en: Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Forty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Hanshan at Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang. Chapter Thirty: The Inconceivable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Regarding the initial intent for this section, there are two points.
First, the general meaning: the preceding three chapters provided specific answers to the previous questions; from here below, the following three chapters...
This section generally clarifies the profound depth of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It is divided into two parts.

First, since the preceding [section] has already established that wisdom is perfected and realization is ultimate, this chapter follows to compare and measure how his practices and virtues are inconceivable.

Furthermore, because the inconceivable virtues of a Buddha are fully exhausted by a Bodhisattva, and also to provide a remote response to the "Ocean of Transformations" (*nirmāṇa-samudra*), the subsequent verses extensively manifest the great function of transformation. Moreover, it is also pervasive...

This is for the purpose of revealing the numerical extent of one section. Second, regarding the explanation of the title: *asaṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇) means "without number" (*a-* meaning "no," and *saṃkhyeya* meaning "number").
It fully bears the name of a number. If the Jin translation reads "The Chapter on the Questions of Bodhisattva Cittarāja on the *Asaṃkhyeya*," it includes both the questioner and the subject;
thus, it mentions both the person and the dharma. Furthermore, it refers to the calculations asked about by the bodhisattva. The Sanskrit original is the same as this.
However, "asamkhyeya" (incalculable) is the very first of the ten great numbers; as it is frequently employed in the sūtras and śāstras, it is used here to designate the title.
Furthermore, to reveal that this number is itself free from number, the name is designated by means of "the incalculable. Regarding the threefold purpose (*abhiprāya*):

the purpose is to manifest the limits of virtue by means of number, while the intent is to cause one to know that the various Buddhas and Samantabhadra transcend number in their manifold layers. Fourth, the correct...

Commentary on the Text: The three chapters below are collectively titled "Profound" (*gambhīra*). They are divided into three distinct sections: this present chapter clarifies the incalculable supreme virtues;

the next chapter clarifies [virtues] throughout all time; and the final chapter pervades all places. Nevertheless, among these three chapters, the first generally clarifies the virtues of both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the second specifically manifests the virtues of the Buddha while incidentally clarifying those of the Bodhisattva; and the last...

This chapter clarifies only the Bodhisattva; the reason for this is that one who is at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is also called a Buddha, and because at the final stage, Samantabhadra is both a Buddha and a Bodhisattva.
At that time, Bodhisattva Mind-King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
expound that which is incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), immeasurable, boundless, unequaled, uncountable, incomparable,
inconceivable, unfathomable, ineffable, and beyond the ineffable."

Now, this first chapter first poses questions and subsequently provides answers. Within the questions, there are two parts: first, restating what the Buddha has taught; second, from "World-Honored One" onwards, formally clarifying the inquiry.

Regarding the first: the reason the Mind-King (citta-rāja) asks these questions is to demonstrate that the counting does not depart from the mind, for both the counted and the uncounted are under its sovereign control.
Furthermore, it reveals that this counting comprehensively subsumes what precedes and follows, thereby establishing its transcendent excellence.

The reason for specifically asking about ten is that by citing the last, the first is included, thereby manifesting their inexhaustibility; this is because this principle is frequently employed throughout the preceding and following texts.
Thus, the text says: "When the Tathāgata expounds [the teachings], he asks only about the fundamental number, which already encompasses all its transformations."
“World-Honored One, what are the ‘incalculable’ (*asaṃkhyeya*) up to the ‘unspeakably unspeakable’ (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*)?
This is the second section, which clearly sets forth the inquiry.
The Buddha addressed Bodhisattva Cittarāja, saying: “Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You now desire to cause all...”
Regarding the meaning of the world entering into the measure of what is known by the Buddha, one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
In the second response, there are four parts. First, praising the question to demonstrate its benefit and cause it to enter into what is known by the Buddha:

"Measure" (*saṃkhyā*) refers to that which is explained in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) as profound, vast, and boundless; only a Buddha can fathom it, for it is not like that which is known by ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle. As [it says]:
The Huangdi Suanfa (Yellow Emperor’s Algorithm) contains only twenty-three numbers, beginning with one and two and ending with the *zhengzai* (correct cycle).

It has already been stated that [the calculations] exceed what heaven and earth can contain. The Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) reaches sixty, already arriving at the "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*). This [text], however, contains one hundred and twenty-four.
It is doubled again and again; therefore, it cannot be measured by anything else. Thus, the ultimate limit of numbers is entrusted to the "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*).
How much more so when, at the beginning of the verse, the "unspeakable" is further multiplied, traversing various atoms and lands to manifest its inexhaustibility.

The reason the Buddha himself provides the answer is to personally demonstrate that it is inconceivable. Furthermore, this chapter comprehensively describes the ultimate virtues of the causal stage; therefore, the Buddha speaks.
"Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mind-King responded, "So be it," and received the instruction.
Second, the instruction to listen and the permission to speak.
The Buddha said: "Good son, one hundred lakṣas make one koṭi; one koṭi times one koṭi makes one ayuta;
one ayuta times one ayuta makes one nayuta; one nayuta times one nayuta makes..."
One *bimbara*; one *bimbara* makes one *kiṃkara*; one *kiṃkara* makes one *agāra*; one *agāra* makes one *jaya*;
one *jaya* makes one *mahābhava*; one *mahābhava* makes one *abhava*. One *abhava*...
One *āpala* makes one *tāvala*; ten *tāvalas* make one *khaṇḍa*; ten *khaṇḍas* make one *pramā*; ten *pramās* make one *nime*;
ten *nimes* make one *ābhyañjana*; ten *ābhyañjanas* make one *mṛgapada*. Mṛga...
Two *bhamiga* make one *villaga*; two *villaga* make one *vigava*;
two *vigava* make one *saṃkhyāma*; two *saṃkhyāma* make one *visara*;
two *visara* make one *vijambha*. Two *vijambha*... [make one... *vijambha*.
One *vīcambā* makes one *vīśaṅga*; two *vīśaṅgas* make one *vīśuddha*;
two *vīśuddhas* make one *vībhava*; two *vībhavas* make one *vīpattha*;
two *vīpattis* make one *vīkhadha*; two *vīkhadhās* make one... [and so on].
Weighing. Each act of weighing is one *dhāraṇī*. One *dhāraṇī* is one *vīthi*.
Each *vīthi* is one *viparyāsa*. Each *viparyāsa* is one *trimaya*.
Each *trimaya* is one *vidūra*. Each *vidūra* is one *khepara*. *Khepara*... [upper tone].
One *rāvi-bhara* makes one *vicāraṇa*; one *vicāraṇa-vicāraṇa* makes one *parivarta*;
one *parivarta-parivarta* makes one *udvaha*; one *udvaha-udvaha* makes one *paramodvaha*;
one *paramodvaha-paramodvaha* makes one *nirava*; one *nirava-nirava* makes one *hali*; one *hali-hali* makes one...
One movement. One movement, one movement makes one *kharipu*. One *kharipu*, one *kharipu* makes one *kharitra*.
One *kharitra*, one *kharitra* makes one *khiluka*. One *khiluka*, one *khiluka* makes one *dharabudha*.
One *dharabudha*, one *dharabudha* makes one *haruna*. One *haruna*...
One *nāharuṇa* is equal to one *maruta*. One *maruta-maruta* is equal to one *saṃmuta*.
One *saṃmuta-saṃmuta* is equal to one *īlita*. One *īlita-īlita* is equal to one *maruma*.
One *maruma-maruma* is equal to one *dānta*. One *dānta-dānta* is equal to one *vigatamada*.
Pride. Freedom from pride and freedom from arrogance constitute one *aniñjya* (immovability).
One *aniñjya* and another *aniñjya* constitute one *paramāṇu* (extreme atom). One *paramāṇu* and another *paramāṇu* constitute one *amatra*.
One *amatra* and another *amatra* constitute one *bhamatra*. One *bhamatra* and another *bhamatra* constitute one *gamatra*. One *gamatra*...
One *roga-mātra* makes one *namata-ra*; one *namata-ra* and another *namata-ra* make one *himata-ra*;
one *himata-ra* and another *himata-ra* make one *vima-tara*;
one *vima-tara*, another *vima-tara*, and yet another *vima-tara* make one *prama-tara*; one *prama-tara*... [and so on].
One *ramaṭra* makes one *śivamaṭra*; two *śivamaṭras* make one *īla*; two *īlas* make one *vela*; two *velas* make one *tela*;
two *telas* make one *gelā*; two *gelās* make one *sūphura*. *Sūphura*...
One *rasubura* makes one *nira*; one *nira* and another *nira* make one *kīra*;
one *kīra* and another *kīra* make one *sīrasīra*; one *sīrasīra* makes one *pīra*; one *pīra* and another *pīra* make one *mīra*.
One *mimira* makes one *sārada*; one *sārada* makes one *meruta*;
one *meruta* makes one *kheruta*; one *kheruta* makes one *madhura*;
one *madhura* makes one *samura*; one *samura* makes one *vamura*.
One ayasa; two ayasas make one kāmara; two kāmara make one magava;
two magavas make one ātala; two ātalas make one heluya; two heluyas make one vīlava. Vī...
One *rava* and one *avara* make one *kalapa*. One *kalapa* and one *kalapa* make one *hahava*.
One *hahava* and one *hahava* make one *vibhara*. One *vibhara* and one *vibhara* make one *nabhara*. One *nabhara* and one *nabhara* make one *mālāra*.
One *mālāra* and one... [mālāra]... make one... [mālāra]... (The text continues with further multiples of these units).
One *lala* makes one *sahavara*. One *sahavara* and another *sahavara* make one *milapū*.
One *milapū* and another *milapū* make one *camara*. One *camara* and another *camara* make one *dhāmara*.
One *dhāmara* and another *dhāmara* make one *phalamada*. One *phalamada* and another *phalama*...
One *da* makes one *vigaṃma*; one *vigaṃma-vigaṃma* makes one *upabaddha*; one *upabaddha-upabaddha* makes one *vyākhyāna*;
one *vyākhyāna-vyākhyāna* makes one *akṣaya*; one *akṣaya-akṣaya* makes one *udbhava*;
one *udbhava-udbhava* makes one *anātman*; one *anātman-anātman* makes one...
Avanta; two avantas make one utpala; two utpalas make one padma; two padmas make one saṃkhyā;
two saṃkhyās make one gati; two gatis make one yāti; two yātis make one asaṃkhyeya; two asaṃkhyeyas [make one mahāsaṃkhyeya].
One asaṃkhyeya-cycle becomes one asaṃkhyeya-cycle; one asaṃkhyeya-cycle multiplied by an asaṃkhyeya-cycle becomes one immeasurable (apramāṇa).
One immeasurable multiplied by an immeasurable becomes one immeasurable-cycle (apramāṇāvarta). One immeasurable-cycle multiplied by an immeasurable-cycle becomes one boundless (ananta).

One boundless multiplied by a boundless becomes one boundless-cycle (anantāvarta). One boundless-cycle multiplied by a boundless-cycle becomes one incomparable (asama). One incomparable multiplied by an incomparable...
One "unequaled revolution" (asamā-parivarta) is equal to one "incalculable" (asaṃkhyeya).
One "incalculable" is equal to one "incalculable revolution" (asaṃkhyeya-parivarta). One "incalculable revolution" is equal to one "inexpressible" (anabhilāpya).
One "inexpressible" is equal to one "inexpressible revolution" (anabhilāpya-parivarta). One "inexpressible revolution" is [equal to one... "inexpressible..."
One *acintya* (inconceivable) becomes one *acintyācintya* (inconceivable-inconceivable). One *acintyācintya* becomes one *acintyāvartana* (turning of the inconceivable).
One *acintyāvartana* becomes one *aprameya* (immeasurable). One *aprameya* becomes one *aprameyāprameya* (immeasurable-immeasurable).
One *aprameyāprameya* becomes one *aprameyāvartana* (turning of the immeasurable). One *aprameyāvartana* becomes one *anabhilāpya* (ineffable). One *anabhilāpya*...
One "unspeakable" may be said to be one "unspeakable transformation. One "unspeakable transformation" and another "unspeakable transformation" constitute one "unspeakably unspeakable.
Furthermore, one "unspeakably unspeakable" constitutes one "unspeakably unspeakable transformation."
The fourth [section] is the correct answer to the doubts raised; it consists of two parts. First, the prose explains the vast number of the counting units themselves;

second, the verse reveals that the virtues being counted are inexhaustible. Now, for the first part: the question raises the latter [number] because it is difficult to know, while the answer provides a complete explanation from beginning to end.
The initial statement that one hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi refers to the medium scale of enumeration.
A *lakṣa* is ten thousand; a *koṭi* is one hundred million. Thus, the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance" (*Prabhābodhiparivarta*) states, "exceeding one *koṭi*.
In all Sanskrit manuscripts, this is rendered as *koṭi*. If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, which takes a *lakṣa* to be one million, then a *koṭi* would correspond to ten billion (*zhào*).
If one also includes the lower numerical units such as one, ten, hundred, thousand, and ten thousand, there are a total of one hundred and thirty-seven [units].
Regarding the numbers: because they were easy to understand from the preceding [section], they are omitted here. All numbers from *koṭi* downward are superior numerical methods;
because they increase by doubling at each stage, many of them retain their original Sanskrit sounds. These are merely names for numbers and possess no further underlying principle.
At the end, it says "this is also unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*). If one were to list them in full as before, there would then be four [such stages].
This is "unspeakable. Therefore, the translators used the two characters "this again" (*cishi*) as a skillful means to translate what was originally "unspeakably unspeakable" (*asabhya-asabhya*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of Citta-rāja Bodhisattva:
Inexpressible and beyond speech, they fill all inexpressible and unspeakable eons;
they speak of inexpressible and unspeakable Buddha-fields that can never be exhausted,
reducing them all to fragments and pulverizing them into atoms of dust.
In a single atom, lands are unspeakable; as it is with one, so it is with all.
These unspeakably many Buddha-lands are, in a single thought-moment, reduced to dust in unspeakable numbers;
every thought-moment of this reduction is likewise so. This continues thus throughout unspeakable eons.
These atoms contain unspeakably many lands; To describe these lands as being like atoms is even more difficult than using the method of unspeakable calculation.
Counting eons in this way by the number of these atoms— One atom contains one hundred thousand unspeakable [eons].
These two verses praise one hundred and twenty verses. They are largely divided into two parts. The first six clarify that the virtues of Samantabhadra are so vast they cannot be fully described;

the remaining verses clarify that the virtues of the Buddha are profound and vast, which Samantabhadra has thoroughly investigated. Within the former part, there are two sections. The first four and a half verses clarify the great number [of virtues];
the latter one and a half verses reveal the vastness of what is being counted. Now, for the first: "The accumulation of numbers... from here on.

There are ten stages to manifest its inexhaustibility. Thus we know that even ascending to the "unspeakably many times unspeakable" (anabhilāpyānabhilāpya-parivarta), it is still merely a provisional accommodation to the capacities of beings;
according to what the Buddha truly knows, it is in fact inexhaustible. Regarding these ten stages: first, one accumulates from the "unspeakable" up to the "unspeakably many times unspeakable.
However, this should logically accumulate up to the final "unspeakably many times unspeakable" stage, yet here it stops at the accumulation [of the preceding].
Regarding "the unspeakable," there are two meanings: first, because it is easy to grasp through words, as many [instances] are used in the following verses;
second, because it expresses a number that is beyond the reach of verbal expression. Next are the second and third lines, which take what was accumulated above and fill all within the unspeakable.
Among these, the first line indicates [the subject], and the latter two lines explain it. That is to say, what is this "one"?

"One must by no means say [it cannot be told]. The commentary explains that "that which cannot be fully told within unspeakable eons" refers to the three and a half verses which take each of those aforementioned unspeakable [realms] and individually crush every one of them into dust.

The four and a half verses mean that within each of those aforementioned particles of dust there are unspeakable numbers of realms. The five and a half verses take the realms within those aforementioned particles of dust for a single moment...
1. To grind them all into dust. 2. Six thoughts: to grind that dust into further particles. This continues for many more kalpas. 3.
One phrase clarifies the dust thus ground; furthermore, there are many lands (*kṣetra*). 4. One phrase: these many lands are again ground into dust. 5. A half-verse:
using many calculations, one passes through many kalpas counting the aforementioned dust, saying "such is the number. 6. Ten and above.
For as many eons as there are atoms in all worlds— wherein each atom contains one hundred thousand unspeakable eons— and for such eons, layered upon layers,
infinitely and inexhaustibly,
one might praise a single Samantabhadra; yet none could exhaust the measure of his merit.
Within the space of a single subtle hair-tip, there are unspeakably many Samantabhadras;
it is the same for every hair-tip. Thus, this extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Second, regarding the manifestation of the vastness of the enumeration, three levels are briefly cited: first, using the aforementioned eons to praise a single Samantabhadra.

The virtues of the Worthy One (Bhadrapāla) are inexhaustible. Second, how much more so when there are many Bhadrapālas within a single atom? Third, how much more so since there are many within every atom throughout the entire dharma-realm?
If one’s mind does not accord with this nature, then the mind that attempts to contemplate it will become deluded and deranged.
All the lands existing upon the tip of a single hair, their number being immeasurable and beyond description;
even if one were to take all the hairs as numerous as the dimensions of space, on each and every such tip, the lands are exactly like this.
Within those lands upon the tips of the hairs, they abide in infinite varieties of distinctions.
There are unspeakably many lands of different kinds; There are unspeakably many lands of the same kind.
Within an unspeakable number of hair-tips, There are unspeakably many pure lands with unspeakably various adornments, And unspeakably many varieties of wonders.

The second section consists of one hundred and fourteen verses. These clarify that Samantabhadra has thoroughly investigated the profound and vast virtues of the Buddha, thereby extensively manifesting the characteristics of his transformations.
Within this, there are two parts; the first ninety-one stanzas clarify the unimpeded nature of the resultant virtues.

The preceding section has already clarified that the causal stage is thoroughly mastered. The subsequent passage, beginning with "the ineffable Tathāgatas," clarifies the profound and vast qualities of the fruition (*phala-guṇa*).
Through the cause, one is able to enter [this state]. Within this [section], there are also two parts: first, the clarification of the unimpeded nature of the dharmas of fruition;

second, from "Bodhisattvas are all able... onwards, the thorough mastery of the causal stage. Within the first part, there are also two sections: first, three verses clarify mastery over the *pariṇāmanavibhūti* (enjoyment-retribution).
Upon each and every tip of those hairs, he proclaims the names of unspeakably many Buddhas;
within each and every name are Tathāgatas, all of whom are unspeakably unspeakable in number.
Within the bodies of each of these Buddhas, they manifest unspeakably many pores.
Within each and every one of those pores, there appear inconceivable and ineffable multitudes of colored forms;
from all those inconceivable pores, light rays are emitted.

Subsequently, the luminosity integrates the environment and its inhabitants, thereby entering into mastery. Within this [section], there are five parts; the first two and a half verses concern the central [subject].
Manifesting clearly:
within each and every one of those rays of light, there appear unspeakably many lotus flowers;
within each and every one of those lotus flowers, there are unspeakably many petals.
Within each of the unspeakably many petals of the unspeakable flowers, there appear unspeakably many forms;
within those unspeakably many forms, there further appear unspeakably many petals;
within those unspeakably many petals, there is unspeakable radiance; and within that radiance, there are unspeakably many forms.
Within these unspeakable forms and appearances, each manifests unspeakable rays of light;
within each unspeakable ray of light, unspeakable moons appear; from each of those unspeakable moons, again unspeakable moons appear;
and within all those unspeakable moons, each manifests unspeakable rays of light.
Within each and every one of those rays of light, there further appear unspeakably unspeakable numbers of suns;
within each and every one of those suns, there appear unspeakably unspeakable colors;
and within each and every one of those colors, there again appear unspeakably unspeakable rays of light.
Within each and every one of those rays of light, there appear unspeakably many lion thrones,
with unspeakably many ornaments for each; within unspeakably many of those rays of light,
there are unspeakably many exquisite colors, and within those colors, unspeakably many pure lights.
Within each of those pure lights, there further appear various wondrous radiances;
these lights again manifest various rays of light, beyond expression and beyond the expressible.
Within such various radiances, there respectively appear exquisite jewels like Mount Sumeru.
Within each and every light, the jewels that appear are ineffable and beyond description.
In the twenty-one and a half verses [of this section], the support appears in the center; first, the lotus and its radiance appear.
That single exquisite jewel, like Mount Sumeru, manifests unspeakably many buddha-fields;
yet even when all such Sumeru jewels have been exhausted, there is no remainder. The manifestation of these fields is likewise in every way.
Taking a single field and reducing it to dust, the color and form of a single mote of that dust is unspeakable.
The lands of all realms become atoms, and each atom possesses characteristics;
such various characteristics of these ineffable and unspeakably many atoms all emit light,
which constitutes the subsequent function of the Pure Land.
The Buddhas appearing within the light are unspeakable; The Dharma taught by those Buddhas is unspeakable;
The sublime verses within that Dharma are unspeakable; The liberation attained upon hearing those verses is unspeakable;
The manifestation of the True Reality within every moment of thought is unspeakable.
Manifesting all Buddhas of the future, They constantly expound the Dharma without end.
Each and every Buddha-dharma is unspeakable; Its various purities are unspeakable.
The utterance of wondrous sounds is unspeakable; The turning of the wheel of the true Dharma is unspeakable.
Within each and every wheel of Dharma, he expounds unspeakable numbers of sūtras;
within each and every sūtra, he analyzes unspeakable numbers of dharma-gates;
and within each and every dharma-gate, he further explains unspeakable numbers of dharmas.
Within each and every one of those dharmas, he tames sentient beings in ways that are unspeakable;
in three or five verses, he manifests and correctly teaches the Dharma within them.
Or again, upon the tip of a single hair, he dwells constantly for unspeakable eons.
As it is with the tip of a single hair, so it is with all others; the number of kalpas they abide is likewise thus.
The four clarities manifest while remaining eternally present;
their minds are unimpeded and ineffable, and the emanations of the Buddhas are ineffable.
Each and every emanated Tathāgata further manifests an ineffable number of further emanations;
The Dharma-body of those Buddhas is ineffable, and their divided bodies are ineffable.
Their adornments are immeasurable and ineffable, as they travel to the ten directions in ineffable numbers.
The universal wandering through lands is unspeakable; The observation of sentient beings is unspeakable;
The purification of sentient beings is unspeakable; The taming of sentient beings is unspeakable;
Those various adornments are unspeakable; Those various spiritual powers are unspeakable.
Those sovereign powers are unspeakable; Those miraculous transformations are unspeakable;
All supernatural faculties are unspeakable; All spheres of experience are unspeakable;
All empowerments are unspeakable; The worlds in which they dwell are unspeakable.
The pure true reality is ineffable; The teaching of the sūtras is ineffable.
Within each and every one of those sūtras, The exposition of dharma-gates is ineffable.
Within each and every one of those dharma-gates, Furthermore, the teaching of all dharmas is ineffable.
Within each and every one of those phenomena, that which is determinate is ineffable;
within each and every one of those determinates, the taming of sentient beings is ineffable.
There are ineffable similar dharmas and ineffable similar minds.
Inexpressible are the diverse phenomena; Inexpressible are the diverse minds;
Inexpressible are the diverse faculties; Inexpressible are the diverse languages.
Moment by moment, in all spheres of activity, The taming of sentient beings is unspeakable.
All miraculous transformations are ineffable; All manifestations are ineffable.
The time and eons therein are ineffable; The distinctions therein are ineffable.
These fifty and a half verses clarify mastery in taming sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva is able to analyze and explain them all; even those skilled in calculation cannot discern [them].
Regarding the second stage, the position of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), one thoroughly masters the middle two. First, the half-verse concludes the preceding and introduces what follows.
Upon the tip of a single hair, there are lands of various sizes—lands that are defiled or pure, coarse or subtle;
all such as these are unspeakable in number. Yet each one can be clearly perceived and distinguished.
If a single land were ground into dust, those particles would be immeasurable and unspeakable.
Thus, lands as numerous as atoms, infinite in extent, all come together upon the tip of a single hair.

These lands are beyond description; though they gather together upon the tip of a hair, there is no crowding, nor does the tip of the hair increase in size, yet those lands all come and assemble there.
Within them, all the various lands— Their forms remain as they were, without confusion;
As one land does not disturb another, So it is with all lands.
The realm of space is boundless, Yet every hair-tip is spread throughout, filling it entirely.
In this way, all the lands upon the tips of hairs, a Bodhisattva can describe in a single thought-moment;
within a single subtle pore, unspeakable numbers of lands enter in succession,
yet those lands can be contained within that pore, for the lands cannot pervade the pore.
The number of kalpas for entering is unspeakable; The number of kalpas for receiving is unspeakable.
While abiding in this array, No one can speak of all the kalpas.
Having thus taken up and abided therein, All realms of experience are unspeakable.
The skillful means for entering [the realm] are ineffable; that which is done after having entered is also ineffable.

The remaining verses correctly manifest the qualities of the cause (*hetu-guṇa*). Among these, there are ten. The first eight verses clarify the body and land of the Indra-net (*indra-jāla*), which is the locus where practice arises.
Furthermore, while the preceding text clarified its pervasive expansion, this clarifies its capacity for inclusion; the wording is merely abbreviated. It says:

Regarding the statement that "the pores can entirely receive all lands": this refers to a single hair-pore of the dharma-nature. Therefore, although many lands are received within it, there is no exterior [to them].
The many lands with their unimpaired characteristics rest pervasively within a single hair-pore of one who has attained awakening.
This is because internal and external dependent origination are neither identical nor separate.
The clarity of the mental faculty is unspeakable; Wandering through all directions is unspeakable;
Valiant diligence is unspeakable; Mastery of miraculous transformations is unspeakable;
All contemplation is unspeakable; All great vows are unspeakable.
All realms are unspeakable; All-pervasive penetration is unspeakable;
The purity of physical action is unspeakable; The purity of verbal action is unspeakable;
The purity of mental action is unspeakable; The purity of resolute faith is unspeakable.
The purity of wondrous wisdom is unspeakable; The purity of wondrous insight is unspeakable.
The elucidation of all true marks is unspeakable; The severance of all doubts and delusions is unspeakable.
Transcending birth and death is unspeakable; Ascending to the stage of certainty is unspeakable.
The profound samādhi is unspeakable; Thoroughly penetrating all things is unspeakable.
(Verse 2) The diligent practice of the three karmas is unspeakable.
All sentient beings are unspeakable; All Buddha-fields are unspeakable. (Verse 3)
Knowing that the bodies of sentient beings are ineffable; Knowing that their mental inclinations are ineffable;
Knowing that their karmic fruits are ineffable; Knowing that their intellectual understandings are ineffable;
Knowing that their categories are ineffable; Knowing that their spiritual lineages are ineffable.
Knowing that the receiving of a body is ineffable; knowing that the place of birth is ineffable;
knowing that the actual process of birth is ineffable; knowing that once born it is ineffable;
knowing that its full comprehension is ineffable; and knowing that its directional movement is ineffable.
Knowing that their speech is ineffable, and knowing that their activities are ineffable,
the Bodhisattva possesses such great compassion as to benefit all worlds through the practice of gathering beings by means of the three types of vessels.
Universally manifesting their bodies is unspeakable; Entering all Buddha-fields is unspeakable;
Beholding all Bodhisattvas is unspeakable; Generating wisdom is unspeakable;
Inquiring about the True Dharma is unspeakable; Proclaiming and spreading the Buddha’s teachings is unspeakable.
Manifesting various bodies is unspeakable; Visiting all lands is unspeakable;
Displaying spiritual powers is unspeakable; Pervading the ten directions is unspeakable;
Everywhere manifesting emanated bodies is unspeakable; Approaching all Buddhas is unspeakable.
The various articles of offering are unspeakable; The diverse, immeasurable, and pure precious jewels are unspeakable; The most exquisite lotus flowers are unspeakable;
The most supreme fragrant garlands are unspeakable; Making offerings to the Tathāgata is unspeakable.
Pure faith is unspeakable; Supreme realization is unspeakable;
Exalted aspiration is unspeakable; Reverence for all Buddhas is unspeakable.
These four and a half verses clarify the practice of traveling to make offerings to the Buddhas.
The practice of giving is unspeakable; that his mind in the past was unspeakably free of seeking anything for himself as he gave it all away is unspeakable.
His pure upholding of the precepts is unspeakable; the purity of his mind and intentions is unspeakable.
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Delighting in the True Dharma is unspeakable;
Accomplishing all patiences is unspeakable; The patience of the non-arising of phenomena is unspeakable;
Being fully endowed with tranquility is unspeakable; Abiding in the stage of tranquility is unspeakable.
The arousal of great diligence is unspeakable; the mind of the past is unspeakable;
the mind of non-retrogression is unspeakable; the unshakable mind is unspeakable;
the treasury of all samādhis is unspeakable; the contemplation of all phenomena is unspeakable.
Tranquil in meditative concentration, it is ineffable; Thoroughly penetrating all dhyānas, it is ineffable;
Wisdom that penetrates everywhere, it is ineffable; Mastery over samādhi, it is ineffable;
Thoroughly penetrating all dharmas, it is ineffable; Clearly beholding all Buddhas, it is ineffable.
The cultivation of immeasurable practices is unspeakable; The arousal of vast vows is unspeakable;
The profound realm is unspeakable; The pure Dharma-gates are unspeakable;
The power of the Bodhisattva-dharmas is unspeakable; The abiding of the Bodhisattva-dharmas is unspeakable.
Those various states of right mindfulness are ineffable; those various dharma-realms are ineffable;
the cultivation of the wisdom of skillful means is ineffable; training in profound wisdom is ineffable;
immeasurable wisdom is ineffable; ultimate wisdom is ineffable.
Those various wisdoms of phenomena are ineffable; That pure wheel of Dharma is ineffable;
That great cloud of Dharma is ineffable; That great rain of Dharma is ineffable;
Those various supernormal powers are ineffable; Those various skillful means are ineffable.
Entering the wisdom of emptiness and stillness is unspeakable; the continuous succession of every thought-moment is unspeakable;
the immeasurable gateways of practice are unspeakable; abiding constantly in every thought-moment is unspeakable;
and the five broad practices and the ten perfections are unspeakable.
The oceans of Buddha-fields are unspeakable; One can travel to all of them, which are unspeakable;
The distinctions among those fields are unspeakable; Their various purities are unspeakable;
Their diverse adornments are unspeakable; And their boundless forms and characteristics are unspeakable.
The various intermingled arrangements are unspeakable; The various exquisite beauties are unspeakable;
The pure Buddha-fields are unspeakable; The defiled worlds are unspeakable.
These two and a half verses describe the sovereign practice of traveling through lands.
Knowing that sentient beings are ineffable, Knowing their spiritual lineages are ineffable,
Knowing their karmic retributions are ineffable, Knowing their mental activities are ineffable,
Knowing their faculties and natures are ineffable, Knowing their understandings and inclinations are ineffable.
The defilement and purification [of beings] are ineffable; The observation and subduing [of them] are ineffable;
The mastery over transformations is ineffable; The manifestation of various bodies is ineffable;
The cultivation of diligence is ineffable; The liberation of sentient beings is ineffable.
The manifestation of supernatural transformations is unspeakable; The emission of great light is unspeakable;
The various colors and forms are unspeakable; Causing sentient beings to be purified is unspeakable.
These seven sets of four verses clarify the practice of taming sentient beings.
Inconceivable are the individual pores; Inconceivable are the nets of light they emit;
Inconceivable are the manifestations of color within those nets of light; Inconceivable is their universal illumination of Buddha-fields;
Inconceivable is their courageous fearlessness; Inconceivable are their skillful means and expedients.
Taming sentient beings is unspeakable; Causing them to transcend birth and death is unspeakable;
The purification of physical action is unspeakable; The purification of verbal action is unspeakable;
The boundless mental action is unspeakable; And the sublime, wondrous conduct is unspeakable.
The accomplishment of the jewel of wisdom is ineffable; The profound penetration of the dharma-realm is ineffable;
The bodhisattvas’ dhāraṇīs are ineffable; Their skillful cultivation and study are ineffable;
The voices of the wise are ineffable; The purity of those voices is ineffable.
Right mindfulness is truly ineffable; Awakening sentient beings is ineffable;
Being fully endowed with dignified deportment is ineffable; Pure cultivation is ineffable;
Accomplishing fearlessness is ineffable; Subduing the world is ineffable.
The multitudes of all Buddha-sons are unspeakable; Their pure and supreme practices are unspeakable;
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Extolling them without end is unspeakable;
The Guides of the World are unspeakable; Expounding and praising them is unspeakable.
The three types of karma, deeply purified by eight verses and a half,
are unspeakable for those bodhisattvas; their pure merits are unspeakable,
their limits are unspeakable, and their ability to abide therein is unspeakable.
The wisdom that abides therein is ineffable; To abide through all kalpas is beyond description.
Delighting in all Buddhas is ineffable; The equality of wisdom is ineffable.
Skillfully entering all phenomena is ineffable; Being unimpeded regarding the Dharma is ineffable.
The three periods of time are like space and are ineffable;
The wisdom of the three periods is ineffable, and the thorough understanding of the three periods is ineffable;
Abiding in wisdom is ineffable, and sublime, wondrous conduct is ineffable; Immeasurable great vows are ineffable.
The pure great vows are unspeakable; The accomplishment of bodhi is unspeakable;
The bodhi of all Buddhas is unspeakable; The arising of wisdom is unspeakable;
The discernment of principles is unspeakable; The knowledge of all dharmas is unspeakable.
The purification of Buddha-fields is unspeakable; The cultivation of the various powers is unspeakable;
Long-term practice is unspeakable; Awakening and understanding in a single thought-moment is unspeakable;
The sovereign mastery of all Buddhas is unspeakable; The extensive exposition of the True Dharma is unspeakable.
The various supernormal powers are unspeakable; Manifesting in the world is unspeakable;
The pure wheel of Dharma is unspeakable; The courageous ability to turn it is unspeakable;
The various ways of expounding it are unspeakable; Compassion for the world is unspeakable.
The ninth and eighth and a half verses describe the practice of mastery over vows and knowledge:
Even if one were to spend unspeakably many eons Praising unspeakable virtues,
Those unspeakable eons might come to an end, But the unspeakable virtues could never be exhausted.
The eleventh verse concludes that these virtues are inexhaustible:
Inexpressible Tathāgatas, with inexpressible tongues, Praise the Buddha’s inexpressible virtues; Even throughout inexpressible eons, they could not reach their end.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions, All simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment;
Within that, a single Buddha can universally manifest Inexpressible numbers of all bodies.
Within these inexpressible bodies, one body Manifests inexpressible numbers of heads.
Within this ineffable, one head is manifested; within this ineffable, one tongue is manifested;
within this ineffable, one voice is manifested; it remains for an ineffable number of kalpas.
As one [Buddha], so are all Buddhas; As one body, so are all bodies;
As one head, so are all heads; As one tongue, so are all tongues;
As one voice, so are all voices— Thus may they praise the Buddha for unspeakable eons.
"Even incalculable eons may come to an end, But praising the Buddha’s virtues can never be exhausted.

This second section clarifies that the fruit-virtues are profound and vast, and that the causal practices can lead one into them. Within this, the fruit is explained first, followed by the cause. This section contains three parts.
The first six verses collectively praise the Buddha’s virtues:
Within a single minute atom, there are entirely present Inexpressible lotus-world realms;
In each and every lotus-world realm, There are inexpressible Buddhas named Bhadraśrī.
Extending throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), All the subtle dust motes within it—
whether worlds forming, abiding, or decaying— Are infinite and beyond description;
even a single mote of dust has no limit, And immeasurable lands universally enter therein.
The distinctions among the ten directions are unspeakable; The distribution of the oceans of lands is unspeakable.
(2) This second verse specifically clarifies the dependent environment.
Within each and every land, there is a Tathāgata, Whose lifespan and number of kalpas are unspeakable.
The conduct of all Buddhas is unspeakable; The profound and wondrous Dharma is unspeakable;
Supernatural powers and great strength are unspeakable; Unobstructed wisdom is unspeakable;
Entering into a single pore is unspeakable; The causes and conditions of that pore are unspeakable.
The accomplishment of the ten powers is unspeakable; The awakening to bodhi is unspeakable;
The entry into the pure dharma-realm is unspeakable; The attainment of the treasury of profound wisdom is unspeakable.
These three sets of three verses separately clarify the primary retribution.
The various quantities are unspeakable, yet they know them all completely;
The various forms and measures are unspeakable, yet there is nothing therein they do not master;
The various samādhis are unspeakable, yet they are able to abide within them for the duration of an eon.
Before unspeakably many Buddhas, their conduct is unspeakably pure;
they attain unspeakably many unimpeded minds; they travel to unspeakably many realms in the ten directions, manifesting unspeakably many spiritual powers; their conduct is boundless and unspeakable.
They travel to unspeakably many buddha-fields; Their thorough realization of all Buddhas is unspeakable;
Their courageous and heroic diligence is unspeakable; Their wisdom and penetration are unspeakable.
Regarding phenomena, they neither act nor do not act; Their entry into all realms of experience is unspeakable.
Inexpressible great kalpas; Constantly wandering through the ten directions with inexpressible skillful means;
Inexpressible wisdom; Inexpressible true wisdom; Inexpressible wisdom of spiritual powers;
Manifesting in every thought-moment in ways that are inexpressible.

Regarding the ineffable qualities of all Buddhas, one understands each and every ineffable cause of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and enters into their virtues; therein, first is the practice of one's own portion (*svabhāga*).
They are able to realize enlightenment at a single moment, or they enter realization at various times;
Inexpressible Buddha-fields as numerous as the hairs on a body, And inexpressible Buddha-fields within a single atom—
To all such Buddha-fields they travel, Beholding the Tathāgatas, beyond all expression.
Penetrating the one reality is ineffable; Skillfully entering the Buddha-lineage is ineffable.
The Buddha-lands are ineffable; Being able to travel to them all to attain enlightenment— The lands, sentient beings, and Buddhas, Their essential natures and distinctions, are ineffable.
Thus, throughout the three periods of time without limit, the Bodhisattva clearly perceives all things;

this is the subsequent superior progress. For now, I have briefly categorized [the stages] according to their manifest characteristics. However, the virtues mentioned above are each perfectly interfused with one another, inexhaustible and beyond exhaustion;
one must realize them by means of forgetting the self. This concludes the Chapter on the Upper Asaṃkhyeya.
The Thirty-first Chapter: On the Lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the initial intent [of this chapter]: Now, the profound mirror of emptiness and luminosity transcends the realm of numerical calculation;

how could there be lifespans of various forms and myriad states, long or short? Nevertheless, in responding to phenomena and according to capacities, there is nothing that does not manifest and nothing that is not [accommodated].

Therefore, the preceding chapter manifested his actual virtues, while this chapter distinguishes them according to the capacities of sentient beings. Although it proceeds from the small to the great, it demonstrates that at no time is he not omnipresent;
thus, it is one aspect of the many virtues previously mentioned. Consequently, it is treated here in a broad and detailed manner, serving as a remote response to the "Ocean of Life Span" [chapter].
Second, regarding the explanation of the title: "Life Span" (*āyus*) refers to the life-force as a karmic retribution, while "Measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to its specific limits.
The retributive lifespan of the purified land is perceived according to the limitations of individual capacities, thereby manifesting an inexhaustible life and an immeasurable quantity.
Because this is the measure of "lifespan" (āyus), the lifespan possesses this specific measure; thus, both interpretations apply. Third, as for the essential purport (abhiprāya):

Taking the long and short durations according to the capacities of beings as its primary principle, it reveals the infinite reach throughout the limits of the future as its ultimate goal. If one approaches this from the perspective of the Shared Teaching (paryāya), it represents the gradual accumulation of the inferior toward the superior;
however, if one approaches it from the perspective of the Distinct Teaching (viśeṣa), the long and short durations are perfectly interfused.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mind-King (Cittarāja) addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"The compilers of the initial collection of the sutras have recorded this; yet it was the Mind-King who spoke it, because he had received the essential meaning and because the Buddha’s life-span is sovereign."
O Son of the Buddha, one kalpa in the realm of Śākyamuni Buddha, this Sahā world, constitutes a single day and night in the realm of Amitābha Buddha, the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One kalpa in the Land of Ultimate Bliss constitutes a single day and night in the realm of Vajradṛḍha Buddha, the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja. One kalpa in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja...
One eon in the world-system of Avivartyasvaracakrā, the Buddha-field of the Buddha Supuṣpita-padma-vikrānta-rāja-prabha,
constitutes one day and night in the world-system of Vimalā, the Buddha-field of the Buddha Dharmadhvaja.
One eon in the world-system of Vimalā constitutes one day and night in the world-system of Sudīpa, the Buddha-field of the Buddha Siṃha...
One kalpa of the Buddha-field *Suloka* constitutes one day and night in the Buddha-field *Prabhāgarbha* of the world *Suprabhā*.
One kalpa of the world *Suprabhā* constitutes one day and night in the Buddha-field *Dharmaprabhāpadmavikāśana* of the world *Duratikrama*. One kalpa of the world *Duratikrama*...
One eon in the world-system of Adorned Wisdom (*Vyūha-prajñā*) constitutes one day and night in the Buddha-field of All-Supernatural-Power Radiance (*Sarva-ṛddhi-prabhāsa*).
One eon in the world-system of Adorned Wisdom constitutes one day and night in the Buddha-field of Moon-Wisdom (*Candra-jñāna*) in the world-system of Mirror Radiance (*Ādarśa-prabhāsa*).
Second, the formal exposition. This consists of three parts. First, the individual enumeration of ten lands in relation to one another:
"O Son of the Buddha, in this manner, proceeding in succession until beyond a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds..."
Next, to illustrate the extensive by means of the concise:
the final world-system’s single eon constitutes one day and night in the Buddha-field of the Victorious Lotus World (Bhadrottara),
where the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and all his fellow great Bodhisattvas fill its entirety.
Third, its ultimate profundity is highlighted. For instance, if a kalpa were taken as a single day, ten such layers would already render the kalpa unspeakable;
how much more so for a million asaṃkhyeyas? Thus, the final stage is already adjacent to the equality of the ocean of lands (kṣetrasamudra).
Therefore, by citing Samantabhadra and others as filling [the realm], it clarifies the abode of the ultimate rank. For this reason, it is called "simultaneously revealing the bodhisattvas."
The "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" concludes.
Regarding the initial intent of the thirty-second chapter, "The Abodes of the Bodhisattvas":
the preceding section treated the benefit of transformation throughout all time; this section clarifies that the bodhisattvas pervade all [realms].
Therefore, he appears next. Thus, in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is clarified that within every single hair-tip of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are countless Samantabhadras;
this is spoken according to ultimate reality. Now, however, as taught in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, he is indicated as having a specific location.
This causes sentient beings to look up with joy and their minds to yearn for a refuge.

If one knows that the Bodhisattva can abide within a single pore to contain oceans of lands, and that the dust motes within his dwelling place can contain the infinite, then there is not a single direction where the Bodhisattva does not dwell.

This also provides a remote answer to the previous question regarding the ocean of lifespan, as the Bodhisattva’s lifespan varies according to the capacities of sentient beings. Second, regarding the explanation of the name: "Bodhisattva" (Bodhisattva-mahāsattva)...
Because the dwelling places of great compassion adapt to the capacities of sentient beings and are not limited to a single location, they are called "the dwelling places of all bodhisattvas";

thus, this serves as their name. Third, regarding the essential purpose (*abhiprāya*): adapting to capacities and responding to stimuli according to specific locations constitutes the essence (*mūla*). Causing beings to rely upon it and leading them to realize that there is no fixed location constitutes the ultimate goal (*prayojana*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mind-King (Cittarāja) addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"Next, in correctly explaining the text, there are two parts. First is the preface composed by the compiler of the sutra, which is also spoken by the Mind-King. This is because all those whom the king governs possess sovereignty;
it also signifies that the mind abides in accordance with wisdom, being free from all obstructions."
O Son of the Buddha, there is a place in the eastern direction called Mount Ṛṣigiri. Since ancient times, multitudes of bodhisattvas have dwelt therein.
Currently, there is a bodhisattva named Vajravikrama who, together with a retinue of three hundred bodhisattvas, constantly resides within it, expounding the Dharma.

Next, the actual locations are explained. There are twenty-two locations. The first ten rely upon the mountains and seas of the eight directions; the upper and lower realms are not accessible to ordinary beings, and thus they are not described here.

Mountains and seas encompass and conceal [all things], serving as the dwelling places for those of benevolence and wisdom; this symbolizes the loftiness and profundity of great wisdom, for it is capable both of stillness and of illumination.
The latter twelve locations consist of cities and towns where people dwell in mixed communities, wherein every capacity of sentient beings is fully accommodated.
Because it manifests great compassion without omission, one knows that the Bodhisattva is not absent from anywhere.
As for the first mountain, Mount Xianren, tradition holds it to be Mount Penglai.
To the south there is a place called Mount Śikhin, where from time immemorial various bodhisattvas have dwelt.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Dharmamati, together with a retinue of five hundred bodhisattvas.
He constantly dwells therein, expounding the Dharma.
Second is Mount Śikhara-vijaya, where Meghashri resides.
To the west lies a place called Vajrajvāla Mountain, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
There dwells a bodhisattva named Vīravikramacaryā (Courageous and Fearless Conduct),
together with a retinue of three hundred bodhisattvas, who constantly expounds the Dharma therein.
The Mountain of Threefold Vajra Flames is on the shore of the Western Sea.
To the north lies a place called Mount Gandhamādana, where from time immemorial the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Gandhahastin, who, together with a retinue of three thousand bodhisattvas,
constantly dwells therein expounding the Dharma.
Fourth is Mount Xiangji (Fragrant Accumulation). It was formerly said that this must be Mount Xiangshan to the north of the Snow Mountains.
To the northeast there is a place named Mount Qingliang (Coolness), where various bodhisattvas have dwelt since ancient times.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue of ten thousand bodhisattvas.
He is always among them, expounding the Dharma.
The Five Qingliang Mountains are the Wutai Mountains of Yanmen Commandery in Daizhou. Within them stands the present-day Qingliang Temple;
because ice accumulates year after year and snow still falls in summer, never experiencing the heat of midsummer, it is called "Qingliang" (Cool).
Five peaks rise upward, their summits devoid of trees, resembling terraces built of stacked wood; hence it is called Wutai.
The mountain’s numinous and sacred traces are fully recorded in various biographies and chronicles.
In the midst of the ocean there is a place called Vajra Mountain, where various bodhisattvas have dwelt since ancient times.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata, together with a retinue of twelve hundred bodhisattvas,
who constantly expounds the Dharma therein.
The six Vajra Mountains. This refers to a mountain named Vajra located to the east, near the Eastern Sea.
Although it is not composed entirely of gold, gold is found throughout its upper and lower regions, its four sides, and even within the sands of its mountain streams and flowing waters;
when viewed from afar, it appears as if its entire body were made of gold.
To the southeast there is a place called Mount Cetiya. Since ancient times, various bodhisattvas have dwelt therein.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Devaputra-mukuṭa, together with a retinue of one thousand bodhisattvas, who constantly expounds the Dharma within that place.
Mount Saptatīrtha (Seven Shrines) is here called the Place for Generating Pure Faith. That which contains śarīra is a stūpa;
that which lacks śarīra is called a caitya. It is named as such either because the mountain's shape is like a stūpa, or because there is a caitya located upon it.
Since ancient times, it has been said that Qingliang is to the east; thus, its shadow and echo lie to the southeast, in the regions of Wu and Yue.
Although there are many sacred mountains in Wu and Yue, the one that resembles [Wutai] in form is Mount Chicheng to the south of Tiantai.
To the southwest there is a place named Mount Prabhāsa. Since ancient times, various bodhisattvas have dwelt therein.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Bhadrajyotis, together with a retinue of three thousand bodhisattvas, who constantly expounds the Dharma within that place.

Regarding Mount Aṣṭāprabhāsa: it was formerly said that this must be connected to Mount Potalaka, because the Chinese translation of the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* identifies the abode of Avalokiteśvara as Mount Aṣṭāprabhāsa.
However, since the present text does not describe it as the abode of Avalokiteśvara but refers to it as "Aṣṭāprabhāsa," it is thus stated to be connected [to Potalaka].
To the northwest there is a place called Mount Fragrant Wind, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
There currently dwells a bodhisattva named Fragrant Light, who, together with a retinue of five thousand bodhisattvas,
constantly expounds the Dharma therein.
To the west of Mount Gandhamādana, within the great ocean,
there is another dwelling place called the Adorned Cave (*vyūha-guhā*). Since time immemorial,
hosts of bodhisattvas have resided therein.
Regarding the Cave of the Ten Adornments: because it faces the sixth ocean mentioned above, it is said that "furthermore" there exists [this cave].
To the south of Vaiśālī, there is a dwelling place named Sthitirāja (Root of Good Abiding), where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
Furthermore, there are twelve locations for cities and towns. First is Vaiśālī, which is also Vārāṇasī;
this is translated here as "City of Vast Splendor" (Guǎngyánchéng) and is also called "Vast and Broad. It is the city where the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) resided in Central India.

Regarding the term "South," according to the *Record of the Western Regions* (Xīyùjì), fascicle seven, it states that fourteen or fifteen *li* to the south of this city is a stūpa. This is the [stūpa of] the Seven... [text continues].
This is the site where one hundred noble ones held a second council. Further south, eighty or ninety *li* away, there is the Saṃghārāma.
Beside it are the sites containing the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas; this must be that very place.
In the city of Mathurā, there was a dwelling place called the Pūrṇa Cave, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
Second, regarding Mathurā: it is also called Mathura, which in this language means "peacock," and is also called "Secret."
All of these are accounts from ancient times. Furthermore, regarding what is called the "Cave of Fulfillment" (Pūrṇaguhā) in Central India:
that country possesses stupas such as those of Śakra and others, as well as a stupa of Mañjuśrī. Five or six *li* to the west of the royal city, there is a mountain monastery built by Upagupta.
To the north of the monastery is a cliff, within which is a stone cave; this is [the site of] Gupta...
In the place where many people were ordained and counting-slips were placed for their records,
there was a dwelling in the city of Kujinana called the Dharma Seat (Dharmāsana), where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
Regarding "Kucina": the full form is *Kucinaya*. *Kuci* is a clan name, which here means "large basin. *Naya* refers to the Vinaya (the rules of discipline).

This means that the shape of the pond was like a large basin; in ancient times, there was a rishi who practiced the Vinaya on its banks, and later generations took this as their clan name, after which the city was named.
In the City of the Pure Other Shore, there is a dwelling place called the Mucilinda Cave, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
This City of the Four Purities of the Other Shore is in South India. "Mucilinda" means "liberation" (mokṣa) in this language; it is [the name of] a dragon.
*Nālanda* means "place" (*sthāna*) in this language; it is the dwelling place of nāgas.
In the country of Mālava, there is a monastery established by the Nāga King Anāvaraṇa, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.

Fifth is the country of Mālava; its location is not clearly known. The Jin-period scriptures do not mention this country, referring instead only to "Wind Land," which refers to places with wind-cavities where dragons dwell.
In the country of Kāmpilya, there is a dwelling place named Jātamaitrī, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
Regarding the six Kāmpilyas, the correct transliteration is Gānpú; this is the name of a fruit. Those fruits are red and white, round and pure.
At first glance, it resembles the crabapples of this land, yet they have three horizontal lines of striations. In this country, there are many beautiful women who resemble dark blue lotus flowers;
thus the country is named after its women. It is here that those who give birth to compassion arise.
In the land of Zhendan, there is a dwelling place called the Nārāyaṇa Cave, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
The seven lands of Zhendan refer to this very Great Tang; it is also called Zhendan or Zhina, all of which are transcriptions of Sanskrit sounds.
"Chu-xia" (楚夏) here means "much deliberation," as human sentiments and considerations are manifold.

Previously, it was established as the eight directions; thus, Qingliang (the Pure Cool Mountain) simply stated "northeast. Now, because it is among various countries, the name of the country is cited.
"Narayana" means "firm and solid" (*jiānláo*). Formerly, it was said that there is Mount Lao to the east of the borders of Qingzhou; currently, there is an ancient [site] there.
This must be the sacred site of the Buddha.
In the kingdom of Shule, there is a dwelling place named Ox-Head Mountain (Gośīrṣa), where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
8. The Kingdom of Śūlī (Shuluo). Its full name is Kharoṣṭhala; it is named after a mountain in that country.

It is sometimes translated as "Evil Nature" (*āśaya*), a name derived from the character of the people. However, Mount Gośīrṣa (Ox-Head Mountain) is currently located in the kingdom of Khotan, which is here called *Dharaṇīkṣīra* (Earth-Milk).
This kingdom was established only one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as detailed in the *Record of the Western Regions*.
This was because when the collection of the scriptures took place, the region had not yet been opened and still belonged to Śākala.
In the kingdom of Kāśmīra, there is a monastery called Anupūrva, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.
*Kāśmīra* is universally translated as "Jibin" (罽賓). This is translated [etymologically] as "Ānanda’s Entry.
It is the site where Madhyāntika resided.
In the city of Vaipulya-nandana (增長歡喜城), there is a dwelling place called the Venerable One’s Cave (*Bhadanta-guhā*). Since ancient times, various bodhisattvas...
The multitude dwelt therein.
The tenth is the City of Increasing Joy (Ratnasaṃbhava-pura). An ancient commentary states that this refers to the Venerable One’s Cave (Ārya-guhā) in South India;
it is the place where the Sthavira school resided.
In the country of Āmrapālī, there is a dwelling place named Vision of the Radiance of the Treasury of Billions (*Koṭigarbhaprabhāsa*).
Since ancient times, multitudes of bodhisattvas have resided therein.
Eleven Āmrapālīs—this is translated as "Stainless" (*vimala*), which is the name of the fruit. This country is abundant and...
It is named after its excellence. Within the borders of Central India,
in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there is a dwelling place called the Śāmbala Cave, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times.

The twelfth is the country of Gandhāra, here translated as "Holder of the Earth" (Chìdì). It is so named because it is protected by many who have attained the fruits of the Path, and thus is not subject to invasion by other countries.
Alternatively, it is called "Pervasive Fragrance" (Xiāngbiàn), because fragrant herbs grow everywhere throughout the country before [others do].
*Campara* is the name of a fragrant flowering tree; because many of these grow near the side of the caves, [the place is so named]. This concludes the text.
There is no definitive conclusion. It may be that the transmission of these sutras was not yet complete.
As it is with Jambudvīpa, so it may be inferred for other regions, other realms, and realms of different categories. The cloud-bodies of the Dharma-realm are neither localized nor non-localized.
According to the general structural outline, from the "Ten Samādhis" chapter down to these six chapters, the Dharma-gate of Equal Enlightenment is expounded; this includes the preceding sections.
The three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are designated as the perfection of the causes of differentiation.

The subsequent three chapters—from the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha" to the "Chapter on the Merit of the Minor Marks and Radiance"—are taught as the fulfillment of the fruits of differentiation.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas."

Chapter Thirty-Three (Part One): The Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha.

Regarding the intent of the initial arrival: first general, then specific. Generally speaking, the five chapters below serve as the response to the ten questions posed at the beginning of the second assembly, such as the "Tathāgata-bhūmi.
Thus, the ancient masters held that only three chapters respond to what precedes them;

that is to say, the preceding section clarifies the causes for the production through cultivation—the perfection of the differentiated causes—whereas the present section examines the fruits produced through cultivation, manifesting the differentiated fruits.

"Full. Because the causes are perfected, the fruit is full; therefore, he comes next. If one asks why he requests again after having already answered the previous question, it is because the cause and fruit are separated.
He longs for the Dharma and yearns to hear it; since the virtue of the cause is still profound, the fruit must be even more mysterious and wondrous, and thus he requests it with longing.

This chapter is explained separately because the preceding chapter concludes with the causes, while this chapter begins with the fruits; thus, it follows immediately after. Second, regarding the explanation of the title:
the fruit-dharma of the Tathāgata utterly transcends words and thought, and therefore this serves as its name; this is precisely the inconceivable dharma of the Buddha.
Third, regarding the essential tenet: first generally, then specifically. Generally, it clarifies the essence of the Buddha’s fruit-virtues.
Usage: Taking the ineffability of the mind as its principle, it aims for the swift fulfillment [of enlightenment] through the total forgetting of words and the severance of conceptualization.
Within this principle, there is a threefold analysis: first, the general and specific qualities of the Buddha; second, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of the meaning;

and third, the revelation of the meaning of the inconceivable. First, regarding the discernment of the Buddha’s qualities: if one speaks of the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), they apply generally to...
The provisional is small. If the five dharmas encompass the nature of great awakening, they still pertain to the provisional.

If one speaks of it as having only the single flavor of real virtue, this is spoken from the perspective of sudden realization regarding principle. If one speaks of its possession of inexhaustible virtues, this is what is clarified here.

Therefore, in the subsequent text, ten questions are first posed, and the answers provide many approaches; these categories pervade the ten directions, each being individually inexhaustible. Second, the specific [analysis].

Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of meaning: the merits of all Buddhas do not transcend two kinds. First, those produced through cultivation; second, those that are originally inherent.
The former refers to qualities such as faith, which were previously non-existent and now exist. The latter refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), which possesses inherent, essential merits.

These two are unimpeded and should be analyzed according to four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, those produced solely through cultivation; second, those that are solely inherently existent—thus distinguishing between their nature and their characteristics.

Therefore, there are three types of "produced-by-cultivation" (xiūshēng) that are "originally existent" (běnyǒu): first, because the *tathāgatagarbha* depends upon its "revealing cause" (*liǎoyīn*), being originally hidden and now manifest;
second, because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is in profound resonance with the principle;

and third, according to what is clarified in the provisional teachings, where the two virtues are not intermingled and even the four permutations (*catuskoṭi*) of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* exhibit distinctions. Although there are these four meanings, according to the tenet of this sutra:
Yet there are no four distinct things. It is like pure gold existing inherently; its cultivation and manifestation are like the ornaments made from it.

However, it is precisely through the ornaments that the qualities of the gold are revealed. Since the ornaments have no independent substance and are entirely formed by gathering the gold, the gold alone does not obstruct the ornaments.

Likewise, the Dharma-body alone does not obstruct the Reward and Transformation bodies, and the same applies to the ornaments alone. Because they are mutually and completely inclusive, they constitute the ten bodies.
There is no obstruction. The eight marks encompass the entire dharma-realm; the sixteen-foot form pervades the ten directions.
Each of the sense organs and every pore is individually limitless, yet there is no obstruction to their measure. Measure and non-measure are without hindrance.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the meaning of the inconceivable, there are generally four aspects: first, the principle is subtle and difficult to fathom; second, the phenomena are vast and difficult to know; third, the practice...
Profoundly transcending the world, the four fruits transcend ordinary sentiment. The present text applies to all four, yet specifically elucidates the last one.

Within this last category, it is further divided into four: first, what is the inconceivable? Briefly stated, there are ten kinds: first, wisdom transcends the realm of the world; second, compassion surpasses ordinary sentiment;
third, accomplishing deeds without deliberation; fourth, remaining eternally pure while appearing to share in defilement; fifth, that which is performed...
1. Secrecy; 2. The vastness of the six karmic functions; 3. Entering through the many and the few; 4. Mastery over the partial and the complete; 5.

The non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants; 6. The single flavor of principle and phenomena. These points are all fully contained therein. Second, regarding that which is inconceivable, there are four aspects:
1. Transcending the mundane world; 2. Surpassing the provisional and the small vehicles; 3. Exceeding the stage of causes; 4. Revealing the self-nature of the Dharma.
III. What is the inconceivable? There are also four kinds: because it is not the object of the wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, cultivation, or retribution.
IV. What is the purpose of the inconceivable? There are also four kinds: to cause one to have faith and incline toward it; to give rise to practice and seek it;

to realize it according to one's capacity; and to attain it in its perfection. The preceding [sections] are all the thesis (*siddhānta*); what is the purpose of the thesis? It is for the sake of the goal (*prayojana*).
This very core tenet can serve to explain the title.
At that time, within the great assembly, there were bodhisattvas who had this thought.

Next is the formal explanation of the text, which is divided into five chapters. The first chapter generally elucidates the Buddha’s virtues; the subsequent four specifically manifest the Buddha’s [qualities].
Regarding the virtues: according to the ancient masters, the latter two constitute the equality of cause and effect. These consist merely of the dharmas of the three grades of fruit.
Now, following Xianshou, the first grade generally reveals the essence and function of the Buddha’s virtues; the second grade specifically reveals the characteristics of these supreme virtues;

and the third grade specifically reveals the beneficial functions of these supreme virtues. Furthermore, the first grade clarifies the brilliance (*māhātmya*), the second grade clarifies the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and the third grade clarifies the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

Now, the first section is divided into four parts: first, the section on the request; second, the section on the empowerment; third, the section on the realization; and fourth, the section on the exposition.
Within the first [the section on the request], there are two sub-divisions. First, the clarification of the requester; this refers to the thought that arises, which constitutes the act of requesting.
How are the buddha-fields of all Buddhas inconceivable? How are the original vows of all Buddhas inconceivable?
How are the spiritual lineages of all Buddhas inconceivable? How is the manifestation of all Buddhas inconceivable?
How are the bodies of all Buddhas inconceivable? How are the voices of all Buddhas inconceivable? How is the wisdom of all Buddhas inconceivable?
How inconceivable is the sovereign power of the Buddhas? How inconceivable is the unimpeded nature of the Buddhas?
How inconceivable is the liberation of the Buddhas?

The following section correctly elucidates that which is recollected. As for the fact that all ten dharmas are called "inconceivable," this means that the aforementioned fruit-function transcends the realm of the intellect and is free from the characteristics of verbal expression.
Therefore, the meanings of these ten phrases are manifold and inclusive; they all pertain to both the Truth-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Nevertheless, these ten phrases subsume the twenty phrases concerning the fruits achieved by the Universal Radiance [Samantaprabhā] mentioned previously. That is to say, "body" subsumes the six sense organs, and "wisdom" subsumes...

The three questions concerning the Buddha’s realm (*buddha-viṣaya*), the Buddha’s stage (*buddha-bhūmi*), and the most excellent [qualities] comprise five categories when subsumed under mastery (*vaśitā*): first, spiritual power (*ṛddhi*); second, supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*);
third, the ten powers (*daśabala*); fourth, the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); and fifth, the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). These are all expanded in the former [section] and consolidated here.

Within the former "realm," the buddha-field (*kṣetra*) was expanded because it constitutes the environment upon which those to be converted depend. Within the former "sphere of activity" (*caryā*), the appearance [in the world] was expanded.
The lineage of the original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna-gotra*). This lineage is precisely the practice of compassion and wisdom, because the original vow distinguishes practice in terms of its cause.

"Manifestation" refers to the conduct of Samantabhadra of the Buddha; thus, manifestation and practice have varying degrees of breadth and narrowness, as the aforementioned "Chapter on Manifesting Conduct" is but one instance thereof.
While the former [chapter] was unimpeded, this [chapter] opens up liberation; the unimpeded nature of its function is called liberation.

Because they are liberated. The reason for their opening and closing is to manifest that the meanings are not limited by direction. That their names are mostly identical is to manifest that they are not different.
Their sounds are clearly distinguished. These characteristics of the ten meanings were already explained in the second assembly; they will be further clarified below in the section on the exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the bodhisattvas, empowered them with his spiritual power and sustained them with his wisdom.
Radiance shone forth and majestic authority filled the space, causing the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha to abide in the fearlessness of the Buddha,
enter the Buddha’s dharma-realm, attain the sovereign supernatural powers of the Buddha’s majesty and virtue, and obtain the Buddha’s unimpeded, vast, and great contemplation.
He observes and knows the sequence of the lineage of all Buddhas, abiding in the inconceivable skillful means of the Buddha-dharma.

Within the second "Augmentation by Others" (parakṛta-adhikāra), there are three parts: first, the initial augmentation, because the [Buddha] uses spiritual power to know the capacities of the [disciples]; second, the manifestation of the characteristics of the augmentation, because of the augmentation of the three karmas;
and third, the specific details. The first phrase is general, while the subsequent phrases are specific, referring to mind, speech, and body; herein, light is used as the teaching.
Because of his radiance. Following the phrase "blue lotus," the purpose [of the passage] is added. This is because it fully explains his virtues; the text contains eight phrases:

first, he restrains external [factors] with fearlessness; second, he internally realizes profound stillness—this refers to the excellence of his mental karma (*manas-karma*); third, his majestic virtue is filled within.

1. The four bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) are the external penetration; this is the excellence of bodily action (kāyakarma). 2. Possessing the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) is the excellence of vocal action (vākkarma).
3. Universally observing the capacities of beings to teach them is "vastness. 4. Knowing that natures are without distinction is "succession. 5.

Skillfulness in bestowing and explaining the teachings is "expedient means" (upāya). These all describe qualities of virtue. As for why the "Blue Lotus Treasury" (Nīlotpalagarbha) is added: it signifies that the qualities of fruition are free from [defilement].
It is said: because it is manifested by means of causes; because cause and effect are simultaneous; because its intrinsic virtue is untainted and most preeminent;
and because each single virtue contains all virtues.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury was able to penetrate the unobstructed Dharma-realm;
was able to dwell securely in profound practices free from hindrances; was able to fulfill the great vows of Samantabhadra; and was able to know and see all Buddha-dharmas.

With a heart of great compassion, they observe sentient beings, desiring to bring them to purity; they practice with diligent effort without weariness or indolence, receiving and practicing all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
