Within a single thought-moment, they give birth to the wisdom of a Buddha and comprehend all inexhaustible gateways of knowledge.
They are fully endowed with dharanis and eloquence.

The third section, the Section on Realization (*abhisamaya*), consists of ten phrases. The first four phrases pertain to self-benefit; the subsequent three phrases pertain to the benefit of others. The preceding [eight] are all of the nature of the "own stage" (*svabhāga*).
The final three phrases, beginning with "in a single thought-moment," represent the "progressive advancement" (*viśeṣa-gati*).
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he addressed the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha.
This fourth section on the exposition is divided into two parts. First is the general address empowered [by the Buddha]. Regarding the address to Padmagarbha:

were it not for the Buddha-mind, there would be no means to receive this merit; thus he is also named "Lotus. The reason he is not called "Blue" is that he is not obstructed in his capacity as the expounder.
Because they are most supreme, O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have immeasurable abodes. That is to say: they abide in great compassion;

they abide in manifesting various bodies to perform the deeds of Buddhas; they abide in an impartial mind to turn the pure wheel of Dharma; and they abide in the four analytical knowledges to preach immeasurable teachings.
They dwell in all the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas; they dwell in the pure sound that pervades immeasurable lands;

they dwell in the ineffable, profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*); they dwell in the manifestation of all supreme spiritual powers (*abhijñā*); and they dwell in the ability to reveal the ultimate dharma that is free from all obstructions.
The subsequent section explicitly reveals the Buddha’s virtues, which briefly comprises two meanings. First, the five chapters below collectively answer ten questions;

this present chapter answers the question regarding the Buddha-nature (*gotra*), for the Buddha takes merit as his nature. Next, two chapters answer the question regarding the body. Next, one chapter answers the question regarding the original vow.
Finally, one chapter answers the question regarding the manifestation [of the Buddha]. As for the question regarding the land, it has already been explained extensively in the first assembly.
The remainder is either yet to be explained in subsequent chapters, or is subsumed within the preceding and following sections. Second, this chapter fully answers ten questions.

That is to say, while the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, they are briefly manifested through thirty-two gates; each gate fully answers the ten questions, resulting in three hundred and twenty virtues to manifest their inexhaustibility.
This is intended to reveal that a single virtue of the Buddha possesses all others, and thus it also manifests—

Because that which was asked is fully encompassed herein, yet the names of the headings for the gates differ from those previously mentioned in order to manifest the boundless nature of the Buddha’s virtues.

The text is divided into ten sections: the first two gates answer the question regarding the land; the next two gates, beginning with "In every thought-moment, he brings forth," answer the question regarding his original vows;
and the third section, beginning with "The inconceivable realm," [answers the question regarding his spiritual power].

The second section, "The Two Gates," answers the question regarding spiritual lineage (*gotra*). The fourth section, "Universal Entry," and the following two sections answer the question regarding manifestation.

The fifth section, "Purity Free from Faults," with its five gates, answers the question regarding the body. The sixth section, "Expounding," and the following two sections answer the question regarding voice.

The seventh section, "Supreme," and the following three sections answer the question regarding wisdom. The eighth section, "Mastery," and the following eight sections [answer the remaining questions].
The answer to the question on mastery consists of the nine gates of the "Definitive" section below, which answer the question on unimpededness.

The answer to the question on liberation consists of the ten gates of the "Abiding in Omniscience" section below. These answers regarding the body and mastery respond to the previous "Universal Radiance.

Because the questions are numerous, the gates employed are likewise many; however, the textual structure generally consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. Here, the first two [are presented].
Regarding the "land of the gate": the land is that which serves as the basis and the dwelling place. The first gate clarifies the dharma-gate of its eternal abiding;
the latter gate clarifies its pervasive abiding throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is not merely that the land does not exist within spatial locations that constitutes the true land.
Now, for the first section, there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. Within the explanation, nine phrases reveal the Tathāgata’s response.
The teaching through the opportune occasion (*tatkāla-dharma*) answers the ten questions such that all ten become places of abiding; the following sections are to be understood accordingly.

First, by giving rise to a responsive mind, he answers the question regarding the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), for compassion is the spiritual lineage. Second, by manifesting the body of the Dharma, he answers the question regarding the body.
Third, by manifesting the intent of the Dharma, he answers the question regarding the original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*), for the original vow is impartial and benefits all beings.
Fourth, the eloquence that can transform answers the question of sound; for it is through eloquence that sound issues forth.
Fifth, the dharma that is transformed answers the question of mastery; for mastery is inconceivable. Sixth, the pervasive resonance of transformation answers the question of the buddha-field;
for the field is where sound reaches. Seventh, the principle revealed answers the question of wisdom; for wisdom is able to abide [therein].

Because of the *dharmadhātu*. Eighth, the power of transformation answers the question regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Ninth, the benefit of expounding the Dharma answers the question regarding unimpededness (*anāvaraṇa*).

The text consists of only nine phrases; the phrase "appearing" (*prādurbhāva*) is omitted, or it may be understood as encompassing the preceding phrases, since appearing is capable of performing all nine functions.
Since the answers to these ten questions are thus established, the analogies for the answers to the first two assemblies can be known by extension.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of dharmas that pervade the infinite and boundless Dharma-realm.

What are these ten? They are as follows: All Buddhas possess a body of infinite limits; their physical marks are pure, and they universally enter all realms of existence without being stained or attached. All Buddhas possess eyes of infinite limits and no obstruction; regarding all...
They are able to clearly perceive all phenomena. All Buddhas possess infinite and unobstructed ears;
they are able to fully comprehend and understand all sounds. All Buddhas possess infinite noses, which reach the shore of the sovereign mastery of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas possess broad and long tongues, from which they emit wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm. All...
All Buddhas possess boundless bodies; according to the minds of sentient beings, they cause all to behold them.
All Buddhas possess boundless intentions; they abide in the unimpeded and equal Dharma-body.
All Buddhas possess boundless and unimpeded liberation; they manifest inexhaustible great supernormal powers. All Buddhas possess boundlessness...

In pure worlds, they manifest various Buddha-lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings, fully endowed with immeasurable and diverse adornments, yet they give rise to no defiled attachment therein. All Buddhas possess boundless bodhisattva practices and vows.
They attain the mastery of sporting in perfect wisdom and are able to thoroughly penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which pervade the entire dharma-realm without limit.
Second, regarding the "pervasive dharma-realm," this clarifies its universal abiding; that is to say, the six sense organs and the three karmas all pervade the single realm of the dharma.
In the heading, "immeasurable" refers to the phenomenal dharma-realm (*śrī-dharmadhātu*), and "boundless" refers to the noumenal dharma-realm (*tattva-dharmadhātu*).

These two are non-obstructive, as is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*); these together constitute that which is pervaded. In the enumeration, the preceding ten are made manifest.
All are pervasive. First, one [characteristic] universally pervades the body, encompassing the answers to three questions: first, it directly answers regarding the body;

its universal presence throughout all realms of existence (*gati*) constitutes the nature of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the sense of manifestation. Next, six are the specific characteristics of the body;

these also answer, in conjunction with the body, the six questions concerning Universal Radiance, the Eyes, and so forth. The production of sublime sounds answers the question regarding sound. The eighth answers three [questions].
Question: The ninth is called the "unimpeded answer," and the tenth is the "liberation answer. The power of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) constitutes mastery.

The ninth provides a specific answer regarding the buddha-fields, while the tenth answers the questions concerning original vows and wisdom. In the preceding two initial sections, the question regarding the buddha-fields was answered.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of wisdom that arise in every thought-moment. What are these ten?
They are as follows: in a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest the descent from the heavens into immeasurable worlds.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the taking of birth by Bodhisattvas in immeasurable worlds.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the leaving of home and training in the Way in immeasurable worlds.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree in immeasurable worlds.

All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma in immeasurable worlds. All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest [these deeds] in immeasurable worlds.
They transform and guide sentient beings and make offerings to all Buddhas.
Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest immeasurable worlds and unspeakably diverse Buddha-bodies. Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas...
They are all able to manifest the various adornments and countless ornaments of immeasurable worlds, as well as the sovereign power of the Tathāgatas and the treasury of omniscience.

Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest immeasurable and innumerable pure sentient beings throughout immeasurable worlds. Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest...
The various faculties, various degrees of diligence, and various modes of practice and understanding of the Buddhas of the three times throughout immeasurable worlds,
who attain equal and perfect enlightenment within the three times— this is the tenth.

The second section consists of two parts that answer questions regarding the original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*). This first part clarifies how the Buddha manifests the eight signs of his appearance through the power of his vows.

The subsequent part clarifies that these vows do not lose their timing. Now, for the first: the essence of the vow is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*); it proceeds from this wisdom of the vow.
The manifestation of the eight signs and so forth is not the arising of wisdom. Among the individual vows, there are ten: first, descending to be born; second, the lineage of birth;
third, training in the path of liberation; fourth, clarifying his appearance; fifth, his voice; sixth, manifesting through transformation to adorn the land; seventh, manifesting the physical body;
eighth, the marks of mastery and the adornment of merit, because he adorns the *tathāgatagarbha*; ninth, this is unimpeded; tenth...
This is because they possess wisdom and perfect, universal knowledge.
Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of non-mistimed actions. What are these ten? They are:

first, all Buddhas never miss the proper time for attaining equal and perfect enlightenment; second, all Buddhas never miss the proper time for bringing those with whom they have a karmic connection to maturity.

All Buddhas bestow predictions upon Bodhisattvas without missing the proper time. All Buddhas manifest spiritual powers in accordance with the minds of sentient beings without missing the proper time.
All Buddhas manifest the Buddha-body in accordance with the understandings of sentient beings without missing the proper time.
All Buddhas abide in great equanimity without missing the proper time. All Buddhas enter all villages...
They do not miss the proper time. All Buddhas gather those of pure faith without missing the proper time. All Buddhas discipline wicked sentient beings without missing the proper time.
All Buddhas manifest the inconceivable supernatural powers of all Buddhas without missing the proper time.

These are the ten. Second, regarding not missing the opportune time: movement and stillness depend upon conditions. When the faculties are mature, one manifests transformation; when they are not yet mature, one desists. It is not that one's vows are incomplete;

rather, if the capacity for response matures and one misses the moment, it constitutes a violation of the original vow. Within the specific [categories], there are two: first, manifestation; second, the fulfillment of the essence.

May there be a connection through shared affinity. Third, knowing the spiritual lineage and bestowing predictions; fourth, mastery; fifth, manifesting the body; sixth, abiding in equanimity with wisdom;
seventh, the non-obstruction of the six sense faculties; eighth, purifying lands to gather those with faith; ninth, using powerful voices to subdue the wicked; tenth, the inconceivable liberation.
These two preceding sections answer the questions regarding the original vows.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of incomparable and inconceivable realms. What are these ten?
They are as follows: first, all Buddhas sit cross-legged, pervading immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
Second, when all Buddhas speak a single phrase of meaning, they are able to reveal and manifest all Buddha-dharmas. Third, all Buddhas emit a single...
Their radiance is able to universally illumine all worlds. All Buddhas are able to manifest all bodies within a single body;
all Buddhas are able to manifest all worlds within a single location;
all Buddhas are able to decisively comprehend all phenomena within a single wisdom, without [obstruction].
Without obstruction. All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully manifest the immeasurable majestic virtue of the Tathāgatas.

All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, universally take as their object the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the minds of sentient beings, without confusion or disorder. All Buddhas, within a single...
In mindfulness, one realizes that they are identical in essence and non-dual with all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; this constitutes the tenth [point].

This third section consists of two gates answering the question regarding the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). This first gate clarifies both the retributive and responsive aspects, as their spiritual lineages are both truly authentic.
The subsequent gate clarifies only the Dharma-realm lineage. Now, for the first [of these], its essence and characteristics transcend words and thought; how so?
It is inconceivable. It is called "matchless" because those in lower stages cannot attain it. Within the distinct [qualities], there are six: first, the single voice; second, the two tones;
third, the emission of light through the power of vows, which is the light obtained according to one's original vows; fourth, manifestation; fifth, the buddha-field; and sixth, wisdom.
Seven, mastery; eight, the lineage of majestic power; nine, the absence of heterogeneous obstructions; ten, the identity of the essence of liberation.
The five preceding sections have briefly pointed out and addressed these ten questions. What follows is omitted for fear of being overly prolix and obscure.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to give rise to ten kinds of wisdom. What are these ten? They are as follows:
all Buddhas know that all phenomena have no direction toward which they tend, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom of dedication and vows.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are entirely without body, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom of the pure body. All...
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are originally non-dual, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom of awakening.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are without self and without sentient beings, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom that disciplines sentient beings.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are originally signless, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom that comprehends all signs. One.
All Buddhas know that all worlds have neither arising nor perishing, yet they are able to produce the wisdom that fully understands arising and perishing.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena have no creator, yet they are able to produce the wisdom that knows the fruits of karma.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom that fully understands verbal expression;
all Buddhas know that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom that knows defilement and purity.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, yet they are able to produce the wisdom that fully understands arising and ceasing.
This is the tenth.
Second, regarding the production of wisdom: this clarifies that the Dharma-body is the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); from within the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this wisdom emerges.
Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*): it is not because it answers the question of wisdom itself. Within the distinct [categories], there are ten pairs of phrases;

in each case, the preceding phrase refers to the nature of knowing—that is, the nature of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*)—which acts as the productive cause. The subsequent phrase refers to the arising of the functional application of wisdom (*jñāna*). These two preceding gates answer the question concerning the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of universal entry methods (*samanta-praveśa-dharma*). What are these ten?
They are as follows: First, all Buddhas possess pure and wondrous bodies that universally enter the three periods of time.

Second, all Buddhas are fully endowed with the three kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*) to universally transform sentient beings. Third, all Buddhas are fully endowed with all *dhāraṇīs*, enabling them to universally...
They uphold all Buddha-dharmas. All Buddhas are fully endowed with the four kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and universally turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with impartial great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and never abandon any sentient being.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and constantly [pervade] everywhere...
He observes all sentient beings. All Buddhas are fully endowed with roots of goodness for the benefit of others, subduing sentient beings without ceasing.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with unobstructed minds, able to dwell universally throughout the entire dharma-realm.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with unhindered spiritual powers; in a single thought-moment...
They universally manifest all Buddhas of the three periods of time. All Buddhas are fully endowed with unimpeded wisdom;
in a single thought-moment, they universally establish the kalpas of the three periods of time. This is the tenth.
The fourth [section] has two gates that answer [the question of] manifestation. This gate clarifies universal and constant manifestation;

the subsequent gate clarifies the characteristics of manifestation. Now, for the first: regarding the clarification of universal and constant manifestation, it is because there is no coming or going that constitutes true manifestation.

As it says in the *Biezhong* (Separate Commentary): "It universally manifests all Buddhas of the three periods of time; how much more so one's own body? Furthermore, a single manifestation is itself [the whole].

All are manifested, because the Buddhas of the three periods of time possess no dual nature. Regarding the "three kinds of mastery" mentioned in the specific section, these refer to the transformations of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of vast dharmas that are difficult to believe and accept. What are these ten? As it is said:
That is to say: all Buddhas are able to utterly destroy all Māras; all Buddhas are able to subdue all non-Buddhists;
all Buddhas are able to tame all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice;
all Buddhas are able to travel to all worlds to transform and guide the multitudes of beings. All...
The Buddhas are all able to realize the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through their wisdom.
All Buddhas are able, by means of their non-dual body, to manifest various bodies that fill all worlds.

All Buddhas are able, by means of their pure voices, to give rise to the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) and preach the Dharma without interruption. For anyone who receives it with faith, the merit shall not be in vain. All Buddhas...
The Buddhas are all able to manifest within a single pore as many Buddhas as there are atoms in all worlds,
without interruption. All Buddhas are likewise able to manifest within a single atom as many lands as there are atoms in all worlds,
fully endowed with various kinds of sublime and wondrous adornments, eternally.
Within that, they turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to transform sentient beings; yet, the atoms do not become large and the worlds do not become small.
They constantly abide in the dharma-realm through realized wisdom. All Buddhas have fully and thoroughly comprehended the pure dharma-realm.

They shatter the darkness of worldly ignorance with the light of wisdom, enabling them to fully comprehend and awaken to the Buddha-dharma, and following the Tathāgata, they abide within the ten powers. These are the ten.
The twenty kinds of vast dharmas clarify the characteristics of their manifestation. They are called "vast" because their great function is boundless;
they are "difficult to believe and accept" because ordinary and inferior beings cannot fathom them. These two preceding sections answer the question regarding manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of great merit that are pure through the elimination of faults. What are these ten?
They are as follows: all Buddhas possess great majestic power and are pure through the elimination of faults;

all Buddhas are born into the family of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, and their lineage is disciplined and virtuous, being pure through the elimination of faults; all Buddhas... [the text continues].
The future limit of the mind has no abiding place; it is pure, being free from faults. All Buddhas have no attachment to the phenomena of the three periods of time;
they are pure, being free from faults. All Buddhas know that various natures are all of one single nature, coming from nowhere;
they are pure, being free from faults. The merit of all Buddhas in the past and future limits is inexhaustible and equal.

The Dharma-realm is pure and free from faults. All Buddhas possess boundless physical forms that pervade the lands of the ten directions, taming all sentient beings according to the time, and are thus pure and free from faults. All Buddhas have attained the four fearlessnesses and are free from all terrors;
amidst the great assemblies, they roar the great lion’s roar, clearly discerning and distinguishing all dharmas, and are thus free from faults.
Pure. Although all Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa after incalculably incalculable eons, sentient beings who hear their names obtain immeasurable merit.
Their virtues are no different from those of a Buddha currently present; they are pure and free from faults.
Even though all Buddhas dwell far away in worlds beyond incalculably incalculable numbers, if there are sentient beings who, with a single-minded focus and correctness...
When one recollects [the Buddha], one attains the vision of his faultless and pure state; this constitutes the tenth [point].
The fifth section, consisting of five gates, answers the question regarding the body and is divided into five parts. First, this gate provides a general exposition:

the three karmas of the Tathāgata are without fault because they proceed in accordance with wisdom, and because all matters pertaining to the three karmas do not transcend the body. [The following] specifically...
Reflect upon this: the ten phrases herein are for the most part identical to the ten marks of the body as they appear in the "Chapter on Manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of ultimate purity.
What are these ten? They are: the ultimate purity of the great vows of all Buddhas in the past; the ultimate purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) maintained by all Buddhas... [and so forth].
Ultimately pure. All Buddhas are ultimately pure, having abandoned all worldly delusions.
All Buddhas are ultimately pure in their adornment of buddha-lands. All Buddhas are ultimately pure in their retinues.
All Buddhas are ultimately pure in their lineages. All Buddhas are ultimately pure in the marks and signs of their form bodies.
Ultimate purity: the dharma-body of all buddhas is unstained and ultimately pure;

the omniscient wisdom of all buddhas is unimpeded and ultimately pure; the liberation, mastery, and fulfillment of what was to be done by all buddhas—having reached the further shore—is ultimately pure. These are the ten.
Regarding the second, ultimate purity (*atyanta-viśuddhi*): this clarifies that [defilements] do not arise again, distinguishing it from causal purity; thus it is called "ultimate.

Because the various stains of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) never arise again, within the specific [categories], there is first the purity of the five bodies of merit (*guṇakāya*), next the three bodies of form (*rūpakāya*), next the one body of dharma (*dharmakāya*), next the one body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*), and finally the purity of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) and so forth.
O Son of the Buddha, throughout all worlds and at all times, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform ten kinds of Buddha-activities.
What are these ten? First, if there are sentient beings who mindfully recollect them with single-minded devotion, the Buddhas appear before them.
Second, if there are sentient beings whose minds are not disciplined or compliant, the Buddhas preach the Dharma for them. Third, if there are sentient beings capable of generating purity...

First, faith will certainly cause one to obtain immeasurable roots of goodness. Second, if there are sentient beings who can enter the stage of the Dharma (dharmatā), they shall all realize it through direct manifestation without anything remaining unknown.
Third, in teaching and transforming sentient beings, one never experiences weariness or fatigue.
Fourth, when traveling to and fro among various Buddha-fields, one does so without obstruction. Fifth, with great compassion, one does not abandon any sentient being. Sixth, [one] manifests...
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is never interrupted; ninth, mastery over supernatural powers (abhijñā) is never-ceasing;
tenth, abiding in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one is able to observe it universally. These are the ten.

The thirty kinds of Buddha-activities clarify the functional applications of the body. Within these specific categories, many are identical to the bodily characteristics described in the "Appearance" chapter.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of inexhaustible oceans of wisdom. What are these ten? They are as follows:
The Dharma of the boundless Dharma-body and inexhaustible ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas;
the Dharma of the immeasurable Buddha-activities and inexhaustible ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas; the Dharma of the realm of the Buddha-eye and inexhaustible ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas;
the Dharma of the immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable roots of goodness and inexhaustible ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas; all Buddhas...

The Dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom that universally rains down the wondrous Dharma of ambrosia; the Dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom that extols the meritorious virtues of all Buddhas;
the Dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom regarding the various vows and practices cultivated by all Buddhas in the past;
and the Dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom through which all Buddhas constantly perform Buddha-works throughout the limits of the future.
The dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom that all Buddhas thoroughly understand the mental activities of all sentient beings;
and the dharma of the inexhaustible ocean of wisdom adorned with the merit and knowledge of all Buddhas, which none can surpass—these are the ten.
Regarding the Dharma of the four inexhaustible oceans of wisdom: it refers to the six sense faculties and the three karmas of the Tathāgata, all of which are in accord with profound and vast wisdom;
furthermore, each is individually characterized by expansive wisdom and depth.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of eternal dharmas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
first, all Buddhas constantly practice all the pāramitās; second, all Buddhas are eternally free from delusion regarding all phenomena;
third, all Buddhas are always endowed with great compassion; fourth, all Buddhas always possess the ten powers; fifth, all [Buddhas...]
The Buddhas constantly turn the wheel of Dharma. All Buddhas constantly manifest perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings.
All Buddhas always delight in taming all sentient beings. The minds of all Buddhas are constantly in right mindfulness of the non-dual Dharma.
Having transformed sentient beings, all Buddhas constantly manifest entry into nirvana without remainder. This is the realm of the Buddhas.
Because the realms are without limit; these constitute the ten.
Regarding the fifty kinds of permanent phenomena (*nityadharma*), this clarifies that the mental karma within the body is constant, as its function is uninterrupted.
The above five gates answer the question concerning the body.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of gateways for expounding the infinite dharmas of the Buddhas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas expound the gateway of the infinite realms of sentient beings;
all Buddhas expound the gateway of the infinite conducts of sentient beings; all Buddhas expound the gateway of the infinite karmic fruits of sentient beings.
All Buddhas proclaim immeasurable gateways for transforming sentient beings;
all Buddhas proclaim immeasurable gateways for purifying sentient beings; all Buddhas proclaim immeasurable gateways of bodhisattva practices;
all Buddhas proclaim immeasurable gateways of bodhisattva vows; all Buddhas proclaim immeasurable [gateways] of all worlds.
The gate of the kalpas of formation and destruction; the gate of all Buddhas expounding the immeasurable gates of the pure Buddha-lands through the profound resolve of Bodhisattvas;

the gate of all Buddhas expounding the immeasurable gates of the successive appearance of all Buddhas of the three periods of time in each and every world throughout the kalpas; and the gate of all Buddhas expounding the wisdom of all Buddhas—these are the ten.

The sixth section consists of two parts that respond to questions concerning sound. This section clarifies the exposition through vocal expression and simultaneously answers the inquiry of Samantaprabha.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform ten kinds of buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings. What are these ten? [As follows:]
That is to say: all Buddhas manifest physical bodies to perform Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings;
all Buddhas emit sublime sounds to perform Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings; all Buddhas have that which they receive to perform Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings;
all Buddhas have nothing that they receive to perform Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings; all Buddhas, by means of...

The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind perform the buddha-work for sentient beings. The sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas manifest all objective spheres of perception to perform the buddha-work for sentient beings. The various names and titles of all Buddhas perform the buddha-work for sentient beings.
All Buddhas take the realms of the Buddha-fields to perform the buddha-work for sentient beings.
[The tenth] matter: All Buddhas perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings by adorning and purifying Buddha-lands;
all Buddhas perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings through silent non-speaking. These are the ten.
The latter ten gates clarify the performance of Buddha-activities through various forms of teaching the Dharma;

that is to say, the six sense objects, the four great elements, and all movements and actions are capable of manifesting the Dharma and bringing about benefit, such that there is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity—not only sound.

As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, regarding the specific [categories], the first is the body and the second is the voice; the third and fourth are both the reception of wisdom, yet one does not receive them in order to perfect that *dāna* (generosity).
This is to cause them to emulate the Buddha’s practice of having few desires. Furthermore, it is because they experience all sensations while remaining without any subjective grasping.
These two preceding sections answer the question regarding voice.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of most excellent dharmas. What are these ten? Namely, all..."
The great vows of all Buddhas are firm and indestructible; what they say must be done, for their words are without duality.
All Buddhas, desiring to fulfill all merits, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all future kalpas without ever giving rise to weariness.
All Buddhas, desiring to subdue all sentient beings, go to unspeakable [realms].
The world may be described as such, yet for all sentient beings it remains uninterrupted.
Toward both those who have faith and those who revile, all Buddhas universally observe with great compassion, viewing them equally and without distinction.
From their first aspiration until their attainment of Buddhahood, all Buddhas never retreat or lose the mind of enlightenment. All Buddhas...
They accumulate immeasurable merits and virtues, dedicating them all toward the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). They remain forever free from attachment to any worldly realm.
Having trained in the three types of action (*trikarma*) under all Buddhas, they practice only the conduct of a Buddha and not that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
All these acts are dedicated toward the nature of omniscience to bring about unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

All Buddhas emit great rays of light; these rays shine equally upon all places and illuminate the teachings of all Buddhas, causing the minds of all Bodhisattvas to become pure and fulfill omniscience.

All Buddhas have abandoned worldly pleasures, being neither greedy nor stained by them, yet they universally vow that the world shall be free from suffering and attain happiness, devoid of all frivolous play.

Treatise: All Buddhas, out of compassion for all sentient beings who undergo various sufferings, protect the lineage of the Buddhas, practice the realm of the Buddhas, transcend birth and death, and attain the stage of the Ten Powers. These constitute the ten.

The seventh section consists of three gates that answer questions concerning wisdom. This first gate generally elucidates the wisdom of the provisional and the ultimate regarding cause and effect, while simultaneously answering the question of Puguang (Universal Radiance) regarding his supreme [attainment].
Because this wisdom is supreme, it concludes by stating that he "dwells in the stage of the ten powers" (*daśabala-bhūmi*), which also answers the Buddha’s question.
Within the specific [explanation], there are four parts, namely the practice of the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the remainder may be inferred accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of unobstructed abodes. What are these ten?
They are: all Buddhas are able to travel to all worlds with unobstructed abiding;
all Buddhas are able to dwell in all worlds with unobstructed abiding; all Buddhas are able, within all worlds...
All Buddhas abide without obstruction in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. All Buddhas are able to expound the True Dharma in all worlds without obstruction.
All Buddhas are able to dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven palace in all worlds without obstruction. All Buddhas are able to enter the Dharma-realm and all three periods of time.
Abiding without obstruction: all Buddhas are able to sit at every site of enlightenment within the Dharma-realm and abide without obstruction.
All Buddhas are able, in every thought-moment, to observe the mental activities of all sentient beings, teaching and taming them through the three kinds of mastery while abiding without obstruction.
All Buddhas are able to abide with a single body in the realm of non-existence...
They abide without obstruction in benefiting sentient beings in all places, as inconceivable as the reach of the Buddhas;
they abide without obstruction in being able to reveal the true Dharma taught by immeasurable Buddhas.
These are the ten.
Second is the dwelling of non-obstruction. This clarifies that wisdom is free from hindrances; because the activities of wisdom are unimpeded, all things are without obstruction.

O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of supreme and unsurpassed adornments. What are these ten? They are as follows: ... [The remainder of the passage] ... what are they? They are as follows: [the list continues].
It is said that all Buddhas are fully endowed with the primary marks and secondary characteristics;
this constitutes the foremost, most supreme, and unsurpassed physical adornment of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with sixty kinds of vocal tones, each tone consisting of five hundred parts, and each part is further adorned by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pure sounds.
They are able to remain without any fear amidst all assemblies within the Dharma-realm and let out the great lion’s roar, expounding the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Among sentient beings who hear them, there are none who do not rejoice; according to their faculties and inclinations, they all attain subduing and transformation.
This is the second supreme and unsurpassed adornment of speech of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas possess the ten powers, the great samādhis, and the eighteen unique qualities that adorn their mental karma. Their sphere of activity is unimpeded and thoroughly penetrating;
they have attained all Buddha-dharmas without exception. They take the adornment of the dharma-realm as their own adornment, and the multitude of the dharma-realm...
The mental activities of beings throughout the past, future, and present, each with their distinct differences, can all be clearly perceived within a single thought-moment.
This is the third supreme and unsurpassed mental adornment of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas are able to emit countless rays of light, and each ray of light has an unspeakable number of networks of light as its retinue.

It belongs to [the Buddhas]. It universally illumines all Buddha-lands, extinguishes all darkness in the world, and manifests the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas. Their bodies are equal and entirely pure;
the Buddha-deeds they perform are never in vain, and they are able to lead sentient beings to the stage of non-retrogression. This is the fourth most supreme and unsurpassed light of the Buddhas.
The Adornment of Clarity: Whenever all Buddhas manifest a smile, they emit from their mouths hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays.
Each individual ray of light possesses immeasurable and inconceivable varieties of colors, which universally illuminate all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Within the great assembly, they utter words of truth and bestow [the prophecy] upon the immeasurable...

The bestowing of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon countless, inconceivable sentient beings—this is the fifth supreme and unsurpassed manifestation of the smile-adornment of all Buddhas, which transcends worldly delusion.
All Buddhas possess the Dharma-body, which is pure and unimpeded; they have attained ultimate penetration into all phenomena and abide within the Dharma-realm.
It is without limit or boundary. Although it exists within the world, it is not mixed with the world; it realizes the true nature of the world and practices supramundane dharmas.
It is cut off from the path of speech and transcends the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. This is the sixth most excellent and unsurpassed adornment of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas possess immeasurable, eternal, and wondrous radiance, which is unspeakably unspeakable.

Adorned with various forms and marks as their ornament, they are treasuries of radiance, producing immeasurable, perfect light that shines universally throughout the ten directions without obstruction.
This is the seventh supreme, unsurpassed, eternally wondrous adornment of light of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas possess boundless sublime colors and lovely, exquisite colors, which are pure.
Exquisite form. Exquisite forms manifested according to the mind, which outshine all exquisite forms within the three realms, reaching the unsurpassed exquisite form of the further shore.
Therefore, this is the eighth most supreme and unsurpassed adornment of exquisite form of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas are born from the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; having accumulated the jewels of manifold virtues, they are ultimately pure and free from all [defilements].
Free from faults and beyond worldly censure, it is the most preeminent among all phenomena.
Adorned with pure and wondrous conduct, it is fully endowed with the wisdom of all-knowledge. Its lineage is pure and cannot be disparaged;
this is the ninth supreme and unsurpassed adornment of the lineage of all Buddhas. All Buddhas, by the power of great compassion...
His body is adorned and ultimately pure; free from all craving, his bodily activities are forever stilled. His mind is well-liberated, and those who behold him never tire of the sight.
With great compassion, he protects and delivers the entire world; he is the foremost field of merit, the unsurpassed recipient of offerings.
Out of compassion, they benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to increase their immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom.
This is the tenth supreme, unsurpassed adornment of the meritorious virtues of the Buddhas' great loving-kindness and great compassion.
The thirty kinds of unsurpassed adornments are the fulfillment of benefit through wisdom. Because one possesses the internal adornment of wisdom, one externally possesses all adornments.
Regarding the general definition: it is "supreme" because it transcends lower stages, and it is called "unsurpassed" because there is nothing superior above it.
Within the specific details, the meaning is concluded and the names are self-evident: first, the body with its marks and signs; second, the perfect voice; third, the adornment of virtues.

[The topics are: first, the mind; second, the four rays of light; third, the smile and the bestowal of prophecy—the conditions for these are very numerous and are also clarified in the "Chapter on Leaving the World";
fourth, within the dharma-body, true suchness emerges from its entanglements, and is thus called "pure and unobstructed," which is precisely the dharma-nature dharma-body.
Because fundamental wisdom reflects back upon itself, it attains ultimate penetration into all phenomena; this is the Wisdom-Dharmakāya.

Wisdom accords with the Dharma-realm, and both are without limit or boundary. Although it exists as the manifested Dharmakāya for those below [the stage of realization], it realizes the Dharmakāya of merit for those below the world;
because it adorns the principle of wisdom, it realizes the true nature of the world, thereby achieving non-intermixture with what precedes and giving rise to what follows.

Worldly practices are transcended; when one enters the supramundane Dharma, its merits are fully perfected. When the path of language is severed, this is the *dharmakāya* of empty space, which is also the *dharmakāya* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Its essence is beyond the hundred negations, and speech ceases within the four propositions. It can only be realized through direct correspondence;

thus, it transcends the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), manifesting as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). By overturning the outflowing aggregates, it becomes the fivefold *dharmakāya*. If one were to overturn the elements...
In this state, the six external sense objects are likewise identical to the body of the land; thus, the ten bodies are perfectly interfused, realizing the true *dharmakāya*.
Seventh is the constant radiance (*nityaprabhā*). Eighth is the wondrous color of gold and so forth. Ninth, within this [body], the true, the responsive, and the causal seeds are complete;

since the seed of the Buddhas of the three periods is the natureless *tathatā*, the responsive and causal seeds may be understood accordingly. Tenth, that which arises necessarily co-exists with wisdom; therefore, there is no...
Craving is stirred when it accords with the Path; thus, bodily formations are forever stilled. When the mind is well-liberated, one achieves supreme non-craving.
For the observer, there is no weariness, and one achieves the stilling of higher formations. These are all merits, yet being free from craving and views, one achieves lower great compassion.
Since one has become the foremost field of merit, there is nothing superior to receiving offerings from such a person.
These are the ten. Third, the summary.
The above seven sections and three gates answer the question regarding wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of sovereign dharmas.
The eighth [section] consists of eight gates answering questions on mastery (*vaśitā*), forming eight segments.

The first segment provides a general clarification of mastery while also encompassing empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It begins with a general heading, followed by ten specific instances of mastery, which constitute ten minor sub-sections.
What are the ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas have attained complete mastery over all phenomena;
they clearly comprehend various collections of phrases and collections of meanings; and they expound all teachings with unhindered eloquence. This is the first sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.

There are ten further [aspects] which are entirely identical to the ten kinds of mastery found within the eighth stage; they differ only in being more profound and vast, and not following the same sequence.
First is mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*). The *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* state that this is because of the manifestation of dharma-gates that have neither center nor periphery.
All Buddhas never miss the proper time in their transformation of sentient beings;
according to their aspirations and inclinations, they preach the True Dharma, causing all to be tamed without interruption. This is the second sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.

Second is mastery over the mind. Because of the wisdom of entering samādhi throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one observes the capacities of beings while remaining in samādhi, thereby ensuring that transformations are never untimely.
All Buddhas are able to cause all manner of infinite and innumerable various adornments to fill the entirety of the realm of empty space.
The world undergoes six kinds of earthquakes, causing that world to either rise or fall, expand or contract, or to coalesce or disperse;
yet not a single sentient being is ever harmed. The sentient beings therein do not perceive it, do not know of it, have no doubt about it, and feel no wonder.
This is the third sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.

Third is mastery over resolute conviction (*adhimukti-vaśitā*). Because [the world] transforms according to one's resolution—whether large or small, pure or impure—all Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā-bala*), are able to purify all worlds.

Within a single moment of thought, they universally manifest the adornments of all worlds; these various adornments could not be fully described even after the passage of incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

All are entirely free from defilement and incomparably pure. All matters concerning the adornment and purification of all Buddha-fields are made equal, such that they enter into every single field. This is the fourth sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.
Fourth is mastery over wealth. Because they maintain and sustain all worlds with infinite adornments,
whenever any Buddha perceives a single sentient being who is ready to be transformed, He remains for them throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, even until the end of the future,
sitting in the full lotus posture with body and mind free from weariness, focusing His mind with single-minded devotion.
They maintain mindfulness without ever allowing it to be forgotten; they employ skillful means to subdue beings without missing the proper time.
As they do for a single sentient being, so they do for all sentient beings. This is the fifth sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.
Fifth is mastery over life, because one maintains the life-span for unspeakable eons.
All Buddhas are able to go everywhere throughout all worlds;
they never abandon any realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) where all Tathāgatas practice. In each of the ten directions, there are immeasurable worlds.

Oceans. Within each ocean of worlds there are immeasurable world-systems. By means of his spiritual power, a Buddha reaches them all in a single thought-moment and turns the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma. This is the sixth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas.
Sixth is mastery over the wish-fulfilling power (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*).
Because they manifest transformations at will within all lands, all Buddhas, desiring to discipline all sentient beings, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in every thought-moment;
yet regarding all Buddha-dharmas, they have neither already realized them nor are they about to realize them. Furthermore...
They do not abide in the stage of those still in training (śaikṣa), yet they possess complete knowledge, vision, and unimpeded penetration.
With immeasurable wisdom and immeasurable mastery, they teach and discipline all sentient beings; this is the seventh sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.

Seventh is mastery over knowledge. Because the Tathāgata manifests the three types of enlightenment (trividha-bodhi), adorned with the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), and the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).

Within this text, it is stated that because the realms of sentient beings are boundless and their capacities for maturation continue in succession, [the Buddha] should manifest realization moment by moment;
yet true realization was already accomplished in the past. Therefore, regarding the three periods of time, the Buddha is neither newly awakened nor unawakened, but dwells [in suchness].

Regarding the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*): it further clarifies that although there is awakening in every moment, because one is free from the characteristics of awakening, this is not an awakening belonging to the three periods of time, nor is it a lack of awakening;

therefore, one does not abide in the stage of training. Furthermore, the phrase "thoroughly penetrating immeasurable wisdoms and so forth" refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*) and other such qualities.
All Buddhas are able to perform the Buddha-work of the ear-faculty through the eye-faculty; they are able to perform the Buddha-work of the nose-faculty through the ear-faculty;
they are able to perform the Buddha-work of the tongue-faculty through the nose-faculty; and they are able to perform the Buddha-work of the body-faculty through the tongue-faculty.
They are able to perform Buddha-works through the sphere of the body as the sphere of mental attention.

They are able to abide within all worlds through the sphere of the mind, dwelling amidst various mundane and supramundane realms; within each and every realm, they are able to perform immeasurable and vast Buddha-works.
This is the eighth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas.
Eighth is mastery over karma. This refers to the vast Buddha-activity of the mutual functioning of the six sense organs, for this is the activity of a Buddha. Yet it does not involve transformation;
a single organ does not change, as it is inherently complete from the beginning.
Within each and every pore of the bodies of all Buddhas, there can be accommodated all sentient beings.
The body of each and every sentient being is equal in extent to unspeakably many Buddha-fields, yet there is no crowding.

Each and every sentient being can, with every step, traverse countless worlds. Continuing in this manner through successive stages for the duration of countless eons, they behold the emergence of all Buddhas.
Manifesting in the world to teach and transform sentient beings, they turn the pure wheel of Dharma and reveal the ineffable teachings of the past, future, and present.

Within the entire realm of empty space, all sentient beings across all realms of existence—whether in their physical forms, their modes of conduct, their comings and goings, or the various articles of enjoyment they receive—are fully provided for, yet within this, there is no obstruction whatsoever. This is...
This is the ninth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas:
mastery over birth. Because they manifest birth in all worlds, in a single moment all Buddhas appear as Buddhas numbering the atoms within all worlds; each and every Buddha...

In every world-realm of the Dharma-dhātu, within the vast and magnificent arrays of exquisite lotus flowers, they attain equal and perfect enlightenment upon lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury; they manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas.
Just as it is in the world-realm of the Vast and Magnificent Arrays of Exquisite Lotuses, so it is throughout all the unspeakably, unspeakably many world-realms of the Dharma-dhātu.
He speaks of various adornments, various realms, various forms, various manifestations, and various kalpas.

Just as he does so within a single thought-moment regarding pure worlds, likewise, throughout all thought-moments across immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, everything is manifested in a single thought-moment;
yet within that single thought-moment, he dwells for immeasurable durations without ever employing even the slightest expedient means.
This is the tenth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas: mastery over vows.
Because they manifest the attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi* in Buddha-lands at whatever time they desire according to their will.

Thus far, only the third and eighth [sovereign dharmas] have been explained by taking their essential meaning; the remainder are all based on the text of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding this tenth sovereignty...
This passage consists of four sections: first, the manifestation of many Buddhas in a single thought-moment within one category of realm;

second, the manifestation of other realms as illustrated by the section beginning with "As in the realm of various wonders"; third, the manifestation of other moments as illustrated by the section beginning with "As in a single moment";

and fourth, the summary of its profound and vast nature in the section beginning with "In a single moment, all are manifested. Regarding "all are manifested": in a single thought-moment, one manifests the Dharma.
Because of the various realms, forms, times, and spiritual powers, that which dwells immeasurably in a single thought-moment is eternally without manifestation;
yet, through even a slight expedient means of the Tathāgata, it is called "sovereign. This concludes the first gate of the aforementioned sovereignty.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of immeasurable, inconceivable, and perfected Buddha-dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: first, every single pure mark of all Buddhas is endowed with a hundred merits;
second, all Buddhas have fully accomplished all Buddha-dharmas; third, all Buddhas have fully accomplished all roots of goodness.
All Buddhas have fully accomplished all merits and virtues. All Buddhas are able to teach and transform all sentient beings. All Buddhas are able to act as sovereigns for sentient beings.
All Buddhas have fully accomplished pure Buddha-fields. All Buddhas have fully accomplished the wisdom of all-knowledge.
All Buddhas have fully accomplished the marks and signs of the form body (*rūpakāya*); those who behold them obtain benefit, and their merit is never in vain.
All Buddhas are endowed with the equal and true Dharma of all Buddhas. All Buddhas, having performed the work of a Buddha...
There is none in whom he does not manifest entry into *nirvāṇa*. This is the tenth.
Regarding the second [point], the inconceivable perfection of the Buddha-dharmas: this clarifies the perfection of mastery.

While it was said that the ten aforementioned masteries might exist in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), this passage reveals the ten kinds of perfection belonging to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that is not...

Because it is sovereign, it is described as "perfect. Regarding the second [category], there are two parts: first, because it realizes and establishes the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth of awakening, it is called "all Buddha-dharmas";
second, because it encompasses both merit and wisdom, it is called "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). Fourth, because it belongs exclusively to the Buddha, it is simply termed "virtues" (*guṇa*).
Ninth, it possesses the teaching of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*); the remaining points may be inferred accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
The third skillful means is mastery over the Dharma (*dharme vaśitā*), for it is characterized by the unimpeded equality of the provisional and the ultimate.
This is the initial general heading.

What are the ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas thoroughly understand that all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet they are able to reveal the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of all Buddhas; this is the first skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Among these, one statement concerns skillfulness in exposition: it means knowing that reality is ineffable and transcends the conceptual proliferation of movement, yet exercising mastery by arising as skillful means to reveal the roots of goodness.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are entirely without anything seen, such that they do not know one another. They are neither bound nor liberated;

there is no receiving, no accumulation, and no accomplishment. Having attained sovereign mastery and reached the ultimate further shore, they nevertheless know the reality of all phenomena as it truly is.
Attaining mastery in a manner that is neither different nor distinct, they are without self and without reception, never violating the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Thus it is.
To attain the stage of great mastery and be able to constantly observe the entire dharma-realm is the second skillful means.

Second is skillfulness in knowledge and vision: this refers to realizing the truth wherein there is neither subject nor object of seeing, yet without being obstructed by phenomena, remaining in the ultimate reality.
Knowing and seeing that there is neither bondage nor liberation, one attains great mastery.
All Buddhas are eternally free from all marks and their minds abide nowhere; yet they are able to know all things without confusion or error.

Although they know that all marks are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are able to skillfully enter into their essential nature as it is, while also manifesting immeasurable physical bodies and the inexhaustible signs of the various adornments of all pure Buddha-lands.
They gather the lamp of wisdom to extinguish the delusions of sentient beings; this is the third skillful means.

Third is the skillfulness of manifestation, which refers to manifesting the characteristic of signlessness within signs, and entering into nature from the absence of nature; it is also able to manifest the harmonizing of beings through both the primary and secondary environments.
All Buddhas abide in the dharma-realm, yet they do not abide in the past, future, or present, remaining within the nature of suchness.

Because it is devoid of the characteristics of the three periods of time— past, future, and present— it is nonetheless able to expound upon the appearance in the world of immeasurable Buddhas of the past,
future, and present, causing those who hear it to universally perceive the realms of all Buddhas.
This is the fourth skillful means.

Fourth is skillfulness regarding the three periods of time. This means realizing the principle that transcends the three limits of time, yet manifesting throughout the three periods of time for the benefit of others.
The physical, verbal, and mental activities of all Buddhas are without fabrication; they neither come nor go, and they likewise have no abiding.
Having transcended all numerical phenomena and reached the further shore of all dharmas, they serve as a treasury of all teachings, possessing immeasurable wisdom.

They thoroughly comprehend various mundane and supramundane dharmas; their wisdom is unimpeded, and they manifest immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers to subdue all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma realm. This is the fifth skillful means.
Fifth is skillfulness regarding the characteristics of nature. This refers to the three karmas being profoundly still, yet encompassing all manifestations.
All Buddhas know that all phenomena are invisible; they are neither one nor different, neither finite nor infinite.
Neither coming nor going, all things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Yet this does not contradict the various phenomena of the world.

The Omniscient One perceives all phenomena within the absence of intrinsic nature; while possessing mastery over phenomena and extensively expounding them, he always dwells peacefully in the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the sixth skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Sixth is skillfulness in maturing sentient beings. This means knowing that all phenomena are neither identical nor different.
All Buddhas, within a single moment, know all times as being endowed with pure roots of goodness; they enter the state of right determination without attachment.
Regarding such periods as days, months, years, eons, and the cycles of formation and destruction, they neither abide in them nor abandon them.
Yet they are able to manifest, whether by day or night, during the first, middle, or last watches; for one day, seven days,
half a month, a month, a year, a hundred years, one kalpa, many kalpas, inconceivable kalpas, unspeakable kalpas, and even until the end of all future kalpas,
constantly turning the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, without interruption, without retreating, and without rest.
This is the seventh skillful means:

skillfulness regarding the seven periods of time. It refers to knowing how to integrate with the proper timing so as to neither remain fixed nor abandon [the teaching], yet without destroying the sequence of years and eons, preaching without ceasing.
All Buddhas eternally abide in the Dharma-realm, having accomplished the immeasurable fearlessnesses of all Buddhas,
as well as incalculable eloquence, unfathomable eloquence, inexhaustible eloquence, uninterrupted eloquence, boundless eloquence, unique eloquence, infinite eloquence, true eloquence,
the eloquence of skillfully revealing all phrases, the eloquence of all dharmas, and eloquence that accords with their respective faculties and natures.

According to their inclinations and understandings, he teaches unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sūtras through various dharma-gates, all of which are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and are utterly consummate. This is the eighth skillful means.

Eighth is skill in eloquence (*pratibhāna-kuśala*). This means that while constantly abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, one is quiescent and has no place of abiding, yet is able to accomplish immeasurable fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Tenth is the eloquence of expounding the Dharma. Regarding this tenth eloquence: first, it is manifold; second, it cannot be fathomed by the mind.
Third, because even if one were to explain a single matter for an entire eon, it would not be exhausted; fourth, because eloquence is unrestrained and without interruption;
fifth, because it forms eloquence upon contact with any category of things; sixth, because it is absent in those of lower stations; seventh, because no one is able to challenge or defeat it;
eighth, because it accords with both phenomena and principle; ninth, because there is not a single sentence or meaning that cannot be revealed; tenth, because there is not a single dharma...
Because it cannot be fully expounded, the excellence of its teaching is clarified through its being "virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 85, states:

first, it is virtuous in the beginning, because joy arises at the time of hearing it; second, it is virtuous in the middle, because there is no hardship during the time of practice, as one remains far removed from the two extremes and proceeds by way of the Middle Way;
third, it is virtuous in the end, meaning that it ultimately brings about the departure from defilement and so forth.
Therefore, all Buddhas abide in the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). They know that all phenomena are fundamentally without names;
they have no past names, no present names, and no names for the past or future. They have no names for sentient beings, no names for non-sentient beings, and no names for lands.
There is no name that is not the name of a land; there is no name of a phenomenon, nor a name of what is not a phenomenon;
there is no name of merit, nor a name of what is not merit; there is no name of a bodhisattva, nor a name of a Buddha; there is no name of number, nor a name of what is not number;
there is no name of arising, nor a name of cessation; there is no name of existence, nor a name of non-existence; there is no single name, nor various names. Why is this? Because all phenomena...
Because its essential nature is ineffable, all phenomena have no direction and no location;
they cannot be described as being gathered together nor as being dispersed, nor can they be described as one nor as many. No sound can reach them and all speech is utterly cut off.

Although various expressions are employed in accordance with worldly convention, they do not rely on any objective referent and involve no creative construction, remaining far removed from all falsehood.
Reflecting thus, one reaches the ultimate further shore; this is the ninth skillful means.
The ninth is skillfulness regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which means that because one speaks while remaining free from speech, there is no conceptual attachment.
All Buddhas know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent. Because they are unarisen, they are not form (*rūpa*).

Because they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they are not feeling (*vedanā*). Because they lack names and numbers, they are not perception (*saṃjñā*). Because they lack volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*), they are not formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because they lack grasping, they are not consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because they lack bases of entry, they are not sense-fields (*āyatana*). Because they are unattainable, they are not elements (*dhātu*). Nevertheless, they do not destroy anything.

The Dharma is by its very nature unarisen, like empty space; thus all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent, devoid of karmic fruit, devoid of cultivation, devoid of accomplishment, and devoid of production.
They are neither numbered nor unnumbered; neither existent nor non-existent;
neither arising nor ceasing; neither defiled nor pure; neither entering nor exiting; neither abiding nor not abiding; neither disciplined nor undisciplined.
He is tamed; he is neither a sentient being nor a non-sentient being, neither a life-span nor a non-life-span, neither dependent on causes and conditions nor independent of causes and conditions.

Yet, he is able to fully understand all sentient beings—those in the category of the rightly determined, the wrongly determined, and the indeterminate—and for their sake, he preaches the sublime Dharma so that they may reach the further shore.
He accomplishes the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, and is able to roar the lion’s roar. He is endowed with...
Abiding in omniscience within the realm of the Buddha is the tenth skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
This refers to the skillful means of quiescence and activity (*śānti-prayoga-kauśalya*), which means realizing quiescence while initiating activity.

Within this, one first realizes primordial quiescence, and subsequently, without abandoning it, is able to initiate activity. This section also has two parts: first, the actual manifestation; second, the subsequent explanation establishing it. That is to say:

The nature of form and so forth does not exist; it is not that they are dispelled to make them non-existent. Therefore, one does not destroy any phenomena. Thus, being empty, there is no karma and so forth;
the subsequent arising of function may be known.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of skillful means accomplished by all Buddhas.
The Great Text has three concluding sections. Within the eighth section on the Gates of Mastery, the third response concerning the ten skillful means is completed.
Below follows the ten great Buddha-activities.
*The Essential Summary of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Forty-six.
Essential Summary of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Volume Forty-Seven Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda,
Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Da Huayan Monastery
Translated by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Kuang at Fayun Monastery, Ming Dynasty.
Part Three of the Thirty-third Chapter: The Inconceivable Buddha-Dharma.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of vast and great buddha-activities, which are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
This deliberation cannot be known by any of the devas or humans in all the worlds;
nor can it be known by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, or present, except through the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority.
The fortieth kind of vast Buddha-activity clarifies the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This directly answers the questions posed by the Buddhas in the preceding two assemblies.
First, regarding the general indication within the section on the eight marks and so forth:

because all these possess great function and subtle mutual containment, they are called "Buddha-activities" (*buddhakṛtya*) as they gather and sustain sentient beings. Within this, first the names are indicated; from "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) onwards, their excellence is revealed.
What are these ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas, throughout all worlds that exhaustively fill space and pervade the Dharma-realm, manifest birth in the Tuṣita Heaven;

there they cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva and perform great Buddha-works, possessing immeasurable physical forms, immeasurable majestic virtue, immeasurable radiance, immeasurable voices, immeasurable modes of speech, and immeasurable [aspects of] the three [karmas].
Obscure. It is the sphere of activity of immeasurable wisdom, encompassing all humans, devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, asuras, and so forth.
His great loving-kindness is unimpeded, and his great compassion is ultimate. He benefits all sentient beings with equanimity:
sometimes causing them to be born in the heavens, sometimes causing them to be born among humans, purifying their faculties, or taming their minds; or at times...
For some, he teaches the distinctions of the three vehicles, while at other times he teaches the perfect single vehicle;
thus universally delivering all beings and causing them to transcend birth and death—this is the first vast buddha-activity.

Within this section, first there is the interrogation, followed by the explanation. In the explanation, the first part clarifies the Buddha-activities of the higher rebirths; herein there are four points: first, a specific clarification of that which is capable of encompassing;
second, the inclusion of the vast multitude of those encompassed; third, the excellence of that which is capable of encompassing, beginning with "great compassion"; [and fourth, the summary].
Fourth, they bring about benefit by being subsumed within the descent [into the womb].

O Son of the Buddha, when all Buddhas descend from Tuṣita Heaven into their mothers’ wombs, they contemplate the dharma of taking birth through ultimate samādhi as being like an illusion, like a transformation, like a shadow, like space, and like a mirage; they take birth according to their wish.

His measure is unimpeded; he enters the dharma of non-contention; he gives rise to non-attached wisdom; he is pure through the departure from desire; and he accomplishes the vast and wondrous treasury of adornments.
Second is the buddha-work of descending the spirit and entering the womb, which has two parts. First, the wisdom and virtue are internally perfected.
Having received his final body, he performs the work of a Buddha while dwelling in a pavilion adorned with great jewels; or he performs the work of a Buddha through supernormal powers;
or he performs the work of a Buddha through right mindfulness; or he performs the work of a Buddha by manifesting supernatural transformations;
or he performs the work of a Buddha by manifesting the sun of wisdom; or he performs the work of a Buddha by manifesting the vast spheres of all Buddhas; or...
They perform buddha-work by manifesting the immeasurable light of all buddhas; or they perform buddha-work by entering countless vast samādhis;
or they perform buddha-work by manifesting their emergence from those various samādhis.

The following clarifies the external manifestations of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). This section has two parts; first, it clarifies how the Buddha performs his buddha-work in a single place at one time.
"O Son of the Buddha, at that time, while the Tathāgata was within his mother’s womb, he performed buddha-work through various manifestations for the sake of benefiting all worlds.
That is to say, he may manifest his initial birth, or manifest as a youth, or manifest as being in the palace."
Sometimes they manifest as renunciants; sometimes they manifest the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment; sometimes they manifest the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma;

and sometimes they manifest entry into parinirvāṇa. In this way, through various skillful means, they perform buddha-work in all directions, all networks, all lineages, all species, and in all worlds. This is [the buddha-work].
The second is the vast Buddha-activity.
Subsequently, when summarizing the times and places, the Buddha-activity is performed. Within this, there are many locations;
following the section on Gopa below up to the ten layers, these five are briefly cited here. Each subsequent one is more extensive than the preceding one. First, "all" refers to the Sahā world and...
1. It can encircle as many worlds as there are atoms in thirteen world-systems, because it dwells without interval throughout the ten directions. 2.
Above those worlds, there are further surrounding worlds and their retinues, which interlace to form a network.
3. It encircles the intermediate oceans and the ten right-turning oceans. 4. It encompasses all the world-systems within the Flower Treasury World-Ocean. 5. All worlds...
Because they have exhausted the entire Dharma-realm.
O Son of the Buddha, all the virtuous karmas of all Buddhas are already pure; all their births and wisdoms are already luminous and immaculate.
Yet, they employ the phenomena of birth to guide the deluded masses, causing them to awaken and fully practice all manner of goodness for the sake of all beings.
Because he is born, he manifests his birth in the royal palace.
