Third, there are two aspects to manifesting the Buddha-activities of the birthplace in the palace. First, it clarifies how he manifests birth despite being unborn; this is the aspect of the birth ceremony.
All Buddhas have already abandoned all forms of sensual desire, palaces, and musical entertainments, remaining free from any attachment or defilement.

They constantly contemplate that all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, and that all instruments of pleasure are entirely unreal. They maintain the pure precepts of the Buddha, bringing them to ultimate perfection.
The subsequent section clarifies defilement within the state of non-defilement; this is the characteristic of the royal palace. Within it, there are four parts:
first, the three trainings are perfected in themselves, for non-defilement is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Observing the ladies of the inner palace, wives, concubines, and attendants, he gives rise to great compassion; observing that all sentient beings are illusory and unreal, he arouses great loving-kindness;
observing that there is not a single thing in the world worth delighting in, he gives rise to great sympathetic joy;
and regarding all phenomena with a mind that has attained mastery, he gives rise to great equanimity.

Second, with a compassionate mind for all beings, he manifests within the Dharma-realm endowed with the merits of a Buddha; his physical marks are perfect and his retinue is pure, yet he remains entirely unattached to anything.
Using voices that accord with the various types of beings, he expounds the teachings for the multitudes, causing them to develop a profound sense of weary detachment from worldly phenomena.
He demonstrates the fruits attained according to his practice, and further employs skillful means to teach and transform beings as appropriate:
causing those who are not yet mature to reach maturity, and causing those who are already mature to attain liberation; thus performing the work of a Buddha so that they do not regress.
Furthermore, with a vast and compassionate mind, he constantly expounds various teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
He also manifests three kinds of mastery, causing them to attain awakening and achieve purity of mind.
Third, the inclusion of those endowed with virtue and benefit:
although he dwells within the inner palace where all may behold him, he performs buddha-activities throughout all worlds;
by means of great wisdom and great diligence, he manifests various buddha-superknowledges that are unimpeded and inexhaustible.
They constantly abide in three types of skillful means: namely, bodily action that is ultimately pure; verbal action that always proceeds in accordance with wisdom;
and mental action that is profoundly deep and free from obstruction. By these skillful means, they benefit sentient beings.
This is the third vast buddha-work. Fourth, the benefit of the four means of attraction is vast and profound.
O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas manifest themselves in various adorned palaces, and having observed them with weary detachment, they abandon them.
He left the household life, desiring to cause sentient beings to understand that all worldly phenomena are mere delusions, impermanent, and subject to decay.
He gave rise to a profound sense of weary detachment, ceased to produce defiled attachments, and forever severed the afflictions of worldly craving and love.

Cultivating pure conduct to benefit sentient beings, at the time of his renunciation, he abandoned secular deportment and dwelt in the Dharma of non-contention, fulfilling his original vows to an immeasurable degree.
Regarding his merit: with the light of great wisdom, he extinguishes the darkness of worldly delusion; he serves as the unsurpassed field of merit for all the world.
He constantly praises the Buddha’s merits for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to plant various roots of goodness before the Buddha and perceive the true meaning with the eye of wisdom.
Furthermore, he praises and explains renunciation for sentient beings, which is pure, faultless, and leads forever to liberation. For a long time...
The high banner of wisdom in the world—this is the fourth vast buddha-activity.

Regarding the four activities of renunciation, there are two parts: first, clarifying the intention for renunciation; second, from "at the time of renunciation" onwards, clarifying the characteristics of renunciation.
This is because of the three karmas and the two benefits.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas are endowed with all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). They have fully known and seen immeasurable dharmas;
they have attained supreme perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, subdued all Māras, and possess preeminent majesty and virtue.

Their bodies pervade all worlds, and the deeds performed through their spiritual powers are boundless and inexhaustible. Regarding all the meanings practiced by those of all-knowledge, they have attained them all.
He is sovereign; having fully perfected all meritorious virtues, his seat of enlightenment is completely adorned and extends throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

Seated upon it, the Buddha turns the sublime wheel of Dharma, proclaiming all the practices and vows of Bodhisattvas, revealing the infinite realms of all Buddhas, and causing all Bodhisattvas to attain realization and enter into their practice.

Through various kinds of pure and wondrous conduct, they are further able to guide all sentient beings, causing them to plant roots of goodness and be born within the ground of equality of the Tathāgatas.
They abide in the boundless wondrous practices of all bodhisattvas, accomplishing all supreme dharmas of merit.
[This applies to] all worlds, all sentient beings, all buddha-fields, and all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands all teachings, all taming of beings throughout the three periods of time, all spiritual transformations,
and the inclinations and desires of the minds of all sentient beings, thereby performing the work of a Buddha. This is the fifth vast buddha-work.

Fifth, the Buddha-activity of attaining enlightenment. This section has two parts. First, it clarifies that true awakening was originally perfect. Second, it shows that under the Bodhi tree, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) has now reached fulfillment.
Following this, it explains how the Dharma was expounded beneath the Bodhi tree for the benefit of these beings, specifically the sudden exposition of the *Avataṃsaka*.
O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma that is non-retrogressive, so as to cause all Bodhisattvas not to fall back.
They turn the wheel of immeasurable dharmas, so that all worlds may fully understand them. They turn the wheel that awakens all beings.

Because he is able to roar the great lion’s roar of fearlessness; because he turns the wheel of the Dharma, the treasury of wisdom regarding all phenomena, opening the gate of the Dharma-treasury to remove the veil of darkness;
because he turns the unimpeded wheel of Dharma, which is equal to space; because he turns the wheel of non-attachment, observing that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent;
and because he turns the wheel of illumination for the world, causing all sentient beings to purify their Dharma-eye.
They turn the wheel of Dharma of omniscience, because it pervades all phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
They turn the single wheel of Dharma common to all Buddhas, because all Buddha-dharmas are not mutually contradictory.

All Buddhas, by means of such immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of wheels of Dharma, act in accordance with the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings.
Thus, they perform inconceivable Buddha-works; this is the sixth vast Buddha-work.

Regarding the Buddha-work of turning the wheel of Dharma, the meaning extends to both the provisional and the ultimate. First, the items are listed, and finally, they are concluded. Within the listing:

first, it concerns only the Bodhisattva vehicle, encompassing the four stages of non-retrogression; second, it encompasses the five vehicles, as all in the world understand them; third, it reveals the ultimate by opening up the provisional.

1. It is real, because it causes one to realize that knowledge and vision are definitively existent. 2. It penetrates the Three Piṭakas, because the Three Piṭakas eliminate delusion and the three obstacles.
3. It is exclusively sudden, because both phenomena and principle are simultaneously transcended. 4. It is the wheel of the Middle Way, because it does not cling to either extreme. 5.
It is the dharma of conventional truth, because it purifies the objects of knowledge. 6. It is exclusively the Buddha-dharma, because its wisdom is all-pervasive. 7. It is exclusively...
Because the perfect Dharma has no diverse flavors, the following section concludes with "thus" and so forth.
That is, the immeasurable vehicles constitute the tenth wheel, as they are expounded according to the capacities of beings; because all ten are complete, they are inconceivable.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas enter all royal capitals and cities to perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings;
that is to say, they enter the capitals and cities of human kings, celestial kings, nāga kings, yakṣa kings,
gandharva kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, and rākṣasa kings.
O King, when kings such as the Piśāca kings and all their capital cities enter the city gates, the earth trembles, and a brilliant light shines everywhere.
The blind regain their sight; the deaf regain their hearing; the insane regain their minds; the naked obtain clothing;
and all who suffer from grief and pain attain peace and happiness. All musical instruments sound spontaneously without being struck, and all manner of ornaments...
Whether they are adorned with ornaments or not, they all emit sublime sounds; no sentient being who hears them fails to rejoice.
The physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas are pure and endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), such that those who behold them never tire of doing so.
They are able to perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings through such acts as looking around, observing, moving about, bending and stretching, walking, or standing still. Or...
Whether sitting or reclining, whether silent or speaking, whether manifesting supernatural powers or preaching the Dharma, or whether issuing instructions— in all such ways,
they perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings. All Buddhas, throughout all the various oceans of the mental inclinations of countless sentient beings in all worlds,
universally exhort them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and constantly observe with diligence, thereby planting [the seeds of enlightenment].
Cultivating all roots of goodness and practicing the bodhisattva path, they extol the Buddha’s physical marks as being most subtle and supreme, difficult for any sentient being to encounter.

If there are those who behold him and give rise to faith, then all immeasurable wholesome dharmas will arise within them, and they will gather the merits of the Buddha until they are universally pure.
Having thus praised the Buddha’s virtues, their bodies manifest everywhere throughout the ten directions.
Throughout the world-systems, they cause all sentient beings to behold and revere them;
by contemplating, observing, serving, and making offerings, they plant various roots of goodness, attain the Buddha’s joy, increase the seeds of Buddhahood, and shall all become Buddhas.

Through such practices, they perform the work of a Buddha: sometimes manifesting a physical body for sentient beings, sometimes emitting sublime sounds, or sometimes acting through subtle means alone.
With faith and joy, they prostrate with their heads, bow deeply with palms joined, extol and praise him,
and inquire after his well-being, thereby performing the work of a Buddha. Through such immeasurable, innumerable, ineffable,
and inconceivable varieties of Buddha-activities as these, all Buddhas, in all worlds, act in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.

With the power of their original vows, the power of great compassion, and the power of all-encompassing wisdom, they skillfully teach and transform all beings, causing them to be fully subdued. This is the seventh vast buddha-work.

The seventh is the Buddha-activity of the seven modes of deportment (*sapta-īryāpatha*). Among these, there are four parts: first, specifically citing the benefit of sentient beings by entering a city;

second, the general manifestation of the benefit of sentient beings through the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas; third, the manifestation of the benefit of sentient beings through speech, as stated in the passage beginning "All Buddhas in the past...";
the word "past" (*xi*) is absent in the Jin edition, which refers to the present benefit; if one speaks of the "past," it refers to the past benefit.

This is an instance of citing the cause to reveal the result; it must refer to the character "Pu" (Universal). From "All Buddhas of the four directions" onwards, the text summarizes the profound and vast [teachings].
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas may perform the work of a Buddha while dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), or they may dwell in tranquility.
They perform Buddha-works while dwelling [in various states]: some perform Buddha-works while dwelling in secluded places; some perform Buddha-works while dwelling in the abodes of Buddhas;
some perform Buddha-works while dwelling in samādhi; and some perform Buddha-works while dwelling alone in groves and forests.
Some perform Buddha-works by remaining hidden and unmanifest; some perform Buddha-works by abiding in profound wisdom;

some perform Buddha-works by abiding in the incomparable realm of all Buddhas; some perform Buddha-works by abiding in various invisible bodily activities, teaching and transforming sentient beings through skillful means according to their mental inclinations, desires, and understandings, without ceasing; or...
They perform the work of a Buddha by seeking omniscience through a celestial body.
Or they perform the work of a Buddha by seeking omniscience through the bodies of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Or they perform the work of a Buddha by seeking omniscience through the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas...
The body of the Bodhisattva seeks all-knowledge and performs the work of a Buddha. At times it performs the work of a Buddha by preaching the Dharma;
at times it performs the work of a Buddha through silence. It performs the work of a Buddha by speaking of a single Buddha, or by speaking of many Buddhas.
It performs the work of a Buddha by explaining all the practices and all the vows of the Bodhisattvas as being a single practice and vow; or it speaks of the single practice of the Bodhisattvas.
With a single vow, they perform buddha-work through immeasurable practices and vows. They may perform buddha-work by teaching that the realm of the Buddha is the very realm of the world;
or they may perform buddha-work by teaching that the realm of the world is the very realm of the Buddha;
or they may perform buddha-work by teaching that the realm of the Buddha is no realm at all. They may abide for a single day, or they may abide for a single night.

They may remain for half a month, or for one month, or for one year, or even for unspeakable eons, performing the work of a Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings. This is the eighth vast deed of a Buddha.

Within the eight types of manifesting Buddha-activities, there are four: First, the practice of abiding with physical and mental tranquility: *araṇya* refers exclusively to mountain forests; "solitude" (*śānta*) extends to cities and towns;
"seclusion" (*vivikta*) refers to places devoid of objects. Second, the practice of descending from a celestial body to respond to those who seek above.
Third, the practice of descending through teaching or remaining silent to transform those below. Fourth, the practice of dwelling for even a single day [in the world].
At that time, one should advance in practice.
O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas are the treasury from which pure roots of goodness arise.

They cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma, to have their faculties subdued, and to forever leave behind the mundane world. They cause all Bodhisattvas to [attain] Bodhi...
Equipped with the tools of wisdom and illumination, they do not attain awakening through another. They may manifest *nirvāṇa* to perform buddha-work;
they may manifest that all things in the world are impermanent to perform buddha-work; they may speak of the Buddha-body to perform buddha-work;
they may speak of having completed all that was to be done to perform buddha-work; or they may speak of the perfection of merit without deficiency to perform buddha-work.

Buddha-activities: sometimes performing Buddha-activities by teaching the eternal severance of the root of all existence; sometimes performing Buddha-activities by causing sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from the world, thereby conforming to the Buddha-mind;
sometimes performing Buddha-activities by teaching that life ultimately ends in exhaustion;

sometimes performing Buddha-activities by teaching that there is not a single thing in the world worth delighting in; or sometimes performing Buddha-activities by proclaiming the exhaustion of what has not yet been exhausted.
They perform Buddha-work by making offerings to all Buddhas throughout the future;
or they perform Buddha-work by proclaiming that all Buddhas turn the pure wheel of Dharma, causing others to hear it and give rise to great joy;

or they perform Buddha-work by expounding the realm of all Buddhas, causing others to resolve their minds for enlightenment and cultivate various practices; or they perform Buddha-work by expounding the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, causing them to...
They resolve their minds to always delight in seeing Buddhas and perform Buddha-work;
or they perform Buddha-work by proclaiming the purification of the faculties and the diligent pursuit of the Buddha-way with a mind free from weariness or retreat;

or they perform Buddha-work by visiting all Buddha-lands to observe various realms and diverse causes and conditions; or they perform Buddha-work by gathering the bodies of all sentient beings and making them all...

The Buddha’s body causes all indolent and heedless sentient beings to abide in the pure prohibitions and precepts of the Tathāgata, thereby performing the work of a Buddha. This is the ninth vast buddha-work.
Regarding the nine points on the Buddha’s activity of manifesting function: first, it reveals the basis for manifesting function, because this [basis] is able to give rise to the treasury of merit;
second, from "or manifesting nirvāṇa" onwards, it correctly elucidates the manifestation of function.
"O Son of the Buddha! When all Buddhas enter nirvana, immeasurable sentient beings wail and weep, giving rise to great sorrow and affliction.
Looking at one another, they say: 'The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great compassion;
he pities and benefits all the world, serving as the savior and refuge for all sentient beings. The appearance of a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.'"
Having encountered this unsurpassed field of merit, which has now forever passed into extinction,
he performs the work of a Buddha by causing all sentient beings to wail with grief and yearn with longing. Furthermore, for the sake of transforming and delivering all devas,
humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, he accordingly...
He desires to shatter his own body into immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable relics,
so that all sentient beings may give rise to pure faith, reverence, respect, and joyful offerings; thereby they may cultivate various merits to full perfection,
and further erect stupas adorned in various ways within the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the yakṣas.
Within the palaces of the gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others,
they shall serve as objects of worship. Their teeth, claws, and hair shall all be used to erect stūpas, causing all who see them to mind the Buddha,
mind the Dharma, and mind the Saṅgha, becoming faithful and joyful, unwavering, and with sincere reverence and respect, wherever they may be.

By practicing generosity, making offerings, and cultivating various meritorious virtues, one may, through this merit, be reborn in the heavens or dwell among humans with noble lineage, honor, and abundant wealth.

All one's retinue shall be entirely pure; one shall not enter the evil realms but will always be born in the good destinies, constantly attaining the vision of the Buddhas and possessing all pure dharmas. Thus, one shall swiftly attain liberation from within the three realms of existence.
Each shall obtain the fruit of their own vehicle according to their respective vows. Having repaid the kindness known by the Tathāgata, they shall forever serve as a refuge for the world.

O Son of the Buddha, although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have entered parinirvāṇa, they still act as inconceivable, pure fields of merit for sentient beings—the supreme field of merit of inexhaustible virtue—causing the roots of goodness in all sentient beings to flourish.
Being fully endowed with perfected merit and virtue constitutes the tenth vast buddha-activity.

The tenth is the buddha-activity of nirvāṇa, which is one specific manifestation among the various functions [of the Buddha]. This section has three parts: first, clarifying the benefit of the compassionate longing for nirvāṇa;

second, "Furthermore, for the sake of transforming and delivering... and below, clarifying the benefit of the dissemination of the relics; and third, from "O Son of the Buddha... and below, the concluding summary.
Increasing fulfillment. If these are correlated with the ten questions: first is the original vow; second is the seed-nature and the land; third is non-obstruction;
fourth is liberation; fifth is manifestation; sixth is voice; seventh is body; eighth is wisdom; ninth is mastery.
O Son of the Buddha, these buddha-activities are immeasurable, vast, and inconceivable. All the gods and humans of the world,
as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present, are unable to know them, except for those who are empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of the Tathāgata.
The Three Bonds. The forty types of vast Buddha-activities within the eighth answer concerning mastery are completed.
O Son of the Buddha! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of sovereign dharmas of non-dual conduct. What are these ten? First, [the sovereignty of... (text continues).
That is to say: all Buddhas are able to skillfully expound the words of prophecy, which are definitive and non-dual;
all Buddhas are able to accord with the mental inclinations of sentient beings to fulfill their intentions, which is definitive and non-dual;
all Buddhas are able to manifest the realization of all dharmas and expound their meaning, which is definitive and non-dual. All...
The Buddhas are all able to fully realize the wisdom of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present as being definitive and non-dual.
All Buddhas know that all moments (*kṣaṇa*) of the three periods of time are a single moment, definitive and non-dual.
All Buddhas know that all Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*) of the three periods of time enter into a single Buddha-field, definitive and non-dual. All Buddhas...
The Buddhas know that the speech of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time is the speech of a single Buddha, which is definitively non-dual.
All Buddhas know that the essential nature of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time and that of all sentient beings they transform are equal, being definitively non-dual.
All Buddhas know that there is no difference between the nature of worldly phenomena and the nature of the Buddhas' teachings.

They are decisively non-dual. All Buddhas know that all the roots of goodness possessed by all Buddhas of the three periods of time are a single root of goodness, decisively non-dual. These are the ten.

The fifth [category], "those who possess mastery over non-dual practice," clarifies mastery over fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) and simultaneously answers the question regarding the fearlessness of Samantaprabha.
Because they are clear and discerning regarding phenomena, and because their certainty is unimpeded, it is called "non-dual. Not fearing the challenges of others is termed "mastery.
Within the ten phrases of this specific section, the first four are understandable; the next three encompass two meanings. First, by...

The principle is fused with the marks. Second, each phenomenon enters into every other phenomenon. Next, two are solely principle. Furthermore, one contains three: first, because they are cultivated as being of the same nature;
second, because they are mutually dedicated; third, because they are mutually principal and attendant. Fifth, there is the single gate of non-dual practice.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of abodes by which they abide in all dharmas. What are these ten? They are:
all Buddhas abide in the awakening to the entire dharma-realm; all Buddhas abide in the speech of great compassion;
all Buddhas abide in their original great vows; all Buddhas abide in never abandoning the taming of sentient beings; all...
All Buddhas abide in the dharma of selflessness. All Buddhas abide in impartial benefit. All Buddhas abide in the dharma of non-forgetfulness.
All Buddhas abide in an unobstructed mind. All Buddhas abide in a mind that is constantly and correctly concentrated.
All Buddhas abide in the equal entry into all dharmas without contradicting the mark of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is called...
Tenth: The sixth section clarifies abiding in all dharmas. This explains mastery over samādhi and simultaneously answers the inquiry regarding the Samādhi of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka*).
Since there is nothing in which the Tathāgata abides that is not samādhi, he dwells pervasively in all things; the meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly.
The sixth dwelling is the single gateway to all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of knowledge of all phenomena without exception.
What are these ten? They are: knowing all past phenomena without exception; knowing all future phenomena without exception... [and so forth].
There is nothing remaining. He knows all present phenomena exhaustively, without remainder. He knows all dharmas of speech exhaustively, without remainder.
He knows all worldly paths exhaustively, without remainder. He knows the minds of all sentient beings exhaustively, without remainder.
He knows all the various levels of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas—superior, middling, and inferior—exhaustively, without remainder.
Furthermore, he knows the perfect wisdom and all roots of goodness of all Buddhas without increase or decrease, leaving nothing remaining.
He knows that all phenomena arise from conditions without exception, leaving nothing remaining. He knows all varieties of world-systems without exception, leaving nothing remaining.
He knows all the diverse manifestations within the entire dharma-realm, like Indra’s net, without exception, leaving nothing remaining.
The remainder constitutes these ten.

Regarding the seventh point, "knowing all phenomena exhaustively without exception," this clarifies the mastery of the ten powers (*daśabala*) and simultaneously answers the question posed by Samantaprabha concerning the ten powers.
Because the wisdom of the ten powers illuminates objects of cognition without omission, it is also evident that they can be known. Seven.
To know all phenomena exhaustively and without remainder through a single gateway.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of powers. What are these ten? They are:

the power of vastness, the supreme power, the immeasurable power, the power of great majesty and virtue, the power difficult to obtain, the non-retrogressive power, the firm and solid power, the unassailable power...
The power that destroys; the inconceivable power of all worlds; the power that no sentient being can move.
These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of great Nārāyaṇa-bannered valiant dharmas.

The eighth is the Power of Vast Strength (*vipulabala*). This clarifies the mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*) and also answers the question regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*) of Samantaprabha.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry and explanation beginning with "What are they..."; and third, the conclusion. Now, for the first part:

"Ten Powers" is a specific designation, while "Great Nārāyaṇa" and so forth are general titles. Therefore, in the following list, only the general titles are used for clarification. This is [the heading].
Thus, the ten powers (*daśabala*) indicated in the heading are each applied throughout the subsequent detailed sections.

Within these ten gates, each one fully possesses the ten powers indicated in the heading, thereby forming one hundred gates. Among these ten, the first is "vast" because it pervades the *dharmadhātu*;
the second is "supreme" because nothing surpasses it; the third is "immeasurable"; the fourth is "to be revered and feared"; the fifth is... [only]...
1. Because it is attained by the Buddha; 2. because its activity is unyielding; 3. because it is to be firm; 4. because its conditions are indestructible;
5. because it transcends words and thought; 6. because it is immovable. These are the ten gates of the lowest-of-the-low grade.
What are these ten? They are as follows: the bodies of all Buddhas are indestructible;
their lives cannot be severed; they cannot be affected by worldly poisons; the calamities of water, fire, and wind in all worlds cannot cause harm to the Buddha’s body;
and all Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras... [and so forth].

The nāgas, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, piśācas, rākṣasas, and others, exerting all their power, rained down great vajras as large as Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, falling simultaneously throughout the trichiliocosm;
yet they could not cause the Buddha’s mind to feel even a moment of alarm or fear, nor could they move even a single hair on his body. He proceeded...

Whether standing, sitting, or reclining, his posture never changes. At whatever place the Buddha dwells, whether in the four directions near or far, he does not allow rain to fall unless it is permitted;
even if it were not restrained and rain were to fall, it would ultimately cause no harm.
If there are sentient beings sustained by the Buddha or dispatched by the Buddha, they cannot even be harmed, let alone the body of the Tathāgata. This is the first [mark] of all Buddhas.
The first is the dharma of great Nārāyaṇa-like strength and valor.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text, there are ten sections. The first is the power of the indestructibility of body and life;
now, following the inverse order, this corresponds to the "immovable power," because not even a single hair can be shaken. Within this section, there are two parts; first—
This clearly explains that it is unshakable and indestructible; that is to say, neither sentient nor insentient conditions can destroy it.

Subsequently, if there are sentient beings, [the text] further provides an illustration to manifest its excellence: "O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas, by means of the Sumeru Kings within all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm, and..."
The Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, the great oceans, forests, mountains, palaces, and dwellings—
[the Tathāgata] places all these within a single pore and sustains them until the end of the future kalpas, yet sentient beings do not perceive or know this,

except for those who are empowered by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, at that time, the Buddhas maintain all those worlds within a single pore until the end of the future.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they do not give rise to even a single thought of weariness.

Son of the Buddha, it is just as space universally sustains all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm without weariness; likewise, all Buddhas sustain all worlds within a single pore. This is the first [of the Buddhas'... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.
The term "this is the first" (*shì wéi zhū fó dì yī*) indicates that this passage likely concludes the description of the first of the ten powers or qualities of a Buddha.*
Second, the dharma of the courageous strength of the two great Nārāyaṇa banners;
second, the power of containment within a single pore, which is inconceivable, yet sentient beings do not perceive it.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas are able, in a single thought-moment, to take steps as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds;
with each step, they pass through lands as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
Thus they practice for as many eons as there are atoms in all worlds.
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a great mountain of diamond equal in measure to all those buddha-fields passed through;
and suppose there were as many such mountains of diamond as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields—yet the Buddhas would be able to [perceive them] with their...
These mountains are placed within a single pore. The number of pores on the Buddha’s body is equal to the number of pores on all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Within each and every pore, he places that many great diamond mountains (*vajraparvata*).
Carrying that many mountains, he travels through the ten directions, entering all worlds throughout the entirety of empty space, from the beginningless past to the endless future.
Throughout all kalpas, they never cease; the Buddha-body is neither impaired nor weary, and the mind is always in meditative concentration without distraction.
This is the Buddhas' third great Nārāyaṇa-banner of heroic vigor.
The power of a single hair holding a great mountain would not fail; for although it holds a massive body with many mountains, the mind suffers no exhaustion or injury.
In this text, "swiftly traversing vast strides" refers to traveling through lands for many eons as if they were the size of a single mountain.
Since even a single mountain is already immeasurable, how much more so are many mountains within a single pore? How much more so when many hairs sustain them throughout the exhaustion of all eons?
It dwells in a state that is truly difficult to conceive.
Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas, having finished eating in a single sitting, remain in the full lotus posture for unspeakable eons throughout the past and future limits of time.
They enter the inconceivable bliss experienced by Buddhas; their bodies abide in tranquility, unmoving, and likewise—

They abandon the work of transforming sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha! Suppose there were someone who, throughout every single world pervading all of space, measured them one by one with the tip of a hair;

and suppose that within the space of a single hair-tip, a Buddha were able to sit in the full lotus posture until the end of the future eons, and as it is for the space of one hair-tip, so it is for the space of every hair-tip. O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose all sentient beings in every world throughout the ten directions were such that the body of each individual being was as vast as the measure of unspeakably many Buddha-fields of atoms, and their weight were likewise so;
yet the Buddhas could place all those beings upon the tip of a single finger for as many kalpas as exist until the end of time. All...

The tips of their fingers are likewise all thus. Holding all such sentient beings, they enter every single world throughout the entirety of space, exhausting the whole dharma-realm without exception; yet the bodies and minds of the Buddhas never experience weariness or fatigue.
This is the fourth great Nārāyaṇa-banner of valorous strength of all Buddhas.
The fourth is the power of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is steadfastness because one abides securely through the power of concentration.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas are able to manifest within a single body as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
from each head, they manifest as many [transformations] as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
From each tongue, there emanate sounds of distinct varieties as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

there is not a single sentient being in the dharma-realm who does not hear them. Each sound expounds collections of sutras as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and each collection of sutras expounds [unspeakably unspeakable...]

One may speak of as many dharmas as there are atoms in a buddha-field. Each dharma possesses as many words, phrases, and meanings as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
One might continue to expound them in this manner for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
Having exhausted those eons, one would further continue to expound them for as many [eons] as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.

Even if one were to count eons as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, continuing in this sequence until the number of atoms in all worlds and the number of mental thoughts of all sentient beings were exhausted—
even throughout the entirety of future eons— the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the emanation bodies of the Tathāgata would never come to an end.
This refers to the turning of the wheel of Dharma through the exposition of wisdom, which severs all doubts and delusions.

The wheel of Dharma; the wheel of Dharma that illuminates all phenomena; the wheel of Dharma of the treasury of unimpeded hearing; the wheel of Dharma that brings joy and subdues immeasurable sentient beings;
the wheel of Dharma that reveals and elucidates all bodhisattva practices; the wheel of Dharma that rises high as the perfect sun of great wisdom;
the wheel of Dharma that universally kindles the bright lamp of wisdom to illuminate the world; the seed of fearless eloquence.

They plant the seeds for the adornment of the wheel of Dharma. Just as a single Buddha-body, through its supernormal powers, turns such various wheels of Dharma that no worldly phenomena can serve as a metaphor, so too, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space—in every location the size of a single hair-tip—there exist worlds numbering as many as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. In each and every world...
Within each realm, in every moment of thought, he manifests emanation bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
Each and every emanation body is likewise so. The sounds, words, phrases, and meanings they proclaim fill every dharma-realm, such that all sentient beings therein attain understanding;
yet the Buddha’s speech remains without change, without interruption, and without end.
Exhausted. This constitutes the fifth great Nārāyaṇa-banner of heroic vigor among the Buddhas:
the constant and universal manifestation of the power of the Dharma. This is non-retrogression; because its vocal expression is unchanging and never ceases or is exhausted.

Within this passage there are two parts: first, the manifestation through a single body; second, from "As with one Buddha... onwards, the manifestation through multiple bodies. Within the former, there are three sections.
First, it reveals the abundance of what is taught; next, from "thus expounding" onwards, it clarifies the permanence of what is taught;
finally, from "that which is called" onwards, it demonstrates the essence of what is taught. This manifold body may be known as the teaching that is eternal and constant, without beginning or end.
Those who are born blind cannot see it even when facing it; according to their respective perceptions, they speak of it as having a beginning and an end.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas have their chests adorned with the marks of virtue, which are indestructible like a vajra.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, they sit in the full lotus posture, while the hosts of Māra’s army are infinite in number and of various kinds.
Their strange forms were most terrifying; among sentient beings, there was none who did not become struck with alarm and dread.
Some fell into madness, while others even met their death. Thus the hosts of Māra filled the void of space. Yet when the Tathāgata beheld them, his mind felt no fear;
his countenance remained unchanged, not a single hair stood on end. He was unmoved and undisturbed, free from discrimination, and remained in silent stillness, transcending all joy and anger.
Pure, abiding in the dwelling of the Buddhas, endowed with the power of compassion, their faculties are subdued and their minds are fearless;
they cannot be shaken by any hosts of Māras, yet they are able to crush all Māra armies, causing them all to turn their hearts, prostrate themselves, and take refuge.
Thereafter, they further employ the three wheels of teaching to cause them all to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The resolve for the three types of awakening never regresses; this is the sixth great Nārāyaṇa-bannered, heroic dharma of all Buddhas.
The power of Māra that obstructs the six marks of virtue is difficult to overcome; yet all ten are difficult to attain. The world abounds in the delusions of Māra.
To establish a one-sided and difficult-to-attain reputation is not the way.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas possess unimpeded voices; these voices pervade the worlds of the ten directions, and sentient beings who hear them are naturally subdued.
All such sounds produced by those Tathāgatas are like Mount Sumeru and all else...
No mountains can obstruct it; no palaces of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, or any other such abodes can obstruct it.
Even the loud sounds of all worlds cannot obstruct it. It reaches all beings according to their capacity for transformation.
There is no one among those born who does not hear it; they all attain complete understanding of its words, phrases, and meanings.
This is the seventh great Nārāyaṇa-banner of valiant strength of all Buddhas.
The seventh is the power of the all-pervading perfect sounds (*saptasvarāṅga*), which is majesty and virtue, for all who hear it are tamed.

O Son of the Buddha, the minds of all Buddhas are without obstruction; throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably unspeakable eons, they have been perpetually and perfectly pure.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present are of one and the same essential nature.

Without turbidity or obscuration, without self or what belongs to self, neither internal nor external, one realizes that objects are empty and quiescent, and thus does not give rise to deluded thoughts.
Having nothing to rely upon and nothing to do, one does not dwell in any signs and forever severs conceptual discrimination. One's original nature is pure;

one abandons all攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging/conditioning) and recollections. Regarding all phenomena, one is always free from conflict and contention, abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and detached.

Desiring purity, they enter the true Dharma-realm and expound it inexhaustibly. Free from all delusive thoughts of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), they sever all verbal expressions regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Having fully and unimpededly mastered the ineffable and boundless realm, their wisdom and skillful means achieve the ten powers (*daśabala*). Adorned with all merits, they are utterly pure as they expound [the Dharma].
They expound various and immeasurable dharmas, all of which are not in contradiction with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding all phenomena within the dharma-realm across the three periods of time, they are entirely equal and without distinction, attaining ultimate mastery. They enter the most supreme treasury of all dharmas;
through right mindfulness, they are undeluded regarding all dharma-gates. They dwell peacefully in all Buddha-fields of the ten directions without wavering or shifting, practicing...
The knowledge of non-interruption knows all phenomena exhaustively without remainder; it has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), and the mind is well-liberated and wisdom is well-liberated.

Abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one penetrates it without obstruction; the mind is always in right concentration, and regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time as well as the mental activities of all sentient beings, one comprehends them in a single thought-moment without any hindrance. This is the [first] of the Buddhas’...
The eight dharmas of the heroic vigor of the Eight Great Nārāyaṇa Banners;
the eight powers of non-obstruction of the mind, which are the powers of immeasurability because they are free from measure and non-measure. First, there is no obstruction of dust-like delusions;
subsequently, there is non-obstruction in the arising of function within the ineffable. This is because the mind is well-liberated.
There are three characteristics: first, the thorough and universal comprehension of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);

second, the realization and attainment of the abandonment of the various afflictions associated with them; and third, having abandoned the afflictions, dwelling free from craving in all circumstances.
O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas share one and the same Dharma-body:

a body of infinite realms, a body of boundless merit and virtue, a body inexhaustible throughout the world, a body unstained by the three realms, a body manifested according to thought, a body that is neither real nor unreal and is equally pure, a body that comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, unconditioned and indestructible—the self-nature of phenomena, which is a single mark yet markless.
The body that is without location or direction, pervading all bodies; the body of sovereign spiritual transformations with boundless forms and marks;
the body that manifests in various ways, universally entering all things; the body of skillful means of the sublime Dharma; the body of the treasury of wisdom that shines everywhere;

the body that demonstrates the equality of all phenomena; the body that is omnipresent throughout the dharma-realm; and the eternally pure body that is unmoving, non-conceptual, and neither existent nor non-existent.

Neither by means nor without means, neither ceasing nor not ceasing, he manifests his body in accordance with the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings as they are to be transformed.
This body is born from the jewels of all merits; it is the Tathatā-body endowed with all Buddha-dharmas;
it is a body that is inherently quiescent and unobstructed; it has accomplished all that is unhindered.
The Dharma-body; the body that dwells pervasively throughout the entire pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); the body that manifests forms universally throughout all worlds;

the body that is without objective support, without regression, eternally liberated, endowed with all-knowledge, and fully penetrating all things—this is the ninth great Nārāyaṇa-banner of heroic vigor of all Buddhas.
The ninth, the subtle and secret power of the Dharma-body, is the most supreme. This encompasses the preceding eight, for there is nothing further to be added by the latter one.

Although the text enumerates twenty-five bodies, these are either the true nature of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the response-body of the true nature, the characteristics of the essence, or the wisdom of the principle;
they are the ten bodies in perfect fusion, a single body of the same Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and thus cannot be [mechanically] correlated [with the preceding categories].
Regarding the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, it is therefore called the "supreme, subtle, and secret.
O Son of the Buddha! All Buddhas equally awaken to all the dharmas of all Tathāgatas and equally cultivate all the practices of all Bodhisattvas.
Whether in their vows or their wisdom, they are pure and equal, like a great ocean that has attained complete fulfillment through the power of their practice.
The Honored One has never retreated or been discouraged; he dwells in the immeasurable realms of all samādhis, demonstrating all paths, exhorting toward good and admonishing against evil.
His power of wisdom is supreme as he expounds the Dharma with fearlessness; whatever is asked, he is able to answer skillfully. His wisdom and his preaching of the Dharma are impartial and pure;
his actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely without confusion. He dwells where the Buddhas dwell—among all the Buddhas.
The lineage performs the Buddha-work by means of the Buddha’s wisdom. Abiding in omniscience, it expounds immeasurable dharmas that have no root and no limit.
Its supernormal powers and wisdom are inconceivable; no one in any world can fully comprehend them.
This wisdom penetrates deeply to perceive all phenomena—subtle, wondrous, vast, immeasurable, and boundless throughout the three periods of time.
They have thoroughly mastered all Dharma-gates and are able to enlighten all worlds.
With supramundane wisdom, they perform unspeakably diverse Buddha-activities within all worldly realms. They have attained non-retrogressive wisdom and entered the ranks of the Buddhas.

Although they have already realized the ineffable Dharma that transcends words and letters, they are nonetheless able to manifest various forms of speech and expression through their universal [compassion].
The wise and virtuous gather all wholesome practices and achieve the sublime wisdom that accords with a single thought-moment, whereby they are able to fully awaken to and understand all phenomena.
Just as they previously resolved, they bestow the Dharma upon all sentient beings according to their respective vehicles.
Thus, regarding all phenomena, all worlds, all sentient beings, and all three periods of time within the realm of reality (dharmadhātu), it is as follows:
The extent of these realms is boundless; with unimpeded wisdom, [the Buddhas] are able to know and see them all.
O Son of the Buddha, in a single moment of thought, all Buddhas appear in the world according to those who are to be transformed, dwelling in pure lands and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
Manifesting supernatural powers, they awaken the minds and consciousnesses of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time without missing the proper moment.
O Son of the Buddha! Sentient beings are boundless; worlds are boundless; the dharma-realm is boundless; the three periods of time are boundless;
and the most supreme Buddhas are likewise boundless. Within them all, they manifest the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, employing the skillful means of buddha-wisdom.
Their awakening is without rest. O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, manifest most wondrous bodies and abide in boundless realms.
With great compassion and skillful means, their minds are without obstruction; at all times, they constantly expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This is the tenth great Nārāyaṇa-bannered, heroic, and courageous dharma of all Buddhas.
The power of knowledge consisting of the ten perfections of conduct is itself the power of vast strength.

Because its causal conduct is like the ocean and its resultant wisdom is universally pervasive throughout the five boundless realms, its great function is limitless. There are four sections in the text: first, the perfection and purity of the ten thousand practices;

second, abiding where the Buddhas abide, wherein the application of wisdom is perfectly pervasive; third, although already having realized [the truth], there is mastery over movement and stillness; fourth, [the remaining section].
O Son of the Buddha, the lower application of all Buddhas is boundless, and their ten powers above do not transcend the three karmas;
this may be inferred through reflection.
O Son of the Buddha, this great Nārāyaṇa-bannered, heroic Dharma of all Buddhas is immeasurable and limitless.

It is inconceivable; all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, as well as those of the two vehicles, are unable to comprehend it, except for those empowered by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
The third major section: A summary of the eight extensive powers in ten gates.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of definitive laws. What are these ten? They are:
all Buddhas definitely descend from Tuṣita upon the exhaustion of their lifespan; all Buddhas definitely manifest birth and entry into the womb."
In the tenth month, all Buddhas invariably grow weary of worldly pleasures and seek to renounce the household life.
All Buddhas invariably sit beneath the Bodhi tree and attain equal and perfect enlightenment, awakening to all Buddha-dharmas.
All Buddhas invariably awaken to all phenomena in a single thought-moment. They manifest spiritual powers throughout all worlds. All Buddhas are certainly able to...

They shall turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma at the appropriate time. All Buddhas will certainly be able to accord with the roots of goodness planted by others, preaching the Dharma and bestowing predictions of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) at the appropriate time. All Buddhas will certainly be able to perform the Buddha-work at the appropriate time.
All Buddhas will certainly be able to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas who have attained accomplishment. All Buddhas will certainly be able to...
To universally answer all the questions of sentient beings in a single thought-moment—this is the tenth.
The ninth major section, "The Decisive Dharma," has three gates. Regarding the first gate, answering unimpeded questions:
it clarifies that what is performed is decisive and capable of being unimpeded. This is termed "decisive" because it refers to one category of world-systems; as for other categories of worlds...
It is not necessarily so. Furthermore, it is said to be "definite" because the Buddhas are certainly able to act as such.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of swift dharmas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
if any sentient beings behold all the Buddhas, they will swiftly attain liberation from all evil realms. If any sentient beings behold all the Buddhas...
Those who see [it] will swiftly attain the perfection of supreme merit. If any among all Buddhas should see it, they will swiftly achieve vast roots of goodness.
If any among all Buddhas should see it, they will swiftly attain rebirth in the pure and wondrous heavens.
If any among all Buddhas should see it, they will swiftly be able to sever all doubts. All...

If those who have already resolved upon bodhicitta are able to behold the Buddhas, they will swiftly achieve vast faith and understanding, never again falling back, and will be able to teach and transform sentient beings according to their needs. If they have not yet resolved upon it, they will be able to swiftly generate the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, if all Buddhas [behold those] who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*)...
Those who behold it will swiftly enter the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Any Buddha whom they behold will swiftly purify all mundane and supramundane faculties. Any Buddha whom they behold will swiftly eliminate all obstacles.
Any Buddha whom they behold will swiftly attain fearless eloquence (*vaiśāradya-pratibhāna*). This is...

There are ten [points]. Regarding the second, the quality of swiftness (*āśu-dharma*): this clarifies that it causes others to be without obstruction, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). One obtains benefit immediately upon seeing it, yet those of meager merit do not behold it.
There are ten phrases in five pairs: first, the perfect and supreme virtues that distance one from the evil destinies; second, the accomplishment of the causes for goodness.
One experiences the fruit of joy. Third, one eliminates doubt and fulfills the great mind. Fourth, from the initial entry into the stage until its final purification.
Fifth, one purifies the two obstacles and possesses the four analytical knowledges.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure dharmas that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should constantly keep in mind. What are these ten?
All Bodhisattvas should constantly recollect all the past causes and conditions of all Buddhas.
All Bodhisattvas should constantly recollect all the pure and supreme practices of all Buddhas. All Bodhisattvas should constantly recollect all Buddhas’ fulfillment of the perfections.
All Bodhisattvas should constantly recollect all Buddhas’ accomplishment of their great vows.
Bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind that all Buddhas have accumulated roots of goodness;
bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind that all Buddhas have already perfected the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind that all Buddhas have manifested perfect enlightenment; [and] bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas.
All bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind the immeasurable [qualities] of all buddhas. All bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind the immeasurable supernatural powers of all buddhas.
All bodhisattvas should constantly keep in mind the ten powers and fearlessnesses of all buddhas. These are the ten.

Third, regarding those who should be mindful of purity: [the text] cites the Buddha’s non-dual unimpededness and exhorts beings to maintain mindfulness of it. Ninth, the answer concerning the three gates of non-obstruction:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of abiding in omniscience. What are these ten? Namely, the first..."
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully know all the karma accumulated by all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, as well as the karmic fruits and retributions thereof.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully know what is appropriate for all sentient beings. By means of...
Through the three wheels of teaching and subduing, all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully know all the mental characteristics of every sentient being throughout the entire dharma-realm.
In all places, they universally manifest the arising of a Buddha to allow them to see him, skillfully gathering and sustaining them.
Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas universally accord with the minds of all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm.
To delight, desire, and liberate them, they manifest and preach the Dharma to bring them under discipline.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, fully know the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm; thus they manifest spiritual powers.
Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas pervade all places and appear for the sake of all sentient beings who are ready to be transformed.

It is taught that the Buddha-body cannot be grasped or clung to. In a single thought-moment, all Buddhas universally reach every place throughout the entire dharma-realm and all sentient beings within their respective paths.
In a single thought-moment, all Buddhas respond to those among sentient beings who have thoughts of them, appearing everywhere without exception to meet their needs. All Buddhas, in a single...
Within their mindfulness, they fully know the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings and manifest immeasurable forms and appearances for them;
this is the tenth. O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-samādhis.
What are these ten? They are as follows: All Buddhas are constantly in right concentration, and within a single thought-moment, they pervade all things.
In all places, they extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. All Buddhas constantly abide in right concentration;
within a single thought-moment, they pervade all places and universally expound the limit of non-self for all sentient beings. All Buddhas constantly dwell in right concentration;
within a single thought-moment, they pervade all places and universally enter the three periods of time. All Buddhas constantly abide in right...
In a single thought-moment, they universally enter all places throughout the vast Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
All Buddhas, constantly abiding in right concentration, universally manifest immeasurable and diverse Buddha-bodies in all places within a single thought-moment.
All Buddhas, constantly abiding in right concentration, in a single thought-moment, pervade all places according to [the capacities of] all sentient beings...

Giving rise to various mental understandings that manifest in body, speech, and mind, all Buddhas constantly abide in right concentration, and within a single thought-moment, they universally expound all dharmas throughout all places—the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) free from desire.
All Buddhas constantly dwell in right concentration, and within a single thought-moment, they universally proclaim the self-nature of all dependent origination throughout all places. All Buddhas...

The Buddha constantly abides in right concentration; within a single thought-moment, he manifests throughout all places the immeasurable, vast adornments of both mundane and supramundane realms, enabling all sentient beings to always behold the Buddha. All Buddhas constantly abide in right concentration;
within a single thought-moment, they pervade all places, causing all sentient beings to fully penetrate and realize the nature of all Buddhas.
The Dharma is immeasurable, and through liberation, they have reached the ultimate, unsurpassed shore. These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of unimpeded liberation. What are these ten?
They are as follows: all Buddhas are able to manifest within a single atom unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas appearing in the world.
All Buddhas are able, within a single atom, to manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas turning the pure wheel of Dharma.
All Buddhas are able, within a single atom, to manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings receiving transformation and being tamed.
All Buddhas are able, within a single atom, to manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands.
Earth. All Buddhas can, within a single atom, manifest the bestowal of predictions upon unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Bodhisattvas.
All Buddhas can, within a single atom, manifest all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
All Buddhas can, within a single atom, manifest all world-systems of the past, future, and present. All Buddhas can, within a single atom...
All Buddhas can manifest all supernatural powers of the past, future, and present; all Buddhas can manifest all sentient beings of the past, future, and present within a single atom;
all Buddhas can manifest all Buddha-activities of the past, future, and present within a single atom.

These are the ten. Regarding the tenth, "Abiding in All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñatā-vihāra*), the answer to the question concerning liberation is provided through the first three gates. The first gate clarifies liberation from the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because wisdom is established in both phenomena and principle, it is called an "abiding. Due to being free from obstacles, one is able to know all things. Second, [the absence of...]

Regarding the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Inconceivability": this clarifies liberation from the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because one is free from these hindrances, its function is vast and immeasurable, and its essence is profound and inconceivable;
therefore, among the ten types [of samādhis], each first clarifies the state of being in concentration, followed by the single-moment universal application.
Regarding the "Three Unhindered Liberations": this clarifies liberation through karmic activity. As the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Treatise on Wisdom) states: "The Bodhisattva..."
There is the inconceivable liberation. The Buddhas possess unimpeded liberation; because they are liberated from all obstructions, their actions are without hindrance.
Thus, within each single atom, they instantaneously perform subtle functions. If one were to answer the ten questions individually:
1. Manifestation; 2. Voice; 3. Original Vow—because the vow is to transform all beings to their ultimate end; 4. Land; 5.

Wisdom—it is able to bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas; 6. Buddha-body; 7. Seed-nature—referred to as the "seed of the world," which is the seed for entering the world to transform sentient beings;
it should not be the seed within the ocean of worlds, as the section on lands has already concluded previously.

Therefore, the eighth is sovereignty; the ninth is non-obstruction, because there is no obstruction in benefiting sentient beings; the tenth is liberation, because there is nothing that is not accomplished.
Since each individual gate answers all ten questions, it encompasses and includes them all; for this reason, it is called "inconceivable.

However, the text lacks a formal conclusion and seems as though it has not yet reached its end. Perhaps this is to manifest that the Buddha’s virtues are inexhaustible; thus, the marks [of the Buddha]...

Chapter Thirty-Four: The Ocean of Marks on the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the intent of this chapter’s opening: the preceding chapter explained the dharmas of fruition in general; this chapter specifically reveals the excellence of its marks.

It answers, both proximately and distantly, the questions concerning the bodies raised in the previous chapter, as well as the six sense organs—such as the eyes—of Universal Radiance. It demonstrates that it is not merely the eyes and other organs that pervade the dharma-realm.

Furthermore, each possesses many marks (*lakṣaṇa*), because their function is inconceivable. Second, regarding the explanation of the names: the "ten bodies of the Tathāgata" indicate the person (*pudgala*) to manifest his virtues;

the term "ocean of marks" indicates the marks based on that person. Both are explained as previously stated. Because the wondrous forms resulting from meritorious retribution are brilliant and renowned, they are called "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*);
because these marks and virtues are profound and vast, they are termed an "ocean. Thus, the text says: "There are ten lotus flowers."

It contains characteristics as numerous as the atoms of the universe; the substance of these characteristics is vast. Each individual function pervades all characteristics and functions, which are likewise vast.

Each is inconceivable, merging with one another; their substance and function are profound. Such characteristics belong exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). They are designated by means of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
Thus, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* distinguishes three categories of characteristics: first, the most concise among the concise.
It is taught that there are thirty-two marks; secondly, they are briefly described as eighty-four thousand marks;

and thirdly, they are extensively described as being immeasurable marks, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the sake of Samantabhadra, Bhadramukha, and others—the *Avataṃsaka* being an alternative name for this very sūtra.
Among these three, the first is common to the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle, as it shows [the Buddha] to be like a human, sitting upright and undisturbed. The next... [is] only...
The Mahāyāna: because Bodhisattvas cultivate eighty-four thousand pāramitās; subsequently, there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), for the One Vehicle cultivates inexhaustible practices.
Furthermore, there is first transformation, then retribution, and finally that which pertains to the ten bodies. This is the ocean-like aspect of the ten bodies.

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound). Furthermore, the first [level] is seen equally by both ordinary beings and sages; the second is seen only by those on the stages (*bhūmi*); and the last is seen only by those of the Perfect Vehicle (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) capacity.
Nevertheless, it pervades all five positions. If one speaks of its essence: the first consists of form and color; the second is precisely meditative concentration and wisdom;

and the last consists of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one speaks of its cause: the last encompasses both the pure and the mixed, as explained in the first assembly. Therefore, each and every mark is a fruit.

All of these pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Regarding the three essential points: taking the manifestation of the inexhaustible ocean of marks as the essence (*śāstra*), and causing the cultivation of inexhaustible practices to reach manifest perfection as the goal (*prayojana*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, I shall now [explain] for you..."
This discourse expounds upon the ocean of marks possessed by the Tathāgata.
The main text is correctly explained in three sections: first, the exhortation to listen and the permission to speak; second, the formal presentation of the characteristics;

third, the summary of the brief and the revelation of the extensive. Now, for the first: the reason why Samantabhadra speaks is that the ocean of marks is universally pervasive, so as to cause [beings] to practice.

Universal Practice. Because he has attained universal marks, Samantabhadra is originally the presiding host of this assembly; as his previous exposition has already reached its conclusion, he now speaks of these [marks].
Second, regarding the top of the Tathāgata’s head, the actual description of their characteristics is presented briefly, enumerating ninety-seven marks.

The text generally consists of five parts: first, the locus; second, the enumeration of names; third, the adornment of the essence; fourth, the functional activity; and fifth, the summary of the number. Alternatively...

Some [details] are omitted and not fully provided; these should be understood from the relevant passages. Alternatively, [certain functions] may be added as beneficial effects, which are subsumed within the category of "karmic activity" (*karman*).

However, names are established based on essence (*svabhāva*), function (*vṛtti*), or both. They are all established by means of essence and function—either following the essence alone, the function alone, or both together.

As for cases where the name and the meaning of the essence or function do not correspond, this is merely a case of textual abbreviation where the full meaning is implicitly contained. A detailed discussion of each point follows.
If each mark were treated according to its individual location, there would be ninety-seven sections, as indicated by the sūtra itself.

Now, following a thematic classification, they are organized into nineteen sections, beginning from the crown of the head and ending at the feet; this constitutes the sequential contemplation of the ocean of marks.
O Son of the Buddha, upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head there are thirty-two marks of a Great Man adorned with jewels.

First: regarding those on the crown, there are three parts. First is the general indication by way of location; next, from "In their midst" onwards, is the detailed enumeration of their names and characteristics.
The section beginning with "Afterward, the sons of the Buddha" concludes [the discussion] by summarizing them as adornments. First, regarding the "Adornments of Jewels":

this generally reveals the adornment of the essence through material jewels, as it states that they are all adorned with *maṇi* gems and so forth; it also reveals the jewel of wisdom, as it is perfectly pure and adorned.
Within each individual mark, there are both the adornments of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*naya*). They are explained according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the "marks of a great man" (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), because they are the marks of a great man, the thirty-two marks listed individually each consist of four aspects;
this is because the single category of "basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) has already been indicated in general. Although there are only thirty-two here, in reality, they should be more numerous. Why? Because...
This reveals that within the one, all are perfectly interfused; thus, within a single crown, the thirty-two locations of the provisional teachings are already complete.

If this is so, why is it not the same for the others? It is because the Crown is manifest as the most supreme. If we consider the person, it is because they possess excellence that makes them superior.
Therefore, they are humbled by humans and surpassed by the various devas; thus, it is said elsewhere that they prefer subtlety.
Within them is a mark of a great man called "Illuminating All Directions," which universally emits an immeasurable net of great radiance.
It is adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels. Jeweled hair covers it everywhere, soft, supple, and dense;
each strand emits the light of maṇi jewels, filling all boundless worlds and manifesting the physical forms and marks of the Buddha in their full perfection.
This constitutes the first [category].
Regarding the four [subdivisions] within the first characteristic, these are distinct names. Their names are established based on their functions:

(1) "Adorned with a body composed of all exquisite jewels," (2) "The individual functions of each jewel," and (4) "This constitutes one" serves as the conclusion of the count. Others should be understood by analogy.

Next is a mark of a great man called Cloud of Buddha-Eye Radiance. Adorned with various kinds of mani-jewel kings, it emits golden light like the radiance emitted from the ūrṇā-kośa between the eyebrows. That light universally illumines all worlds.
These are the two.
Within these two, the lower part is adorned with mani-jewels; this explains the meaning of "light.
The downward activity of that light explains the meaning of the "Buddha-eye," for there is nothing the Buddha-eye does not illuminate.

Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud Filling the Dharma Realm. It is adorned with exquisite jewel wheels and emits the lamp-light of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom, universally illuminating all oceans of worlds throughout the dharma realms of the ten directions.
Within it, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are universally manifested. This is the third. Next is a mark of greatness called...
They manifest clouds of universal illumination, adorned with various kinds of true gold and maṇi jewels;
all these exquisite treasures radiate light that shines upon inconceivable Buddha-lands, wherein all Buddhas appear. This is the fourth.
Next is a mark of a great man called Cloud Emitting Jewel Radiance. It is adorned with the pure majesty of the king of maṇi jewels, with lapis lazuli forming its filaments.

Its light illuminates all dharma realms throughout the ten directions, universally manifesting various spiritual transformations therein and praising the wisdom and merit practiced by the Tathāgata in the past. This is the fifth. Next is...
The mark of a great person is called the Cloud of Great Sovereignty Manifesting the Tathāgata Pervading the Dharma Realm.
It has a crown made of the jewel-flame *maṇi* of the bodhisattvas' spiritual transformations; it possesses the powers of a Tathāgata that awaken all beings;
it has a wreath of jewel-flame light-circles whose radiance universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions, within which all Tathāgatas are manifested sitting.
In the site of enlightenment, clouds of omniscience fill the void of the immeasurable Dharma-realm; this is the sixth.
Next is a mark of greatness called the Tathāgata’s Universal Lamp Cloud, which can shake the lands of the Dharma-realm and is adorned by a great sovereign ocean of jewels.
It emits pure light that fills the Dharma-realm, within which it universally manifests throughout the ten directions.
The ocean of merits of all bodhisattvas; and the ocean of wisdom-bannered clouds of the Buddhas of the past, present, and future—this is the seventh.
Next is a mark of a great man named "Universally Illuminating Vast Clouds of All Buddhas," adorned with Indra-ratnas, wish-fulfilling king jewels, and maṇi king jewels.
It constantly emits the radiant light of the bodhisattva-flame lamp, universally illuminating the ten directions.
In every world-system, there appear therein oceans of the various physical marks of all Buddhas, oceans of great sounds, and oceans of the power of purification; these constitute the eighth.
Within the eighth enclosure, there is a maṇi named "Intention" (Manas), which is therefore not the same as the "Wish-fulfilling" (Cintāmaṇi).

Next is a mark of a great man named "Cloud of Perfect Radiance. It is adorned with various jewel-flowers made of exquisite lapis lazuli maṇi-kings, and all manner of precious gems spread a great network of flames that fills all the ten directions.

In all worlds, all sentient beings see the Tathāgata sitting before them, praising the merits of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and causing them to enter the pure realm of the Tathāgata; this is the ninth.
Next is a mark of greatness called "Cloud of Radiant Light that Universally Illumines the Treasury of All Bodhisattva Practices," which consists of exquisite flowers made of various jewels.
Adorned with splendor, their precious light universally illuminates immeasurable worlds; their precious flames universally cover all lands;
they penetrate the dharma-realm of the ten directions without obstruction; and they cause the Buddha’s voice to resound, proclaiming the ocean of Dharma. These are the ten.
