Next is the mark of a great man called Cloud of Universal Radiance, adorned with *vaiḍūrya*, *indra-vajra*, and *maṇi* jewels.
As for their adornment, the light and color of lapis lazuli jewels are clear and penetrating, universally illuminating all oceans of worlds and emitting sublime sounds that fill the Dharma-realm;
all such things are manifested from the great ocean of merit and wisdom of the Buddhas. This is the eleventh.
In these eleven [sections], the functional activities are all explained from below; the causes are likewise subsumed under functional activities.
Next is a mark of a Great Being named Cloud of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-megha*), adorned with various jewel flowers.
All those jewel flowers emit radiance, and within them there are Tathāgatas seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), filling all infinite worlds.
The realm: it causes all worlds to attain universal purity and forever severs all false conceptualizations and discriminations; this is the twelfth.
Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud of Radiant Illumination, adorned with the heart-king maṇi-jewels of the ocean-treasury of jewel-flames.
It emits great light, within which appear immeasurable bodhisattvas and various bodhi...
The practices performed by the Bodhisattvas fill the Dharma-realm with oceans of all Tathāgatas’ wisdom-bodies, dharma-bodies, and various physical forms;

this is the thirteenth. Next is a mark of greatness called the Cloud of Universal Illumination Adornments, adorned with *vajra*-flowers and *vaiḍūrya* jewels, which emits great radiance; within that light is a great precious lotus throne.
Fully adorned and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it spontaneously proclaims the four practices of bodhisattvas;
its sound universally permeates the ocean of all Dharma-realms. This is the fourteenth.

Regarding the "four bodhisattva practices" mentioned in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In brief, all bodhisattvas have four types of practice:

first, the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā-caryā*); second, the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma-caryā*); third, the practice of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-caryā*);
and fourth, the practice of maturing sentient beings (*sattvaparipācana-caryā*)."
Next is a mark of greatness called the Cloud of the Ocean-like Practice of Manifesting the Samādhis of the Buddhas.
Within a single thought-moment, it manifests the infinite adornments of the Tathāgatas, universally adorning all inconceivable oceans of worlds throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
This is the fifteenth. Next is a mark of greatness called the Cloud of Universal Illumination of the Ocean of Transformations. It is like a wondrous jewel lotus...
Mount Sumeru serves as its adornment; the radiance of various jewels arises from the vows of the Buddha, manifesting infinite transformations without end.
This is the sixteenth. Next is a mark of a great man, named Cloud of Liberation of All Tathāgatas.

Adorned with pure and wondrous jewels, it radiates great light, adorning all the lion thrones of the Buddhas, manifesting the physical forms of all Buddhas, as well as immeasurable Buddha-dharmas and oceans of Buddha-lands. This is the seventeenth.
Next is a mark of a Great Being named Sovereign Expedient Means Universally Illuminating Cloud, consisting of *vaiḍūrya* flowers and true gold.
It is adorned with clouds of the sublime Dharma-flames from the lamp of the lotus-maṇi king.
It emits pure light from dense clouds of jewel-flames of all Buddhas, filling the entire dharma-realm. Within it, all manner of exquisite ornaments are universally manifested.
This is the eighteenth. Next is a mark of a great man called Cloud of Awakening to the Buddha-lineage, which is immeasurable.
Adorned with precious light, it is fully endowed with a thousand spokes, pure both within and without, born from roots of goodness cultivated in the past.
Its radiance shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, giving rise to clear wisdom and daily proclaiming the ocean of the Dharma;
this is the nineteenth.
Nineteenth, regarding those "endowed with a thousand wheels," the Sanskrit original says "endowed with a thousand-spoked wheels.
Next is a mark of a Great Being called the Cloud of Sovereignty Manifesting the Marks of All Tathāgatas. It is adorned with various precious necklaces and *vaiḍūrya* jewel flowers;
it extends great jewel-flames that fill the Dharma-realm, within which all things are universally manifested.

The twenty[th] are the immeasurable Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, who are as courageous and fearless as lion kings, fully endowed with physical marks and wisdom. Next is the mark of a Great Man.

It is named "Cloud Pervasively Illuminating the Entire Dharma Realm. Adorned with the pure and majestic marks of a Tathāgata, it emits great radiance that universally illuminates the dharma realm, manifesting the wondrous treasury of wisdom of all infinite and boundless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the twenty-first.
The twentieth is the manifestation of both body and wisdom, which reveals wisdom.
Next is a mark of a great man called the Cloud of the Tathāgata Vairocana’s Marks, consisting of exquisite jewel-flowers and Vairocana...

It is adorned with pure and wondrous lapis lazuli moons, which emit immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of light rays from mani jewels, filling all of space and the dharma-realm.
Within them, immeasurable buddha-fields are manifested, each containing a Tathāgata sitting in the full lotus posture.
This is the twenty-second. Next is a mark of a great man called "Universally Illuminating One."
The clouds of light of all Buddhas are adorned with exquisite lamps of various jewels.
They emit pure radiance that universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, manifesting all Buddhas turning the wheel of Dharma. This is the twenty-third.
Next is a mark of greatness called "Cloud Universally Manifesting All Adornments," which is adorned with various jewel-flames. It emits...

Pure radiance fills the dharma-realm. In every thought-moment, there constantly appear unspeakably unspeakable numbers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas seated at their sites of enlightenment. This is the twenty-fourth.
Next is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Sounds of All Dharma Realms Emerging," adorned with exquisite sandalwood upon a sea of mani jewels.
He spreads a great net of flames that fills the dharma-realm. Within it, he universally proclaims subtle and wondrous sounds, revealing to all sentient beings the ocean of all karmas.
This is the twenty-fifth. Next is a mark of greatness called "Cloud of the Transformation-Wheel of All Buddhas Universally Illuminating.
It is adorned by the Tathāgata’s pure eyes, and its light shines upon all worlds throughout the ten directions. At...
Within it, he universally manifests all the ornaments belonging to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
furthermore, he emits wondrous sounds that expound the inconceivable and vast ocean of Dharma. This is the twenty-sixth.
Regarding the twenty-sixth point on adornment, it says: "The Tathāgata’s pure eyes are the adornment. This refers to the ten eyes.

"Illuminating below" reveals their functional activity; this also encompasses both the light of the body and the light of wisdom. The "pure eyes" and the "light" explain the aforementioned "universal illumination.
Their manifestation as ornamental implements is the meaning of the upper wheel, for it is the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
Next is a mark of a great man called "Clouds of the Buddha-Ocean Illumined by Light.

Its light shines universally upon all worlds, reaching throughout the entire dharma-realm without obstruction; within it, there are Tathāgatas sitting cross-legged everywhere. This is the twenty-seventh.
Next is a mark of greatness called Jewel Lamp Cloud. It emits the vast radiance of the Tathāgata, universally illuminating all dharma realms throughout the ten directions.
Within it, there are universally manifested all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and inconceivable oceans of sentient beings.
This is the twenty-eighth. Next is a mark of greatness called Non-differentiation of the Dharma Realm.
Separating from the clouds, he emitted the great wisdom-light of the Tathāgata, which universally illumined the Buddha-lands of the ten directions,
the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Bodhisattvas, and the infinite oceans of Dharma. Within these,

he universally manifested various kinds of spiritual powers and further produced sublime sounds that accorded with the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, expounding the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva so as to cause them...
Dedication. This is the twenty-ninth. Next is a mark of a great person called the Cloud of Universal Illumination Abiding in All Oceans of Worlds.

It emits jewel radiance that fills all of space and the dharma-realm, universally manifesting within it pure and wondrous sites of enlightenment as well as the adorned physical forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, causing those who see them to attain the state of non-seeing. This is...
This constitutes the thirtieth. Next is a mark of a great man called Cloud of Pure Radiant Flames of All Jewels.
It emits immeasurable pure light from mani-jewels belonging to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, universally illuminating all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions.
Within it, oceans of Bodhisattvas appear everywhere, each fully endowed with the spiritual powers of a Tathāgata, constantly roaming through the ten [directions].
This extends throughout the entire network of lands within the realm of empty space; this is the thirty-first.
From the twenty-seventh to the thirty-first, the descriptions of their adornments are all omitted, as these are already contained within their respective names.
Next is a mark of a great being called "Cloud Adorned by the Universal Illumination of the Entire Dharma Realm.
It is situated at the very center, gradually rising upward, and is adorned with a Jāmbūnada-gold Indra-net.

It emits clouds of pure light that fill the dharma realm, constantly manifesting in every thought-moment the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds. This is...
It consists of thirty-two parts.

Regarding these thirty-two primary names: next, the most prominent part adorns the lower body; this [mark] resides at the very summit of the head, specifically manifesting as a distinct location, and is therefore called "situated in the center.
Thus, one should know that all the remaining [marks] encircle this characteristic; they are simply not explained here in detail. It gradually rises upward.

The term "protruding" (*utsaṅga*) precisely clarifies its characteristic. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "The Tathāgata has a bone-protuberance on his crown, shaped like a fist.
The *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* states: "It is like a clenched fist. This refers to the characteristic of being prominently raised.
O Son of the Buddha, upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head there are thirty-two such marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) that serve as adornments;
these three together constitute the final adornment.
O Son of the Buddha, between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows there is a mark of a great man called the "Mani-jewel Cloud of Light Pervading the Dharma-realm."
Adorned with flowers, it emits great radiance endowed with the colors of various jewels; like the sun and moon, it is transparent and pure.
Its light shines universally upon the lands of the ten directions, wherein the bodies of all Buddhas are manifested.
Furthermore, it produces wondrous sounds that proclaim the ocean of Dharma. This is the thirty-third.
Second, between the eyebrows there is one mark, namely the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft). From this point downward, each [mark] has its respective locus;

therefore, the text for each consists of five parts: first, the locus; second, the manifestation of the name; third, the adornment of the lower body by the *maṇi*; fourth, the specific characteristics;

and fifth, the radiance. Regarding the first, the locus: as for this *ūrṇā-kośa*, when retracted it curls to the right like a crystal bowl; when extended, it possesses ten facets (*daśakoṭi*) and emits a great radiance.
The adornment is the unique jewel; its radiance possesses many colors. Being empty both within and without, it is thus thoroughly penetrating.
Its fourth function is the downward application of light; furthermore, that which issues forth below is the light of the Dharma. Therefore, this light is named according to its function.
The number of the five fetters can be known.
The Tathāgata’s eye possesses the mark of a great man called "Cloud of Sovereign Universal Vision.
It is adorned with various exquisite jewels, and the light of the maṇi gems is pure and translucent. It universally perceives all things without any obstruction. This is the third.
14. The Tathāgata’s nose possesses the mark of a great man, called "Cloud of All Supernormal Powers and Wisdom.
It is adorned with pure and wondrous jewels, and the radiant light of various precious gems completely covers it.
Within this, immeasurable transformation Buddhas appear, sitting upon jeweled lotuses and proceeding to all worlds to expound the [Dharma] for all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings.
To contemplate the ocean of all Buddhas' teachings—this is the thirty-fifth.
The third eye and the fourth nose each possess one mark.
The Tathāgata’s tongue possesses a mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting the Images of Sound," adorned with various colors and exquisite jewels.
It is for the sake of adornment, accomplished by the roots of goodness from past lives. His tongue is broad and long, pervading all oceans of worlds.
Whenever the Tathāgata smiles with a serene countenance, he necessarily emits the light of all *maṇi* jewels.
This light universally illumines the dharma-realm of the ten directions, enabling the minds of all beings to attain refreshing clarity throughout the past, future, and present.
There are Buddhas who all appear vividly within the light, universally proclaiming vast and subtle sounds throughout all lands for immeasurable eons;
this is the thirty-sixth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s tongue possesses another mark of a great man.

It is named the Cloud of the Dharma Realm. Its palms are level and even, adorned with various jewels, emitting wondrous jewel-light whose color and form are perfectly complete, just like the light emitted from between the eyebrows.
This light universally illumines all Buddha-fields, which are composed solely of atoms and lack inherent nature.
Within the light, there further appear immeasurable Buddhas, all of whom emit sublime sounds to expound all dharmas.
These are the thirty-seven.
Regarding the fifth [mark], the tongue has four characteristics. The first is the characteristic of the broad and long root of the tongue.

Among the adornments of the body, this refers to those perfected through past roots of goodness; this citation of the adornment of causes is intended to cause one to praise and expound the One Vehicle. As for its...
The length and breadth of the tongue refers to its substance. For those of merit, it reaches the nose; for a provisional Buddha, it reaches the hairline.

In other Mahāyāna teachings, it is clarified that through the manifestation of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), it reaches the Brahma-world or even covers the trichiliocosm. "Gold" refers directly to the substance; thus, it immediately covers everything.
Subsequently, the Tathāgata descends to distinguish its functional activity: "Expounding the Dharma" explains the vocal sound, while "Manifesting the Buddha" explains [the physical form].
The image has two aspects: that of the tongue and that of the palm. "Palm" refers to the area near the root.

Its downward activity involves illuminating all lands with light, so that those who are ready for deliverance need not wait for the destruction of their delusions; they understand spontaneously upon being gathered together. Since it merely joins with sensory objects, what inherent nature could there be?
The Tathāgata’s tongue possesses the mark of a great man, called the Cloud of Radiance Illuminating the Dharma Realm.
It is adorned with the king of wish-fulfilling jewels and naturally and constantly emits golden jewel-flames, within which the oceans of all Buddhas are reflected.
Furthermore, it vibrates with sublime sounds that fill all boundless worlds; within each sound, all sounds are fully contained. All...
When he expounds the wondrous Dharma, those who hear it find joy in their hearts; for immeasurable kalpas they savor and contemplate it without forgetting. This is the thirty-eighth.
Furthermore, on the tip of the Tathāgata’s tongue is another mark of a great man called Cloud Illuminating the Dharma Realm.
It is adorned with the sovereign king of maṇi jewels, which radiates various colors and subtle, wondrous light that fills immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions. To its very end...

There is no part of the dharma-realm that is not pure. Within it, there are entirely immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, each emitting sublime sounds to provide various teachings and elucidations. All Bodhisattvas listen to and receive them in their presence. This is the thirty-ninth.
The latter two are both located at the tip of the tongue; they may reside on the left and right, or above and below.

Examining their textual descriptions and functional applications, there is only a difference between expansion and contraction: the former contracts the ocean of Buddhas into the tip of the tongue, while the latter expands all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm.
Upon the palate of the Tathāgata’s mouth is a mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting the Inconceivable Dharma-realm.
Adorned with *indranīla* and *vaiḍūrya* jewels, it emits clouds of pure light from the flames of fragrant lamps, filling all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions.
It manifests various supernatural powers and skillful means, pervading all worlds.
The ocean of realms. He expounds the profound and inconceivable Dharma; this constitutes the fortieth.
Regarding the "single mark of the upper palate": since it exists on the upper palate, it is likewise appropriate for the lower. Alternatively, it may be an omission in the Sanskrit original.
On the lower right molar of the Tathāgata’s mouth there is a mark of a great man called the Buddha-tooth Cloud (*buddhadanta-megha*).
It is adorned with various precious *maṇi* jewels and *svastika* wheels. It emits a great radiance that universally illumines the Dharma-realm.
Within it, the bodies of all Buddhas are universally manifested, circulating throughout the ten directions to awaken all sentient beings. This is the forty-first [mark].
The seventh tooth has four characteristics, namely, because it consists of the four great teeth on the left, right, above, and below.
Therefore, when the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa and his body was cremated, these four teeth were not crushed. They are the bones of the cheeks; they are also called the mandible.
On the upper right molar of the Tathāgata’s mouth is a mark of a great man called Jewel Flame Sumeru Treasury Cloud.
It is adorned with a treasury of maṇi jewels and emits the pure radiance of adamantine fragrant flames.
Each ray of light fills the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting the spiritual powers of all Buddhas and further revealing the purity of all worlds throughout the ten directions.
The Sublime Place of Enlightenment (Sudharmā-maṇḍala). This constitutes the forty-second.
The upper right auxiliary tooth is named Sulu; it manifests the Sublime High Mountain (Sumeru).
On the lower left auxiliary tooth of the Tathāgata’s mouth, there is a mark of a Great Man named Jewel Lamp Illuminating Everywhere Cloud (Ratnapradīpa-samantāvabhāsa-megha), which is all-sublime.

It is adorned with the fragrance of blossoming jewel-flowers. Clouds of lamp-flames emit pure radiance that fills all oceans of worlds, within which all Buddhas appear, seated upon lion-thrones of lotus-treasury, surrounded by hosts of bodhisattvas.
This is the forty-third [mark], located above the left cheek of the Tathāgata’s mouth.
The tusks possess the marks of a Great Being. They are named the Tathāgata Cloud of Manifest Illumination;

they are adorned with pure radiance, Jambūnada-golden jewel nets, and precious flowers. They emit great wheels of flame that fill the Dharma-realm, within which all Buddhas are universally manifested.
By means of their supernormal powers, they distribute the milk of the Dharma, the lamp of the Dharma, and the jewels of the Dharma throughout the void, providing instruction.
It transforms the entire assembly of bodhisattvas; this constitutes the forty-fourth [point].

Among these four, regarding the "Dharma-milk," "Dharma-lamp," and "Dharma-treasure": they are called "milk" in reference to nourishing the *dharmakāya*; they are termed "lamps" for illuminating and discerning the myriad objects;

and they are designated as "treasures" because they cause [the *dharmakāya*] to be perfectly pure. This is precisely the unfolding of the Dharma of the *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), which also brings about [this realization].

Regarding the benefits of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*, the Tathāgata’s teeth possess the mark of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) called "Universal Manifestation of Clouds of Radiance. Each space between the teeth is adorned with an ocean of marks;
when he smiles, they all emit light endowed with the colors of various jewels, and the flames of *maṇi* gems swirl to the right.
It revolves and spreads throughout the dharma-realm, filling it entirely. It articulates the Buddha’s melodic voice to expound upon the practices of Samantabhadra.
This is the forty-fifth.
On the eighth tooth there is one mark.
The Tathāgata’s lips possess a mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting the Radiance of All Jewels.
It emits vast light of the color of Jāmbūnada gold, the hue of lotuses, and all precious gems, illuminating the entire Dharma-realm and causing it all to be purified. This is the forty-sixth.
The ninth [mark] is on the lips. The upper two [lips] should each be distinguished as upper and lower. Their lower parts are adorned with the radiance of Jambudvīpa;
for the color of the lips is beautiful and red, like the rising sun or the petals of a red lotus. Subsequently, they illuminate the lower [realms] through their functional activity.
The Tathāgata’s neck possesses a mark of a great man called "Cloud Illumining All Worlds.
It is adorned with the king of maṇi-jewels, perfected in deep blue hue, soft, supple, and smooth, emitting the pure light of Vairocana.
It fills all worlds throughout the ten directions, and within it, all Buddhas appear universally; this is the forty-seventh.
On the tenth neck, there is one mark.
On the Tathāgata’s right shoulder is a mark of a great man called the Buddha’s Vast Cloud of All Jewels.
It emits the radiance of all jewel colors, true gold, and lotus flowers, forming a net of jewel-flames that universally illumines the Dharma-realm.
Within it, all bodhisattvas are universally manifested. This is the forty-eighth. Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s right shoulder is another mark of a great man, named...
The most supreme jewel-cloud of universal illumination is pure in color like Jāmbūnada gold;
it emits mani-light that fills the dharma-realm, within which all bodhisattvas are universally manifested. This is the forty-ninth.
On the Tathāgata’s left shoulder is a mark of a great man called the Cloud of Supreme Light Illuminating the Dharma-Realm; it is like the [mark] upon the crown of the head and between the eyebrows.
This is the fiftieth kind of adornment. They emit the light of various jewels, such as Jāmbūnada gold and lotus-colored gems, forming a great web of flames that fills the Dharma-realm.
Within it, they manifest all spiritual powers. This constitutes the fiftieth.
Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s left shoulder is another mark of a Great Man called Cloud of Universally Radiant Light. This mark spirals to the right and is the color of Jāmbūnada gold.
It is adorned with the king of maṇi jewels, emitting the radiant light of various jewel-flower incenses that pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Within it, all Buddhas and all pure, adorned lands are universally manifested. This is the fifty-first.
On the Tathāgata’s left shoulder there is another mark of a great man called Cloud of Universal Radiance; its form spirals to the right and is subtle.
The fifty-second is the Secret Adornment. It emits clouds of Buddha-lamp flames and pure radiance that pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
within them appear all the various adornments of all bodhisattvas, all of which are exquisitely beautiful. This is the fifty-second.
The eleventh shoulder has five marks: two on the right and three on the left, though some may also be missing.
On the Tathāgata’s chest is the mark of a Great Man, shaped like the *svastika* (卍), named Auspicious Ocean-Cloud (*Śrī-sāgara-megha*).
It is adorned with *maṇi* jewel flowers and emits various wheels of light-flames in all jewel colors, filling the entire Dharma-realm. Universally...
They cause all to be purified. Furthermore, they produce wondrous sounds that proclaim the ocean of Dharma. This is the fifty-third.
To the right of the auspicious mark is a mark of a great man called Cloud Manifesting Radiant Light.
It is adorned with Indra’s net, which emits great circles of light that fill the entire dharma-realm. Within these, immeasurable Buddhas appear everywhere. This is the fifty-fourth.
To the right of the auspicious marks, there is further a mark of a great man called the Tathāgata-Cloud of Universal Manifestation.
It is adorned with the maṇi-jewel crowns of all bodhisattvas and emits great radiance that universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions.

He causes all to be completely purified. Within that [assembly], he manifests the Buddhas of the past, future, and present seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), universally displaying spiritual powers and extensively proclaiming the ocean of Dharma.
This is the fifty-fifth. To the right of the auspicious marks, there is another mark of a great man called "Cloud of Blooming Flowers.
It is adorned with *maṇi* jewel flowers and emits the pure light of jewel-fragrant flame-lamps.
It is radiant, shaped like a lotus flower, and fills the world. This is the fifty-sixth.
To the right of the auspicious marks, there is another mark of a great being called "Delightful Golden Cloud.

It is adorned with the *maṇi* kings of the treasury of the heart-king of all jewels, emitting pure light that illuminates the entire *dharmadhātu*. Within it, he appears universally, just like a Buddha.
The Eye of Vast Radiance Maṇi Jewel Treasury is the fifty-seventh.
On the right side of the auspicious mark, there is another mark of a great man called Buddha-Ocean-Cloud, adorned with Vaiḍūrya jewels, incense lamps, and flower garlands.
He emits from his left side the Great Flame of Pure Radiance of the Maṇi-jewel King that Fills Empty Space with Fragrance and Light, which pervades all lands throughout the ten directions.
Within it, he universally manifests the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment. This is the fifty-eighth [mark].
On the left side of the Auspicious Mark is a mark of a great man called Manifesting Clouds of Light, wherein countless bodhisattvas sit upon precious lotus flowers.
They serve as adornments, emitting various intermingled jewel-flame radiances from the sovereign maṇi-kings that universally purify all oceans of the dharma-realm.
Within them, they manifest immeasurable Buddhas and the sublime voices of those Buddhas as they expound all dharmas.
This is the fifty-ninth. On the left side, there is another mark of a great man called "Manifesting Clouds of Radiance Pervading the Dharma Realm.
It is adorned with layers of mani-jewel nets that emit great light pervading all lands.
Within it, the assemblies of all bodhisattvas are universally manifested; this is the sixtieth.
To the left of the auspicious mark, there is another mark of a great being named Universal Victorious Cloud (*Samanta-jaya-megha*).

It is adorned with garlands of jewel wheels from the sun-light mani-kings, emitting great flames that fill the oceans of worlds throughout the dharma-realm. Within them, he manifests every world as one.

All Tathāgatas and all sentient beings—this is the sixty-first. On the left side of the auspicious mark, there is another mark of a great man called "Cloud of Wondrous Sound Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
It is adorned with the pure fragrant filaments of the lamp of all dharmas and emits great radiance that fills the dharma-realm, within which the marks of all Buddhas appear everywhere.
The ocean and the ocean of the mind—these constitute the sixty-third. On the left side of the auspicious mark, there is another mark of a great man called Cloud of Adornment.
It is adorned by the oceans of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
it emits pure light that purifies and adorns all Buddha-lands, and within it, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions appear universally.
As well as the practices performed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—these constitute the sixty-three [marks].
Regarding the twelfth, the eleventh mark on the chest: the first is in the center, with five on each side, left and right. Now, for the first, the *svastika*:
The direct translation is "Auspicious Ocean-Cloud. Since the name is established based on its form, the form is first indicated;
it should be moved to follow the title to be subsumed under the essence, which involves no contradiction.
The Tathāgata’s right hand possesses a mark of a great man called Ocean-Illuminating Cloud (*sāgarāvabhāsa-megha*).
Adorned with various jewels, it constantly emits pure light like moonbeams that fills all worlds throughout space. It produces a great sound praising the practices of all bodhisattvas.
This is the sixty-fourth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s right hand possesses another mark of a great man called Shadow (*chāyā*).
There appeared clouds of radiance, adorned with *vaiḍūrya* and deep-blue *maṇi* jewel flowers.
They emitted great light that universally illumined all worlds, such as the Lotus Treasury and Maṇi Treasury where Bodhisattvas dwell.
Within them, infinite Buddhas were fully manifested, sitting beneath Bodhi trees with their pure *dharmakāya*, shaking the [universe].

Pervading all lands in the ten directions—this constitutes the sixty-fifth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s right hand possesses a mark of a great man called Lamp-Flame Garland Universal Adornment Pure Cloud. It is adorned with Vairocana jewels and emits great radiance that forms a net of transformations.
Within it, the assemblies of all bodhisattvas appear universally, all wearing jeweled crowns and expounding the ocean of all practices.
This is the sixty-sixth. Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s right hand there is another mark of a great man called "Universal Manifestation of All Jewel Clouds.
It is adorned with lotus-flame lamps that bestow the light of the ocean-treasury, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Within it, immeasurable Buddhas are universally manifested sitting upon lotus thrones. This is the sixty-seventh. Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s right hand...

There is a mark of a great man called Cloud of Radiance. It is adorned by an ocean of maṇi-flames, emitting the pure light of various jewel-flames, incense-flames, and flower-flames, which fills all the networks of worlds.
Within it, the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas are universally manifested. This is the sixty-eighth.
The thirteenth hand possesses thirteen marks, divided into three parts. The first nine are the marks of the "Direct Speech" (pratyakṣa-vāk) hand: five on the right and four on the left;

this is either because one [mark] was omitted from the left, or to indicate that the right side is more commonly used. Regarding the sixth mark on the middle finger of the right hand, the *Shi-er-men lun* states:
"It forms a net of transformations," because its light transforms into a net.
The Tathāgata’s left hand possesses a mark of a great man called "Pure Lamp Cloud of Vaiḍūrya.
Adorned with the exquisite colors of precious ground, it emits the golden radiance of the Tathāgata, constantly manifesting all manner of supreme and wondrous ornaments in every thought-moment.
This is the sixty-ninth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s left hand possesses another mark of a great man called "One..."

The cloud-sound of the wisdom-lamp of all lands is adorned with Indra-net vajra-flowers, emitting the pure radiance of Jāmbūnada gold that universally illuminates all worlds in the ten directions; this is the seventieth.
Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s left hand there is another mark of a great man, named "Cloud of Radiance of Abiding Jewel Lotuses. The multitude...
It is adorned with exquisite jewel flowers and emits great radiance like the lamp of Mount Sumeru, universally illuminating all worlds in the ten directions;

this is the seventy-first. Furthermore, on the Tathāgata’s left hand there is another mark of a great man called Cloud Illuminating the Dharma Realm, which, by means of exquisite jewel garlands, jewel wheels, jewel vases, Indra-nets, and various wonderful signs, [is adorned].
To adorn [them], they emit great radiance that universally illumines all lands throughout the ten directions.
Within this, they manifest the entire dharma-realm and all oceans of worlds, wherein all Tathāgatas sit upon lotus thrones. This is the seventy-second.
The seventy-second [section] in the middle of the left [volume] states: "Adorned with Indra’s net" means that the nets and their coverings interpenetrate one another.
On the right hand of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) called "The Cloud-Spiral of All Kalpas and Oceans of Lands Appearing," which is like the moon in water or a flame.
The mani-kings of the treasury are adorned with all manner of jewel flowers.
They emit great radiance that fills the dharma-realm, and from within them there constantly issue subtle and wondrous sounds that pervade the lands of the ten directions. This is the seventy-third.
On the left hand of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man called "Abiding in All Jewel Clouds," which, by means of indranīla-vajra jewels, [is adorned].
As an adornment, he emits the light of various jewels from the king of maṇi-gems, filling the dharma-realm.
Within it, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are universally manifested. This is the seventy-fourth.
On the palm of the Tathāgata’s right hand is a mark of a great man called Cloud of Radiance, adorned with a thousand-spoked jewel wheel of the king of maṇi-gems, which emits precious light.

It is luminous; its light spirals to the right, filling the dharma-realm. Within it, all Buddhas appear universally, each Buddha’s body with blazing flames, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and purifying all worlds. This is the seventy-fifth.
On the palm of the Tathāgata’s left hand is a mark of a great man called "The Universal Increase of the Flame-Wheel Manifesting Clouds of Dharma-Realm Bodhimaṇḍas."
It is adorned with the thousand-spoked wheels of the Sunlight Maṇi King, emitting great radiance that fills all oceans of worlds.

Within them, all bodhisattvas are manifested, proclaiming the ocean of practices of Samantabhadra and universally entering all Buddha-lands, each awakening immeasurable sentient beings. This is the seventh.
Sixteenth: On the palms of both his left and right hands in the final two [marks], there are each a thousand wheels, complete with the three features of hub, spokes, and rim,
spontaneously perfected.
The Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man known as the "Secret Organ," which universally emits clouds of Buddha-sounds.
It is adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels and radiates the brilliant light of mani-lamp flames; that light is intensely blazing and possesses the colors of all kinds of precious gems.
It universally illumines the entire void dharma-realm, wherein all Buddhas are everywhere manifested as they travel to and fro, pervading every place. This is the seventy-seventh.
The fourteenth is the mark of the concealed organ, like that of a horse-king.
On the Tathāgata’s right hip is a mark of a great man called Jewel Lamp Garland Universal Illumination Cloud.
It is adorned with various maṇi jewels and emits inconceivable jewel-flame radiance that pervades all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions. Together with...
The void and the dharma-realm are of one and the same mark, yet they are able to give birth to all marks.
Within each and every mark, the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas are fully manifested. This is the seventy-eighth.
On the left hip of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Light Pervading the Void that Manifests the Ocean of All Dharma Realms," which is like a lotus flower.

Adorned with pure and wondrous jewels, they emit networks of light that universally illuminate all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions, wherein clouds of various manifestations appear everywhere. This is the seventy-ninth.
The fifteenth seat has two characteristics.
On the Tathāgata’s right thigh is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Universal Manifestation. It is adorned with *maṇi* jewels of various colors.
The thigh and calf are in perfect proportion to one another, emitting the wondrous light of the Dharma from *maṇi* flames in a single thought-moment.
Within it, he can universally manifest all jewel-kings and the ocean-like marks of his gait; this is the eightieth.
On the Tathāgata’s left thigh is a mark of a great man called "Manifesting the Ocean-like Clouds of the Infinite Marks of All Buddhas.
It is adorned by all oceans of jewels that abide in accordance with it. As he wanders extensively, he emits pure light that universally illuminates all sentient beings. All...
Causing them to aspire to the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma; this is the eighty-first.

Regarding the sixteenth pair of marks on the thighs: the left is called "conforming abiding. Because the thighs involve much movement, they must be adorned with many jewels in accordance [with that movement].
On the right side of the Tathāgata’s calf, there is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the king of the eneya deer, named Cloud of All Dharmadhātus of Empty Space.
It is adorned with exquisite jewels of radiant light; its form is perfectly round and straight, enabling him to stride with grace.
It emits a pure radiance of Jambu-river gold that illuminates all Buddha-worlds, and it issues forth a great sound that pervades everywhere.
All were shaken. Furthermore, all the buddha-fields appeared, abiding in the void adorned with jewel-flames. From within them, immeasurable bodhisattvas manifested through transformation.
This is the eighty-second. On the left side of the Tathāgata’s leg, upon the calf of the Enīya deer-king, there is a mark of a great man called Adorned Ocean Cloud (*vyūha-samudra-megha*).
Its color is like pure gold, and it is able to travel everywhere throughout one...
In all Buddha-fields, they emit pure light of all kinds of jewels that fills the Dharma-realm and performs the work of Buddhas.
This is the eighty-third [mark]. The Tathāgata’s hair on his precious calves possesses a mark of a Great Man called "Clouds of Universal Manifestation of the Dharma-realm Images.
These hairs curl to the right; from the tip of each hair, jewel-light is emitted, filling all the ten directions.
The Dharma-realm manifests the spiritual powers of all Buddhas; from every one of its pores, light rays are emitted, within which all Buddha-fields appear. This is the eighty-fourth.
The seventeenth [mark] consists of three features on the calves. The third feature, the body hair on the upper arms, extends down to both calves.

If one follows the Jin translation, which simply says "the tips of the hair," it refers to all the hair on the entire body. If the meaning is to be understood as in previous [traditions], then the locations [of the marks] total nineteen.
Beneath the feet of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of the Secure Abiding of the Ocean of All Bodhisattvas.
Its color is like that of vajra-Jāmbūnada gold and pure lotuses, emitting jewel-light that universally illumines the oceans of worlds in the ten directions.
Clouds of precious fragrant flames pervade everywhere; as he lifts his foot to take a step, the fragrance flows forth, endowed with all manner of jewels.
The physical form fills the Dharma-realm; this is the eighty-fifth [mark].
The eighteenth foot has thirteen characteristics, which together comprise seven [groups]. The first is a single mark on the sole of the foot;

the left and right are omitted for brevity. However, the Jin translation includes a separate "thousand-spoked wheel" mark on the soles of the feet following the description of the insteps; this must certainly be...

It is indeed so. Therefore, the subsequent chapter explains the characteristics of the lower wheels, naming them the "Universal Illumination King. The mention of "thousand wheels" in this current scripture actually refers to the spaces between the fingers.
Perhaps because they are constantly luminous and easy to perceive, while the spaces between the fingers are distinct, these [spaces] are specifically cited here.
He is named "Abiding in Peace" because the soles of his feet are level and firm, such that no needle could penetrate where they touch the ground.
Upon the right foot of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Universal Radiance," adorned with all manner of precious jewels;
it emits great light that fills the Dharma-realm, manifesting the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Sa. This is the eighty-sixth. Upon the Tathāgata’s left foot is a mark of a great man called "Cloud Universally Manifesting All Buddhas.
It is adorned with *maṇi* jewels from the treasury of gems and radiates precious light.

In every thought-moment, it manifests the supernatural transformations and the ocean of teachings of all Buddhas, as well as their seats of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
Without interruption—this is the eighty-seventh.
Regarding the two supreme marks of the two-footed ones:
between the toes of the Tathāgata’s right foot is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Light Illuminating the Ocean of All Dharmadhātus. It is necessary...

The thousand-spoked wheel of flames of the Mīḍhamaṇi King is adorned with various ornaments and emits great radiance that fills all the oceans of worlds throughout the ten directions of the entire Dharma-realm.
Within it, there universally appear all the various jewel-ornamented forms of all Buddhas. This is the eighty-eighth. Between the toes of the Tathāgata’s left foot is a mark of a Great Man.
It is named "Clouds of Oceans of All Buddhas Manifesting," adorned with mani-jewel flowers, fragrant flames, lamps, garlands, and all manner of jewel wheels.
It constantly emits the pure radiance of oceans of jewels, filling the void and pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Within it, there are manifested the perfect voices and the *svastika* marks of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The characteristic of the equality of syllables benefits all immeasurable sentient beings; this is the eighty-ninth.
Between the three toes, there are two marks.
On the right heel of the Tathāgata, there is a mark of a great man called Sovereign Radiant Cloud, [adorned] with powdered indranīla jewels.
As an adornment, he constantly emits the wondrous jewel-light of the Tathāgata. This light is exquisite and fills the entire Dharma-realm;
it is all of one single mark without distinction. Within it, he manifests all Buddhas seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) expounding the sublime Dharma.
This is the ninety-first [mark]. On the left heel of the Tathāgata is a mark of a great man called "Manifesting the Wondrous."

The ninety-first is the Ocean-Cloud of the Sound Explaining All Dharmas, adorned with oceans of transformation-maṇi jewels, fragrant flames of maṇi jewels, Sumeru-flowers of maṇi jewels, and lapis lazuli;
it emits great radiance that fills the dharma-realm, within which the spiritual powers of all Buddhas are universally manifested. This is the ninety-first.
The fourth is the mark of two heels.
On the right foot of the Tathāgata, there is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Radiant Light Manifesting All Adornments.
It is composed of various jewels, exquisitely adorned, and emits a pure, clear light the color of Jambūnada gold, universally illuminating the ten [directions].
Throughout the entire dharma-realm, its marks of radiance are like great clouds that universally cover the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas;
this is the ninety-second. On the left foot of the Tathāgata’s ankle is a mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting All Colors.
It is formed from the *vairocana-ratna-indranīla* jewel of the treasury of all moon-flames.
Adorned, they traverse the ocean of all dharma-realms in every thought-moment, emitting the radiant light of mani-lamp incense flames;
this light pervades and fills all dharma-realms. This is the ninety-third.
Regarding the two marks of the five-toed feet:
on the circumference of the Tathāgata’s right foot, there is a mark of a great man called Universal Cloud Treasury (*Samantagarbha-megha*).
It is adorned with *indranīla* vajra-jewels that emit precious light, filling all of space, within which everything is manifested.
All Buddhas sit upon lion thrones made of the king of *maṇi* jewels at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This is the ninety-fourth.
On the circumference of the Tathāgata’s left foot is a mark of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) named "Cloud of Light Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm.
It is adorned with *maṇi* jewel flowers and emits great radiance that fills the dharma realm, being of a single, equal nature. Within it, he manifests...

He manifests the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and with a great, wondrous voice, he expounds the inexhaustible Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm. This is the ninety-fifth.
It has six sides and is surrounded on all four sides. *Indranīla* means "Imperial Blue" in this language.
On the tip of the Tathāgata’s right toe is a mark of a great man called "Cloud of Manifesting Adornments.
It is exceedingly lovely and is adorned with pure Jāmbūnada gold. It emits a great radiance that fills the ten directions.
Throughout the entire dharma-realm, he manifests within it the various meritorious virtues, spiritual powers, and transformations of the inexhaustible ocean of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This is the ninety-sixth. On the tip of the Tathāgata’s left toe is a mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting the Spiritual Transformations of All Buddhas," which possesses the inconceivable Buddha-light, moon-flames, and universal fragrance.
It is adorned with wheels of mani-jewel flames, emitting pure light of various jewel colors that fills all oceans of worlds.
Within them, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear, expounding the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas. This is the ninety-seventh.
The seven toes have two at each end, left and right; their patterns are clear and thus easily known.
Thus far, we have briefly listed ninety-seven marks, with their sequence and names arranged by the translator. Since they are not stated exhaustively, how could they not exceed one hundred?
Not a single foot is missing, nor are the lips and palate unopened. Even if these two were closed, the six sense organs would all be functional; why then should the ears alone be absent?
If one adds two for the ears and one for the soles of the feet, the total becomes a hundred, thereby manifesting inexhaustibility—how wonderful!
Moreover, the items listed here among the thirty-two are still not exhaustive; how could the power of Samantabhadra be limited to only a hundred?
The Jin translation omits some, listing only ninety-four, and it lacks the sequential numbering. Thus we know [the current version is incomplete].
The ninety-seven categories do not exist apart from their association with the various phenomena that give rise to conceptualization.
Son of the Buddha, Vairocana Tathāgata possesses such great marks of a person as these, numbering as many as the atoms within ten oceans of Lotus Treasury worlds;
every part of his body is adorned with the wondrous signs of various jewels.
The third section concludes the concise exposition to reveal the extensive. Since a detailed explanation would be difficult to encompass, it is necessary to conclude with the concise;
yet, as the concise cannot exhaust the meaning, it is necessary to reveal the extensive. The characteristics of a single flower-receptacle world-dust are already boundless;

how much more so for ten such flower-receptacles, which are infinitely inexhaustible. Who but one with the Universal Eye could behold them? Furthermore, since the thirty-two marks differ in their provisional and ultimate aspects, they are mutually...
Because they are mutually exclusive, there is no combined explanation.
Regarding the introductory intent of the thirty-fifth chapter, "The Chapter on the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance":
the preceding chapter elucidated the major marks (*lakṣaṇa*), while this chapter elucidates the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). Although the major and minor marks differ, both serve to adorn [the body].

The body [is discussed] to answer the previous inquiry concerning the body, as well as the eyes and so forth, together with the question regarding mastery (*vaśitā*). The secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) exist based upon the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*);

since their qualities are inferior to those of the marks, they are explained next. The function of these inferior qualities brings about immediate benefit, thereby conversely revealing that the qualities of the great marks are inconceivable.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Tathāgata" designates the person to indicate his virtues; "secondary marks" and so forth manifest the virtues as dependent upon the person.
The secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are the essence, because they follow and enhance the beauty of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Radiance is their function;
as for "merit" (*guṇa*), it refers to the light emitted from the secondary marks, which is able to benefit sentient beings and manifest the merit of those marks—hence the name.
Whether one says "the secondary marks of the Tathāgata" or "the Tathāgata possesses secondary marks," both interpretations apply. This is the third point: the essential purport.
This clarifies that manifesting auspicious signs and virtuous qualities is the primary purpose, while inspiring sentient beings to practice with reverence is the ultimate goal.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King of Perfection.
From within this secondary mark, a great radiance issues forth, called Blazing Intensity, [measuring] seven million..."
It has incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) rays of light as its retinue.

Next, regarding the explanation of the text, there are two parts: first, the brief; second, the detailed. Within the brief, there are two sections: first, the indication of the marks of fruition; second, from "O Sons of the Buddha, for my sake...
onwards, the citation of the causes to manifest them by contrast. Now, for the first [point]: there are two intentions for the Buddha’s own explanation. First, the *saṃgha*...
This concludes the section [on the marks]. Since this chapter reaches the ultimate fruit, both [the primary marks and the secondary signs] were spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the two excellent uses of inferior characteristics, the Buddha spoke of them himself out of fear that sentient beings might not believe in their inconceivable application. Furthermore, there are two meanings for addressing "Precious Hand" (*Ratnapāṇi*):

first, it indicates that the hand follows the [secondary] marks, and he is the master of this gate; second, it causes those who possess jewels to give rise to faith in the hand. There is that which follows...

"Good" (*bhadra*) refers to the general characteristic. It is precisely your "goodness," which is identical to the name mentioned later; thus, its virtuous functions are all-encompassing and complete, hence it is called "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*).
As for the King named Most Victorious (*Vasavatti*), who is sovereign in gathering and benefiting others, his "light" (*prabha*) is called "blazing" (*jvalita*);

like the sun, he possesses these virtues. By means of this, he is further able to gather his retinue. The mention of "one million" and so forth indicates their great number. Furthermore, it says "seven."

This refers to purifying the seven branches, cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, and illuminating the seven stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the seven stages: first, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*);

third, the stage of purified superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*); fourth, the stage of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*); fifth, the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*); sixth, the stage of certain practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*);

and seventh, [the stage of the bodhisattva]. (The first corresponds to the stage of faith; the second to the three levels of the virtuous; the third to the first ground; the fourth from the second to the seventh grounds; the fifth to the eighth ground; and the sixth to the ninth ground.)
"Reaching the ultimate stage" (from the tenth bhūmi to the stage of the Tathāgata). Supplementary note:
This chapter speaks of the merit of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). Their great function is inconceivable; the intent is to reveal that the Buddha’s virtues are beyond thought.
Because the Buddha’s virtues are inconceivable and without parallel, [the text] cites the most inferior of the secondary marks as an illustration.
This refers to the virtue of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), which serves to manifest the excellence of his complete physical form.
Now, the sutra mentions "the one with secondary marks named King Paripūrṇa. The term "secondary marks" here is used as a general designation for the common characteristics of all such marks.

The name "King Paripūrṇa," however, specifically indicates the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet; therefore, its specific location is only revealed later. This is the very last [mark].
It is merely the least excellent of the marks. If it were the wheel-mark on the Buddha’s foot, it would be superior;

however, as the following text describes the wheel-mark during the causal stage, it is even more inferior. Nevertheless, even this most inferior mark among the causal qualities emits a single ray of light capable of causing sentient beings suffering extreme agony in the hells to be liberated from their pain and reborn in heaven. Furthermore, it is obtained...

The benefits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are perfected all at once in three layers. If the light within the causal stage possesses such great benefit, then it can be known that the inferior light within the resultant stage does as well.
Furthermore, if the benefit of the inferior light at the feet is thus, how much more so for the excellence among the other marks?
If the excellence is already like this, how much more so for the superior marks? If the causal stage is already like this, how much more so...
If such is the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana) among the fruits of virtue, how much more so for the many secondary marks?
If such is the merit of a single primary mark (lakṣaṇa) and a single secondary mark, how much more so for the many primary marks and secondary marks covering the entire body?

If the benefit of the primary and secondary marks of a single body is thus, how much more so for the marks and secondary marks numbering as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury (Puṣpa-garbha) worlds? By means of this, they increase in layers of ever-greater excellence and expand.
Reflect upon this: how could the merit and benefits of that Buddha possibly be conceived by thought?
Because the meaning contained within the scriptural text is so profound, although several layers have been raised in this commentary, it remains difficult to point them all out exhaustively.

Since his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are so vast and numerous, one can know the greatness of that Buddha’s body. To contemplate the Buddha in this way—how could this be for those of inferior understanding?
Is it possible? Son of the Buddha,
when I was a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita heaven palace, I emitted a great light named King of Light Banners,
which illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields.
Second, regarding the presentation through the contrast of causes: this is done for the sake of manifesting excellence. This has several layers.

First, because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and virtues are so profound and vast that words cannot fully encompass them, they are set aside and one speaks instead of "excellence" (*śubha*). Second, these excellent virtues are further manifold;

since there are already eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) accompanying the thirty-two primary marks, the marks and excellences are as numerous as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*).
There are many such marks. First, regarding one of the primary marks: among the three types of excellence, he speaks only of the inferior. Therefore, he mentions the soles of the feet.
Fourth, beneath each sole there are many rays of light, yet he speaks of only one ray. Fifth, even a single ray at the stage of fruition (*phala*) cannot be fully described;
thus, it is manifested by way of the causal stage (*hetu*). Since the light of the cause accomplishes benefit, the three levels are suddenly perfected—how much more so the fruition!
"A single ray of light. Thus it is by successive extension; how much more so for the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and how much more so for the general description of the Tathāgata’s virtues?
That "the ocean of fruition transcends words" is precisely this meaning. The text has two parts: first, the extent of the light’s illumination.

This refers to the emission of light from within the previously mentioned "perfect secondary mark" (*anuvyañjana*); therefore, no specific location of emission is designated. Yet, this is not the same as the previous light, for that [secondary mark] possesses manifold rays.
This is merely one among seven million asaṃkhyeya rays of light.
Those beings in the hells within that world who encounter these rays find their manifold sufferings stilled. They obtain ten kinds of pure eyes;
the same applies to their ears, noses, tongues, bodies, and minds. All give rise to joy and exultation, offering praise and celebration.
Next is the benefit accomplished by light. Within this, there are two parts. First is the benefit of causing them to leave suffering and purify their past roots of goodness.
Upon passing away from that life, they are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. In that heaven, there is a drum named "Exceedingly Delightful.
Once those devas have been born, this drum emits a sound and addresses them, saying: "O sons of the gods, because you were not heedless in mind regarding the Tathāgata..."
Having planted various roots of goodness and previously attended upon many spiritual friends, through the great majestic power of Vairocana,
they passed away from that life and were reborn in this heaven.
Later, through the transformation of karmic retribution, he was born in heaven and obtained the benefit of hearing the Dharma. Within this, the first part indicates the past causes:

namely, that in the past he drew near to virtuous friends, whereby he surely heard the Universal Dharma and became of the Vajra lineage; his mind was not negligent, manifesting that he had previously practiced and planted various roots of goodness, including those of seeing and hearing.
Next, from "Vairocana" onwards, it reveals the present conditions. Finally, from "At that time" onwards, it provides the conclusion.

The cause belongs to the fruit; this is stated briefly in the text. As for the conclusion that [the light] belongs to rebirth in heaven, in reality, the cessation of suffering and the attainment of the pure eye and so forth all arise from these causes and conditions.
Thus we know that although the Buddha’s light shines equally upon all, without planting the seeds of wholesome causes, there is no such supreme benefit.
How can a single ray of light suddenly produce such benefits? It is because it is manifested by inexhaustible merit. It is purely immaculate.
Because it flows from the Dharma-realm, it is not like the eighty secondary marks of the provisional teachings, which merely adorn the physical form to inspire faith.
Herein, the causes for falling into hell are briefly omitted; this is because, although one practices the vehicle and precepts, one's conduct is broad and expansive.
Supplementary Commentary: This light illuminates those in the hells who were not of "swift practice and lax precepts.
Rather, they were those who in the past had personally approached spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and heard various Mahāyāna sūtras, thereby giving rise to the resolve to practice.

However, because upon hearing the perfectly integrated (*pariṇata*) Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka*, they failed to believe and instead slandered it, they fell into the evil destinies. This is because it was precisely those who had previously slandered [the teaching] who now hear it.
The name "Avataṃsaka" is the seed-syllable of the Vajra; therefore, having now encountered these causes and conditions, one emerges from suffering and attains benefit.
This is also clearly explained within the *Yaochao* (Excerpts), which points out that the *Shu* (Commentary) has missed the meaning of the Sūtra.
O Son of the Buddha, the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet is named King Universal Illumination.
It possesses an auspicious mark named King Perfection, which constantly emits forty kinds of light rays.
Among them is one ray named Pure Merit, which can illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, according to the various karmic actions of sentient beings.

All those who indulge in various sensual pleasures were brought to spiritual maturity. Those sentient beings in the Avīci Hell suffering extreme agony who encountered this light all passed away and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
The second part is the detailed exposition. This focuses solely on the cause, as the fruit is difficult to describe. Within this section, there are also two parts:
first, the detailed exposition on the benefit of purifying past wholesome roots; second, the benefit of hearing the Dharma extensively after being born in the world. Now, for the first:

it crushes the suffering of the lower miserable realms and emits light from the wheels beneath the feet. The forty rays of light signify that there are no forty stages that are not illuminated. [End of] middle section.
Regarding the first point: setting aside the detailed explanation for brevity, [the light] can illuminate that which follows, surpassing the previous [level] in its lack of unevenness.

From "according to each" onwards, it purifies afflictions and accomplishes virtues; therefore, the preceding light receives names such as "pure. By using the heavy to illustrate the light, it cites Avīci [as the example].
Once they had been born in heaven, they heard the sound of celestial drums proclaiming: "Excellent, excellent!
O sons of the gods, the Bodhisattva Vairocana has entered the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement; you should pay him homage."
Next, regarding the benefit of extensively hearing the Dharma, it is divided into six sections: first, a brief presentation of the exhortation; second, from "At that time, the sons of the gods...
onwards, the arising of doubt after having heard [the sound]; third, from "At that time, the celestial drum... onwards, a general indication of the cause; fourth, from "The sons of the gods...

onwards, the explicit clarification of the exhortation and instruction; fifth, from "At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard this sound... onwards, approaching [the Buddha] in accordance with the exhortation.
The Buddha. When these six teachings were spoken, those who saw and heard them gained even deeper benefit.
At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard the sound of the celestial drum thus exhorting them, all conceived this thought: "How marvelous! How rare!
For what cause has this subtle and wondrous sound been produced? Then the celestial drum addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "As for me..."
It is accomplished through the power of the roots of goodness produced by uttering these sounds.
The first three [points] may be understood.
O sons of the gods, just as I speak of "I" yet do not cling to an "I" nor cling to "mine," so too do all Buddhas.
It is likewise. He himself declares that as a Buddha he is not attached to a self, nor is he attached to what belongs to a self.

O sons of the gods, just as my voice does not come from the east, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below, so too is the attainment of Buddhahood through the ripening of karma; it does not come from the ten directions.
The fourth [section] has four parts. First, using oneself as an analogy for the Buddha: there is no self and no coming.
O sons of the gods, it is just as when you were formerly in hell; neither the hell nor your body came from the ten directions.
It was merely because you were bound by the delusions of inverted, evil karma and ignorance that you took birth in a hellish body. This has no root and no...
"There is a source, O sons of the gods. By the power of the majestic virtue of the Bodhisattva Vairocana, he emits great radiance;
yet this radiance does not come from the ten directions. Sons of the gods, my Drum of Celestial Sound is likewise:
it does not come from the ten directions, but arises solely through the power of the roots of goodness of samādhi and the power of the majestic virtue of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Such pure sounds are produced, and such various forms of mastery are manifested.
O sons of gods, it is just as, for example, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, possesses the exquisite palaces and various instruments of pleasure belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
yet these instruments of pleasure do not come from the ten directions. My celestial drum sound is likewise: it does not come from the ten directions.
Second, by using others as metaphors for oneself, it is shown that coming is itself non-coming. There are three metaphors in the text, all of which can be understood through their manifestation.
However, evil karma and roots of goodness are the causes and conditions of coming; since these causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), coming is itself non-coming.
It is not that some pre-existing phenomenon exists within the ten directions and comes from there. Therefore, causes and conditions are themselves wisdom. Wisdom...
The fundamental nature of wisdom is not produced by causes and conditions. Why, then, do you think there are causes and conditions?
O sons of the gods, it is as if all the worlds, numbering as many as the atoms in a hundred million nayutas of buddha-fields, were ground to dust.
For as many sentient beings as there are motes of dust, I preach the Dharma according to their inclinations, causing them great joy;
yet toward them, I feel no weariness, no discouragement, no pride, and no negligence.
O sons of the gods, it is likewise for the Bodhisattva Vairocana when he dwells in the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement.
From within a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana) upon the palm of his right hand, he emits a single ray of light, manifesting immeasurable powers of sovereign spiritual authority (*vibhutva*).
This is such that even all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know it, let alone ordinary sentient beings.

Third, one uses oneself as an analogy for the inconceivable realm of the Buddha. Regarding the raising of the hand among the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): this is mentioned specifically to manifest its excellence.
The light of the feet is raised because they rescue those above and lead those below; here, however, the hand is raised to manifest universal penetration.
"O sons of the gods, you should go to where that bodhisattva is, draw near to him, and make offerings to him. Do not again become greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires.
Thus he exhorted them four times to go and cautioned them not to remain. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general exhortation and caution.

Attachment to the pleasures of the five desires obstructs all roots of goodness. O sons of the gods, it is just as when the fire at the end of an eon burns Mount Sumeru, reducing it entirely to nothingness so that not even a trace remains;
likewise, when the mind is entangled by craving and desire, one can never give rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Next is the detailed explanation. This also consists of two parts. First is the explanation of the preceding admonition, which includes the teaching, the analogy, and the application.

"O sons of the gods, you should recognize kindness and repay it. O sons of the gods, those sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness frequently meet with untimely deaths and are reborn in the hells. O sons of the gods, when you were formerly in the hells..."
Illuminated by the light from within, they abandon that realm and are born here. You all should now swiftly dedicate yourselves to increase your roots of goodness.

O sons of gods, just as my celestial drum is neither male nor female, yet can produce immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable things, so too it is with you, sons and daughters of gods; though neither male nor female, you are able to receive [these benefits].
By means of various sublime palaces and gardens, just as my celestial drum is neither born nor extinguished,
so too are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither born nor extinguished. If you can attain awakening and understanding regarding this,
you should know that you have entered the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom.

The subsequent section provides an exegesis on the exhortation; herein there are six parts: first, the concordant exegesis for the sake of repaying kindness; second, the inverse exegesis beginning with "Those sons of gods who... and so forth;

third, the demonstration of the nature of that kindness beginning with "O sons of gods, you all... and so forth; fourth, the exhortation to proceed toward the increase of goodness beginning with "You all now...
and so forth; fifth, the demonstration of the Dharma for practice beginning with "O sons of gods, like my celestial drum... and so forth.

This refers to the teaching of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*). It is neither male nor female; it is used as a metaphor for non-arising and non-ceasing to manifest the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Sixth, "If you all can... and so forth, encourages practice to achieve benefit. Regarding the term "seal of non-reliance" (*anāśraya-mudrā*):

once one has realized non-arising, both subject and object are simultaneously stilled, and there is nothing whatsoever to rely upon; hence it is called "non-reliance. By means of this seal of wisdom, one seals and determines all phenomena.
Neither grasping nor retaining, the mind rests in its own natural ease; therefore, it is called samādhi.
At that time, having heard these sounds, the sons of the gods attained what they had never experienced before, and they immediately all transformed themselves into ten thousand clouds of flowers.
Ten thousand clouds of incense, ten thousand clouds of music, ten thousand clouds of banners, ten thousand clouds of canopies, and ten thousand clouds of songs of praise—
having thus performed these transformations, they immediately proceeded together to the palace where the Bodhisattva Vairocana dwells.
With palms joined in reverence, he stood to one side; desiring to pay his respects and behold [the Buddha], he was unable to see him.
Regarding the fifth section, "Following the Exhortation to Approach the Buddha," there are five parts. First: Offering oblations and not encountering [him].
At that time, a certain son of heaven spoke these words: "The Bodhisattva Vairocana has already passed away from here and been born into the human world in the household of King Śuddhodana.
He has ascended a sandalwood pavilion and now dwells within the womb of Queen Māyā."
Second, they heard of his location.
At that time, the sons of the gods, observing with their divine eyes, saw that the Bodhisattva’s body was dwelling among humans in the house of King Śuddhodana,
being served and honored by the Brahmā and Kāmadhātu devas.
Second, regarding the vision of descending to be born:

the assembly of devaputras all had this thought: "If we do not go to the Bodhisattva’s abode to inquire after his well-being, and if we allow even a single moment of attachment to arise toward this celestial palace, it would be improper. At that time, each individual deva...
The son, together with a retinue of ten nayutas, was about to descend to Jambudvīpa;
four of them resolved to go.
At that time, a sound issued from the celestial drum, announcing: "O sons of the gods, it is not by this death that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas pass away."
And he was born in that realm. However, by means of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he causes sentient beings to see him according to what is appropriate for their minds.
Fifth is the ritual for seeing the Buddha, which consists of two parts: first, teaching the recognition of rebirth so as to cause them to abandon distorted views;

second, teaching the arousal of the bodhicitta and the repentance of transgressions so that they may certainly behold him. Now, regarding the first: because he did not encounter [the Buddha] previously, he now beholds his descent into birth.
Not departing from existence and non-existence, their minds remain attached to "this" and "that. Therefore, the essence and function are revealed to manifest that there is neither death nor birth.
Within the text, there are the elements of principle, analogy, and application. Regarding the principle, it first warns against distorted views and subsequently demonstrates correct view.
Thus, one knows that what is produced through the Buddha’s transformation is not a matter of dying and being reborn.
"O sons of the gods, just as I am able to produce sound now without being seen by the eye,
so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who enters the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*): though not seen by the eye, he is able to manifest birth in various places,
free from conceptual discrimination, having eliminated pride, and remaining without attachment."
Second, the analogies; third, the application to the Bodhisattvas and below. Within this, first it is clarified that the Dharmakāya is unborn and all-pervasive yet invisible;
yet, its responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) are nowhere non-arising, being present everywhere, and appearing here as well for those who have the capacity to perceive them.

Why then need one go further down to Jambudvīpa? The section beginning with "Free from conceptual discrimination" reveals the virtues of these manifested births and dispels various views. By means of...
Non-conceptual wisdom arises; it is not said that there is a place selected for its arising. Although dwelling in the royal palace, he is free from arrogance;
although surrounded by devas, he is free from defiled attachment. In the second part of the subsequent text, [it says]:

"O sons of the gods, you should give rise to the resolve for awakening and repent your transgressions. This section has three parts: first, stating the intent of the outline; second, explaining according to the outline. Within the first:
This is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation of the characteristics. Now, for the first part, the presentation of the headings:

One who wishes to repent must recognize the ten minds of contrariness and conformity. That is to say, one must first recognize the ten kinds of minds that conform to birth and death as the objects to be remedied:

(1) recklessly calculating a personal self, giving rise to the view of a body; (2) possessing afflictions within while encountering adverse conditions without, such that the mind of "I" becomes exalted.

1. Having already fulfilled both internal and external conditions, one abandons wholesome deeds and takes no joy in the virtues of others. 2. One gives free rein to the three types of action (karma), committing every kind of evil.
3. Although one’s activities are not extensive, an evil mind pervades them all. 4. An evil mind continues in succession, uninterrupted day and night. 5.
One conceals and denies one’s faults, unwilling to let others know of them. 6. One is arrogant and impudent, acting with reckless violence and having no fear of evil.
The Path. Ninth, being shameless and lacking remorse, having no fear of either ordinary beings or sages. Tenth, repudiating cause and effect and becoming an icchantika.

Next, one gives rise to ten kinds of thoughts that oppose the cycle of birth and death, which are to be overturned and eliminated starting from the last: first, clearly believing in cause and effect; second, feeling personal shame and self-reproach;
third, fearing the evil realms; fourth, not concealing one's flaws; fifth, severing the continuous stream of [afflictive] mind; sixth...
1. To resolve upon Bodhicitta; 2. To cultivate merit and remedy transgressions; 3. To rejoice in the virtues of others; 4. To be mindful of the Buddhas of the ten directions; 5.
To contemplate the emptiness of the nature of offenses. These five points are all fully contained within these three sections, though their sequence differs.
The previous [section] followed the order of the arising of the mind, whereas this follows the order of superiority and inferiority.
"O sons of the gods, you should all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the first section of the initial instruction, which consists of four parts that remedy six faults; the first is the resolution for *bodhicitta*."
This serves as the basis for repentance; because it is the root of practice that encompasses all virtues, it is explained first and foremost.
