Whereas formerly his malevolent mind was pervasive and he brought peril upon others, now his compassion covers the entire Dharma-realm, extensively benefiting sentient beings.

Purifying one’s mind and abiding in virtuous deportment constitute the two aspects that take the purification of the three karmas as the essence of confession. Purifying one’s mind refers to the practice of mental stillness (*śamatha*).

Abiding in virtuous deportment encompasses both the prohibitions and the prescriptions; it means one should disclose [one's faults] without concealing defects, and sever the continuity of the [defiled] mind.

Reversing the previous six or seven [sections], one repents and eliminates all karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and obstructions to vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*).

Third, regarding the elimination of karmic obstructions—namely, the three of delusion, karma, and suffering, or the two obstructions of karma and its retribution—these are distinguished according to cause and effect. Since...

Regarding the confession of obstructive karmas: whereas [ordinary beings] fear the evil realms, here one turns that into fearlessness. Because the Son of Heaven has newly arrived from that realm, it is not explained in detail.
Among the afflictions, there are two types—sharp and dull—and among these, the severing of the roots of goodness through false views is the most fearsome.
This is explained separately as an obstruction to vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, because it obstructs both the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and vision, it is so designated;

the rest is as explained elsewhere. With bodies as numerous as all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), with heads as numerous as all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena, with tongues as numerous as all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena, and with virtuous bodily actions and virtuous speech as numerous as all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena...
Karma. With wholesome mental karma, one repents and eliminates all obstructive faults and evils.
One universally directs the four modes of mental activity until none remain. Since past transgressions have already pervaded all objects, one now repents those former errors;
thus, one universally employs the three karmas before every Buddha and before every sentient being, equalizing them throughout the realm of beings.
One should confess and repent all [faults]. Since both humans and devas, as well as ordinary beings and sages, are present for this confession, one must reproach oneself;

otherwise, one would lack shame and remorse. Because the mind operates universally, it causes the body and speech to operate universally. One first prostrates with the head, using the body as the whole;

the five wheels (the two knees, two elbows, and forehead) touch the ground. Regarding the term "universally" (*pian*), by what means is it universal? Therefore, the next line speaks of the "three virtuous karmas."
"Universal! This is precisely cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions, reversing the indulgence of the three karmas.
When the sons of the gods heard these words, they attained what they had never experienced before; their hearts were filled with great joy, and they asked him, saying:
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva repent and eliminate all faults and evils?
This second inquiry seeks the method for doing so. The previous statement was still brief; since the meaning of "elimination" was not fully exhausted, this question follows next.
At that time, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi, the celestial drum emitted a voice, proclaiming:

"The third is the True Teaching according to the Dharma. This True Teaching contemplates the emptiness of the nature of offenses, while simultaneously revealing those who falsely conceptualize a self or person and deny cause and effect, as well as those who encounter adverse external conditions."
"O sons of the gods, the bodhisattva knows that all karmas do not come from the east, nor do they come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below;
rather, they accumulate and abide within the mind. They arise solely from inversion and have no place of abiding.
Thus does the bodhisattva clearly perceive with certainty, free from doubt."

Next is the formal explanation of the instructions, which is divided into five parts: first, the specific contemplation on the emptiness of karma; second, the general contemplation on the four obstacles;
third, the specific contemplation on the afflictions of views; fourth, contemplating retribution in relation to karma; and fifth, a summary of the benefits of repentance. Regarding the first:

since karma is the cause of retribution and the foremost of the three obstacles, it has no pre-existing essence and does not come from the ten directions; this precisely reveals the meaning of emptiness.
It arises solely from inversion. This explains the reason for emptiness: because the ocean of karmic obstructions arises from false conceptualization, it lacks intrinsic nature.
When this wisdom of emptiness is made to correspond with the mind, one will be certain and free from doubt; being able to know in this way, [one realizes the truth].
They are then called Bodhisattvas.

O sons of gods, just as I, the celestial drum, speak of karma, speak of its retribution, speak of conduct, speak of precepts, speak of joy, speak of peace, and speak of various samādhis, so too do all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They speak of "I" and "mine," and they speak of sentient beings.
The various karmas of greed, hatred, and delusion are in reality devoid of a self and devoid of what belongs to a self;
though one searches throughout the ten directions for the retributions of the six realms resulting from all such actions performed, they are entirely unfindable.

Second, there is the general contemplation of the four obstacles, using the metaphor of the celestial drum preaching the Dharma without speaking. This metaphor illustrates that while the conventional exists, the ultimate is non-existent.

In the initial part of the metaphor, the objects to be remedied are presented, namely the two obstacles of karma and its retribution. Subsequently, the five practices and so forth are taught; these are the remedies, namely:

performing good deeds, ceasing evil, rejoicing in others' merit, establishing others in virtue, and abiding in samādhi. Finally, the section beginning with "all Buddhas" correlates these points with the actual teaching.

Within this, first, following worldly convention, it is said that "I" and "mine" exist; these are the obstacle of views (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*). It is further stated that greed, hatred, and delusion are the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Subsequently, however, in reality, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they do not exist. These two textual passages—existence and non-existence—are concise summaries of the three obstacles.
Since there is no "mine," the first false conceptualization of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) is overturned.

"O sons of the gods, it is just as when the sound of my voice neither arises nor ceases, yet the various devas who have committed evil do not hear any other sound, but hear only the sound that awakens them regarding the hells. All karmic actions are likewise: they neither arise nor cease."
According to what one cultivates and accumulates, one receives its retribution.
Third, the specific refutation of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Because these delusions of view are deep and perilous, they are extensively refuted.

The text contains three metaphors. First, the metaphor of the drum having no arising or ceasing yet following sound; this illustrates that although karma has no arising, it evokes retribution according to cultivation. This refers to the aforementioned contemplation.
Karma is empty; this is to dispel the attachment to its existence. If one were to claim that it is [merely] empty, such a person could not be transformed by any Buddha.
Therefore, what is now revealed is that it is not a nihilistic non-existence, overturning and refuting the denial of cause and effect.
O sons of the gods, just as the sounds produced by my celestial drum cannot be exhausted throughout immeasurable eons and are without interruption, yet neither coming nor going can be apprehended;
so it is with these sounds. O sons of the gods, if there were coming and going, there would be the extremes of annihilation and permanence.
All Buddhas do not proclaim any dharma of annihilation or permanence, except as a skillful means for the sake of maturing beings.
Sentient beings.

Second is the analogy of sound having neither coming nor going, which illustrates the return to the Middle Way. To hold that things definitely exist is eternalism; to hold that they definitely do not exist is nihilism. Both are dualistic extremes;
therefore, both views are simultaneously refuted to reveal the transcendence of annihilation and permanence. In the text, the analogy is presented first: "O sons of the gods..."

If there were a lower conjunction, or if there were something that could come, it would be eternal; if it departs and does not return, it would be annihilated. Therefore, although it is empty, it is not annihilated;
although it exists, it is not eternal.
O sons of the gods, it is like my voice: throughout immeasurable worlds, it is heard by all sentient beings according to their respective mental dispositions.
All Buddhas are likewise; they cause all sentient beings to behold them according to their respective mental dispositions.
The third analogy, the sound of the drum following the mind, illustrates that the Buddha is perceived through the mind.

It dispels the fixed attachment to a ritual master existing outside the mind, causing one to truly contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions and thereby overturning and breaking external adverse conditions.
O sons of the gods, it is as if there were a crystal mirror called "The Illuminator," pure, translucent,
and equal in measure to ten worlds, wherein all mountains and rivers and all sentient beings within immeasurable and boundless lands are reflected.
"Even down to the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts—all their reflected images appear therein.
O sons of the gods, what do you think? Can those various images be said to come into the mirror or go out from the mirror?"
He replied, "No, O sons of the gods. It is the same with all karmas; although they can produce the retributions of karma, they have no place from which they come or to which they go.
O sons of the gods, it should be known that all karmas are just like a magician who deceives the eyes of men."

The fourth pair examines the retribution of karma. The text contains two metaphors. First, the metaphor of the illusory substance of a mirror-image, which illustrates that although something exists, it is non-existent.
That is to say, a mirror-image appears in dependence upon a mirror; the image neither comes nor goes. How could retribution, which arises in dependence upon karma, have coming or going?
Second, the metaphor of a magician deluding the eyes, which illustrates how karma summons retribution: though it does not exist, it appears to exist. Furthermore, karma is also like this.
It is an illusion. Furthermore, that illusion is neither existent nor non-existent; it is precisely the Middle Way.
To know it thus is true repentance, whereby all evils and transgressions are entirely purified.

The fifth section is a summary of the benefits of repentance, which may be understood as follows. The preceding portion clarifies how those who have come from the hells to be born as sons of gods hear the Dharma and repent;
the following portion clarifies the benefits.
At the time this Dharma was being taught, within worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, [the beings of] Tuṣita...
The various devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) devaputras of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
All the celestial maidens within the six heavens of the desire realm relinquished their female bodies and gave rise to the aspiration for supreme enlightenment.

The sixth is the benefit of seeing and hearing. This section has two parts. First, it clarifies the benefit for the other assemblies: because the sound [of the teaching] is heard everywhere through the power of samādhi.
At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard the exposition of Samantabhadra’s Vast Dedication and attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*), obtained the various powers (*bala*).

Because of the Adornment Samādhi, the text next correctly establishes the benefits for those who are the appropriate recipients. This section has two parts: first, the primary benefit; second, the successive benefits beginning with "the fragrant clouds therein.
Within the first part, there are also two sections: first, obtaining the benefit of the Dharma; second, the benefit of sentient beings seeing the Buddha.
First, all [versions] contain the character "hence" (故). This seems to function as a restatement of what preceded as a reason, implying that seeing the Buddha serves as a benefit;

yet, since there was no prior text stating that one attains the stages of the ten directions, of what would this be a restatement? For this reason, the Jin translations all lack the character "hence."

It should be said that by hearing the exposition of Samantabhadra’s vast and extensive dedication, one immediately attains the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and acquires the samādhi adorned with all powers (*bala*).
The former phrase refers to attaining the [spiritual] positions, while the latter phrase refers to accomplishing the practices; for one partially attains the ten powers as an adornment.

By means of the purification of the three karmas equal in number to all sentient beings, and through the repentance and removal of all heavy obstructions, one immediately beholds lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems, as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.

Upon each flower, there is a bodhisattva sitting in the full lotus posture, emitting great radiance; from each of those bodhisattvas' secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), multitudes [of light rays] are emitted.

There arise lights equal in number to all sentient beings. Within those lights, there are Buddhas equal in number to all sentient beings, seated in the full lotus posture, preaching the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings;
yet they have not yet manifested even a small portion of the power of the *vimala-samādhi* (Stainless Samādhi).

At that time, those devaputras, with the aforementioned various flowers, further emanated from each and every pore of their bodies clouds of exquisite flowers equal in number to all sentient beings, as an offering to Vairocana Tathāgata; they held them and scattered them over the Buddha.
All [beings] abide within the body of the Buddha.

Second, clarifying the benefit of seeing the Buddha, which has three parts: first, clarifying the cause for seeing; second, "that very seeing" (the initial phrase), which correctly clarifies the act of seeing the Buddha.

Third, at that time, they offered worship with a reverent mind. Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned," it refers to the fact that the flowers previously held while approaching the Buddha had not yet been scattered.
As for the flowers emerging from the pores, this is because they have already attained the stages (*bhūmi*). Since the flowers were mentioned first, they are cited here briefly;
however, among what was held above were incense, canopies, and so forth, and thus below one sees incense and canopies, all of which are likewise accomplished.
Furthermore, those clouds of incense rain universally upon worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable Buddha-fields.

If there are sentient beings whose bodies are touched by this fragrance, their bodies become peaceful and blissful, just like a bhikṣu who has entered the fourth dhyāna. All karmic obstructions are... [purified].

It is extinguished. Regarding the second [section], the benefits of successive progression, there are two: first, the benefit of smelling the fragrance; second, the benefit of seeing the covering. Both are accomplished based on the previous offerings. Now, for the first:

it consists of the dharma, the metaphor, and their synthesis. Within the dharma, because one is freed from obstructions, one attains the bliss of liberation; therefore, it is illustrated by a metaphor.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are no eight calamities.

If there are those who hear this, those sentient beings possess five hundred internal afflictions regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and likewise five hundred external afflictions.
Those whose conduct is dominated by greed number twenty-one thousand; those whose conduct is dominated by hatred...

Those with a predominance of desire are twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of delusion are twenty-one thousand; and those with equal proportions of the three poisons are twenty-one thousand.
Next, by means of the cessation of obstacles, one attains pure roots of goodness; this constitutes the characteristic of benefit. In the text, that which is manifested first is...
"Extinction" refers to eighty-four thousand [afflictions]. Regarding this, there are two ancient interpretations. The first states: "Sentient beings have ten root afflictions;
however, each of these delusions further possesses ten powers, thus totaling one hundred. These should be calculated as being divided into nine grades."
However, because the superior grade is heavy, it is divided into three grades; because the middle and lower grades are light, each is made into one grade.

Combined, these constitute five hundred [types of afflictions]. They arise with respect to internal and external objects; that is, one's own five sense-objects are considered internal, while the five sense-objects of others are considered external.

Each of these five categories has five hundred types, totaling five thousand. When these are further distinguished according to delusion regarding each of the Four Noble Truths, they become twenty thousand.
Adding the original one thousand, there are twenty-one thousand. Based on their distribution among the three poisons and so forth, they constitute eighty-four thousand.
This is fully detailed in the sutra text itself; other matters are not the intent of the sutra and are therefore not recorded here at length.
Having understood that all these are entirely false and illusory, and having known them thus, one accomplishes the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of Fragrant Banner Clouds.
Subsequently, this reveals the capacity for cessation; that is, by understanding that the essence of delusion is empty, it naturally does not arise. Thus, the Jin translation says: "These various..."
All afflictions are completely extinguished. Because they are extinguished, there is purity; delusion vanishes and wisdom manifests, which is the light of mastery.
The roots of goodness are perfected. The phrase "clouds of fragrant banners" refers to the roots of goodness of the ninth stage.
If there are sentient beings who see this canopy, they plant as many roots of goodness as the sands of one Ganges River, becoming a Wheel-Turning King of a Pure Golden Net.
Regarding the second benefit of seeing the canopy, there are two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the benefits obtained; second, "The Buddha-sons dwelling here... and so forth.
This clarifies the increasing benefit of the transformation through gathering and conversion. First, according to the Jin translation of the sutra:

"The roots of goodness planted by as many wheel-turning sage-kings as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River—such as the wheel-turning king *Śuklavimalaratnajāla* and others. This refers to many wheel-turning kings, not merely the many roots of goodness of a single wheel-turning king.
The Sanskrit original is likewise. As for the phrase "one Ganges River [of sands]": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)*
This refers to those from the nine stages prior up to the copper-wheel [stage] of the tenth abiding (*daśabhūmi*).

The scope of those transformed by these ten stages is compared to the sands of the Ganges as being greater than before; thus, the Jin translation states, "The wheel-turning kings such as Ratnajāla," where the term "such as" (*ādi*) includes the preceding categories.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this station of the universal monarch, they teach and transform sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.

Regarding the second section, "The Transformation through Gathering and Benefiting," there are two parts. First, the stage of attaining benefit is explained; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, as if having attained the first dhyāna" onwards, the actual attainment of benefit is established.
Now, for the first part, there is the teaching, the analogy, and the synthesis. Within the teaching, the limits of gathering and transforming beings are directly clarified.
This has already been explained as before.

O Son of the Buddha! For example, in the world-system of the Tathāgata Candraprabhajñāna, there are always immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās from various worlds who manifest their bodies and come to hear the Dharma.
He extensively expounded upon the accounts of his past lives without a single moment of interruption.
Any sentient being who hears the name of that Buddha will certainly attain rebirth in that Buddha’s land.
Among the two similes, the first—where transformation is continuous and uninterrupted—illustrates the teaching and transformation of sentient beings within the superior dharma.

The latter—where those who hear the name will certainly be born in that land—illustrates the correspondence in the inferior [dharma], wherein encountering this light results in attaining the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
It is likewise for a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the position of a Universal Monarch with a pure golden net:
if anyone should even briefly encounter its light, they will certainly attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva, by virtue of the power of the roots of goodness previously cultivated.

Regarding the initial general synthesis within the subsequent section, according to the Jin translation, there is likewise the phrase "furthermore, below, he emits the sovereign light of the *māndārava* flowers.
In the present scripture, this is implicitly contained within the subsequent analogy of synthesis; it refers to the "emission of the pure light from the *maṇi* crest.
If one were to simply say "he encountered this light," there would be no prior textual basis for the emission of light. Therefore...

It is as previously stated. Regarding the phrase "attaining the ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*): this chapter contains three successive layers of the sudden and perfect attainment of the ten stages, and is therefore called "progressive benefit.
First, the sons of the gods hear the drum preaching the Dharma and attain the ten stages. Second, from the hair-pores of these sons of the gods, clouds of flower-canopies emerge;
those who see them attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), which is itself the ten stages. Third, the Wheel-Turning King emits...

Light. Those who encounter it further attain the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). These three stages are all equal; they are simultaneously and instantaneously accomplished in as many varieties as there are atoms.
This is the benefit produced within a single light of a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*). It is even more difficult to describe the benefits of the remaining lights and marks.
The phrase "by the power of roots of goodness previously cultivated" clarifies that this is an instantaneous benefit.
This is due to the cause. Because they have heard the Universal Dharma and cultivated universal goodness,

O Son of the Buddha, just as one who has attained the first dhyāna sees all the palaces in the Brahma-heaven and experiences the bliss of the Brahma-world even before their life has ended, so it is for all who attain the various dhyānas.
In the second section on the benefit of accomplishing virtue, there is first the analogy, followed by the application to the Bodhisattva below. The meaning of the analogy is as follows:

just as one who has attained the form-realm concentrations (*rūpadhyāna*) through cultivation in the desire realm sees objects of the form realm with eyes belonging to the desire realm, so too does the Bodhisattva, through the power of the Dharma, suddenly realize and see the realms of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) while not yet having transformed his ordinary body.
Thus, that which would otherwise require three great eons (*tri-kalpa-asaṃkhyeya*) can be reached in a single thought-moment.
Because it clarifies that the one encompasses all; and because it clarifies that throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes, not even a single stage is exhausted, for all are encompassed by the one.
Such mastery over slowness and speed belongs to this Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) alone, and not to other schools.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the station of a Wheel-Turning King with a Pure Golden Net. He emits the pure radiance from his maṇi-crest.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they all attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva.
They achieve immeasurable radiance of wisdom and obtain the ten kinds of pure eyes, up to the ten kinds of pure minds, fully endowed with them.
He has attained immeasurable and profound samādhis and has accomplished such pure fleshly eyes.

In this combined section, the first part correctly clarifies the attainment of benefits, while the subsequent part, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, even if," reveals the boundaries of the objective realm.
Regarding the first part: the phrase "attaining the tenth stage of a bodhisattva" reiterates the preceding combined section, wherein the virtues are based upon the stages.
It is established. This is why it is restated; otherwise, it would imply that light was emitted twice, and each time one would have attained the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the statement "to achieve such pure physical eyes" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): this means that the aforementioned virtues of the ten eyes are all achieved through the physical eyes of an ordinary body (*pṛthagjana-kāya*);
therefore, he concludes by referring to them in this way.

O Son of the Buddha! Suppose there were a person who took as many buddha-fields as there are in a hundred million nayutas of buddha-fields and ground them into atoms, such that each atom represents one buddha-field.

Then, taking as many buddha-fields as there are in those atoms and grinding them again into atoms, he places all these atoms in his left hand and travels eastward, dropping a single atom after passing as many worlds as there are atoms. In this manner...
Proceeding eastward until these atoms are exhausted, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below— thus,
all worlds throughout the ten directions, whether they are occupied by atoms or not, are entirely integrated to form a single buddha-field.
Next, regarding the clarification of the boundaries of the objective realm (*viṣaya-pramāṇa*): this demonstrates that the range of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is vast.

If even the fleshly eye is thus, how much more so the other eyes, which are profound and wondrous beyond description. This section consists of two parts; first, a provisional illustration is provided to demonstrate the multiplicity of the objective realm.
Next, the capacity to perceive is correctly elucidated; finally, the conclusion of these virtues and their ultimate destination is presented. The first section is divided into three parts.
First, the single-layered vastness is explained: "O Ratnapāṇi, what do you think? Is such a buddha-field as vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable? He replied, "No.
Such a buddha-field is indeed vast, immeasurable, rare, extraordinary, and inconceivable. If...
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this parable, are able to give rise to faith and understanding, you should know that they are even more rare and wondrous.
The Buddha said, "Ratnapāṇi, it is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who hear this parable and give rise to faith, I bestow upon them the prediction that they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
...anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. One shall obtain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.
Next, the extensive [teaching] is revealed through question and answer:
"Bhadrabāhu, suppose there were another person who, with [offerings as vast as] the number of atoms in a thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields as described above..."

Grind a buddha-field into fine dust. Using these particles as a basis for the previous analogy, exhaust them one by one until even a single buddha-field has been reassembled and ground again into dust.
Proceeding in this manner through successive iterations, continue until eighty such cycles have passed.
Multiplying the previous number three times further reveals its vastness.
Thus, all the atoms within such vast Buddha-fields, a bodhisattva’s pure physical eye can clearly perceive in a single thought-moment.
They also see Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten billion vast Buddha-lands.
Just as a crystal mirror of pure radiance illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, the second part clearly explains the capacity for vision.
First, one sees the atoms of the aforementioned vast fields; that the physical eye can see this is already transcendent, let alone in a single thought-moment.
Next, it also sees below, clarifying the vision of many Buddhas. Finally, "just as a crystal... and so forth.
This is the mark of clear vision; for there is no mind and no coming or going.
Ratnapāṇi, all such things are accomplished through the roots of merit and the profound samādhi of the Universal Monarch of the Pure Golden Net.

The third section concludes by dedicating the merit to the excellence of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). This chapter of the sutra is not yet complete. The preceding section on the differentiated causes and effects is finished.
Supplementary Note: These three chapters of the sutra on the inconceivable Dharma clarify the cultivation and arising of the sublime within the context of differentiated causes.

This is the fruit-virtue of awakening. First, the "Inconceivable Dharma" reveals the inconceivable ocean of marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) of the virtues of the *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya*.
Next, the two chapters clarify the inconceivable virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Because in the causal stage each and every practice was cultivated while being accorded with the universal Dharma-realm, the resultant marks of reward now each and every one are bodies that pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is said that there are "marks of a great man as numerous as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury worlds."
The characteristics are such as these; his body may likewise be known. Yet within each individual mark there are many excellent secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

Taken collectively, the merits of the bodily marks are inconceivable and difficult to express in words. Therefore, I shall briefly cite the very last mark, that of the wheels on the soles of the feet.
This mark possesses many excellent secondary signs; now, I shall mention one among them, which constantly emits forty...
Various kinds of light rays emanate; now there is but a single ray that shines downward to illuminate the sentient beings in the hells who suffer extreme agony.
These beings are freed from suffering and reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where they hear the Dharma being preached by celestial drums and immediately realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Having realized the ten stages, they offer the incense, flowers, canopies, and other items they carry to the Buddha. Those who smell the fragrance or see the canopies likewise ascend [to the same state].
The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding this second turning, those who ascend to the Ten Grounds emit light, causing all who encounter that light to likewise realize the Ten Grounds.

Thus, the merit of the Ten Grounds being perfected instantaneously through these three stages is entirely accomplished by the light emitted from within a single auspicious mark (*lakṣaṇa*) on the sole of the foot. Now, the merit of even the lowest of these auspicious marks is such as this.

If even this is inconceivable, how much more so are the merits of his manifold virtues and marks? If the radiance of his physical body is thus, how much less conceivable can be the light of wisdom of the Dharma-body?
This is precisely what is meant in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* when it says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. This is for those who study the Buddha-dharma.
To speak of the merit of these three grades while explaining the wisdom of the Buddhas is like using a firefly’s glow to illuminate the four continents.
*The Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 48.

The Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Kuang at Fayun Temple, Hanshan, provides this exegesis on the thirty-sixth chapter, "The Practice of Samantabhadra.

Regarding the initial intent [of this section], there is first the general and then the specific. The general refers to how these two chapters clarify the causes and effects of manifestation; therefore, it follows next...
It comes forth. It is also called "Equal Cause and Effect. This means that by synthesizing the previously mentioned differentiated causes, one accomplishes this perfect cause of Samantabhadra;
and by synthesizing the differentiated fruits, one accomplishes the fruit of the manifestation of the nature-arising (*xingqi*).

Furthermore, while the former was based on cultivation through production (*xiusheng*), this is based on cultivation through manifestation (*xiuxian*). If this is so, why is there no further separate question? And why does it conclude with the "differentiated fruits"?
Yet there was no auspicious sign. Does an auspicious sign occur only at the conclusion of the causes of equality? It is precisely by this principle that it is revealed as preceding this assembly;
if one were to ask about it separately, there would be a disjunction. Because it is intended to connect with what precedes, it is not separated by an auspicious sign.

The Universal Dharma (Pufa) is rare and extraordinary; there are distinct auspicious signs for both cause and fruit. Furthermore, there ought to have been an auspicious sign previously, but it is absent because the scripture has not yet reached its end.

"Separately" means that because the sequence of meaning in this chapter proceeds from cause to effect, it also serves as a remote response to the question regarding "the practice" at the beginning of the second assembly, as well as the questions concerning the "inconceivable" chapter and the invocation of original vows.

Thus, although these have already been answered previously, they are clarified again here because the latter two are profound and subtle—just as the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are the most exquisite among the primary marks (lakṣaṇa). — Ancient Commentary.

The specific virtues constitute a single section on cause and effect. Second, regarding the explanation of the names: first, to generally reveal the meaning of the two categories, it is called "cultivation arising based on nature" and "function arising based on nature.
Because their differentiated characteristics are exhausted and the essence of cause and effect is uniform, it is termed "equal cause and effect.
Furthermore, the cause is the cause of fruition, its measure pervading the Dharma-realm; the fruit is the fruit of fruition, its objective sphere being like space.
Because cause and effect together exhaust [all obstacles] to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings in the future, it is called "Manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*).

Specifically, the title of this chapter is "Samantabhadra," which indicates the person to manifest the Dharma; it clarifies that this practice is not a sequential method. "The Practitioner" (*caryā*) manifests the Dharma rather than the person;

the chapter clarifies the practice itself, not the human body of the practitioner. Its virtue pervades the *dharmadhātu*, thus it is "Universal" (*samanta*); it is supremely compliant, harmonious, and virtuous.
It is called "Worthy" (*bhadra*). To cultivate practice based on one's nature is called "conduct" (*caryā*).

Although the conduct of Samantabhadra appears frequently by name in various sutras and is explained extensively within this chapter, I shall now briefly manifest ten meanings to represent its inexhaustibility: 1. **The Universality of What is Sought**:

This means that one must seek to realize that which all Tathāgatas have equally realized. 2. **The Universality of Those to be Converted**: Within the space of a single hair-tip, there are... [text continues]
1. Universality of sentient beings: because all sentient beings are transformed and perfected. 2. Universality of what is severed: because there is not a single delusion that is not severed.
3. Universality of the practice of phenomena: because there is not a single phenomenon that is not practiced. 4. Universality of the practice of principle:
because the aforementioned practices of phenomena all penetrate the source of principle, as the nature is fully endowed. 5. Universality of unimpeded practice: as mentioned above...
2. Universality of mutual penetration: because the two are mutually pervasive. 7. Universality of the practice of fusion: because each and every practice is fused and subsumed without end.
8. Universality of the arising of function: because there is no function that is not possible, and none that is not all-pervasive.

9. Universality of the spheres of practice: because the aforementioned gates are practiced throughout the Indra-net of lands. 10. Universality of the timing of practice: because it exhausts the three periods of time.

Because the contemplation of eons and kalpas is perfectly interfused without end; and because the aforementioned ten practices are interpenetrating yet unmixed, and though traversed they are infinitely layered, when Sudhana enters a single pore of Samantabhadra, the Dharma-gates he attains exceed those from all his other spiritual friends by unspeakably many times.
Furthermore, these aforementioned ten practices may be collectively subsumed into two: if one considers Samantabhadra as being after the stages, then one has attained the fruit.
Abandoning causes and penetrating to the ultimate limit constitutes the conduct of Samantabhadra.

To manifest the Dharma through persons, the conduct of Samantabhadra is such that if one is Samantabhadra prior to or during a stage, one becomes a person through virtue; yet if one simply cultivates universal conduct, one is called Samantabhadra.
Thus, Samantabhadra is itself the conduct, and the name is derived solely from this conduct. This applies even if one is Samantabhadra only after the stages.
[The Bodhisattva] practices. There is no bestowing upon those of lower station. A detailed explanation of Samantabhadra is as distinguished in the first assembly.

Regarding the three points of essential purport (*piṇḍārtha*), there is again both a general and a specific [explanation]. Generally, the two chapters clarify equality of cause and fruit as the essential purport, while the reconciliation of previous distinctions constitutes the goal.
Specifically, this chapter clarifies the perfect cause of equality as the essential purport, and the non-duality of the accomplishment of the fruit of equality as the goal.
[The Buddha] proceeded. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra again addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, what has been expounded just now is merely a brief description of a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realm, presented in accordance with the capacities and dispositions of the various sentient beings."
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of sentient beings who, out of ignorance, commit evil deeds;
who conceive of a self and what belongs to a self, clinging to the body; who are subject to perversions, doubt, false views, and conceptual discrimination;
and who are constantly bound by the fetters of affliction, following the stream of birth and death and remaining far removed from the path of the Tathāgata. Therefore, they manifest in the world.

The text consists of two parts: this chapter distinguishes the cause, while the subsequent chapter clarifies the result. Within the former, there are also two sections: first, a direct exposition in prose; second, a restatement in verse.

Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the formal teaching; second, the auspicious signs as proof. Regarding the first of these, there are also two sections: first, the clarification of the causes for the teaching;
second, the formal presentation of the present subject matter, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... Within the first of these, there is also...

Two: First, the preceding brief explanation is indicated; second, the reasons for this are investigated and explained. Regarding the first: "Spoken by Samantabhadra" uses a person to represent the Dharma.

"As previously mentioned" refers back to the Chapter on the Secondary Marks (*anuvyañjana*), because for sentient beings in the hells who possess heavy obstructions, he briefly explained a small portion of the application of the secondary marks;
a detailed explanation would be inconceivable. Second, this generally refers back to what preceded.

The fruit described therein constitutes a limited scope, for the ocean of fruition transcends all words. Although these three—the distant, the pervasive, and the differentiated—involve cause and effect, they possess the principle of perfect interfusion;

yet, because they distinguish the causes and effects of the five stages sequentially and adapt to the capacities and ailments of beings without exhausting the source of the Dharma, they are termed "limited.
This, in turn, reveals that the subsequent [stage] of equal cause and effect accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
To speak of the perfect integration of cause and effect is called the "vast teaching. Within the two sections of inquiry and explanation, the intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Why was the former termed the "lesser teaching"? Regarding the explanation, there are two points. First, it establishes why the various Buddhas appear in the world:
because sentient beings possess the ten faults such as ignorance (*avidyā*), it is not yet appropriate to teach extensively; therefore, the distinctions and so forth were first clarified. Second...
This refers to what arises subsequently. That is to say, once sentient beings have passed beyond [the initial stage], their obstructions and karmic burdens are inexhaustible;
thus, when one is treated, all are treated, and when one manifests, all manifest. Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, cause and effect likewise extend to the furthest limits of time.
Because that which preceded continues to follow without end, ten faults are mentioned: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, unwholesome volitional formations (*akuśala-saṃskāra*). These two—

This serves as a general summary. Next, all six [factors] are ignorance (*avidyā*). Third, they involve conceiving of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*). Fourth, it is because of attachment to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

As the *Six Grounds* (*Ṣaḍbhūmika*) states: "The worldly acquisition of a body is entirely due to attachment to the self. Fifth, they consist of the three inversions (*viparyāsa*) and the four inversions, which cannot be decisively severed.
Sixth, deviating from correct principle; seventh, pervasive conceptual construction; eighth, being constantly bound by fetters;

ninth, following the stream of birth and death—the meaning of this applies to both karma and suffering, as it refers to the stream of causes and the stream of results; tenth, being far removed from the conduct of the Tathāgata and following a wrong path—this constitutes the fault.
The designations such as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth are as explained in the standard treatises.
"O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater fault than for Bodhisattvas to give rise to a mind of anger toward other Bodhisattvas.
Second, the formal presentation of the conduct of Samantabhadra has two parts: first, clarifying the vastness of what is to be remedied; second, "therefore, all... [and so forth].
The Bodhisattva is able to remedy what is profound and subtle from below. Now, since a single delusion constitutes a million obstacles, then one obstacle is all obstacles;
thus it is for every delusion. For now, we follow the general explanation. The text has three parts: first, the heading;
second, the inquiry and explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first part: among all [afflictions], hatred is the heaviest. Apart from hatred, if one searches everywhere else, none [is found].
There is no evil as grave as anger. Thus, the Jin (Chinese) translation of the sutra states:
"Among all evils, there is none that surpasses this single thought of anger. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:

"A bodhisattva would rather give rise to a hundred thousand thoughts of greed than a single thought of anger, for nothing violates and harms great compassion more than this. Regarding the phrase "toward another bodhisattva," if...
To give rise to anger toward a bodhisattva is an even more grievous fault, because it causes the bodhisattva to abandon the Great Practice.
For this reason, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that when the celestial Māra sees various bodhisattvas mutually criticizing one another, he always rejoices greatly.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of anger toward other bodhisattvas, they immediately bring about hundreds of thousands of millions of gateways to obstruction.
Second, the interrogation and explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts.

First, the general manifestation: What are the one million obstacles? They are as follows: the obstacle of not seeing bodhi; the obstacle of not hearing the true Dharma; the obstacle of being born in impure worlds;
the obstacle of being born in the various evil destinies; the obstacle of being born in places of difficulty; the obstacle of having many diseases; and the obstacle of having much... [text truncated]
The obstacle of being slandered and defamed; the obstacle of being born in dull and obtuse realms of existence; the obstacle of losing right mindfulness; the obstacle of lacking wisdom;

the obstacle of the eye; the obstacle of the ear; the obstacle of the nose; the obstacle of the tongue; the obstacle of the body; the obstacle of the mind; the obstacle of evil spiritual friends; and the obstacle of evil associates.

The obstacle of delighting in practicing the Hīnayāna; the obstacle of delighting in associating with the vulgar and ordinary; the obstacle of lacking faith in those of great majestic power; the obstacle of delighting in dwelling together with those who are devoid of right view;
the obstacle of being born into non-Buddhist sects; the obstacle of abiding within the realm of Māra; the obstacle of being separated from the Buddha’s true teaching;
the obstacle of not seeing virtuous friends; the obstacle of hindrances to the roots of goodness; the obstacle of increasing unwholesome dharmas; and the obstacle of attaining inferior states.
The obstacle of dwelling [in such states]; the obstacle of being born in a borderland; the obstacle of being born into a family of evil people; the obstacle of being born among evil deities;
the obstacles of being born among evil nāgas, evil yakṣas, evil gandharvas, evil asuras, evil garuḍas, evil kiṃnaras, evil mahoragas, and evil rākṣasas;
the obstacle of taking no delight in the Buddha-dharma; the obstacle of practicing the ways of the ignorant; and the obstacle of attachment to [worldly] pleasures.
The obstacle of the Hīnayāna; the obstacle of taking no delight in the Mahāyāna; the obstacle of being naturally prone to alarm and fear; the obstacle of constant mental anxiety and distress;

the obstacle of attachment to birth and death (saṃsāra); the obstacle of not being single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-dharma; the obstacle of not rejoicing in seeing or hearing of the Buddha’s sovereign supernormal powers;

the obstacle of not attaining the various faculties of a bodhisattva; the obstacle of not practicing the pure conduct of a bodhisattva; and the obstacle of retreating from the profound resolve of a bodhisattva. Not...

It creates obstacles to the great vows of a bodhisattva; it creates obstacles to generating the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*); it creates obstacles to indolence regarding the practices of a bodhisattva;

it creates obstacles to being unable to purify and treat all karmas; it creates obstacles to being unable to gather great merit; it creates obstacles to the power of wisdom being unable to become clear and sharp; it creates obstacles to severing vast wisdom;
it creates obstacles to not protecting and upholding the various practices of a bodhisattva; and it creates obstacles to delighting in slandering [the One Vehicle].

The obstacle to the speech of omniscience; the obstacle that distances one from the bodhi of all Buddhas; the obstacle of delighting in dwelling within the realm of Māras; the obstacle of not single-mindedly cultivating the realm of the Buddhas;
the obstacle of not resolutely generating the great vows of a Bodhisattva; the obstacle of not delighting in dwelling together with Bodhisattvas;

the obstacle of not seeking the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva; the obstacle of a nature characterized by excessive views and doubt; the obstacle of a mind that is constantly dull and darkened; the obstacle of not...
Because they are unable to practice the bodhisattva’s impartial giving, the obstacle of non-renunciation arises;

because they are unable to uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts, the obstacle of breaking the precepts arises; because they are unable to enter the gate of patience, the obstacles of delusion, affliction, and hatred arise;

because they are unable to practice the bodhisattva’s great diligence, the obstacle of the stain of indolence arises; and because they are unable to attain the various samādhis, the [obstacle of distraction] arises.
The obstacle of distraction; the obstacle of impaired wisdom arising from not cultivating the *prajñāpāramitā*;
the obstacle of lack of skill regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); the obstacle of lack of skillful means regarding the deliverance of sentient beings;
the obstacle of being unable to investigate the wisdom of a bodhisattva; and the obstacle of being unable to comprehend the bodhisattva’s methods of renunciation. These are not accomplished.

Because the Bodhisattva lacks the ten kinds of vast eyes, there is the obstruction of being like one born blind; because the ears do not hear the unimpeded Dharma, there is the obstruction of being like a mute sheep;

because the marks and signs are incomplete, there is the obstruction of the impaired faculty of the nose; because one cannot discern the languages of sentient beings, there is the obstruction of failing to perfect the faculty of the tongue;
because one treats sentient beings with contempt, there is the obstruction of failing to perfect the faculty of the body; [and] the mind...

Because of much mental derangement, one accomplishes the obstacle to the faculty of mind (*manas*). Because of not maintaining the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), one accomplishes the obstacle to physical action (*kāyakarman*).

Because of constantly giving rise to the four kinds of faults, one accomplishes the obstacle to verbal action (*vākkarman*). Because of frequently generating greed, hatred, and wrong views, one accomplishes the obstacle to mental action (*manaskarman*).
[These are] the obstacle of seeking the Dharma with a thieving mind, and the obstacle of severing the sphere of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the Bodhisattva...
There is the obstacle of generating cowardice within the courageous Dharma; the obstacle of generating indolence regarding the bodhisattva’s path of renunciation;
the obstacle of generating cessation within the gateways of the bodhisattva’s wisdom-light;
the obstacle of generating weakness within the bodhisattva’s power of mindfulness; the obstacle of being unable to uphold the Tathāgata’s teaching; and regarding the bodhisattva...
The obstacle of being unable to approach the path that transcends birth; the obstacle of being unable to cultivate the unerring path for bodhisattvas;
the obstacle of conforming to the fixed positions of the two vehicles; and the obstacle of distancing oneself from the lineage of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
Next, regarding the enumeration of the obstacles: although they are designated as being in the hundreds of thousands, I shall briefly list one hundred categories.

Ancient masters categorized them into five stages based on their positions; while this is not without reason, consider this: if one seeks the Dharma with a thieving mind, how could it merely obstruct the first stage?

It is known that these obstacles pervade all stages; if even faith does not arise, what need is there to mention the subsequent stages? Furthermore, the Dharma-realm which is the object of obstruction is like an imperial net of Indra, layered and interwoven.
They are grave. They are able to obstruct the same objects [of practice], and they are likewise all inexhaustible. Therefore, know that even one million [obstructions] is merely a brief explanation.
O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a single thought of anger toward other bodhisattvas, they will then bring about as many as these one million doors of obstruction.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater fault or evil than these.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva,
three fetters are thereby established.
Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly fulfill the practices of a bodhisattva should diligently cultivate the ten [perfections].
The various dharmas.

Second, the treatment of the two [categories] that are profound and subtle. First, the actual exposition; second, the concluding exhortation. Now, for the first [section], there are six stages, each containing ten lines.
The first is the initial cultivation; the latter five constitute the realization of benefits. These five subsequent sections rely upon one another in succession.

First: this initial [section] subsumes what follows; it is the treatment of one that is the treatment of all. Although the exposition has a sequence of before and after, the attainment occurs simultaneously.
Now, the first part is divided into two: first, the presentation and exhortation to practice.
What are these ten? They are: not abandoning any sentient being; conceiving the thought of a Tathāgata toward all bodhisattvas;
never slandering any of the Buddha-dharmas; knowing that all buddha-lands are inexhaustible;
generating deep faith and delight in the practices of a bodhisattva; not forsaking the mind of enlightenment—which is equal to space and the dharma-realm—and observing...
Awakening enters into the powers of the Tathāgata; one diligently cultivates unimpeded eloquence; one teaches and transforms sentient beings without weariness;
and one dwells in all worlds with a mind free from attachment—these are the ten.
Following this are the enumeration and the conclusion. Within these, ten dharmas are subsumed into five pairs to distinguish five kinds of cultivation.

The first two relate to persons and clarify the cultivation of humility and respect, because one respects superiors and loves inferiors. The next two relate to dharmas and clarify authentic cultivation.

Because one understands the matters through compliance with the teachings. Next, the two [stages] clarify extensive cultivation in terms of mental activity, because one delights in great practice and a great mind.
Next, the two [stages] clarify superior cultivation in terms of wisdom, because one internally realizes the wisdom of the result and externally gives rise to supreme discernment.

Finally, the two [stages] clarify long-term cultivation in terms of compassion and vow; for sentient beings are inexhaustible, yet one does not weary of transforming them through compassion, and worlds are... [inexhaustible].
...the limit. This is because they abide in non-attachment.
Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is established in these ten dharmas, they are able to fulfill ten kinds of purity.
What are these ten? They are: the purity of penetrating the profound Dharma; the purity of attending upon spiritual friends; [and so forth].
Purity: purity in upholding the teachings of all Buddhas; purity in thoroughly understanding the realm of empty space;
purity in deeply entering the dharma-realm; purity in observing the boundless mind; purity in sharing the same roots of goodness as all bodhisattvas;
purity in non-attachment to all eons; purity in observing the three periods of time; and purity in practicing all the teachings of the Buddhas. This is...

It consists of ten [points]. Regarding the second, "purity": because one achieves freedom from defilement based on the aforementioned correct practice, there are two parts in the text. First, the transition from the preceding to the subsequent;
second, the inquiry into the number and the enumeration of the names. The following sections all follow this pattern. Within the enumeration, there are ten phrases in sequence.
This is accomplished through the preceding ten phrases: first, by not abandoning sentient beings, one attains purity in the profound Dharma;
because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they are true within their very delusion, and thus constitute the profound Dharma. Second, by revering those above, one is able to draw near.
Third, by not slandering, one is able to protect. Fourth, by knowing [the Dharma] to be inexhaustible, one realizes it to be like space. Fifth, by...
The Bodhisattva’s practice does not depart from the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is "profound entry. Sixth, because one knows that the bodhicitta is equal to space, it is "boundless.
Seventh, observing that all Bodhisattvas share this same contemplation, they are able to enter the power of the Buddhas; thus, it is called a "root" (*mūla*).

Eighth, because of diligent cultivation without indolence, one does not become attached to the duration of kalpas. Ninth, because of tireless transformation [of others], one contemplates the transformed and the untransformed among the sentient beings of the three periods of time.
Tenth, by virtue of the vow to abide in the world, one is able to cultivate all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these ten dharmas, they become fully endowed with ten kinds of vast wisdom.
What are these ten? They are: the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows the karmic retributions of all sentient beings;
the wisdom that knows all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom that knows the profound and secret principles of all Buddha-dharmas; and the wisdom that knows...
The wisdom of all dharani-gates; the wisdom of eloquence that knows all syllables and characters;
the wisdom of skillful mastery in the languages, sounds, and expressions of all sentient beings; and the wisdom that universally manifests one's body in all worlds.
The wisdom that universally manifests reflections within all assemblies; the wisdom of omniscience present in all places of rebirth—these are the ten.
Regarding the third, the vast wisdom:
once defilements have been brushed away, fundamental wisdom is spontaneously luminous; it accords with the nature of reality and knows through its own likeness. Thus it is said.
It is called "Vastness. It is also formed from the preceding ten and the subsequent ten, which can be understood through the power of the mind.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in these ten knowledges, they then attain entry into ten kinds of universal entries.
What are these ten? They are: the entry of all worlds into a single hair-pore; the entry of a single hair-pore into all worlds; and so forth.
The realms: the bodies of all sentient beings enter into one body, and one body enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.

Unspeakable eons enter into a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment enters into unspeakable eons. All Buddha-dharmas enter into a single dharma, and a single dharma enters into all Buddha-dharmas.
Unspeakable places enter into a single place, and a single place enters into unspeakable places. Not...

One may say that a single faculty enters into all faculties, yet a single faculty cannot be said to enter into a single faculty. All faculties enter into non-faculties, and non-faculties enter into all faculties.
All perceptions enter into a single perception, and a single perception enters into all perceptions.
All sounds and voices enter into a single sound and voice, and a single sound and voice enters into all sounds and voices. All three periods of time enter into a single period of time.
One world enters all worlds of the three periods of time; this constitutes the ten [entries]. Regarding the fourth, "Universal Entry":
phenomena accord with principle and are fundamentally integrated. Wisdom realizes that such is the nature of things (*dharmatā*), so that there is no realm through which it does not penetrate.

Thus, both body and mind enter [all realms]; this also arises from the preceding three [entries] and can be understood through the intellect. It is not something accessible by the [ordinary] faculties.
Objects, consciousness, and principles are all not faculties.
Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has observed in this way, he dwells in ten kinds of sublime and wondrous minds.
What are these ten? They are: dwelling in the sublime and wondrous mind that [perceives] all worlds as being neither speech nor non-speech; dwelling in the one...
The sublime mind that has no basis for the conceptual thoughts of all sentient beings; the sublime mind that abides in the ultimate realm of empty space;
the sublime mind that abides in the boundless dharma-realm; the sublime mind that abides in all profound and secret Buddha-dharmas;
the sublime mind that abides in the extremely profound and undifferentiated Dharma; the sublime mind that abides in the eradication of all doubts and delusions; the sublime mind that abides in...
The supreme and wondrous mind of the equality and non-differentiation of all worlds; the supreme and wondrous mind abiding in the equality of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
the supreme and wondrous mind abiding in the immeasurable powers of all Buddhas—these are the ten.

Regarding the fifth, the Supreme and Wondrous Mind (*parama-vicitra-citta*): because one previously realized that the essence of all phenomena is fundamentally integrated, there is no obstruction between phenomena and principle.

Thus, one brings about benefit in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; this is called the Supreme and Wondrous Mind. It arises from the preceding four minds and can also be understood through reflection.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these ten kinds of sublime and wondrous minds, they attain ten kinds of skillful wisdom regarding the Buddha-dharma.
What are these ten? They are: skillful wisdom that thoroughly comprehends the profound Buddha-dharma; skillful wisdom that gives rise to the vast Buddha-dharma;
skillful wisdom that proclaims the various Buddha-dharmas; and skillful wisdom that enters into the equality [of the Buddha-dharma].

Skillful knowledge of the equality of the Buddha-dharma; skillful knowledge of the clear discernment of the distinctions within the Buddha-dharma; skillful knowledge of the realization of the non-distinction of the Buddha-dharma;
skillful knowledge of the profound entry into the adornments of the Buddha-dharma; skillful knowledge of entering the Buddha-dharma through a single expedient means;
skillful knowledge of entering the Buddha-dharma through immeasurable expedient means; and knowing the non-differentiation of the boundless Buddha-dharmas.

The skillful knowledge of differentiation; the skillful knowledge of non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas through the self-power of one’s own mind—these are the ten. Regarding the sixth skillful knowledge:

because of the aforementioned non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, it now involves the definitive resolution of the provisional and the real; thus it is named [the skillful knowledge of definitive resolution].
Skillful wisdom consists of eleven phrases; the last two are combined as one, while the remainder follow their respective order, all being established from the preceding ten.
First, it is profound because it transcends words yet employs words. Second, it is vast because it is without dependence.
Third, it can expound various things because it is like the arising of form based on space. Fourth, it realizes equality because it dwells beyond the two extremes. Fifth, it comprehends the seeds...

Because wisdom is profound and subtle, it realizes distinctions. Sixth, non-distinction is entirely identical [to this]. Seventh, if there are no obstructing afflictions, then there is the adornment of the Buddha-dharma.
Eighth, through equality, one achieves a single skillful means. Seventh, the dharmas of the three periods of time are categorized according to the gate of distinction.
This constitutes immeasurable skillful means. Tenth, by abiding in the power of the Buddha, one comes to know that the Buddha’s own power is boundless and non-retrogressive.
As it was with the preceding ten [points], so it is with the preceding four sections as well. Thus, through this successive progression, one does not depart from the initial cultivation.
Therefore, each single dharma possesses all [dharmas].
Sons of the Buddha, once Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard this teaching, they should all resolve their minds to respectfully receive and uphold it.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold this dharma will, with little exertion of effort, swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and fully possess all Buddha-dharmas, which are entirely equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This is the second exhortation: because a single practice can encompass everything, one swiftly attains *bodhi*.
At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma,
worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.

There rained down clouds of all manner of flowers surpassing those of the devas, clouds of incense, clouds of powdered incense, and clouds of robes, parasols, banners, pennants, mani jewels, and so forth, as well as one...
Clouds of all kinds of ornaments; clouds raining various musical performances; clouds raining all bodhisattvas;
clouds raining the unspeakable physical forms and marks of the Tathāgatas; clouds raining unspeakable praises of "Excellent! for the Tathāgatas;
clouds raining the voices of the Tathāgatas filling the entire dharma-realm; clouds raining unspeakable adornments of worlds; clouds raining the unspeakable...
Increasing the clouds of enlightenment; raining down unspeakable clouds of radiant illumination;

raining down unspeakable clouds of teaching the Dharma through spiritual powers—thus, within the Bodhisattva palaces at the sites of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi trees in the four continents of this world, one beholds the Tathāgata attaining perfect awakening and expounding this Dharma. In all worlds throughout the ten directions, [it is likewise].
It is exactly the same throughout all realms.

In the second major section, "Establishing through Proof," there are two parts: first, the manifestation of auspicious omens as proof; first, regarding this realm, and subsequently, the concluding generalization beginning with "In this way... and so forth.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came to this land bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, filling the ten directions.
They spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent! Son of the Buddha, you are indeed able to expound this."
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have bestowed the profound Dharma of the great vow of prediction. O Son of the Buddha!
We are all named Samantabhadra, and we have each come from the world Samantavijaya to this land from the presence of the Tathāgata Samantadhvaja-īśvara.
By the spiritual power of the Buddhas, we expound this Dharma in all places, just as it is in this assembly. Thus...
It is said that all things are equal, without increase or decrease. We have all come to this site of enlightenment by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to serve as witnesses for you.
Just as we, bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, have come to this site of enlightenment to bear witness, so it is likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Second, regarding the realization of all Bodhisattvas: it likewise occurs first in this land and subsequently as described below; this concludes the general application.

As for the "profound Dharma of the prediction," it means that one attains *bodhi* with little exertion of effort. As for those "all named Samantabhadra," it is because they all possess this very practice.

As for the "World of Universal Excellence" (*Samantavijaya*), it is because this universal Dharma is the most supreme therein. [The phrase] "Universal Banner Sovereign" (*Samantadhvaja-vaśavartin*)...
This is because this practice results in a fruit that is preeminent and unimpeded.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of his own roots of goodness, surveyed the ten directions as far as the Dharma-realm.
He desired to reveal the bodhisattva practices and desired to proclaim the realm of the Tathāgata’s awakening. He desired...
He spoke of the realm of great vows. He wished to declare the number of kalpas of all worlds; he wished to clarify that the Buddhas appear according to the times;
he wished to explain how the Tathāgatas appear in accordance with the ripening of sentient beings' faculties to enable them to make offerings;

he wished to clarify that the merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is never in vain; he wished to clarify that the roots of goodness planted will inevitably yield their fruit; and he wished to clarify his own great majestic virtue.
The Bodhisattva manifests forms and preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings to bring them to awakening.

He then speaks in verse. Regarding the second section, which further elucidates the middle two [points] by means of verses: first is the introductory narrative, followed by the formal verses. First, the ritual protocol is stated; subsequently, the intention for the exposition is revealed.
This involves ten points, all of which are fully contained within the verses. The text is clear and may be understood accordingly.
"You all should rejoice and abandon all hindrances; listen with single-minded reverence.

This second section of the *Bodhisattvapraṇidhānacaryā* consists of one hundred and twenty-one verses, divided into two parts. The first twenty-four verses constitute the Section on Manifesting the Teachings.
The preceding section was in prose; the remainder all correctly elucidates the characteristics of Samantabhadra’s practice. This is in verse (*gāthā*).
It alternates with the preceding prose to collectively manifest the conduct of Samantabhadra. The former briefly clarifies how ten dharmas arise sequentially from one another;

this [section], however, extensively reveals various gateways without such sequential progression. In the former, the essence (*tattva*) is mostly revealed; here, the function (*vṛtti*) is mostly analyzed. Within the former, there are two parts.
First, having exhorted them to listen and granted permission to speak:
"I shall now explain in due order the practices cultivated by those former Bodhisattvas, the most excellent lions among men;
I shall also describe the number of kalpas, the worlds, and their various karmas."
And as for the Peerless Honored One who has arisen therein— just as these past Buddhas appeared in the world through their great vows—
how may I, for the sake of sentient beings, extinguish all sufferings and afflictions?
May I fulfill the continuity of the conduct of all Lions of Debate and attain the equal Dharma of the Buddhas.
The realm of omniscience beholds the past; All those lions among men emit great nets of light, Universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions. Reflecting thus, they make this vow:
"I shall become a lamp for the world, Fully endowed with the merits of a Buddha, Possessing the ten powers and omniscience."
All sentient beings are ablaze with greed, hatred, and delusion; I shall rescue and liberate them all, causing them to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms.
Having made such a vow, firm and non-retrogressive, I shall fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and attain the ten powers of non-obstruction. Thus the vow was made.
His practice is without retreat or cowardice, and all that he does is not in vain; this is called the Lion of Speakers, and the following section provides the correct demonstration of its limits.
Within this, there are two parts; the first nine verses authorize the narration of the past conduct of the Bodhisattva.
Within a single Bhadrakalpa, a thousand Buddhas appear in the world;
I shall explain their Universal Eye in due order. As it is within one Bhadrakalpa, so it is throughout immeasurable kalpas;
I shall explain the practices of those future Buddhas, just as for a single Buddha-field system.
So too are the immeasurable lands; the future Lords of Ten Powers—now I shall speak of the practices of all these.
Following this, below the section on a single Bhadrakalpa, he permits the exposition of the practices of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. This section consists of two parts:
the first three verses cite the time and place of the exposition; the first two [verses] concern the time, and the last one concerns the place.
The successive appearance of the Buddhas in the world, In accordance with their names, In accordance with the predictions they received,
In accordance with their lifespans, In accordance with the True Dharma they cultivated, Dedicatedly seeking the unobstructed path, In accordance with the sentient beings they transformed,
The duration for which the True Dharma remains in the world, And in accordance with the Buddha-fields they purified.
Sentient beings and the wheel of Dharma, The preaching of it at the proper and improper times,
The sequential purification of the multitudes according to the karma of all sentient beings, Their conduct and their inclinations— Distinguishing between superior, middling, and inferior,
one transforms them to cultivate practice, Entering into such wisdom, One cultivates that most excellent conduct.
Constantly performing the deeds of Samantabhadra, Universally delivering all sentient beings;
With unimpeded physical actions, And speech that is entirely pure, The mental conduct is likewise so. In the three times, there is nothing otherwise.
The Bodhisattva practices in this way, Ultimately perfecting the path of Samantabhadra, Becoming a sun of pure wisdom born into the world.
Universally illuminating the entire Dharma-realm throughout all kalpas of future ages, One fully understands in a single thought inconceivable lands, yet remains free from discrimination therein.
The practitioner is able to enter such a most supreme stage; Of these dharmas of the bodhisattvas, I shall now speak a small portion.
With wisdom that is boundless, Thoroughly penetrating the realm of the Buddhas,
Entering skillfully into all things, never retreating from their practice, Endowed with the wisdom of Samantabhadra, Fulfilling the vows of Samantabhadra,
And entering into incomparable knowledge— I shall now describe their conduct.
The subsequent eleven verses clarify the practices that have been taught. Among them, the former—the practice of the appearance of all Buddhas in the world—is the practice of Samantabhadra;
thus, cause and effect are perfectly integrated. The latter—the sevenfold practice of the Bodhisattvas’ vows, wisdom, and the three wheels—is likewise the practice of Samantabhadra.

Within a single atom, all worlds are clearly seen; if sentient beings were to hear this, their minds would become confused and they would go mad. Just as it is within one atom, so it is with all atoms:
all worlds enter therein, in such an inconceivable manner, within each and every atom.
The dharmas of the ten directions and three periods of time, And the realms and lands, are all infinite;
One can fully discern and know that within every single atom There are infinite varieties of Buddha-lands, Each and every one of them being infinite;
Within the entire Dharma-realm, All its various and diverse characteristics— [One knows them all.]
The various distinctions among the realms of existence are all able to be discerned and known.

This second section clearly reveals the conduct of Samantabhadra in ninety-seven verses, divided into two parts: first, sixty-seven verses clarify the conduct of great wisdom that is itself compassion;
second, the final thirty verses, beginning with "those who are not yet at peace," clarify the conduct of great compassion that is itself wisdom.
Now, first: there are ten kinds of practices. The first five verses clarify the practice of entering the Indra’s Net (*indrajāla*).
