Profoundly penetrating subtle wisdom, One discerns all worlds; The formation and destruction of all eons (*kalpa*) Can all be clearly explained.
Knowing the long and short duration of all eons, The three periods of time are but a single thought-moment.
They are able to discern and know all practices, whether they are identical or different;
They enter deeply into all worlds, both vast and non-vast; Within a single body are infinite lands, and within a single land are infinite bodies;
All the various types of worlds throughout the ten directions, With their vast and immeasurable characteristics.
They are able to know all things throughout the entirety of the three periods of time;
possessing profound wisdom, they fully comprehend the formation and destruction of immeasurable lands.
Regarding the worlds of the ten directions—those that are forming and those that are decaying—they understand all such ineffable matters with deep clarity, O Virtuous One.
There are some lands where the various grounds are adorned with all manner of beauties, and the same is true for the various realms of existence;
this arises from the purity of karma. There are some worlds that are defiled in immeasurable ways;
this arises from the karmic retribution of sentient beings. All things correspond to their own actions within these infinite and boundless fields.
Knowing that a single kṣetra is thus, one enters all kṣetras; their number is unknowable.
All world-systems enter entirely into a single kṣetra; yet the worlds do not become one, nor is there any confusion.
Some worlds are upright, some are inverted; some are high, and others are low.
All are the perceptions of sentient beings, Which they can all discern and know.
The vast and expansive worlds are immeasurable and boundless; They know that the manifold is one, And that the one is manifold.
O Samantabhadra, sons of the Buddhas, By means of the wisdom of Samantabhadra, You thoroughly understand the number of all lands.
Their number is without limit; they know the transformations of all worlds:
the transformation of lands, the transformation of beings, the transformation of phenomena, and the transformation of Buddhas—all of these are ultimately perfected.
All the subtle and vast lands within every world, with their various and diverse adornments, all arise from karma.
Innumerable sons of the Buddhas, Skillfully training and entering the Dharma-realm,
With sovereign power of spiritual penetrations pervading the ten directions, Even for eons equal in number to all sentient beings,
They could not exhaustively describe the names of those worlds, Except as revealed by the Buddha.
The second [section] consists of seventeen verses on the subtle conduct regarding time and place:
The worlds and the various names of the Tathāgatas— Even after speaking for immeasurable eons, they could not be exhausted;
How much more so the supreme wisdom Of all the Buddhas of the three times!
Born from the *dharmadhātu*, Pervading the stage of the Tathāgata, With pure and unimpeded mindfulness and boundless, unobstructed wisdom, He analyzes and expounds the *dharmadhātu*.
Having attained the further shore—these three verses clarify the secret conduct of the Buddha’s mind. The first verse and a half summarize the preceding introduction.
Next, the following one and a half verses clearly demonstrate that which is difficult to understand can be understood:
All past worlds, Whether vast or subtle, Adorned by their cultivation— In a single thought-moment, he can know them all.
Within those [worlds], the Lions among Men Cultivated the various practices of the Buddhas.
Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, they manifest all sovereign powers.

Thus, throughout the succession of immeasurable eons in future ages, all those Honored Ones among Men—the Bodhisattvas—are able to know all their practices and vows, as well as all their spheres of experience; thus they diligently practice.

Therein they attain perfect enlightenment, And they also know those assemblies; Through these various Dharma-gates, they extend their lifespans to transform sentient beings, And for the sake of the multitudes, they turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Bodhisattva knows thus, dwelling on the stage of Samantabhadra’s conduct; With wisdom, all is clearly understood, As they give birth to all Buddhas.
All the Buddha-fields encompassed within the present age— having entered deeply into these lands, they penetrate the Dharma-realm.
Within those worlds, all Buddhas of the present have attained mastery over the Dharma;
their discourse is unimpeded, and they also know those assemblies.
Through the power of manifesting transformation in the Pure Land, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas,
the World-Honored One, the Tamer of Beings, constantly contemplates this matter; all his majestic spiritual powers and his inexhaustible treasury of wisdom,
he is able to know them all completely.
The fourth section consists of ten verses concerning the practice of the Buddhas of the three times in their gathering and transforming of beings.
Born with unimpeded eyes, Unimpeded ears, nose, and body, And unimpeded broad and long tongues that can cause all beings to rejoice;
Possessing the most supreme and unimpeded mind, Vast and universally pure.
Wisdom is all-pervasive and fills [all things], Fully knowing the phenomena of the three periods of time.
(Verse 5) There are two verses regarding the unimpeded activity of the six sense faculties:
Skillfully training in all transformations: The transformation of lands, the transformation of sentient beings, The transformation of worlds, and the transformation of subduing.
Having ultimately transformed to the other shore, Though the various distinctions of the world exist, They all arise from dwelling in conceptualization;
Entering the Buddha’s wisdom of skillful means, He understands them all with complete clarity.
To the unspeakable multitudes in every assembly, He manifests his body for each one, Causing them all to behold the Tathāgata, And delivering infinite beings.
The sixth [chapter] has three verses: Like a magical emanation, their activity is without fixed direction.
The profound wisdom of the Buddhas Is like the sun appearing in the world;
It manifests everywhere throughout all lands without ceasing. Having thoroughly understood all worlds, They realize that provisional names have no reality.
Sentient beings and the world are like dreams and like reflections; Regarding all worldly phenomena, one does not give rise to discriminatory views.
One who is well-detached from discrimination does not perceive even an immeasurable and incalculable number of eons as being distinct from a single thought-moment.
To understand this is to realize that even the thought-moment is itself non-thought.
Thus one perceives the world: Countless lands are all transcended in a single thought-moment;
Though passing through immeasurable eons, one does not stir from one's original place.
Inexpressible eons are but a mere instant; Do not perceive length or brevity— This is the ultimate nature of the kṣaṇa.

The mind dwells in the world, and the world dwells in the mind; herein one does not falsely give rise to the dualistic or non-dualistic discrimination of sentient beings, worlds, and eons, nor of the Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma—all are like illusions and transformations.
The dharma-realm is entirely equal throughout all lands in the ten directions.
Manifesting immeasurable bodies, Knowing that the body arises from conditions, Ultimately free from attachment,
relying on non-dual wisdom, He appears as a lion among men; Unattached to the dharma of non-duality,
He knows that non-duality is not dual.
The seventh [chapter] consists of ten verses. It concerns the sovereign conduct of the three worlds; its profound subtlety should be carefully contemplated.

Having thoroughly understood that all worlds Are like flames, like shadows, and like light, Like echoes, as well as dreams, Like illusions and magical transformations— In this way one enters accordingly The sphere of activity of all Buddhas.
Having achieved the wisdom of Samantabhadra, universally illuminating the profound Dharma-realm,
they abandon all attachments to sentient beings, lands, and defilements, yet give rise to great compassion. Universally purifying all worlds,
these Bodhisattvas maintain constant right mindfulness as they discourse upon the lion-like sublime Dharma, which is as pure as space.
They give rise to great skillful means, seeing that the world is constantly deluded;
they resolve to save and deliver all beings, and their conduct is entirely pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Whether it be the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas—if one perceives their true reality, there is no distinction whatsoever among them.
The eighth [section] consists of six verses, which specifically clarify the conduct of the World-Lord, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The *dharmakāya* treasury of the Tathāgata pervasively enters into the world;
though it exists within the world, it is unattached to the world. It is like pure water: reflections neither come nor go.
The Dharma-body pervades the world; know that it is likewise so.
Thus, free from defilement and attachment, body and world are all pure, serene like space. All things are without birth;
know that the body is without end. It is neither born nor does it perish; it is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Manifesting throughout all worlds, He eliminates all false views.
He reveals the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which neither comes nor goes; He is unattached to self or what belongs to self.

The ninth [chapter] contains five verses that clarify how, though not possessing a body, he manifests bodily conduct. Regarding the "Dharmakāya-garbha," this refers to the aforementioned "Garbha-body."
The statement that the essential body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is omnipresent is likewise the same as this.

For example: Just as a skilled illusionist Manifests all manner of things, Their coming has no point of origin, And their going reaches no destination; The nature of illusion is neither finite, Nor is it infinite.
Within that great assembly, he manifests both the measurable and the immeasurable.
By cultivating all roots of goodness with this mind of tranquil concentration, he gives birth to all Buddhas.
That which is measurable, immeasurable, finite, and infinite—all these are but conceptual constructions; he has thoroughly realized the nature of all realms of existence.
Not clinging to the measurable or the immeasurable, the profound Dharma of all Buddhas—vast, deep, and quiescent;
with profound and immeasurable wisdom, they know the depths of the various realms of existence.
Bodhisattvas, free from delusion and with pure minds in constant succession, skillfully employ the power of supernormal faculties to deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
The tenth chapter contains sixteen verses: They demonstrate the practice of non-measurement as measurement;
they cause those who are not yet settled to find stability, and for those already settled, they show the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Thus pervading the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), their minds are without attachment; they do not abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nor do they enter into nirvāṇa.

Thus pervading the entire world, they awaken all living beings; understanding the number of dharmas and the number of sentient beings without attachment, they rain down the rain of Dharma everywhere to saturate all worlds.
Throughout all realms, in every thought-moment, they attain perfect enlightenment while cultivating the practices of a Bodhisattva.
The second major section, "Never Regressing," concerns the compassionate activity of wisdom itself. Within this, there are also ten sections of practice. The first consists of four verses:
the practice of gathering and transforming beings through non-abiding.
All the various bodies in the world, He understands them all completely. By knowing the nature of these bodies in this way, he attains the body of all Buddhas.

Universally knowing all sentient beings, All kalpas, and all lands throughout the ten directions without limit— There is no ocean of wisdom into which he does not enter; The bodies of sentient beings are immeasurable.
For each [being], he manifests his body; the Buddha-body is without limit. The wise behold it all:
that which is known in a single thought-moment gives rise to all Tathāgatas, such that even after passing through immeasurable eons, one could never finish praising it.
The second section consists of four verses: The Buddhas can manifest bodies that are not physical bodies;
They manifest their forms everywhere and enter parinirvāṇa; Within a single thought-moment, immeasurable śarīras appear, each distinct from the others.
A single verse concerning the distribution of the relics throughout the three realms of existence:
"In this way, in future ages, those who seek the fruit of Buddhahood—those with immeasurable bodhicitta and decisive wisdom—know them all.
Thus, among all the Tathāgatas existing within the three periods of time..."
One is able to know all things; this is called abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
(Verse 4) One knows the great mental activities of the Buddhas through such discernment, and one enters the stages of immeasurable practices through the conduct of wisdom.
That wheel is non-retrogressive; it is subtle, wondrous, and vast wisdom.
Having deeply entered the realm of the Tathāgata, one does not retreat once entered; this is called the wisdom of Samantabhadra.
The Most Victorious One of all universally enters the Buddha-realm; practicing without retrogression, he attains unsurpassed bodhi.
The fifth [section] consists of three verses. Regarding the profound practice of the Wheel of Dharma:
The immeasurable and boundless minds, And their various distinct karmas, Are all accumulated through conceptualization;
He fully understands them all as equal, Whether they are defiled or undefiled, And whether they are the minds of those in training or those beyond training.
Inconceivable numbers of minds, he knows them all within every single thought-moment;
He understands them to be neither one nor two, neither defiled nor pure, And likewise without confusion;
he clearly perceives them all as arising from their own conceptualizations. The mental conceptions of all sentient beings are each different.
Arising in various worlds through such skillful means, Cultivating all supreme practices, Born through transformation from the Buddha-dharma, One is named Samantabhadra.
(These are the six verses. [He] thoroughly understands the faculties and conduct [of beings].
Sentient beings all falsely give rise to The perceptions of good and evil destinies;
Because of this, some are born in heaven, While others fall into hell. When Bodhisattvas contemplate the world, They see it arises from the karma of false imagination;
Since false imagination is boundless, The worlds are likewise immeasurable— All the various lands throughout the universe.
Manifested by the net of conceptualization, through the skillful means of the net of illusion, one is able to enter all seven realms of existence in a single thought-moment.
These three verses clarify the activities of worldly karma and afflictions.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and likewise the mind-faculty— They are able to enter into the various distinctions and equalities of worldly perceptions.
Within the objective realm of each individual eye, Infinite eyes all enter into the differentiation of various natures;
These are infinite and ineffable, Yet that which is seen is without distinction.
Furthermore, they are without confusion; each according to their own karma, they experience their respective fruits.
The power of Samantabhadra is immeasurable; he knows all of them entirely.
Within the realm of all eyes, great wisdom can enter completely; thus, all these worlds he is able to discern and know.
And they cultivate all practices, never again falling back from them.
These eight verses on existence and non-existence describe the unimpeded conduct regarding faculties and objects;
the Buddha’s teaching, the teaching on sentient beings, and the teaching on lands—all such teachings throughout the three periods of time.

The single verse "thoroughly knowing all varieties of the nine states of existence" refers to knowing the four types of methods for preaching the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "preaching in a land and so forth," there are briefly three meanings:
first, in terms of supernormal power; second, in terms of interpenetration, because by preaching one thing, one preaches all things; third, in terms of revealing the principle. This...
It is said that Bodhisattvas fully comprehend all objects of contact; thus, the various categories of contact constitute the teaching, as in the case of the fragrant rice and so forth.
Within the past, they see the future; within the future, they see the present.
They clearly perceive each instance of the three times interacting with one another. In such infinite ways, they awaken all the worlds.
The skillful means of omniscience; its limits cannot be found.
These are the final two verses of the tenth chapter. This concludes the practice subsumed within the three periods of time. Thus ends the chapter on the Equal Cause.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Volume Forty-nine and Volume Fifty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery;
Excerpts by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Huishan Fayun Monastery.
Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part One: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the intent of the initial arrival: the preceding chapter elucidated the cause that accords with the fruit; this chapter distinguishes the fruit that accords with the cause.

Although their essence is equal, the two aspects are not conflated. Because the sequence of meaning follows "cause first, then fruit," it also serves as a response to the manifestation of mindfulness mentioned in the previous "Inconceivable" chapter, and as a response to the question concerning "practice" asked in the second assembly. Second, the explanation of the title.
The term "Tathāgata" refers to one who possesses the Dharma; it is a general designation for the three bodies and the ten bodies.
"Manifestation" (prādurbhāva) refers to the Dharma that relies upon the person, distinguished as the fruition-function and the transformation-function. This collectively clarifies the Tathāgata.

Although this was seen in the preceding text, because it is contrasted with "manifestation," it is here further explained that all ten bodies possess manifestation. For now, this is clarified by way of the three bodies; however, as for "coming" (āgama)...
It immediately appears. Because it is necessary to clearly explain and illustrate the distinction between the person and the Dharma, this is further clarified.
If one relies on the *dharmakāya*, "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; its constant manifestation according to reality is termed "appearing. Thus, the text says:
"It universally manifests all things, yet there is nothing manifested. It also says: "Its essential nature is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing," and so forth. If...
Relying on the reward body (*sambhogakāya*), one comes by means of the path of reality as it is to achieve perfect enlightenment; thus, one is called a Tathāgata.

When the merits of one's original nature are suddenly manifested all at once, this is termed "appearing. Therefore, the text says: "When the Tathāgata achieves perfect enlightenment, he has no doubt regarding any phenomena;
he universally perceives all sentient beings achieving perfect, equal enlightenment. If one relies on the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)...
As for the body, it rides upon the vehicle of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) to come and transform sentient beings; therefore, it is called the Tathāgata.

Thus, the great function that responds to capacities manifests all at once. A text states: "By the power of original vows, he manifests the Buddha-body, causing [beings] to see the great spiritual transformations of the Tathāgata.
It further states: "According to their capabilities and according to their powers, beneath the Bodhi tree, he plants..."

The various bodies achieve equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Now, because there has never been a duality between the new Buddha and the anciently accomplished one, the newly accomplished and the ancient Buddha appear to be distinguished as Dharma-body and Reward-body;

yet, because there is nothing that does not respond to the opportune moment, they are the Response-body while being the True-body. Because the Response arises in accordance with the Nature, it is the True-body while being the Response-body.
Thus, the three Buddhas are perfectly interfused and the ten bodies are unimpeded. Therefore, by discerning the response and manifestation, the Truth itself is revealed.

This is established. For this reason, the Jin dynasty named it "Arising from Nature" (*xingqi*). Although the character "nature" (*xing*) is an added interpretive term, it does not deviate from the underlying principle, because although phenomena arise from conditions, they do not contradict nature;
and because there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, the pure supersedes the defiled.

Because nature itself arises; because if one were separated from conditions, nature could not be described; and because the Bodhisattva Xingqi (Nature-Arising) is added below to represent what is being explained.
Although delusion is identical to nature, it does not accord with nature. Now, because the meaning of "arising" has many connotations, it is directly termed "manifestation" (*chuxian*).
This is because manifestation occurs through nature, through causes, through reality, and through response. If one were to distinguish only the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*):
It appears. This does not merely lose the meaning of the previous two [explanations], nor is it sufficient to manifest the profound. How, then, could it integrate the previously distinct fruits?
If "coming" (*āgata*) is taken as the meaning of "appearing," then *Tathāgata* is simply "appearance"; this is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*).
Alternatively, if one distinguishes between person and dharma, all three are the appearance of the *Tathāgata*; thus, the third doctrinal intent is "equal appearance."
This is established as the thesis. The merging of differentiated fruits constitutes the goal.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the white tuft between his eyebrows a great radiance named "The Manifestation of the Tathāgata."
With immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays as its retinue,
that light universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, the entirety of space and the dharma-realm, circling them ten times to the right.
It manifests the infinite sovereignty of the Tathāgata, awakens countless multitudes of bodhisattvas, and causes all worlds in the ten directions to tremble.
It extinguishes all sufferings of the evil realms; it outshines all the palaces of the māras;
and it reveals all the Tathāgatas sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, as well as all the assemblies at their sites of enlightenment.
Having performed these actions, they came and circumambulated the assembly of bodhisattvas to the right.

Fourth, the formal explanation of the text: the general structure of this chapter is divided into seven sections: first, the section on the empowerment (*adhikāra*); second, the section on the essence (*svabhāva*); third, the section on the request (*adhyeṣaṇā*);

fourth, the section on the exposition (*nirdeśa*); fifth, the section on revealing the name and upholding [the teaching] (*nāmanirdeśa-parigraha*); sixth, the section on manifesting auspicious signs as proof (*prātihārya-saṃsiddhi*); and seventh, the section of verses (*gāthā*).

The Section on General Compendium. Herein, there are first two parts: first, the empowerment of the petitioner by means of light from the hair-tuft; second, the empowerment of the speaker by means of light from the mouth.

Within the former, there are three sections: first, the light; second, the empowerment; third, the benefit. Within the section on the light, there are ten points, divided into three parts. First, the source from which the light issues.

The space between the eyebrows symbolizes the penetration of realization, for it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence; it symbolizes the path of non-abiding, for it is free from the two extremes of the real and the responsive.
The white tuft of hair symbolizes that which is manifested, for its nature is stainless and it serves as the basis for manifesting all the teachings through verbal expression.
Third, from "immeasurable" onwards, the names and essences of the light are distinguished, as they have been described. Fourth, from "immeasurable" onwards... [text continues].

There are eight sections, all of which pertain to the activity of light (*prabhā-karman*). First is the light of the retinue, which is the causal activity (*hetu-karman*), for it universally encompasses all phenomena as they are produced thereby.
Fourth is the activity of extending the light downward; fifth is the activity of manifesting reverence below; sixth is the awakening to joy below;
seventh is the activity of correct elimination below; eighth is the activity of eclipsing and subduing obstacles below; ninth is the manifestation below...
The manifestation of activity. Tenth, this is the activity of the lower fascicle.
[The light] enters the crown of the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue Arising from the Nature of the Tathāgata.
Second, the correct clarification of the characteristics of the empowerment. As for why this bodhisattva is empowered: it is because he is manifested according to his name; his nature possesses...

There are two meanings: first, the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*), because it is that which arises from causes; second, the meaning of "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), because whether true or responsive, all things arise from this.
There is also an interpretation which says: "This Sublime Virtue (*Sudhana*) is none other than Mañjuśrī, who expounds this Dharma-gate."
Regarding the title *Jiaxingqi* (Manifestation of the Added Nature): this interpretation does not contradict the great principle.

This is because Mañjuśrī, as the Great Wisdom, acts as the manifestor, while Samantabhadra, as the Dharmadhātu, acts as that which is manifested; together they bring about the appearance of Vairocana.

Furthermore, it is the manifestation of the Buddha because his practice and realization have reached fulfillment. That [the light] enters through the crown of the head is the sign of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), representing the ultimate limit of wondrous wisdom.
Only then could it be manifested.
At that time, the entire great assembly in this *bodhimaṇḍa* leaped for joy with body and mind, giving rise to great delight, and thought:
"How extraordinary and rare! Now the Tathāgata emits a great radiance; he must surely proclaim the most profound Great Dharma."
Among the three additions, two are presented first. The great assembly rejoices together because they know that the Dharma is about to be bestowed.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotra-vyuha-guṇa, seated upon a lotus throne, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and with a single-minded focus directed toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:

First, at that time, Samantabhadra received the instruction; because he knew himself to be the one who would cause the Dharma to be taught, there are two parts within this section. First is the prose:
he paid homage with body and mind. "Kneeling" (跽) means to squat on the ground.
The Great Wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment emerges, Universally penetrating all realms to reach the further shore;
Equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
I now pay respectful homage to you who have ascended To the shore of the signless realm, And manifest a body adorned with wondrous marks.
He emits a thousand stainless rays of light, Which utterly destroy the hosts of Māra throughout all worlds in the ten directions, leaving none untouched;
Yet he never causes a single sentient being to feel fear— Such is the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata.
The nature of the void and the dharma-realm is equal; having been able to abide thus, one causes all sentient beings, in their infinite number, to extinguish evil and remove all defilements.
Through diligent practice over countless eons, they achieve the path of supreme bodhi.
Regarding all objects of experience, your wisdom is unimpeded; you share the same nature as all Buddhas.
The subsequent verses of praise and supplication consist of ten stanzas, divided into two parts: the first five are praises, and the latter five are supplications.

Within the praises, the first stanza offers general praise and prostration, while the remaining four offer specific praise for the emission of light. These include praises of the cause, the fruit, and the activity [of the light].
The Teacher has emitted this great radiance, Shaking all worlds throughout the ten directions;
Having manifested immeasurable supernormal powers, He has returned once more and entered my body.
Those who have well trained in the definitive Dharma— Immeasurable bodhisattvas have all gathered here.
May I give rise to the mind that seeks the Dharma; for this reason, I now entreat the Lord of Dharma.
This present assembly is entirely pure, and they are all able to skillfully deliver the world.
Their wisdom is boundless and free from attachment; such noble and excellent ones have all gathered here.

O Honored Teacher who benefits the world, whose wisdom and diligence are both immeasurable, you now illuminate the great assembly with your radiance; please allow me to inquire about the unsurpassed Dharma.
Who is it that can truly and fully expound upon the profound realm of the Great Sage?
"Who is the eldest son of the Tathāgata’s Dharma? O Honored Guide of the World, please reveal him.

In the latter five [verses], the first one describes the personal attainment of benefit; this is the reception of the instruction. The subsequent verse receives the intention of the assembly and makes the request.

The next verse praises the assembly as being worthy of hearing [the teaching]. The following verse describes how the Buddha prompted them to request it. The subsequent verse correctly identifies the Master;
having already grasped the Buddha’s intention, he did not need to request it from the Buddha himself.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted from his mouth a great radiance named "Unobstructed and Fearless," with hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light as its retinue.
It universally illumined all worlds throughout the ten directions, as far as the reaches of space and the Dharma-realm, circling them ten times to the right.
It manifested the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgata and awakened immeasurable beings.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas caused all worlds throughout the ten directions to tremble, extinguished the sufferings of all evil realms, eclipsed all the palaces of the Māras,
and manifested all the Tathāgatas sitting upon the seat of enlightenment and attaining perfect awakening,
as well as all the assemblies at their sites of enlightenment. Having performed these deeds, they came and circumambulated [the Buddha] to the right.
The assembly of bodhisattvas entered the mouth of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra. Once the light had entered,
the body and lion throne of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra became a hundred times greater than they were before, as did the bodies and thrones of all the other bodhisattvas—
except for the lion throne of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the second light from the mouth, which bestows the status of the Master [of the teaching], this is shown because it represents the request for instruction. This section consists of three parts: first, the light; second, the empowerment; and third, the benefit.

Now, for the first part, there are also ten points. First, the source: that it is emitted from the mouth signifies the guidance, teaching, and transmission of the Dharma. Second, the name of the light:
"Causing the Attainment of Unobstructed Eloquence," because it enables one to face the great assembly and profound principles without fear. The remaining points are as explained previously.
Second, regarding "the two enter the mouth below the universal [syllable]": this is because the teaching is transmitted orally, as the Buddha has taught.
Regarding the addition of Samantabhadra: this is because it is the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct; and because the Dharma-realm that is realized is manifested through principle.
Third, regarding "its light enters below" within the section on clarifying the benefits: this is because the Tathāgata alone is excluded, thereby distinguishing between teacher and disciple.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-vyūha-guṇa asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, this great and vast miraculous manifestation displayed by the Buddha causes all Bodhisattvas to give rise to joy;
it is inconceivable and unknown to the world. What auspicious sign is this? The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra replied: "O Son of the Buddha, I..."
"In the past, I beheld various Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who manifested such vast and great supernormal transformations and then preached the Dharma-gate of the Appearance of a Tathāgata.
As I reflect upon it now, it is appropriate that he should preach that very Dharma.
When these words were spoken, the entire great earth shook in its entirety, and immeasurable light illuminating the questions of the Dharma was produced.
Second, within the subsequent section of the fundamental portion (*mūlabhāga*), there are three parts: first, an inquiry that raises a point;
second, an answer that cites an example; and third, the manifestation of auspicious omens following these words to confirm and demonstrate the marvelous.
Since the inquiry regarding the name itself already contains a sign, the shaking of the great earth indicates that the Great Dharma is about to manifest and the great delusions are about to collapse.
Therefore, those who hear this light should augment their wisdom to assist in its proclamation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, whose nature is the arising of wondrous virtue, asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"O Son of the Buddha, how should a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understand the manner in which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear? I pray that you will explain this to me."
O Son of the Buddha, this assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas has all long cultivated pure deeds and achieved mindfulness and wisdom.
They have reached the ultimate shore of great adornment and are endowed with the conduct of the majestic demeanor of all Buddhas.
With right mindfulness, they never forget the Buddhas; with great compassion, they observe all sentient beings, having attained definitive certainty.
They understand the spheres of supernatural power of the great bodhisattvas; they have already attained the empowerment of the spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
they are able to receive the sublime Dharma of all Tathāgatas; and they are endowed with such immeasurable merits as these—all of whom have now assembled.
Son of the Buddha, you have already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, and have accomplished Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva’s supreme and wondrous conduct brings mastery over all gates of samādhi.
He enters the secret realm of all Buddhas and, knowing the teachings of all Buddhas, severs all doubts and confusion.

Empowered by the spiritual authority of all Tathāgatas, he knows the faculties of sentient beings and their inclinations, and for them he preaches the true Dharma of liberation. In accordance with the Buddha-wisdom, he expounds the Buddha-dharma.
The Dharma has reached the other shore. There are immeasurable merits such as these. Well done, Son of the Buddha!

We pray that you will explain the manner in which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears: his physical marks and voice, the sphere of his mind, his practiced conduct, his attainment of the Way, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and even his manifestation of entry into parinirvāṇa—how those who see, hear, or draw near to him give rise to [merit].
The roots of goodness. I pray that you will explain all such matters as these.
Within this third section of requests, there are both prose and verse. In the prose portion, there are four parts: first, a general request for the Dharma;
second, from "O Son of the Buddha, these [beings]... onwards, praising the capacity of sentient beings to hear it; third, from "O Son of the Buddha, you have already... onwards, praising the teacher.
Endowed with virtue. The four "Excellent! sections below mark the headings for specific requests. The first two are understandable. In the third, ten matters are specifically praised:
(1) making offerings to many Buddhas, because he must have heard [the teachings] from them; (2) accomplishing wondrous conduct, because he has already practiced it;

(3) mastery over meditative concentration, because there is that upon which he relies; (4) personal realization and entry; (5) knowing the path of the teachings; (6) removing [afflictions] in others...
Because of doubt; because of the application of the seven higher powers; because of examining the faculties; because of being able to teach accordingly;

and because of attaining the profound meaning through the wisdom that accords with reaching the other shore—thus is the summary at the end. Since there are such qualities for teaching, he is fit to speak.
In the fourth section, the specific request following the headings, the first phrase praises his excellence, building upon the preceding three sections. The latter...

Ten matters are enumerated to manifest their inexhaustibility. First is the manner in which a Tathāgata appears; this is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), as it is a phenomenon produced through the collective convergence of many conditions.

"Dharma" (phenomenon) contains the meanings of "normative rule" (*dharana*) and "support" (*dhṛti*). The remaining nine are specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The first three are the secrets of the three types of action (*trividha-karma*).
The fourth is the objective sphere, which is the object of wisdom and also the sphere of its limits. The fifth is the practice based upon that objective sphere.
Pervading both cause and fruit: sixth, accomplishing the path to Bodhi; seventh, turning the wheel of the Dharma; eighth, necessarily entering Nirvana;
ninth, whether present or absent, all who see or hear receive benefit. Being complete with these nine matters, the beginning and end of one transformation are thus concluded.
Thus concludes the section below.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha-vyūha-guṇa, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and spoke in verse:
“Excellent is your unimpeded great wisdom, Which perfectly awakens to the boundless realm of equality.”
I pray that you will speak of the immeasurable conduct of the Buddhas; having heard it, the sons of the Buddha shall all rejoice.
How do Bodhisattvas accord with and enter [this path]? How do the Tathāgatas appear in the world?
What are the spheres of their body, speech, and mind, and the domains of their practice? I pray that you will explain them all.
How do the Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment? How does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma?
How does the Sugata enter parinirvāṇa? Having heard this, the great assembly rejoices in their hearts;
If they behold the Buddha, the Great Dharma King, And draw near to him, their various roots of goodness will increase.
I pray that you will explain that treasury of merits: what do sentient beings gain upon seeing it?

If there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata—whether while he is in the present world or has entered parinirvāṇa—and conceive deep faith in that treasury of merit, what benefits will they receive? I pray that you will proclaim them.
All these bodhisattvas join their palms in reverence, gazing up at the Tathāgata, the Benevolent One, and me—the realm of the Great Ocean of Merit. O Purifier of Sentient Beings, please speak!
We pray that you will expound the wondrous Dharma and its corresponding meanings through causes, conditions, and parables.
Having heard this, sentient beings give rise to the Great Mind;
their doubts are exhausted and their wisdom is pure like space, pervading all lands.
May you, through wondrous sounds, causes, and analogies, reveal the Bodhi of the Buddhas, just as they manifest their adorned bodies throughout all realms.
In the hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, for immeasurable billions of nayutas of eons,
such an assembly of bodhisattvas as has now gathered would be entirely difficult to behold.
All these bodhisattvas pay reverent homage, giving rise to a yearning thirst for the subtle and wondrous meaning.

"May you, with a pure mind, fully expound the vast Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world"—these five verses praise his virtues and entreat him to teach, encompassing the final three sections [of the treatise]. Among them, the first verse offers a general praise and request;
the next two verses concern the method of teaching. Because the Dharma is profound and difficult to comprehend, the request is made by means of analogies. The final [verse]...
The first one and a half verses praise the assembly as being worthy of hearing [the teaching]. The final half-verse concludes by requesting that what is to be said be expounded.
With a pure mind, free from fault-finding, he fully elucidates the words and their meaning with complete perfection.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Tathāgatagotra-samudgata-vimala and others, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this place is inconceivable."

The fourth section, the Section on Exposition, is divided into two major parts: first, the individual answers to the ten questions; second, the general conclusion and response beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, as the Tathāgata uses all parables...
Now, for the first part, the ten sections answer the ten preceding questions, each consisting of both prose and verse, and each containing the ten [aspects].
Herein is the first: the answer regarding the method of manifestation. Within the prose, there are two [parts]; first—
The proclamation and praise of its profundity:
namely, that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared by means of immeasurable dharmas.
Second, the detailed explanation according to the meaning, which consists of three parts. First, the explanation of the profound and vast nature of the Dharma, responding to the preceding cause.

The conditions. Second, "O Sons of the Buddha," and so forth, uses analogies to clarify the profundity and vastness [of the Tathāgata], thereby doubly responding to the preceding metaphors for the causes.

Third, from "O Sons of the Buddha" up to "knowing that the Tathāgata appears in the world," it summarizes the benefits achieved, concluding the ten preceding metaphors. Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. Herein, many causes collectively bring about the fruit of the appearance [of the Tathāgata].
Why is this? It is not by means of a single condition nor by means of a single matter that the appearance of a Tathāgata is accomplished;
rather, it is accomplished through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya matters.

The second section explains this through a commentary. It consists of two parts: first, a general explanation by means of an inquiry; second, a detailed clarification by enumerating the specific items, beginning with "What are they? and so forth. Regarding the first part:
first, the conditions (*pratyaya*) are explained through a reductio ad absurdum, identifying the causal entities that constitute the conditions as being identical to the resultant essence.

Subsequently, the ten [factors] are explained in a direct, affirmative manner. What was previously termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) was a general characteristic; now, it is clarified that there are specifically ten.
"Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) signifies inexhaustibility. In reality, however, there are hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* immeasurables.

These ten immeasurables all pervade the ten metaphors. Regarding the term "hundreds of thousands," the ancients said that by incorporating the ten immeasurables into the ten metaphors, one forms a hundred;
subsequently, through the ten phrases in the concluding summary, each one summarizes the preceding hundred gates.

A thousand. Within this, there are further distinct meanings that only then constitute "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). Now, below, when listing the ten intermediate gates, each gate is described as "immeasurable";
thus, they do not overlap. From this we know that the terms "hundred" and "thousand" are merely general designations for numbers.
What are the ten? They are: because it is accomplished through the bodhicitta that has encompassed all sentient beings throughout immeasurable past eons;
because it is accomplished through immeasurable past pure and sublime aspirations;

because it is accomplished through immeasurable past great loving-kindness and great compassion that protect all sentient beings; and because it is accomplished through immeasurable past continuous practices and vows.

Because it is accomplished through [the following]: because it is accomplished by the past infinite cultivation of various merits and wisdom with a mind never weary or satisfied; because it is accomplished by the past infinite making of offerings to the Buddhas and the teaching and transforming of sentient beings; because it is accomplished by the past infinite paths of pure wisdom and skillful means; because it is accomplished by the past infinite treasury of pure merit; and because it is accomplished by... Because it is accomplished through the wisdom of the path of immeasurable adornments; because it is accomplished through the past immeasurable penetration of the meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding the two specific enumerations explained separately, the first is the initial arousal of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), which is the vow to appear [in the world]. What is this mind?
1. The marks; 2. clarifying the superior aspiration for upward-seeking; 3. clarifying the compassion for downward-transforming; 4. practice as the continuation of the vow. What is this practice? 5.
Clarifying that it does not depart from merit and wisdom; 6. specifically revealing the adornment of merit; 7. specifically revealing the adornment of wisdom.

Eighth, purifying prior merits; ninth, adorning prior wisdom—namely, because they adorn the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*), the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*), the non-abiding path (*apratiṣṭhita-mārga*), the true path (*samyak-mārga*), the auxiliary path (*sahāya-mārga*), the single path (*eka-mārga*), the twofold path (*dvi-mārga*), and so forth;
tenth, thoroughly investigating the source of phenomena through true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata is perfected through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Dharma-gates.
Within the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), since all have already been fully perfected through manifold causes in the past, the fruits of the two benefits manifest simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that the manifestation of speech penetrates both the Real and the Responsive.
O Son of the Buddha! For example, a trichiliocosm is not accomplished by a single condition nor by a single event;
rather, it is only through immeasurable conditions and immeasurable events that it comes to be formed.

The second analogy clarifies the ten analogies within the "Profound and Vast" section; each consists of three parts: the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The illustration responds to the parable, while the application responds to the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Thus, the text states: "It does not appear through a single condition or a single event.

Furthermore, whereas the preceding exposition of the Dharma primarily concerned the causes of phenomena, the present application primarily concerns manifest conditions. Among the ten, the first is "Great Arising."

This is an analogy. This analogy serves as a general one; it generally illustrates how [phenomena] appear through the convergence of various conditions. Therefore, it says, "by means of immeasurable conditions," and so forth.
What follows regarding the clouds and rain is all that is showered by this [analogy]. Within the first analogy, there are four parts: first, a general explanation of the multiplicity of the general.
First, the specific manifestation of the conditions; second, the manifestation of their causal arising; third, the establishment through their essential nature and characteristics.

Now, for the first [section]: first the reverse order, then the direct order. "Conditions" refers to causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), such as the karma of sentient beings, wind, rain, and so forth.
"Phenomena" refers to the objective characteristics, namely the water and palaces that are supported, and so on.
This refers to the arising and spreading of great clouds and the pouring down of heavy rain, which are supported by a succession of four kinds of wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). What are these four?
First is named "Able to Support" (*dhara*), because it can support the great waters. Second is named "Able to Dissipate" (*vidhara*), because it can dissipate the great waters.

There are three types of establishment (*vyavasthāna*): first, because it establishes all locations; second, because it is called "ornamentation" (*vyūha*), as it is skillful in the distribution of ornaments.

Within the detailed explanation, first there is the raining down from above like clouds, and subsequently the supporting from below by the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). As for that which is capable of supporting: if...
Without this wheel, there would be no place for it to rest. Second, if the waters did not recede, there would be no room for the celestial palaces to arise.

Third, although the waters have already receded, it is by means of this [wheel] that they are established; that is to say, as each stage of water recedes, a corresponding tier of heavens arises, just as layers of ice form one after another in a swift current during a severe winter.
Fourth, although the general locations have arisen, they lack specific adornments; therefore, the fourth [element] is required.
All of this arises from the collective karma of sentient beings and the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas,
enabling all sentient beings therein to receive and enjoy it according to their respective needs and capacities.
Third, the manifestation of its causes arising: namely, that the aforementioned clouds and so forth arise briefly from two causes. First, the external dominant karma of sentient beings.
Regarding "common karma," this refers to the collective transformation of many sentient beings who are destined to be born in this realm;
herein there are four permutations, such as "common among the common" and so forth. Second, the roots of goodness of Bodhisattvas. This has two meanings. First, regarding...
"Co-residing" refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages [of the path]. Second, regarding the capacity to transform:
according to the needs of sentient beings, whatever kind of land might give rise to the roots of bodhisattvahood and so forth, one cultivates the causes for that very land to assist it.

Thus, there are classes of sentient beings who are themselves the Buddha-land of the bodhisattva; this is shown below as the enjoyment fruit within which they abide. This means first establishing the receptacle world.
Later, sentient beings are formed and dwell depending upon it, each according to what is appropriate for them; that is to say, aquatic beings receive the enjoyment of water and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction to the palaces of humans or rākṣasas, and bodhisattvas and sentient beings cohabit in both pure and impure realms.
O Son of the Buddha, through such immeasurable causes and conditions as these, the trichiliocosm is formed. Such is the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*):
there is no one who gives birth to it, no one who creates it, no one who knows it, and no one who brings it into existence;
yet that world is nonetheless accomplished.

The fourth [section] concerns the formation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Within this, first the preceding is joined to the subsequent; then, from "the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus" onwards, it is formally joined.
This sentence serves as the general [statement]. The term "nature of phenomena" applies to both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The phrase "there is no arising" specifically clarifies that the essence is determinate, and furthermore, it negates false conceptualizations—namely, that [phenomena] do not arise from a primordial material cause (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, nor from Īśvara or Brahmā.

...and so forth. There is no self (ātman) that can know; the preceding three [lines] manifest the agent, while "emptiness" manifests that there is no one who accomplishes, thereby manifesting the object of action.
Although both agent and object are empty, this does not obstruct the existence of their characteristics; therefore, it is said that "it is accomplished.
Such non-obstruction is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

The appearance of a Tathāgata is also like this. It is not accomplished through a single condition nor through a single matter, but is accomplished through immeasurable causes and conditions and immeasurable phenomena.

That is to say, having in the past heard, received, and upheld the great Dharma-cloud from the presence of former Buddhas, one is thereby able to give rise to the four kinds of great wisdom-winds of a Tathāgata.

The wheels. What are the four? First is the wind-wheel of great wisdom of the dhāraṇī of mindful retention without forgetting, because it can sustain the great rain-clouds of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
Second is the wind-wheel of great wisdom that gives birth to śamatha and vipaśyanā, because it can exhaust and dry up all afflictions.
Third is the wind-wheel of great wisdom of skillful dedication, because it can bring about accomplishment...

Because of all roots of goodness. Fourth, it gives rise to the great wind-wheel of wisdom, adorned with the distinction of being free from defilement, which purifies the roots of goodness of all sentient beings who were previously transformed, thereby accomplishing the power of the Tathāgata’s untainted roots of goodness.
Thus does the Tathāgata attain equal and perfect enlightenment; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): unarisen and unconditioned, yet [it] is attained.
It is accomplished. O Son of the Buddha, this is the first sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
Next, regarding the application [of the metaphors], the third is briefly not applied in order to reveal its specific cause, because the two subsequent metaphors are each applied individually.
Among the four wheels, the first three are the causes, while the latter one is the fulfillment of the twofold benefit, which is the fruit;

thus, through the perfection of cause and the perfection of fruit, the Buddha appears. Within this chapter, most of the metaphors are applied according to their primary meaning, not merely by way of general category.
They are similar; in reality, the external world arises through the transformation of the internal. Therefore, it causes the external vessel-world to correspond entirely to the internal [mind].
This is why it was stated above that it is "arisen from the roots of goodness of Bodhisattvas" and "produced by the collective karma of sentient beings," and so forth.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: for example, when the trichiliocosm is about to be formed, a great cloud sends down rain called "the Great Deluge.
No place whatsoever can receive it, nor can anything sustain it, except for those places within the trichiliocosm that are about to be formed.
Son of the Buddha, in the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, likewise brings forth the Great Dharma.
The clouds rain down the great rain of the Dharma, which is named "The Accomplishment of the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

It cannot be received nor can it be sustained by any of the followers of the two vehicles whose mental dispositions are narrow and inferior; it can only be sustained by the power of the continuous mental stream of the great bodhisattvas. O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand it thus.
This is the second analogy of the great rain showering upon the trichiliocosm. This cloud and rain are precisely the clouds arising and the rain falling from the previous analogy.
The Dharma-gate of the Perfect Parable is vast and difficult to know, for it pervades the ten directions. Regarding the "power of the continuity of the mind":

if considered in terms of faith and acceptance, it refers only to those of perfect capacity, whose firm seeds continue on so that they can receive the profound meaning. If considered in terms of fully receiving [the teaching], [it refers to all who are capable].
Thus, only those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, having attained the *akṣaya-dhāraṇī*, are able to receive and uphold [the teachings];

even until the tenth stage do they receive the Tathāgata’s rain-like preaching of the Dharma. For this reason, the text states that "great Bodhisattvas" are excluded; according to the primary sense, it merely excludes those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: for example, by the power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds send down rain;

it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by the power of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas, raises a great cloud of Dharma and sends down a great rain of Dharma; likewise, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. The Buddha...
"Son, this is the third sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand it thus.
The third [sign] is beyond comparison to rain from clouds; the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas, arising through shared karma, bring about that appearance."
The Dharma-cloud and Dharma-rain manifest in response to the capacity for awakening; they do not first exist in some location from which they come.
When the capacity for awakening ceases, they depart; yet they do not return to their former place. Therefore, their essence is without birth or extinction.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha: it is like a great cloud that pours down heavy rain;
no sentient being within the great trichiliocosm is able to know its measure, and if one were to attempt to calculate it, it would only drive one mad.

Only Maheśvara, the Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, by virtue of the power of the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, clearly perceives every single drop without exception. Thus it is with the Buddha.

Son, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, is also like this. He raises a great cloud of Dharma and rains down the great rain of Dharma, which all sentient beings—whether Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—cannot know.
Should they attempt to fathom it, their minds would surely become deranged;
with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are lords of the world, because of the power of the wisdom they have cultivated in the past.
"Even down to a single word or a single phrase, there is nothing that does not enter the minds of sentient beings with perfect clarity.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the fourth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus."
The fourth is the parable of the great rain being difficult to know. This illustrates that which is profound and not within the realm of the ordinary mind;
it can only be known by those of great capacity who are lords of the world, for whom there is neither subject nor object of practice.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha: for example, when a great cloud sends down rain, there is a great cloud-rain called "Able to Extinguish," which can extinguish fires;
there is a great cloud-rain called "Able to Raise," which can raise up great waters; there is a great cloud-rain called "Able to Cease," which can cease great waters;
and there is a great cloud-rain called "Able to Accomplish," which can accomplish all things.
There are mani-jewels and various treasures, and there is a great cloud-rain called "Discrimination," which discriminates the trichiliocosm.
Sons of the Buddha, the appearance of the Tathāgata is also like this: he raises a great Dharma-cloud and rains down a great Dharma-rain.
There is a great Dharma-rain called "Able to Extinguish," which is able to extinguish the afflictions of all sentient beings. There is a great Dharma-rain called...

It can give rise [to virtue]. It can give rise to the roots of goodness in all sentient beings. There is a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Cease," which can cease the delusions of view in all sentient beings.
There is a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Accomplish," which can accomplish the jewel-treasures of all wisdom.
There is a great rain of Dharma called "Discernment," which discerns the inclinations of the hearts of all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should know it thus.

This is the fifth analogy of the great rain regarding formation and destruction. How much more so for the Buddha’s extinguishing of afflictions and perfecting of virtues? In this analogy, the first [rain] corresponds to destruction.

At the time of the realms (*dhātu*): the first two immediately use water to stop water; among these, the first two eliminate delusions to accomplish merit (*puṇya*), while the next two eliminate obstacles to accomplish wisdom (*jñāna*).

This is the simultaneous integration of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). The final one is the skillful wisdom that illuminates the capacities of sentient beings. Furthermore, having no second is not the same as the Two Vehicles;

having no third is not the same as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); having no fourth does not increase ignorance (*avidyā*); and having no fifth is not [limited to] the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is—
Within the general category of "parts," the rain of Dharma causes distinctions to arise.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great cloud that rains water of a single flavor, yet according to where it falls, there are immeasurable differences.

The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so. He rains down the water of the Dharma of a single flavor of great compassion, yet he teaches the Dharma with immeasurable distinctions according to what is appropriate.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth sign of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.

The sixth is the single rain that accords with individual metaphors, which illustrates how the Buddha’s single flavor accords with the capacity of the vessel; according to the vessel, there is a corresponding differentiation.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the trichiliocosm is first being formed:

first the palaces of the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are formed, next the palaces of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are formed, and finally those of humans and other sentient beings are formed.
O Son of the Buddha, in all places where beings dwell, the manifestation of the Tathāgata is likewise: first, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of bodhisattvas;
next, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of pratyekabuddhas; and next, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of the roots of goodness of śrāvakas.
Next, one gives rise to the wisdom of the various conditioned wholesome roots and practices of other sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a great cloud raining down water of a single flavor; yet, because the wholesome roots of sentient beings differ, the palaces that arise are various and not the same.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion rains down the Dharma rain of a single flavor, yet it manifests distinctions according to the capacities of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the seventh sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.

The seventh stage of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) first establishes the analogy. This analogy illustrates the Buddha’s virtue of providing superior conditions and rescuing beings beforehand. In the text, this is first explicitly clarified;

subsequently, the "sons of the Buddha" analogy follows to address and resolve doubts. Their prior accomplishment arises from the maturation of karma; their diversity in the Dharma arises from the differences among those with capacity (*yogya*), yet this does not contradict the single flavor (*ekarasa*).
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the world is first about to be formed, a great body of water arises, filling the trichiliocosm.
A great lotus flower named "Jeweled Adornment of the Meritorious Virtues of the Tathāgata’s Appearance" grows, covering the surface of the water.
Its light illuminates all worlds in the ten directions. At that time, Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others behold it.
Having seen these flowers, he immediately and with certainty knew that during this kalpa there would appear in the world that many Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, at that time there arose therein a wind-circle named "Pure Radiance," which was able to form the palaces of the various heavens of the Form Realm;
there was a wind-circle named "Adornment of Pure Light," which was able to form the palaces of the various heavens of the Desire Realm; and there was...
There is a wind-circle named Firm and Dense, which nothing can destroy; it is able to form the various great and small Cakravāḍa mountains as well as the Vajra Mountains.
There is a wind-circle named Supreme Height, which is able to form Sumeru, the King of Mountains. There is a wind-circle named Immovable, which is able to form the ten great mountain kings.

What are these ten? They are: Mount Khadiraka, Mount Ṛṣigiri, [Mount Yugandhara, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Vinataka, Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Sudarśana, Mount Cakravāḍa, and Mount Mahācakravāḍa].
Mount Mārabhañjana, Mount Mahāmārabhañjana, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Munindara, Mount Mahāmunindara, Mount Gandhamādana, and Mount Himavat.
There is a wind-circle named "Abiding" (*anurakṣa*) which is able to form the great earth.
There is a wind-circle named "Adornment" (*vyūhana*) which is able to form the palaces of the terrestrial devas and the palaces of the nāgas.
There is a wind-circle named Inexhaustible Treasury that can form all the great oceans of the trichiliocosm.
There is a wind-circle named Universal Radiance Treasury that can form all the maṇi jewels of the trichiliocosm.
There is a wind-circle named Firm Root that can form all the [bodies] of the Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha, the tree of the mind is like the rain of a single flavor poured by the great cloud, which itself makes no distinction;
yet because the roots of goodness of sentient beings differ, the wind-circles differ. Because the wind-circles differ, the worlds differ.
The eighth matter distinguishes [the Buddha] by means of causes and analogies. The analogy illustrates the virtue of the Buddha’s accomplishment of the great task;
furthermore, this excellence of virtue is distinguished by means of an analogy for wisdom. This analogy is divided into three parts. First, the lotus represents the Buddha.

Although it is omitted in the general summary, it is called "manifesting" (*prādurbhāva*) because it symbolizes the manifestation of the Buddha. As for the term "great," according to the third chapter of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, it is because it possesses one thousand petals.
"Light illuminating the ten directions" refers to golden light. Regarding the phrase "that many Buddhas," it is because there are a thousand branches of flowers representing a thousand Buddhas;
therefore, the eon is named Bhadra (Worthy), as there are many who are worthy and virtuous. Other details are mostly the same as this.

Second, regarding the passage "At that time, O sons of the Buddha, from below the wind-wheel arises... this refers to the powerful wind that holds [the world] from afar, extensively establishing the wind-wheel as previously described. Second.
The Buddha’s great cloud descends, forming a causal connection.

O Son of the Buddha, the appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: he is fully endowed with all roots of goodness and merit, and emits the light of supreme, great wisdom called "the inconceivable wisdom that perpetuates the lineage of the Tathāgatas," which universally illumines the ten directions.
In all worlds, they receive the empowerment and prophecy of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas that they shall attain perfect awakening and appear in the world.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Tathāgata appears, there is furthermore a supreme light of great wisdom called "Pure and Stainless," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s untainted and inexhaustible wisdom. There is also another supreme light of great wisdom.
It is named Universal Illumination; it can accomplish the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom that universally enters the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named Sustaining the Buddha-lineage; it can accomplish the Tathāgata’s unshakable power.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named Transcending the Indestructible; it can accomplish the Tathāgata’s fearless and indestructible wisdom. Furthermore...
There is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom called "All Supernatural Powers," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s unique qualities and the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom called "Production of Transformations," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s wisdom that ensures the roots of goodness produced by seeing, hearing, and drawing near to him are never lost or destroyed. Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom...
The light is named Universal Accordance; it can accomplish the Tathāgata’s body of inexhaustible merit and wisdom, bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is a supreme light of great wisdom named Inexhaustibility.
It can accomplish the profound and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata; according to what it awakens, it causes the lineage of the Triple Gem to never be severed.

Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named "Various Adornments," which can accomplish the marks and signs that adorn the body of the Tathāgata, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy. Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named "Not..."
It can be destroyed; yet it can accomplish the supreme, inexhaustible lifespan of the Tathāgata’s *dharmadhātu*, the *ākāśadhātu*, and so forth.
Within the second combination there are also three [points]. First, the combination of the lotus serves as a metaphor for the Buddha.

Because all roots of goodness and merit therein combine with the aforementioned large and small [elements] to pervade everywhere, the lotus in every birth signifies that the lineage (*gotra*) is never severed. Universally...

Illuminating the ten directions corresponds above to the light illuminating the ten directions; it corresponds below to the passage "together with all bodhisattvas," signifying that one knows the Buddha is about to appear.
The second section, beginning with "the sons of the Buddha," corresponds to the place where the wind-circle arises; this serves as a metaphor for the sequence of these ten wisdom-lights.

This corresponds to the previous section on the "sole fruit-virtue" (*phala-guṇa*), which can establish both the general cause and fruit, and can also establish the provisional (*upāya*) within the real (*tattva*). That which is established is solely the differentiated [phenomenal].
This is the virtue of their distinction. Therefore, the conclusion below states that they share the same essential nature:
"O Son of the Buddha, the water of the Tathāgata’s great compassion is of a single flavor and is without discrimination;

yet, because the desires and inclinations of sentient beings differ and their faculties are each distinct, various wind-circles of great wisdom arise, causing all Bodhisattvas to achieve [their goals]."

Regarding the manner in which the Tathāgata appears, O Son of the Buddha: from within the great wheel of wisdom, the single essential nature of all Tathāgatas, there arise various radiances of wisdom.

The third section contains the causes for the inclusion [of the elements] and their respective attributes; herein there are three parts. First, the cause of inclusion is the wisdom capable of accomplishment, which merges with the water of a single flavor.
The wind-wheel is not uniform; this wheel arises as each successive layer of the water-element diminishes by one unit, like the sediment settling from clear water.
This demonstrates that the capacity for accomplishment arises through the single flavor of great compassion. Second, all the Buddha-sons... [text truncated].
The lower result is the great wisdom that is thus accomplished. It arises from the single reality-wisdom (*ekasatya-jñāna*) in accordance with skillful means (*upāya*).
Because it accords with the distinctions of the upper wind-circle, there are distinctions in the world-systems.
"O Sons of the Buddha, you should know that from a single taste of liberation, the Tathāgata produces immeasurable and inconceivable varieties of merit.
Sentient beings think to themselves, 'This is created by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata. O Sons of the Buddha, this is not created by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
O Sons of the Buddha, it is because even a single bodhisattva has never planted [the seeds] before a Buddha..."
It is impossible for roots of goodness to attain even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

It is solely by the power of the majestic virtue of all Buddhas that all sentient beings are made to possess the merits of a Buddha; yet the Buddha-Tathāgata is without discrimination, without formation, and without destruction.
There is no agent, nor is there any action. Son of the Buddha, this is what constitutes a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The eighth sign appears. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand it in this way:

there are three conditions for connection. This is because sentient beings differ; thus, by combining the previous point regarding the differences in the roots of goodness of sentient beings, the doubts of outsiders are also addressed.
Within this, there are again three parts. First, the preceding correct principle is restated: the flavor of liberation is that which is capable of accomplishment.
Water. Water possesses two meanings: compassion and liberation; the two phrases [in the text] are abbreviated by mutual implication.
The various merits pertain to both the wisdom that acts as the means and the wisdom that is the goal. The two thoughts regarding sentient beings raise external doubts.

However, the Way of Resonance and Response briefly has three meanings: first, mutual fulfillment; second, mutual sublation; third, the emptiness of nature established through conditions. Now, because sentient beings...
Regarding the sublation of conditions by causes: this solely attributes [the result] to the power of the Buddha, thereby losing the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
O sons of the Buddha, this is not so; it is for the sake of explaining the Tathāgata’s intent. Within this, first, causes sublate conditions and categorically state that they are not [the cause].

Next, starting from "but rather," the correct meaning is explained. In the first phrase, cause and condition are established as mutually constitutive. Subsequently, within the passage beginning with "but the Buddha," there are two meanings: first, it establishes the aforementioned cause.

Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): although they follow the minds of sentient beings, they are without discrimination. Because the third meaning—that the nature of things is empty—is realized through the three [aspects], there is no establishment because of the establishment of conditions.

Because there is no establishment, there is no disintegration. Since that which is established is already empty, how could there be an establishing agent, an act of establishing, or an object of establishment?
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, just as four wind-wheels arise depending on space and are able to support the water-wheel—what are these four?
First is named Abiding; second is named Constantly Abiding; third is named Ultimate; and fourth is named Solid.

These four wind-wheels are able to support the water-wheel, and the water-wheel is able to support the great earth so that it does not disintegrate. For this reason, it is said that the earth-wheel depends [on the water-wheel].

The water wheel rests upon the wind wheel; the wind wheel rests upon space. Abiding in space, it has no support, yet, though it has no support, it is able to cause the trichiliocosm to remain securely established.
The ninth is the analogy of four wheels leaning against one another, illustrating the Buddha’s essence, function, support, and qualities.

It also extensively establishes the specific meanings of the winds. Within this analogy, there are two parts; first, clarifying the winds that provide support. There are four types: first, supporting water at a single moment, called "abiding" (*sthiti*);
