second, remaining unmoved for a long duration, called "constant abiding" (*nitya-sthiti*); third, having a measure equal to the duration of a kalpa; and fourth, its essential nature...
Its nature is firm and dense. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Suppose there were a great *yojana* [in height] which, when struck with force by a wheel of vajra, might cause the vajra to shatter, yet the wind-wheel would suffer no damage. Its extent is immeasurable and its thickness is sixteen *lakṣas*.
That [wind-wheel] exists as only one, whereas this is not the case. Second, the characteristics of the four wheels below these four.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, above that is a water wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*) eight lakṣas thick—where one lakṣa equals one hundred million (*koṭi*).
Above that, there is further a golden wheel (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*) three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas thick.
Regarding this world-system, some say it is composed of three wheels—namely, water, wind, and gold; others say it consists of five wheels, adding space below and the great earth above. Now...
If one wishes to calculate the elements that constitute the four wheels, since the earth contains gold and is itself the earth, so it is with the appearance of a Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha.

Relying upon the light of unimpeded wisdom, the Tathāgata gives rise to the four great wind-wheels of buddha-knowledge, which are able to sustain the roots of goodness of all sentient beings. What are these four? They are called: universal gathering...
The great wisdom wind-wheel that causes all sentient beings to rejoice; the great wisdom wind-wheel that establishes the true Dharma so that all sentient beings may give rise to love and joy;
the great wisdom wind-wheel that protects the roots of goodness of all sentient beings;

and the great wisdom wind-wheel that possesses all skillful means and penetrates the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). These are the four, O Son of the Buddha. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones...
The Honored One, with great kindness, protects and rescues all sentient beings; with great compassion, he delivers all sentient beings.
His great kindness and great compassion universally benefit all. This great kindness and great compassion rely upon great skillful means;
great skillful means relies upon the appearance of the Tathāgata; the appearance of the Tathāgata relies upon the light of unimpeded wisdom; and the light of unimpeded wisdom...
It is clear that there is nothing upon which it relies. O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.

Second, within the middle [section], one first correlates [the text] with the four winds that sustain: (1) for those who have not yet entered through faith, one universally gathers them by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and demonstrates the correct principle;
(2) for those who already have faith and affection, one establishes the teachings; (3) for those who have already entered the Dharma, one causes them to accomplish the practice;

(4) for those who have already accomplished the practice, one causes them to attain the fruit. Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, one correlates [the text] with the four wheels.

They are mutually dependent: first, the ground of the union of compassion, for it can support all things with thickness; second, the water of the union of skillful means, for it bends and conforms to the vessel;
third, the wind of manifestation, for its power can sustain all; fourth, the space of non-obstruction, for it is unobstructed like space.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "That unobstructed wisdom has no diversity."
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: once the trichiliocosm has been fully formed, it brings benefit to immeasurable and diverse classes of sentient beings.
That is to say, aquatic beings receive the benefit of water; terrestrial beings receive the benefit of land;
beings of the palaces receive the benefit of their palaces; and beings of space receive the benefit of space.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so. He brings manifold benefit to immeasurable sentient beings. That is to say:
those who see the Buddha and give rise to joy obtain the benefit of joy; those who abide in pure precepts obtain the benefit of pure precepts;

those who abide in various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) obtain the benefit of noble, supramundane, great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and those who abide in the radiance of the Dharma-gates obtain the benefit of the cause...
The benefit of non-destruction: those who abide in the light of non-existence attain the benefit of the non-destruction of all dharmas.
Therefore it is said that the appearance of the Tathāgata brings benefit to all immeasurable sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the tenth sign of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
The tenth is the analogy of great benefit. How much more so the Buddha’s virtue in benefiting the world!

This specifically reveals that within the general [benefit], all sentient beings each receive and enjoy it according to what is appropriate for them. Within the synthesis, the sequence corresponds to the four previous benefits:
seeing the Buddha and giving rise to joy is like a fish obtaining moisture; morality is like level ground because all myriad virtues arise from it; and meditative concentration is like a palace.

Because they have attained peace; because wisdom is like space and cannot be destroyed. Within these two phrases, the first concerns the indestructibility of phenomena, and the latter concerns the indestructibility of principle.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows the appearance of the Tathāgata, they know the immeasurable and know the accomplishment of the infinite.
Because it is measured by conduct, one knows it is vast; because it knows it pervades the ten directions, one knows it has no coming or going;

because it knows it is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing, one knows it has no activity and no object of activity; because it knows it is free from mind, thought, and consciousness, one knows it has no body;
because it knows it is like empty space, one knows it is equal; because it knows all sentient beings are without self, one knows...
One knows it is inexhaustible because it pervades all lands without end; one knows it is without regression because it continues through the future limit without interruption;
one knows it is indestructible because the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no counterpart; one knows it is non-dual because it observes the conditioned and the unconditioned with equanimity;
and one knows that all sentient beings thereby obtain benefit. [End of] Chapter on the Fundamental.

Because of the vow for the fulfillment of mastery in dedication, there are eleven phrases in the third section on the formation of benefits. Each phrase individually concludes one of the preceding ten gates;
since the ninth gate is concluded by ninety-two phrases, there are eleven [sections] in total. First, because many causes appear; second, because it is extensive.
1. Difficult to perceive. 2. Because the three [realms] are non-arising, there is no source. 3. Because it is not mind or consciousness, thought would surely drive one mad.
4. Because it is like space, delusion and views are both forgotten. 5. Because it is equal and selfless, it is of a single flavor. 6.

Because it is inexhaustible, all vehicles manifest transformations. 7. Because its future limit is uninterrupted, the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed. 8. Being without opposition is itself non-existence.
The tenth is the equality of the conditioned and the unconditioned, which subsumes the three wheels and returns them to unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*).
The eleventh is that, for the sake of sentient beings, one brings their benefit to fulfillment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The Great Hero of Ten Powers is most unsurpassed; Like space, his realm is peerless, vast, and immeasurable; His merit is supreme, transcending the world."
The second verse consists of thirty-seven stanzas divided into three parts: first, fourteen stanzas praising the profundity and granting permission to speak;
next, twenty-two stanzas versifying the ten preceding metaphors; and finally, one stanza concluding that the teaching is inexhaustible, rather than versifying the preceding prose.

The first part is now divided into two sections: the first eleven verses praise [the Buddha] as profound and immeasurable; the final three verses exhort the audience to listen. Within the first section, there are also two parts:
the initial verse offers a general praise, echoing the preceding introductory statement regarding the inconceivable; the subsequent ten verses provide specific praises.
This verse immediately follows and summarizes the eleven lines of the preceding [section], just as the ninth verse summarized the ninety-two lines.

Since that previous section concluded with a metaphorical summary, this one likewise provides a comprehensive summary of the preceding metaphors. While the metaphors clarify both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this passage primarily speaks in terms of essence.
There is a further reason for the ancient tradition of the *Tathāgatagarbha* (Nature-Arising) being so extensive.
The merit of the Ten Powers is boundless and immeasurable, beyond the reach of thought or mental calculation;
this single Dharma-door of the Lion among Men cannot be known by sentient beings even in hundreds of millions of eons—
this "one" is itself immeasurable, meaning it is infinite in significance.

Even if the lands of the ten directions were ground into dust, and someone could calculate and know their number, the measure of the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata could not be told even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;
two such hairs are likewise immeasurable. This is the meaning of "vast."
Just as a person holding a measuring rod attempts to measure space, and another follows along counting its units, yet the limit of space cannot be found;
so too is the realm of the Tathāgata—within the three limits of emptiness, it is unattainable.
This is precisely the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Only this third verse seems to summarize the fifth [chapter], "The Nature of Reality" (*Tathatā*).

Emptiness. The sixth verse appears to be a parallel summary of the third [verse] on non-arising and non-ceasing; however, as the meanings they convey differ, both are presented according to their sequence.
Or there may be one who, in a single instant, fully knows the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Even if one were to pass through kalpas equal in number to all sentient beings, one could not know the nature of a single thought-moment of the Buddha.
As for the four things that cannot be known: because it is free from mind and consciousness, it is like the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which pervades all yet cannot be seen or grasped as "all."
The sphere of the Ten Powers is likewise: it pervades all and yet does not pervade all.
That which "pervades all and yet does not pervade all" is precisely the meaning of emptiness.
True Suchness is free from delusion and eternally quiescent; Without birth and without cessation, it is universally pervasive.
The realm of all Buddhas is likewise so; Its essential nature is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
(Regarding) "the six essential natures are equal": this refers to the meaning of equality and selflessness.
For example, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is not a limit; likewise, it is universally present throughout the three periods of time, yet it is not universal.
The realm of the Teacher is also like this: it is entirely unimpeded throughout the three periods of time.
The previous [verse] spoke of pervading all lands; this speaks of pervading the three periods of time—the phrasing is merely varied.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without action and without change; it is like space, fundamentally pure.
The purity of the nature of all Buddhas is likewise so: this original nature is neither a "nature" nor a "non-nature," transcending existence and non-existence.
Because it is free from the eight kinds of change, it endures until the very limit of the future.
The nature of phenomena does not reside in verbal discourse; it is beyond speech, free from expression, and eternally quiescent.
The nature of the realm of the Ten Powers is likewise; no words or phrases can ever fully describe it.
Because it transcends all verbal expression, it is non-dual and without counterpart.
Knowing that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent, like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace,
he manifests a form-body through the power of his original vows, enabling beings to behold the Tathāgata’s great spiritual transformations;
because he manifests his body through these ten original vows, he is able to bring about benefit.

If there are those who wish to know the realm of the Buddha, They should purify their minds like space, remaining far removed from false conceptualizations and all forms of grasping, Causing the mind to be unimpeded wherever it turns.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, you should listen well; I shall clarify the Buddha-realm through a few similes.

The merits of the Ten Powers are immeasurable; for the sake of awakening sentient beings, I shall now briefly explain the realms manifested by the Guide through his physical, vocal, and mental actions:
his turning of the sublime Wheel of Dharma and his entry into Parinirvāṇa—all these roots of goodness I shall now proclaim.
The second section, the admonition to listen and permission to speak, is divided into two parts. First, the initial admonition to listen encourages practice:

"Purify the mind so that it is like space. This is illustrated generally by means of a metaphor; the following two lines illustrate it specifically: First, one must be free from false grasping, because, like that pure sky, it is devoid of clouds and obscurations;
this is *zhengzhi* (true stillness). Second, one must encounter objects without obstruction, because, like that pure sky, it is free from hindrances.
This is true contemplation. When this contemplation does not employ intentional effort to illuminate objects, that which is illuminated becomes boundless.

Because the essence of this stillness is free from attachment and delusion ceases, all grasping is stilled. If one reaches this state, one is neither obstructed nor polished, yet is spontaneously pure.
This purity that is without the concept of purity is to silently tread upon the realm of the Buddhas. This is the essential core of the mind; I pray you, take it to heart.

"Later students should contemplate and practice. The latter two lines permit the delineation of the boundaries [of the teaching]. Within these, the first half-verse concludes the preceding and introduces what follows;
the subsequent half-verse properly demonstrates the boundaries by citing the ten gates. The "practice" is omitted because it is subsumed within the two types of karma;
the "Perfectly Awakened One" is omitted because he is subsumed within the "Teacher," or alternatively, it was simply omitted for brevity.
Just as when the world was first established, it could not have been formed by a single cause and condition,
but rather through immeasurable skillful means and various causal conditions that brought this trichiliocosm into being;
so too is the appearance of a Tathāgata, which is achieved only through immeasurable merit.
The thoughts within the atoms of all lands may still be known, But the causes for birth throughout the ten directions cannot be measured.
Just as when clouds pour down rain at the beginning of a kalpa, Four kinds of great wind-circles arise;
Through the roots of goodness of sentient beings and the power of Bodhisattvas, This trichiliocosm is formed and each abides securely.
The clouds of Dharma in the ten directions are likewise; Rising from the wind-wheel of wisdom, they purify the mind.
For all sentient beings toward whom one has previously directed merit, They universally guide them to achieve the unsurpassed fruit.
Just as there is a great rain called "the torrential downpour," There is no place capable of containing it.
Except for the time when the world is about to be formed, When the great power of the wind blows through the pure void, The appearance of a Tathāgata is likewise so:
He rains down the Dharma everywhere to fill the entire Dharma-realm;
All those of inferior intent are unable to sustain it, Except for those with pure and vast minds.
Just as when great rain pours from the sky, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
so too are the agent and the recipient. Spontaneously and thus, it universally saturates all;
the Dharma-rain of the One of Ten Powers is likewise: without going, without coming, and without fabrication.
With this conduct as their cause, the power of the Bodhisattvas— may all those of great resolve listen!
Just as a great rain pours from clouds in the sky, no one is able to count its drops,
except for the Sovereign Kings of the Three Thousand Worlds, who possess the power of merit and are fully enlightened.
The Dharma-rain of the Sugata is likewise; no sentient beings can fathom it, Except for those who are masters of the world, who see clearly as if beholding a jewel in the palm of their hand.
Just as empty clouds pour down great rain, which can extinguish, can raise, and can sever.
All precious jewels can be accomplished; The entirety of the three thousandfold world is thoroughly discerned.
The rain of the Dharma of the Ten Powers is likewise: It extinguishes delusions, gives rise to goodness, and severs all views.
It causes the jewels of omniscience to be fully realized, And thoroughly discerns the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.
For example, when rain of a single flavor falls from the sky, That which it rains upon appears variously according to the recipient;
Yet how could there be any distinction in the nature of that rain? Rather, it differs according to the objects it meets.
In this same way, the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is neither one nor many; It is equal, quiescent, and free from conceptual discrimination.
Yet, according to the various differences of those to be converted, there are naturally such infinite manifestations:
just as when the world is first formed, the palaces of the gods of the Form Realm are established first,
followed by those of the gods of the Desire Realm, then the human abodes, and finally the palaces of the gandharvas.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise: first he initiates the boundless practices of bodhisattvas;
next he transforms the pratyekabuddhas who delight in tranquility; then the assembly of śrāvakas, and finally all sentient beings and devas.
Upon first seeing the auspicious sign of the lotus, they know that a Buddha is about to appear and rejoice.
The world arises through the power of wind upon water; Palaces, mountains, and rivers are all established.
Through the great radiance of the Tathāgata’s past roots of goodness, He skillfully distinguishes Bodhisattvas and grants them their predictions.
The essence of his entire wheel of wisdom is pure, And he is able to reveal each of the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as forests depend upon the earth, and the earth depends upon water so that it does not disintegrate,
the water-circle depends upon wind, and wind depends upon space, yet that empty space has nothing upon which it depends—
so all Buddha-dharmas depend upon compassion, and compassion in turn is established upon skillful means.
Skillful means rely on knowledge, and knowledge relies on wisdom; The body of unimpeded wisdom has no dependence.

Just as once the world has been established, All sentient beings obtain its benefit— Those dwelling on earth or water, and those dwelling in space, Whether two-legged or four-legged, all receive its grace.
The appearance of the Dharma King is likewise: All sentient beings obtain its benefit;
Should they see, hear, or draw near to him, He causes all their delusions and afflictions to be extinguished.
This second verse summarizes the ten preceding metaphors, which thus constitute ten sections. The first metaphor consists of four verses, as it serves as the general [introduction] for the others.

The nine [analogies] each have two [parts]. Now, for the first [analogy], there are two sections: the first two verses generally manifest the manifold conditions, while the latter two verses specifically manifest the characteristics of those conditions.
Regarding the ninth analogy, the application (*yōjaku*) states: "Skillful means rely upon wisdom. Here, "wisdom" refers to that which appeared in the preceding verse.

However, the first unimpeded wisdom is the Buddha’s true wisdom, while the middle two are both provisional. Within this, wisdom is the knowledge of phenomena, while skillful means adapt to the capacities of sentient beings;

when combined with the former, they constitute the non-obstruction of the provisional and the real, and when contrasted with the first, they represent the simultaneous movement of compassion and wisdom.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is a boundless Dharma, which the deluded of the world are unable to know;
desiring to awaken all sentient beings, he provides metaphors for that which is beyond metaphor,
explaining the three fetters without end.
O Son of the Buddha! How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

The second part provides a specific answer by first clarifying the physical activity (kāyakarman) through nine gateways of manifestation, followed by the eight bases. Within the prose section, there are two parts:
first, the formal presentation.
O Son of the Buddha! All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should perceive the body of the Tathāgata in immeasurable locations. Why is this?
Because all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not perceive the Tathāgata through a single dharma, a single phenomenon, a single body, a single land, or a single sentient being;
rather, they should perceive the Tathāgata pervading all places.

Next, the characteristics are explained. This section consists of three parts: first, a general clarification based on the Dharma; second, a specific elucidation by means of analogies; and third, a summary based on the Dharma.

Within the general section, five points pervade throughout the ten bodies in the analogies; in the summary, ten phrases specifically correspond to the ten analogies, which are identical to their appearance in the preceding [section].
Now, for the first part, there are four sections: (1) the general instruction to see extensively; (2) "For what reason? [and so forth].
To investigate the reasons for this: third, from "The various bodhisattvas... onwards, there is a reverse explanation of the reasons; fourth, from "It should apply universally to all...

onwards, there is a concluding response in accordance with the principle. Within the reverse explanation, five dharmas are raised in general: "Dharma" refers to the dharma-realm that is to be known and the dharma of subduing;
"matter" (vastu) refers to the activities for subduing sentient beings—thus the Jin translation names it "practice" (*caryā*); "body" (*kāya*) is itself "correctness."

The buddha-field is the support; sentient beings are those to be transformed. Among the four types of concordant fetters (*anuloma-saṃyojana*), one should reverse the aforementioned five to establish the five immeasurable realms (*apramāṇa-dhātu*).

The body serves as that which pervades, while the four serve as that which is pervaded: first, the pervasion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); second, the pervasion of the realm of those to be tamed (*vineya-dhātu*).
Third, the realm of the application of subduing; fourth, the pervasive world-realm; fifth, the pervasive realm of sentient beings. There are only these five realms; it is not an abbreviation.
Second, regarding the "Son of the Buddha," in the section explaining the distinct metaphors by way of analogy, it clarifies that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten kinds of bodies:
first, the body that pervades the ten directions; second, the unattached and unimpeded body; third...
1. The body that universally enters and brings about benefit; 2. The body that accords with others through the fourfold equality; 3. The body that benefits beings secretly through non-arising; 4.

The body that abides in universal equanimity through circular transformation; 5. The body that responds universally without thought; 6. The body that reaches the furthest limit of the future; 7. The body that adorns lands and increases benefit; 8.
The body that fulfills vows through the perfection of marks and signs. These constitute the sequence of the ten bodies of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*).
The same. [These are: first, the *dharmakāya*; second, the *jñānakāya*; third, majestic power (*prabhāva*); fourth, *bodhi*; fifth, adornment (*vyūha*);
sixth, the mind-born (*manomaya*); seventh, transformation (*nirmāṇa*); eighth, sustaining power (*baladhara*); ninth, merit (*puṇya*); and tenth, vows (*praṇidhāna*). Regarding "fourth is *bodhi*":

because it first illuminates upon its initial attainment. As the verse says: "Because the sun and moon appear. Regarding "fifth is adornment": the light from each and every pore and secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).
This is clear because it serves as an adornment; the remainder of the text is self-evident. To manifest these ten bodies, ten similes are adduced as illustrations.
Within each simile, there are three parts: the illustration (the simile itself), the application (the correspondence), and the conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like space, which pervades all places, whether they be material or immaterial; yet it neither arrives nor does it not arrive.
Why is this? Because space has no body. The body of the Tathāgata is also like this:
it pervades all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, and all lands; yet it neither arrives nor does it not arrive. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata is bodiless, he manifests a body for the sake of sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, this is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way.

Now, first is the analogy of space pervading all. This illustrates how the body pervades the ten directions; thus, the conclusion below states: "Because the mind is immeasurable and pervades the ten directions.

In the analogy, there is first a direct demonstration, followed by an inquiry and an explanation. The inquiry asks: "How can both [the pervasive and the non-pervasive] be identical, given the distinction between reaching and not reaching?
It is explained that because it is without a body, the two aforementioned meanings are established. Due to being without a body, it is non-existent [in terms of spatial limitation].
It can reach [all places]. Furthermore, because it is non-existent, there is nowhere it does not reach. It is like the emptiness within form (*rūpa*).
If emptiness possessed a body, that body would be a solid mass, and it would thus obstruct form—just as when iron enters water, the water does not enter the iron.

Now, because it lacks a body, it penetrates universally into form. This principle is known by analogy with the example. Here, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is used to illustrate the emptiness of principle (*tattva-śūnyatā*). Principle...
Emptiness is itself the Dharmakāya. Therefore, a verse in the Sūtra says: "The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure like empty space.
This explanation was given for the sake of sentient beings to dispel external doubts.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha: Just as space is vast and wide, and though it is not material, it can manifest all forms, yet that space is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation; so too is the body of the Tathāgata.
Because it universally illuminates with the light of wisdom, it causes all sentient beings to [cultivate] the various roots of goodness and karmic deeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
All are accomplished, yet the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, all attachments and all conceptual proliferations have been eternally severed.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way.
The second is the analogy of emptiness and non-discrimination; how much more so for the unattached and unimpeded body? Therefore, it concludes:

"That which is practiced is unimpeded like space. Just as empty space is non-discriminative and does not obstruct manifest colors, so too is wisdom non-discriminative and does not obstruct the benefiting of sentient beings.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising of the sun over Jambudvīpa, whereby immeasurable sentient beings all receive benefit.
That is to say: it destroys darkness and creates light; it transforms moisture into dryness; it causes grasses and trees to grow; it brings grain crops to maturity;
it makes the void vast and transparent; it causes lotus flowers to bloom; travelers see the road, and those at home attend to their work. Why is this? Because the solar orb is universal...
Because it emits immeasurable light, O Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise. It universally benefits sentient beings through immeasurable means;
that is to say, it extinguishes evil and gives rise to good, destroys ignorance and produces wisdom, provides protection through great kindness, and brings liberation through great compassion.
It causes the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment to increase, inspires deep faith and the abandonment of turbid minds, and enables them to behold [the Truth].

Hearing this, one does not destroy the law of cause and effect; it enables one to obtain the divine eye to see the places of death and rebirth; it causes the mind to be unimpeded and prevents the destruction of roots of goodness;

it causes wisdom to be cultivated and clarified, causing the flower of awakening to bloom; and it causes one to resolve the mind toward enlightenment and accomplish one's original practice. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is the sun-body of vast wisdom, for he radiates immeasurable light that shines everywhere.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way.
The third is the analogy of the sun’s benefit through light, which illustrates the body that universally enters and accomplishes benefit, because it universally enters the *dharmadhātu*.

Both the analogy and its application (*yōga*) include general and specific explanations for their establishment. Within the specific section of the application, there are ten kinds of benefits, which correspond to the preceding eight phrases.
The first and second [stages] correspond to the first phrase, because the mundane and supramundane are distinct. Third, it uproots the suffering of the four torrents and bestows supramundane bliss;

it rescues those of the Two Vehicles from the suffering of sinking into the waters of meditative concentration and bestows the bliss of Bodhi—both instances embodying the meaning of taking what is moist and making it dry.
Fourth, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) universally nourish the grasses and trees of the Two Vehicles. Fifth, faith has two meanings: first, it perfects the aforementioned.
Meaning: Faith is able to increase all dharmas; thus, it is "conjoined with maturation. Faith is able to lead one inevitably to the stage of the Tathāgata;

thus, [it is conjoined with] "vastness. Sentences six and seven together signify "pervading like space": first, one attains the wisdom that perceives and hears the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths;

second, one attains the wisdom of the three types of clairvoyance (*traividyā*) and the ten powers (*daśabala*). This is because, like the sun in the sky, there is vast purity and penetrating illumination. Eight has...

There are two meanings. First, it causes the mind to be unimpeded, thereby fulfilling the aforementioned "penetrating emptiness without destroying the roots of goodness" (akṣaya-kuśalamūla). Second, it fulfills the "lower lotus":

just as a red lotus cannot survive if deprived of sunlight and will undoubtedly wither and die, so too the roots of goodness of the Two Vehicles would perish if they did not encounter the sun of wisdom;
however, once they meet it, they do not perish. Regarding the nine [lotuses], those already open and unfading are fulfilled; now, those not yet open are caused to bloom.
The latter two lines of the tenth [verse] state: "Upon generating the bodhicitta, one immediately beholds the Great Way; accomplishing the fundamental practices is the settling of the family estate.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising of the sun over Jambudvīpa, which first illuminates all the Sumeru mountains and so forth.
The sun first illuminates the various great mountain kings, then the Black Mountains, then the high plateaus, and finally it shines universally upon the entire earth.

Yet the sun does not form the thought, "I shall first illuminate this and afterwards illuminate that. It is only because the mountains and lands have elevations and depressions that there is a sequence of illumination.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, likewise accomplishes the boundless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Jñānacakra (Wheel of Wisdom) constantly emits the unimpeded light of wisdom. First it illuminates the great mountain kings, such as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

next it illuminates the pratyekabuddhas; next it illuminates the śrāvakas; and next it illuminates those sentient beings with determined roots of goodness, manifesting vast wisdom according to their mental capacities.
Thereafter, it universally illuminates all sentient beings, even those fixed in the wrong path.

It is for the sake of universal dissemination, acting as the causal condition for future benefit and bringing beings to maturity. Yet, that Tathāgata, the sun of great wisdom, does not form such a thought:
"I shall first illuminate the great practices of Bodhisattvas, and only later illuminate those sentient beings fixed in error.
Rather, he simply radiates light, shining equally and universally, without obstruction, without hindrance, and without discrimination.
The fourth is the analogy of the sun’s light shining equally, which illustrates the body that accords with all beings through equality.
Because it abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is impartial and equal. This section has two parts: first, the primary analogy; second, a restatement to resolve doubts.

Within the first part, the "black mountains" represent those of the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle, because they lack the light of the emptiness of phenomena and do not manifest meritorious qualities, unlike the ten [stages] of the bodhisattva.
The Great Mountain King represents the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The high plateau is a metaphor for the *śrāvakas*, because they do not produce the lotus flowers of the Buddha-dharma.

The single type of great earth universally encompasses the three groups (*tri-rāśi*): taking the land where growth is certain as a metaphor for the group of those destined for correctness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*);

taking that which requires conditions to grow as a metaphor for the group of those not yet destined (*aniyata-rāśi*); and taking saline or barren lands as a metaphor for the group of those destined for error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). Nevertheless, even these are not abandoned.
Therefore, they all shine equally.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the sun and moon appearing according to the seasons; they illuminate great mountains and deep valleys universally and without partiality.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it illuminates all things universally without discrimination, in accordance with the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings.

They are not the same; the various radiances of their wisdom differ. O Son of the Buddha, this is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Later, he resolves this doubt by stating: "The sunlight is one, whereas the Buddha’s wisdom is manifold; how can they serve as a comparable analogy? He replies:

"Did we not previously state that it merely follows the variations in height of the mountain terrain? Therefore, know that it is simply according to the differing degrees of wisdom among sentient beings that [the manifestations] differ;

the Buddha possesses no private wisdom, nor does he have any multiplicity. This does not contradict the previous analogy. Furthermore, since this was spoken in reference to the capacities of those to be taught (*yogya*),"
This is different. Illuminating the high cannot simultaneously encompass the low; yet when illuminating the low, it still illuminates the high.

Furthermore, if there were to be a relinquishing of transformation, one would first relinquish the small, then the middling, while only the high mountain of the Bodhisattvas would receive illumination throughout the entire day. Reflect on this.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising of the sun. Beings born blind, because they lack the faculty of sight, have never seen it;
yet even though they have never seen it, they are benefited by its light. Why is this?
Because through it, they know day and night, the seasons, and they enjoy various garments and food and drink, which keep their bodies in harmony and free them from all ailments.
The fifth is the parable of the congenitally blind person benefiting daily. This illustrates that the Buddha’s unarisen, hidden benefit reaches those with eyes who behold it;
yet it is not for them alone. It is never extinguished even for the congenitally blind who do not see, because it benefits them in a hidden manner.

The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise. Those who lack faith and understanding, who violate the precepts and hold false views, and who live by wrong livelihoods—such as those born blind who lack the eye of faith—do not see the solar orb of the Buddhas’ wisdom.
Although they do not see the solar orb of the Buddha’s wisdom, they are nonetheless benefited by that sun of wisdom. Why is this? Because, through the Buddha’s majestic power, he causes them...
Because all bodily suffering, afflictions, and future causes of suffering belonging to those sentient beings have been extinguished, there are two points within the "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*):
first the brief, then the detailed. Within the brief section, there are five matters; being blind and lacking faith is the general theme, hence it says, "because they lack the eye of faith.
This refers to the three offenses of *icchantika* in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Lacking faith and severing the roots of goodness constitute one [of these].

The icchantika who lacks understanding and possesses destructive views slanders the Vaipulya sutras; one who destroys the precepts and lives by wrong livelihood commits the four grave prohibitions and the five heinous crimes.
Although these four are the ultimate evils, they still possess Buddha-nature and are likewise benefited [by the teaching], which enables them to leave behind suffering and its accumulation.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata possesses a light named "Accumulation of All Merit"; a light named "Illuminating All Universally";
a light named "Pure Sovereign Illumination"; a light named "Emanating Great and Sublime Sounds";
a light named "Universally Understanding All Languages and Dharmas to Gladden Others"; and a light named "Manifestation."
The sphere of mastery that forever severs all doubt; a light named "Universal Illumination of the Mastery of Non-abiding Wisdom";
a light named "Mastery-Wisdom that Forever Severs All Proliferations of Conceptual Elaboration"; a light named "Emitting Wondrous Sounds According to What is Appropriate";
and a light named "Emitting the Pure Sound of Mastery. These adorn the buddha-fields and bring beings to maturity.
"Sentient beings, sons of the Buddha, from each and every pore of the Tathāgata’s body, he emits thousands of such rays of light.

Five hundred rays of light universally illuminate the lower directions, while five hundred rays of light universally illuminate the Buddhas and their assemblies of bodhisattvas within the various lands in the upper directions."
The subsequent detailed exposition of the middle [section] has two parts: first, the light that benefits; second, the assembly that is benefited. Now, of these two, the first [part] has two sections:
first, the listing of the ten lights; second, the conclusion regarding their limits. Regarding the first of these ten, the initial three constitute the two adornments within the wisdom section.

First, the universal illumination of phenomena; second, the illumination of the pure principle. The next three constitute the three types of wisdom: the first two constitute the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and the latter one constitutes the wisdom of reflection and cultivation (*cintāmayī* and *bhāvanāmayī*).
The final four constitute the four wisdoms: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) because it universally illuminates without abiding;

the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) because it is utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) because it expounds according to the needs [of beings]; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
This is because they adorn the lands and are born through transformation. The passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" concludes by defining the numerical limit;

since the sun possesses a thousand rays, it is concluded as "a thousand," though in reality they are innumerable. The "five hundred illuminating downward" refers to the self-contained stages of the five positions, while the "five hundred illuminating upward" refers to the superior progress through the five positions.
When those bodhisattvas beheld this radiance, they simultaneously attained the realm of the Tathāgata;
their ten heads, ten eyes, ten ears, ten noses, ten tongues, ten bodies, ten hands, ten feet, ten stages, and ten wisdoms were all rendered utterly pure.
Those bodhisattvas perceive that the various stages and grounds they had previously accomplished become even more purified through that light;
all their roots of goodness reach full maturity as they proceed toward omniscience, while those dwelling in the two vehicles have all their defilements extinguished.
As for the remaining portion of those born blind, their bodies are already joyful and their minds are pure; they are supple, disciplined, and capable of cultivating mindfulness and wisdom.
Within these two types of benefit, there are four: first, benefiting bodhisattvas; second, benefiting those of the two vehicles; third, benefiting those born blind; and fourth...

This further benefits those in the evil realms. There are two ways in which a bodhisattva benefits others: first, by benefiting those with complete capacity (*paripūrṇa-yogya*), enabling them to suddenly realize the realm of the Buddha;

second, by benefiting those with provisional capacity (*upāya-yogya*), causing them to mature and incline toward the ultimate reality. "Various places" refers to the five eyes and so forth; "various stages" refers to the stage of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*) and so forth.
All sentient beings belonging to the various realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals all obtain happiness and are liberated from all suffering;

at the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the heavens or among humans. O Son of the Buddha, those sentient beings do not perceive or know by what causes and conditions or by what spiritual power they have come to be born here. That person born blind thinks thus: "I am..."
"Brahmā, I am a transformation of Brahmā. At that time, the Tathāgata dwelt in the Samādhi of Universal Sovereignty and uttered sixty kinds of wondrous sounds, addressing them, saying:
"You are not Brahmā, nor are you a transformation of Brahmā, nor were you created by Śakra or the World-Protectors;
all this is through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata. When those sentient beings heard these words, they [realized the truth].
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they all came to know their past lives and gave rise to great joy.

Because their hearts were filled with joy, clouds of *udumbara* flowers, clouds of incense, clouds of music, clouds of robes, clouds of parasols, clouds of banners, clouds of streamers, and clouds of powdered incense spontaneously emerged.

Clouds of precious clouds, clouds of lion-bannered crescent-shaped pavilions, clouds of songs and hymns of praise, and clouds of various adornments all made offerings to the Tathāgata with a heart of reverence. Why was this? Because these sentient beings had attained the pure eye.
The Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Son of the Buddha, in this way the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom benefits sentient beings who are blind from birth, causing their roots of goodness to become fully matured.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should view it in this manner.

The fourth section, "The Light Beneath the Four Hells Benefits the Evil Realms," consists of six parts: first, the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" downward, the arising of false views due to causes;

third, from "At that time" downward, the manifestation of the correct path through compassionate sound; fourth, from "Those various [beings]" downward, the turning away from error as a repayment of kindness;
fifth, from "The Tathāgata" downward, the Buddha’s conferral of a prophecy; and sixth, from "O Son of the Buddha" downward, the conclusion regarding the benefits of the light.
The benefits herein are for the most part identical to those of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the lunar disc possessed four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities. What are these four?
First, it eclipses the light of all the stars and constellations. Second, it manifests waxing and waning in accordance with the seasons.
Third, its reflection appears without exception in the clear and pure waters of Jambudvīpa. Fourth, for all who behold it, it stands directly before them;
yet this lunar disc is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation. O Son of the Buddha, so it is with the Tathāgata.
The moon of the body is likewise so. It possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities. What are these four? They are:
first, it outshines the entire assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, both those in training and those beyond training;

second, it manifests lifespans of varying lengths according to what is appropriate for beings, yet the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases; third, [it appears] to all sentient beings with pure minds throughout every world-system...
Within the vessel of Bodhi, no reflection fails to appear. All sentient beings who behold it each think that the Tathāgata appears before them alone;
according to their inclinations, he preaches the Dharma for them, and according to their respective stages, he causes them to attain liberation.
According to those who are to be transformed, they cause them to see the body of the Buddha; yet the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation.
All the benefits he performs reach ultimate fulfillment. Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.

The sixth is the parable of the moonlight’s marvels, which illustrates the Buddha’s body that abides in perfect equanimity. This means that he abides equally throughout the three periods of time without increase or decrease.
Among the four dharmas presented in the analogy: first, his perfect wisdom outshines the two vehicles; second, his eternal body manifests both extension and brevity;
third, its presence or absence is perceived according to the capacity of the vessel; and fourth, what is seen is without partiality or bias. The first and the last two [of these] are all...
Regarding the meaning of "perfectly revolving": as for the "vessel of bodhi," this refers to a person capable of receiving bodhi who beholds the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*).
If the ocean of the mind is clarified and deluded thoughts are entirely stilled, then one truly sees the Buddha.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm, who, by means of a slight expedient, manifests his body throughout the great trichiliocosm so that all sentient beings see the Brahmā King appearing before them;
yet this Brahmā King does not divide his body, nor does he possess various distinct bodies. O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise.
It is likewise; there is no distinction, no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and no division of bodies, nor any variety of bodies.
Yet, in accordance with the inclinations of all sentient beings, he manifests his body for them, without forming the thought that he is manifesting various bodies.
Son of the Buddha, this is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.

The seventh is the parable of the Universal Manifestation of the Brahma King, which illustrates how the Buddha’s mindless body universally responds; for it pervades everywhere without differentiation.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like a king of physicians who is well-versed in all medicines and various incantations and treatises, such that there is no medicinal substance in Jambudvīpa he does not employ.
Moreover, by the power of his roots of goodness from past lives and the power of great vidyā-mantras, [he heals all beings].
For the sake of skillful means, there was no illness among those who saw him that was not cured. That great King of Physicians, knowing his life was about to end, thought to himself:
"After my death, all sentient beings will have no one to rely upon. I should now manifest a skillful means for their sake.
At that time, the King of Physicians prepared medicine and anointed his body; through the power of a secret mantra, he caused it to remain after his death.
The body is neither dispersed, nor withered, nor parched; its deportment, vision, and hearing are no different from before.
Whatever is treated is entirely healed and cured.

This is the eighth analogy, that of the King of Physicians Prolonging Life, which illustrates the Buddha’s body reaching the end of the future limit. Within this analogy, there are two parts; first, [the text] clarifies...
Manifesting virtue, he subsequently sustains his body through the power of great [medicinal] herbs.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians, is likewise.
Having refined the medicinal drugs of the Dharma for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, he has attained their perfection and mastered all skillful means.
Through the power of skillful great vidyā-mantras, they have all reached the other shore.

They are well able to eliminate the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings, and they abide for immeasurable kalpas. Their bodies are pure, free from discursive thought and devoid of active exertion;
yet, they never cease performing any of the Buddha-deeds. All sentient beings who behold them find that their various diseases of affliction are entirely cured.
It is extinguished. O Son of the Buddha, this is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way.

Next, within the section on "Combining," there are also two parts. The first combines the manifestation of virtues. First, regarding the application of medicine, there is nothing that is not exhausted. Second, the cultivation and study.

The lower "concordant application" (*anuloma-yukti*) serves as the skillful means; subsequently, for those who are well able to apply the lower "concordant vision" (*anuloma-dṛṣṭi*), the illness is cured.

Each instance of abiding in the lower "concordant application" sustains the body through the power of the preceding analogies as medicine; because it is maintained and stabilized for many eons, it endures.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean which possesses a great maṇi-jewel named "Vairocana-treasury that gathers all light.
If there are sentient beings who touch its radiance, they all become the same color as it.
If there are those who see it, their eyes attain purity. Wherever that radiance shines, it rains down maṇi-jewels called "Peace and Bliss."
It causes all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain composure. Son of the Buddha, the body of the Tathāgatas is likewise so:

it is a great mass of jewels, a treasury of all merits and great wisdom. If there are sentient beings who touch the jewel of the Buddha’s body and its light of wisdom, they become the same color as the Buddha’s body.
If there are those who see it, their Dharma-eye becomes pure, following wherever that radiance shines.
...places. It causes all sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of poverty and even become fully endowed with the bliss of the Buddha’s bodhi.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation, yet it is able to universally perform great Buddha-works for all sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, [known by] all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
It should be viewed in this way.

The ninth is the analogy of the mani jewel that benefits sentient beings. This illustrates how the Buddha adorns the realm for the sake of living beings by raining down precious objects; it is precisely for the purpose of adorning the realm.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean, which possesses a sovereign *maṇi* jewel-king named "Treasury Adorned by All Worlds.
It is fully endowed with a million virtues; wherever it dwells, it causes all calamities and afflictions of sentient beings to be eliminated and their aspirations to be fulfilled.
Yet, this sovereign *maṇi* jewel-king does not appear for those with meager merit.
This is what can be seen by those who are born [into this world].
The tenth analogy is that of the King of Jewels Fulfilling All Wishes, which illustrates the Buddha’s body adorned with the marks of perfection and the fulfillment of all vows.
The Tathāgata’s body, like the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels, is likewise called that which enables all sentient beings to...
All shall be filled with joy. Should any behold his body, hear his name, or praise his virtues, they shall all be forever freed from the suffering and afflictions of birth and death.
Even if all sentient beings in all worlds were to simultaneously focus their minds on desiring to see the Tathāgata, he would cause them all to see him and fulfill every one of their aspirations.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddha-body is not something that sentient beings with meager merit can behold; it is only...

Except for those who are to be tamed by the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata, if there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha’s body, further plant roots of goodness until they reach maturity—it is for the sake of their maturation that they are enabled to see the body of the Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, this is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should view it in this way.

Next, within the section on the application [of the analogy], there is first the formal application itself; subsequently, from the words "O Son of the Buddha, the Buddha-body... onwards, there is the resolution of doubts.

Within this, although the initial application of the analogy already constitutes a resolution of doubt—namely, in response to the doubt: "If by recollecting them all can be seen, why is it that I do not see them now?"—it is therefore said that those with little merit do not see them.
Next, another doubt arises: "There are also those who are poor, lowly, and of meager merit; how is it that they are able to see [the Buddha]? The explanation states:
Except for those who can be tamed, because their minds are immeasurable and pervade the ten directions; because their conduct is unimpeded like space; because they universally enter the Dharma-realm;

because they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); because they are without birth or cessation; because they dwell equally throughout the three periods of time; and because they are forever free from [duality].
Because of the complete elimination of all conceptual discrimination; because of abiding in vows that extend to the very end of time; because of purifying all worlds;
and because of adorning each and every Buddha-body.
Third, the summary according to the Dharma: the ten phrases in sequence conclude with the ten bodies.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
Within the second section there are twenty stanzas; they are arranged in sequence as verses of analogy, consisting of two stanzas for each analogy and its application.
Just as empty space pervades the ten directions— whether in form or formless, existence or non-existence,
throughout the bodies of sentient beings and the lands of the three periods of time—
so too does the true body of all Buddhas universally exist without limit; there is no part of the entire dharma-realm that it does not pervade.
Invisible and ungraspable, yet manifesting forms for the sake of transforming sentient beings;
first, the analogy of the all-pervading void:
just as empty space cannot be grasped, it causes all sentient beings everywhere to create their various karmas.
He does not think, "What am I doing now? or "How do I act? or "For whom do I act?

The bodily actions of all Buddhas are likewise; they cause all living beings everywhere to cultivate wholesome dharmas, yet the Tathāgata never makes any discrimination, thinking, "I am now performing these various deeds for them."
The second is the simile of non-differentiation through the two kinds of emptiness:
Just as when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, Its radiance destroys all darkness without exception;
Mountains, trees, ponds, lotuses, the earth, and all things— All varieties of beings receive its benefit.
The emergence of the Buddhas from the sun is likewise: they cause the multitude of beings in the human and celestial realms to grow in virtuous conduct,
forever eliminate the darkness of ignorance to attain the light of wisdom, and constantly enjoy honor, glory, and all happiness—
this is the analogy for the benefit of the three suns.

Just as when the sun’s light appears, it first illuminates the King of Mountains, then the other mountains, and finally the high plateaus and the great earth, yet the sun never engages in discrimination;
so too is the radiance of the Sugata: it first illuminates the Bodhisattvas, then the Pratyekabuddhas.
Later, he illuminates the śrāvakas and sentient beings; yet the Buddha is fundamentally without a stirring thought.
This is illustrated by the metaphor of the four suns shining equally:
just as one born blind does not see the sun, the sunlight nonetheless brings them benefit.
May they know the proper time and receive food and drink, forever free from all ailments with bodies at peace.
Those beings who lack faith and do not see the Buddha—yet for them too, the Buddha brings forth benefit and profit;
by hearing his name or being touched by his light, they shall thereby attain even to Bodhi.
The Parable of the Five Days’ Increase for the Blind:
Just as the pure moon in the void Can obscure sentient beings' perception of its waxing and waning,
Yet manifests its reflection in every body of water, Appearing before all who gaze upon it.
The Tathāgata’s pure moon is likewise: it can obscure other vehicles and manifest both long and short durations;
appearing universally before the waters of the pure minds of devas and humans, all perceive him as being right before them.
This is the extraordinary metaphor of the moonlight in the sixth month.

Just as the Brahma King, dwelling in his own palace, manifests universally in all the Brahma abodes throughout the three thousandfold world-system so that all humans and devas may behold him, yet does not actually divide his body to go to them;
so too do the Buddhas manifest their bodies, pervading every direction in the ten quarters without exception.
His body is countless and beyond measure; neither dividing himself nor making distinctions, he manifests universally like the seven Brahma-kings.
Just as when a king of physicians skilled in medical arts appears, all who see him are healed of their ailments.
Though his life has come to an end, by applying medicine to his body, he enables him to perform all tasks just as before;
the Supreme King of Physicians is likewise so, possessing skillful means and omniscience.
Through his past sublime conduct, he manifests a Buddha-body, and those sentient beings who behold him have their afflictions extinguished.
The eighth is the parable of the King of Physicians, Yanshou.
For example, there is a king of jewels in the ocean that universally emits immeasurable rays of light;
those sentient beings who touch it take on its color, and those who behold it have their eyes purified.
The most supreme King of Jewels is likewise: those who touch its light all become the same color;
those who behold it have their five eyes opened; they shatter the darkness of all defilements and abide on the stage of Buddhahood.
This is the ninth analogy of the mani-jewel benefiting sentient beings.
Just as the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel satisfies every request that arises,
yet beings with little merit cannot see it— because this king of jewels has no discrimination—
so too is the Sugata, the king of jewels; he completely fulfills all desired joys and aspirations.
Sentient beings who lack faith do not see the Buddha; it is not that the Sugata has abandoned them with his mind.
[This concludes] the Parable of the Ten Jewel Kings Fulfilling Vows.
