This is likely a provisional teaching intended for a limited scope. As for what secular classics say—that the "Wojiao Stone" (the Water-Evaporating Rock) consumes the oceanic waters—this may have been known through inference, or perhaps it was seen as a precious substance but misidentified as a mere stone. Furthermore, it is said:
As for those who pour into the abyss of the Wei-lu, they merely perceive its depletion and name it accordingly.
Son of the Buddha, the great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise.
It is fully endowed with four kinds of great treasures of wisdom and possesses immeasurable majesty, virtue, and radiance. When the light of these wisdom-treasures touches the various Bodhisattvas...
This leads to the attainment of the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata. What are these four? They are: the great wisdom-treasure that extinguishes all waves of dispersed goodness;
the great wisdom-treasure that eliminates all craving for dharmas; the great wisdom-treasure whose light of insight shines universally;
and the great wisdom-treasure that is equal to the Tathāgata’s—boundless and effortless.
Within the section on "Conjunction," there are also two parts; first, the conjunction that generally clarifies essence and function.
"O Son of the Buddha, when all bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate all factors conducive to enlightenment, they give rise to immeasurable waves of non-concentrated wholesome states."
It cannot be destroyed by any in the world, including devas, humans, or asuras.

The Tathāgata, with the light of the great wisdom-jewel that extinguishes all waves of distracted virtue, touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon all waves of distracted virtue and to maintain one-pointedness of mind while abiding in samādhi.
Furthermore, by means of the great wisdom-jewel that removes all craving for dharmas—
The light touches that bodhisattva, causing them to relinquish attachment to the flavor of samādhi and to give rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Furthermore, the light of the jewel-radiance of great wisdom shines everywhere; this light touches that bodhisattva, causing them to relinquish the great supernormal powers that have arisen and to abide in the practice of the function of great illumination. Moreover, it bestows equality with the Tathāgata—boundless and effortless.
The light of the jewel of great wisdom touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish the practices of great luminous effort until they attain the stage of equality of the Tathāgata.

All effort is brought to rest so that nothing remains. O Son of the Buddha, if it were not for the touch of this great illumination of the four jewels of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, there would not be even a single bodhisattva who attains the stage of the Tathāgata.
This is impossible. O Son of the Buddha, this is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it thus.

Hereafter, the individual characteristics of its functions will be explained separately. Regarding these four wisdoms, there have been different traditional assignments in the past; here, we shall now indicate what they accomplish.

This refers to the four dhyānas. Regarding the wisdom that accomplishes them, one should establish distinct names for each stage. To correlate these vertically with the various stages is particularly different from previous interpretations.

This means that the Buddha, by means of the wisdom that realizes the reality within phenomena (*dharmatā*), counteracts the stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis and accomplishes the first four bhūmis, enabling the attainment of the "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*) samādhi.
Because this samādhi can maintain the virtuous and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms, it is so called. The preceding three...
The first stage is the mundane; the four stages are the supramundane. Once one realizes that phenomena are themselves reality, then distraction itself is meditative concentration.

Second, by means of the wisdom of the function inherent in the essence, one remedies the inability to initiate activity in the fourth stage, enabling entry into the conventional world at the fifth stage to achieve the "King of Accumulated Merit" samādhi.
Third, by means of the wisdom of equality and signlessness, one remedies the [limitations] of the fifth stage, although it is already capable of...

Conforming to worldly convention, one has not yet attained equanimity; thus, through the final limit of the functional application of the great light of *prajñā* in the sixth and seventh stages, one accomplishes the Samādhi of Radiance (*ābhāsvara-samādhi*).

Fourth, by means of the equanimous wisdom that is without effort (*anābhoga-jñāna*), one remedies the effortful application of the seventh stage, causing entry into the eighth stage and up to the fruit of Buddhahood, where one attains the Śūraṅgama Samādhi because what was to be done is perfected. Since the fruit is thus complete...
Fourth: The cause is also common to all stages of cultivation. This vertical correlation has been presented here merely to clarify their characteristics;

it must not be taken as a restrictive limitation. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha: from the water’s edge up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, all the great trichiliocosm worlds contained therein—the abodes of sentient beings in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—all arise depending upon empty space.
It abides in space. Why? Because space is all-pervasive. Although that space universally contains the three realms, it is without discrimination.

Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise. Whether it be the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, the wisdom of conditioned practices, or the wisdom of unconditioned practices, all depend upon it.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata arises; the wisdom of the Tathāgata abides. Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata pervades all things.

Although it universally encompasses immeasurable wisdom, it is free from conceptual discrimination. O Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.

The sixth is the analogy of empty space containing all. This illustrates the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom as the support and sustenance [of all things], and it further explains the meaning of "reliance" mentioned previously.

While the preceding section merely spoke of "relying," that term could still imply external reliance upon the power of others (*paratantra*). Now, it clarifies that the essence is all-pervasive and universally inclusive;
thus, the wisdoms of the five vehicles and so forth are all contained within the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata. Master Zhao also said: "As for the mind of a sage..."
The void and profound illumination encompasses all principles without exception. Containing the six directions within the breast, its spiritual discernment is more than sufficient;
reflecting the myriad existents within the square inch of the heart, its spirit remains eternally empty. It is precisely according to this principle.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the King of Medicinal Trees on the summit of the Snowy Mountains, named Inexhaustible Root (*Akṣayamūla*).

The roots of that medicinal tree grow from a depth of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas down to the diamond-hard earth (*vajramaya-bhūmi*) and the limits of the water-circle (*āpa-maṇḍala*).

When that King of Medicinal Trees produces its roots, it causes all the roots of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow; when it produces its trunk, it causes [all the trunks of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow].
In Jambudvīpa, all trees grow from their trunks; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all likewise.
This King of Medicine tree, however, its roots can produce trunks, and its trunks can produce roots; the roots are inexhaustible, and thus it is called the "Inexhaustible Root.
O Son of the Buddha, that King of Medicine tree causes growth in all places, yet there are only two places where it cannot provide the benefit of growth.
Furthermore, it refers to the deep pits of hell and within the water-wheel (*āpa-maṇḍala*). Yet, even there, from the very beginning, there is no weariness or abandonment.

The seventh is the analogy of the growth of the medicinal king (*bhaiṣajyarāja*). This illustrates the Buddha’s benefit and happiness throughout kalpas. Within this analogy, there are four parts: first, the manifestation of essence and function;

second, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of its function, starting from "the root of that medicine" (*tasya bhaiṣajyamūla*); third, [the section] starting from "this medicinal king" (*ayaṃ bhaiṣajyarāja*), which concerns the basis for its name; [and fourth, the conclusion].

"By means of the four [qualities], the sons of the Buddha exclude those who are in improper places; first they exclude them, and then they include them. As for inclusion, it is because they do not loathe [sentient beings].
The Jin translation says: 'They do not abandon the nature of birth.'"
O Son of the Buddha, the great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise.

By means of the wholesome dharmas of all-encompassing wisdom that were accomplished through vows made in the past, it universally covers the realms of all sentient beings and eliminates the sufferings of all evil destinies.
With vast compassionate vows as its roots, it [rests] upon the true wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Born from the lineage of spiritual potential (*gotra*), it has skillful means as its firm and immovable trunk;
the various *pāramitās* of wisdom pervading the *dharmadhātu* as its branches; and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the great samādhis as its leaves.
The dhāraṇīs and eloquence, as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), serve as its flowers; the ultimate, unchanging liberation of all Buddhas serves as its fruit.

This section also consists of four parts, though the textual order is not sequential. First, the synthesis reveals the essence and function, which has six [subsections], beginning with a single compassionate vow.
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) corresponds to the roots; this is the foundation of all Buddhas, for it is profound and difficult to uproot.
Second, the skillful means (*upāya*) arising from true wisdom (*jñāna*) constitutes the trunk, as it is capable of supporting the task, being the very essence of enlightenment.

Third, based on the two preceding types of wisdom, they are divided into the various perfections (*pāramitā*), which provide lateral shade as branches. Fourth, ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are specifically designated by the term "cooling," as they extinguish the heat [of afflictions]. Fifth, eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The *mārga-pakṣa* (factors of the path) and so forth are born directly from it, developing into flowers; the six fruits may be known [therefrom].
O Son of the Buddha, why is the Great King of Medicine Tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom called "Inexhaustible Root"?
Because it is ultimately without rest, and because it does not sever the bodhisattva practices. Bodhisattva practice is itself the Tathāgata-nature. The Tathāgata...
Nature itself is the bodhisattva practice; therefore, it is named the "Inexhaustible Root.
Next, regarding the reason for its designation as "conjoined": because it extends to the limits of the future, it is called "ultimately without rest";
because one attains the fruit without abandoning the cause, it is called "never ceasing the bodhisattva practice. By means of this, cause and effect mutually penetrate and revolve.
They arise together.

O Son of the Buddha, when the root of the Tathāgata’s great medicinal king tree of wisdom arises, it causes all bodhisattvas to produce the root of great compassion that never abandons sentient beings. When its trunk arises, it causes all bodhisattvas to increase their firmness.
It has firm diligence and the profound mind as its trunk. When its branches grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to increase the branches of all the pāramitās.
When its leaves grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to produce the leaves of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), ascetic practices (*dhūta*), merit, fewness of desires, and contentment.
When its flowers grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to be endowed with the marks of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

It is like a beautiful, magnificent flower. When its fruit ripens, it causes all bodhisattvas to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the fruit of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of all Buddhas.

The third [point] combines with the preceding to specifically reveal the characteristics of its function: the profound mind that delights in practicing wholesome deeds is the aforementioned skillful means (*upāya*), namely, pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

It can also extinguish heat. Its marks and signs are like flowers as adornments. As for the abundance of the text and the brevity of the commentary, it is for the sake of distinguishing between the means of accomplishment and that which is accomplished.
O Son of the Buddha, the great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom cannot bring about growth in only two places.

Benefit. That is to say, the two vehicles have fallen into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as sentient beings who are not vessels due to their destruction of the roots of goodness.
They are submerged in the waters of great false views and craving. Yet, even toward them, the Buddha-son has never felt weariness or abandonment. Buddha-son!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases, for his faculties are well-established and his activity arises without cessation.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus.

Fourth, the exclusion of those who are not suitable vessels. This also involves first excluding and then subsequently admitting. Because the state of unconditioned reality (asaṃskṛta-dhātu) is difficult to emerge from once one has fallen into it, it is likened to a deep pit.

Furthermore, because they lack the water of compassion and grasp at the severance [of existence] like ashes, they are like those in hell who, through wrong views, repudiate the existence [of cause and effect].

The soaking and rotting by craving are all likened to water; it cannot accommodate the roots of goodness. Furthermore, because it lacks the condition of earth, it is not a place where [the roots] can grow.

As for the later statement regarding "those who have no weariness or renunciation," the previous section relied on the manifest evil and lack of conditions to induce weariness and fear, thereby leading them directly toward the One Vehicle;
thus, those two groups were excluded. However, they equally possess Buddha-nature and shall eventually attain realization over time; therefore, they do not feel weariness.
[The Buddha] set it aside. This knowledge that present evil is clearly absent implies that if there were no evil, it would necessarily exist [in another form].

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Although an icchantika has severed all roots of goodness, they still possess buddha-nature; if they can resolve their minds toward awakening, they are no longer icchantikas. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Having definitively understood the Dharma for śrāvakas, the other members of the śrāvaka assembly shall likewise do so. Thus it concludes with "Good."

Regarding the phrase "the faculties are firmly established": because they abide eternally in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), there is an implication that it excludes the meaning of the non-existence of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) and fixed natures.
This is so even when not considering the subsequent phrase "without abandoning," let alone the tenth simile, which is shared equally by all.

This would diminish the Buddha-nature and I fear it would lead to the slander of the One Vehicle. I pray that all future students shall exercise caution and refrain from being obstructed by provisional teachings.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the kalpa-fire arises in a trichiliocosm, burning everything to ashes.
The grasses, trees, and forests, even unto the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, are all completely ablaze without exception.
Son of the Buddha, suppose someone were to take dry grass in their hand and cast it into that fire; what do you think?
Would it not burn? He replied, "No, World-Honored One. Son of the Buddha, while the grass thrown into it might possibly not burn, such is not the case with the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
There is nothing among all sentient beings of the three periods of time, all lands, all kalpas, or all dharmas that he does not know through discernment.
It is impossible for him to say that he does not know. Why is this? Because his wisdom is impartial and he has attained complete and clear penetration.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind. All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should...
Thus it is known.

The metaphor of the eighth kalpa fire burning everything to exhaustion illustrates that there is nothing the Buddha’s wisdom does not know exhaustively; by virtue of this, the Buddha’s wisdom has no further basis upon which to rely.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha: for example, when the world-system is destroyed by the calamity of wind, there arises a great wind named "Dissolution" (*vikiraṇa*), which can destroy the trichiliocosm, reducing even the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*) to fine dust.
Furthermore, there is another great wind named "Obstructing" (*pratibandha*) that surrounds the trichiliocosm and obstructs the Dissolution wind, preventing it from reaching [the core].
O Son of the Buddha, in other buddha-worlds, if this great obstructing wind did not exist, there would be no world in the ten directions that would not be destroyed.
It is the same for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he possesses a wind of great wisdom called "The Able to Extinguish."
It can extinguish all the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the great bodhisattvas. There is a wind of great wisdom called "Skillful Sustenance" (*Sukhādhāra*).
This wind of skillful sustenance prevents bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature from having the wind-wheel of great wisdom extinguish all their afflictions and habitual tendencies.
O Son of the Buddha, if there were no such wind of the Tathāgata’s skillfully sustained wisdom, immeasurable bodhisattvas would all fall away.
The stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: by means of this wisdom, bodhisattvas transcend the levels of the two vehicles and abide securely in the ultimate position of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind;
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it thus.

The ninth analogy concerns the wind that sustains destruction during the kalpa of dissolution. This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s skillful means in causing [bodhisattvas] to retain their afflictions and wisdom. It indicates that he is not only able to sever them, but is also able to retain them.
This refers to the Buddha possessing such skillful means to bestow [this teaching] upon bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature and who have not yet perfected the ten thousand practices.
They cause the delusions that sustain rebirth to remain; through this retention of delusion, those delusions eventually reach exhaustion, whereby they attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This differs from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who do not aspire for bodhicitta and seek only swift emergence [from saṃsāra].
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere. Why is this? Because there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

The tenth is the analogy of the dust particle containing a sutra scroll, which illustrates that the Buddha-nature is pervasive and equal. This section consists of four parts: the teaching, the analogy, the application, and the conclusion.
First, as for how we know that the Buddha-wisdom is all-pervasive: there is not a single sentient being who does not possess original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).
Because it is non-different from the essence of the Buddha. The preceding discussion on the "hidden flow" (潛流) suggested that the Buddha’s wisdom pervades other sentient beings;
now, it is revealed that sentient beings themselves inherently possess [this nature]. This has three points:

first, to clarify that there is not a single sentient being who does not possess it, one thereby knows that those lacking this nature are not counted among sentient beings—referring to things such as grasses and trees. This already transcends the view of the five natures (pañca-gotra). Second...

This refers to the cause of sentient beings being enmeshed in bondage, which already possesses the fruit-dharma of emerging from that bondage; therefore, it is said that they possess Tathāgata-wisdom.
It is not merely that they have the nature [of Buddhahood] and will only later become Buddhas, nor is it logical that wisdom exists first and [the state of Buddhahood] later.

Thus, we know that when Nirvāṇa speaks of "possessing the nature" in contrast to former expedient means, even those who have studied further would say this is merely speaking of having a treasury while lacking the actual substance; how much more so for those who hear [this teaching]?
Who would believe in such "knowledge of the fruit within the cause"? Third is the "knowledge of the fruit within that cause," which is precisely the fruit-knowledge of other Buddhas.
This is because, according to the school of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the causes and fruits of self and others are non-dual in essence.

Otherwise, if this teaching were merely stating that sentient beings possess the fruit, how could it be called the teaching of Buddha-wisdom? This would be a mystery upon a mystery; it would not be the Huayan school.
There is no such principle.
It is merely because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachment that one does not realize it.
Next, the doubt is explained: The doubt says, "If *nirvāṇa* is called 'Buddha-nature,' it is termed wisdom. When wisdom exists..."

Then there would be no afflictions; now that the Buddha-wisdom has been attained, how could one still be a sentient being? This explanation first answers the preceding point in accordance with its meaning:

because of perversion, one does not realize it; how can it be said that it does not exist? It is like a strong man who is confused about the jewel on his forehead; can it be said that there is no treasure within his skin?
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*asanga-jñāna*) will manifest before one.
Next, to further establish this through reasoning by means of a reductio ad absurdum: if these were originally non-existent, how could they exist once one is free from inversion?

Since they manifest as soon as one is free from inversion, it is clear that they were not originally absent—just as when a poor person finds a jewel, it was not bestowed upon them at that moment. Therefore, [the teaching of] *nirvāṇa* is intended to dispel fear.
Because they do not practice accordingly, it is said that to claim something definitely exists is to be attached.
Fearing that one might disbelieve its existence, it is said that to claim it definitely does not exist is to speak falsely. One may perhaps be attached, but one must not speak falsely.
As for "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), it refers to the self-awakened sagely wisdom. As for "unimpeded wisdom," beginning and end are non-dual; it is the severance of the two obstacles.
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were a great scripture scroll equal in size to a trichiliocosm,
upon which all the events within that trichiliocosm were inscribed in their entirety— namely, the events occurring within the Great Iron Ring Mountains were all inscribed.
Equal in measure to the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*Mahācakravāḍa*), it records the events within the great earth;
equal in measure to the great earth, it records the events within a medium chiliocosm; equal in measure to a medium chiliocosm, it records the events within a small chiliocosm;
equal in measure to a small chiliocosm, it likewise records the events of the four continents, the great oceans, Mount Sumeru, and the terrestrial devas.

The palaces—whether the palaces of the gods dwelling in the void of the desire realm, the palaces of the form realm, or the palaces of the formless realm—are each written out, all being equal in measure.
Although this great sutra scroll is equal in size to a trichiliocosm, it remains entirely within a single minute atom; as it is with one minute atom, so it is with all minute atoms.
At that time, there was a person of wise and penetrating insight who possessed the fully perfected, pure divine eye.
Seeing this sutra scroll within a mote of dust, providing no benefit whatsoever to sentient beings, he thought:
"I shall, by the power of diligence, shatter that mote of dust and bring forth this sutra scroll, so as to enable all sentient beings to obtain abundant benefit. Having made this thought...
Having formed this thought, he immediately employed skillful means to break apart those atoms and bring forth this great sutra, so that all sentient beings might universally obtain benefit.
It should be understood that this applies to every single atom, just as it does for one.

In the second analogy, there are two parts. First, it clarifies that the great scripture is submerged in dust, serving as a metaphor for how, as stated above, delusion entangles the Buddha’s wisdom (*buddhajñāna*).
"The scroll of the Great Scripture" refers to the boundless Buddha-wisdom in which innate virtues (*prakṛtiguṇa*) are perfected.

"Each letter corresponds to its object" means that wisdom accords with reality (*yathārtha*). "Submerged by a single speck of dust" has three brief meanings: first, because delusion obscures the True; second, because the small contains...
Because it is great. First, because it possesses many [qualities]. As for "all dust," there is not a single sentient being who does not possess Buddha-wisdom.
Later, when one person emerges from below to bring forth the sutras and benefit beings, this is a metaphor for the aforementioned transcendence of delusion appearing before one.

O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it is immeasurable and unimpeded, universally able to benefit all sentient beings, and is fully present within the bodies of all beings.
Yet, because ordinary and ignorant people cling to deluded thoughts, they do not know, do not perceive, and thus fail to obtain its benefits.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure eye of wisdom, surveys them all.
Regarding all sentient beings within the dharma-realm, he spoke these words: "How marvelous, how marvelous!
How is it that these sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet through folly and delusion, they neither know nor see it? I shall instruct them in the noble path."
He causes them to forever be free from deluded thoughts and attachments, so that within their own bodies they may perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata as no different from that of the Buddha.
He then instructs those sentient beings to cultivate the noble path, causing them to leave behind deluded thoughts.

Once they have left behind deluded thoughts, they realize the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata, thereby bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, this is...
This is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way. Within the third synthesis, there are also two parts.
First, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* synthesizes the submerged dust; being immeasurable and unimpeded, it is universally able to benefit others.

This synthesizes the aforementioned "many matters of copying," as well as the bodies and deluded thoughts of sentient beings, both of which correspond to the aforementioned dust. Hereafter follows the subsequent [section].
At that time, the Tathāgata descended to harmonize with and emerge from the sūtras to benefit sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s unified state is like a single person;

his eye of wisdom is like the unified divine eye. This shows that although sentient beings who lack faith possess the Buddha-wisdom, their eye of wisdom has not yet opened—how could this be considered strange?
Furthermore, sūtras such as the *Tathāgatagarbha* speak of nine similes to illustrate the *tathāgatagarbha*, comparing it to a blue lotus.
A lotus flower in muddy water is not esteemed by people as long as it has not emerged from the mud. It is like a poor woman who carries a holy embryo;
like a priceless jewel wrapped in soiled garments; like a *maṇi* gem fallen into a deep latrine; like a statue of pure gold covered by tattered rags;
like the flowers and fruit of the *āmra* tree before they have matured; and likewise like rice [before it has ripened].
Rice within its husks; gold within its ore; an image within its mold—all these illustrate the principle that the Buddha-body exists within the defilements.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should, by means of such immeasurable, unimpeded, and inconceivable [teachings], [realize this].
The aspect of vastness: knowing the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This is the third major section of the text, which summarizes the ten preceding metaphors: first, the general clarification of being the reliance for those without reliance;

second, the capacity to give birth; third, the capacity to pervade invisibly; fourth, the horizontal possession of the four wisdoms; fifth, the vertical possession of the four wisdoms; sixth, the essence that extensively encompasses.
1. Inclusiveness; 2. Pervasiveness; 3. Unobstructedness; 4. Non-duality; 5. Non-differentiation; 6. Non-abiding; 7. Infinite application; 8. Exhaustive knowledge;
9. Skillful retention; 10. Universal sufficiency. The first nine directly manifest the Buddha-wisdom, while the tenth integrates self and others.

These ten are perfectly interfused, briefly revealing the characteristics of Buddha-wisdom by way of the Tathāgata’s mind; yet they do not exhaust even a single hair’s breadth of the Buddha-mind. Therefore, one should further...
This is known through immeasurable and unimpeded cognition.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
If you wish to know the minds of all Buddhas, You should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddhas.
The second verse consists of twenty-two lines and is divided into two parts. The first two lines provide a general exposition in terms of the Dharma:
The Buddha’s wisdom has no place of dependence; Like space, it has nothing upon which to rely.
The various pleasures of sentient beings and the wisdom of all skillful means All depend upon the Buddha’s wisdom; The Buddha’s wisdom has no support.

The remaining verses illustrate the preceding metaphors. Among them, the first metaphor consists of one and a half verses; the latter consists of four verses; and the remaining eight each consist of two verses—all of which can be understood as they appear.
The liberation of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas alike, is entirely dependent upon the dharmadhātu.
The dharma-realm has neither increase nor decrease; the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise.
It gives rise to all-knowledge without increase or decrease, being neither born nor exhausted.
These two verses follow the first two [of the preceding section].
Just as water flows secretly beneath the earth, Seeking it, one never fails to find it; Without thought and yet inexhaustible, its power pervades the ten directions.
The Buddha’s wisdom is also like this: It is universally present within the minds of sentient beings.
If one practices with diligence, One will swiftly attain the light of wisdom.
The two verses summarize the preceding three:
Just as a dragon possesses four jewels that produce all manner of treasures, yet are placed in a deep and secret place such that ordinary people cannot see them;
so too are the Buddha’s four wisdoms, which give rise to all-encompassing knowledge.
No other person is able to see it, except for the great Bodhisattvas.
[Three verses; the first four are as follows:
Like the ocean which possesses four treasures, It can drink all waters Without causing the ocean to overflow.
Nor does it increase or decrease; the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise. It stills the waves and removes attachment to dharmas, vast and without limit.
This verse concerning the capacity to give birth to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is the fifth of the four preceding verses.
From the lowest realm up to the Peak of Existence—throughout the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—all things depend upon space, yet space itself is without discrimination.
So too, the wisdom of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas all depends upon the Buddha’s wisdom; yet the Buddha’s wisdom is without discrimination.
The first five verses precede the sixth.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicines named "Inexhaustible Root," which can produce all trees—roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
The Buddha’s wisdom is also like this; it is born from the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Having already attained awakening, he further gives rise to the practices of a bodhisattva.
(The preceding seven verses are as follows:
Just as if one were to take dry grass and place it within the conflagration at the end of an eon, even a diamond would be consumed by its blazing heat.
There is no principle here that is not incinerated— The kalpas and lands of the three periods of time, And the sentient beings within them;
Even those grasses might not be burned, But there is nothing this Buddha does not know.
(Seven verses preceding the eighth.)
There is a wind named "Dissolution" That can destroy the great trichiliocosm.
If there were no other wind to stop this dissolution and the immeasurable realms, The wind of great wisdom would likewise [cease].
To extinguish the delusions of all bodhisattvas, There is a distinct wind of skillful means That causes them to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata.
The eight verses precede the ninth:
Suppose there were a great sutra scroll, equal in size to the triple-thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust;
and so it is with every mote of dust. Suppose there were a person of wisdom who, with pure eyes, could see them all clearly.
Breaking through the dust, the sutra scrolls emerge, universally benefiting all sentient beings.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise omnipresent within the minds of sentient beings; yet, shrouded by delusive thoughts, they neither perceive nor know it.
Out of great compassion, the Buddhas cause them to eliminate these delusions, and thus [the wisdom] appears.
Three verses on benefiting all bodhisattvas, following the preceding ten. The section on the manifestation of mental activity is concluded.
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 51.
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang.
The Third Part of the Thirty-Seventh Chapter, "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Hanshan at Fayun Monastery on Mount Kuang, clearly elucidates the fifth point:
the realm of appearance. This section precisely reveals the realm of boundaries while simultaneously distinguishing the realm of objective conditions (*ālambana*).
Regarding the first intention: previously, the mind was revealed by means of wisdom; here, the limits of the function of wisdom are precisely clarified.

Regarding the second intention: previously, the knower was explained; now, the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are distinguished. Because these objects are boundless, the difficulty of fathoming their limits is revealed;
thus, one finally exhausts the realm of the objects of cognition. These two meanings mutually complete one another, like a box and its lid fitting perfectly.
O Son of the Buddha, how should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva understand the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
In this passage, the prose section is divided into three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, by means of unobstructed and unhindered wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that all worldly realms are the realm of the Tathāgata.
He knows the realms of all three periods of time, the realms of all lands, the realms of all phenomena, the realms of all sentient beings,
the realm of non-differentiated true suchness (tathatā), and the unobstructed realm of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
The realm of obstruction; the realm of the limitlessness of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); the realm of the measurelessness of space;
the realm of no-realm—this is the realm of the Tathāgata.

The explanation consists of two parts: first the teaching (*dharma*), then the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Within the teaching there are also two parts: first, extensively taking up the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) to reveal the scope of the domain;
second, closely taking up various states of mind to serve as analogies for the Buddha’s domain. Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts:

first, listing the boundlessness of the objects of cognition; second, revealing the immeasurability of their scope. Now, for the first [of these], one is first instructed to take non-obstructive wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) as the cognizer.
This is because there is nothing that cannot measure the Buddha’s realm. Hereafter, the object of focus (*ālambana*) is correctly revealed through ten phrases:

first, a general mention of those to be transformed; second, the time of transformation; third, the place of transformation; fourth, the method of transformation; fifth, the persons to be transformed; and sixth, seventh, and eighth—these three all clarify what is realized.
Among these, *tathatā* (suchness) refers to its essence, which is eternally of one flavor; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent" [in terms of conceptual proliferation].

Regarding the distinctions: the *dharmadhātu* is the basis for the arising of all phenomena, and is thus called "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*). The *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) is the ultimate realization of things as they truly are, and is thus called "boundless" (*ananta*).
As for the nine spheres of transformation, the first eight have specific limits while the last one is universally pervasive.

If categorized according to the two truths (*satyadvaya*), the first five belong to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the latter three to the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Yet all nine penetrate both the conventional and the ultimate, because both the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) and the emptiness of principle (*tattvaśūnyatā*) are equally empty.

The final pair is "non-existence," which reveals that the preceding nine objects are likewise non-existent. If categorized according to the Three Truths, emptiness is the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya), and the three types of emptiness constitute the Middle Way.
If these are subsumed within the five realms (pañca-dhātu), the first three correspond to the immeasurability of the world-realm (loka-dhātu).
The fourth is subduing and the application of subduing; the fifth is sentient beings. The next three are the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
the remaining two are neither.
O Son of the Buddha, just as the objects of all worlds are immeasurable, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata immeasurable. As with one...
The realms of the three periods of time are immeasurable; the realm of the Tathāgata is likewise immeasurable.

Even as the realm of non-realm is immeasurable, the realm of the Tathāgata is likewise immeasurable. Just as the realm of non-realm does not exist anywhere at all, so too the realm of the Tathāgata does not exist anywhere at all.
The realm of the Tathāgata is likewise non-existent in all places.
Second, the manifestation of its boundaries is immeasurable. First, these boundaries are manifested by means of the ten realms; because the object and the wisdom are in accord, both are immeasurable.
However, by means of the absence of objects, it is revealed that they do not exist; thus, even up to true suchness (tathatā), nothing can be apprehended.
Therefore, all objects arise like clouds yet remain eternally quiescent. Just as it is with "thusness" (*tathatā*), so it is with true thusness (*bhūtatathatā*) and the absence of change;
it is likewise for all such states.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that the realm of the mind is the realm of the Tathāgata, just as the realm of the mind is [the realm of] thusness.
The realms are immeasurable, boundless, unbound, and unliberated. The realm of the Tathāgata is likewise immeasurable, boundless, unbound, and unliberated.
Why is this? Because through such and such conceptualization and discrimination, there is such and such immeasurable manifestation.

The second [section] takes various states of mind as a proximate analogy for the Buddha’s realm. This consists of two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the interrogation and explanation. Now, for the first:
"Immeasurable and boundless" refers to the vastness of its characteristics and functions; "neither bound nor liberated" clarifies that its essential nature is profoundly quiescent.
Next, the intent of the interrogation is: "How can one use the mind to serve as an analogy for the Buddha’s realm? The intent of the explanation is: "Bodhi..."
The *sattva* manifests spontaneously according to one's own thoughts; therefore, it has no fixed dimensions. The Buddha-realm is likewise: it manifests according to the capacities of beings.

Whether as body or as wisdom, how could there be any measure? Since wisdom manifests through the mediation of thought, its nature is neither bound nor liberated, for it is not bound by characteristics and thus has no subsequent liberation.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great dragon king who sends down rain according to his will; that rain does not emerge from within, nor does it emerge from without.
The realm of the Tathāgata is also like this: according to such thoughts and conceptualizations, there are such infinite manifestations.
Throughout the ten directions, they have no place of origin. O Son of the Buddha, it is like the waters of the great ocean, all of which arise from—
Just as it is produced by the mental power of the dragon kings, so too is the ocean of all-knowledge of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
it arises entirely from the great vows made by the Tathāgatas in the past.
The second analogy clarifies this through two metaphors. The first metaphor illustrates the absence of bondage and liberation;

the second metaphor illustrates the immeasurable and boundless, which applies to both preceding sections. Now, for the first: the previous section explained the metaphor of rain falling from nowhere, which directly illustrates the absence of bondage and liberation.

Since there is no place of origin, how could there be bondage or liberation? The subsequent section explains the metaphor of the ocean water arising from the mind, which illustrates the absence [of limit].

The causes of bondage and liberation are as follows: water takes the power of the mind as its cause; it is not fixed as being either internal or external. Wisdom arises through the conditions of past vows;
therefore, though it comes, there is no coming.
O Son of the Buddha, the ocean of all-knowledge is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and ineffable.
Nevertheless, I shall now briefly provide a simile; you should listen attentively.

The second is the analogy of the vast and deep waters of the ocean, which illustrates that which is immeasurable and boundless. This section has three parts. First, the headings are presented and the audience is cautioned to listen:
"O Son of the Buddha, in this Jambudvīpa, two thousand five hundred rivers flow into the great ocean;
in Aparagoyānī to the west, five thousand rivers flow into the great ocean; and in Pūrvavideha to the east, seven thousand five hundred rivers flow [into the great ocean]."
The great ocean. To the north, in Uttarakuru, ten thousand rivers flow into the great ocean.
Son of the Buddha, in these four continents, twenty-five thousand such rivers flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean.
What do you think? Is this water much? He replied, "It is very much. Son of the Buddha, furthermore, there are ten *prabhāsa* dragon kings who rain down upon the great ocean.
The water was twice as much as before. The Dragon King Hundred Radiances rained water into the great ocean that was again twice as much as before.
[There were] the Dragon Kings Great Adornment, Mānasvin, Thunder-Resonance, Nanda and Upananda, Immeasurable Radiance, Uninterrupted Continuous Pouring, Great Victory, and Great Exertion. Just as...
These eighty billion great dragon kings each rained upon the great ocean, and they all successively exceeded the former by multiples.
The crown prince of the Dragon King Sāgara is named Jambudhvaja; the water he rained into the great ocean again exceeded the former by multiples.
O Son of the Buddha, the water flowing from the palace of the Dragon King Ten Radiances into the great ocean exceeds the former by a factor of ten.
The water flowing from the palace of the Dragon King Hundred Radiances into the great ocean exceeds the former by another factor of ten.

[The waters from the palaces of] the Dragon King Great Adornment, the Dragon King Mānasa, the Dragon King Thunder-Resonance, the Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda, and Immeasurable Light [flow into the great ocean, each exceeding the previous by a factor of ten].
The Dragon King Vimala, the Dragon King Uninterrupted Torrential Rain, the Dragon King Mahājayanta, the Dragon King Mahāvikrama, and so forth—
these eighty billion great dragon kings each have their own separate palaces, from which water flows into the great ocean.

All of these increase successively, doubling in volume compared to the preceding. The water from within the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara’s son, Yaśodhara, flows into the great ocean, doubling again compared to what went before.
Son of the Buddha, when the Dragon King Sāgara rains continuously upon the great ocean, the water doubles once more;
furthermore, the water from within the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara surges out into the sea, doubling yet again.

It is twice as much as before. Two similes illustrate three points; the Bodhisattvas should know that the following section applies the teaching to the dharma. Within the similes, there are three parts;

first, the specific manifestation of the abundance of water, which consists of four sections: (1) the water emerging from the four continents; (2) the rain falling from the dragon kings; and (3) the water emerging from the palaces.
The four Sāgara kings both rain and produce [waters], each succeeding one doubling the amount of the preceding to manifest their depth and vastness.
The water they produce is the color of dark lapis lazuli; it surges forth at specific times, and for this reason the great ocean’s tides do not miss their appointed time.
Second, this further clarifies the characteristics of the water: because it surges upward, the tide rises quickly; because the various jewels dissolve within it, the tide falls.
This is the ultimate explanation.
O Son of the Buddha, thus the waters of this great ocean are immeasurable, its various jewels are immeasurable, and the sentient beings who depend upon it are immeasurable.
The great earth is likewise immeasurable.
Thirdly, three points reveal its immeasurability.
"O Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is that great ocean immeasurable? He replied, "Indeed, it is immeasurable."

It cannot be used as a metaphor. Son of the Buddha, this great ocean is immeasurable, yet compared to the immeasurable ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it does not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part.
I merely provide analogies according to the minds of sentient beings; however, the realm of the Buddha cannot be reached by analogy.

Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know that the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable, because from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they have practiced all bodhisattva deeds without interruption.
They should know that the accumulation of jewels is immeasurable, for it consists of all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the seeds of the Three Jewels.
Because it is uninterrupted, one should know that the sentient beings who dwell therein are immeasurable, for they are the beneficiaries of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,

both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). One should know that the stages (*bhūmi*) wherein they dwell are immeasurable, for they range from the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate Stage of Non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇā-bhūmi*), being the abodes of all Bodhisattvas.
In the second section on "Conformity," there are two parts. First, it conforms to the immeasurability of water: the Buddha’s wisdom is infinite in a single thought-moment;

how much more so when it exhausts the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions? Layer upon layer, it is beyond all analogy or manifestation. Second, from "O Sons of the Buddha, you should know that the Tathāgata...
onwards, it conforms by universally manifesting immeasurability: it is not only wisdom that constitutes the Buddha's realm, but also the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
These are all the respective boundaries of their domains. It should be understood that the ocean of wisdom merges with the water, while the others merge with the jewels and so forth.
O Son of the Buddha, it is for the sake of entering immeasurable wisdom and benefiting all sentient beings that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva acts thus.
Regarding the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, one should understand it in this way.
This concludes the third major section. It summarizes by stating "one should know," implying that if the mind does not know the Buddha’s realm, how could it possibly benefit sentient beings?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
As the realms of the mind are immeasurable, So too are the realms of all Buddhas.
Just as the realms of the mind arise from the intellect, One should observe the realm of the Buddha in this same way.
The second verse consists of five stanzas divided into two parts; the first stanza provides the explanation through the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).

Just as a nāga does not leave its original abode, Yet pours down great rain through the power of its mind— Although the water has no place from which it comes or goes, It completely saturates all things in accordance with the nāga’s intention.
The Muni of Ten Powers is likewise: He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
If there is a pure mind, he manifests his body. His measure equals the dharma-realm, yet he enters a single pore.
The remaining verses repeat the previous metaphors, also in two parts. The first two combined verses repeat the first two metaphors; they share the same metaphor of neither bondage nor liberation.
As the ocean’s rare treasures are immeasurable, so too are sentient beings and the great earth.
The nature of water is of one single flavor, equal and without distinction; those born within it each receive benefit.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise; all that exists therein is immeasurable.
Those who dwell on the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) all obtain benefit therein.
The final two verses employ the metaphor of the great ocean’s vast depth; they merely summarize and manifest its immeasurability, while the remaining text is omitted.
This is the sixth [topic], the conduct of manifestation. Previously, the boundlessness of the objective sphere and wisdom was clarified; now, the application of these is revealed as compassion.
Wisdom is inexhaustible; for although the ocean of wisdom is already full, compassion never ceases.
Son of the Buddha, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
The prose section has two parts: first, the formal presentation; second, the explanation of the characteristics.
"O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that unimpeded conduct is the conduct of a Tathāgata; he should know that the conduct of suchness is the conduct of a Tathāgata."
Within the explanation of the characteristics, there are three parts: first, the dual presentation of the two practices; second, the dual explanation of the two practices;

and third, the dual conclusion of the two practices. Now, for the first part: the meaning contains many implications. First, the "unimpeded practice" is the phenomenal activity of principle; the "true-suchness practice" is the noumenal activity of phenomena.
The former is the aspect of the practice (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter is the essence of the practice (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the former is identical with wisdom.
The former is the wisdom within compassion; the latter is the wisdom of compassion itself. The former is the conventional within the ultimate; the latter is the ultimate within the conventional.
Their seamless integration and non-obstruction constitute the practice of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, just as True Suchness (tathatā) is not born in the past, does not move in the future, and does not arise in the present,
so too the practice of the Tathāgata is likewise unborn, unmoving, and unarisen.
In the second pair of explanations, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the practice of *tathatā* (suchness); second, the explanation of unimpeded practice. This is the first part.

Regarding the term "*tathatā*," it contains both a literal meaning and a metaphorical one. Within the text, there are three sections. First, the name is cited to provide an explanation, clarifying that its essence transcends the three temporal limits;
therefore, it is identical to *tathatā*. By acceding to suchness, practice is perfected, and practice is itself suchness. Since the past and future are not conditions, [it is beyond them].
Unborn and immovable, it is currently free from conditions; therefore, it does not arise.

Son of the Buddha, just as the dharma-realm is neither measurable nor immeasurable because it is formless, so too is the practice of the Tathāgata neither measurable nor immeasurable because it is formless.

Second, he further cites that the *dharmadhātu* is formless to clarify the Middle Way through the simultaneous negation of both extremes. Thus, one knows that the marks of reality (*lakṣaṇasatya*) and so forth are all the practices of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a bird flying through space; after passing through hundreds of thousands [of leagues], there is the place already traversed and the place not yet traversed.
All are immeasurable. Why is this? Because the realm of space is without limit. The conduct of the Tathāgata is likewise.

Even if someone were to spend hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas analyzing and expounding it, that which has been explained and that which remains unexplained would both be immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the conduct of the Tathāgata is without limit.
Third is the analogy of a bird flying through the void, which explains the meaning of non-measurement (*apramāṇa*). There are two aspects to this non-measurement:

first, its practice is vast and immeasurable, as it is said that "the Tathāgata’s practices are without limit"; second, because phenomena share the same essence, they are inherently without measure or boundary.

Therefore, it is illustrated by the analogy of emptiness. Since there is no measure, how could there be "immeasurability"? If one were to claim that immeasurability is itself a measure, both [measure and immeasurability] would be eternally quiescent in their mutual negation;
this constitutes the practice of the Tathāgata. Thus, the mind is ever more void and the practice is ever more vast;

though practicing all day long, one has never practiced. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely, the Great [Vehicle]."
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, abides in unimpeded conduct; though he has no fixed dwelling place,
he is able to universally manifest his activities for all sentient beings, so that upon seeing them, they may transcend all paths of obstruction.

The second [section] explains unimpeded conduct. This passage consists of two parts: first, a general clarification based on the Dharma; second, a specific illustration by means of analogies. Now, for the first:
wisdom has no abiding place, while compassion demonstrates the sphere of practice; this is the non-obstruction of compassion and wisdom, being itself free from the two-fold obstruction.
To cause others to be without obstruction is entirely the practice of non-obstruction.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the king of golden-winged birds (garuḍa) flying through the void, circling and soaring without departing,
who uses his pure eyes to observe all the dragon palaces within the ocean, and exerting fierce and courageous power, lashes up the waters of the sea with his left and right wings.
He causes both wings to spread wide; then, perceiving those male and female nāgas whose lives are about to end, he seizes them.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the King of Garuḍas, abides in unimpeded conduct and, with his pure Buddha-eye, observes all sentient beings within the various palaces of the Dharma-realm.
If there are those who have previously planted roots of goodness that have already matured, [he perceives them] as follows:

Come, O valiant one endowed with the ten powers! With the two wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā, stir up and split asunder the great ocean of the waters of saṃsāra, seize [beings] therein, and place them within the Buddha-dharma.
Cause them to sever all conceptual constructions and frivolous disputations, and cause them to dwell securely in the non-conceptual and unimpeded conduct of the Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the sun and moon, which are peerless and without equal, circling...
They travel through space to benefit sentient beings, yet they do not form such thoughts as, "From where have I come, or to what place have I gone?
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: their nature is fundamentally quiescent and free from discrimination. They manifest traveling throughout all dharma realms;
desiring to bring benefit and joy to all sentient beings, they perform the works of a Buddha without ceasing. They do not...
Thus arises the conceptual proliferation and discrimination: "I have come from that place and am going toward that place.
These two distinctions are illustrated by metaphors: first, the metaphor of the golden-winged bird parting the ocean, which illustrates compassion within wisdom;
second, the metaphor of the sun and moon being impartial, which illustrates wisdom not losing its compassion.
O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, by means of such immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable natures and characteristics,
know and see the conduct practiced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The third pair of verses concludes the two lines: the essential nature is bound to true thusness (*tathatā*), and its characteristics are bound to non-obstruction.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:

Just as true suchness (tathatā) is neither born nor extinguished, Having no location and being invisible, the practice of those who bring great benefit is likewise: It transcends the three times and is immeasurable;
it is neither a realm (dharmadhātu) nor not a realm, Neither finite nor infinite.
The conduct of those of great merit is likewise: It is neither measurable nor immeasurable, for it has no body.
Just as a bird flies for billions of years, There is no difference between the space before and the space behind;
So too, though one were to expound the Tathāgata’s conduct for many eons, That which has been said and that which has not yet been said cannot be measured.
The golden-winged bird soars in the void and gazes upon the great ocean; It cleaves the waters to seize the male and female dragons.
The One of Ten Powers can uproot those with wholesome roots, Causing them to emerge from the sea of existence and eliminate all delusions.
Like the sun and moon traveling through space, They illuminate all things without discrimination.
The World-Honored One wanders throughout the dharma-realm, Teaching and transforming sentient beings without a single stirring thought.
This second verse has five lines. The first three verses praise *tathatā* (suchness); the latter two verses praise non-obstruction.
O Son of the Buddha! How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has attained perfect enlightenment?
Because it is the fruit of the perfection of practice, the seventh manifestation of bodhi, which is necessarily achieved through cultivation directed toward conditions.

Because it is awakening (*bodhi*). The text consists of three parts: the inquiry, the explanation of the characteristics, and the summary. The inquiry concerns "perfect awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and briefly sets forth five gates. First, the explanation of the name:

the Jin [dynasty] calls it *bodhi*, retaining the Sanskrit term; this translates as "awakening. This specifically distinguishes it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and establishes its difference from the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when "bodhi" is mentioned alone, it refers merely to the path that is to be awakened to; now, it is said to be "accomplished" (*siddha*).
This is the name for the perfect union of wisdom and reality (*jñāna-tattva*). Second, the clarification of its essential nature (*svabhāva*):

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the two types of wisdom and the two types of abandonment constitute the essence of bodhi. The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that both "bodhi" and "the abandonment of bodhi" are termed bodhi.
If one follows this sutra, it encompasses all phenomena, as detailed in the full text. Third, the discernment of its categories: some speak of it as being only one, as [in the following passage].
Wisdom is in accord [with suchness], because it is devoid of dual characteristics. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is such (tathatā) is neither dual nor differentiated.

Therefore, although it is manifested as two, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that there is both naturally pure bodhi (*prakṛti-viśuddha-bodhi*) and that which is accomplished through cultivation; thus, it is also termed "naturally pure."
It is the purity of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*). Alternatively, it may be divided into three, based on the three vehicles (*triyāna*), as in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.

Or it may be expanded into four; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that those who observe with inferior wisdom attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, up to those who observe with the highest-of-the-high wisdom attaining the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Furthermore, the four types of wisdom-enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*) also represent these four meanings. Or it is explained as five, as in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and so forth; in some instances, it clarifies all ten [perfections], as in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-parivarta*), where these ten alone constitute the complete [path].
This is what is being analyzed here. As for the manifestation of their functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there is nothing that is not subsumed within it.

Regarding the fourth [section] on functional activity, the text contains ten gates, wherein essence and function are revealed in tandem, each established with a specific title according to its distinct meaning. Now, to synthesize and encompass them, they are as follows:

It takes the two truths as its object, severs the two obstacles, realizes the two emptinesses, gives rise to the two wisdoms, seals all capacities for awakening, manifests the myriad phenomena, possesses the ten bodies, and pervades the ten directions, reaching even into places as minute as atoms and the tips of hairs. Its activity, encompassing both cause and fruit, is boundless, as detailed below in the text.
Fifth is the "Discernment of Characteristics," which shall now be explained according to the text; herein, the ten gates are briefly discerned. First:

This provides a general clarification of the essence and characteristics: first, the two seals manifest according to the myriad capacities; second, the essence and characteristics are profoundly deep;
third, the three wheels are equal; fourth, cause and effect penetrate one another; fifth, the essence is free from deficiency or fullness; sixth, the characteristics are without increase or decrease;

seventh, the function encompasses both movement and stillness; eighth, it pervades the dharma-realm; ninth, it is universally present in all minds. These shall now be explained individually according to their respective gates.
O Son of the Buddha, you should know that when a Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he does not observe any objective referents.
Regarding all phenomena, he is equanimous and free from doubt; he is non-dual and signless, without activity and without cessation, immeasurable and boundless.
He remains far removed from the two extremes, abiding in the Middle Way, transcending all written characters and verbal expressions.

For now, let us take the first as the general [heading] and the remaining nine as the specific [sections]. Although there are nine distinct sections, they explain ten meanings: the first explains the first meaning;
the second explains the tenth, thereby citing the first to encompass the subsequent ones; and from the third onward, the explanations proceed in sequential order.
The eleventh section explains the eighth and ninth meanings; these should be understood from the text itself, as the explanation of the passages is self-evident.

This should be interpreted differently. First, it is explained in general that there are ten gates, all of which encompass the three aspects of essence (*tattva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*).
First, quiescence and illumination constitute the essence of bodhi; thus, it is said that "all meanings" refers to the objects of both the ultimate and conventional truths.

Contemplation culminates in non-contemplation; as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Non-contemplation is bodhi, because it is free from all conditions," like the ocean being without [discursive] mind.
Yet it is able to discern instantaneously; this is not because there is nothing understood. The Jin translation says, "To understand all meanings.

Understanding is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); contemplation is precisely non-contemplation. Since the mind and its objects are thus quiescent, there are no seeds of delusion or habituation. Non-contemplation is the essence (*svabhāva*); illumination and severance are the function (*vṛtti*).
Taken together, these constitute the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). These two are identical with the myriad dharmas as the essence of *bodhi*. This refers to wisdom and—
The principle is profound and dark; it is identical to the single Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that while remaining equal toward all phenomena, one does not lose the illumination.
To be decisive and clear is called being without doubt. Since there is nothing to doubt, what is known is eternally quiescent. When the three are perfected, all are perfected;
one does not perceive any difference between sentient beings and Buddhas. Therefore, it is said to be non-dual. This is because one knows that all sentient beings are themselves Bodhi.
Because it characterizes the essence, it is also the non-duality of subject and object. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "Non-duality is bodhi," because it is free from mind and dharmas.
Fourth, this collectively points to the essence and characteristics of the preceding three: the quiescence of sentient beings is bodhi, because all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) have been extinguished.
Fifth, this is precisely the cessation of the sphere of mental activity; it is profound stillness without transition. It is also "non-practice" that is bodhi, for there is no...
1. Because of mindfulness. 2. Although awakened, one is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because one does not abide in concentration.
3. It has two meanings: first, it is horizontally pervasive throughout the ten directions, being immeasurably vast; second, its essence is without arising or ceasing, transcending all limits.
4. It also has two meanings: first, vertically, every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) becomes boundless; second, once attained, it is eternally constant and has no future limit.

The mind has no initial characteristic; it darkly accords with principle because it has no prior limit. Ninth, "leaving extremes to accord with the mean" means that one leaves behind all such extremes as defilement and purity, bondage and liberation, existence and non-existence, identity and difference, and so forth. Because one does not dwell or cling to them universally, it is called "leaving extremes.
This is not a matter of seeing extremes as existent; rather, since the extreme is itself the mean, when there is neither extreme nor mean, one truly abides in the Middle Way. Tenth.
This collectively reveals that which transcends words. The preceding nine [sections] rely on words to manifest the profound; yet they do not exhaust the depths of bodhi.
Therefore, they are brought back to the nature that is free from [conceptualization], so that one may transcend words and accord with it.
He knows the mental activities, faculties, dispositions, inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings.
To state the essential point: in a single thought-moment, he fully knows all phenomena of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean, which can universally reflect the physical forms and images of all sentient beings within the four continents; therefore, it is described as such.

It is like the great ocean. The bodhi of all Buddhas is also thus: it universally manifests according to the mental activities, faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet there is nothing that is manifested. For this reason, it is called the bodhi of all Buddhas.
The second [section] concerns the knowledge of all sentient beings, which manifests ten thousand capacities through the "Seal" (mudrā); this is the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

This passage consists of three parts: first, the teaching; second, the analogy; and third, the application. First, the teaching: knowing the three periods of time in a single thought-moment is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). Second, the analogy:

this refers to the Ocean-Seal, used as a metaphor for how Bodhi manifests instantaneously without deliberate thought. Third, the application: regarding the statement that "there is nothing manifested," there are three meanings. First, there is no...

First, because it manifests, it is like the ocean. Second, because that which is manifested is empty, it is like a reflection. Third, because it has no separate substance, it is like water; it cannot be distinguished from the reflection.
Because its own essence manifests, it is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*). The *Awakening of Faith* states:

"The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are free from the characteristics of seeing and perceived objects; they are all-pervasive because the mind is the reality, and thus they are the [nature] of all phenomena."
The nature itself clearly illuminates all delusive phenomena and possesses the great function of wisdom. This is precisely the non-conceptual, manifest illumination;
as the境 (object) of the same essence, it constitutes the characteristic and function of bodhi. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Regarding all meanings, there is nothing observed."
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhi of all Buddhas cannot be proclaimed by any written characters; it cannot be reached by any sounds;
it cannot be expressed by any speech. It is only revealed through skillful means according to what is appropriate for each being.
The characteristics of the three natures are profoundly deep, for their nature transcends words, yet their principle is perfect and their expression is all-pervasive.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha attains perfect enlightenment, he acquires bodies equal in measure to all sentient beings.
One attains a body equal in measure to all dharmas; one attains a body equal in measure to all buddha-lands; one attains a body equal in measure to all three periods of time;
one attains a body equal in measure to all Buddhas; one attains a body equal in measure to all languages; one attains a body equal in measure to True Suchness (*tathatā*);
one attains a body equal in measure to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); one attains a body equal in measure to the realm of empty space; one attains the unobstructed realm.
He attains a body equal in measure to all objects of cognition; he attains a body equal in measure to all vows; he attains a body equal in measure to all practices;
he attains a body equal in measure to the realm of quiescent nirvana.

The fourth is the equality of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-samatā*). This explains the aforementioned equality regarding phenomena (*dharma-samatā*); because it is equal to all phenomena, the wheel of mind (*manas-cakra*) is also equal.
What, then, is there to doubt? The text consists of two parts: first, the individual enumeration of the body and so forth; second, the general conclusion that reveals their multiplicity.

Now, for the first part: there are thirteen bodies. The first six are equal in terms of phenomena (*vastu*); the next three are equal in terms of principle (*tattva*); the next one is equal in terms of both phenomenon and principle. Regarding phenomena:
The fourth is the unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharmāvyāghāta*). Regarding the latter three types of equality, which concern cause and effect, thirteen instances are briefly cited;

therefore, they are concluded as being "immeasurable. The term "measure" (*mātra*) refers to the extent or dimension of that which is equalized. The term "equality" (*samatā*) refers to the three wheels that perform the equalizing.
There are two meanings to this "equality": first, it is equal to the measure of those phenomena and principles; second, it is equal to the essence of those phenomena and principles. This is why...
Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): those various principles and phenomena are precisely what I have realized. Subject and object are merged in profound stillness;

since even they are identical to me, how could anything else be difficult? Therefore, the Sage is empty and void, without form; there is nothing that is not the self. He unifies all things to constitute his own being.
O Son of the Buddha, just as it is with the body one has attained, so it is with speech and mind;
one attains such infinite and innumerable purities of the three spheres.
Subsequently, the three wheels are linked together.
Son of the Buddha, when the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment,
and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvāṇa.

The fifth section clarifies the mutual penetration of cause and effect, explaining the aforementioned non-duality because they share the same nature. This passage consists of three parts: first, the heading;
second, the explanation beginning with "All are the same," etc.; and third, the conclusion beginning with "Knowing all," etc. Now, for the first part:

among the eight aspects [of the bodhisattva], two are briefly cited, hence the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*). This text is identical to what is said in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "If Maitreya were to attain bodhi..."
"Attainment" (prāpti) means that all sentient beings should likewise attain it; all sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of bodhi.

Maitreya showed that those who are deluded regarding this principle merely regard these words as logical refutations, not realizing they have truly attained bodhi. Indeed, it is just as you have questioned.

Furthermore, in the preceding chapter, [it was shown that] because "we" are equal to "them," we are universally identical to their measure; now, it is clarified by means of "them" being equal to "us."
Therefore, I manifest myself entirely within me; thus one knows that the single nature is equal, and that these aspects mutually establish one another.
Within this, does the establishment refer to principle (*li*) or to phenomena (*shi*)? If it were an establishment as a phenomenon, why would the commentary say, "because they share the same nature"?
If it were an establishment as principle, why would it say here, "attaining perfect enlightenment" or "entering nirvana"? This is the Great [Avataṃsaka Sūtra].
Section: The doctrine of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) differs from that of the other schools and is difficult to comprehend.

Nevertheless, if one examines it from the perspective of the realms of humans and devas, [beings] are fully possessed of both the self of persons and the self of phenomena. In the Hīnayāna, these are regarded solely as the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

In the Mahāyāna, some say they are merely manifestations of the mind, while others say they are illusory existence which is itself emptiness; thus, both the self of persons and the self of phenomena are discarded.
