"How should it be upheld? To this, there is now a response, which is divided into two parts: first, the manifestation of the names;

second, under the section "O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate," the explanation of receiving and upholding, so that one may know the general title, seek the essential meaning through the names, recognize the method of upholding, and practice in reliance upon it.
Now, for the first part, there are ten names, divided into five pairs. The first pair is the contrast between the profound internal and the absolute external.
This means that internally, one personally realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues; externally, it cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle.

Second is the correspondence between the realization of quiescence and the opening of wisdom; third is the correspondence between the manifestation of the fruit and the formation of the cause. That is to say, the nature-purity of all virtues is itself the Buddha-seed.
Now, the manifestation of these ten gates is the demonstration of their meaning. Fourth, the response that transcends the world and accords with the Buddha:

since even the world does not know them, how could they possibly be destroyed? These ten are universally within the domain of the Buddha’s own realization. Fifth, the response that purifies the faculties and expounds reality:

because one knows that sentient beings and Buddhas share the same source, one can thereby achieve purification; for the nature that remains unchanging amidst conditions is the fundamental basis of all Buddhas. And...
The non-obstruction between nature and characteristics and the perfect interfusion of cause and effect constitute the inconceivable. Beyond this, there is no further ultimate dharma.
The preceding nine points represent specific meanings, while the final one encompasses them all collectively.
O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate is not taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings;
it is taught only for Bodhisattvas who are intent upon the Mahāyāna, and only for Bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle.
This Dharma-gate does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the various Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The second section, clarifying the upholding [of the teaching], has two parts: first, distinguishing the vessels and non-vessels; second, from "Therefore, a bodhisattva...

onwards, citing the benefits to encourage practice. Now, for the first part, there are the dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis. Within the dharma, there are two sections. First, designating the vessels and non-vessels.

Those who are non-vessels are not [suitable] objects [for this teaching]. These are those of the provisional Hīnayāna and the conceivable vehicles; they are called "other sentient beings" because they practice through successive stages.

This vessel is that which is called the "perfect capacity" (yuanji). It does not discriminate between ordinary beings and sages; it inclines toward the Mahāyāna while excluding the Hīnayāna, and toward the inconceivable vehicle (acintya-yāna) while excluding the provisional vehicles.
It carries all at once; when the mind is fulfilled through the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā), it immediately encompasses all other positions in a state of perfect fusion and non-obstruction.
This is named the inconceivable vehicle. Having explained the arousal of this dharma-gate, the following clarifies its reception.
It is not received. This explains why it was [previously] said that it is "not done. There are those with the hand of perfect faith who are able to receive all practices;
for those of the provisional [vehicles] above, they are not yet fully capable of receiving them, and therefore it is "not done" for them. The *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra* says:
"Although this sūtra may circulate in Jambudvīpa, it shall always abide within the hearts and hands of those sentient beings who are able to believe in the profound Dharma."
Practice. Furthermore, there is the sense that faith, understanding, practice, and realization all possess the meaning of "hands.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the seven treasures possessed by a universal monarch (cakravartin); it is because of these treasures that he is manifested as a wheel-turning king.
These jewels do not fall into the hands of other beings, except for the crown prince born of the first queen who is fully endowed with the marks of a noble wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

If the wheel-turning monarch lacks such a son possessed of these manifold virtues, then after the king’s death, all these jewels will completely vanish within seven days. Son of the Buddha, this sutra is a precious jewel.

It is likewise so. It shall not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, with the sole exception of those true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted the roots of goodness that produce the marks of a Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, if there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon be dispersed and extinguished. Why is this? Because all followers of the two vehicles do not hear this.
[Sūtra]. How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, analyze, and explain it? Only bodhisattvas are able to do so.
The third analogy can be understood. Regarding the correspondence [in the allegory], this sūtra is equated with the seven treasures; if this Dharma did not exist, it would not be [so].
Because he is the True Buddha, he is born into the family of the Tathāgata, like a crown prince born of the First Lady.
As for the marks of a Tathāgata, it is because from the very first thought, one suddenly practices the conduct of a Buddha. Regarding "dispersal and extinction," there are two meanings:

first, being unable to receive [the teaching], whereby the instruction does not proceed; second, being unable to practice, whereby the practice does not proceed. The *Prajñā-śāstra* says: "When the Dharma is about to..."
Regarding "the time of cessation," it refers to the cultivation of cessation; the subsequent explanation of the causes for dispersal and cessation can be understood accordingly.
For this reason, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears this Dharma-gate, they should experience great joy, receiving it with a respectful heart and reverently upholding it upon their heads.
Why is this? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has faith and delight in this sutra will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are three parts within the second section, which exhorts practice by highlighting the benefits: first, a brief presentation and explanation; second, a detailed explanation of the reasons for this, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, suppose...";
and third, a summary of the resulting benefits, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a king has accomplished such merit..."
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas,

practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). If such a person has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majestic power of the Tathāgata,
or if, having heard it at some time, they do not believe it, do not understand it, do not comply with it, and do not enter into it, they cannot be called a true [bodhisattva].
A true bodhisattva is so called because they are unable to give birth into the family of the Tathāgata.
In the subsequent detailed explanation, there are two parts: first, an indirect demonstration by way of contrast; second, a direct explanation. Regarding the first:

if one does not rely on this sutra, then even if one practices for many kalpas, it is still not truly [the path]; how much less could one quickly attain Bodhi? Within this, there is what is established...

This statement seems to be a provisional assumption. In comparison with Maitreya’s praise of Sudhana, it says that while other bodhisattvas require hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas to fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, Sudhana has accomplished this in a single lifetime.
"Thus one can purify Buddha-lands and so forth. This is an instance of employing the provisional to reveal the real; it is not a mere hypothetical assumption.

If there truly were such a person who does not believe, in what stage would they reside? The text provides no definitive judgment, but by implication, they must belong to the stage of the Three Worthies (san-xian).

This is because upon entering the realization of the Sages, one necessarily believes in the Perfect [Teaching]. If we consider the path of the teachings (jiao-dao), even after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one has still not entered the profound mystery. Therefore, ordinary beings...

As for those who are able to believe all at once, it is because the seeds of their past causes—the permeation of hearing [the Dharma]—are distinct. If they do not believe now, how could they hear it in the future?
If they should obtain and hear this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, [they will attain liberation].
Having heard this, they believe, understand, comply with, and enter into it. It should be known that such persons are born into the family of the Tathāgatas;
they accord with the realm of all Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with all the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and abide securely in the realm of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They remain far removed from all worldly dharmas; they give birth to all that is practiced by the Tathāgatas; they penetrate the dharma-nature of all bodhisattvas;
they possess no doubt or hesitation regarding the sovereign mind of the Buddhas; they abide in the teacherless Dharma; and they enter deeply into the unimpeded realm of the Tathāgatas.
In the second section, the sequential explanation, there are two parts. First, it clarifies the benefit of being born into the family through hearing and faith;

second, it clarifies that once a son of the Buddha has heard this Dharma, he is able to achieve the benefit of practicing based on the hearing and faith previously established. Now, for the first part: first, hearing and faith are clarified;

second, from "one should know" onwards, the achievement of the benefit is explained. Regarding "being born into the family of the Tathāgata": this means that because one realizes and attains the Buddha’s Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) herein, it is called "birth."
Second, taking the practice of the mind as one’s home, because it possesses the characteristics of a home. Third, taking the mundane realm as one’s home; Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
"Because this enables the lineage of the Buddhas to remain unbroken. Fourth, distancing oneself from what is not a home.
Fifth, taking the conduct of the Buddha as one’s home. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states: "Now, this bodhisattva’s conduct is like..."

1. Coming to the Way, because it continues without interruption. 2. Taking the dharma-nature of bodhisattvas as their home, because this is also the lineage of the Buddhas and is identical to the single realm of the Tathāgata.
3. Purifying the future Buddha-family. 4. Abiding in the fundamental Buddha-family.

The ninth [section] generally clarifies the family of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle regarding cause and effect. The first six belong to the family of self-perfection (*svabhāva*), while the latter three belong to the family of superior progress (*viśeṣa*).

Because one previously perceived the nature of the mind at the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is called the "family of birth. Because the Fourth Stage is associated with the supramundane, it is so designated.

It is born into the family of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*), because the eighth stage is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*). It is born into the family of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

here, it encompasses all three [stages], while also revealing that the understanding-mind of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is likewise called "born into the family," because cause and effect are unimpeded.
O Son of the Buddha, once Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard this Dharma, they are then able, by means of the wisdom of equality, to know immeasurable dharmas;
they are then able, by means of an upright mind, to remain free from all conceptual discrimination; they are then able, by means of superior aspiration and joy, to manifestly behold all Buddhas;
they are then able, by the power of mental attention, to enter the realm of equalized space; and they are then able to practice with sovereign mindfulness.
One can, through the power of wisdom, fully possess all merits within the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
One can, through spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), remain free from all worldly defilements. One can, through the bodhicitta, enter the net of all ten directions.
One can, through great discernment, know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time share a single essential nature. One can, through roots of goodness, dedicate [merit]...

The wise one universally enters such dharmas; they enter without entering. They do not have any攀缘 (pān-yuan, objective attachment) toward even a single dharma, yet they constantly contemplate all dharmas through a single dharma.
The second [section] concerns the benefit of establishing practice through faith and hearing; it consists of ten phrases divided into five pairs of non-obstructions:

first, contemplation does not obstruct cessation (*śamatha*); second, seeing the Buddha does not obstruct entry into the Dharma; third, the wisdom-practice of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) does not obstruct the arising of merit.

The four wisdoms are unstained by the world and unimpeded in their entry into compassion; the five bodies transcend the three periods of time and are unimpeded in their application while dedicating merit.
"Entering without entering" explains the meaning of the aforementioned "entry. "Not [entering] what has already... and below further explains "not entering while entering."
The essence of wisdom is itself suchness (*tathatā*). Since there is no dharma external to suchness that can be taken as an object of perception, there is nothing into which one can enter.
The sphere of mental activity ceases; it is tranquil and without entry. Yet, it does not lose its illuminating function;

therefore, one always contemplates all dharmas through the single suchness, and thus it is called "entering. Only when these two are non-obstructed is it truly entering. Furthermore, the one is itself suchness; thus, within the one—
Having already seen all within,
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has accomplished such merit attains untaught, spontaneous wisdom with little exertion of effort.
The third section, the summary, may be understood accordingly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The merit obtained from seeing, hearing of, and making offerings to all Tathāgatas is immeasurable."
Within the conditioned, one never reaches exhaustion; Only by extinguishing afflictions can one leave behind all suffering.
It is like a person who swallows a small diamond: It will never be digested, but must eventually pass through.
By making offerings to the merits of the Ten-Powered One, One extinguishes delusions and shall surely attain Vajra-wisdom.

Just as a heap of dry grass equal to Mount Sumeru would be entirely consumed by a fire of mustard seeds, so too the small merit of making offerings to the Buddhas will surely sever the afflictions and lead to Nirvāṇa.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a medicinal herb called Sudarśana; seeing, hearing, smelling, or touching it eliminates all maladies.
"If there are those who see or hear the One of Ten Powers, they shall obtain supreme merit and reach the Buddha-wisdom.

(Verse 10) This verse pertains to the tenth benefit of seeing and hearing. It does not praise the "holding by name" (*nāmadheya-dhāraṇa*), as the praise for holding by name occurs naturally in the subsequent text.
This verse should have been placed before the section distinguishing the Dharma from the parable, because... [the preceding].
The prose sections are linked like hooks and chains; the explicit names [of the Buddhas] also provide benefit through being seen and heard.

If this verse were moved to follow the manifestation of omens and connected with the subsequent verses, the logic and phrasing would be much more coherent. These four verses are divided into two parts: the first verse explains the teaching by way of Dharma (dharmadeśanā).
The latter three [verses] correspond respectively to the first three metaphors in the preceding verses.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways;
that is to say, the east rose and the west sank, and the west rose and the east sank.
The south surged and the north subsided; the north surged and the south subsided; the periphery surged and the center subsided; the center surged and the periphery subsided.

There were eighteen modes of movement, namely: shaking, universal shaking, and total universal shaking; rising, universal rising, and total universal rising; surging, universal surging, and total universal surging.
It shook, shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere.

It rained down clouds of all kinds of flowers surpassing those of the devas, clouds of all kinds of canopies, clouds of banners, clouds of flags, clouds of incense, clouds of garlands, clouds of ointments, clouds of ornaments, clouds of great radiant maṇi-jewels, and clouds of the praises of all bodhisattvas. Not...
One may speak of the various clouds of distinct bodies of Bodhisattvas, raining down clouds of perfect enlightenment;
clouds that adorn and purify inconceivable worlds; and clouds of the Tathāgata’s speech and sounds, filling the boundless Dharma-realm.
Just as in these four continents, the Tathāgata’s spiritual power manifests in this way, causing all Bodhisattvas to rejoice throughout the ten directions.
In all worlds, it is likewise so.
This is the sixth major section, "Manifesting Auspicious Omens as Proof. It consists of two parts: first, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, the proof. Now, for the first.
First this realm, and subsequently these categories; as for the vast number of worlds shaken and so forth, it is because the Dharma is inconceivable.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were likewise eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
Tathāgatas as numerous as atoms, all named Samantabhadra, appeared before him and spoke these words: "Excellent, O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able, through the majestic power of the Buddhas, to accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and expound the inconceivable dharma of the Tathāgata’s manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, we [reside] in the eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions."
Buddhas of the same name, as numerous as atoms, all teach this Dharma just as I have taught it;
likewise, all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions also speak thus.

Regarding the two types of proof: first is proof by the person who has attained the fruit, and second is proof by the person who follows the cause. The reason for providing both is that the Dharma is profound and subtle;
it is a Dharma in which cause and fruit mutually penetrate, and a Dharma in which the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.

The fact that only Bodhisattvas appear in the preceding assemblies is because they represent only the practice of the cause. The fact that only the realization of the fruit appears in the "Chapter on the Arising of the Mind" is because it represents the fruit.

Because it is the fundamental source; because the initial aspiration to attain Buddhahood is difficult to believe and accept; and because [other teachings] are distinct according to their respective meanings and thus ultimately reach nothingness, only this [teaching] possesses both [aspects].

Now, the first part is divided into four sections: first, the manifestation of the body; second, the praise and exposition beginning with "and then"; third, the citation of scriptural proof beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha, we...
which also clarifies the conclusion and the universal application of what has been taught, for it is the teaching of all and the teaching of everything.

"O Son of the Buddha! In this assembly today, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields who have attained all the supernormal powers and samādhis of bodhisattvas.
We have all bestowed upon them the prediction that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in one more birth.
Furthermore, beings as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."

Third, regarding the bodhicitta: we also bestow upon you the prediction that in a future age, after as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, you shall all attain buddhahood under the same name, Buddha Viśiṣṭaviṣaya (Buddha of the Supreme Realm).
In order to cause the bodhisattvas of the future to hear this Dharma, we shall all together protect and uphold it, just as [we have protected] the multitudes delivered within these four continents.

Birth. In all worlds throughout the ten directions—numbering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas, incalculable, immeasurable, and even unspeakably unspeakable, equal to the dharma-realm and space—all sentient beings who are thus delivered are likewise so.
Fourth, the demonstration through the benefits of advancement. This section has four parts: first, the benefit of attaining the fulfillment of the fruits of the four stages;

this is because one attains enlightenment in a single lifetime, and because the supernormal powers and samādhis refer to the ten powers and the ten concentrations. Second, the benefit of generating the resolve for awakening from as low as a speck of dust within a Buddha-field;
this is because those who receive distant predictions do not expect rapid accomplishment. Furthermore, what was previously explained as "one lifetime" refers to many [lifetimes].

This is the first [point]. This clarifies how many eons (*kalpa*) are identical to one; since the one and the many are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), why fixate on a definite number of eons and falsely conceive of them as many?
The sun of wisdom does not shift. If one obstinately clings to length or brevity, one will not expect to achieve Buddhahood.

Regarding the phrase "identical in name" (*tonghao*) and the "extraordinary realm" (*shushengjing*): it is because this is the realm in which the Buddha appears. Third, the benefit of long-term protection and endurance.
Fourth, as follows, the concluding summary of the benefits is extensive and universal: at that time,
by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, by the power of Vairocana’s original vows, by the suchness of the Dharma, by the power of roots of goodness,
because the Tathāgata gives rise to wisdom that does not transcend a single thought-moment, and because the Tathāgata responds to conditions without fail.
It is for the sake of the time; it is for the sake of awakening all bodhisattvas according to the occasion; it is so that past deeds may not be lost or destroyed;
it is to cause them to attain the vast conduct of Samantabhadra; and it is to manifest the sovereignty of omniscience.
Second is the proof by means of the person as the cause. This section has four parts. First, the explanation of the causes for the accumulation [of merit].

Regarding the previous proof of the person as the result, because it relied upon the causes for the manifestation of auspicious signs mentioned previously, those causes were not recounted in detail. Now, in order to clarify the distinction between cause and result, the causes for the accumulation are set forth extensively; the text is clear and can be understood on its own.
Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions,

there came from each direction bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields, filling all the dharma-realms of the ten directions.
Second, the manifestation of the body: although he comes from the ten directions, he pervades the entire Dharma-realm; thus, his coming is without coming.

He manifests the vast and magnificent adornments of a Bodhisattva, emits great nets of light, causes all worlds in the ten directions to tremble, shatters all the palaces of Māras, and extinguishes the sufferings of all evil realms. He manifests one...
They fully manifest the majestic power of all Tathāgatas; they sing praises of the immeasurable and diverse qualities of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas;
they universally rain down all kinds of rains; they manifest immeasurable and diverse bodies; and they receive and uphold the immeasurable teachings of all Buddhas.
Third, the explanation of their virtuous functions: the meaning of these ten phrases is clear.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, each spoke these words: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound this indestructible Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, all of us are named Samantabhadra; we have each come from the world-system of Universal Radiance."
They have come here from the presence of the Tathāgata Dhvajavaśavartin. In all those places as well, this Dharma is being taught;
these very same words, these very same meanings, these very same explanations, and these very same determinations are identical to those here, neither more nor less.
It is by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because we have attained the Dharma of the Tathāgata that we have come to this place.

Bear witness: as it is for me who have come here, so it is likewise in all the worlds throughout the ten directions, equal to space and pervading the Dharma-realm, within every one of the four continents.
Fourth is the proof by means of verbal testimony. All are identical to Samantabhadra because their universal Dharma is the same.

Although the names of the Buddhas of the realms differ, this does not negate the relationship between principal and attendant. "Universal Radiance" (Samantaraśmi) refers to the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, for there is nowhere it does not pervade.

The Buddha’s name "Universal Banner Sovereign" (Samantadhvaja-vijaya) signifies that fundamental wisdom rises loftily, crushing all that is not subdued, as phenomena and principle are unimpeded. Furthermore—
To demonstrate the connection between what has been taught and its universal application:
at that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas.
Desiring to further clarify the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, as well as the indestructibility of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma and his immeasurable goodness—
The faculties are entirely not empty. When the Buddhas appear in the world, they necessarily possess all supreme dharmas;

they are well able to observe the minds of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma according to their needs without ever missing the proper time. They give rise to the immeasurable light of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas.
All Buddhas are adorned with sovereign mastery. All Tathāgatas are one body without difference, from the beginning great...
The arising of this practice is explained through verses.

The seventh major section summarizes [the preceding] in verse. This section has two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the actual verses. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
first, the description of the ritual procedure; second, the intent for re-explaining below. This is because one wishes to further clarify the manifestation of the ten gates mentioned previously.
The text contains ten phrases, each phrase representing a distinct gate. These are arranged in a sequence based on the benefit of sentient beings, though the order is not uniform.

First is the attainment of perfect enlightenment; second is the turning of the Dharma wheel; third is the generation of wholesome roots through seeing and hearing—these three explicitly manifest the benefits.
Fourth is the manifestation of the Dharma itself, which serves as the general gate for the preceding [three]. Fifth is the mind, which is revealed in terms of wisdom. Sixth is the perfection...
1. Sound; 2. Seven is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Since the objective realms are immeasurable, the light produced is also manifold. 3. Eight is *nirvāṇa*.

It is the mastery over movement and stillness, for the Great Parinirvāṇa serves as the adornment of the Buddha. 4. Nine is the body (*kāya*), because it is spoken of as one in reference to its fundamental nature.
5. Ten is practice (*caryā*), because the cause is spoken of within the context of the fruit.
The various deeds performed by all Tathāgatas cannot be matched by any worldly analogy;
in order to bring sentient beings to awakening and understanding, he reveals this subtle, secret, and profound Dharma through analogies that are not truly analogies—
something difficult to hear even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Only those who have been disciplined by diligence and wisdom shall hear this secret and profound meaning.
Those who, upon hearing this Dharma, give rise to joy, have in the past made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
they are sustained by the Buddhas' empowerment and are constantly honored and praised by humans and devas.
This is the supreme wealth that transcends the world; This can deliver all classes of beings;
This can give birth to the pure path. You should uphold this and not be negligent.

The first verse of these four verses in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the "Correct Verses") serves as the conclusion for the section on distribution. By means of this, the ten sections are brought to a close.

Because of the intention [to uphold it]. The final three verses clarify what is named as the "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*). The first line clarifies the name; the remainder all constitute exhortations to uphold it.
For now, they may be divided into three parts: the first verse praises its profundity and difficulty of hearing; the next verse clarifies that hearing it depends upon manifold roots of goodness;

and the final verse cites its excellence to urge its upholding. Now, this chapter is vast and profound in its textual intent; it is both sudden and complete, investigating the [nature of] sentient beings...
The Source exhausts the profound ocean of all Buddhas. Within the fundamental Wheel of Dharma, one further dwells in its heart.
Born into the lineage of the Golden Wheel, one is moreover the legitimate heir—the most wondrous among wonders, the most profound among profundities.

Abiding within the minds of ordinary beings, one can realize swift realization through minor effort. How could one deceive oneself by refusing to accept this and remain long submerged in the cycle of birth?
"Among those who have died, I now hear that you can rejoice in liberation; you ought especially to congratulate yourself on your past merits. The supplementary commentary states:
"The final section of this chapter is titled 'The Section on Receiving and Upholding. At first glance, it appears to conclude this specific chapter;

however, upon careful examination of the general purport of the entire work, it is seen to be a comprehensive conclusion to the texts of the preceding seven assemblies. How is this evident? Because in the first assembly, [the Bodhisattva]..."

Dìchǎng. When Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he sat upon the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), wherein both the primary and secondary retributions were adorned with inexhaustible majesty.

Thereupon, the ten bodies pervaded everywhere with a full and resonant voice—limitless and limitless, principal and satellites layered upon one another, the two aspects hanging down simultaneously, and the two beginnings occurring at once. This is the simultaneous manifestation of the ten gates.
It is fully endowed. Because the nature-virtues of this dharma-realm’s perfect interfusion are identical to those of the Buddhas, the Tathāgata has realized these fruits and virtues.
Yet, because sentient beings are deluded regarding these nature-virtues, he has specifically appeared in the world to guide them.
Fearing that sentient beings might find it difficult to believe or enter through such inconceivable matters, this sutra first raises [the following].
The "Fruit-Ocean of Unobstructed Wondrous Adornment" is presented to exhort sentient beings of great resolve, so that upon seeing or hearing it, they may give rise to faith.
Therefore, this initial section is titled "Lifting up the Fruit to Exhort toward Joyful Arising of Faith.

Now, although those who see or hear of these fruits of virtue can indeed generate faith, they cannot ascend to them without practice; for if one does not fully understand the methods of cultivation and progress, [one cannot attain them].
Thus, there would be no means by which realization could be attained. Therefore, from the second assembly onward, the gate of faith was first opened;

based on faith, one arouses the bodhicitta and fully cultivates all practices. Consequently, the stages and positions are sequentially distributed as the causes and effects of the six levels (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*).

One ascends through the stages of *caryā*, *vihāra*, and *pratipatti* to reach the ten *bhūmis*, and finally the two awakenings of *sama* and *viśiṣṭa*. Initially, these sequential positions and ranks serve to differentiate [the path].

Distinct causes and effects. Next, it clarifies that by relying on the equal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra until the manifestation of wondrous enlightenment;

this constitutes the equality of cause and effect. Therefore, these ten gates of manifestation comprehensively subsume the two preceding types of causal practice to achieve the ultimate fruit, serving as the final consummation. Hence, the conclusion states: "This [is the] immeasurable and... of the Tathāgata.
This is the dharma-gate of inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom. Having heard it, one should believe and understand it, and accordingly enter into realization.

It should be known that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgata; thus, through faith one gives rise to understanding, and subsequently, based on that understanding, one initiates practice.

Therefore, the first six assemblies are judged to constitute the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding. Thus, it is said at the stage of the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*):
"Knowing that all dharmas are the self-nature of the mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom (*jñāna-kāya*) without depending on others for awakening;

this is called being born into the family of the Tathāgata. This signifies that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit. At this point, the *Sūtra of Exhortation to Practice* states: "Hearing and believing [the teaching] results in birth in the family. This...
Thus, the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. In this single assembly of the Dharma, the gates of the Dharma expounded from beginning to end form a single, coherent thread;
as cause and effect are perfectly integrated, the meaning of the entire work from start to finish is now complete. Therefore, this general conclusion is provided.
Therefore, auspicious signs and proofs appear in tandem. How could such profound contemplation be limited merely to this present chapter?

By means of this sutra, one investigates the causes and effects of the six stages through three cycles; yet, while the preceding section only spoke of them in a general sense to inspire faith and understanding, it did not yet constitute actual realization.
Thus, in the latter two sections, one advances to cultivate the practices and enters through the realization of others. Only then...
The four gates of faith-understanding, practice, and realization constitute the ultimate fruition of the cause and effect of the One Vehicle.

The above concludes the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata. Below begins the eighth section, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), wherein the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra expounds the Dharma-gate of Leaving the World at the Universal Radiance Hall during the third assembly. This begins from the fifty-third fascicle and continues as follows:
Fascicle Fifty-nine ends. Together with one chapter of sutra, this constitutes the section on Entrusting the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct.
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifty-two;
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning commented upon by the śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
and the essential points extracted by the śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
The eighth assembly, the "Dharma Gate on Leaving the World" (Lishi jian famen) spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguangming dian),
spans from scroll fifty-three to scroll fifty-nine. It comprises one chapter of the sutra, namely the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (Lishi jian pin).
Regarding "The Thirty-eighth Chapter on Transcending the World, Part One:
The Third Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance," the term "Universal Radiance" symbolizes the Buddha's fundamental wisdom of universal radiance.
It originated when, at the site of enlightenment, Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained perfect awakening;

he manifested clouds of bodies of the dharma-realm, seated within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), and based himself upon this Sūtra of Universal Illumination, which flows forth from the light of wisdom and pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Therefore, the ocean-like assembly of the Dharma-realm gathers simultaneously upon the bodies of oneself and others as inexhaustible adornments;

this is the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala*). Desiring to cause sentient beings of great resolve to arouse the mind, cultivate the causes, and realize this fruit, the text first clearly presents the fruit to encourage them to aspire with faith. Thus, it first cites the sublime fruit to exhort them to initiate [the practice].
With a mind of vast faith and aspiration, one intends to attain this fruit;
since this must necessarily rely upon the true cause, the second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance to explain the causes and fruits of the six stages.

Because the cultivation of the cause must have faith as its primary element, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths was taught in this assembly, with Mañjuśrī serving as the presiding leader, the intent being to emphasize this essential point.
Because the wisdom of the fruit is taken as the causal mind of the self, it is explained in reference to the Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā).

As for the stages of dwelling, practice, direction, and the grounds (*bhūmi*) being explained after ascending to the four heavens, this is because the Samādhi of Universal Radiance had not yet arisen;

rather, based on discriminative wisdom, the forty-stage dharma-gate was established as the cause of differentiation. Therefore, [the Buddha] met again in the Hall of Universal Radiance to explain [it].

The two types of awakening—the equal and the wondrous—and the two kinds of cause and effect, the differentiated and the equal, manifest the virtue of perfect interfusion by means of the gate of sequential practice.
Therefore, the fact that one is called a Buddha upon the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith precisely reveals that the original mind takes the fruition-awakening as its fundamental cause.
Thus, a single stage is fully endowed with all stages; this is what is meant by "the cause encompassing the fruition."

...and so on, until the end of the "Manifestation" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), where it concludes that [enlightenment] arises from understanding based on faith; this constitutes the fruit reaching back to the source of the cause.
Therefore, the second assembly is titled "The Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding. Its intent is that by means of such causes, one attains such a fruit.
This is the first instance of investigating the causes and effects of the six stages (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*). Now, this [text] does not...
The Dharma assembly was convened once again in the Hall of Universal Radiance, with only the presiding teacher changed; thus it is called the "Third Assembly.
It was not that [the Buddha] departed and later returned for a renewed gathering. Furthermore, this chapter consists of two hundred questions arising like clouds from the universal assembly.
Because Fabei asked about the practices within the six positions, Samantabhadra answered ten with one and repaid two thousand with a single jar.
This universally reveals that the practices within the aforementioned six positions do not reside within the positions themselves;

thus, the names of the positions are omitted to manifest the practice of the perfect interfusion of the universal Dharma-realm. Although the preceding positions were explained as being interfused, their sequential arrangement remains distinct and manifold.

The profound meaning of perfect interfusion has not yet been revealed. Therefore, this section specifically reveals that a single stage is fully endowed with all stages, wherein each stage is perfectly interfused, encompassing and integrating all others;
this constitutes the wondrous practice of Samantabhadra. Only by means of this practice can one accord with the wondrous fruit.
Since one is currently engaged in the practice, this clearly establishes the "Section on Progressing in Practice through Entrusting to the Dharma. This is...
The second section investigates the causes and effects of the six stages (*ṣaḍ-vastu*). Regarding the title of this chapter, "Leaving the World" (*lokottara*):
there are three kinds of worlds, namely, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of the perfectly awakened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha-loka*).

As for the term "leaving," the intent is that the aforementioned sequential arrangement of the six stages does not transcend these three worlds and has yet to manifest the practice characterized by transcendence.

Now, by means of the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra, one realizes that the nature of the dharma-realm is empty; therefore, one universally enters all buddha-fields without perceiving the marks of fields.
Thus, one is detached from the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). One realizes that the ultimate nature of sentient beings is empty;

therefore, one does not abandon sentient beings, yet universally performs the work of delivering them. Thus, one is detached from the marks of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*). Although...

Realizing the ocean of fruits without abandoning the gateway of causes, and likewise remaining free from the marks of the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment—this impartial and wondrous practice is the true cause for attaining the fruit. Therefore, in each of the two thousand responses, every mark is transcended;
thus, the title of this chapter is established to signify this.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest of Aranya-dharma, within the Hall of Universal Radiance.
He sat upon the lion throne of the Lotus Treasury, his wondrous awakening fully perfected and the two paths forever severed.

He had realized the dharma of signlessness, abided in the dwelling of Buddhas, attained the equality of Buddhas, reached the state of non-obstruction, and his conduct was such that it could not be turned back.
Unimpeded, they establish the inconceivable and universally perceive the three periods of time. Their bodies are eternally pervasive throughout all lands;
their wisdom is eternally clear and penetrating regarding all phenomena. They comprehend all practices and exhaust all doubts.

No one can fathom the wisdom sought by them, which is equal to that of all bodhisattvas. Having reached the Buddha’s non-dual, ultimate other shore, they are fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s impartial understanding.
He had attained liberation, realizing the Buddha’s ground of equality, which is without middle or limit, exhausting the entire dharma-realm and equaling the realm of empty space.

He was accompanied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields, all of whom were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single lifetime. Each had come from various lands in other directions.
They had all gathered together, fully endowed with the skillful means and wisdom of bodhisattvas. That is to say:
they were well able to observe all sentient beings and, through the power of skillful means, cause them to be tamed and established in the bodhisattva-dharma;
they were well able to observe all worlds and, through the power of skillful means, travel to them all; and they were well able to observe the realm of nirvāṇa and contemplate it.
Deliberating thus, they cultivate sublime conduct free from all conceptual proliferation and discrimination without interruption.

They are skillfully able to gather in and sustain all sentient beings, and they skillfully enter immeasurable methods of expedient means. Knowing that all sentient beings are empty and non-existent, yet they do not destroy the retribution of karma.
They skillfully understand the minds of sentient beings, as well as their faculties, spheres of experience, expedient means, and seeds.

Regarding the distinctions of lineages: they are able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time; they attain personal understanding and subsequently explain them to others.
Regarding the immeasurable mundane and supramundane dharmas, they dwell securely in them all and know their reality.
Regarding all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, they skillfully observe them all and know them to be non-dual. Within a single thought-moment, they are able to attain them all.

The wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is able, in every thought-moment, to manifest the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, causing all sentient beings to resolve their minds toward the Way and achieve realization.
Within the mental objects of a single sentient being, they fully know the spheres of experience of all sentient beings.
Although they have entered the ground of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, they do not abandon the practices of a bodhisattva. All...
Regarding the deeds performed, through wisdom and skillful means, they are without deliberate action. For the sake of each and every sentient being, they remain for immeasurable eons;
yet within incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, they are difficult to encounter. They turn the wheel of the true Dharma and subdue sentient beings, all of which is never in vain.
They have fully perfected the pure conduct and vows of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, thus accomplishing such immeasurability.
The merits of all Tathāgatas cannot be fully exhausted even if they were to speak for boundless eons. Their names are:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantavikurvita Bodhisattva, Samantajñāna Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantavyūha Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Samantadhvaja Bodhisattva, and Samantabodhi Bodhisattva. Such as these...
[They were as numerous as] the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields;
they had all fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. Their profound resolve and great vows were entirely perfected.

They were able to travel to every place where all Buddhas appeared in the world to request them to turn the wheel of Dharma. They were skillfully able to receive and uphold the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas, never interrupting any...

The Buddha-lineage: thoroughly knowing the sequence of all Buddhas appearing in the world, their bestowal of prophecies, their names, their lands, their attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, and their turning of the wheel of Dharma; manifesting as a Buddha in worlds where no Buddha resides;
being able to purify all defiled sentient beings; being able to extinguish all karmic obstructions of Bodhisattvas; and entering into unimpeded purity.
The Pure Dharma Realm. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered a vast samādhi called "Adorned with Buddha-Flowers.

When he entered this samādhi, all worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners, and a great sound issued forth that was heard by all. Thereafter, he arose from that samādhi.
Regarding the statement in the opening preface, "When the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment," and so forth:

this refers precisely to his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment within the original Bodhimaṇḍa, not a separate or subsequent realization. Furthermore, it is said that he ascended to the fourth heaven without departing from the Bodhi tree;
yet, since the assembly at the Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā) had never moved from its place, how could there be any principle for a further attainment? Nevertheless...

The ten bodies appear universally, and a single voice is proclaimed in unison. Thus, while the four heavens are preaching the *paryāya* (sequential) Dharma-gate, it does not hinder the primary assembly from preaching the *yuanrong* (perfectly integrated) practice-gate.

A bodhisattva has ten kinds of reliance. What are these ten? They are: reliance upon the bodhicitta, because it is never forgotten;
reliance upon spiritual friends, because they are harmonized as one; reliance upon roots of goodness, because they are cultivated and increased;
reliance upon the perfections, because they are fully practiced; and reliance upon all dharmas...
Because it is the ultimate departure; because it relies upon great vows to increase awakening; because it relies upon all practices to achieve universal accomplishment;
because it relies upon all bodhisattvas through their shared wisdom; because it relies upon making offerings to all Buddhas so that faith becomes pure;
and because it relies upon all Tathāgatas as if they were the instructions of a compassionate father.
Because their instruction is uninterrupted; these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the state of being the locus for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions.
What are the ten? They are as follows: regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are one’s own roots of goodness;
regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are seeds of enlightenment; regarding all sentient beings, one conceives the thought that they are vessels for enlightenment;

regarding all vows, one conceives the thought that they are one’s own vows; regarding all phenomena, one conceives the thought of renunciation; and regarding all practices, one conceives the thought that they are one’s own practice.
To conceive the thought of the Buddha-dharma regarding all phenomena; to conceive the thought of the path of language regarding all linguistic dharmas;
to conceive the thought of a compassionate father toward all Buddhas; and to conceive the thought of non-duality toward all Tathāgatas—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme skillful perception. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: the practice of all sentient beings, in order to bring them all to full maturity;
the practice of seeking all dharmas, in order to cultivate and study them all; and the practice of all roots of goodness, in order to cause them all to increase.
Because they are long-lasting; because all practices of samādhi maintain a single mind without distraction; because all practices of wisdom possess complete and unobstructed knowledge;
because all practices of cultivation involve nothing that cannot be cultivated; because all practices regarding Buddha-fields involve their total adornment;
because all practices regarding spiritual friends involve respectful service and offerings; and because all practices regarding Tathāgatas involve honoring and upholding them.

This is because all supernatural powers and transformations are exercised with mastery. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, great wisdom-practice of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). What are the ten? They are: the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the bodhicitta; [the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the vow of the bodhisattva path]; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the practice of the bodhisattva path; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the maturation of sentient beings; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the purification of buddha-fields; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the service of the Tathāgatas; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the hearing of the Dharma; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the retention of the Dharma; the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the realization of the Dharma; and the spiritual friend who causes one to dwell in the teaching of the Dharma. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas rely upon these ten kinds of spiritual friends, they will never abandon the bodhicitta until they reach the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Why is this? Because it is by relying on these spiritual friends that Bodhisattvas attain the unsurpassed, great wisdom of the Buddhas. Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should always rely upon and serve these ten kinds of spiritual friends. Why is this? A bodhisattva possesses ten kinds of mental states through which they attain peace and security. What are these ten? They are as follows: dwelling themselves in the bodhicitta and likewise causing others to dwell in the bodhicitta, thereby attaining peace and security of mind;
being themselves ultimately free from anger and contention and likewise causing others to be free from anger and contention, thereby attaining peace and security of mind;
and being themselves free from the dharmas of the foolish and ordinary, and likewise causing others to be free from the dharmas of the foolish and ordinary.

Their minds attain peace and security. They themselves diligently cultivate roots of goodness and also cause others to diligently cultivate roots of goodness, so their minds attain peace and security.
They themselves abide in the path of the *pāramitās* and also cause others to abide in the path of the *pāramitās*, so their minds attain peace and security.

They themselves are born into the family of the Buddhas and shall also cause others to be born into the family of the Buddhas, so their minds attain peace and security. They themselves deeply enter into non-self...
They themselves enter the true dharma of the nature of reality, which is the absence of intrinsic nature, and cause others to do so, thereby attaining peace of mind.
They themselves do not slander any of the Buddha-dharmas, and they cause others not to slander any of the Buddha-dharmas, thereby attaining peace of mind.
They fulfill their own vow for the enlightenment of omniscience and cause others to fulfill their vows for the enlightenment of omniscience, and their minds attain peace and security.

They themselves enter deeply into the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas and cause others to enter the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, and their minds attain peace and security. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, [they shall attain the supreme enlightenment].

What are these ten? They are: bringing sentient beings to maturity through giving; bringing sentient beings to maturity through the form-body (*rūpakāya*);
bringing sentient beings to maturity through preaching the Dharma; bringing sentient beings to maturity through practicing together with them; [bringing sentient beings to maturity] through non-...
They accomplish sentient beings by means of passionate attachment; they accomplish sentient beings by revealing and teaching the bodhisattva practices;
they accomplish sentient beings by manifesting with blazing intensity throughout all worlds; they accomplish sentient beings by manifesting the great majestic power of the Buddha-dharma;
they accomplish sentient beings by manifesting various supernatural transformations; and they [accomplish sentient beings] by means of various subtle, secret, and skillful methods.
Thus they bring sentient beings to maturity; these are the ten. By means of these, the Bodhisattva brings the realm of sentient beings to maturity.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of precepts. What are the ten? They are: the precept of not abandoning the bodhicitta.
The precept of remaining far removed from the stages of the two vehicles; the precept of observing and benefiting all sentient beings;
the precept of causing all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma; the precept of cultivating all that is studied by bodhisattvas; and the precept of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena.
The precept of dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment; the precept of non-attachment to the bodies of all Tathāgatas;
the precept of contemplating all phenomena as free from grasping and attachment; and the precept of restraint over the sense faculties—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and vast perfection of the precepts of a Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...

Bodhisattvas have ten ways of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). By means of these, a bodhisattva knows for themselves that they have received the prediction. What are these ten? They are as follows:

knowing for themselves that they have received the prediction by generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) with a sublime intention; knowing for themselves that they have received the prediction by never becoming weary of or turning away from the various practices of a bodhisattva;
knowing for themselves that they have received the prediction by dwelling through all eons practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva; cultivating one...

One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction [of enlightenment] regarding all Buddha-dharmas. One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction through single-minded, profound faith in all the teachings of the Buddhas.

One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction by cultivating all roots of goodness so that they are fully accomplished. One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction by establishing all sentient beings in the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction through being in harmonious union with all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without duality.
Regarding all spiritual friends, one conceives of them as Tathāgatas and knows for oneself that one has received the prediction of enlightenment;
one constantly and diligently guards the original vow for bodhi and knows for oneself that one has received the prediction of enlightenment—these are the ten.

O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of entries by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter into the various Bodhisattvas. What are these ten? They are: entry into the original vow, entry into practice, entry into the accumulations, entry into the various pāramitās...

The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Entering into accomplishment; entering into the differentiation of vows; entering into various understandings; entering into the adornment of Buddha-lands;

entering into mastery of spiritual powers; and entering into the manifestation of taking birth—these are the ten. By means of these, Bodhisattvas universally enter into all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of entries by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into all Tathāgatas. What are they?
There are ten, namely: entering infinite perfect enlightenment; entering infinite turning of the wheel of Dharma;
entering infinite skillful means; entering infinite differentiated sounds; entering infinite taming of sentient beings; entering infinite sovereign mastery of spiritual powers;
entering infinite various and differentiated bodies; entering infinite samādhis; and entering infinite powers.
Fearlessness; entering the manifestation of nirvana that is boundless—these are the ten. By means of these, a bodhisattva universally enters all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the conduct of sentient beings.
What are the ten? They are: entering the past conduct of all sentient beings; entering the future [conduct] of all sentient beings...
They enter into the present conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the wholesome conduct of all sentient beings;
they enter into the unwholesome conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the mental conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the conduct of the faculties of all sentient beings;

they enter into the conduct of the inclinations of all sentient beings; they enter into the conduct of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings; they enter into all sentient beings...
To teach and discipline beings according to the appropriate and inappropriate times—this is the tenth. By means of these, a bodhisattva universally enters into the conduct of all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters worlds. What are these ten?
These are: entering defiled worlds; entering pure worlds; entering small worlds; entering large worlds; entering worlds within atoms;
entering subtle worlds; entering inverted worlds; entering upright worlds; entering worlds where a Buddha resides;
and entering worlds where no Buddha resides. These are the ten. By means of these, the Bodhisattva universally enters all [worlds] throughout the ten directions.
"World-Honored One, Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of entry into eons for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: entering past eons; entering future eons; entering present eons; entering countable eons;
entering uncountable eons; entering countable eons as uncountable eons; entering uncountable eons as countable eons; entering [uncountable eons as uncountable eons];..."
All kalpas are non-kalpas; entering non-kalpas is entering all kalpas; entering all kalpas is entering a single thought-moment. These are the ten.
By means of these, Bodhisattvas universally enter all kalpas. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of speaking of the three periods of time.
What are the ten? They are: speaking of the past as the past; [speaking of] the past...
The future world speaks of the future world; the past world speaks of the present world; the future world speaks of the past world;
the future world speaks of the present world; the future world speaks of the inexhaustible. The present world speaks of the past world;
the present world speaks of the future world; the present world speaks of equality; the present world speaks of the three periods of time as being one.
[He] reflects. These are the ten. By means of these, the Bodhisattva universally expounds the three periods of time.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of knowledge of the three periods of time possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: knowing all established arrangements;
knowing all languages; knowing all discourses; knowing all conventions; knowing all designations; knowing all regulations; knowing their provisional names; knowing...
They know it to be inexhaustible; they know it to be quiescent; they know all things to be empty—this constitutes the ten.
By means of these, the Bodhisattva universally knows all phenomena throughout the three periods of time. Sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to ten kinds of tireless minds.
What are these ten? They are: a mind free from weariness in making offerings to all Buddhas; a mind free from weariness in attending upon all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
a mind free from weariness in seeking all dharmas; a mind free from weariness in hearing the true Dharma;
a mind free from weariness in proclaiming the true Dharma; and a mind [free from weariness] in teaching and disciplining all sentient beings...
A mind free from weariness; a mind free from weariness in establishing all sentient beings in the bodhi of the Buddha;
a mind free from weariness in practicing the bodhisattva conduct for unspeakably unspeakable eons in each and every world;
a mind free from weariness in wandering through all worlds; and a mind free from weariness in observing and contemplating all Buddha-dharmas. This is...
There are ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, tireless great wisdom.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of differentiated wisdom for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the wisdom that knows the differentiation of sentient beings;
the wisdom that knows the differentiation of faculties; the wisdom that knows the differentiation of karmic retribution; the wisdom that knows [the differentiation of] reception...
They produce the wisdom that discerns births; the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of worlds; the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of the dharma-realm;
the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of all Buddhas; the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of all phenomena; the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of the three periods of time;

and the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of all paths of linguistic expression. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the unsurpassed [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
The Vast and Differentiated Wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dhāraṇīs possessed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, because it retains all dharmas without forgetting them;
the dhāraṇī of practice, because it skillfully contemplates all dharmas according to reality; the dhāraṇī of reflection, which thoroughly understands all... [dharmas].
Because of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because the *dhāraṇī* of the light of phenomena illuminates the inconceivable teachings of all Buddhas;
because the *dhāraṇī* of samādhi hears the true Dharma at the presence of all present Buddhas with an undistracted mind;
because the *dhāraṇī* of the perfect voice understands inconceivable sounds and languages; and because of the *dhāraṇī* of the three times for expounding [the Dharma].
Because they are the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they expound the boundless dharmas of the Buddhas through various eloquences and *dhāraṇīs*;
because they give rise to the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded hearing, whereby one can hear all the teachings spoken by unspeakably many Buddhas;
and because they are the *dhāraṇī* of all Buddha-dharmas, abiding securely in the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata.

These are the ten. If bodhisattvas wish to attain these dharmas, they should diligently practice and study them. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of Buddhas spoken of by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

What are the ten? They are: the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha of Vows, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution, the Buddha of Sustenance, the Buddha of Nirvāṇa, the Buddha of the Dharma Realm, the Buddha of Mind, the Buddha of Samādhi, the Buddha of Original Nature, and the Buddha of Accordance with Desire.
The Buddha. These constitute the ten [categories].
The first two hundred phrases of the main text answer the ten gates of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). The text is divided into three sections:

first, from "the ten kinds of reliance" (*daśavidha-niśraya*) downward, nine gates clarify the fulfillment of one's own practice (*svacaryā-paripūri*); next, from "entering among the bodhisattvas" downward, eight gates clarify... [the fulfillment of the practice of others].

The section on "Excellence in Practice" is complete. The three gates following the "Discriminative Wisdom" clarify the culmination of the two practices. However, at the end of the twentieth gate, it concludes by stating:
"The teaching of the ten kinds of Buddhas clearly reveals that upon the fulfillment of the mind of the ten stages of faith, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment.
That is to say, knowing that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom, not [by means of...]"
He attained awakening. Taking that wisdom of fruition as his initial resolve, he fulfilled the practices of the initial resolve so that the Buddha-fruit was immediately perfected.

This precisely reveals that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause; all distinctions of stages are entirely obliterated, manifesting only the practice of perfect interfusion and non-obstruction.
From this point forward, each stage penetrates the preceding and succeeding ones, fully revealing the universal Dharma’s boundless practices, wondrously transcendent.
Regarding thought and reflection: one must deeply illuminate the mind through contemplation to attain its essential principle.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to ten kinds of Samantabhadra-minds. What are these ten? They are:

giving rise to the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings; giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*karuṇā*), to undergo [suffering] on behalf of all sentient beings...
Because of suffering, one gives rise to the mind of universal giving, relinquishing all that one possesses.

One gives rise to the mind that takes the recollection of omniscience as its primary focus, joyfully seeking all Buddha-dharmas. One gives rise to the mind adorned with merit, training in all bodhisattva practices.
They resolve upon a mind like a vajra, because they do not forget or lose [their resolve] in any place of rebirth;
they resolve upon a mind like the ocean, because all pure and white dharmas flow into it; they resolve upon a mind like the king of great mountains, because they endure all evil words;
they resolve upon a mind of peace and security, because they bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; they resolve upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Because they ultimately skillfully contemplate that all phenomena are non-existent, this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these states of mind, they will swiftly achieve the skillful wisdom of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of Samantabhadra practices. What are the ten? They are: the vow to abide through all future eons...
The Dharma-practice of Worthy Conduct: May I offer worship and respect to all future Buddhas;
may I establish all sentient beings in the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
may I accumulate all roots of goodness; may I enter into all perfections; may I fulfill [the path].
The method for practicing all bodhisattva practices and the practices of Samantabhadra; the method for adorning all worlds through the practices of Samantabhadra;
the method for being born in all buddha-fields through the practices of Samantabhadra; and the method for skillfully observing all phenomena through the practices of Samantabhadra.
"I vow to attain unexcelled bodhi in all buddha-fields through the practice of Samantabhadra. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas diligently cultivate these dharmas, they will swiftly fulfill the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate sentient beings and give rise to great compassion. What are the ten? Namely, they observe:
One arouses great compassion because sentient beings are without refuge or protector; one arouses great compassion by observing that the nature of sentient beings is unruly;
one arouses great compassion by observing that sentient beings are destitute and lack roots of goodness; one arouses great compassion by observing that sentient beings sleep through the long night;
one arouses great compassion by observing that sentient beings practice unwholesome dharmas; one observes...

One gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings are bound by the fetters of desire; one gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of birth and death;
one gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings are long afflicted by the suffering of illness;

one gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings lack the desire for wholesome dharmas; and one gives rise to great compassion by observing that sentient beings have lost all Buddha-dharmas. This is [the meaning].
10. Bodhisattvas constantly observe sentient beings with this mind. O Son of the Buddha! There are ten causes and conditions for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to resolve upon bodhicitta.
What are these ten? They are: resolving upon bodhicitta for the sake of teaching, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings;
resolving upon bodhicitta for the sake of eliminating the mass of suffering of all sentient beings.
With the mind, one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of endowing all sentient beings with complete peace and happiness;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of severing the ignorance of all sentient beings; one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing the Buddha-wisdom upon all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of reverently making offerings to all Buddhas; and one generates the bodhicitta in order to follow the Tathāgata.

One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of pleasing the Buddhas through their teachings and commands. One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of beholding the physical bodies, marks, and signs of all Buddhas.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of entering the vast wisdom of all Buddhas.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of manifesting the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva...
One should generate the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhicitta*) for the sake of awakening into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
When approaching and making offerings to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should give rise to ten kinds of minds. What are these ten? They are: the mind of service, and the mind of joy.

The mind free from contrariness; the compliant mind; the mind free from seeking anything else; the one-pointed mind; the mind sharing the same roots of goodness; the mind sharing the same vows; the Tathāgata-mind;
and the mind sharing the same fulfillment of practices. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to such minds, they will attain ten kinds of purity.
What are these ten? They are: the purity of the profound mind; reaching... [the purity of the ultimate destination].
The physical body is pure because it is ultimately indestructible; the voice is pure because it manifests in accordance with what is appropriate for beings and thoroughly masters all languages;
eloquence is pure because it skillfully expounds the infinite teachings of the Buddhas;
wisdom is pure because it abandons all darkness of ignorance; and the manner of birth is pure because it is fully endowed with...

Because they have perfected the sovereign power of a bodhisattva; because they have purified their retinue by bringing to fruition the roots of goodness of sentient beings who practiced together with them in the past;
because they have purified their karmic retribution by eliminating all obstacles of karma;

because they have purified their great vows by being non-dual in nature with all other bodhisattvas; and because they have purified their practices by attaining liberation through the vehicle of Samantabhadra. This is...
It is tenfold, O Son of the Buddha. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pāramitās. What are these ten? They are:
the pāramitā of giving, because of relinquishing all that one possesses; the pāramitā of ethical discipline, because of purifying the precepts of a Buddha;
the pāramitā of patience, because of abiding in the patience of a Buddha; and the pāramitā of vigor, because of not retreating from anything undertaken.
Because it transforms; because the dhyāna-pāramitā consists of mindfulness on a single object; because the prajñā-pāramitā consists of observing all phenomena as they truly are;
because the jñāna-pāramitā consists of entering the powers of a Buddha; because the praṇidhāna-pāramitā consists of fulfilling all the great vows of Samantabhadra;
because the abhijñā-pāramitā consists of manifesting all sovereign functions; [and] the dharma-pāramitā...

Because they universally enter into all the teachings of the Buddhas—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of wisdom that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize. What are the ten? They are: the wisdom of the infinite distinctions of all worlds;...
He realizes accordingly: he realizes accordingly with inconceivable wisdom the realm of all sentient beings;
