For this reason, one gives rise to a great vow for their sake, desiring that they all attain mastery over mind and intention, that their actions be unimpeded, and that they abandon evil thoughts and the various afflictions arising toward others. This is the eighth mountain-like superior mind of a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflects: "It is not another who causes me to resolve upon bodhicitta, nor do I wait for others to assist me in my practice.

I myself have resolved to gather all Buddha-dharmas; I vow to exert myself and, throughout all future kalpas, practice the bodhisattva path to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, I now cultivate bodhi..."

In the practice of the bodhisattva, one should purify one's own mind and also purify the minds of others; one should know one's own sphere of experience and also know the spheres of experience of others.
"I shall become entirely equal to the spheres of experience of all Buddhas of the three times"—this is the ninth mountain-like superior resolve.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way, there is not a single dharma through which they practice the bodhisattva path. There is...
There is not a single dharma that fulfills the bodhisattva practice; there is not a single dharma that teaches and tames all sentient beings;
there is not a single dharma that makes offerings to and reveres all Buddhas;

there is not a single dharma that has been, is being, or will be realized in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and there is not a single dharma that has been, is being, or will be taught.
Both the speaker and the Dharma are unattainable; yet one does not abandon the vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva seeks all dharmas and finds them all unattainable;
it is in this way that they give rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, although there is nothing to be attained regarding dharmas, they diligently practice and cultivate them.
Their superior wholesome karma is pure, their remedial wisdom is perfected, and they increase in every thought-moment until all things are fully endowed.
Their minds are neither startled nor terrified by this, nor do they form such a thought as: "If all phenomena are entirely quiescent."
"What meaning do I have for seeking the path of unsurpassed bodhi? This is the tenth mountain-like superior mind.

O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of mountain-like superior minds of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If Bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
They increase their superior resolve toward the Great Mountain King of Supreme Wisdom. O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of ocean-like wisdom through which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What are these ten? They are as follows:
entering into all infinite realms of sentient beings—this is the first ocean-like wisdom. Entering into all worlds without giving rise to [conceptualization]...

This is the second ocean-like wisdom: discerning that all realms of empty space are immeasurable and unimpeded, universally entering the net of all differentiated worlds throughout the ten directions. This is the third ocean-like wisdom:
the bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully enters the dharma-realm—namely, the unimpeded entry, the uninterrupted entry, the non-eternal entry, and the immeasurable entry.
Because they thoroughly understand all entrances of non-arising, non-ceasing, and all-pervading entrance, this is the fourth ocean-like wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Regarding the roots of goodness accumulated— already accumulated, currently accumulating, and yet to be accumulated— by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Dharma-preachers, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all ordinary beings of the past, future, and present throughout the three times...
Regarding all roots of goodness—those already accomplished, those being accomplished now, and those yet to be accomplished by the Buddha in his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

and regarding all roots of goodness from the teachings already given, currently being given, and yet to be given by the Buddhas of the three periods of time as they subdue all sentient beings—he understands them all completely.
With deep faith, he rejoices in them, and vows to practice them with delight.
There is contentment; this is the fifth ocean-like wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. In every thought-moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters unspeakable eons of the past.

Within a single eon, there may be ten billion Buddhas appearing in the world, or a thousand billion Buddhas appearing in the world, or a hundred thousand billion Buddhas appearing in the world, or an incalculable number, or an immeasurable number, or an infinite number, or...
Incomparable; or incalculable; or immeasurable; or inconceivable; or unfathomable; or inexpressible;

or inexpressibly inexpressible—buddhas, world-honored ones, beyond all calculation, appear in the world, together with their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment consisting of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, preaching the Dharma and subduing all beings.
He clearly perceives all such things as birth, the lengthening or shortening of lifespans, and the duration for which the Dharma remains.

As it is with one eon, so it is with all eons. He fully understands that even in eons devoid of Buddhas, there are sentient beings who plant roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who are virtuous...
Once their faculties have matured, they shall behold the Buddhas in future ages and will fully comprehend them all.
Thus observing unspeakably unspeakable eons of the past, their minds never grow weary or satisfied; this is the sixth ocean-like wisdom.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the future world and observes and discerns all kalpas, which are immeasurable and boundless.
He knows which kalpa has a Buddha and which kalpa has no Buddha; in which kalpas how many Tathāgatas appear in the world;
what the name of each individual Tathāgata is; in which world they dwell; what the name of that world is; how many sentient beings they deliver; and the length of their lifespan.
For how long? Thus observing until the end of the future, they fully comprehend it all; being inexhaustible, they never grow weary.

This is the seventh ocean-like wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Entering the present world, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes and contemplates, and in every moment of thought, they universally behold the unspeakably many worlds of infinite categories throughout the ten directions.
There are Buddhas who have already attained, are now attaining, or will attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
They proceed to the site of enlightenment and sit upon auspicious grass beneath the Bodhi tree, where they subdue the armies of Māra and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having arisen from this state, he enters cities and towns, ascends celestial palaces, and preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
He turns the great wheel of Dharma, manifests supernatural powers to subdue sentient beings, and even entrusts them with the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having relinquished his life-span, he enters parinirvāṇa; having entered nirvāṇa, the treasury of the Dharma is compiled so that it may endure for a long time.

They dwell in the world, adorning Buddha-stūpas with various offerings. They also see all sentient beings in those worlds encountering the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, receiving and upholding it, reciting it, and through mindfulness, reflection, and contemplation, increasing their wisdom and understanding.
Observing in this manner throughout the ten directions, they have no error regarding the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has realized...
Knowing that all Buddhas are entirely like dreams, yet being able to go to the abodes of all Buddhas to pay them respect and make offerings—
at that time, the bodhisattva does not cling to their own body, does not cling to the Buddhas, does not cling to the worlds,

does not cling to the assemblies, does not cling to the teaching of the Dharma, and does not cling to the number of eons; nevertheless, they see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, observe the worlds, and enter into the succession of eons.
There is no satiety. This is the eighth ocean-like wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, in each and every eon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes offerings to and reveres unspeakably unspeakable, immeasurable Buddhas.
He manifests his own death here and rebirth there, using all manner of offering requisites that transcend those of the triple world.
To make offerings, and furthermore to make offerings to the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the entire great assembly;
after each and every Tathāgata has entered Parinirvāṇa, they shall all make offerings to the relics with unsurpassed ritual implements and extensively practice giving to satisfy sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with an inconceivable mind and a mind that seeks no recompense, thoroughly...
With a resolute mind and a mind intent on benefiting others, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons,
they make offerings to all Buddhas, benefit sentient beings, protect and uphold the true Dharma, and reveal and expound it.
This is the ninth ocean-like wisdom. Therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the presence of all Buddhas,
all bodhisattvas, and all Dharma teachers, single-mindedly and exclusively seeks the teachings spoken by bodhisattvas, the teachings studied by bodhisattvas, the teachings taught by bodhisattvas,
the teachings practiced by bodhisattvas, the teachings purified by bodhisattvas, and the teachings for the maturation of bodhisattvas.
The Dharma; the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s discipline; the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s equanimity; the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s renunciation; and the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī.
Having attained these Dharmas, they uphold, recite, analyze, and explain them without ever becoming weary.
They cause immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to a mind corresponding to omniscience within the Buddha-Dharma, to enter into the true nature of reality, and toward *anuttara*...
They attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus, for unspeakably unspeakable eons, these bodhisattvas never experience weariness or satiety. This is the tenth ocean-like wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of ocean-like wisdom through which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If any...
When a bodhisattva dwells securely in this Dharma, they attain the ocean of the unsurpassed, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
In the third major section, "The Support of the Ten Powers," there are thirty gates that answer the thirty questions posed in the preceding ten verses.
These successively reveal the practices within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The first stage has three gates; the second and third stages likewise have three gates each.
Each has one gate. The fourth line has two gates. The fifth line has six gates.
The four positions—the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth lines—each have two gates. The tenth line has nine gates. As for the reason for the varying number of gates:
because *dāna* (generosity) is at the beginning, it possesses all three; whereas *śīla* (precepts) and *kṣānti* (patience) pertain to the mundane world, they possess only one.

Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are preeminent, they have many gateways. Since these are already numerous within the category of knowledge (*jñāna*), they are treated briefly here in the context of *prajñā*.

As for the remaining [perfections], because they are progressively superior, only two gateways are employed. Nevertheless, these ten practices fully cultivate the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*); thus they are called the "gateways of the ten pāramitās.
They serve to adorn the fruit of Buddhahood by bringing both merit and wisdom to fulfillment. Apart from these ten practices, there is no other distinct dharma. However—

That which is cultivated according to the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles is merely called the "six perfections" (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and is not yet termed *pāramitā*, because it does not yet accord with reality.

Now, regarding these ten practices and ten perfections, the fact that "power" (*bala*) is placed at the beginning is due to the fact that in the preceding ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), one has realized the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Now, as one initiates practice in accordance with the Dharma-realm, each and every one is termed a "Buddha-practice," for the entire Dharma-realm is fully present therein.
The essence [of this stage] consists in the power that sustains these practices, much like the great wind-circle which possesses the power to sustain the world-system.

Now, by means of the power of wisdom and vows arising from the dharma-realm, one establishes all practices; therefore, the sustaining power is explained first. Thus, the commentary (*śāstra*) explains:

"Sustaining power" is also synonymous with the meaning of "establishing," because one establishes these practices through the power that exhausts the entire dharma-realm. Although this follows the sequence of the ten perfections...
There is no difference, for all are subsumed within this single gate of sustaining power. Next is the single gate of the ten kinds of great consolation.
By means of the previous single gate of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), all other perfections are harmoniously integrated.

Because one perceives that every aspect of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is mutually penetrating, whatever is given accords with the dharma-realm; thus it becomes signless, true practice. This practice...
Since it is already real, one may joyfully anticipate the attainment of the wondrous fruit with absolute certainty.

However, while the third gate involves ten kinds of profound entry, once one has entered the *dharmadhātu*, what need is there to wait for future attainment? It is immediate realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Therefore, this particular gate focuses exclusively on the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), whereby one enters the three worlds and comes to know the essence of the causes and effects of various lands.

Regarding the distinctions among the natures and the fivefold natures of sentient beings: although the *dharmadhātu* is equal, it does not preclude the teaching of various dharmas according to the capacities of beings in accordance with their natures.
One who acts thus is truly called a teacher of the Dharma. Therefore, this single perfection (*pāramitā*) completely subsumes all perfections.
Thus, it concludes by stating that one attains entry into the profound *dharmatā* of bodhi. These three gates have fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dāna*).

Because of deliverance, one accomplishes the practice of joy (*muditā*). Through the twenty kinds of reliance on a single gate, the practice of benefiting others (*hita*) is clarified, thereby accomplishing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Through the thirty kinds of fearless mind in a single gate, the practice of non-opposition (*avirodha*) is clarified, thereby accomplishing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Because one attains great conformity by relying on the *dharmadhātu*, one is able to practice the ten kinds of difficult practices and endure what is difficult to endure;

since the objective realm is like space, what could there be to oppose? The forty kinds of mind free from doubt—the two gates below—clarify the practice of being unbending and the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). By deeply realizing the *dharmadhātu*, the objective realm is like [space].
Because it is empty, all difficult practices and difficult endurances are not in conflict with it;
thus, one gains confidence in one’s own mind as being like a vajra—certainly able to destroy all things and certainly incapable of being destroyed by anything.

Therefore, whether emerging from the ultimate or entering into the conventional, within all activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, one proceeds directly and without obstruction, with certainty.
There is no doubt. Because there is no doubt, all that one undertakes cannot be obstructed by the ultimate (*paramārtha*) nor hindered by the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction; they do not require further integration, for they are equal in their very essence.
Being thus, who could ever bend or weary them? Such diligence and valor arise from this lack of bending or weariness; therefore, the provisional and the real are practiced in tandem.
The two truths are harmoniously integrated; all practices are inconceivable. Thus, it is called the inconceivable gathering of wholesome conduct.
Through the five existences, the six gates, the ten kinds of secret language, and so forth, one clarifies the practice free from delusion and confusion, thereby perfecting the perfection of dhyāna.

Because of the aforementioned practice of being unyielding, one emerges from the ultimate truth and enters into conventional reality, skillfully benefiting sentient beings without obstruction. Therefore...
These first two gates clarify the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*), demonstrating how a single word can manifest all phenomena.

Skillful wisdom (*jñāna-kauśalya*) consists in correctly discerning the appropriate capacities of beings. The next two gates concern the essence of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon which this relies;

through ten kinds of samādhis, one universally enters all places for benefiting sentient beings simultaneously and pervasively, without sequence, just as the tides of the great ocean respond without fail.
At that time, because both essence and function are manifested together, the latter two gates clarify liberation, supernatural powers, and mastery in benefiting sentient beings.
Because of skillful wisdom, non-delusion is precisely the wisdom of concentration; because of universal penetration, non-distraction is precisely the concentration of compassion.
Since this accords with the true *dharmadhātu* and is naturally so, the sixth [perfection] has two gates clarifying the excellent manifestation of conduct.
This constitutes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). It precisely reveals the essential nature of the practice for benefiting sentient beings.

Because one previously entered the realm of all sentient beings universally through the power of samādhi—and the reason for entering was for the sake of benefiting them—this section now precisely clarifies how, within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) thus entered, one teaches and transforms sentient beings by manifesting various types of conduct. However, these sublime practices must necessarily rely upon the fundamental Great [Vehicle].
Taking wisdom as its essence, it employs ten kinds of skillful knowledge to simultaneously illumine both phenomena and principle, and to practice both provisional and ultimate truths in tandem.

Although it contemplates arising and non-arising, it does not abandon the salvation of sentient beings; although it contemplates conditions and the transcendence of conditions, it is not hindered from benefiting others by following along with conditions.

Furthermore, it fully knows the mental activities of sentient beings and tames them according to their faculties, such that every action and every transformation accords perfectly with [the needs of those being taught].
The nature of the *dharmadhātu* is to teach and transform beings with equanimity; thus, one attains the gate of great unimpeded liberation.

This is the practice of "skillful manifestation" (*sukṣaṇa*). This liberation differs from the aforementioned: while the former merely involves the two states of quiescence and illumination without being bound by phenomena, this is called "great liberation" within the midst of active practice.
The seventh stage has two gates, which are termed the "practice within the state of non-attachment. Thus it is established.
The "Skillful Means" (upāya) refers to the gardens and groves, which are places for wandering and delight; the "ten palaces" refer to places of peace and comfort.

Through the superior practice of benefiting sentient beings, one wanders through the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) as if strolling in gardens and groves, taking the realm of sentient beings as one's place of peace and comfort.
The reason it is so is that its essence consists of having attained fundamental great wisdom (*mūla-mahājñāna*), while [employing] skillful means.

Wisdom serves as the function; thus, one dwells and moves with mastery. By accomplishing the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one is called "unattached" because of possessing wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
In the eighth stage, there are two gates that clarify practice within the difficult-to-attain position, whereby one accomplishes the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Because one traverses the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) above and extensively transforms sentient beings while delighting in those to be transformed, there is a profound internal aspiration and joy for their benefit.
He brings the merit of his transformative activities back to himself; every single practice becomes his own virtue.

Thus, he takes the virtue of benefiting sentient beings as his own adornment, vowing to be adorned by virtue so that both his inner realization and outer manifestation become increasingly sublime—this is truly rare.

Chapter Nine has two sections clarifying the conduct within the stage of wholesome dharmas (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) in order to perfect the power of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); this is because his previous aspiration and joy have become even deeper.
The practice becomes increasingly vast and great. Because the sphere of contact is entirely true, external objects do not move;

because compassion and wisdom increase further, the inner mind does not abandon [its resolve]. Thus, the practice becomes ever more profound and great, its power expansive. This constitutes the wholesome dharmas.

Nineteen gates clarify the practice within the stage of reality (*tattvabhūmi*), thereby perfecting the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This stage of practice subsumes the nine preceding practices.

All are unified within the single mind of the Dharma-realm; thus, there are ten kinds of wisdom. First is the wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which refers to skillfully observing all Buddha-dharmas.
Second is the wisdom of preaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanājñāna*), which, through skillful observation, enables one to preach the Dharma well.

Third is the wisdom of *li-zhi* (transcendence/purity), which, by preaching in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), is pure and free from obstructions. Fourth is the wisdom of definitive discernment (*niścayajñāna*), which, through skillfulness...
The Seal of Skillful Wisdom definitively certifies all phenomena; therefore, the mind is certain to achieve Buddhahood without doubt.

This constitutes the Seal of the Ten Wisdoms: Fifth is the Wisdom of Thorough Illumination. Because it definitively certifies all phenomena through careful discernment, the light of wisdom shines through, comprehending all phenomena without exception.
Sixth is Peerless Wisdom. Because of the aforementioned thorough illumination, one does not become biased or attached; one dwells simultaneously in both principle and phenomena without [obstruction].
7. Knowledge of being without inferiority: Since one knows there is no one equal to oneself, one strives for further advancement;
because there is no timid or weak mind regarding all superior matters, one is without inferiority. 8. Knowledge of eminent transcendence:

Because of the absence of inferiority, the myriad practices transcend far beyond, proceeding directly toward Bodhi and remaining unshakable. 9. Knowledge of profundity and vastness: That is to say, not...

One merely seeks advancement. Furthermore, the essence of practice is profound and vast, encompassing and integrating all; it is like the ocean receiving the hundred rivers, fusing them into a single flavor.
Therefore, this single gate of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) integrates the preceding nine practices and nine perfections, each being gathered back into the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Through this superior progress, one enters the mind of dedication (pariṇāmanā-citta).
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volumes 54 and 55.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple.
Extracted and clarified by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Kuāngshān.
The first thirty questions have been answered above, concluding with the Ten Practices; the twenty-nine sections below answer the remaining twenty-nine [questions].
Section on the Inquiry into the Ten Stages of Dedication,
Part Three of Chapter Thirty-Eight, "Transcending the World.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of [qualities] for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It is like the abiding as a jewel. What are the ten? Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to travel to the abodes of all Tathāgatas in countless worlds, where he gazes upon them, pays homage, serves, and makes offerings.
This is the first abiding as a jewel. In the presence of inconceivable Tathāgatas, he hears the True Dharma, receiving, upholding, and recollecting it so as never to forget.
Through the loss [of such views], analytical reflection and awakening wisdom increase. Such actions fill the ten directions;
this is the second jewel-like dwelling. Passing away from this world-system, one manifests birth in other places, yet remains without confusion regarding the Buddha-dharma.

This is the third jewel-like abiding: knowing that all phenomena arise from a single phenomenon, yet being able to analyze and expound upon each of them individually, because the various meanings of all phenomena ultimately converge into a single meaning.
This is the fourth jewel-like abiding: knowing weariness with and detachment from afflictions, knowing the cessation of afflictions, and knowing the protection against afflictions.
They eliminate and sever the afflictions; they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet ultimately reach the further shore of that very limit.
Being skillful in means, they are well-trained in what is to be learned, causing their former vows and practices to all be fulfilled completely, without their bodies ever becoming weary.
This is the fifth jewel-like dwelling. They know that all conceptualizations of sentient beings have no locus.

Furthermore, it is taught that there are various locations and directions; although there is no conceptual differentiation and no distinct volitional activity, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, there is cultivation and there is purposeful action. This is the sixth jewel-like abiding.

They know that all dharmas are of a single nature—that is to say, they are without nature, without various natures, without immeasurable natures, without calculable natures, and without measurable natures.
They are without color and without marks; whether as one or as many, they are all unapprehendable.
Yet they definitively and fully understand that "this is the Dharma of the Buddhas," "this is the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas," and "this is the [Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas]."
He discerns phenomena: "This is the dharma of the śrāvakas; this is the dharma of ordinary persons; this is wholesome dharma;
this is unwholesome dharma; this is mundane dharma; this is supramundane dharma; this is faulty dharma; this is faultless dharma;
this is contaminated dharma; this is uncontaminated dharma; and so on, up to: this is conditioned dharma."
This is the unconditioned dharma. This is the seventh jewel-like abiding. A bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the Buddha and does not find him;
seeks the bodhisattva and does not find him; seeks the dharma and does not find it; seeks sentient beings and does not find them.
Yet, they do not abandon the taming of sentient beings, causing them to form the vow for perfect awakening in all dharmas. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva skillfully observes and knows the conceptual discriminations of all sentient beings and knows the spheres of experience of all sentient beings.

Through skillful means, he transforms and guides them so that they may attain nirvāṇa. Because he desires to fulfill his vow to transform sentient beings, he ardently practices the bodhisattva conduct.
This is the eighth jewel-like abiding. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows skillfulness.
The teaching of the Dharma, the manifestation of nirvāṇa, and all skillful means employed for the sake of liberating sentient beings—all these are established by the mind’s conceptualization.

They are neither inverted nor false. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time, unshakable like suchness, and non-abiding within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); they do not perceive even a single sentient being as existing.
Those who have been transformed, those who are being transformed now, and those who will be transformed in the future—these too he personally understands as having nothing to cultivate.
He realizes that not even the slightest dharma can be found that either arises or ceases; yet, by relying upon all dharmas, he ensures that his vows do not go in vain.
This is the ninth jewel-like dwelling of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva regarding the inconceivable and immeasurable Buddhas. One...
The dharma of receiving predictions as heard from a single Buddha is unspeakably unspeakable; their names and titles are each different, and the number of eons varies.
From a single eon up to unspeakably unspeakable eons, one should hear it in this manner.

Having heard it, one practices without being startled, without fear, without confusion, and without delusion, because one knows that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable. Thus, the Tathāgata...
Because the words of the prophecy are non-dual; because of the supreme power of one’s own conduct and vows;

because they cause those to be transformed according to their needs to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and because they fulfill all vows equal to the entire dharma-realm—this is the tenth jewel-like dwelling.
O Son of the Buddha, this is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [abides] in *anuttara-samyak-*.
The three types of enlightenment abide like ten kinds of jewels. If bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they will obtain the jewel of the unsurpassed, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of Mahāyāna vows that are like vajras.
What are these ten? O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought: first—
All phenomena are without limit and cannot be exhausted; I shall, by means of the wisdom that exhausts the three periods of time, universally awaken to them all without exception.
This is the first adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Within the space of a single hair-tip, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. How..."
How much more so for the entire dharma-realm; I shall bring all beings to extinction through the unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
This is the second adamantine bodhicitta of the Mahāyāna vow. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects:
"The worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable, boundless, without limit, and inexhaustible; I shall [purify] them with the buddha-fields."
The earth is the supreme adornment; it adorns all such worlds, and all these adornments are entirely real.
This is the third adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:
"All sentient beings are immeasurable, boundless, without limit, and inexhaustible. I shall..."
One dedicates all roots of goodness toward that [state], and the illumination of the light of unsurpassed wisdom shines upon it.
This is the fourth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects:
"All Buddhas are immeasurable, boundless, without limit, and inexhaustible; I shall, with the roots of goodness I have planted..."
With all their faculties, they dedicate these offerings so that they may be entirely pervasive and without any deficiency;
only then shall I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This is the fifth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see all Buddhas and hear the Dharma they preach, they give rise to great joy, yet they do not cling to it.

One’s own body does not cling to the Buddha-body. One understands that the Tathāgata’s body is neither real nor false, neither existent nor non-existent, neither having a nature nor lacking a nature, neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor markless, neither arising nor ceasing;
it truly has nothing whatsoever, yet it does not destroy existence. Why is this? Because one cannot grasp or cling to it by means of any natures or marks. This is...
This is the sixth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. O Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is reviled, insulted, beaten, or tortured by sentient beings;

or if their hands and feet are severed, their ears and noses cut off, their eyes gouged out, or their heads decapitated—they are able to endure all such things and never give rise to anger because of them.
A mind of harm. For unspeakably, unspeakably many incalculable eons, one practices the bodhisattva path to gather in and sustain sentient beings, never ceasing or abandoning them.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already skillfully observed that all phenomena are devoid of dual characteristics;
with a mind unmoved or distracted, they are able to relinquish their own bodies and endure their suffering. This is the [first].
Seventh is the adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"The kalpas of future ages are immeasurable, boundless, limitless, and inexhaustible.

I shall, throughout those kalpas, practice the Bodhisattva path within a single world-system to transform sentient beings; and as I do in one world-system, so shall I do throughout the entire Dharma-realm."
It is the same for all worlds within the realm of empty space; yet the mind is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of the Dharma of the bodhisattva path, as he practices for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is the eighth adamantine vow-mind of the Mahāyāna. Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva further...
This is the reflection: Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi has the mind as its root.
If the mind is pure, one can fulfill all roots of goodness and will certainly attain mastery over the Buddha’s bodhi.
If one wishes to achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is accomplished at will. If one wishes to eliminate and sever all conditions for grasping, one should abide in the One.
He said: "I am also able to attain it, yet I do not sever [the path], because I desire to bring the Buddha-bodhi to ultimate completion.

Furthermore, I do not immediately realize unsurpassed bodhi. Why? Because I wish to fulfill my original vow by practicing the bodhisattva conduct throughout all worlds to transform sentient beings. This is the ninth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind, O Son of the Buddha."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that the Buddha is unapprehendable; awakening is unapprehendable; the Bodhisattva is unapprehendable; all phenomena are unapprehendable;
sentient beings are unapprehendable; the mind is unapprehendable; conditioned activities are unapprehendable;
the past is unapprehendable; the future is unapprehendable; the present is unapprehendable; and all worlds are unapprehendable.

They attain it. Yet conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are not to be apprehended. The Bodhisattva thus dwells in tranquility, dwells in profundity, dwells in cessation, dwells in non-contention, dwells in the ineffable, dwells in non-duality, dwells in equality, dwells in self-nature, dwells in accordance with reality, dwells in liberation, dwells in nirvāṇa, and dwells in the limit of reality;
and yet they do not abandon any of their great vows, nor do they abandon omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If the mind does not abandon the bodhisattva practice; does not abandon the teaching and transforming of sentient beings;
does not abandon the various pāramitās; does not abandon the taming of sentient beings; does not abandon the serving of all Buddhas; does not abandon the expounding of all dharmas;
and does not abandon the adornment of worlds—for what reason? Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has made great vows. Although they have realized and penetrated the one...
Regarding all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), his great compassion increases ever further; he fully practices immeasurable merits and never abandons sentient beings in his heart.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-existent, yet ordinary, deluded people neither know nor perceive this.
I shall cause them all to attain awakening and clearly discern the nature of all phenomena.

Illumination. Why is this? All Buddhas abide in quiescent extinction (*śānti*), yet through their great compassionate heart (*mahākaruṇā-citta*), they preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings throughout all worlds without ever ceasing. How could I now abandon great compassion?
Furthermore, I have previously made vast vows, generating the resolve to definitively benefit all sentient beings and the resolve to accumulate [merit].
The mind of all roots of goodness; the mind that resolves upon skillful dedication and abides therein;
the mind that gives rise to profound wisdom; the mind that embraces all sentient beings; the mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings. To speak words of truth and not of falsehood;
to vow to bestow the unsurpassed Great Dharma upon all sentient beings; to vow never to sever even a single...

The lineage of all Buddhas is such that, as long as all sentient beings have not yet attained liberation, have not yet achieved perfect enlightenment, have not yet perfected the Buddha-dharmas, and their great vows are not yet fulfilled, how could one wish to abandon great compassion?
This is the tenth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of adamantine [vows] that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas generate.
This is the adamantine bodhicitta of the Great Vehicle. If Bodhisattvas abide in this dharma, they will attain the supreme, great supernormal knowledge of the Tathāgata’s vajra-nature.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of great undertakings.
What are the ten? Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought: "I shall offer worship and respect to all Buddhas.
This is the first great arousal of the mind. Furthermore, he forms this thought:
"I shall nurture all the roots of goodness possessed by all bodhisattvas. This is the second great arousal of the mind. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I..."

After the parinirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas, one should adorn their stūpas, making offerings to them with every kind of flower, every kind of garland, every kind of incense, every kind of unguent, every kind of powdered incense, every kind of robe, every kind of canopy, and every kind of banner and flag.
One should uphold and protect the true Dharma of those Buddhas; this is the third [practice].

The fourth great resolve: Furthermore, one forms this thought: "I shall teach and discipline all sentient beings, causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the fourth great resolve. Furthermore, one forms this thought:
"I shall adorn all worlds with the unsurpassed adornments of the Buddha-fields. This is...

The fifth great arousal of the mind. Furthermore, he reflects: "I shall arouse the mind of great compassion and, for the sake of even a single sentient being, practice the bodhisattva conduct in every world, individually, throughout each and every kalpa until the end of the future.
As I do for one sentient being, so shall I do for all sentient beings, causing them all to attain the unsurpassed awakening of a Buddha," and so forth.
Not giving rise to even a single thought of weariness or indolence—this is the sixth great undertaking. Furthermore, one should think:
"Those Tathāgatas are immeasurable and boundless; I shall, for the sake of a single Tathāgata, pass through inconceivable eons in respectful service and offering.
As I do for one Tathāgata, so shall I do for all Tathāgatas. This is the seventh great undertaking.

He generates the resolve. Furthermore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva thinks: "After those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall erect for each and every Tathāgata a precious stūpa for their relics, equal in height and breadth to unspeakably many worlds;
likewise, I shall create images of the Buddhas for an inconceivable number of eons."
They offer worship with all manner of jeweled banners, flags, canopies, incense, flowers, and garments, without giving rise to even a single thought of weariness.
This is for the sake of accomplishing the Buddha-dharma; for the sake of making offerings to all Buddhas; for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
and for the sake of protecting, upholding, revealing, and expounding the True Dharma. This is the eighth great undertaking of a bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva further reflects: "By means of these roots of goodness, I shall attain unexcelled Bodhi and enter the stage of all Tathāgatas, becoming equal in essence with all Tathāgatas.
This is the ninth great undertaking. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reflects: "After I have attained perfect enlightenment, regarding all..."
Throughout unspeakable eons of the world, they expound the True Dharma and manifest inconceivable, sovereign supernormal powers;
their body, speech, and mind never experience weariness, nor do they ever depart from the True Dharma.

This is because they are sustained by the power of the Buddha, because they diligently practice great vows for the sake of all sentient beings, because they take great loving-kindness as their primary motive, because they bring great compassion to ultimate fulfillment, and because they have realized the non-...
Because they accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because they abide in true speech; because they have realized that all phenomena are utterly quiescent;

because they know that all sentient beings are ultimately unapprehendable while yet not contradicting the workings of karma; because they are of one and the same essence as the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

because they pervade the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of empty space; because they have attained penetration into the signlessness (*animitta*) of all phenomena; and because they have achieved perfection.

Because they are unborn and unceasing; because they are fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas; and because, through the power of their great vows, they subdue sentient beings and perform great Buddha-activities without rest. This is the tenth great undertaking.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of great undertakings of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will not sever the path to enlightenment.
The Tathāgata’s supreme great wisdom is fully perfected through the practice of the *sādhana*. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of ultimate great undertakings for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: the ultimate great undertaking of reverently making offerings to all Tathāgatas;
the ultimate great undertaking of being able to protect and deliver all sentient beings according to their needs; and the exclusive pursuit of all Buddhas...
The ultimate great matter of the Dharma; the ultimate great matter of the accumulation of all roots of goodness;
the ultimate great matter of contemplating all Buddha-dharmas; the ultimate great matter of fulfilling all vows;
the ultimate great matter of accomplishing all bodhisattva practices; the ultimate great matter of serving all spiritual friends; proceeding to...
The ultimate great task of all Tathāgatas in all worlds; the ultimate great task of hearing and upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas—these constitute the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the ultimate matter of the great wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten [qualities].
One plants indestructible faith. What are the ten? They are: indestructible faith in all Buddhas; indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas;
indestructible faith in the noble Saṅgha; indestructible faith in all Bodhisattvas;
indestructible faith in all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); indestructible faith in all sentient beings; [indestructible faith] in the One...
Unbreakable faith in all the great vows of bodhisattvas; unbreakable faith in all bodhisattva practices;
unbreakable faith in reverently making offerings to all buddhas; and unbreakable faith in the skillful and secret means by which bodhisattvas teach and discipline all sentient beings.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will then attain...
The unshakable faith in the unsurpassed great wisdom of all Buddhas. O Son of the Buddha! There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
What are these ten? They are: receiving the prediction through having profound internal understanding;

receiving the prediction through being able to give rise to the various roots of goodness of a bodhisattva in accordance with that understanding; receiving the prediction through cultivating vast practices; receiving the prediction through manifest presence...

Recorded. One receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa) even when not present before [the Buddha]. One receives the prediction through the realization of bodhi by means of one’s own mind. One receives the prediction upon accomplishing patience (kṣānti).
One receives the prediction for the purpose of teaching and taming sentient beings. One receives the prediction upon reaching the ultimate end of all kalpas.
They receive the prediction of enlightenment through mastery over all bodhisattva practices. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will receive the prediction of enlightenment in the presence of all Buddhas.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dedication of roots of goodness by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to dedicate all their roots of goodness.
What are these ten? They are: may my roots of goodness be identical with the vows of the spiritual friends; may they be accomplished in this way and not otherwise.
May my roots of goodness be identical with the minds of the spiritual friends; may they be accomplished in this way and not otherwise.
May my roots of goodness be accomplished in the same way as the conduct of spiritual friends, and not otherwise accomplished.
May my roots of goodness be accomplished in the same way as the roots of goodness of spiritual friends, and not otherwise accomplished.

May my roots of goodness be accomplished in the same way as the equanimity of spiritual friends, and not otherwise accomplished. May my roots of goodness be accomplished in the same way as [the qualities] of spiritual friends...

May I achieve such recollection as the spiritual friend has achieved, and not achieve anything else; may I achieve through my roots of goodness the same purity as that of the spiritual friend, and not achieve anything else;
may I achieve through my roots of goodness the same dwelling as that of the spiritual friend, and not achieve anything else;
may I achieve through my roots of goodness the same fulfillment as that of the spiritual friend.
May there be no other attainment; may my roots of goodness, in accord with those of spiritual friends, achieve such non-destruction—may there be no other attainment.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed dedication of roots of goodness.
Disciple of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of attaining wisdom. What are the ten? They are as follows:
One attains wisdom by gaining mastery over giving; one attains wisdom by deeply understanding all Buddha-dharmas; one attains wisdom by entering the boundless knowledge of the Tathāgata;
one attains wisdom by being able to sever doubts regarding all questions and answers; one attains wisdom by entering into the meaning for the wise;
and one attains wisdom by deeply understanding the excellence of the vocal expressions of all Tathāgatas within all Buddha-dharmas.
They skillfully attain wisdom. They deeply understand that even a small root of goodness planted under the Buddhas will inevitably fulfill all pure and white dharmas;
they attain the wisdom of obtaining the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge. They attain the wisdom of accomplishing the inconceivable dwelling of a Bodhisattva.
They attain the wisdom of being able to travel to unspeakably many Buddha-fields within a single thought-moment. They awaken...
The enlightenment of all Buddhas; entering the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); hearing and retaining all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas;
and attaining wisdom that deeply penetrates the various adorned voices and sounds of all Tathāgatas—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, directly realized wisdom of all Buddhas. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of immeasurable, boundless, and vast resolve. What are these ten? They are: generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast resolve toward all Buddhas;
generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast resolve by contemplating the realm of all sentient beings;
and generating [an immeasurable, boundless, and vast resolve] by contemplating all lands, all worlds, and all dharma-realms.
One generates an immeasurable, vast, and great mind by contemplating that all phenomena are like space;
one generates an immeasurable, vast, and great mind by contemplating the vast conduct of all bodhisattvas.
With right mindfulness, they resolve upon an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind directed toward all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

They resolve upon an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating the inconceivable karmic fruits and retributions. They resolve upon an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
They resolve upon an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind to universally enter all great assemblies of Buddhas.
The great mind: observing all Tathāgatas and producing a vast mind that is immeasurable and boundless in its wondrous sounds.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these minds, they will attain the ocean of immeasurable, boundless, and vast wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of hidden treasures (*nidhi*). What are the ten?
That which is called knowing all dharmas is the treasury for initiating meritorious conduct; knowing all dharmas is the treasury of right reflection;
knowing all dharmas is the treasury of the illumination of *dhāraṇī*; knowing all dharmas is the treasury of eloquence for exposition;
knowing all dharmas is the treasury of the ineffable, well-awakened reality; knowing all Buddhas for oneself...
In supernormal powers, it is the treasury of observation and manifestation. It is the skillful treasury of the equal emergence of all phenomena.
It is the treasury of knowing all phenomena and constantly beholding all Buddhas.
It is the treasury of thoroughly understanding that all inconceivable eons are like illusory abodes. It is the treasury that generates joy toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The treasury of pure faith. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the treasury of the supreme wisdom-dharma of all buddhas and will be able to fully subdue all sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of discipline for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows: not giving rise to slander toward any of the Buddha-dharmas.
The discipline of not slandering; the discipline of having an indestructible mind of faith and joy toward all Buddhas;
the discipline of giving rise to respect and reverence toward all bodhisattvas; the discipline of never abandoning a mind of affection and delight toward all spiritual friends;
and the discipline of not giving rise to thoughts of recollection toward any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—[these are] far removed from...
The discipline of never retreating from the bodhisattva path; the discipline of never giving rise to thoughts of harming sentient beings;
the discipline of cultivating all roots of goodness until they reach ultimate perfection; and the discipline of being able to subdue all māras.
To bring all the perfections (*pāramitā*) to fulfillment through the discipline of restraint—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the discipline of supreme great wisdom. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of mastery for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: mastery over life, by which one dwells for an unspeakable number of eons; [mastery over mind...]
Therefore, there is mastery over the mind, because wisdom is able to enter incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) samādhis;
mastery over requisites, because one is able to adorn all worlds with immeasurable ornaments; and mastery over karma, because one receives retribution according to the appropriate time.
Mastery over birth, because of manifesting birth in all worlds; mastery over resolve, because of seeing Buddhas filling all worlds;
mastery over vows, because of attaining perfect enlightenment in various lands according to one’s desire and at any time;
mastery over spiritual power, because of manifesting all great miraculous transformations; and mastery over the Dharma, because of manifesting... [the unobstructed teaching of the Dharma].
Because they encompass all dharma-gates, they possess mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
Because they manifest the ten powers and fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata and achieve perfect enlightenment in every moment of thought, these constitute the ten.

If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the fulfillment of all the *pāramitās* of all Buddhas, as well as wisdom, spiritual power, and mastery over enlightenment. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded functions. What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded function regarding sentient beings;

the unimpeded function regarding buddha-lands; the unimpeded function regarding phenomena; the unimpeded function regarding bodies; the unimpeded function regarding vows; the unimpeded function regarding spheres of activity;

the unimpeded function regarding wisdom; the unimpeded function regarding supernormal powers; the unimpeded function regarding spiritual might; and the unimpeded function regarding the powers of a Buddha.
"Son of the Buddha, what is the unimpeded activity of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding the equality of sentient beings?
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded activities of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas concerning sentient beings. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded activity of knowing that all sentient beings are without a [substantial] self; the unimpeded activity of knowing that all sentient beings are sustained merely by conceptualization."

The unimpeded function of preaching the Dharma for all sentient beings without ever missing the proper time; the unimpeded function of universally manifesting and transforming all realms of sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of placing all sentient beings within a single pore without causing any crowding;
and the unimpeded function of manifesting all worlds in other directions for all sentient beings so that they may see them all.
The unimpeded function of manifesting the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting devas for the sake of all sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of manifesting the tranquil deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas for the sake of all sentient beings;

the unimpeded function of manifesting the practices of bodhisattvas for the sake of all sentient beings; and the unimpeded function of manifesting the physical forms of all buddhas for the sake of all sentient beings.
The unimpeded function of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment through the physical marks and signs of excellence and the power of all-knowledge—this is the tenth.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding the buddha-lands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded function of making all lands into a single land; the unimpeded function of causing all lands to enter into a single pore; knowing all...
The unimpeded function of exhausting all lands; the unimpeded function of filling all lands while sitting cross-legged in a single body;
the unimpeded function of manifesting all lands within a single body; the unimpeded function of shaking all lands without causing sentient beings to feel fear;
and the unimpeded function of adorning a single land with the ornaments of all lands. With one...
The unimpeded function of adorning all buddha-fields with the ornaments that adorn a single field;
the unimpeded function of manifesting to sentient beings through a single Tathāgata and a single assembly throughout all buddha-fields;

and the infinite varieties of the net of all directions, including all small fields, great fields, broad fields, deep fields, upward-facing fields, downward-facing fields, sideways fields, and upright fields. By means of these...
This is the unimpeded function that universally manifests to all sentient beings; this constitutes the tenth.

O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding phenomena. What are these ten? They are as follows: namely, knowing that all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon.
The unimpeded function of a single dharma entering all dharmas, yet not contradicting the mental inclinations of sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of giving birth to all dharmas from the *prajñāpāramitā* and explaining them to others so that they all attain awakening;
the unimpeded function of knowing that all dharmas are free from words and letters, yet causing all sentient beings to realize and enter this truth; and the knowledge of all [dharmas]...
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is a single characteristic, yet it possesses the unimpeded function of being able to expound immeasurable characteristics of phenomena.
It possesses the unimpeded function of knowing that all phenomena transcend verbal expression, yet being able to teach others boundless dharma-gates.

It possesses the unimpeded function of skillfully revolving the universal wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) regarding all phenomena. By means of all phenomena entering into a single dharma-gate, they do not contradict one another. Regarding this non-...

The unimpeded function of explaining kalpas that can never be exhausted; the unimpeded function of causing all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding by means of the fact that all phenomena are entirely contained within the Buddha-dharma;
and the unimpeded function of knowing that all phenomena have no limits or boundaries.

To know that all phenomena have the limit of non-obstruction, like an infinite variety of illusory nets, and to possess the unimpeded function of teaching inexhaustibly for immeasurable eons for the sake of sentient beings—this is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions of the body of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows: by means of the bodies of all sentient beings...
The unimpeded function of entering one’s own body; the unimpeded function of entering the bodies of all sentient beings by means of one’s own body;
the unimpeded function of all Buddha-bodies entering the body of a single Buddha; and the unimpeded function of the body of a single Buddha entering the bodies of all Buddhas.
The unimpeded function of causing all lands to enter one's own body; the unimpeded function of filling all phenomena of the three periods of time with a single body to manifest to sentient beings;
and the unimpeded function of manifesting infinite bodies within a single body while entering samādhi.
The unimpeded function of manifesting within a single body as many bodies as there are sentient beings and thereby attaining perfect enlightenment;

the unimpeded function of manifesting the body of a single sentient being within the bodies of all sentient beings, and manifesting the bodies of all sentient beings within the body of a single sentient being;
the manifestation of the Dharma-body within the bodies of all sentient beings; and the manifestation of all sentient beings within the Dharma-body.
The unimpeded function of the body. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions of the vows of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: the unimpeded function of making all the vows of all Bodhisattvas one’s own vow;

the unimpeded function of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment with sovereign mastery through the power of the vows of all Buddhas to achieve Bodhi; and according to... [the rest of the passage]... what is intended.
The unimpeded function of maturing sentient beings and spontaneously attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the unimpeded function of never severing great vows throughout all boundless eons;
the unimpeded function of distancing oneself from the body of consciousness and not clinging to the body of wisdom, yet manifesting all bodies through the power of sovereign vows;
and the unimpeded function of relinquishing one’s own body to fulfill the vows of others.
The unimpeded function of universally teaching and transforming all sentient beings without abandoning the great vow;
the unimpeded function of practicing the bodhisattva path throughout all eons without the great vow being interrupted;
and, by the power of the vow, manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment within a single pore to pervade all buddha-fields throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds.
For each and every sentient being, he thus manifests unimpeded power: he proclaims a single phrase of Dharma that pervades the entire realm of reality;
he raises great clouds of the True Dharma; he flashes the lightning of liberation; he thunders the sound of the true Dharma; and he rains down the nectar of ambrosia.
By the power of his great vows, he saturates the realms of all sentient beings with unimpeded power. These are the ten. Thus it was said by the Buddha.
Son, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding the spheres of activity of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
They are: the unimpeded function of abiding in the sphere of the Dharma-realm while not abandoning the sphere of sentient beings;

the unimpeded function of abiding in the sphere of the Buddhas while not abandoning the sphere of Māra; and the unimpeded function of abiding in the sphere of Nirvāṇa while not abandoning the sphere of saṃsāra.
The unimpeded function of entering the realm of all-knowledge while not severing the realm of the bodhisattva lineage;
the unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of tranquility while not abandoning the realm of distraction;
and the unimpeded function of abiding in a realm that is without going or coming, without conceptual proliferation, without marks, without essence, and beyond verbal expression—like space—and yet...
They possess the unimpeded function of abandoning the realm of conceptual proliferation regarding all sentient beings,

yet they do not abandon the unimpeded function of the realm of all directions and locations while abiding in the realm of the powers and liberations. They enter the realm of the limit of non-existence of sentient beings,
yet they do not abandon the unimpeded function of teaching and transforming all sentient beings while abiding in meditative concentration, liberation, supernormal powers, and clear wisdom.
The realm of tranquility; yet, the unimpeded function of manifesting birth within all worlds.
Abiding in the realm of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment adorned with all practices, yet the unimpeded function of manifesting the tranquil deportment of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of knowledge possessed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The unimpeded functions. What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded function of inexhaustible eloquence; the unimpeded function of all dhāraṇīs being free from forgetfulness;
the unimpeded function of being able to definitively know and definitively explain the faculties of all sentient beings;
and, within a single thought-moment, knowing through unimpeded wisdom the mental activities of all sentient beings.

The unimpeded function of knowing the desires, inclinations, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), habitual perfumes (*vāsanā*), and the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings, and accordingly administering the medicine;
the unimpeded function of being able to enter the ten powers of a Tathāgata in a single thought-moment;

the unimpeded function of knowing all kalpas of the three periods of time and the sentient beings therein through unimpeded wisdom; and manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment in every moment of thought.

Awakening. It is the unimpeded function of manifesting to sentient beings without interruption; the unimpeded function of knowing the karma of all sentient beings through the perception of a single sentient being;
and the unimpeded function of understanding the speech of all sentient beings through the sound of a single sentient being.
These are the ten. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded applications of the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded application of manifesting the bodies of all worlds within a single body;

the unimpeded application of hearing and receiving the teachings spoken in all the assemblies of Buddhas within a single assembly of a Buddha; [the unimpeded application] toward a single sentient being...
Within a single thought-moment, one accomplishes the ineffable, unsurpassed enlightenment; this is the unimpeded function that awakens the minds of all sentient beings.
With a single sound, one manifests the diverse vocal expressions of all worlds; this is the unimpeded function that causes all sentient beings to each attain understanding.
Within a single thought-moment, one manifests all karmic fruits and seeds from throughout the entirety of past kalpas.
The distinction of types: the unimpeded function by which all sentient beings are enabled to know and see;
the unimpeded function by which a single atom manifests vast Buddha-fields with infinite adornments; the unimpeded function by which all worlds are made fully adorned;
the unimpeded function by which one universally enters all three periods of time; and the emission of the great light of Dharma, manifesting all things.
The unimpeded function of the Buddha’s bodhi, the practices, and the vows of sentient beings;

the unimpeded function of skillfully protecting all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors, as well as all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
and the unimpeded function of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas. This is [the unimpeded function].
Tenth: If Bodhisattvas attain this unimpeded function, they are able to universally enter into all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions of spiritual power. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded function of placing unspeakably many worlds within a single atom; manifesting within a single atom that which is equal to the Dharma-realm; [and so forth].

The unimpeded function of all Buddha-fields: placing the waters of all great oceans within a single pore and traveling back and forth through the worlds of the ten directions, yet without causing any disturbance or harm to sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of manifesting all miraculous powers within one's own body by containing unspeakable numbers of worlds therein; and with a single hair...
They bind together incalculable mountains of vajra-enclosures and carry them while traveling through all worlds, yet they do not cause sentient beings to give rise to a mind of fear;

this is their unimpeded power. They make unspeakable eons into a single eon, and a single eon into unspeakable eons, manifesting within them the distinctions of formation and destruction, yet they do not cause the minds of sentient beings to feel fear; this is their unimpeded power.
The unimpeded function of manifesting various transformations and destructions of water, fire, and wind calamities throughout all worlds, yet without afflicting sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of being able to protect and sustain all sentient beings when the three calamities destroy all worlds, ensuring that their means of livelihood are not diminished or lacking;
and the unimpeded function of taking an inconceivable world in one hand and casting it [into another].
Beyond unspeakable worlds, he employs the unimpeded power that causes sentient beings to have no thoughts of alarm or fear;
he employs the unimpeded power that explains all lands to be identical to empty space, causing all sentient beings to fully attain awakening and understanding. These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded applications of power possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
They are: the unimpeded application of the power of sentient beings, because they teach, transform, and subdue them without ever abandoning them;

the unimpeded application of the power of buddha-fields, because they adorn them with unspeakably many manifestations of ornamentation; the unimpeded application of the power of dharmas, because they cause all bodies to enter therein...
Because there is no body, the power of the *kalpa* functions without obstruction through the uninterrupted cultivation of practice;
the power of the Buddha functions without obstruction through awakening those who are asleep; the power of conduct functions without obstruction through the gathering of all bodhisattva practices;

the power of the Tathāgata functions without obstruction through the liberation of all sentient beings; and the power of being without a teacher functions without obstruction through the self-awakening to all [phenomena].
Because of the Dharma; because the power of all-knowledge functions without obstruction, having attained perfect enlightenment through all-knowledge;
and because the power of great compassion functions without obstruction, never abandoning any sentient being. These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha, these are called the ten kinds of unobstructed functions of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. If there are those who attain these ten unobstructed functions, regarding the [Buddha-]...
Whether the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is realized or not is entirely according to his will, without contradiction.
Although he has attained perfect enlightenment, he nevertheless does not cease practicing the bodhisattva conduct. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has made great vows to enter the gate of infinite and unobstructed activity, skillfully manifesting it. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses...

There are ten kinds of playful manifestations (*vikrīḍita*). What are the ten? They are as follows: manifesting the body of a buddha-field (*kṣetra-kāya*) by means of the body of a sentient being, yet without destroying the body of the sentient being—this is the playful manifestation of a bodhisattva.
Manifesting the body of a sentient being by means of the body of a buddha-field, yet without destroying the body of the buddha-field—this is the playful manifestation of a bodhisattva.
Manifesting the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within the body of a Buddha... [and so forth].

To diminish the body of a Tathāgata is the playful mastery of a bodhisattva. To manifest the body of a Tathāgata within the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without increasing those bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is the playful mastery of a bodhisattva.

To manifest the body of one who has attained perfect awakening within the body of bodhisattva practice without interrupting that body of bodhisattva practice is the playful mastery of a bodhisattva. Regarding...

Manifesting the body of a fully awakened Buddha while appearing as the body that practices the bodhisattva path, yet without diminishing the body of one who has attained enlightenment—this is the bodhisattva’s play.
Manifesting the body of birth and death within the realm of nirvāṇa, yet without being attached to birth and death—this is the bodhisattva’s play.
Manifesting nirvāṇa within the realm of birth and death, yet not ultimately entering into nirvāṇa—this is [the bodhisattva’s play].
The Bodhisattva’s play consists of entering into samādhi and manifesting all activities—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—without ever relinquishing that samādhi-equipoise.

This is the Bodhisattva’s play: while remaining in the presence of a single Buddha, hearing the Dharma and upholding it with a body that does not move, he manifests his form individually within the assemblies of unspeakably many Buddhas through the power of samādhi. Furthermore, [he...]
Without dividing their bodies and without emerging from meditative concentration, they hear the Dharma and maintain it in an uninterrupted succession.
Thus, in every thought-moment, from each single body of samādhi, they produce unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodies of samādhi.
Even if all kalpas were to be exhausted in this sequential manner, the bodhisattva’s bodies of samādhi could never be exhausted.

These are the playful manifestations of the Bodhisattva; these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the playful manifestation of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spheres of activity. What are the ten? They are:
manifesting gateways to the boundless Dharma-realm to enable sentient beings to enter—this is the sphere of the Bodhisattva.
The realm: manifesting the infinite, wondrous adornments of all worlds so that sentient beings may enter them—this is the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity.
Transforming to go to all realms of sentient beings and awakening them through every skillful means—this is the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity.
Producing the body of a bodhisattva from the body of a Tathāgata, and producing the body of a Tathāgata from the body of a bodhisattva—this is the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity.
To manifest world-systems within the realm of empty space, and to manifest the realm of empty space within world-systems—this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
To manifest the realm of nirvāṇa within the realm of saṃsāra, and to manifest the realm of saṃsāra within the realm of nirvāṇa—this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
To produce the speech of all Buddha-dharmas from within the speech of a single sentient being is the domain of the Bodhisattva.
To manifest as a single body with an infinite body, and to manifest as all differentiated bodies from a single body, is the domain of the Bodhisattva.
To fill the entire Dharma-realm with a single body is the domain of the Bodhisattva. Within a single thought-moment, to...
All sentient beings resolve upon bodhicitta; each manifests immeasurable bodies and attains equal and perfect enlightenment—this is the realm of the Bodhisattva.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the realm of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of power. What are the ten? They are as follows:
That is to say: the power of the profound mind, because it is unmixed with any worldly sentiments; the power of the superior profound mind, because it does not abandon any of the Buddha-dharmas;
the power of skillful means, because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion; the power of wisdom, because it thoroughly understands all mental activities;
the power of aspiration, because it fulfills all that is sought; and the power of practice, because it remains uninterrupted throughout the limits of the future.
The power of the vehicles (*yāna-bala*): being able to give rise to all vehicles while not abandoning the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-bala*):
manifesting within each and every pore all pure worlds and the appearance in the world of all Tathāgatas.
The power of awakening (*bodhi-bala*): causing all sentient beings to resolve to attain Buddhahood without interruption. Turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
Power. Because he speaks a single phrase of Dharma that perfectly accords with the faculties, inclinations, and desires of all sentient beings—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the ten powers of the supreme, all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas. O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of fearlessness. What are the ten?
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to hear and retain all speech. They form this thought:

"Even if there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings coming from the ten directions to question me regarding hundreds of thousands of great dharmas, I would not see [any deficiency] in my response to those questions."
The subtle and slight marks are difficult to answer; because they do not see them, the mind attains fearlessness.
Having reached the ultimate shore of great fearlessness, one is able to respond to whatever is asked, severing all doubts without any timidity.
This is the first fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the unimpeded consecration of the Tathāgata.
Possessing eloquence that reaches all written characters, speech, and sounds, he reveals the secret ultimate further shore.
