He forms this thought: "Even if there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings coming from the ten directions to question me with immeasurable teachings, I would not perceive even the slightest aspect of difficulty in answering those questions. Because I perceive no such difficulty, my mind attains..."
Fearlessness. Having reached the ultimate shore of that great fearlessness, they are able to respond to whatever questions are asked and sever all doubts without any trepidation.
This is the second fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are empty;
they are devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self; they are without action and without an agent; they are without a knower and without...

There is no life-principle (*jīva*), no nourisher, and no person (*pudgala*). Being free from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and having forever transcended all views, their mind is like space.
They form this thought: "I do not perceive even the slightest characteristic in sentient beings that could harm my physical, verbal, or mental karma. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva has distanced themselves from "self" and "what belongs to self," and they do not perceive even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in any phenomena.
Because they do not perceive [such signs], their minds attain fearlessness; they ultimately reach that great shore of fearlessness, remaining firm, courageous, and indestructible.

This is the third fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is protected by the power of the Buddhas, sustained by the power of the Buddhas, and abides in the majestic deportment of the Buddhas; their conduct is true and without change.
He forms this thought: "I do not see even the slightest aspect of my deportment that would cause sentient beings to give rise to reproach.
Because I see none such, my mind attains fearlessness, and I teach the Dharma with composure amidst the great assembly.
This is the fourth fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the physical, verbal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are entirely pure and bright.
Pure, gentle, and far removed from all evils, he reflects thus: "I do not perceive even the slightest aspect of my own physical, verbal, or mental karma that is worthy of reproach.
Because I see nothing such as this, my mind attains fearlessness, enabling me to establish sentient beings in the Buddha-dharma.
This is the fifth fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s vajra...
The Māras, non-Buddhists, and sentient beings with views—such as the *ṛṣis*, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings—constantly follow and guard him.
All Tathāgatas protect and keep him in mind without abandoning him. The bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"I do not see any Māras, non-Buddhists, or sentient beings with views who could come to obstruct my practice of the bodhisattva path."
He perceives the characteristics of even a small portion of the Path; because he does not see [any faults therein], his mind attains fearlessness.
Having ultimately reached that great shore of fearlessness, he gives rise to a heart of joy and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva. This is the sixth fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already achieved the first faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*); his mind is free from forgetfulness, and he is pleasing to the Buddhas.

He forms this thought: "Regarding the words, phrases, and methods of the path to awakening taught by the Tathāgata, I do not perceive even the slightest sign of forgetfulness therein. Because I perceive no such thing, my mind attains fearlessness.
I shall uphold all the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva. This is the seventh fearlessness of a bodhisattva. O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva...
This Mahāsattva has attained complete mastery over wisdom and skillful means. He has reached the ultimate perfection of all the powers of a Bodhisattva.
He constantly and diligently teaches and transforms all sentient beings, and always binds his aspirational mind to the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of bringing them to maturity, he manifests birth within a world of afflictions and defilement, yet from a lineage of supreme nobility.
With his retinue complete, he enjoys all his desires according to his heart’s wish and dwells in joy and happiness. Yet, he reflects thus:

"Although I am gathered here with this retinue, I do not see even the slightest sign upon which I might become attached, such that it would cause me to neglect my practice of dhyāna, vimokṣa, the various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the eloquence of the bodhisattva path. Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, they have reached the further shore. They cultivate the bodhisattva practices with a vow never to interrupt them.
Not seeing a single worldly object capable of deluding or confusing the bodhisattva path, their minds attain fearlessness because of this non-perception.
Ultimately reaching that great shore of fearlessness, by the power of their great vows, in all worlds...
Manifesting birth within the realms is the eighth fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva never forgets the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*). Riding upon the Great Vehicle, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
By the power of the great mind of all-knowledge, they manifest the tranquil deportment of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, thinking thus:
I do not perceive within myself even a trace of the characteristics of renunciation that would lead me to emerge from the two vehicles.
Because I do not perceive such things, my mind attains fearlessness, reaching the supreme and great shore of fearlessness, where I am able to universally manifest all paths of the vehicles.
To be ultimately fulfilled in the equality of the Mahāyāna— this is the ninth fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes all pure and white dharmas, is endowed with roots of goodness, perfects the supernormal powers,
dwells ultimately in the enlightenment of all Buddhas, fulfills all bodhisattva practices, and receives [them] from all Buddhas...
This is the seal of the consecration of omniscience. Yet, they constantly transform sentient beings and practice the bodhisattva path with this thought:
"I do not see even a single sentient being who should be brought to maturity whom I am unable to mature by manifesting the sovereign power of all Buddhas.
Because they see no such being, their minds attain fearlessness, and they ultimately reach the shore of that great fearlessness.
They do not interrupt the bodhisattva practices; they do not abandon the bodhisattva vows;
and according to the needs of all sentient beings to be transformed, they manifest the realm of a Buddha to deliver them. This is the tenth fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of fearlessness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the [fearlessnesses] of all Buddhas.
They attain supreme fearlessness, yet they do not abandon the fearlessness of a bodhisattva. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unique qualities of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas naturally practice the six *pāramitās* without being taught by others;
they always delight in great giving and do not give rise to stinginess; they constantly maintain pure precepts.
They are free from transgressions; they are fully endowed with patience and their minds are unshakable. They possess great vigor that never regresses;
they skillfully enter the various dhyānas and are forever free from distraction. They are adept at cultivating wisdom and completely eliminate all evil views.

These, O Son of the Buddha, are the six perfections—the uncommon dharmas—cultivated by following the path of the pāramitās through one's own power, without depending on the instruction of others. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
A Mahāsattva is universally able to embrace all sentient beings. That is to say, they practice giving through both material wealth and the Dharma;
they maintain right mindfulness before them with a gentle countenance and affectionate speech; their hearts are joyful as they reveal the meaning of reality as it is;
they cause others to awaken to and understand the Bodhi of all Buddhas; they harbor no hatred or partiality, but provide equal benefit. This is the second [quality] that does not depend on others.

The uncommon dharma of diligently gathering sentient beings by following the path of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). O Son of the Buddha, the skillful dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is as follows:

namely, dedication that does not seek karmic retribution; dedication that accords with the *bodhi* of the Buddhas; dedication that is unattached to all worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and samādhis;
dedication for the benefit of all sentient beings; and dedication for the sake of... [not]... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

Dedicating the severance of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the third uncommon dharma: to initiate roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings and seek the Buddha’s wisdom without relying on the instruction of others.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reaches the ultimate perfection of skillful means;
his mind constantly looks back upon all sentient beings, never wearying of the mundane world of ordinary fools.

Regarding their spheres of activity: they take no pleasure in the path of renunciation of the two vehicles; they do not cling to their own happiness but exert themselves solely in transforming and delivering others.
They are skillfully able to enter and emerge from meditative concentrations and liberations, attaining complete mastery over all samādhis.

Coming and going through birth and death as if wandering through gardens and pavilions, they never for a moment give rise to a mind of weariness or aversion. At times they dwell in the palaces of Māra; at other times they act as Śakra, Brahmā, or the Great Kings.
Lord of the World, there is no place of birth where he does not manifest his body.
Sometimes he leaves the household life within the assemblies of non-Buddhists, yet he remains forever far removed from all false views.
Regarding all worldly literature, incantations, scripts, seals, mathematics, and even the arts of play, song, and dance, he manifests them all with such skill that none are not exquisite. At times...
She manifested as a beautiful woman whose wisdom and talent were foremost in the world.
Regarding all mundane and supramundane dharmas, she was able to inquire and to explain; in questioning and answering, she severed doubts and attained ultimate perfection.
She thoroughly mastered all mundane and supramundane matters and reached the further shore. All sentient beings constantly came to gaze upon her with reverence. Although she appeared...

They maintain the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without losing the mind of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Although they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment in every moment of thought, they do not cease their bodhisattva practices.
This is the fourth unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*), the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that reaches the ultimate further shore without depending on the instruction of others.
O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva well understands the path of the dual practice of skillful means and reality (*tattva*).
Mastery of wisdom reaches its ultimate consummation: namely, dwelling in nirvāṇa while manifesting birth and death;
knowing there are no sentient beings while diligently practicing the work of teaching and transforming them; abiding in ultimate quiescence while manifesting the arising of afflictions;

dwelling in the single, solid, and dense Dharma-body of wisdom while universally manifesting the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings; and constantly entering profound meditative concentration while...
They manifest the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, yet they constantly remain far removed from the three realms without abandoning sentient beings.

They always delight in the joy of the Dharma, yet they manifest the presence of court ladies, singing, and playful diversions. Although their bodies are adorned with the various marks and signs of excellence, they manifest the forms of the ugly, the impoverished, and the lowly.
Though they constantly accumulate a multitude of virtues free from all faults and evils, they manifest birth in the hells and among animals.
They are born as hungry ghosts. Although they have already reached the further shore of the Buddha’s wisdom, they do not abandon the bodhisattva’s body of wisdom.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such immeasurable wisdom that even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know it.

How much more so for all ignorant sentient beings! This is the fifth unshared quality: the simultaneous practice of both the provisional and the ultimate without depending on the instruction of others.
Son of the Buddha, the physical, verbal, and mental actions of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva follow wisdom and are entirely pure.
That is to say, being fully endowed with great compassion, they are forever free from the intent to kill; and so on, until being fully endowed with right understanding, they possess no...
Wrong view. This is the sixth unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) of not following the wisdom of body, speech, and mind through the instruction of another.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, being fully endowed with great compassion, does not abandon sentient beings;
he undergoes all sufferings on behalf of all sentient beings—namely, the sufferings of hell, the sufferings of animals, and the sufferings of hungry ghosts—for the sake of their benefit.

They do not give rise to weariness or fatigue, but focus solely on liberating all sentient beings. They never become addicted to or defiled by the realms of the five desires, but always exert themselves diligently to extinguish all forms of suffering.
This is the seventh unique quality (āveṇika-dharma), which arises through great compassion without depending on the instruction of others.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are always joyfully beheld by sentient beings, [just as] by Brahmā.
Śakra, the Four Great Kings, and all sentient beings never tire of beholding him. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has practiced pure conduct for a vast period of time and is free from any fault; therefore, sentient beings never weary of seeing him.
This is the eighth unique quality, not derived from the instruction of others, by which all sentient beings delight in beholding him.
Dharma. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is adorned with the great vow for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), their resolve and aspiration are firm and steadfast.
Although they may dwell in the perilous places of ordinary worldlings, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas, they never lose or diminish the bright, pure, and wondrous jewel of the mind of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a precious gem named "Pure Adornment" (*viśuddhālaṃkāra*); even if placed in the midst of mud and mire, its radiance and color...
It does not change. It is able to make turbid water entirely clear and pure. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:
although he dwells among the impure and turbid places of the foolish and ignorant, he never loses or destroys the pure jewel-mind that seeks all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Furthermore, he is able to cause those evil sentient beings to distance themselves from the defilements of false views and afflictions, so that they may attain the seeking of all-knowledge.

The jewel of the pure mind. This is the ninth uncommon quality (āveṇika-dharma): not losing the jewel of the mind of omniscience while dwelling in places of great hardship, without depending on the instruction of others.
Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the wisdom of the realm of self-awakening.
Awakening spontaneously without a teacher, he has attained ultimate mastery and reached the further shore.
With the stainless Dharma-ribbon crowning his head, he does not abandon his proximity to virtuous friends; he always delights in honoring all Tathāgatas. This is the tenth unique quality:
attaining the supreme Dharma without instruction from another, while never being separated from spiritual friends and never ceasing to honor the Buddhas.
Dharma. Sons of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of uncommon dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
If Bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the supreme, vast, and uncommon dharmas of the Tathāgata. Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of karma.
What are the ten? They are: the karma of all worlds, which is entirely identical in its adornment and purification.
Therefore, it is because they are able to make offerings to all the deeds of all Buddhas; because they plant the same roots of goodness as all Bodhisattvas;
because they are able to teach and transform all sentient beings; because they purify and encompass all future deeds throughout the limits of the future;
and because, through all their deeds of supernatural power, they do not leave a single world-system while reaching all world-systems.
The karma of all-encompassing radiance, because it emits rays of light of immeasurable colors, and within each ray there appear lotus thrones upon which bodhisattvas sit in the full-lotus posture;

the karma of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem never ceases, because after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, it protects, maintains, and upholds the teachings of all Buddhas; and the karma of all transformations, throughout all worlds...
Because they teach the Dharma within the realms to transform and guide all sentient beings;

because they perform all acts of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), manifesting whatever the minds of sentient beings desire within a single thought-moment so that all their aspirations are completely fulfilled—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and vast activity of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of bodies. What are the ten? They are: the non-coming body, because they do not undergo birth in any world;
the non-going body, because they cannot be found by seeking them in any world; the non-substantial body, because they perceive all worlds as they truly are;
and the non-false body, because they demonstrate the world through the principle of suchness.
Therefore, it is the inexhaustible body because it continues without interruption until the end of the future; the firm body because all Māras cannot destroy it;
the immovable body because all Māras and non-Buddhists cannot shake it; the body endowed with marks because it manifests the pure marks of a hundred merits;
the markless body because the ultimate nature of phenomena is entirely without marks; and the universally reaching body because it...

Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time are of one and the same body—this constitutes the ten. If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and inexhaustible body of a Tathāgata.

The fourth major section, following the "Abiding Like a Jewel," consists of twenty-nine gates that answer twenty-nine questions regarding the practice within the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Among these, the first dedication has four gates; the second and third dedications each have two gates;
the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh each have one gate; and the eighth dedication consists of ten gates, namely the ten non-obstructions (*daśāsaṅga*).
The ninth dedication has three gates; the tenth dedication has four gates.
Regarding "dedication," it refers to taking each of the ten *pāramitā* practices previously cultivated and dedicating them toward three destinations, namely, dedicating them to sentient beings.

If one abandons sentient beings, then there is no basis for the bodhisattva’s practice. Second is dedication toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), because one vows that all sentient beings shall reach unsurpassed enlightenment.

Third is dedication toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this means that if one does not ultimately return to the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-bhūtakoṭi*), one has not yet abandoned signs and thus remains within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which is not what is called the bodhisattva path.
Because it is the practice of the *dharmadhātu*. Since sentient beings lack the characteristic of being sentient beings, this is itself *bodhi*.

Since *bodhi* is without attainment, one returns to the ultimate *dharmadhātu*. This is the gathering of practice through vows, ensuring that practice is not in vain because there is a destination toward which it tends.

If categorized by sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), then the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) involve entering principle as emptiness, while the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) involve emerging from the mundane to benefit sentient beings.

This is provisional. This dedication culminates in the convergence of the one mind as the Middle Way. Now, this Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is not so, for it is entirely inseparable from the essence and function of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is the general purport of this dedication. Now, within each of the ten stages, they are all mutually fused and subsumed.
First, regarding the Dedication of Protecting and Delivering Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Appearance of Sentient Beings, there are four sections. The first is as follows:
1. The Jewel Mind: clarifying that the roots of goodness dedicated are noble and perfect. 2. The Vajra-like Mahāyāna Mind: namely, the great vow of protection. 3. Universal Arousing:
namely, the dedication for the sake of others. 4. Ultimate Great Task: namely, the fulfillment of what has been transformed and accomplished.
The above four gates collectively clarify the first dedication. Second is indestructible faith.
The final two gates clarify the second, the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*). In the first gate, the indestructibility is properly elucidated;

in the subsequent gate, the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is bestowed, which signifies the completion of the practice of dedication. Regarding the practice of dedicating roots of goodness equal to those of all Buddhas within the ten types of roots of goodness, the final two gates clarify this.
In the first gate, equality with the Buddhas is properly elucidated, taking the Buddha as the true and virtuous knower.

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth are identical to the Buddha because they are non-dual. Since the two minds of compassion and wisdom are equal to those of the Buddha, one subsequently attains ten kinds of wisdom;

this constitutes the fulfillment of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The fourth gate, the single section on the "Vast Mind," clarifies the practice of dedication that reaches all places (*sarvatragatā-pariṇāmanā*);
for since wisdom is like the ocean, immeasurable and boundless, there is nothing it does not [pervade].
This concludes the section on the fiftieth type of treasury: the practice of dedication within the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
This is called a "treasury" because all phenomena encompass these ten meanings; it is called "hidden" because those who are deluded do not perceive them.
Each of these consists of ten aspects, which constitute the inexhaustible merit. Sixth is the fiftieth type of restraint (*saṃvara*).
The first gate is the practice of dedication that accords with making all roots of goodness firm.

This refers to the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-paṭala*), which all accord with the equal *dharmadhātu* and thus pervade all roots of goodness. Because the root of the precepts is firm, it serves as the foundation for practice;
therefore, it is said that "all roots of goodness are brought to ultimate fulfillment. Ultimate fulfillment is precisely what is meant by firmness. Seventh.
The tenth gate, "Ten Sovereign Powers," clarifies the practice within the dedication that accords with all sentient beings in an equal manner.
Because each and every root of goodness reaches the stage of ultimate firmness, one accords with sentient beings and attains great sovereignty.
The eightieth [chapter], "Ten Gates of Unimpeded Function," clarifies the practice within the dedication that reveals the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness). That is to say:
Each and every practice is like suchness, because it is without obstruction. Therefore, the *Commentary on the Stages* (*Jiwei guo*) states:
"Abiding in this stage, one attains the equality of all lands, an equality that is perfectly equal. Within these ten gates, there is a general manifestation of the body and land, self and other;
whether it be wisdom or its object, each is mutually integrated, unobstructed, and unhindered. This is their general characteristic, which reveals that they are none other than the Dharma-realm.
Because the essence gives rise to great function, there are extensively many meanings; here, they are briefly presented through ten gates to manifest their inexhaustibility.
The nine and ten types of "playful manifestations" (vīlāsa) are explained in the final three gates as the practice of dedication free from bondage and attachment.

Through this freedom from bondage and attachment, one accomplishes the sovereign wisdom and function of Samantabhadra. The first gate manifests the accomplishment of playful appreciation through conduct that accords with one's own will.
"Abiding" means manifesting bodies with sovereign mastery throughout the ten dharma realms, entering and exiting, coming and going, and sporting therein without obstruction.

The next section reveals that within a single realm, the scope is immeasurable and inconceivable. The final section reveals that the functional power of this mastery is able to accord with the dharma-realm;
through wisdom-illumination, it penetrates to the ultimate source, wherein defilement and purity are interfused, and everything follows only the turning of wisdom. Therefore, there is no bondage.
There is no liberation. The ten sets of ten types of fearlessness clarify the practice of entering the Dharma-realm through the four gates of immeasurable dedication.
Because one is neither bound nor attached as described above, one universally enters the Dharma-realm, manifesting bodies according to the capacities of beings and preaching the Dharma;
thus, both self-benefit and benefiting others attain fearlessness. The reason for this is that one has attained the Dharma-realm’s power of hearing and retention. Therefore...

Having attained unimpeded eloquence, they enter and emerge from the two kinds of emptiness. Manifesting dignified deportment, their three karmas are pure; thus they receive the external protection of the Ten Kings.
Internally possessing right mindfulness and externally employing manifold skillful means, they are endowed with all-knowledge; therefore, their conduct is fearless.
By means of this, they preach the Dharma for the benefit of themselves and others, such that every single action accords with the Dharma-realm. Thus it is said.

One attains the ten unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), which do not share in common with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). These all arise from the nature (*dharmatā*) and are not shared with others;
thus, the provisional and the real are practiced in tandem. Consequently, the substance and function of the realized virtues are fully perfected.
Because each and every practice door is dedicated toward this end, one accomplishes the body of the supreme adornment of the practices of Samantabhadra. Thus it is accomplished.
Having already attained the essence of the practice of dedication, one relies upon this very body to enter the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is precisely upon this body that one initiates the practice of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Volumes 55 and 56. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Sī;
Explanatory Outline by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Sī on Kuāngshān.

Part One: Answers to the Previous Twenty-nine Questions. Section Ten: The Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). End of the Practice within the Ten Stages of Dedication. Part Two: Fifty Sections.
Answering the previous fifty questions, this clarifies the characteristics of practice within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Four: "The Departure from the World" (*Lokottara-varga*).
"O Son of the Buddha! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of physical action (*kāyakarman*). What are the ten? They are as follows: first, the body..."
The bodily action that fills all world-realms; the bodily action that is able to manifest before all sentient beings;
the bodily action that is able to take birth in all realms of existence; the bodily action that travels through all world-realms;
the bodily action that proceeds to the assemblies of all Buddhas; and the bodily action that is able to universally cover all world-realms with a single hand.
The physical activity of being able to grind all the Vajra-perimeter mountains of all worlds with a single hand until they are crushed into fine dust;
the physical activity of manifesting within one’s own body the formation and destruction of all Buddha-fields to show them to sentient beings;
the physical activity of containing all realms of sentient beings within a single body; and the physical activity of universally manifesting all pure Buddha-fields within one’s own body.
Within this, all sentient beings accomplish the path through the karma of the body; these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed Buddha-karma of the Tathāgata and be able to awaken all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas further possess ten kinds of bodies. What are the ten? They are: the body of the various pāramitās;... [and so forth].
It is the body of perfect practice because it practices all things correctly; the body of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) because it does not abandon any sentient being;

the body of great compassion because it undergoes immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without weariness; the body of great loving-kindness because it protects and rescues all sentient beings;
the body of merit because it benefits all sentient beings; and the body of wisdom because it is identical to the bodies of all Buddhas.
Because of their single nature; because the Dharma-body is eternally free from birth within the various realms of existence; because the expedient body manifests before all places;

because the power-body displays all manner of miraculous transformations; and because the enlightenment-body attains perfect awakening according to one's aspiration and at the appropriate time—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed [state] of the Tathāgata.
The Body of Great Wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of speech of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
gentle speech, because it brings peace and security to all sentient beings; nectar-like speech, because it causes all sentient beings to become completely cool;
non-deceptive speech, because all that is spoken is in accordance with reality; and truthful speech...
Because he speaks no falsehood even in dreams; because his vast speech is revered by all Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Great Kings;
because his profound speech reveals the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because his steadfast speech teaches the Dharma inexhaustibly;
because his upright speech is easy to understand when uttered; because his diverse speech manifests according to the occasion; and because he awakens all sentient beings.

Because speech causes understanding according to one's inclinations and desires, these constitute the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous speech of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to purify their vocal karma.
What are the ten? They are: purifying vocal karma by delighting in hearing the voice of the Tathāgata.

They cultivate pure verbal karma by delighting in hearing the explanation of the bodhisattva’s merits; they cultivate pure verbal karma by not speaking words that all sentient beings find unpleasant to hear;
they cultivate pure verbal karma by truly distancing themselves from the four faults of speech; they cultivate pure verbal karma by joyfully exulting and praising the Tathāgata;
and they cultivate pure verbal karma by loudly praising the Buddha’s true merits at the stūpas of the Tathāgata.
They purify their verbal karma by practicing pure speech; they purify their verbal karma by bestowing the Dharma upon sentient beings with a profoundly pure mind;

they purify their verbal karma by praising the Tathāgatas through music and song; they purify their verbal karma by listening to the True Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas without begrudging body or life;
and they purify their verbal karma by sacrificing their bodies to serve all Bodhisattvas and Dharma masters while receiving sublime [teachings].

Purifying verbal action through the purity of the Dharma—this constitutes the ten. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies verbal action by means of these ten matters, they will obtain ten kinds of protection. What are the ten? They are:
being protected by the entire host of devas, headed by the King of Devas; being protected by the entire host of nāgas, headed by the King of Nāgas; [and being protected by] the yakṣas...
The King was at their head; the Gandharva Kings were at their head; the Asura Kings were at their head; the Garuḍa Kings were at their head;
the Kiṃnara Kings were at their head; the Mahoraga Kings were at their head; and the Brahmā Kings were at their head.
Each one, together with his own retinue, acted as a protector. With the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, at their head, all the Dharma-preachers [were likewise protected].

They all provide protection. These are the ten. Son of the Buddha, once Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have obtained this protection, they are able to accomplish ten kinds of great tasks. What are these ten? They are: causing all sentient beings to rejoice;
being able to travel to all worlds; being able to fully understand all faculties; [and] all that is supreme...
They cause all things to be completely purified. They cause all afflictions to be severed and eliminated. They cause all habitual tendencies to be abandoned.
They cause all desires and pleasures to be made bright and clean. They cause all profound intentions to fully increase.
They cause the entire dharma-realm to be universally pervaded. They cause all nirvāṇas to be clearly perceived. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of mind. What are the ten? They are: 1. A mind like the great earth, because it can sustain and cause all sentient beings' roots of goodness to grow;
2. A mind like the great ocean, because the waters of the immeasurable and boundless great wisdom of all Buddhas flow entirely into it;
3. A mind like Sumeru, the king of mountains, because it places all sentient beings...
Because it abides in the supreme roots of goodness that transcend the world, it is like a *maṇi* jewel-king mind;
because it delights in purity and is free from defilement, it is like a vajra mind; because it decisively penetrates all phenomena, it is like a vajra-circled mountain mind;
and because no māras or non-Buddhists can shake it, it is like a lotus mind, such that no worldly dharmas can [defile it].

Because it is unstained, like the heart of the udumbara flower; because it is difficult to encounter throughout all eons, like the heart of the pure sun which destroys the veil of darkness; and because it is immeasurable, like the heart of space. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure mind. O Son of the Buddha, these are the [qualities] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
There are ten kinds of generating the mind of awakening. What are these ten? They are: the generation of the mind thinking, "I shall deliver all sentient beings";

the generation of the mind thinking, "I shall cause all sentient beings to sever and eliminate their afflictions"; the generation of the mind thinking, "I shall cause all sentient beings to extinguish their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
the generation of the mind thinking, "I shall sever and eliminate all doubts and delusions"; the generation of the mind thinking, "I shall..."
I resolve to extinguish the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings. I resolve to eliminate all hardships and obstacles of the evil realms.
I resolve to reverently accord with all Tathāgatas. I resolve to skillfully train in all that is studied by all Bodhisattvas.
I resolve that I shall manifest all Buddhas at every single hair-tip throughout all worlds.

The mind of attaining perfect enlightenment; the resolve: "I shall strike the unsurpassed Dharma drum throughout all worlds, so that all sentient beings may, according to their faculties and inclinations, fully attain awakening and understanding. This is the tenth.

If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme mind of great exertion in performing enlightened activities. O Son of the Buddha, these are the [vows] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
There are ten kinds of all-pervading minds. What are the ten? They are: the all-pervading mind that encompasses all space, because its resolve is vast;

the all-pervading mind that encompasses the entire dharma-realm, because it penetrates the infinite; the all-pervading mind that encompasses all three periods of time, because it knows them all in a single thought-moment;
and the all-pervading mind that encompasses the appearance of all Buddhas, [extending] from their entry into the womb to their birth...
Because they have fully understood everything from birth, renunciation, attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa;

because they pervade the minds of all sentient beings, fully knowing their faculties, desires, and habitual tendencies; because they pervade the mind of all wisdom, understanding and following the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
because they pervade all boundless minds, knowing the distinctions within the various nets of illusion; because they pervade the one...
The mind of universal non-arising, because it does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any phenomena;

the mind of universal unimpededness, because it does not dwell upon its own mind or the minds of others; the mind of universal sovereignty, because it manifests the attainment of Buddhahood universally in a single thought-moment.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the immeasurable, unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas that pervade all.
Adornment. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of faculties for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
the faculty of joy, because of unshakable faith upon seeing all Buddhas; the faculty of aspiration, because of awakening to and understanding all the Buddha-dharma one has heard;
the faculty of non-retrogression, because all undertakings are brought to ultimate completion; and the faculty of steadfast abiding, because of never severing all roots of enlightenment...
Because it is the practice of the bodhisattva; because its subtle faculties enter into the subtle principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
because its tireless faculties bring all matters concerning sentient beings to ultimate completion; and because its adamantine faculties realize and know the nature of all phenomena.
The adamantine flame-root, because it universally illumines the spheres of all Buddhas; the undifferentiated root, because all Tathāgatas share a single body;
and the unobstructed limit-root, because it penetrates deeply into the ten powers of the Tathāgata. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the roots of the Tathāgata’s supreme, great wisdom, which are perfectly fulfilled.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of profound resolve for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the profound resolve that is unstained by any worldly phenomena;
the profound resolve that is not mixed with the paths of the two vehicles; and the thorough comprehension of all Buddhas...
The profound mind of awakening; the profound mind that accords with the path of the knowledge of all-knowledge; the profound mind that cannot be shaken by any demons or non-Buddhists;
the profound mind that purely cultivates the perfect wisdom of all Tathāgatas; the profound mind that receives and upholds all teachings as they are heard;
the profound mind that does not cling to any place of rebirth; and the profound mind that is endowed with all subtle [qualities].
The profound mind of wisdom; the profound mind that cultivates all the Buddha-dharmas—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide within them, they will attain the supreme, pure, and profound mind of omniscience. Children of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of superior profound minds.
What are these ten? They are: the superior profound mind of non-retrogression; [and so forth].
The superior profound mind that accumulates all roots of goodness; the superior profound mind that resolves all the secret words of the Tathāgatas by being free from doubt and hesitation;
the superior profound mind that correctly maintains [the teachings] as it flows from great vows and great practices;
the superior profound mind that is most excellent because it penetrates deeply into all Buddha-dharmas; and the superior profound mind that acts as a sovereign over all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, there is the superior profound resolve of vast increase, because it universally enters into various gateways to the Dharma;

the superior profound resolve of preeminence, because all that is undertaken is accomplished; the superior profound resolve of mastery, because it is adorned by all samādhis, supernormal powers, and transformations;
the superior profound resolve of abiding, because it sustains one's original vows; and the superior profound resolve of non-resting...
The profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), because it brings all sentient beings to maturity—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, pure, and superior profound mind of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of diligent cultivation. What are the ten? They are: diligent cultivation of giving, relinquishing everything entirely;...

Because they do not seek recompense, they diligently practice the precepts; because they are free from deception through the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), austerities, fewness of desires, and contentment, they diligently practice patience;
because they are free from the notions of self and other and endure all evils, they ultimately give rise to no mind of anger or malice.
One diligently cultivates vigor; the activities of body, speech, and mind are never distracted, for all that is done proceeds without regression until reaching the ultimate goal.
One diligently cultivates meditative concentration; through liberation and samādhi, supernormal powers appear, as one is freed from all desires, afflictions, strife, and worldly entanglements.
One diligently cultivates wisdom; one practices and accumulates all meritorious virtues.

Because they are free from weariness, they diligently cultivate great loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Because they know that all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they diligently cultivate great compassion (*karuṇā*).

Because they know all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty and universally take upon themselves the suffering of all sentient beings without fatigue, they diligently cultivate the awakening to the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata.
Because they have fully realized unimpeded understanding and manifest it to sentient beings, they diligently cultivate the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), turning it until—
Because it is the mind of all sentient beings. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the diligent cultivation of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of resolute understanding (*adhimukti*). What are the ten? They are:
first, the supreme resolute understanding, because of planting and honoring roots of goodness; second, the... adornment... [text fragment].
The resolute conviction of solemnity, because it gives rise to various kinds of adornments; the resolute conviction of vastness, because its mind has never been narrow or inferior;

the resolute conviction of quiescence, because it is able to enter the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); the resolute conviction of universality, because the arousal of the thought of enlightenment reaches everywhere;
the resolute conviction of capability, because it is able to receive the empowerment of the Buddha’s power; and the resolute conviction of firmness...
It is the resolute understanding that crushes and destroys all demonic activities; the resolute understanding of clarity and discernment that thoroughly knows all karmic retributions;
the resolute understanding of manifestation that can manifest supernormal powers at will; the resolute understanding of succession that receives the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
and the resolute understanding of mastery that attains Buddhahood according to one’s will and at any time. This is...
There are ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, definitive understanding.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of definitive understanding by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know all worlds. What are these ten?
That is to say: knowing that all worlds enter into one world; knowing that one world enters into all worlds;
knowing that all worlds are entirely pervaded by the body of a single Tathāgata and a single lotus seat;
knowing that all worlds are like empty space; knowing that all worlds are endowed with the adornments of a Buddha; and knowing all worlds...
The Bodhisattvas are fully pervasive. They know all worlds entering into a single pore; they know all worlds entering into the body of a single sentient being;
they know that all worlds, with their single Buddha-bodhi tree and single Buddha-maṇḍala, are entirely encompassed;
they know a single sound pervading all worlds, causing all sentient beings to each individually understand and give rise to thoughts.
Rejoicing. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the vast and definitive understanding of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Buddha-field.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of definitive understandings by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know the realm of sentient beings.
What are the ten? They are: knowing that the fundamental nature of the entire realm of sentient beings is without reality; knowing...
They know that the entire realm of sentient beings enters the body of a single sentient being; they know that the entire realm of sentient beings enters the body of a bodhisattva;
they know that the entire realm of sentient beings enters the Tathāgatagarbha; they know that the body of a single sentient being universally enters the entire realm of sentient beings;
they know that the entire realm of sentient beings is all capable of being a vessel for the Buddhadharma; they know one...
They manifest the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors according to the desires of all realms of sentient beings.
They know how to manifest the tranquil deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas according to the desires of all realms of sentient beings.
They know how to manifest the bodies adorned with the merits of bodhisattvas for all realms of sentient beings. They know how to manifest the body of a Tathāgata for all realms of sentient beings.
Their marks and signs are serene, and their majestic deportment awakens sentient beings. These are the ten.

If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great power of certain understanding. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of habitual tendencies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: the habitual tendency of the bodhicitta; the habitual tendency of roots of goodness; [and so forth].
The habitual tendencies of teaching and transforming sentient beings; the habitual tendency of seeing Buddhas; the habitual tendency of taking birth in pure worlds;
the habitual tendency of practice; the habitual tendency of vows; the habitual tendency of the perfections (*pāramitā*); the habitual tendency of contemplating the equality of all phenomena;
and the habitual tendency of the distinctions between various realms—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will forever be free from [the view of] a single [self].
They sever all habitual tendencies of affliction and attain the Tathāgata’s great wisdom—the wisdom that discerns between habitual tendencies and the absence of habitual tendencies.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of "grasping" by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not cease their bodhisattva practices. What are these ten? They are:
grasping the realm of all sentient beings in order to bring them ultimately to transformation; grasping all worlds in order to ultimately adorn them...
Because it is pure; because it takes up the practice of the bodhisattva path as an offering to the Tathāgatas;

because it takes up the accumulation of roots of goodness that result in the marks and signs of excellence of all Buddhas; because it takes up great compassion that extinguishes the suffering of all sentient beings;

because it takes up great loving-kindness that bestows upon all sentient beings the bliss of omniscience; and because it takes up the perfections that accumulate the various adornments of a bodhisattva.
They grasp through skillful means because they manifest [themselves] in all places; they grasp for the sake of awakening because they attain unimpeded knowledge.
In brief, Bodhisattvas grasp all phenomena because they clearly perceive them everywhere with wise intelligence.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these graspings, they will be able to continue the Bodhisattva practices without interruption.

They attain the unsurpassed, non-apprehendable Dharma of all Tathāgatas. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of cultivation for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the cultivation of the various pāramitās;
the cultivation of study; the cultivation of wisdom; the cultivation of meaning; the cultivation of the Dharma; the cultivation of renunciation; the cultivation of manifestation;
the cultivation of diligent practice without indolence; the cultivation of the attainment of perfect enlightenment; and the cultivation of turning the wheel of the True Dharma.
The wheel of Dharma—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unsurpassed cultivation of all dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the Buddha-dharmas. What are these ten?
That is to say: by not being separated from spiritual friends, one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma; by deep faith in the Buddha’s words, one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma;
by not slandering the True Dharma, one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma; and by dedicating immeasurable and inexhaustible roots of goodness, one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma.
They achieve the Buddha-dharma by resolving with faith in the boundless realm of the Tathāgata; they achieve the Buddha-dharma by knowing the realm of all worlds;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by not abandoning the realm of the Dharma-realm; they achieve the Buddha-dharma by remaining far removed from the realms of all Māras;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by maintaining right mindfulness of the realm of all Buddhas; they joyfully seek the Tathāgata...
The accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma through the sphere of the ten powers—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will achieve the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.

O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may fall away from the Buddha-dharma that they should avoid. What are the ten? They are: falling away through disparaging spiritual friends;...
One loses the Buddha-dharma by fearing the suffering of birth and death; one loses the Buddha-dharma by wearying of practicing the bodhisattva path;
one loses the Buddha-dharma by not delighting in abiding in the world; one loses the Buddha-dharma by being attached to meditative absorption;
one loses the Buddha-dharma by grasping at roots of goodness; one loses the Buddha-dharma by slandering the true Dharma; and one loses the Buddha-dharma by severing the bodhisattva practice.
The Dharma. These ten lead to the loss of the Buddha-dharma: delighting in the paths of the two vehicles, and harboring resentment toward bodhisattvas.
If bodhisattvas abide in these [teachings], they enter the bodhisattva path of non-retrogression (*niyāma*).
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of paths of non-retrogression for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows: the birth of *prajñāpāramitā*...
First, to practice the *pāramitās* while constantly observing all sentient beings;
second, to distance oneself from all views while liberating all sentient beings bound by views;
third, to not dwell upon any signs while not abandoning sentient beings who cling to signs; fourth, to transcend the triple world while remaining ever-present in all worlds.
To be eternally free from afflictions while dwelling together with all sentient beings is the fifth.
To have attained the dharma of freedom from desire, yet always to feel great compassion and pity for all sentient beings who are attached to desire, is the sixth.
To always delight in tranquility, yet constantly manifest among all retinues, is the seventh. To be free from birth in the world, yet to die here and arise there.
The bodhisattva’s practice of these constitutes the eighth. To remain unstained by any worldly phenomena while not ceasing any worldly activities constitutes the ninth.
To have the awakening of all Buddhas already manifest before one while not abandoning any of the bodhisattva’s vows and practices constitutes the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten paths of transcendence for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. They emerge [from them].
They transcend the world and do not share in it, yet they do not mix with the practices of the two vehicles.
If bodhisattvas abide in this Dharma, they will attain the definitive Dharma of a bodhisattva. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of definitive Dharmas for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: being definitively born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas; being definitively...
They dwell within the realm of all Buddhas; they definitively understand the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas; they definitively abide in the various *pāramitās*;
they definitively attain entry into the assemblies of the Tathāgatas; and they definitively manifest the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
They are firmly established in the powers of the Tathāgata; they decisively penetrate the bodhi of the Buddha;
they are decisively of one body with all Tathāgatas; and they are decisively non-dual with the dwelling place of all Tathāgatas. These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give birth to the path of the Buddha-dharmas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
Following virtuous friends is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it plants roots of goodness in common with them.

Profound faith and understanding is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it knows the sovereign power of the Buddhas. Making great vows is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma.
Because their minds are vast and expansive, it is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma; because they know that karma is never lost, it is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma;
because they practice through all kalpas without weariness until the end of the future limit, it is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma;
because they manifest throughout incalculable worlds to bring sentient beings to maturity, it is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, which never ceases.
The bodhisattva practice is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it increases great compassion.
The immeasurable mind is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because in a single thought-moment it pervades the entirety of the realm of empty space.

Sublime conduct is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because what was originally practiced is never lost or destroyed. The lineage of the Tathāgata is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it causes one—
May all sentient beings joyfully resolve upon bodhicitta, for they are sustained by all wholesome dharmas. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall obtain the title of "Great Being" (Mahāpuruṣa).
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten titles of the Great Beings for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows: they are called Bodhisattvas...
Because they are born from the wisdom of bodhi, they are called mahāsattvas. Because they dwell securely in the Mahāyāna, they are called the foremost sattvas.
Because they realize the supreme dharma, they are called the victorious sattvas. Because they awaken to the supreme dharma, they are called the most excellent sattvas.
Because their wisdom is most excellent, they are called the superior sattvas; they give rise to superior diligence.
Therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed *Sattva*, because he reveals the unsurpassed Dharma.
He is called the Powerful *Sattva*, because he extensively knows the ten powers (*daśabala*). He is called the Peerless *Sattva*, because he is without equal in the world.
He is called the Inconceivable *Sattva*, because he attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment. These are the ten. If all Bodhisattvas obtain these titles, they then achieve perfection.
The Bodhisattva Path. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of paths for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
First, the single path is the bodhisattva path, because of not abandoning the solitary mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Second, the twofold path is the bodhisattva path.
Because they give rise to wisdom and skillful means, the three gates of liberation are the bodhisattva path.
Because they practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without attachment to the triple world, the four practices are the bodhisattva path.

Because they repent and eliminate karmic obstacles, rejoice in merit, respectfully honor and entreat the Tathāgatas, and skillfully dedicate [merit] without ceasing, the five faculties are the bodhisattva path.
The Path: Abiding securely in pure faith, steadfast and immovable; giving rise to great diligence until all tasks are brought to completion;
maintaining one-pointed right mindfulness without any divergent objects of focus; being skillful in knowing the methods for entering and emerging from samādhi;

and being well able to discern the sphere of wisdom—for these reasons, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) constitute the bodhisattva path. These are: the divine eye, by which one sees everything that exists within all worlds.

Through the knowledge of various forms, one knows the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings in this and other worlds. Through the divine ear, one hears the Dharma preached by all Buddhas and upholds it with mindfulness, extensively expounding it for the sake of sentient beings according to their faculties.
Through the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the minds of others with mastery and without obstruction.
Through the recollection of past lives, one remembers and knows all the kalpas of the past in order to increase roots of goodness.
The supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery manifests in various ways according to the needs of all sentient beings to be converted, so as to cause them to delight in the Dharma.

The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and gives rise to the bodhisattva practice without interruption. These seven recollections are the path of the bodhisattva.
What is called "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti) is seeing immeasurable Buddhas within a single pore in order to awaken the minds of all sentient beings.

"Recollection of the Dharma" (dharmānusmṛti) is never departing from the assembly of a single Tathāgata while personally receiving the sublime Dharma within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, expounding it according to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all beings to lead them to realization and entry. "Recollection of the Sangha" is constant...
He perceives them as a continuous succession without interruption, because he sees Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds.
He recollects relinquishment, because he understands and realizes the increase and expansion of the Bodhisattvas’ practice of relinquishment and their mind of great generosity.
He recollects ethical discipline, because he does not abandon the bodhicitta and dedicates all roots of goodness to sentient beings. He recollects the devas, constantly mindful of the Tuṣita Heaven.

Because he is a Bodhisattva who has reached the stage of being born only once more before attaining Buddhahood; because he constantly contemplates sentient beings and employs wisdom and skillful means to teach, transform, and subdue them, extending his reach universally to all without interruption;

and because he accords with the Eightfold Noble Path, which is the path of the Bodhisattva—namely, practicing the path of right view by remaining far removed from all false views, and giving rise to right thought by abandoning deluded discrimination.
Because their minds always accord with omniscience; because they constantly practice right speech, remaining free from the four faults of speech and conforming to the words of the noble ones;

because they perpetually cultivate right action to teach and transform sentient beings so that they may be tamed; because they abide securely in right livelihood, practicing the dhūtas, contentment, and correct deportment;
because they follow the four noble lineages in accordance with the conduct of enlightenment; and because they have forever abandoned all faults.
They give rise to right diligence and zealously cultivate all the ascetic practices of a bodhisattva, because they enter the ten powers of a Buddha without obstruction.
Their minds are always in right mindfulness, enabling them to remember and maintain all sounds and speech, because they have eliminated the distracted and agitated minds of the world.
The mind is constantly in right concentration, skillfully entering the inconceivable gates of liberation of a bodhisattva, because within a single samādhi one gives rise to all samādhis.
Entering the nine successive concentrations is the path of a bodhisattva; that is to say, they are free from desire, ill-will, and harm.
Yet, through all vocal actions, they preach the Dharma without obstruction, having extinguished applied and sustained thought, yet through all...
With wisdom and discernment, they teach and transform sentient beings; abandoning both craving and delight, they behold the mind of all Buddhas with great joy.

Leaving behind worldly pleasures, they accord with the supramundane bliss of the bodhisattva path. From this state of immovability, they enter the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*), yet they do not relinquish rebirth within the realms of desire and form.
Although they abide in the meditative absorption that extinguishes all perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), they nevertheless...
Because they have stilled the practices of bodhisattvas, training in the ten powers of a Buddha is the path of a bodhisattva. These are:
the wisdom that skillfully knows what is possible and what is impossible; the wisdom that skillfully knows the causes and effects of the karma of all sentient beings—past, future, and present;

the wisdom that skillfully knows the differences among the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to their needs; and the wisdom that skillfully knows all sentient beings...

The wisdom of various and immeasurable natures; the skillful wisdom that knows the distinctions among the inferior, middling, and superior understandings of all sentient beings and enables them to enter the Dharma through skillful means;

the wisdom that universally manifests the physical forms, marks, and majestic deportment of the Tathāgatas throughout all worlds, all lands, all three periods of time, and all kalpas, yet does not abandon the practices of a bodhisattva; and the skillful knowledge of all things.

The wisdom that gives rise to the gates of liberation for all bodhisattvas through skillful means—whether they be the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, whether defiled or pure, timely or untimely;
the wisdom that knows the distinctions of all sentient beings as they die here and are born there within the various realms of existence;
and the wisdom that, in a single thought-moment, fully knows the number of all kalpas throughout the three periods of time. [He] skillfully knows all...

To attain the knowledge that extinguishes the desires, latent tendencies, afflictions, and habitual traces of sentient beings, yet not to abandon the various practices of a bodhisattva—this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed path of skillful means of all Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have immeasurable paths, immeasurable aids to the path, and immeasurable cultivations.
The Path. The Path of Immeasurable Adornments. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of immeasurable paths for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

What are these ten? They are as follows: because space is immeasurable, the path of the Bodhisattva is also immeasurable; because the dharma-realm is boundless, the path of the Bodhisattva is also immeasurable;
because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the path of the Bodhisattva is also immeasurable; because the world... [is immeasurable], the path of the Bodhisattva is also immeasurable.
Because the realms are boundless, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable. Because the number of kalpas cannot be exhausted, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
Because the linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings are immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
Because the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable. Because the voice of the Buddha is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also [immeasurable].

Immeasurable. Because the power of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable. Because the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of immeasurable aids to the path for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, namely:
as the realm of empty space is immeasurable, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path immeasurable.

As the dharma-realm is boundless, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path boundless. As the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path inexhaustible.
As the world-systems are limitless, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path limitless.
Just as the number of kalpas cannot be fully described, so too the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path cannot be fully described by all the worlds.

Just as the linguistic conventions of sentient beings are immeasurable, so too the wisdom produced by the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path in knowing these linguistic conventions is immeasurable.
Just as the body of a Tathāgata is immeasurable, so too the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path pervades all sentient beings.

The births in all lands, all worlds, and all eons are likewise immeasurable. Just as the Buddha’s voice is immeasurable, a single word or sound uttered by a bodhisattva pervades the entire dharma-realm; because there is not a single sentient being who does not hear and know it, the aids to the path they accumulate are also immeasurable.
Just as the Buddha’s powers are immeasurable, the bodhisattva, relying on the power of the Tathāgata, accumulates the aids to the path.
It is also immeasurable. Just as the wisdom of all-knowledge is immeasurable, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the factors conducive to enlightenment immeasurable.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of immeasurable paths of cultivation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? First, [the path of]...

It is the cultivation of neither coming nor going, because there is no activity of body, speech, or mind; the cultivation of neither increase nor decrease, because it is according to its original nature;
the cultivation of neither existence nor non-existence, because it lacks intrinsic nature;

and the cultivation that is like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, a mirage in the heat, or the moon in water, because it is free from all attachment. It is emptiness.
The cultivation of signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action, because one clearly perceives the three realms while accumulating merit without ceasing;
the cultivation that is ineffable, beyond speech, and detached from verbal expression, because it is far removed from the establishment of conventional designations;

the cultivation of the indestructible dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because wisdom directly knows all phenomena; and the cultivation of the indestructible *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because one universally enters into reality.
Because it is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the limit of space (*ākāśakoṭi*); because one cultivates vast wisdom, for all that is performed has inexhaustible power;

because one dwells in the cultivation of the equality of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), seeing all phenomena directly without doubt;
these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the state of a Tathāgata.
The cultivation of the supreme skillfulness of omniscience. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of paths of adornment for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

What are these ten? O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not depart from the desire realm, yet enters the meditative concentrations, liberations, and various samādhis of the form and formless realms; furthermore, they do not undergo rebirth therein because of them. This is the first.
The first path of adornment is to manifest wisdom and enter the path of the śrāvakas, yet not to attain liberation through this path;

this is the second path of adornment. To manifest wisdom and enter the path of the pratyekabuddhas, while giving rise to great compassion without ceasing, is the third path of adornment. Although surrounded by a retinue of humans and devas...
Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of beautiful women who attend to him with song and dance, he never for a moment abandons dhyāna, liberation, and the various samādhis.
This is the fourth adornment of the path: to experience all sensual pleasures together with all sentient beings while sharing in their enjoyment.
Even for a single moment, they have never abandoned the Bodhisattva’s samādhi of equanimity; this is the fifth adornment of the path.
Having reached the further shore of all worlds, they are entirely unattached to worldly dharmas, yet they do not abandon the practice of delivering sentient beings;
this is the sixth adornment of the path. They abide securely in the right path and right wisdom.

Possessing right view, they are able to demonstrate entry into all false paths without taking them to be real or grasping at them as pure, thereby causing those sentient beings to distance themselves from false teachings;
this is the seventh adornment of the path. They constantly and skillfully uphold the pure precepts of the Tathāgata, such that their actions of body, speech, and mind are free from all faults;
desiring to transform sentient beings who have violated the precepts, they manifest the practice of one [precept].

Regarding all the conduct of ordinary fools: although they have already perfected pure merit and dwell in the bodhisattva path, they manifest birth in all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and in various perilous and difficult places such as poverty, so as to cause those sentient beings to attain liberation.
Yet, in reality, the bodhisattva is not born into those realms. This is the eighth adornment of the path.
Without relying on the instruction of others, they attain unimpeded eloquence and the light of wisdom that universally illuminates all Buddha-dharmas.
They are sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas and share the same Dharma-body as all Buddhas.
They accomplish all firm, great-person, pure, and secret dharmas, and abide securely in all equal vehicles. All Buddhas...
All realms appear before him. Possessing the full radiance of all worldly wisdom, he perceives the realms of all sentient beings.
He is able to act as a Dharma-teacher for sentient beings, demonstrating the quest for the True Dharma without ever resting.
Although he is in truth the unsurpassed teacher of sentient beings, he demonstrates the practice of honoring his ācāryas and upādhyāyas. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through skillful means, dwells upon the bodhisattva path and manifests itself according to what is appropriate for each being.

This is the ninth adornment of the path: the perfection of roots of goodness, the culmination of all practices, the collective consecration by all Tathāgatas, the reaching of the further shore of mastery over all dharmas, and the crowning of the head with the turban of unimpeded dharma.
His body pervades all worlds, universally manifesting the unimpeded body of a Tathāgata. He possesses supreme mastery over all phenomena and has reached the ultimate consummation.
He turns the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma and has fully accomplished all the sovereign qualities of Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests birth in all lands, together with the three...

The Buddhas of all worlds share the same realm, yet they do not abandon the practices of a bodhisattva; they do not forsake the dharma of a bodhisattva; they do not slacken in the karma of a bodhisattva;

they do not depart from the path of a bodhisattva; they do not relax the decorum of a bodhisattva; they do not sever the aspirations of a bodhisattva; they do not cease the skillful means of a bodhisattva;
they do not terminate the deeds performed by a bodhisattva; and they do not grow weary of the bodhisattva’s function of generating and sustaining beings. Not...

This halts the bodhisattva’s power of maintenance. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva desires to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they contemplate the gateways to all-knowledge and cultivate the bodhisattva practices without ceasing.
This is the tenth adornment of the path. If bodhisattvas abide in this dharma, they will attain the unsurpassed, great adornment of the Tathāgata.
The Way. Furthermore, one does not abandon the bodhisattva path. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of feet for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these ten? They are:
the foot of ethical discipline, because all supreme great vows are fully accomplished; the foot of diligence, because one does not regress in gathering all factors conducive to enlightenment;
and the foot of supernormal powers, because one causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their inclinations.
The foot of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) is so called because one travels from one buddha-field to all buddha-fields without ever leaving a single one.

The foot of profound resolve (*adhyāśayapāda*) is so called because one seeks and aspires to all supreme dharmas. The foot of firm vow (*praṇidhānapāda*) is so called because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion.

The foot of compliance (*anulomapāda*) is so called because one does not contradict the instructions of any venerable one. The foot of delighting in the Dharma (*dharmārāmapāda*) is so called because one hears and retains all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas without weariness.
Because they are free from indolence; because they preach the Dharma rain for the sake of the multitude with no timidity;

and because they have fully distanced themselves from all evils through their practice. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and most supreme feet of the Tathāgata.
With a single step, they are able to reach every world-system. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of hands. What are the ten? They are: the hand of profound faith, because they resolutely accept and ultimately uphold all that is spoken by the Buddha;
the hand of generosity, because they satisfy all those who come seeking according to their desires;
the hand of greeting with a welcoming mind, because they extend their right palm to receive and welcome others; the hand of making offerings...
The hands of all Buddhas are those that gather a multitude of merits without weariness; the hands of great learning and skillful means are those that completely sever all doubts of sentient beings;
the hands that cause one to transcend the triple world are those that bestow [liberation] upon sentient beings to pull them out from the mire of desire;
