the hands that place [beings] on the other shore are those that rescue drowning beings from within the four violent currents; the hands that do not begrudge the True Dharma are those that [bestow] all that is wondrous...
Because they fully reveal all dharmas; because they skillfully employ the hands of various treatises to use the medicine of wisdom to extinguish the diseases of body and mind;
and because they constantly hold the jewel-hand of wisdom to open the light of Dharma and shatter the darkness of afflictions—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed hand of the Tathāgata, which universally covers all worlds throughout the ten directions.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of bellies belonging to Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the belly free from flattery and crookedness, because the mind is pure;
the belly free from illusion and hypocrisy, because the nature is straightforward; the belly that is not false or artificial, because it is without treachery or partiality;
the belly free from deception and plundering, because there is no greed for any object; and the belly that severs afflictions, because it is endowed with wisdom.
Therefore, it is because the belly of the pure mind is free from all evils; because the belly of observing food contemplates the Dharma as it truly is;
because the belly of observing non-action awakens to dependent origination; because the belly of awakening to all paths of renunciation brings the profound mind to full maturity;
because the belly that is free from the stains of all extreme views causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-belly.

Therefore, these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast, and great belly of a Tathāgata, which is fully capable of containing all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of treasuries.
What are these ten? They are as follows: the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, because it reveals the immeasurable majesty and virtue of the Buddha-dharma;
the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which increases the seeds of the Dharma, because it gives rise to the vast radiance of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which sustains the lineage of the monastic community, for it enables them to enter the wheel of non-retrogression.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which awakens those sentient beings fixed in right determination, for it skillfully accords with the proper time without exceeding even a single thought-moment.

The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which brings to ultimate maturity those sentient beings of indeterminate nature, for it ensures that their causal continuity remains uninterrupted. [It is also for the sake of those] fixed in error...
The arousal of great compassion by sentient beings is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it causes all future causes to be fully accomplished.
The fulfillment of the ten powers of a Buddha through indestructible causes is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it possesses the invincible roots of goodness that subdue the armies of Māra.
The supreme, fearless Great Lion’s Roar is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it causes all sentient beings to rejoice.
Because of joy, attaining the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Because wisdom universally enters all places, universally knowing all sentient beings, all lands, all dharmas, and all Buddhas is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because one clearly perceives them all within a single thought-moment. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain them.
Then one attains the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed storehouse of great wisdom, which consists of indestructible roots of goodness.

O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of mind possessed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the mind of diligent application, because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion;
the tireless mind, because of the accumulation of the merit of the marks and signs of excellence; the mind of great valor, because it crushes and destroys...

Because of all the hosts of Māras, one practices according to the principle; because the mind eliminates all afflictions, one possesses a non-retrogressive mind that never ceases until reaching Bodhi;
because one gives rise to a pure mind, knowing the mind is unmoving and free from attachment;

because one knows the minds of sentient beings and, according to their inclinations and desires, seeks to lead them to liberation; and because one causes them to enter the Great Brahma of the Buddha-dharma.
The mind that abides in knowing the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings, so as not to rescue and protect them by means of separate vehicles;
the mind of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action, which perceives the characteristics of the triple world without grasping or attachment;
and the mind adorned with the supreme treasury of the *svastika* mark, firm and adamantine like a vajra—such a mind cannot be moved even by as many māras as there are sentient beings.
Because of its hairiness. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s heart, which is the treasury of the light of supreme great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of donning of armor. What are the ten? They are:
donning the armor of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), in order to rescue and protect all sentient beings; donning the armor of great compassion (*karuṇā*), in order to endure...
They don the armor of great vows because of all sufferings; they don the armor of dedication because they bring all actions to ultimate completion;
they don the armor of merit because they benefit all sentient beings.
They don the armor of the *pāramitās* in order to deliver all sentient beings; they don the armor of wisdom in order to extinguish the darkness of afflictions for all living beings;
they don the armor of skillful means in order to give rise to roots of goodness through universal gates;
they don the armor of the firm and undistracted mind of omniscience in order not to delight in other vehicles; and they don the armor of single-minded resolve.
Because they are free from doubt and hesitation regarding all phenomena—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they are clad in the unsurpassed armor of the Tathāgata and are able to utterly crush and subdue all the armies of Māra.
Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of weapons. What are the ten? They are as follows: giving is the weapon of the Bodhisattva.
The precepts are the weapon of the bodhisattva for the sake of destroying all stinginess.
Equanimity is the weapon of the bodhisattva for the sake of abandoning all transgressions. Wisdom is the weapon of the bodhisattva for the sake of extinguishing all afflictions.
Right livelihood is the weapon of the bodhisattva for the sake of remaining far removed from all [unwholesome ways].
Because of wrong livelihood, skillful means are the weapon of a bodhisattva, for they are manifested in all places.
Briefly stated, all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they deliver sentient beings through the gateway of the afflictions.
Birth and death are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they do not sever the bodhisattva practice while teaching and transforming sentient beings. Thus it is said.
The reality of things as they are (*yathābhūta-dharma*) is the weapon of the bodhisattva, for it can shatter all attachments.
Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the weapon of the bodhisattva, for it does not abandon the gateways of bodhisattva practice. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they are able to eliminate all the afflictions and fetters accumulated by sentient beings throughout the long night. O Son of the Buddha, the bodhi...
The Mahāsattva has ten kinds of heads. What are the ten? They are: the head of *nirvāṇa*, because its crown cannot be seen;
the head of veneration, because it is honored and saluted by all humans and devas; the head of vast resolute conviction, because it is the most supreme within the trichiliocosm;
the head of the foremost roots of goodness, because all sentient beings of the three realms offer it worship; the head of bearing... [the burden].
It is the head of all sentient beings, because it accomplishes the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head;
it is the head that does not disparage others, because it is always supreme and honored in all places; it is the head of Prajñāpāramitā, because it nurtures all dharmas of merit;
it is the head corresponding to skillful means and wisdom, because it universally manifests bodies identical to all classes of beings; it is the head that teaches and transforms all sentient beings.
Because they take all sentient beings as their disciples; because they protect the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas and are foremost in ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, great wisdom-eye of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of eyes, namely: the fleshly eye...
The eye [of flesh] because it sees all forms; the divine eye because it sees the minds of all sentient beings;
the wisdom-eye because it sees the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings; the Dharma-eye because it sees the true reality of all phenomena;
the Buddha-eye because it sees the ten powers of the Tathāgata; the knowledge-eye because it cognizes and perceives all phenomena; and the light-eye because it sees the radiance of the Buddhas.
The eye of birth and death sees nirvana; the unimpeded eye sees without obstruction;
the all-knowing eye sees the universal dharma-realm. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great eye of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of ears. What are they?
There are ten [aspects]: namely, hearing sounds of praise, one eliminates craving; hearing sounds of disparagement, one eliminates anger;
hearing explanations of the two vehicles, one does not cling to them nor seek them; hearing of the Bodhisattva path, one rejoices with exultation;

hearing of the various places of suffering and hardship such as the hells, one gives rise to great compassion and makes vast vows; and hearing of the superior and wondrous matters of humans and devas.
Knowing that all these are impermanent phenomena, upon hearing the praises of the Buddhas' merits, they apply themselves with diligent vigor to bring them quickly to fulfillment.
Upon hearing the teachings on the six perfections, the four means of integration, and other such dharmas, they resolve to practice them, vowing to reach the further shore.
Hearing all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they know them all to be like echoes; they enter into ineffable, profound, and wondrous meanings.

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly hear the true Dharma without even a moment’s rest, yet they never abandon the work of transforming sentient beings. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas accomplish these...
Dharma, one then attains the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of noses belonging to Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: hearing various foul odors, they do not perceive them as foul; hearing various fragrant scents, they do not perceive them as fragrant;
hearing both fragrance and stench, their minds remain equanimous; and being neither attracted by fragrance nor repelled by stench, they abide in impartiality (*upekṣā*).
If they hear the scents of the clothing, bedding, and limbs of sentient beings, they are able to know their conduct characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, or their equal proportions.
If they hear the scents of hidden treasures, grasses, trees, and so forth, they clearly discern them all as if they were right before their eyes.
If they hear the sounds of sentient beings from as low as the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), [they likewise understand them].
Through the fragrance of these [bodhisattvas], they know all the practices performed by those in the past.

If they smell the fragrance of the generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom of the śrāvakas, they abide in the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) without allowing it to be distracted or moved.

If they smell the fragrance of all bodhisattva practices, they enter the stage of the Tathāgata through impartial wisdom (samatā-prajñā). Upon smelling the fragrance of the realm of the wisdom of all Buddhas, they likewise do not abandon it.
Abandoning all bodhisattva practices—this is the tenth. If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s immeasurable and boundless pure nose.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of tongues. What are the ten? They are:
the tongue that reveals and expounds the inexhaustible conduct of sentient beings; the tongue that reveals and expounds the inexhaustible... [and so forth].
The tongue of the Dharma-gate; the tongue that praises the inexhaustible merits of all Buddhas; the tongue that expounds eloquence and rhetoric without end;
the tongue that elucidates the Mahāyāna and aids the Path; the tongue that universally covers the empty space of the ten directions; and the tongue that shines universally upon all Buddha-fields.
The tongue that causes all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding; the tongue that causes all Buddhas to rejoice;
the tongue that subdues all demons and non-Buddhists, eliminates all birth-and-death and afflictions, and leads them to nirvana—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas accomplish these qualities, they shall attain the supreme [tongue] of the Tathāgata that pervades all Buddha-lands.
Tongue. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of bodies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the human body, for the sake of teaching and transforming all humans;
the non-human body, for the sake of teaching and transforming those in the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm;

the celestial body, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; and the body of a learner (*śaikṣa*), which is manifested as a demonstration.

Because of the stage of training; because of manifesting the stage of an Arhat through the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); because of teaching and transforming others to lead them into the stage of a Pratyekabuddha through the body of a Pratyekabuddha;
because of bringing about the fulfillment of the Mahāyāna through the body of a Bodhisattva; because of the consecration with the water of wisdom through the body of a Tathāgata;
because of the skillful production of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*); and because of manifesting the untainted Dharma-body (*anāsravadharmakāya*) through effortless spontaneity.
Because it is the body of all sentient beings; these are the ten. If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed body of a Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of intention. What are the ten?
What is called the foremost mind, because it gives rise to all roots of goodness; the abiding mind, because its profound faith is firm and unshakable;
the deeply penetrating mind, because it understands in accordance with the Buddha-dharma; the internally comprehending mind, because it knows the inclinations of the hearts of all sentient beings;
the undisturbed mind, because it is not mixed with any afflictions; and the luminously pure mind, because adventitious defilements cannot stain it.
Because they are focused; because they skillfully observe the thoughts of sentient beings without missing a single moment;
because they skillfully discern their actions so that no error ever arises in any instance; because they closely guard the sense faculties, keeping the mind subdued and preventing it from wandering;
and because they skillfully enter samādhi, deeply entering the Buddha’s samādhi without notions of self or what belongs to a self. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas...
Abiding in this Dharma, one attains the supreme intention of all Buddhas. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: the practice of hearing the Dharma, because of loving and delighting in the Dharma; the practice of expounding the Dharma...
Because they benefit sentient beings; because they practice the subduing of their own minds, free from greed, hatred, delusion, and fear;

because they practice the teachings of the desire realm to transform sentient beings of the desire realm; because they practice the samādhis of the form and formless realms to swiftly cause [the mind] to turn back;
because they practice the conduct directed toward the meaning of the Dharma to swiftly attain wisdom; and because they practice with mastery in all places of birth to transform sentient beings.

Therefore, it is because of the practice of performing prostrations and making offerings to all Buddhas in all Buddha-fields; the practice of not severing the continuity of birth and death within nirvāṇa;
and the practice of fulfilling all Buddha-dharmas by not abandoning the bodhisattva practices. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s practice of neither coming nor going.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of abodes for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the abode of the bodhicitta, because it is never forgotten;
the abode of the pāramitās, because one does not grow weary of the factors conducive to enlightenment; and the abode of teaching the Dharma, because it increases wisdom.

He dwells in *araṇya* because he has realized great meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). He dwells in accordance with all-knowledge through the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), contentment, and the four noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*), characterized by few desires and few activities.
He dwells in profound faith because he bears the burden of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). He dwells in proximity to the Tathāgata because he trains in the Buddha’s majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
He dwells in the production of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because he has perfected great wisdom (*mahājñāna*). He dwells in the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*) because he is fulfilled.

Because of the bestowal of prophecy; because of abiding at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and being fully endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the Buddha-dharmas. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme abode of omniscience. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of seats for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the seat of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), which brings forth the ten paths of wholesome action; ... [text continues] ... [The text continues with the remaining nine seats. ... [text continues] ... [The text concludes with: ... because of the bestowal of prophecy; because of abiding at the site of enlightenment and being fully endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the Buddha-dharmas. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme abode of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of seats for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the seat of a wheel-turning monarch, which brings forth the ten paths of wholesome action.
Therefore, the Four Heavenly Kings sit because they establish the Buddha-dharma with sovereign mastery over all worlds;
Śakra sits because he serves as the supreme lord for all sentient beings; and Brahmā sits because he has attained mastery over the minds of both himself and others.
The Lion’s Seat is so called because it is able to preach the Dharma; the Seat of the True Dharma because it reveals and teaches through the power of dhāraṇī and eloquence;
the Firm Seat because of the ultimate fulfillment of one's vows; the Seat of Great Loving-kindness because it causes all evil sentient beings to rejoice;
the Seat of Great Compassion because it endures all suffering without weariness; and the Vajra Seat because it subdues all māras and non-Buddhists.
Therefore, these constitute ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the seat of the Tathāgata’s unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of reclining for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: reclining in tranquility, because the body and mind are serene;
reclining in meditative concentration, because of practicing according to the principle; reclining in samādhi, because the body and mind are supple...

Because it is gentle; because Brahmā lies down without causing affliction to himself or others; because one who has performed good deeds lies down without regret later on; because one with right faith lies down unshakable;
because one on the right path lies down to be awakened by virtuous friends; because one with sublime vows lies down through skillful dedication;
because one whose every task is finished lies down having accomplished what was to be done; and because one who has relinquished all effort lies down in total mastery.

Because of cultivation. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great Dharma-resting of the Tathāgata and will be able to awaken all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten places of abiding. What are the ten? They are:
taking great loving-kindness as their place of abiding toward all sentient beings; [taking great compassion as their place of abiding]; ... [and so forth].

Because they give rise to an impartial mind, they take great compassion as their dwelling place; because they do not disparage those who have not yet studied, they take great sympathetic joy as their dwelling place;
because they are free from all sorrow and affliction, they take great equanimity as their dwelling place;
and because they are equal toward the conditioned and the unconditioned, they take all the *pāramitās* as their dwelling place, with the bodhicitta as their foremost.
Therefore, because they skillfully observe all things as empty as their place of abiding; because they do not emerge from the state of correctness by taking the signless as their place of abiding;
because they observe the taking of birth by taking the wishless as their place of abiding;
because the dharma of patience is brought to fulfillment by taking mindfulness and wisdom as their place of abiding; and because they take the equality of all phenomena as their place of abiding.

Because they receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and unimpeded dwelling place of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of spheres of activity for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: taking right mindfulness as the sphere of practice, because of fulfilling the foundations of mindfulness;

taking the various realms of existence as the sphere of practice, because of correctly awakening to the course of the Dharma; taking wisdom as the sphere of practice, because of attaining the joy of the Buddhas;
taking the perfections as the sphere of practice, because of fulfilling the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); and taking the four means of integration...
Because they take the sphere of activity for teaching and transforming sentient beings as their domain; because they take the accumulation of roots of goodness within birth and death as their domain;
because they take engaging in various conversations and play with all sentient beings as their domain to teach them according to their needs so that they may forever be liberated;
and because they take supernatural powers as their domain to know the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings. By means of...
Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the sphere of activity because it is associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*);
the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the sphere of activity because one accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) without interrupting the bodhisattva practices. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
The fifth major section, "The Fifty Kinds of Bodily Action," contains fifty gates that answer fifty questions, clarifying the modes of practice within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Now, these are distributed according to the gradual progression of the ten stages: the first stage has ten gates; the second stage has six gates;
the third and fourth stages each have five gates; the fifth stage has two gates; the sixth stage has one gate; the seventh and eighth stages each have three gates; and the ninth...
There are two sections. Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are thirteen gates. Now, first, the ten gates clarify the practice within the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
What is called "stage" refers to the stage of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the ultimate *dharmakāya* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) realized by the Buddhas.
Because it is now the ground traversed by Bodhisattvas, it is termed a "stage" (*bhūmi*); for a stage can both support all things and give birth to them. This refers to the preceding three...

The seeds of causes cultivated by the wise were previously entirely dispersed; now they are gathered into the stages (*bhūmi*), from each of which arise the merits that adorn the *dharmakāya*, thereby adorning the substance of the *saṃbhogakāya*. For this reason, they are designated by the name "stages.
Thus, at the conclusion of the preceding dedication, it is summarized as ten types of bodies. This is because all prior practices are subsumed within the *dharmakāya*. Now...

Regarding the fact that the first stage (bhūmi) takes the three karmas of body, speech, and mind as primary: this precisely reveals that the two practices of merit and wisdom adorn and constitute the resultant body.
Therefore, the first stage encompasses all previous deep planting of roots of goodness, the accumulation of the aids to the path, and so forth.

Thus, one accomplishes the ten kinds of bodies of great wisdom. If it were not for the adornment of the wondrous practice that is, in its singular progression, identical with the nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), how could one possibly attain the merits of the ocean of marks and minor characteristics of the ten bodies on the level of fruition?

Therefore, at the beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*), immediately following the conclusion of the preceding stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one attains the most supreme purity of body, speech, and mind.

Purifying the three karmas: because sentient beings are deluded regarding the fundamental Dharma-body and falsely accept the sense-faculties and physical body, they have accumulated immeasurable and boundless defiled karma through the three karmas over countless kalpas; it is only upon reaching this stage that these are finally purified.

All merits are perfected to adorn the Dharma-body; therefore, in the first, second, and third stages, those who rely upon the vehicles of humans and devas clearly demonstrate that as their status is higher, their practice is more fundamental. If there were even a single speck of impurity, it would obstruct and obscure the celestial nature; how then could they be called the perfect Sambhogakāya? Although there are many interpretations for each of the ten gates according to the text, the general meaning is as follows: [The remainder of the passage concerns the specific meanings of the ten gates, such as the gate of the basis, the gate of the cause, the gate of the fruit, the gate of the activity, the gate of the benefit, the gate of the manifestation, the gate of the duration, the gate of the entry, the gate of the exit, and the gate of the ultimate attainment. ...the ultimate attainment is the Tathāgata’s stage, which is the perfection of all virtues. It is the fulfillment of the three bodies, the completion of the two benefits, and the ultimate destination of the four practices. It is the supreme fruit of the ten stages, the finality of the ten perfections, the culmination of the ten powers, and the ultimate realization of the ten knowledges. It is the source of the ten powers, the treasury of the ten powers, and the sovereign lord of the ten powers. It is the great master of the ten powers, the great king of the ten powers, and the great wheel-turning monarch of the ten powers. It is the great commander of the ten powers, the great leader of the ten powers, and the great guide of the ten powers. It is the great teacher of the ten powers, the great preacher of the ten powers, and the great illuminator of the ten powers. It is the great light of the ten powers, the great radiance of the ten powers, and the great brilliance of the ten powers. It is the great sun of the ten powers, the great moon of the ten powers, and the great constellation of the ten powers. It is the great ocean of the ten powers, the great mountain of the ten powers, and the great jewel of the ten powers. It is the great cloud of the ten powers, the great rain of the ten powers, and the great harvest of the ten powers. It is the great medicine of the ten powers, the great mantra of the ten powers, and the great liberation of the ten powers. It is the great path of the ten powers, the great vehicle of the ten powers, and the great city of the ten powers. It is the great palace of the ten powers, the great throne of the ten powers, and the great canopy of the ten powers. It is the great banner of the ten powers, the great drum of the ten powers, and the great conch of the ten powers. It is the great mirror of the ten powers, the great sword of the ten powers, and the great armor of the ten powers. It is the great net of the ten powers, the great hook of the ten powers, and the great noose of the ten powers. It is the great bell of the ten powers, the great staff of the ten powers, and the great wheel of the ten powers. It is the great wisdom of the ten powers, the great compassion of the ten powers, and the great skillful means of the ten powers. It is the great vow of the ten powers, the great practice of the ten powers, and the great fruition of the ten powers. It is the great merit of the ten powers, the great wisdom of the ten powers, and the great liberation of the ten powers. It is the great power of the ten powers, the great fearlessness of the ten powers, and the great unobstructedness of the ten powers. It is the great sovereignty of the ten powers, the great mastery of the ten powers, and the great autonomy of the ten powers. It is the great purity of the ten powers, the great clarity of the ten powers, and the great perfection of the ten powers. It is the great equality of the ten powers, the great non-duality of the ten powers, and the great non-conceptuality of the ten powers. It is the great emptiness of the ten powers, the great signlessness of the ten powers, and the great wishlessness of the ten powers. It is the great non-arising of the ten powers, the great non-ceasing of the ten powers, and the great non-abiding of the ten powers. It is the great non-coming of the ten powers, the great non-going of the ten powers, and the great non-existence of the ten powers. It is the great non-grasping of the ten powers, the great non-rejecting of the ten powers, and the great non-attachment of the ten powers. It is the great non-increase of the ten powers, the great non-decrease of the ten powers, and the great non-change of the ten powers. It is the great non-birth of the ten powers, the great non-death of the ten powers, and the great non-suffering of the ten powers. It is the great non-self of the ten powers, the great non-person of the ten powers, and the great non-living-being of the ten powers. It is the great non-soul of the ten powers, the great non-individual of the ten powers, and the great non-substantiality of the ten powers. It is the great non-dharma of the ten powers, the great non-mark of the ten powers, and the great non-characteristic of the ten powers. It is the great non-cause of the ten powers, the great non-condition of the ten powers, and the great non-result of the ten powers. It is the great non-effect of the ten powers, the great non-activity of the ten powers, and the great non-function of the ten powers. It is the great non-entering of the ten powers, the great non-exiting of the ten powers, and the great non-staying of the ten powers. It is the great non-beginning of the ten powers, the great non-middle of the ten powers, and the great non-end of the ten powers. It is the great non-past of the ten powers, the great non-future of the ten powers, and the great non-present of the ten powers. It is the great non-world of the ten powers, the great non-direction of the ten powers, and the great non-location of the ten powers. It is the great non-form of the ten powers, the great non-sound of the ten powers, the great non-smell of the ten powers, the great non-taste of the ten powers, the great non-touch of the ten powers, and the great non-phenomenon of the ten powers. It is the great non-eye of the ten powers, the great non-ear of the ten powers, the great non-nose of the ten powers, the great non-tongue of the ten powers, the great non-body of the ten powers, and the great non-mind of the ten powers. It is the great non-form of the ten powers, the great non-sound of the ten powers, the great non-smell of the ten powers, the great non-taste of the ten powers, the great non-touch of the ten powers, and the great non-dharma of the ten powers. It is the great non-consciousness of the ten powers, the great non-contact of the ten powers, the great non-feeling of the ten powers, the great non-thirst of the ten powers, the great non-grasping of the ten powers, and the great non-becoming of the ten powers. It is the great non-birth of the ten powers, the great non-aging of the ten powers, the great non-sickness of the ten powers, and the great non-death of the ten powers. It is the great non-grief of the ten powers, the great non-lamentation of the ten powers, the great non-suffering of the ten powers, the great non-distress of the ten powers, the great non-despair of the ten powers, and the great non-uprooting of the ten powers. It is the great non-ignorance of the ten powers, the great non-view of the ten powers, the great non-affliction of the ten powers, and the great non-purification of the ten powers. It is the great non-defilement of the ten powers, the great non-purity of the ten powers, and the great non-liberation of the ten powers. It is the great non-bondage of the ten powers, the great non-release of the ten powers, and the great non-attainment of the ten powers. It is the great non-knowledge of the ten powers, the great non-wisdom of the ten powers, and the great non-enlightenment of the ten powers. It is the great non-Buddha of the ten powers, the great non-Dharma of the ten powers, and the great non-Saṅgha of the ten powers. It is the great non-preaching of the ten powers, the great non-hearing of the ten powers, the great non-understanding of the ten powers, and the great non-practice of the ten powers. It is the great non-realization of the ten powers, the great non-attainment of the ten powers, and the great non-fruition of the ten powers. It is the great non-merit of the ten powers, the great non-virtue of the ten powers, and the great non-liberative action of the ten powers. It is the great non-skillful means of the ten powers, the great non-expedient of the ten powers,
Nothing lies outside of this. Regarding the twenty kinds of profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), the following six gates clarify the practice within the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), the first stage is designated as the Path of True Vision (*darśanamārga*), while from the second stage onward begins the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Whereas the previous teaching involved the singular cultivation of precepts, here there is complete cultivation. Having already realized and attained the wondrous principle of perfect interfusion, it is therefore called "profound mind."

Because practice that accords with principle pervades the entire dharma-realm in each and every instance, the first two gates clarify the purity of initiation, explicitly demonstrating the conformity to principle.
The latter four gates are termed the purity of essence, as they manifest cultivation in accordance with the nature [of reality].

Furthermore, the ten perfections (pāramitās) that constitute this cultivation comprehensively encompass both the "virtuous dharma-gathering precept" and the "restraint-discipline precept" within the three categories of pure precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara). Its...

This definitively elucidates the precept of benefiting sentient beings. Because one possesses definitive understanding that the dharma-realm of sentient beings is equal, non-dual, and pure by nature, one practices in accordance with this essence. Each and every such practice accords with the nature of *tathatā*.

Because it is perfectly interfused and unimpeded, it is the foremost of the paths of cultivation. The thirtieth section, "The Ten Kinds of Habitual Tendencies," explains the practice within the third stage through five gates.
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): because sentient beings are deluded regarding the one true nature, they are perfumed by ignorance to form all manner of afflictive habitual tendencies.
Since the entire substance of *tathatā* (Suchness) universally constitutes these defiled habits, now—
When a Bodhisattva cultivates the practice of the Dharma-realm through the contemplative wisdom of the three preceding stages of worthiness, they disregard the nature of their afflictions.
Rather, they directly and single-mindedly rely upon the wisdom of the Dharma-realm to extensively cultivate various kinds of immeasurable and wondrous practices.
Because their contemplative wisdom is perfectly luminous, they no longer perceive any afflictions that need to be severed; thus, this is "severing without severing. Now that...

Entering the ground of the single reality (*eka-tathatā-bhūmi*), one integrates and subsumes all prior practices; each of the former defiled habits is transformed through perfuming into pure habits of bodhi.
However, were it not for these ten kinds of habitual tendencies serving as the seeds for attaining Buddhahood, there would be no means to realize the fruit of bodhi.
Therefore, from this point onward, whatever practice is cultivated is all perfumed by these ten habits, giving rise to the present manifestation.

Therefore, this constitutes true cultivation. However, while the Separate Teaching (biejiao) correctly severs the innate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from the second stage onward, in this Perfect School (yuanzong), there is no necessity to sever them further.
It suffices to cultivate by simply designating these ten habitual tendencies; thus, those tendencies are severed spontaneously without being severed.
Therefore, cultivation takes habitual tendencies as its primary focus. Next, the ten kinds of grasping [are explained].
Sentient beings, through their defiled habits, grasp at birth and death and undergo the five aggregates.
Now, the Bodhisattva, by means of these ten practices, grasps the Dharma-body; each and every practice-gate adorns and perfects the Reward-body.

Yet, were it not for this grasping, there would be no manifestation of the Reward-body’s marks and signs within the nature of the Dharma-realm. This is therefore the grasping of non-grasping. Thus it is said:

Because that which is grasped is vast, it is termed "superior grasping. The first two gates constitute the practice of aversion, while the latter three gates constitute the practice that gives rise to aversion.

The first gate correctly reveals the characteristics of cultivation; the second clarifies the superior conditions for the completion of cultivation; and the third clarifies the avoidance of regression.
Taken together, these constitute a thorough elucidation of the characteristics of cultivation throughout this single stage; therefore, the [first] three...
The first three stages are associated with the vehicles of humans and devas; the latter four stages are associated with the supramundane.

The fourth stage is the "Path of Leaving Birth" (*niyāmāvakrānti*), and the following five sections clarify the practice within these four stages. Because this stage is associated with the supramundane, it is called the "Stage of Leaving Birth.

One cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) upon reaching this position; therefore, it is the "Path of Leaving Birth. As for what is meant by "birth," it refers to the preceding three stages.

By means of ten kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one grasps the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhi*). Seeing therein both aversion and grasping is like having raw food in the stomach that has not yet been digested;
furthermore, it is because of its astringent nature and because it has not yet reached full maturity.
Therefore, one relies on superior external conditions while internally preventing decline. Upon reaching the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), the antidotes become pure and cultivation increases.

Therefore, it is established as "the ability to depart" because it can bring about the departure from that birth; it is called the "path of departing from birth" because one attains non-arising by departing from conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), thereby manifesting the maturity of practice and the departure from its coarseness.
Because internal qualities increase and become superior through the growth of cultivation, a superior external designation is established, calling him a "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*).
The subsequent section correctly reveals the antidotes; the *Bhūmi-sūtra* relies on the stages to explain them extensively.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are clarified here. Now, based on the actual stages (*bhūmi*), this single section comprehensively clarifies the methods of counteractive cultivation (*pratipakṣa*);

as these are all the true path (*mārga*), they are collectively included. The five immeasurables (*pañcāpramāṇa*) and the two subsequent sections clarify the practice within the fifth stage (*bhūmi*).
However, both the true path and the auxiliary path are "immeasurable" because the noble ones (*ārya*) of the fifth stage engage with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings.
Conforming with the world, they extensively practice all manner of deeds; because they accord with suchness through the right path, their minds are equal to the dharma-realm.
Since this is already immeasurable, they take true suchness as that which is traversed; all encountered objects are suchness, and the Path is nowhere not present.
Therefore, the conditions and resources for all the myriad practices performed serve as aids to the Path. Thus, the more vast the objective realm, the greater the Path becomes.
Consequently, worldly speech, the activities for sustaining life, and so forth, are all in accord with the True Dharma-realm;
each and every one is immeasurable and boundless. This is why they constitute the practice of the Non-abiding Path. Sixth, the Immeasurable Cultivation of the Path, part one.

This section clarifies the practice of the sixth stage (*bhūmi*). Since the manifestation of *prajñā* constitutes true cultivation, although one was able to cultivate unimpeded conduct in accordance with the world during the preceding five stages, one had not yet been able to forget the dualistic views of defilement and purity; now, in this sixth stage, [this is overcome].
By means of the manifestation of *prajñā*, one observes that the *dharmadhātu* is free from defilement and purity, and that *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* are equal;
therefore, it is called "immeasurable cultivation. This is because each and every practice accords with the measure of the *dharmadhātu*.

Since this [level] is manifested precisely through the cultivation of the preceding stage, the seventh ground is explained below under three sections as the path of adornment. By means of this ground...
Having already attained the equality of defilement and purity, one practices both the provisional and the real, adorning them with these two modes of conduct; thus it is called "ornamentation.
Because the provisional and the real are unimpeded, one’s own practice remains undefiled while being able to manifest defilement in accordance with those to be transformed.

Abiding in the correct yet entering the deviant, one maintains both the provisional and the real regarding precepts and transgressions. Because the essence of the cause is already perfected, and because the great function is generated, one attains the ten [powers].

Because [the Bodhisattva] is complete, there is no movement and no reaching; yet they attain ten kinds of mastery in taking and bestowing with the hands. Therefore, in every thought-moment, they advance in the cultivation of all Buddha-dharmas.

Because they are directed toward Buddha-wisdom, they are able to extensively transform sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Because there is no movement that does not reach within the full extent of the Dharma-realm, this is called "Far-reaching" (*dūramgamā*). [The eighty secondary marks, the three... (Note:

The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, specifically the section concerning the second stage, the *Vimalā-bhūmi*. The final characters "八十種腹下三" likely refer to the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*) and the beginning of a discussion on the three [marks], though the text is incomplete.)
This section clarifies the practice within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding the term "abdomen": the abdomen of worldly people generally contains impurities and evils.
Now, it is said that the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage has already realized the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*). All pure merits cultivated from above are fully gathered here.
Because the essence of this True Suchness is equal to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and empty space, there is nothing it does not encompass.
"Yong" (容) signifies that there is no wholesome [quality] that does not accumulate therein. "Zang" (藏) refers to the five internal organs within the abdomen;
it means that the Dharma-body, as the accumulation of the aforementioned merits, serves as a treasury of merit.

Furthermore, it is able to produce benefits for sentient beings, for both those established in right concentration and those in wrong concentration are all embraced by great compassion. As for the "ten kinds of mind," the mind is the single body of the whole.

The Lord of this refers to the fact that the *tathatā* thus realized is the Lord of the *dharmakāya*. All effortless and spontaneous (*anābhoga*) activities that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings constitute its great function (*mahopāya*).
While the body [of the first stage] previously possessed the substance but was minute, this [stage] possesses the entire substance and great function without exception.
By briefly citing these three, the entirety has already been revealed; therefore, [the text speaks of] the ninth stage...
Manifesting the body to preach the Dharma is entirely due to this great function. The section on the "Donning of the Armor" in the ninth stage clarifies the practice within the nine stages.

Since this stage emerges from the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*) yet manifests the body to preach the Dharma while entering the realm of Māra, these ten kinds of armor are used to protect the person, and these ten kinds of weapons are used to defeat the enemy. That is to say:

One battles against the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the demon of birth and death (*mṛtyumāra*). If one lacks the means to prevent and guard against harm, there will inevitably be injury and damage.
How much more so when it comes to transforming the realm of Māras into the realm of Buddhas—how could this be a trivial matter?

Regarding the tenth stage, the "Ten Heads" section below clarifies the practice within the tenth bhūmi. First, as for the term "ten heads," it refers to the ten [aspects] of the Bodhisattva of this stage.

The virtue of the Ground is perfected. Abiding in and receiving the position of rank, it stands preeminent among all sages; therefore, its head is designated as the foremost. This Ground consists of thirteen gates:
first, by relying on the six sense organs, the perfection of its virtuous characteristics is manifested;

subsequently, by relying on the four modes of deportment, its subtle and minute functional activities are revealed. The two gates of walking and standing represent the Dharma-realm as the locus of abiding. In summary:
This reveals that the practices cultivated by those of the Three Worthies accord with the Dharma-realm; they adorn the Dharma-body to constitute the retributive essence (*vipākakāya*).

Now, in the tenth stage, the retributive essence is perfected and its virtuous marks are fully complete, thereby accomplishing the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and dwelling securely within the Dharma-realm.

This is to await the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. Just as the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King is installed as the heir apparent, so too the Bodhisattva of this stage can fully receive the Dharma-clouds and Dharma-rains of the Buddha and is capable of performing Buddha-works;

thus, they are like the heir apparent who concurrently manages the affairs of state. The practices of the ten stages above are now concluded; below follows the perfection of causes and the realization of the fruit.
Complete.

Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Five: On Transcending the World.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of observations for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:

the observation of knowing all karmas, because of seeing them in their subtle details; the observation of knowing all realms of existence (*gati*), because of not grasping at sentient beings; the observation of knowing all... [text fragment ends]
The observation of the faculties is because they are realized to be without faculties. The observation of all phenomena is because the dharma-realm is known to be indestructible.
The observation of seeing the Buddha-dharma is because one diligently cultivates the Buddha-eye. The observation of attaining wisdom is because one teaches the Dharma according to reality.

The observation of the patience of non-arising is because one definitively understands the Buddha-dharma. The observation of the stage of non-retrogression is because one extinguishes all afflictions and transcends them.
Because it observes the stages of the three realms and the two vehicles; because it observes the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as being sovereign and immovable regarding all Buddha-dharmas;
and because it observes the performance of all Buddha-activities throughout the ten directions through the samādhi of excellent awakening wisdom—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great observing wisdom. Buddha.
Son, there are ten kinds of universal observation for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
universally observing all those who come seeking [something], by fulfilling their intentions with a mind free from opposition;

universally observing all sentient beings who violate the precepts, by establishing them within the pure precepts of the Tathāgata; universally observing all sentient beings with harmful intent, by establishing them...
By virtue of the Tathāgata’s power of patience, he universally observes all indolent sentient beings and exhorts them to be diligent so that they do not abandon their burden of carrying the Mahāyāna.
He universally observes all sentient beings with distracted minds and causes them to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, free from dispersion and agitation.
He universally observes all sentient beings with evil wisdom and causes them to eliminate doubt and destroy [the view of] existence.
Because of this vision: one universally contemplates all as equal spiritual friends, so as to abide in the Buddha-dharma by following their instructions;
one universally contemplates all teachings heard, so as to swiftly realize and perceive the supreme meaning;
one universally contemplates all infinite sentient beings, so as to never abandon the power of great compassion; and one universally contemplates the dharma of all Buddhas, so as to swiftly attain...
Because they accomplish all-knowledge. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom of universal observation.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of prowess of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
What are the ten? They are: the prowess of the bull king, which outshines all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and...
Because of the great assembly of gandharvas and others, he is the majestic display of the Elephant King, for his mind is well-tamed and gentle as he bears the burden of all sentient beings.

He is the majestic display of the Dragon King, raising the dense clouds of the Great Dharma, flashing the lightning of liberation, thundering the roar of the meaning of reality, and raining down the nectar of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. The Great Golden...
The King of Winged Birds exerts his prowess; he dries up the waters of craving and destroys the eggshell of ignorance.
He seizes the various venomous dragons of affliction and brings them forth from the great ocean of birth-and-death suffering. The Great Lion King exerts his prowess;
dwelling securely in fearless, impartial great wisdom as his weapon, he subdues all Māras and non-Buddhists. He is valiant and exerts his prowess, able to...
Because he crushes and destroys all enemies that are the afflictions within the great battle-array of birth and death, he possesses the prowess of great wisdom (*mahājñāna-vaikṛtya*).
Because he knows the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as dependent origination, and freely reveals all phenomena, he possesses the prowess of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇī-vaikṛtya*).
By the power of mindfulness and wisdom, he upholds the Dharma without forgetting it;

because he proclaims it according to the faculties of sentient beings, his eloquence is vigorous, unimpeded, and swift, discerning all things so that all may receive benefit and their hearts rejoice—this is the Tathāgata’s vigor.

All the dharmas that assist the path to omniscience are fully perfected. By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, all that is to be attained is attained, and all that is to be realized is realized.
Sitting upon the lion throne, he subdues Māra and his adversaries, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These are the ten. If there are bodhisattvas...
Abiding in this Dharma, one attains the supreme, sovereign, and powerful mastery over all phenomena of all Buddhas.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of lion’s roars of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. What are these ten? They are as follows:
first, proclaiming, "I shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment"—this is the great lion’s roar of the bodhicitta. "I shall cause all..."
To deliver those sentient beings who have not yet been delivered; to liberate those who have not yet been liberated; to settle those who have not yet found peace;

and to cause those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*—this is the Great Compassionate One’s lion’s roar: "I shall ensure that the lineages of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are never severed."
"This is the Great Lion’s Roar of repaying the kindness of the Tathāgata: 'I shall adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
This is the Great Lion’s Roar of ultimate and firm resolve: 'I shall eliminate all evil realms and places of hardship.
This is the Great Lion’s Roar of personally upholding pure precepts: 'I shall fulfill the marks of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas.'"
"Adorned with excellence! This is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of merit:
'I shall bring to full completion all the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas. This is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of knowledge:
'I shall eliminate all Māras and all demonic activities. This is the great lion’s roar of practicing correct conduct to sever all afflictions: 'I shall realize..."
To know that all dharmas are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without a person (pudgala); that they are empty, signless, and wishless;
and that they are as pure as space—this is the Great Lion’s Roar of the Forbearance toward the Non-arising of Dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When a Bodhisattva in his final birth causes all Buddha-lands to tremble and makes them entirely pure, at that time, all the Śakras, Brahmās, and Four Heavenly Kings...
They all came to offer praise and entreaty, saying: "We pray that the Bodhisattva will manifest birth through the dharma of non-arising.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, with his unimpeded eye of wisdom, surveyed all sentient beings in the world and saw none who were his equal.
He then manifested his birth within the royal palace; immediately after taking seven steps, he proclaimed, "I am the most supreme and foremost in the world."
"I shall forever bring an end to the limits of birth and death"—this is the great lion’s roar as it is spoken and acted upon. This is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great lion’s roar of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure giving. What are the ten? They are: giving with equanimity, because they do not discriminate among sentient beings;
giving according to their wishes, because they fulfill their aspirations; giving without distraction, because it causes them to obtain benefit;

giving as is appropriate, because they know the superior, middling, and inferior capacities; giving without dwelling [on the act], because they do not seek karmic rewards; and giving through the opening of renunciation.
Because the mind does not cling; because all giving is ultimately pure; because the giving dedicated toward Bodhi is free from the conditioned and the unconditioned;
because the giving that transforms sentient beings is never abandoned until the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
and because the giving with the three spheres purified observes the giver, the recipient, and the gift with right mindfulness as being like space. This is...
There are ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, pure, and vast giving of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure precepts for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
the pure precept of body, because of guarding against the three evils of the body; the pure precept of speech, because of being free from the four faults of speech; the pure precept of mind...

Pure ethical discipline is that which is forever free from greed, hatred, and wrong views; pure ethical discipline is that which does not violate any precepts and acts as a sovereign lord among all gods and humans;
pure ethical discipline is that which guards the bodhicitta and takes no pleasure in the Lesser Vehicle;
pure ethical discipline is that which guards the precepts established by the Tathāgata and gives rise to great dread even toward the most subtle of transgressions.
The pure precept of secret protection, because it thoroughly uproots sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts;

the pure precept of non-action regarding all evils, because it vows to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; the pure precept of distancing oneself from all views of existence, because it is unattached to the precepts themselves;
and the pure precept of protecting all sentient beings, because it gives rise to great compassion. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, faultless, and pure precepts.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure patience for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
the pure patience of peacefully accepting verbal abuse, because of protecting all sentient beings; the pure patience of peacefully accepting blades and staves, because of skillfully protecting...
Pure patience regarding self and others is because it does not give rise to anger or malice and its mind remains unshakable;

pure patience regarding the lowly is because it does not reproach them and is supreme in its capacity for forbearance; pure patience regarding those who seek refuge is because it saves them all, even at the cost of one's own life;

pure patience regarding the removal of pride is because it does not look down upon those of limited learning; and pure patience regarding injury and destruction is because it observes [the nature of things].
Because it is like an illusion; because it is the pure patience of non-offense and non-retribution, as one perceives neither self nor other;

because it is the pure patience that does not follow afflictions, as one is detached from all objective spheres; because it is the pure patience of conforming to the true wisdom of a bodhisattva, knowing that all phenomena are unborn;
and because it is the pure patience of entering the sphere of omniscience without depending on the instruction of others—these are the ten. If any bodhisattvas...
When the Bodhisattva dwells therein, they attain the supreme Dharma-patience that is realized by all Buddhas without depending on another.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure diligence for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
pure diligence of body, which consists of serving, making offerings to, and honoring all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, teachers, elders, and fields of merit.
Because it is non-retrogressive, there is the pure diligence of speech, which tirelessly and extensively expounds to others the Dharma as it has been heard and praises the virtues of the Buddha.

There is the pure diligence of mind, which skillfully enters and emerges from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and various samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity without rest. There is the pure diligence of the true mind, which is without deception...
Because they are free from flattery, crookedness, and deceit, they cultivate all things with diligence and without regression;
they increase their supreme mental purity and vigor, constantly aspiring toward the highest of high wisdom, and vow to be endowed with all pure and white dharmas.
Thus, they do not let their pure vigor go to waste, but rather embrace generosity, ethical discipline, patience, learning, and heedfulness, continuing until enlightenment.
Because it is the cessation of intermediate [distractions], it is the pure diligence that subdues all Māras;
because it can completely eliminate all afflictions, fetters, and hindrances—namely greed, hatred, delusion, and false views—it is the pure diligence of the light of perfected wisdom.
Whatever one undertakes, it is thoroughly examined so that all things are brought to ultimate completion without subsequent regret, thereby attaining all...

Because of the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), he practices pure diligence that is neither coming nor going. Having attained knowledge as it truly is, he enters the gateway of the *dharmadhātu*.

Since his body, speech, and mind are entirely equal, and because he realizes that characteristics are not characteristics and thus remains unattached, he accomplishes the pure diligence of the light of the Dharma.
Transcending all stages (*bhūmi*), he receives the Buddha’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and manifests his passing away with an untainted body (*anāsrava-kāya*).
Birth; leaving home; attaining the Way; preaching the Dharma; and passing into parinirvāṇa. Because they fulfill such universal virtuous deeds (samantabhadra-karma), these constitute the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, pure vigor.
Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure dhyāna. What are the ten? They are as follows: always delighting in...
The pure dhyāna of renunciation, because of relinquishing all that one possesses; the pure dhyāna of true spiritual friends, because they demonstrate and teach the right path;
the pure dhyāna of dwelling in an araṇya and enduring wind, rain, and so forth, because of being free from the notions of "I" and "mine";

the pure dhyāna of being free from the clamor of worldly beings, because of always delighting in stillness; and the pure dhyāna of mental activity being pliant and supple, because of guarding [the mind].
The pure dhyāna for guarding the sense faculties, because all sounds cannot disturb it as it is a samādhi of mental tranquility and purity;
the pure dhyāna of the skillful means of awakening, because it directly realizes the observation of all things;
the pure dhyāna free from attachment to flavor, because it does not abandon the desire realm; and the pure dhyāna that initiates supernormal clarity, because it knows all things.

Because of the various dispositions and natures of sentient beings; because of sporting with mastery in pure meditative absorption and entering the Buddha-samādhi through the knowledge of non-self—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure meditation.
Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure wisdom. What are the ten? They are as follows:
Pure wisdom that knows all causes, because it does not destroy the maturation of results; pure wisdom that knows all conditions, because it does not conflict with their conjunction;
pure wisdom that knows neither annihilation nor permanence, because it thoroughly penetrates dependent origination as it truly is.
The pure wisdom that uproots all views, because it neither grasps nor rejects the characteristics of sentient beings;
the pure wisdom that contemplates the mental activities of all sentient beings, because it understands them to be like illusions;

the pure wisdom of vast eloquence, because it is unimpeded in analyzing all phenomena and in answering questions; [a wisdom] which cannot be known by any māras, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
Vimalamati, because he has deeply entered the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, he perceives the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
he perceives that the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is pure; he perceives that all phenomena are entirely quiescent;
and he perceives that all lands are identical to empty space. Vimalamati, this is because he knows that all marks are without obstruction, and thus possesses all dhāraṇīs and eloquence.
The wisdom of pure skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) that brings about the attainment of all supreme knowledge;

and the wisdom of the equality and purity of all phenomena through the vajra-wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samāyukta-vajrajñāna*), which attains the most honored knowledge of all phenomena—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unobstructed great [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
Wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure loving-kindness for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
first, pure loving-kindness of equanimity, because it universally gathers all sentient beings without discrimination; second, pure loving-kindness of benefit...
Pure compassion that gathers beings as one’s own kin, because it causes all that is done to bring them joy;

pure compassion that does not abandon the world, because it ultimately causes all to transcend birth and death; pure compassion that reaches liberation, because the mind constantly contemplates and accumulates roots of goodness;
and [the compassion] that gives rise to [liberation], because it universally causes sentient beings to eliminate all afflictions.
The pure compassion of bodhi, because it causes all sentient beings everywhere to resolve to seek the mind of omniscience;
the pure compassion that is unimpeded in the world, because it emits great radiance that shines equally and universally;

the pure compassion that fills empty space, because it rescues and protects sentient beings, reaching every place; and the pure compassion with dharmas as its object, because it realizes the true dharma of suchness.
Therefore, there is objectless, pure loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because one enters the bodhisattva’s nature of transcendence (*niyāma*). These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure loving-kindness.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure compassion (*karuṇā*). What are the ten? They are as follows: peerless, pure...
Compassion: because it arises from a solitary resolve; pure compassion free from weariness, because one undergoes suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without regarding it as toil;

pure compassion for taking birth in difficult circumstances, for the sake of delivering sentient beings; pure compassion for taking birth in fortunate realms, for the purpose of manifesting impermanence;
and pure compassion for those sentient beings fixed in error, which is never abandoned throughout the succession of kalpas.

Because of their great vows, they possess the pure compassion that does not cling to their own happiness; because they universally bestow joy upon all sentient beings, they possess the pure compassion that seeks no reward for their kindness;
because they cultivate and purify their minds, they possess the pure compassion that can eliminate perversions;
and because they teach the Dharma according to reality, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, free from attachment, and free from feverish affliction.
Because of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), they undergo manifold sufferings. Having understood this, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all sentient beings.

This is called "innate purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). For the sake of teaching the stainless, pure, and luminous Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are like the tracks of birds in the sky;
yet sentient beings, due to the cataracts of ignorance (*moha-timira*), are unable to perceive or understand them. Thus he contemplates.
To observe that [suffering] and give rise to a mind of great compassion is called true wisdom, because it reveals the Dharma of Nirvāṇa to them.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure compassion.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure joy. What are the ten? They are as follows:
The pure joy of generating the bodhicitta; the pure joy of relinquishing all possessions; the pure joy of teaching and bringing to maturity those who break the precepts without reviling them;
the pure joy of enduring the sight of sentient beings who commit evil while vowing to rescue them;
the pure joy of sacrificing one’s body to seek the Dharma without giving rise to regret; and the pure joy of constantly delighting in [the Dharma] while renouncing personal sensual pleasures.
The pure joy of the Dharma’s delight causes all sentient beings to relinquish the joy of material requisites and always delight in the pure joy of the Dharma.
It is the pure joy of the equality of the Dharma-realm, which consists in seeing and reverently making offerings to all Buddhas without ever feeling satiated.
To cause all sentient beings to love and delight in the pure joy of entering and emerging from the play of *dhyāna*, liberation, and *samādhi*;

and to cause their hearts to delight in fully practicing all ascetic austerities in accordance with the Bodhisattva path, thereby realizing the jewel-like, tranquil, immovable, and unsurpassed purity of concentration and wisdom—this is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain them.
The Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure joy. O Son of the Buddha! There are ten kinds of pure relinquishment for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: the pure relinquishment of not giving rise to attachment when all sentient beings show respect and make offerings;
the pure relinquishment of not giving rise to anger when all sentient beings treat them with contempt or insult; always practicing...

Pure equanimity that is not defiled by the eight worldly concerns; pure equanimity that waits for the proper time to transform those sentient beings who are vessels of the Dharma, yet does not give rise to aversion toward those who are not vessels;
pure equanimity that does not seek the dharmas of the two vehicles, whether in training or beyond training;
and pure equanimity in which the mind is always far removed from all sensual pleasures and dharmas conducive to affliction. Not...
They praise the pure relinquishment of the two vehicles that involves wearying of and renouncing birth-and-death;

they remain far removed from all worldly speech, speech that is not [conducive to] nirvāṇa, speech that is not free from desire, speech that does not accord with principle, speech that disturbs others, the speech of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and—in brief—all speech that obstructs the path of a bodhisattva, having completely abandoned them through pure relinquishment. Or there may be sentient beings...
There are those whose faculties have already matured and who have given rise to mindfulness and wisdom, yet are unable to know the supreme Dharma;

they await their time before being transformed through pure relinquishment. Or there may be sentient beings whom the Bodhisattva has already taught in the past, but who can only be tamed upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood;
these too await their time for pure relinquishment. Regarding these two types of persons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [remains equanimous].
It is lofty and not low; it is without grasping and without abandoning; it is far removed from all various forms of conceptual discrimination;
it dwells constantly in right concentration; it enters into the dharma of suchness; and the mind attains patient endurance and pure equanimity—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure equanimity. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has...
There are ten kinds of meanings. What are these ten? They are: the meaning of extensive learning, because of firm practice; the meaning of the Dharma, because of skillful discernment;

the meaning of emptiness, because of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the meaning of tranquility, because of being free from the clamor and confusion of all sentient beings;
the meaning of the ineffable, because of not clinging to any speech; and the meaning of reality as it is, because of penetrating the equality of the three periods of time.
Because they are equal; because the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* is that all phenomena are of one taste; because the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) is that all Tathāgatas accord with and enter it;
because the meaning of the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are;
because the meaning of *mahāparinirvāṇa* is the cessation of all suffering while cultivating the various practices of a bodhisattva. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, then...
One attains the supreme meaning of all-knowledge. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dharmas for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

What are these ten? They are: the dharma of reality, because one practices according to what has been taught; the dharma of detachment from grasping, because one is entirely free from both the grasper and the grasped;
the dharma of non-contention, because there is no contention whatsoever arising from delusion; and the dharma of quiescence, which extinguishes all feverish afflictions.

Because it is free from affliction; because all craving is severed through the dharma of detachment from desire; because the conceptualization of objects of perception has forever ceased through the dharma of non-discrimination;
because it is immovable like space through the dharma of non-arising; because it is free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing through the dharma of the unconditioned;
because its own nature is unstained and pure through the dharma of the fundamental nature; [it is] the relinquishing of all *upapatti-nyāya*.
The dharma of *paryaṅka* (the cross-legged posture) is able to give rise to all bodhisattva practices because their cultivation is uninterrupted. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast dharma of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of requisites for merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*).
What are the ten? They are as follows: namely, exhorting sentient beings to generate the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Maintaining mindfulness is a supportive equipment for the bodhisattva’s merit, because it ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed.
Following the ten kinds of dedication is a supportive equipment for the bodhisattva’s merit, because it severs all unwholesome dharmas and gathers all wholesome dharmas.
Wisdom that provides instruction is a supportive equipment for the bodhisattva’s merit, because it transcends the merit of the three realms.
Therefore, a mind free from weariness is a supportive tool for the merit of a bodhisattva, because it brings all sentient beings to ultimate liberation.
Completely relinquishing all internal and external possessions is a supportive tool for the merit of a bodhisattva, because there is no attachment to any object.
Diligently striving without retreat in order to fulfill the primary and secondary marks is the merit of a bodhisattva.

The requisites for practice: because they open the gates of great giving without limit, they dedicate all roots of goodness—superior, middling, and inferior—toward unsurpassed bodhi without any sense of contempt; this is the Bodhisattva’s requisite of merit, as it accords with skillful means.
