O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva is born, he causes all Buddha-lands to tremble, liberates all sentient beings, and extinguishes [all afflictions].
It eclipses all evil realms and outshines all Māras. Immeasurable Bodhisattvas all assemble there.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of births of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; they are manifested in this way for the sake of taming sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests a smile and makes a vow within his own mind for ten reasons. What are they?
Tenth: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reflects, "All the world is submerged in the mire of desire;
except for me alone, there is no one capable of providing rescue. Having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his own mind.
He further reflects, "The entire world is blinded by the afflictions (*kleśa*); I alone now possess perfect wisdom. Having known this, [he acts accordingly].
With a joyful and smiling countenance, he made a vow within his own mind. He further thought:

"By means of this provisional name-body, I shall now attain the unsurpassed Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, which fills the three periods of time. Having known this, with a joyful and smiling countenance, he made a vow within his own mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with unobstructed eyes, surveyed everywhere throughout the ten directions, from all the Brahmā heavens down to...
All the Maheśvaras thought to themselves: "These sentient beings all claim for themselves to possess great power of wisdom.

Having known this, they smiled with serene joy and made a vow within their own minds. At that time, the Bodhisattva observed that these sentient beings, who had long planted roots of goodness, were now all regressing and sinking. Having known this, he smiled with serene joy and made a vow within his own mind.
The Bodhisattva observes that the seeds of the world, though few when sown, yield very abundant fruit.

Having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his mind. The Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings who receive the Buddha’s teaching will certainly obtain benefit.
Having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his mind. The Bodhisattva observes the past...

Having realized that bodhisattvas who practice together in this world become attached to other matters and fail to attain the vast merit of the Buddha-dharma, he smiled with a joyful countenance and made a vow within his own mind:

"The bodhisattva observes that all the devas and humans who have gathered together throughout the past and future worlds remain even now in the stage of ordinary beings; they are unable to abandon [worldly attachments] and yet do not grow weary."
Feeling weary, having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his own mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva is touched by the light of all Tathāgatas; his joy and comfort increase manifold as he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his own mind. This is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva manifests in this way for the sake of taming sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
For ten reasons, he manifested the act of walking seven steps. What are these ten? They are: he manifested the power of a bodhisattva, therefore he manifested walking seven steps;
he manifested the bestowal of the seven riches, therefore he manifested walking seven steps; he fulfilled the vows of the earth goddesses, therefore he manifested walking seven steps;
he manifested the sign of transcending the three realms, therefore he manifested walking seven steps; he manifested that the supreme conduct of a bodhisattva surpasses [that of] an elephant...
He took seven steps because he was a king of kings, a bull among men, and a lion among men; he took seven steps to manifest the sign of the adamantine ground;
he took seven steps to manifest his desire to bestow upon sentient beings the power of valor; he took seven steps to manifest his cultivation of the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment;
he took seven steps to manifest that the Dharma he had attained was not derived from the instruction of another. He manifested...
Because he is supreme and peerless in the world, he demonstrates walking seven steps; this is the tenth.

Sons of the Buddha, for the sake of taming sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests such displays. Sons of the Buddha, there are ten reasons why a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests in the stage of childhood.
What are these ten? They are: to manifest mastery of all worldly scripts...
One dwells in the stage of a youth (*kumārabhūmi*) for the sake of manifesting mastery over various activities such as writing, calculation, books, and seals;
one dwells in the stage of a youth for the sake of manifesting mastery over all worldly activities such as elephants, horses, chariots, bows, arrows, swords, and halberds;
and one dwells in the stage of a youth for the sake of manifesting mastery over all worldly matters such as calligraphy, discourse, gambling, and games.
The Stage of the Youth (*kumārabhūmi*): One dwells in the stage of the youth in order to manifest the complete distancing from all faults of the actions of body, speech, and mind;
one dwells in the stage of the youth in order to manifest the entry into meditative concentration and abiding in the gate of nirvāṇa throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
He dwells in the stage of a youth (*kumārabhūmi*) in order to manifest a power that surpasses all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), humans, and non-humans;
he dwells in the stage of a youth in order to manifest the physical form and majestic radiance of a bodhisattva that surpasses all Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors.
The Stage of the Son (*putrabhūmi*). He dwells in the Stage of the Youth (*kumārabhūmi*) in order to cause sentient beings who are attached to sensual pleasures to rejoice in the Dharma;
he dwells in the Stage of the Youth in order to honor the True Dharma and diligently make offerings to the Buddhas throughout all worlds in the ten directions;
he dwells in the Stage of the Youth in order to manifestly receive the empowerment of the Buddhas and be illumined by the light of the Dharma. These are the ten. — The Buddha.
Once the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has manifested the stage of a youth, he manifests his dwelling in a royal palace for ten reasons. What are these ten? They are:
he manifests his dwelling in a royal palace in order to bring to maturity the roots of goodness in those sentient beings with whom he practiced together in previous lives;
he manifests his dwelling in a royal palace to demonstrate the power of the Bodhisattva’s roots of goodness; [he does so] for all humans and devas who are addicted to...
He manifests dwelling in a royal palace to demonstrate the Bodhisattva’s great majestic power and the splendors of pleasure;

he manifests dwelling in a royal palace to accord with the minds of sentient beings in the world of the five turbidities; he manifests dwelling in a royal palace to demonstrate that the Bodhisattva possesses the great majestic power and strength to enter samādhi even within the deep inner chambers; and he does so to fulfill the aspirations of those sentient beings who shared the same vows in past lives.
Therefore, he manifests his presence in the royal palace; he manifests his presence in the royal palace because he wishes to fulfill the aspirations of his parents, relatives, and kinsmen.
He manifests his presence in the royal palace because he wishes to offer the sounds of the sublime Dharma through music and song as an offering to all Tathāgatas.
He manifests his presence in the royal palace because he wishes to dwell within the palace in subtle samādhis, demonstrating them from the moment of attaining Buddhahood until his final nirvāṇa.
He manifests by dwelling in a royal palace; he manifests by dwelling in a royal palace in order to accord with and protect the teachings of all Buddhas.
These are the ten. After a Bodhisattva in his final existence has thus manifested dwelling in a royal palace, he subsequently renounces the household life.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten reasons why a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests the renunciation of the household life. What are these ten? They are as follows:
He manifests leaving the home life in order to inspire weariness with domestic life; he manifests leaving the home life in order to cause sentient beings attached to the household to renounce it;

he manifests leaving the home life in order to accord with those who have faith and delight in the path of the noble ones; he manifests leaving the home life in order to proclaim and praise the merits of the renunciant life;
and he manifests leaving the home life in order to reveal the eternal departure from the two extreme views.
He manifests leaving the household life in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the pleasures of desire and the pleasure of self;

he manifests leaving the household life in order to first manifest the characteristics of transcending the three realms; he manifests leaving the household life in order to manifest sovereignty that is not dependent on others;
and he manifests leaving the household life in order to reveal that he shall attain the Tathāgata’s dharmas of fearlessness throughout the ten directions. This is the final dharma of a bodhisattva.
Because it was appropriate to do so, he manifested the act of leaving the household life. This is the tenth. It is by these means that Bodhisattvas discipline sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, for ten reasons Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas manifest the practice of asceticism. What are these ten? Namely:

they manifest the practice of asceticism in order to bring to fulfillment those sentient beings of inferior understanding; they manifest it in order to uproot sentient beings with false views; they manifest it... [and so forth].
He practices asceticism. He manifests the practice of asceticism so that sentient beings who do not believe in karmic retribution may see it.

He manifests the practice of asceticism because it is appropriate for conforming to the dharmas of a defiled world. He manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate his ability to endure toil and diligently cultivate the Path.
He manifests the practice of asceticism in order to cause sentient beings to joyfully seek the Dharma. For...
He manifests the practice of asceticism because he desires the happiness of sentient beings;
he manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate the excellence of the Bodhisattva’s undertaking of practice, showing that even in his final birth he does not abandon diligent vigor;

he manifests the practice of asceticism to cause sentient beings to delight in the dharma of tranquility and to increase their roots of goodness; [and] for the sake of the faculties of gods and worldly people...
Because those who are immature must wait for the time of their maturation, he demonstrates the practice of asceticism.

These are the ten. By these skillful means, the Bodhisattva subdues all sentient beings. Son of the Buddha, there are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
What are the ten? They are as follows: at the time of proceeding to the site of enlightenment, he illuminates all worlds; he proceeds to the site of enlightenment...
At that time, he causes all worlds to tremble. When proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he manifests his body universally throughout all worlds.
When proceeding to the site of enlightenment, he awakens all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings who were his companions in past lives.

When proceeding to the site of enlightenment, he displays all the adornments of the site of enlightenment. When proceeding to the site of enlightenment, he acts in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings.
Manifesting various physical forms, modes of deportment, and all manner of adornments for the Bodhi tree according to what beings desire;

upon approaching the site of enlightenment, manifestly beholding all Tathāgatas of the ten directions; at the moment of stepping onto the site of enlightenment, constantly entering samādhi with every lift and placement of the foot;
achieving Buddhahood in every thought-moment without interval; and at the moment of approaching the site of enlightenment, [surrounded by] all devas, nāgas, and yakṣas...
The *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, *asuras*, *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, and *mahoragas*, as well as Śakra, Brahmā,
and all the world-protecting kings, each unaware of the others, offered various kinds of supreme and wondrous offerings. When they arrived at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*),
they universally beheld all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, through unimpeded wisdom, as they cultivated bodhi in all worlds.
By practicing these, one attains perfect enlightenment. These are the ten. It is by means of these that Bodhisattvas teach and transform sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there are ten things. What are the ten? They are as follows:

at the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment, they cause all worlds to tremble in various ways; at the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment, they radiate light equally upon all worlds...
The realm. When sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one eliminates all suffering of the evil destinies.

When sitting at the site of enlightenment, one causes all worlds to be composed of vajra. When sitting at the site of enlightenment, one universally manifests the lion-thrones of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, the mind is like space, free from all discrimination. When sitting at the site of enlightenment, according to its...
The majestic deportment of the body as it should appear; when sitting at the site of enlightenment, dwelling in accordance with the vajra-samādhi;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, receiving the pure and wondrous place sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas;

when sitting at the site of enlightenment, being able to empower all sentient beings through the power of one's own roots of goodness—these are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, these are the [qualities] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When a Bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there are ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events. What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, all Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions appear before him.
They all raise their right hands and proclaim in praise: "Excellent, excellent! O Unsurpassed Guide! This is the first.

First, it is an unprecedented occurrence: when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all Tathāgatas protect and mindfully attend to him, bestowing upon him their majestic power. This is the second unprecedented occurrence:

when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, the assembly of Bodhisattvas who were his companions in practice throughout past lives all come to surround him, adorned with various kinds of ornaments.

They were endowed with reverence and made offerings; this was the third unprecedented event. When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all the grasses, trees, shrubs, forests, and insentient things in all worlds bowed their bodies and lowered their shadows, turning toward the site of enlightenment;
this was the fourth unprecedented event. When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sat at the site of enlightenment...
He enters a samādhi called "Contemplating the Dharma Realm. By the power of this samādhi, he is able to bring all the practices of a bodhisattva to complete fulfillment.

This is the fifth unprecedented event. When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he attains a dhāraṇī called "The Supreme, Stainless, Wondrous Light Ocean-Treasury," by which he is able to receive [the teachings] of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata’s great cloud of Dharma rain—this is the sixth unprecedented event.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), by the power of his majestic virtue, he produces supreme and wondrous offerings and makes them as offerings to all Buddhas throughout all worlds—this is the seventh unprecedented event. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he dwells in the most...
Supreme Wisdom: He fully perceives and understands the faculties, intentions, and mental activities of all sentient beings. This is the eighth unprecedented event.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he enters a samādhi named "Excellent Awakening.
By the power of this samādhi, his body fills all worlds throughout the three periods of time and the entirety of the realm of empty space. This is the ninth...

Ninth, the unprecedented event: when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they attain the stainless radiance of unimpeded great wisdom, causing their physical actions to universally enter the three periods of time. This is the tenth unprecedented event.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events that occur when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he manifests the subduing of Māra by contemplating ten meanings.

What are these ten? They are as follows: first, because the sentient beings of the degenerate age delight in combat, he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to manifest the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue;
second, in order to sever the doubts of those among the devas and humans who harbor uncertainty.
He manifests the subduing of Māra. He manifests the subduing of Māra for the purpose of teaching and taming the various hosts of Māras.

He manifests the subduing of Māra because he wishes to cause those among the devas and people of the world who delight in military arrays to all come together to witness it, thereby bringing their minds to subdual.
He manifested the subduing of Māra to demonstrate that all the power possessed by Bodhisattvas is invincible in the world;

he manifested the subduing of Māra out of a desire to inspire the courageous strength of all sentient beings; he manifested the subduing of Māra out of compassion for all sentient beings in the final age;
and he manifested it to show that even at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there are still armies of Māra.
They come to provoke and disturb him. Thereafter, because he is able to transcend the realm of Māra, he manifests the subduing of Māra.

Because he wishes to demonstrate that the power of afflictions and karma is weak and inferior, while the force of the roots of goodness of great compassion is powerful and flourishing, he manifests the subduing of Māra.
Because he desires to accord with the practices of this turbid and evil world, he manifests the subduing of Māra. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of accomplishments that constitute the powers of a Tathāgata. What are these ten? They are:

the accomplishment of the power of a Tathāgata by transcending all Māras, afflictions, and karmic actions; the accomplishment of the power of a Tathāgata by fulfilling all bodhisattva practices and sporting within all bodhisattva samādhi-gates;
and the accomplishment [of the power of a Tathāgata] by fulfilling all the vast meditations of a bodhisattva...
Because of meditative concentration, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata. Because he has perfected all pure factors conducive to enlightenment, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata.
Because he has attained the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena and possesses excellent discernment through right reflection, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata.
Because his body pervades all worlds, he is a Tathāgata. The sounds of the speech that issue from him are entirely in harmony with all sentient beings.
Because he gives rise to an equal mind, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata. Because he is able to empower all things through his supernormal powers, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata.

Because his physical, verbal, and mental karma is identical and no different from those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and because he comprehends the phenomena of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata.
Having attained the Samādhi of Excellent Awakening Wisdom, he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, namely:
The powers of a Tathāgata are established by virtue of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, up to the power of the destruction of the outflows; these constitute the ten.
If Bodhisattvas are endowed with these ten powers, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten matters concerning the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma by a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. What are these ten? First, being fully endowed with...
1. Purifying the wisdom of the four fearlessnesses; 2. Producing the four analytical knowledges and voices that accord with [the needs of beings];
3. Skillfully elucidating the characteristics of the four noble truths; 4. Accordance with the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas; 5.
Able to cause the minds of sentient beings to be filled with pure faith; 6. Ensuring that all speech is never in vain and is able to uproot sentient beings [from suffering].
1. All the poisonous arrows of suffering; 2. Being sustained by the power of the vows of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
3. Emission of sounds that pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions; 4. Teaching the Dharma without interruption for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); 5.

According to the teachings expounded, being able to give rise to the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis.
Dharma. Son of the Buddha, when the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, turn the wheel of Dharma, there are such immeasurable kinds of matters as these.

Son of the Buddha, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, turns the wheel of Dharma, he plants seeds of pure and white dharmas within the minds of sentient beings through ten matters, so that none pass by in vain.
What are these ten? They are: first, by the power of past vows; second, by the Great [Compassion]... [and so forth].
Because they are sustained by compassion; because they do not abandon sentient beings; because they teach the Dharma according to their inclinations through mastery of wisdom;
because they invariably act at the appropriate time without ever missing it; because they speak without falsehood according to what is suitable;

because they possess the knowledge of the three periods of time and understand them thoroughly; because their physical form is supreme and without equal; and because their mastery of speech is unfathomable.
Therefore, because they possess mastery of wisdom and awaken all who hear their speech, these are the ten.
Son of the Buddha, after the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha has performed his buddha-work, he manifests parinirvāṇa for the sake of observing ten kinds of meanings.
What are these ten? Namely: to demonstrate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are truly impermanent; to demonstrate that all conditioned things are not secure.
He demonstrates that Great Nirvāṇa is a place of peace and security, free from fear.

Because all humans and devas are attached to the physical body (*rūpakāya*), he manifests the physical body as an impermanent phenomenon, so as to cause them to aspire to abide in the pure *dharmakāya*.

He demonstrates that the power of impermanence cannot be overturned. He demonstrates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not abide according to one's will and are not autonomous. He demonstrates all...
Because the three realms of existence are all like illusions and transformations, lacking solidity; because it demonstrates that the nature of nirvāṇa is ultimately solid and indestructible;
and because it demonstrates that while all phenomena are without birth or arising, they possess the characteristics of aggregation and disintegration. O Son of the Buddha!

When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have performed their Buddha-work, fulfilled their vows, turned the wheel of Dharma, and brought to completion the transformation and deliverance of all those who were to be saved;

and when there are Bodhisattvas who have received their honorable titles and attained their predictions of enlightenment—it is by the nature of the Dharma that they enter the unchanging Great Parinirvāṇa.
O Son of the Buddha, this is how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha contemplates the tenth [aspect].
For the sake of the ultimate meaning, he demonstrates parinirvāṇa. O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-door is called "The Vast and Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas.

It is proclaimed by immeasurable Buddhas; it enables the wise to comprehend immeasurable meanings and gives rise to joy, and it causes the great vows and great practices of all bodhisattvas to continue uninterrupted.
The second major section, "Dwelling in Tuṣita," consists of nineteen gates that clarify the perfection of the activity of the fruit.

The reason this activity of the fruit is primarily manifested through the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] is to demonstrate that it is the fruit of the great activity of Samantabhadra, rather than being explained from the perspective of the actual retribution of the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is because the actual retribution is inexpressible; moreover, it is to show that the eight phases encompass both cause and fruit.

Therefore, this is the meaning of the commentary (*śāstra*). To speak according to the actual reality: as previously stated, the equal fruit realized at the conclusion of the five stages of causes is explained in detail in each instance in the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*).

Now, since Samantabhadra has perfected the causes that accord with the *dharmadhātu*, the fruit realized therein—adorned by the aforementioned merit and wisdom—should be described as the fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* realm.

In this context, only the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) is clarified, while the *vipākaphala* (retribution fruit) is not mentioned. If one were to discuss the fruit resulting from the perfection of causes, that has already been explained in the preceding appearance.

If one were to rely on the actual adornments of the *vipākaphala*, those have already been explained in the first section where the fruit was presented to encourage delight, detailing the various adornments of both the primary and secondary [realms]. To explain this exhaustively here would result in needless redundancy; such is the case.

First: although these various passages all speak of the fulfillment of the fruit and the simultaneous manifestation of the ten bodies, these are merely the functioning of the universal dharma-realm and have not yet definitively established the specific phenomena that are manifested.
Therefore, in this chapter on the perfection of causes, only a single transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is cited.
The eight phases of attaining enlightenment are merely one category among the manifestations of the Dharma-realm;
they are like seeing boundless spring by observing a single leaf, or perceiving the limitless sky through a single crack.

Thus, even when viewed through the single gateway of dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven, all ten gateways herein are the great functions of the Dharma-realm. This is what is required of those who would practice.

One must understand that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) arises from the *dharmakāya* (truth body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), serving as the source of the emanation body, thereby demonstrating the equality of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is not like the various other teachings which speak merely of a Buddha accomplished through the severance of delusions.
Therefore, those who contemplate the teachings must recognize this source. Now, the nineteen sections are condensed into ten; the first section concerns abiding in the heavens.
Two [sections] in one gate show the passing away; three in one gate show entry into the womb; four in one gate show dwelling in the womb;
five in three gates show birth; six in two gates show life at home; seven in two gates show leaving home; eight in five gates show the attainment of enlightenment;
nine in two gates show the turning of the wheel of Dharma; ten in eleven gates show entry into nirvana. The first two gates are combined and belong to the third. Therefore...

These are the eight aspects. In the first stage, there is one gate consisting of ten matters; therefore, these constitute the practices within the fruits [of the path]. First, transforming the desire-realm heavens;
second, transforming the form-realm heavens; third, transforming the great trichiliocosm; fourth, conversing with those of the same class; fifth, preaching the Dharma for those of the same class;
sixth, skillfully subduing Māra; seventh, preaching the Dharma through musical sounds; eighth, approaching the Buddha to hear the Dharma; ninth...

He makes offerings to many Buddhas; he benefits sentient beings through ten types of manifestations. Because these ten kinds of activities exist while dwelling in celestial palaces, they are categorized as practices within the state of fruition.
This is intended to demonstrate that even within the state of fruition, one does not abandon the practices of the cause;

it is only by manifesting birth here that one can perceive this. This is the function of manifesting the body in a single location, let alone manifesting the body everywhere throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
How could these various functions possibly be conceived by thought? One should observe that the functions of each successive gate below are subtle and difficult to know;
this is sufficient evidence. Thus far, from the Great Vows up to the Great Practices, all have been shown to be continuous.
This concludes the section on the General Response to the Two Hundred Questions.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Volumes 58 and 59 Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, a Śramaṇa.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery.
Extracted and clarified by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Huishan Fayun Monastery.
The above demonstrates that both the Great Vows and the Great Practices have attained continuity. This concludes the exposition answering the two hundred questions of Puhui.
The division is concluded. Below follows the exhortation to practice and study.
Chapter Thirty-Eight of the *Lokadhātu-parivarta*, Part Seven:
"O Sons of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma, and having heard it, believe and understand it; and having understood it, practice it—they will certainly attain [it]."
One shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? Because one practices according to what has been taught.
Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas do not practice according to what has been taught, you should know that such persons are eternally separated from the *buddha-bodhi*.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice according to what has been taught. Son of the Buddha, these are all the meritorious practices of the bodhisattvas.

The Chapter on the Worldly Dharma-Gate for Transcending the World, which is the Flower of the Meaning of the Determination of Abodes; it universally enters into all dharmas, universally gives birth to all-knowledge, transcends all worlds, and departs from the paths of the two vehicles.
It is not shared with any sentient beings and is able to illuminate all dharma-gates, increasing the supramundane roots of goodness in all beings.
This chapter on the worldly dharma-gate should be honored, should be heard and received, and should be...
One should recite and uphold it; one should contemplate it; one should aspire to it; and one should practice it.
If one can do so, it should be known that this person will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When this chapter was being spoken, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of this dharma-gate, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds in the ten directions all shook violently.
It quivered, and a great light shone everywhere. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and praised him, saying:

"Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound this 'Chapter on the Door of the World-transcending Dharma Universally Entering All Buddha-Dharmas,' which is the Flower of the Definitive Meaning of the Spheres of Action and Merit of these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. Son of the Buddha, you have already..."
You have well studied this Dharma; you have well expounded this Dharma. By your power, you shall protect and uphold this Dharma.
We Buddhas all rejoice in this. Just as we Buddhas rejoice in you, so do all Buddhas likewise.
Son of the Buddha, we Buddhas all with one mind protect and uphold this sutra, so that for the present and the future...
All the assemblies of bodhisattvas who had never heard it before shall now hear it. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the entire great assembly throughout the ten directions and as far as the Dharma-realm, and spoke these verses:
Having practiced austerities for immeasurable eons, born from the true Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas, he causes immeasurable multitudes to abide in Bodhi. Listen as I describe his peerless conduct:
having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, he has abandoned all attachment; he extensively delivers all living beings without forming any conceptual notions.
Seeking the Buddha’s merit with a mind free of dependence, I shall now describe those supreme and wondrous practices.
Having transcended the three realms, māras, afflictions, and karma, they possess supreme merit and most excellent conduct;
their delusions and confusion are extinguished, and their minds are tranquil. I shall now describe the path they have traveled.
Forever free from all worldly deceptions and illusions, you manifest various transformations for the sake of sentient beings;
you display the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind to manifest myriad phenomena, and by explaining these powers, you cause the multitude to rejoice.
You behold the birth, aging, and death of all beings, as they are oppressed and constrained by afflictions, grief, and calamities.
To cause those seeking liberation to resolve their minds upon awakening, you should listen to and receive his meritorious conduct:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

as well as skillful means, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity—practicing these constantly for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons. You, O Benevolent One, should listen to the merits of that person.
Seeking Bodhi for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, He was not stingy with his body or life;
Vowing to benefit all beings and not himself, I shall now describe his practice of loving-kindness and compassion.
To expound upon his virtues for immeasurable billions of kalpas Would be like a single drop from the ocean—not even that much would suffice.
His merit is peerless and beyond comparison; through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall now briefly describe it.
His mind is neither high nor low, and he seeks the Way without weariness.
He causes all sentient beings everywhere to abide in goodness and increase pure dharmas. His wisdom universally benefits others, like a tree, a river, or a spring.
Just as the great earth is the foundation for all things, so too is the Bodhisattva like a lotus flower:
with compassion as its root, tranquility as its stalk, wisdom as its many filaments, and the precepts as its pure fragrance.
The Buddha emits the light of the Dharma to cause it to blossom, yet it remains unstained by the waters of conditioned existence.
All who behold it rejoice in the Bodhisattva’s wondrous Dharma-tree: Born from the seed of faith in the upright mind, with compassion as its roots;
With wisdom as its trunk, skillful means as its branches, and the five perfections as its dense foliage;
With meditative concentration as its leaves and supernormal powers as its flowers; And omniscience as its fruit.
With supreme power as its parasitic vine, it casts a shade that covers the three realms.
The Bodhisattva, the Lion King, has the pure white Dharma for his body; the Four Truths are his feet, right mindfulness his neck, compassion his eyes, and wisdom his head.
With the silken band of liberation bound upon his crown, he dwells within the valley of ultimate emptiness.
Roaring the Dharma to terrify the hosts of Māras, the Bodhisattva acts as a caravan leader.
Seeing all sentient beings throughout the wilderness of birth and death, in the perilous and evil places of affliction, seized by the bandits of Māra—
foolish and blind, having lost the right path— he shows them the straight road and leads them into the city of fearlessness.
The Bodhisattva beholds sentient beings afflicted by the diseases of the three poisons and various sufferings,

tormented throughout the long night; for their sake, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion and extensively expounds eighty-four thousand gates of remedial methods to eliminate all suffering and affliction— the Bodhisattva is thus the Dharma King.
Transforming sentient beings through the True Path, Causing them to distance themselves from evil and cultivate goodness;
Dedicatedly seeking the merits of the Buddhas, At the abodes of all Buddhas, they receive the consecration and the noble prediction.
Extensively bestowing upon others the wealth of the sages— The precious jewels of the factors of enlightenment— The Bodhisattvas turn the Wheel of Dharma, Just as the Buddhas have turned it.

With the hub of precepts and the rim of samādhi, with wisdom as its adornment and insight as its sword, he has already destroyed the thieves of affliction and utterly eliminated the host of demonic enemies.
When all those of the various external paths behold him, there are none who do not scatter.
The Bodhisattva’s ocean of wisdom is deep and vast, without limit or shore; it is filled to overflowing with the flavor of the True Dharma.
Filled with the jewels of the factors of enlightenment, the great mind has no shore or limit;
the ocean of omniscience cannot be fathomed by sentient beings, for its description is inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva is Mount Sumeru, transcending the world; with the peaks of supernormal powers and samādhi, his great mind rests unmoving.
If there are those who draw near, they share in his wisdom and appearance;
he transcends all realms of experience, seeing everything without exception. The Bodhisattva is like a vajra;
his resolve to seek all-knowledge, his faith, and his ascetic practices are firm and unshakable, and his mind is free from fear.
Benefiting all living beings, He utterly destroys all Māras and afflictions.
The Bodhisattva’s great compassion Is like a dense and heavy cloud; The three types of knowledge flash as lightning, And supernormal powers resound as thunder.
Universally employing the four analytical eloquences, He rains down the water of the eight meritorious qualities.
Moistening and satisfying all beings, it causes them to remove the heat of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva’s city of the True Dharma has Prajñā as its walls, shame and remorse as its deep moats, and wisdom as its defensive ramparts.
It opens wide the gates of liberation; right mindfulness constantly guards it, and the Four Noble Truths form its broad royal road.
Gathering the weapons of the six supernormal powers, he further erects the great banner of the Dharma;
beneath it, throughout the three realms of existence, the hosts of all māras are utterly unable to enter.
With the bodhisattva-garuḍa’s *cintāmaṇi* as his firm feet, the wings of skillful means and valor, and the clear, pure eyes of compassion.
Abiding at the tree of omniscience, he gazes upon the great ocean of the three realms of existence; grasping gods, humans, and nāgas, he establishes them on the shore of nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva, the sun of the True Dharma, has appeared in the world with the perfect wheel of the precepts;
traveling swiftly by means of the bases of psychic power, he illuminates all with the light of wisdom.
The medicinal herbs of the powers of the long faculties extinguish the darkness of afflictions;
The moon of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-light dries up the ocean of craving and desire. Taking the Dharma-realm as its wheel, it wanders through ultimate emptiness;
there is no world that does not behold it. Within the consciousness-mind of the three realms, it increases or decreases according to the occasion.
Among the constellations of the two vehicles, there is none to equal him; The Bodhisattva, the Great Dharma King,
his body adorned with merit, Perfectly endowed with all the marks and signs, Gazed upon by humans and devas alike,
With the pure eyes of skillful means and the wisdom-vajra mace, He has attained mastery over all phenomena.
Transforming all living beings through the Way, the Bodhisattva is like a Great Brahma King; Mastery transcends the three realms of existence, and karma and delusions are entirely severed.
Possessing both compassion and equanimity, he manifests his body everywhere, awakening others with the sound of the Dharma.
Within those three realms, he uproots the foundations of all false views.
The Bodhisattva Sovereign Deva, Transcending the realms of birth and death, Whose sphere is ever pure and whose wisdom never regresses,
Who has severed the paths of the Lesser Vehicles, Receiving all methods of consecration,
Endowed with merit and wisdom, Whose fame is heard everywhere— such is the Bodhisattva’s mind of wisdom.
Pure as space, without intrinsic nature and without a place of dependence, where nothing at all can be apprehended;
possessing great sovereign power, able to accomplish the affairs of the world; naturally endowed with pure conduct, causing sentient beings to be likewise;
this is the Bodhisattva’s stage of skillful means, which brings benefit to all living beings.
The water of the Bodhisattva’s compassion washes away all afflictions; The fire of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom burns the fuel of delusive habits;
The wind of the Bodhisattva’s non-abiding wanders through the three realms of existence;
The Bodhisattva is like a precious jewel, able to rescue those in poverty and distress; The Bodhisattva is like a vajra.
The Bodhisattva is like a necklace, able to destroy perverted views; The Bodhisattva is like a *maṇi* jewel, adorning the bodies within the three realms of existence and increasing all practices.
The virtue of the Bodhisattva is like a flower, constantly emitting the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*);
The vow of the Bodhisattva is like a garland, eternally bound upon the heads of sentient beings.
The fragrance of the Bodhisattva’s pure precepts is firmly maintained without transgression;
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom as unguent universally perfumes the triple world; The Bodhisattva’s power is like a curtain, able to shield against the dust of afflictions;
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom is like a banner, able to destroy the enemy of self-conceit; Sublime conduct serves as the silken brocade.
Adorned with wisdom, wearing the robes of shame and remorse, universally covering all sentient beings—this is the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded vehicle.
With this, one departs from the three realms. The Bodhisattva is a mighty elephant whose mind is well-tamed;
the Bodhisattva is a horse of divine power, leaping across all states of existence.
The Bodhisattva is a Dharma-preaching dragon, universally raining upon the minds of sentient beings;
The Bodhisattva is the Utpala flower, difficult to encounter in the world; The Bodhisattva is a great heroic general, who completely subdues all māras;
The Bodhisattva turns the wheel of Dharma, just as the Buddha has turned it; The Bodhisattva is a lamp that destroys darkness.
Sentient beings behold the true path; The river of the Bodhisattva’s merit flows ever in accordance with that true path.
The bridge of the Bodhisattva’s diligence extensively delivers all multitudes of beings.
With great wisdom and vast vows, together they form a sturdy ship, To guide and receive all sentient beings, And establish them upon the shore of Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva’s pleasure garden, truly bringing joy to sentient beings;
The Bodhisattva’s palace of wisdom, adorned with the flowers of liberation; The Bodhisattva is like a wondrous medicine, eradicating the disease of afflictions;
The Bodhisattva is like the Snowy Mountains, producing the medicine of wisdom; The Bodhisattva is equal to the Buddha.
Awakening all sentient beings—the Buddha-mind has nothing else to it. Just as the Perfectly Awakened One comes to awaken the world, so does the Bodhisattva come.
Just as the All-Knowing One enters the universal gate through wisdom, the Bodhisattva skillfully guides all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva naturally awakens to the realm of all-knowledge;

the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable power cannot be destroyed by the world. With fearless wisdom, the Bodhisattva knows all sentient beings and phenomena throughout the entire world—their various distinct physical forms, as well as their sounds and names.
They are able to discern and know all things; though detached from name and form (*nāmarūpa*), they manifest various appearances.
No sentient beings whatsoever can fathom their way. Such virtues as these the Bodhisattvas have fully accomplished.
They realize that all natures are devoid of inherent nature, remaining unattached to both existence and non-existence.
Such is omniscience— Inexhaustible and without dependence. I shall now expound it To bring joy to all sentient beings.

Though they know the characteristics of all phenomena To be like illusions, entirely empty and quiescent, Yet through the heart of compassionate vows And the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, They manifest supernatural transformations.
These various and immeasurable matters, Such as all these meritorious qualities— You all should listen and receive them:
A single body can manifest Infinite and diverse bodies; Without mind and without objective realm, Universally responding to all beings;
Within a single sound, it fully expounds All manner of speech and sounds.
They can produce the languages of all sentient beings according to their respective types;
Having forever left behind the body of afflictions, they manifest bodies of sovereign mastery. Knowing that dharmas are ineffable, they yet provide various explanations;
Their minds are eternally in a state of quiescence, pure as space, Yet they universally adorn the buddha-fields.
Manifesting before all assemblies, they are without attachment to the body;
yet they are able to manifest bodies throughout all worlds, taking birth according to what is appropriate.
Although they are born in all places, they do not dwell upon that birth; knowing the body to be like space, it appears in various ways according to the mind.
The body of the Bodhisattva is boundless, manifesting universally in all places; always with deep and pure mind,
they reverently offer worship to the Most Victorious among Two-Legged Beings— incense, flowers, various musical performances,
banners, pennants, and precious canopies— never departing from the assembly of a single Buddha.
Universally present before all Buddhas, amidst their great assemblies, they pose difficult questions and listen to the Dharma;
hearing the Dharma, they enter samādhi through each and every immeasurable gateway.
Their emergence from concentration is likewise so, manifesting without end through wisdom and skillful means, realizing that the world is entirely like an illusion.
Yet they are able to manifest within the world all manner of infinite illusory phenomena;
they display various forms, as well as minds and speech, entering into the nets of conceptualization while remaining forever unattached.
Sometimes they manifest the initial aspiration for enlightenment to benefit the world; at other times, they manifest long-standing cultivation of the path.
Vast and boundless, the supreme dharmas— generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom; the four Brahma-vihāras, the four means of attraction, and so forth— whether they are manifested in practice, brought to fulfillment,
attained through patient endurance free from conceptualization, or manifested as being bound to only one more birth, the Buddhas bestow the empowerment.
Sometimes manifesting in the form of a śrāvaka, Or again manifesting as a pratyekabuddha, Attaining parinirvāṇa in various places yet never abandoning the bodhisattva practice;
Sometimes manifesting as Śakra, Or manifesting as Brahmā, surrounded by celestial maidens; Sometimes remaining alone in silent contemplation, Or manifesting as a bhikṣu.
Tranquil, he disciplines his mind; Or he appears as a Sovereign King, Governing the laws of the world.
Or he appears as a woman skilled in arts; Or he appears practicing virtuous deeds; Or he appears experiencing the five desires;
Or he appears entering various meditative absorptions; Or he appears at the very moment of birth; Or appearing as a child, or as one old and dying.
If there should be one who attempts to conceive of this, their mind will fall into doubt and become deranged.
Whether manifesting in a celestial palace or manifesting his initial descent of spirit; whether entering or dwelling in the womb;
whether attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, being born, or entering nirvana; whether manifesting entry into a school or remaining among the ladies of the harem.
Some leave the mundane world to practice dhyāna; some sit beneath the Bodhi tree and spontaneously attain perfect enlightenment;
some manifest the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; some manifest the initial seeking of the Way;
some manifest the body of a Buddha, sitting in meditation for immeasurable kalpas; some cultivate the path of non-retrogression, accumulating the requisites for bodhi.
Deeply entering incalculable eons, they have all reached the other shore.
Infinite eons are a single thought-moment; a single thought-moment is infinite eons. All eons are non-eons;
for the sake of the world, they manifest eons— Without coming and without accumulation—yet they accomplish the affairs of all eons. Within a single mote of dust...
Universally beholding all Buddhas throughout all places in the ten directions, there is nowhere that the lands, sentient beings, and dharmas do not exist;
he sees them all in succession, and even after the passing of immeasurable eons, they can never be fully exhausted.
The Bodhisattva knows that sentient beings are vast and without limit.
The body of that single sentient being arises from immeasurable causes and conditions; just as one knows this one [body], so it is with all others.

According to what they have realized, he teaches those who have not yet learned, fully knowing the various faculties of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and also knowing how those faculties shift and transform.
Those who should be transformed and those who should not; the single faculty and all faculties;
the subtle distinctions of their mutual causal conditions; their sequential order without confusion;
furthermore, he knows their inclinations and understandings, as well as all habitual tendencies of affliction; and he also knows all mental activities of the past, future, and present.

Having thoroughly understood that all conditioned phenomena neither come nor go, and having realized their nature, he preached the unsurpassed Dharma. He fully comprehended all manner of defiled and pure practices;
in a single thought-moment he attained Bodhi and perfected all-knowledge, abiding in the inconceivable state of a Buddha.
With the mind of ultimate wisdom, one can know all in a single thought.

Having attained mastery over the power of the bodhisattva’s supernatural knowledge and wisdom regarding the conduct of all sentient beings, one is able to travel to immeasurable lands within a single thought. Thus swiftly one travels, throughout countless eons.
There is nowhere it does not pervade, yet it does not stir even a fraction of a hair’s breadth.
It is like a skilled illusionist who manifests all manner of forms; if one seeks within that illusion, there are no forms and no non-forms.
So too is the Bodhisattva: through the illusory power of skillful wisdom, they manifest all things in their various forms.
Pervading the world like the pure sun and moon, Like a bright mirror in the void whose reflection appears in all waters,
Yet not being mixed with the water— Know that the Bodhisattva’s pure wheel of Dharma is likewise:
It appears in the waters of the minds of the world, Yet is not mixed with the world.
Just as a person in a dream performs various deeds, which, though passing through billions of years, do not end even after a single night;

so too, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they manifest all manner of activities that may last for immeasurable eons, yet their wisdom in a single thought-moment is inexhaustible. It is like [the echo] within a mountain valley.
And within the various palaces, all things resonate in response; yet in reality, there is no discrimination.

When Bodhisattvas dwell in the Dharma-nature, they are able, through their sovereign wisdom, to extensively produce sounds according to the various types of beings, yet they likewise remain without discrimination. It is like seeing a mirage and perceiving it as water.
Chasing after [it], they cannot drink; as they toss and turn, their thirst increases all the more. One should know that the afflicted minds of sentient beings are likewise so.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion and rescues them, causing them to transcend [suffering].
He contemplates form as being like a mass of foam, sensation as being like a bubble upon the water, and perception as being like a mirage in the heat.
All conditioned phenomena are like the trunk of a plantain tree; The mind and consciousness are like a magical illusion.
Manifesting all manner of things—knowing the aggregates thus, The wise have no attachments.
The sense bases are entirely empty and still, Like the movement of mechanical puppets; The nature of the elements is eternally detached, Yet falsely appears within the world.
The Bodhisattva dwells in reality, the supreme meaning of tranquil extinction;
he proclaims it extensively in various ways, yet his mind has no point of reliance. There is neither coming nor going, nor is there any abiding.
The causes of afflictions, karma, and suffering—these three constantly revolve; dependent origination is neither existent nor non-existent.
Neither real nor unreal, thus one enters the Middle Way; In teaching, there is no attachment, and within a single thought-moment, One universally manifests the minds of the three periods of time.
Regarding all the various phenomena of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, One accords with the three codes of discipline And expounds the three gates of liberation.
Establishing the paths of the three vehicles, Accomplishing all-encompassing wisdom, Thoroughly understanding what is possible and impossible,
The various karmas, the faculties, The elements, the analytical knowledges, and meditative concentrations,
The path leading to all destinations, Recollection of past lives, the divine eye, And the eradication of all delusions— One knows the ten powers of a Buddha.
Yet they have not yet achieved full realization of the emptiness of all phenomena;
they constantly seek the sublime Dharma without being joined with afflictions, nor do they exhaust their outflows.
Having extensively known the path of deliverance, they bring sentient beings across and attain fearlessness therein, never abandoning the cultivation of all practices.
Without error and without contradicting the Way, Nor losing right mindfulness; Vigor, aspiration, samādhi, contemplation, and wisdom Are all without diminution;
The three clusters are entirely pure, And one clearly penetrates the three periods of time.
With great compassion for sentient beings, There is no obstruction whatsoever— All this arises from entering this Dharma-gate.
I have described only a small portion of such conduct; though one were to spend countless eons explaining the meaning of its majestic virtues, that conduct would never be exhausted.
What I have now spoken is but a tiny fraction, like a single mote of dust upon the great earth. Abiding in the wisdom of the Buddha, one should conceive of it as something truly extraordinary.
Practicing the most supreme conduct, endowed with great compassion, Diligent and self-serene, they transform all sentient beings.
Abiding securely within pure precepts, they possess the practices for receiving predictions;
They are able to enter into the merits of the Buddhas, And fully know the conduct of sentient beings, their lands, As well as their eons and worlds.
Free from thoughts of weariness, possessing the *dhāraṇī* of discerning wisdom, they penetrate the true meaning;
their contemplation and teaching are peerless. They are the tranquil, perfectly awakened ones who have given rise to the mind of Samantabhadra and cultivated its practices and vows.
Through the power of the causes and conditions of compassion, their resolve for the Path is pure.
Practicing the perfections, they fully realize the wisdom of subsequent cognition;
through the power of realization and mastery, they achieve unsurpassed enlightenment. Having accomplished equalizing wisdom, they expound the most supreme Dharma;
possessing excellent eloquence, they attain the station of the Dharma King and remain far removed from all attachments.
He proclaims the equality of mind, which gives birth to wisdom; through transformation he attains enlightenment and sustains all kalpas.
The wise one experiences great joy, deeply entering and relying upon fearlessness and freedom from doubt;
having realized the inconceivable, he skillfully and subtly discerns with excellence.
Skillfully entering all samādhis, universally perceiving the realm of wisdom, Ultimate in all liberations,
sporting in the supernormal powers and clarities, Permanently free from all fetters, wandering at will through groves and gardens,
Taking pure dharmas as their palace, all their practices are delightful, Manifesting immeasurable adornments.
With a mind unmoved by the world, deeply observing with a virtuous heart, you can eloquently expound the seal of sublime, pure enlightenment.
The light of your wisdom illuminates all things; that which you abide in is peerless.
Your mind is not inferior; you stand firm in wisdom like a great mountain, and your planting of virtue is like a deep ocean.
Abiding in the Dharma like a treasure, with the armor of the mind of vow, they initiate the great task that can never be destroyed;
they receive the prophecy of enlightenment, abiding in the secret treasury of the vast mind which is inexhaustible;
awakening to all phenomena, they possess mastery over all worldly knowledge.
Their wondrous functions are unimpeded throughout all sentient beings, lands, and various dharmas;
their vows, realms, wisdom, and supernormal powers are manifested in the world in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions.
Their playful displays and spheres of activity are sovereign and cannot be restrained.
The powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities, adorned by all karmas;
the various bodies and bodily actions, as well as speech and the purification of speech— because they have attained protection,
the bodhisattva’s mind first gives rise to ten kinds of activities, and through the pervasiveness of that mind, the faculties remain undistracted and unshaken.
Having attained the most excellent faculties, with a profound mind and an ever-increasing resolve, far removed from all flattery and deceit, they possess various forms of definitive understanding.

Pervasively entering into the world, they abandon the habitual tendencies of those afflictions and take up this most excellent path; skillfully cultivating it to perfection, they attain all-knowledge.
Having departed from regression and entered the stage of certainty, they decisively realize nirvāṇa.

They give birth to the path of the Buddha-dharma, achieve its merits, and attain its titles; whether it be the path itself or the immeasurable paths, even down to the stages of the path’s adornments, they dwell securely in their sequence, yet remain entirely free from attachment—even toward their own hands, feet, and internal organs.
Taking the vajra as his heart, he is clad in the armor of compassion;
Fully equipped with all weapons, he has wisdom as his head and clear insight as his eyes; The practice of bodhicitta serves as his ears, and pure precepts as his nose;
With the extinction of darkness and the absence of obstruction, eloquence is his tongue, and his body reaches everywhere.
With supreme wisdom as his mind, he performs all activities while walking or staying;
on the lion throne at the site of enlightenment, he dwells in the Brahma-posture amidst the sky. His conduct and his observations universally illumine the realm of the Tathāgata;
he surveys the conduct of all sentient beings with vigor and roars like a lion, practicing pure giving free from attachment.
Abandoning pride, they maintain pure precepts; free from anger, they are ever patient. Without indolence, they are constantly diligent;
having attained mastery in meditative concentration, their wisdom is beyond all activity. With compassion they rescue others without weariness;
rejoicing in the Dharma, they relinquish afflictions. Amidst all sensory realms, they understand both meaning and the Dharma.
May merit be fully perfected, and wisdom be like a sharp sword; May they universally illuminate the joy of much hearing and clearly understand the direction toward the Dharma;
Knowing Māra and the path of Māra, may they vow to abandon them all;
Beholding the Buddhas and the deeds of the Buddhas, may they resolve to embrace them all; Free from pride, may they cultivate wisdom.
Not held by the power of Māra, but sustained by the Buddha and likewise upheld by the Dharma, he manifests dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven;
he further manifests the end of his life there, manifests dwelling in the mother’s womb, and manifests entering the subtle realm of rebirth.
He manifests birth and a smile, and also manifests taking seven steps.
He demonstrated the mastery of all arts and sciences, and also showed himself dwelling in the deep inner palace.

He left the home life to practice austerities and proceeded to the site of enlightenment. There he sat upright, radiating light, awakening all living beings, subduing Māra, and attaining perfect enlightenment.
He turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; all that he manifested has now come to its end.
Entering into Great Parinirvāṇa— those practices of the Bodhisattvas, cultivated for immeasurable eons, vast and boundless—
I shall now describe but a small portion. Although they cause immeasurable multitudes to dwell securely in the Buddha’s virtues,
within both sentient beings and phenomena, there is ultimately nothing to be grasped.
Endowed with such practices, they sport in the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):

placing myriad lands upon the tip of a hair for billions of eons, holding infinite lands in their palms, traveling everywhere without bodily fatigue and returning to place them back in their original locations—all this without sentient beings being aware of it; by means of all these, the Bodhisattvas...
Various adorned lands are placed within a single pore, yet they are all made visible in their true reality.
Furthermore, with a single pore, one universally contains all oceans; though the great oceans neither increase nor decrease, sentient beings are not harmed.
Immeasurable Iron Ring Mountains are grasped in the hand and crushed into dust.
From a single atom, one enters a world-system; exhausting the number of all such atoms, one further grinds these world-systems into dust;
such atoms may be known. The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is immeasurable;
from within a single pore, they emit infinite rays of light, surpassing the light of the sun, moon, and stars.
The light of the maṇi jewel and the radiance of all the devas— All these are eclipsed and extinguished;
He brings an end to the suffering of the evil realms And preaches the unsurpassed Dharma.
With the various and diverse sounds of all the worlds, The Bodhisattva, with a single voice, Is able to manifest them all.
He definitively and analytically expounds all the teachings of the Buddhas,
causing all living beings to hear them and rejoice greatly. He places all past eons within future and present eons,
and likewise shifts future and present eons back into the past, manifesting infinite lands.
The blazing, the formation, and the abiding of all worlds, And the past, future,
and present Buddhas of all ten directions— All are clearly manifested within a single pore;
Deeply knowing the nature of transformation, He skillfully responds to the minds of sentient beings.

Manifesting various bodies, yet remaining entirely without attachment—whether manifesting as the bodies of all sentient beings within the six realms of existence, or as the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, or the World-Protectors;
or as the bodies of the multitudes of devas and humans, or the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or the bodies of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas; or manifesting as the body of a bodhisattva.

Practicing all-knowledge, skillfully entering the soft, medium, and superior [capacities], they manifest the attainment of enlightenment within the web of sentient beings' various conceptions, as well as throughout all Buddha-fields.
Having thoroughly understood the web of all conceptions, they attain mastery over conception; they manifest the cultivation of bodhisattva practices and all matters of expedient means.
Manifesting such vast and wondrous supernatural transformations, these various realms are unknown to all the world.

Though they manifest, there is nothing manifested; ultimately, they further increase [the roots of virtue] by acceding to the minds of sentient beings, causing them to practice the path of reality through body, speech, and mind.
Equanimity is like space; pure precepts are the ointment and incense. Various practices are the garments; the Dharma-silk adorns the pure topknot.
The maṇi-jewel of omniscience—there is no merit that does not pervade it.
Through consecration, he ascends to the royal throne; the pāramitās are his wheels. The various supernormal powers serve as his elephant.
Divine power serves as his horse; wisdom is his bright pearl; sublime conduct is his retinue of court ladies;
the four means of attraction are his treasurers; skillful means is his commander-in-chief;
the Bodhisattva Universal Monarch has samādhi for his city walls and emptiness and stillness for his palace; compassion is his armor and wisdom is his sword.
Mindfulness is the bow and clear wisdom the sharp arrow; The canopy of spiritual power is raised high.
The banner of wisdom is erected aloft; The power of patience remains unshakable. It directly shatters the army of Māra.
Dhāraṇīs serve as level ground, And various practices are the flowing rivers. Pure wisdom is the gushing spring, And sublime insight forms the grove of trees.
Emptiness is the clear and pure pool; the factors of enlightenment are the blooming lotuses. Adorned by their own supernormal powers, they constantly delight in samādhi.
Contemplation serves as their maidservants; nectar is their choice food and the taste of liberation is their drink.
They sport within the three vehicles—this is the practice of all bodhisattvas.
Subtly and increasingly superior, Having practiced for immeasurable eons,
Their minds never weary of making offerings to all Buddhas, Adorning and purifying all lands,
Universally causing all beings to dwell securely in omniscience; Even the atoms within all lands— Their number could all be known.
The entire realm of empty space might be measured by a single grain of sand;
The thoughts and moments of every sentient being’s mind might be counted and known; But the merits of the Buddha-sons can never be fully told.
Desiring to possess these merits and all supreme, wondrous dharmas, And desiring to cause all sentient beings [to attain them as well]...

Free from suffering and always at peace, desiring that one’s body, speech, and mind may become entirely equal to those of all Buddhas, one should generate the vajra-mind and train in these meritorious practices.
This concludes the seventh major section, the exhortation to practice and study. The Sūtra states: "This dharma-gate is named 'The Vast Purity of the Bodhisattva'."
"Purifying Conduct. This is the title of the Dharma taught by immeasurable Buddhas. Furthermore, it says:

"If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and believe, understand, and practice it, they will surely swiftly attain Bodhi. This is the exhortation to believe and practice. Finally, it says:
"The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate for Increasing the World-transcending Roots of Goodness in Sentient Beings and Departing from Worldly Dharmas. This is the conclusion.
This is the title. Subsequently, the worlds of the ten directions shook and emitted light, manifesting as auspicious signs that confirmed [the teaching].

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all offered praise; this constitutes the confirmation by others. Furthermore, it is protected and circulated so that it may be heard in the final age.
This concludes the discourse of this single assembly as the ultimate Dharma. Thus, this chapter serves as the entirety of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The subsequent verses, numbering two hundred and fifteen and a half, may be understood by following the commentary (*śāstra*).
The above concludes the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), which is the second time the causes and effects of the six stages (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*) are elucidated.

Below, in the ninth assembly at the Jetavana Grove, the "Dharma-gate of Entering the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-praveśa-dharmaparyāya*) is taught; this is the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm" (*Dharmadhātu-praveśa-parivarta*), spanning from volume sixty to volume eighty.
End. This concludes the third cycle clarifying the causes and effects of the six stages, collectively forming the section on "The Realization and Attainment of Virtue Based on Persons.
The "Chapter on Transcending the World" is finished.
