It is because what is seen in a dream cannot be seen by that great multitude. It is the same for all bodhisattvas and the kings of the world:
it is because of the power of the roots of goodness accumulated over a long time, and because they have made the vast vow for omniscience.
Because they study all the virtues of the Buddhas; because they practice the path adorned by the bodhisattvas;
because they fulfill the dharma of the knowledge of all-knowledge; because they satisfy all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra; because they enter into all the stages of bodhisattva wisdom;
because they sport in all the samādhis wherein bodhisattvas dwell; and because they have already been able to examine all the [qualities of] bodhi...
Because the realm of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is unobstructed, he perceives all the inconceivable, sovereign, and miraculous transformations of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
All the śrāvakas and great disciples are unable to see or know them, for they lack the pure eye of a bodhisattva.
It is like the Snowy Mountains, which abound with various medicinal herbs; when a skilled physician arrives...
They are all able to distinguish them; yet those hunters and herdsmen who constantly dwell on that mountain do not see those medicinal herbs.
This is also like this: because Bodhisattvas enter the realm of wisdom and possess the power of mastery, they are able to see the vast and great spiritual transformations of the Tathāgata.
The Great Disciples, however, seek only their own benefit and do not desire to benefit others; they seek only for themselves...
One who seeks peace does not desire to bring peace to others. Although they dwell within the forest, they neither know nor see it.
It is like a treasure trove within the earth, completely filled with all manner of rare and wondrous jewels;

there is a man of great wisdom and discernment who is skilled in identifying all hidden stores, and he possesses such great power of merit that he can exercise mastery over them according to his will.
They take [the treasure] and provide for their parents, relieve their kinsmen, and ensure that the elderly, the sick, and the destitute are all equally supported.
Those who lack wisdom and merit, even if they arrive at the place where the treasure is hidden, do not know it, do not see it, and thus gain no benefit from it;
this case is exactly like that. The great Bodhisattvas possess the eye of pure wisdom and are able to enter the inconceivable [realm] of the Tathāgata.
They deliberate upon the most profound realm; they are able to perceive the Buddha’s spiritual power; they are able to enter all dharma-gates; they are able to roam within the ocean of samādhis;
they are able to make offerings to all Buddhas; they are able to awaken sentient beings through the True Dharma;

and they are able to gather and sustain sentient beings through the four means of integration. Even the great śrāvakas cannot perceive the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, nor can they see the bodhisattvas.
"O Assembly, it is like a blind person who has reached a great island of jewels; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they are unable to see any of the various treasures.
Because they do not see them, they cannot gather them or enjoy their use. It is just so with these great disciples:
although they dwell in the forest in the presence of the World-Honored One, they do not see the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual powers."
Furthermore, they were unable to see the great assembly of bodhisattvas. Why was this?
Because they lacked the unimpeded, pure eye of a bodhisattva, and thus could not sequentially awaken to and enter the dharma-realm to behold the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
It is like a person who has obtained a pure eye called "Stainless Radiance," which no darkness or color can obstruct. At that time, that person...

Suppose a person, in the darkness of night, stands amidst a multitude of immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and millions of people—whether they are walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
A person with clear vision sees every detail of those people’s forms and deportments without exception;
yet that person with clear vision cannot be seen by any of those people in their various movements and gestures. The Buddha is also like this.
It is so. Having achieved the pure and unimpeded eye of wisdom, he is able to clearly perceive all worlds.
The supernormal powers and transformations he manifests are surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, such that none of the great disciples can see them.

It is, for example, like a bhikṣu who, in the midst of a great assembly, enters the meditative concentration of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), namely, the concentration on the universal base of earth, water... [and so forth].

The totalities (kṛtsnāyatana): the totality of fire, the totality of wind, the totality of blue, the totality of yellow, the totality of red, the totality of white, the totality of space, the totality of the bodies of various sentient beings, the totality of all languages and sounds, and the totality of all objects of perception. One who enters these meditative absorptions sees...
As for its object of focus, the rest of the great assembly is entirely unable to see it, except for those who dwell in this samādhi.
It is likewise with the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas manifested by the Tathāgata; the Bodhisattvas perceive it fully, while the Śrāvakas cannot behold it.
It is, for example, like a person who applies a drug that makes the body invisible to their own eyes and remains within a great assembly.
Though he comes and sits, there is no one who can see him, yet he is able to perceive all matters within the assembly. You should know that the Tathāgata is likewise:

transcending the world, he perceives the world universally, and cannot be seen by any śrāvakas, except for those great bodhisattvas who are advancing toward the realm of omniscience. It is like when a person is born, two deities constantly...
They follow one another. First is being born together; second is having the same name. While devas constantly see humans, humans do not see the devas.
One should know that the Tathāgata is likewise: when he manifests great supernormal powers within the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas are entirely unable to see him.
It is like a bhikṣu who has attained mastery over the mind and enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Six.
The functions of his sense faculties were entirely inactive; he was neither aware of nor cognizant of any speech.
Because he was sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he did not enter parinirvāṇa. All the śrāvakas were likewise:
although they resided within the Jeta Grove and possessed the six sense faculties, they did not know, see, understand, or enter the Tathāgata’s sovereign assembly of bodhisattvas.

All such activities [are performed]. Why is this? The realm of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep, vast, and great; it is difficult to see and difficult to know, difficult to fathom and difficult to measure.
It transcends all worlds, is inconceivable, and cannot be destroyed. It is not the realm of any of the followers of the two vehicles.
Therefore, the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and the Jeta Grove [pervade everywhere].
Pervading all pure worlds—such matters as these are entirely unknown and unseen by the great śrāvakas, for they are not their proper vessel.
The second major section, "The Son of the Buddha: The Similes Beginning with the Ganges," clarifies this through ten similes, each one following in sequence.
This is an analogy. It generally illustrates the failure to perceive the realms of the Tathāgata’s causes and effects, and it also illustrates the failure to perceive the realms of the Bodhisattvas.
However, each analogy possesses both a general and a specific meaning, illustrating two kinds of qualities. First is the analogy of the hungry ghosts in the Ganges.

The general analogy illustrates that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not perceive the profoundly deep virtue of their beneficial influence. The specific analogy illustrates that they do not perceive the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
The intent is to reveal that the two vehicles possess cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and therefore do not see the Buddha-realm;
this is like a hungry ghost who, due to the power of its karma, does not see water. The second analogy, the dream of traveling to a celestial palace, serves as a general illustration.

The lofty, eminent, and vast virtues of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—specifically illustrated by the Tathāgata’s playful supernatural transformations (*vikrīḍita-ṛddhi*) and the various adornments of the great assemblies of Bodhisattvas—are compared to dreams to illustrate the Bodhisattva’s actual realization; thus, those of the Two Vehicles are like those who have not yet seen such a dream.
Third, the analogy of the excellent medicines of the Snowy Mountains serves as a general metaphor for the profound and difficult-to-penetrate [qualities] of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
Seeing Virtue. The first analogy illustrates how a bodhisattva dwells securely in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to rescue and deliver sentient beings; thus, they are like a skilled physician.

Because the followers of the two vehicles lack such compassion, they do not see [this virtue]. The fourth analogy, that of the hidden treasure difficult to know, generally illustrates the Tathāgata’s secret and difficult-to-know virtues, and specifically illustrates the bodhisattva’s entry into samādhi for observation; it is like a person of clear wisdom who recognizes a treasure. There is...
Merit is able to grasp it. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not plant roots of merit, and furthermore, they lack the eye of wisdom;

therefore, they are unable to see it. This is like the analogy of five blind men who cannot see a treasure island. Generally, this serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s transcendent and inconceivable virtues.

Specifically, it serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s wondrous conduct and the perfection of his accumulated practices. Because the bodhisattvas’ roots of goodness have matured, they receive the prediction [of enlightenment]. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not.
Because of these roots of goodness, it is like a blind person who does not see the treasure on the island.

The analogy of the six pure eyes being unobstructed serves as a general metaphor for the immeasurable virtues illuminated by the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and specifically as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s majestic power (*pratāpa*).

Only when the Bodhisattvas’ eye of wisdom is clear and pure do they perceive the Tathāgata’s sovereign mastery; because the eye of wisdom of the followers of the two vehicles is not clear, they do not perceive the Tathāgata’s sovereign mastery.
7. The metaphor of the spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) universally illustrates the inconceivable, all-pervading virtues of the Tathāgata;

specifically, it illustrates the adornments of the Tathāgata’s pure lands. Because Bodhisattvas enter this samādhi, they see them; because those of the two vehicles lack this samādhi, they do not see them. 8.
The metaphor of the wondrous medicine that obscures the form universally illustrates the Tathāgata’s transcendent virtue of concealment and manifestation; specifically, it illustrates...
The Tathāgata’s sustaining power enables Bodhisattvas to give rise to the virtue of transformations; because the followers of the Two Vehicles lack this liberation, they do not perceive it.
Ninth, the analogy of the celestial beings following humans serves as a general metaphor for how the Tathāgata’s adorned and excellent Bodhisattva bodies pervade the ten directions.
The perfection of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is not seen by those of the two vehicles because they lack compassion and abandon sentient beings;

this is illustrated by the metaphor of the ten meditative absorptions of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This serves as a singular metaphor for the śrāvakas who abide in their own vehicle, utterly devoid of the thought to mature sentient beings or purify buddha-fields, because they lack the causes possessed by Buddhas and bodhisattvas; therefore, they do not now see the Tathāgata’s awakening.
This is merely the realm of the supreme and wondrous Tathāgata. At the conclusion, it summarizes by asking: "For what reason do those of the Two Vehicles not perceive it? The Sūtra states:
"The realm of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep, vast, and expansive; it is difficult to know, difficult to fathom, and difficult to measure, transcending all worlds."
It is inconceivable. There is no one who can fathom its depth. It is not within the domain of any of the followers of the two vehicles.

Therefore, the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the Jeta Grove—all these things that pervade every pure world—were entirely unknown and unseen by the great śrāvakas, for they were not vessels for such matters. This...
This concludes the section on the Dharma-realm gate. It is certain that this is not something known or seen by those of the Two Vehicles, for they are not suitable vessels for it.

Question: This sutra is the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle, intended solely for those of the highest faculties. Since it is said that the Two Vehicles are not suitable vessels, how could they have been present in the assembly?
If they were already seated there yet did not hear or see [the teaching], what was the intention behind this? Answer:
It is said that there are two meanings here. First, according to the *Avataṃsaka*’s doctrine of the equal Dharma-realm, all sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If those of the Two Vehicles were truly and ultimately excluded from this, it would entail the fault that Buddha-nature is not universal.
Those currently seated here are precisely manifesting the equal Buddha-wisdom, for not a single sentient being is abandoned.

However, as for those who were present yet neither saw nor heard [the teaching], it was because those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) delight in abiding in their own vehicles and do not plant superior roots of goodness;
this is precisely the fault of delusive conceptualization and attachment, whereby they fail to realize [the truth]. Their mental faculties and wisdom are inferior.

Therefore, they are not suitable vessels; this is the first point. Second, since the Buddha’s wisdom is fundamentally impartial, if those of middling or inferior faculties were without the potential for Buddhahood, it would entail the fault that the Buddha abandons sentient beings and severs his great compassion of shared essence (*samatā-karuṇā*).
Now, those of inferior faculties have no affinity for the Great Dharma; they must necessarily be enticed and led by means of various skillful expedients.
Therefore it is said: "I guide sentient beings through immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients, desiring that all people attain Buddhahood, so that my original vow may be fulfilled.
Since the One Vehicle is difficult to traverse, it is essential to reveal the provisional. Thus, [the Buddha]...
The One Vehicle Dharma is explained as three; this constitutes the simultaneous manifestation of two aspects.

When manifesting the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya, if it is absolutely necessary for the Tathāgata to appear in the human realm—even while engaging in the same activities as others—the Dharma he teaches to ordinary worldlings on the broad ground and to those with the false views of external paths would not be easily understood without skillful means.

Transformation necessarily relies upon great expedient power; the Bodhisattva conceals within while manifesting without, appearing to engage in the same activities as others to gradually lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.

Thus, those among the śrāvakas at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who previously came from among the non-Buddhists were all great bodhisattvas of this assembly who manifested as śrāvakas through skillful means, acting as a responsive retinue to strike the bellows of the Dharma.

This is the transformation through the Dharma. Therefore, the roots were first buried here in this Root Chapter (Honmon) as a preliminary provision for those with the capacity for provisional manifestations.

The intent was that these traces of transformation, which will be displayed alongside the Buddha, must necessarily begin from here; it serves as the foundation for subsuming the derivative (shumoku). These are the two meanings.
However, these two meanings are still discussed from the perspective of provisional manifestations (*traces*).

If one relies upon the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm, the Buddha’s ten bodies are all-pervading, and the Dharma is expounded in a single sound, heard equally by all diverse classes of beings; it is fundamentally equal.

It is only according to the capacity—whether great or small—of sentient beings that there are differences in what is seen and heard. Thus, when the Tathāgata is actually present in the Jeta Grove, he is precisely [the manifestation of] the ultimate reality.
However, regarding the Flower Treasury [World], those Bodhisattvas who perceive it see the Dharma-realm body; those of inferior capacity see only the six-foot form.
When the single voice preaches the Dharma, Bodhisattvas who hear it perceive only the One Vehicle, while those of small faculties hear the preaching of the Three Vehicles.
Thus, though they are in the same time and the same assembly, they have different views and hear differently, without waiting for the manifestation of provisional means—just as with a single rain.
[The moisture] is universally moistened; yet the three faculties receive this nourishment individually. If this were the case, then the Śrāvakas seated here would truly be of inferior capacity.
As stated in the sutras, they are indeed like the blind and the deaf. Only by understanding it in this way does one enter the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).

However, regarding the simultaneous manifestation of the two aspects of the dual descent [of light], this is merely a matter of what is perceived according to the capacities of the recipients. The Commentary states: "Since it is not their..."

The vessel [of Śāriputra] was originally not fit to be ranked among them; however, in order to manifest the superiority of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva of Great Authority manifested himself as blind and deaf.
Thus we know that blindness and deafness possess the power to manifest superiority over the excellent, and for this reason it is profoundly profound and mysterious.
If one refers to the later passage where Śāriputra causes six thousand bhikṣus to contemplate Mañjuśrī’s virtues and they immediately attain realization, this is a manifestation.

This serves as the foundation for opening up the provisional; it is the dharma of the non-obstruction between the provisional and the real, for they are perfectly interfused and fundamentally lack fixed definition.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vairocanapraṇidhānaraśmi, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"You all should contemplate the inconceivable path of the Buddha. Within this Jetavana Grove, he has manifested supernormal powers;
through the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, he has displayed countless worlds throughout all the realms.
Yet those who are deluded cannot comprehend them—such is the profound and wondrous Dharma of the King of Dharma."
Immeasurable and inconceivable are the various supernormal powers he manifests; none in the world can fathom them.
Because he has realized that all phenomena are signless, he is called a Buddha.
His majestic marks and adornments are so vast that they cannot be fully extolled; now, within this grove, he displays great supernatural power.
Profound and without limit, it cannot be fathomed by words.
Behold this assembly of bodhisattvas of great majesty and immeasurable power, who have come from the lands of the ten directions to see the World-Honored One.
Their vows are all fulfilled; their conduct is unimpeded throughout all worlds.
No one is able to measure it; neither all the *pratyekabuddhas* nor those great *śrāvakas* can fully know the sphere of the Bodhisattva’s practice.
Having perfected all the stages of the Bodhisattva’s great wisdom, he stands high with a banner of valor, difficult to crush and impossible to move.
"O Greatly Renowned Sages, through the power of immeasurable samādhis, the various spiritual transformations you manifest fill the entire dharma-realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Invincible King of Diligence, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke:
The verse says:
Observe these sons of the Buddhas, Treasure-stores of wisdom and merit, Who have perfected the practices for enlightenment And bring peace and security to all the world;
Their minds are fundamentally luminous and penetrating, Skillfully entering into all samādhis.
Your wisdom is boundless and your sphere of activity is immeasurable; you cause this Jetavana Grove to be adorned in manifold ways.
A multitude of bodhisattvas has gathered here and dwells in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Behold this ocean-like assembly of immeasurable beings who have come from the ten directions to this place, free from all attachment.
Seated upon a precious lotus throne, neither coming nor abiding, Without dependence and free from conceptual proliferation,
with a stainless mind unimpeded, He has reached the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm; Establishing the banner of wisdom, firm and immovable,
He knows the nature of phenomena is without transformation, Yet manifests the affairs of transformation.
To all the infinite lands of the ten directions, Where all the Buddhas reside, He simultaneously visits them all without dividing his body.
Behold the Lion of the Śākyas and his sovereign power of supernatural faculties;
He is able to cause the assembly of Bodhisattvas To gather together from everywhere, And to hear all the teachings of the Buddhas.
The Dharma-realm is entirely equal, yet through verbal expression it appears as different.
This assembly has fully realized that all Buddhas eternally abide within the state of equality of the Dharma-realm, expounding the various distinct teachings with inexhaustible eloquence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Victorious Unsurpassed Majestic Virtue King, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Behold the Unsurpassed One, Whose vast wisdom is perfectly complete, And who skillfully understands the timely and the untimely."
He expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, Subduing all those of external paths.
Regarding all various heterodox arguments, He universally manifests supernatural powers in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Perfect Awakening is neither finite nor infinite; Whether finite or infinite, The Muni has completely transcended them both.
Just as the sun in the sky Shines upon all places, So too is the Buddha’s wisdom, Thoroughly penetrating the phenomena of the three times.
Just as on the night of the fifteenth, The lunar disk is without wane or defect, So it is with the Tathāgata:
All pure dharmas are perfectly complete. It is like the sun in the sky.
His activity never ceases for even a moment; the Tathāgata is likewise thus.

His spiritual transformations are constantly continuous, just as the lands of the ten directions are unimpeded within space. The Lamp of the World manifests transformations in the world in exactly the same way.
Just as the earth of the world is that upon which all living beings depend, so too is he.
The wheel of the Dharma of the Lamp that Illumines the World is likewise the support;
Just as a fierce and swift wind moves without obstruction, So too is the Buddha-dharma, swiftly pervading the world.
Just as the great water-wheel is that upon which the world rests, So too is the wheel of wisdom.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Unobstructed Supreme Treasury, who is the locus of reliance for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, received the Buddha’s spiritual power, surveyed the ten directions, and spoke these verses:
Just as a great mountain of jewels Benefits all sentient beings, So too is the Buddha-mountain, Universally benefiting the world.
Just as the waters of the great ocean Are clear, pure, and free from turbidity, Seeing the Buddha is likewise so: It can eliminate all thirst and craving. Just as Mount Sumeru...
Emerging from the great ocean, the Lamp of the World is likewise;
Arising from the ocean of Dharma, like a sea replete with myriad jewels, It satisfies all who seek. The Teacherless Wisdom is also thus:
All who behold it attain awakening. The Tathāgata’s profound wisdom Is immeasurable and beyond counting.
Therefore, the power of spiritual transformations manifests in ways that are inconceivable.
Just as a skilled illusionist displays various phenomena, so too is the Buddha’s wisdom; it manifests all powers of mastery.
Like a wish-fulfilling jewel that can satisfy every desire, the Most Victorious One is likewise.
Fulfilling all pure vows, like a bright and pure jewel, the Buddha’s wisdom likewise shines universally upon all things, illuminating the minds of all sentient beings.
Just as an eight-faceted jewel reflects all directions equally, so too is the unobstructed lamp, shining universally throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Just as the water-purifying jewel can clear all turbid waters, so too is it when one sees the Buddha:
all the faculties become completely pure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Moon of Vows, who had manifested throughout the dharma-realm, observed the ten directions by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power. And...
He spoke in verse:
"Just as the sapphire jewel can turn all colors blue, so too do those who see the Buddha all resolve to practice for bodhi.
Within each and every atom, the Buddha manifests his supernormal powers."
Causing immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas to all become pure;
The profound, subtle, and infinite power of the bodhisattvas' realm is unknowable; The world cannot fathom it.
The manifestations of the Tathāgata’s body, Adorned with pure marks, universally enter the dharma-realm.
Having accomplished all the bodhisattvas and inconceivable buddha-fields, therein they attain perfect enlightenment;
all these bodhisattvas and lords of the world fill them completely.
Śākyamuni, the Unsurpassed Honored One, possessing complete mastery over all dharmas, manifests supernatural powers that are boundless and immeasurable.
The various practices of the Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and inexhaustible; the Tathāgata, through his sovereign power, manifests them all.

O Son of the Buddha, you have well cultivated and studied them, attaining unimpeded wisdom regarding the profound realms of phenomena and clearly understanding all dharmas—this is the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata.
Turning the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the multitude, Your spiritual transformations fill everywhere; You cause the world to be entirely pure,
With the Tathāgata’s wisdom perfected And his sphere of activity likewise purified— Just like a great dragon king who universally relieves all living beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Radiance of Dharma-Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, And their great disciples, the śrāvakas— None of them can know the Buddha.”
The act of lifting and lowering the feet throughout the past, future, and present— this,
even all the Pratyekabuddhas do not know regarding the Tathāgata; how much less could ordinary worldlings,
bound by the fetters of afflictions and with their consciousnesses shrouded by ignorance, know the Teacher?
The Perfectly Awakened One’s unimpeded wisdom transcends the path of language; its measure is unfathomable, and who is able to know or see it?
Just as the light of the bright moon, whose limits cannot be measured, so too are the Buddha’s supernormal powers;
one cannot perceive their end or limit. Such is each and every skillful means.
The emanations produced in every thought-moment exhaust themselves throughout immeasurable eons; one cannot fathom them through contemplation.
Contemplating the Omniscient One’s inconceivable Dharma, the limits of each and every door of skillful means cannot be found. If there is one who, regarding this Dharma, arouses vast and great vows,
For such a person, it is not difficult to know and see these realms; Bravely and diligently practicing the inconceivable great ocean of Dharma, their mind is without obstruction.
Having entered this gateway of skillful means, their minds are already tamed; With aspirations vast and wide, they shall attain Great Bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketudhvaja-rāja, who dwells in the most supreme state, having received the Buddha’s spiritual power,
surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
The body of wisdom is not a physical body; it is unimpeded and inconceivable.
Were there anyone capable of conceiving of it, none could ever equal it. From inconceivable karma arises this pure body, uniquely and wondrously adorned;
it does not cling to the three realms, its radiance illuminating all.
The Dharma-realm is entirely pure, Opening the gateway to the Buddha’s Bodhi;
It gives birth to manifold wisdoms like the sun in the world, Universally radiating the light of insight.
Far removed from all dust and defilement, It eliminates every obstruction, Purifying everywhere throughout the three realms of existence, Forever severing the flow of birth and death.
Having accomplished the Bodhisattva path, He gives birth to unsurpassed enlightenment. He manifests infinite forms;

yet these forms have no locus of dependence. Though that which is manifested is immeasurable, All inconceivable bodhi Can awaken to all phenomena in a single moment— How could one possibly seek to measure it?
The Tathāgata’s limit of wisdom is fully and clearly realized in a single thought-moment;
because he knows all phenomena of the three periods of time, he is called the Buddha’s Wisdom. It is inexhaustible and indestructible.
The wise should thus single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha’s Bodhi; this contemplation is inconceivable, for when one contemplates it, it cannot be grasped.
Awakening is ineffable, transcending the path of language; from this all Buddhas are born—this Dharma is inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Banner of Light of Vow and Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke:
The verse says:
If one can skillfully observe The inexhaustible ocean of bodhi, Then one will be free from deluded thoughts and resolutely uphold the Dharma.
If one attains a resolute mind, Then one is able to cultivate sublime conduct.
In silent meditation, one reflects within; forever severing all doubts and delusions, the mind knows no fatigue nor does it succumb to indolence.
Progressing ever further in cultivation, one ultimately accomplishes the Buddha-dharma through perfected faith and wisdom.
From moment to moment, these qualities are made to increase, as one always delights in and constantly observes them.

Without attainment and without reliance on anything, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, all the meritorious deeds one has cultivated are entirely dedicated toward the path sought by all Buddhas.
Though remaining within birth and death, the mind is free from defilement and attachment;
dwelling securely in the teachings of all Buddhas, one always delights in the conduct of the Tathāgatas.
All phenomena existing in the world, such as the aggregates and elements—having relinquished them all, one seeks exclusively the virtues of the Buddha.
Ordinary beings, fettered by delusions, constantly wander through the world;
the Bodhisattva’s mind is unimpeded as he rescues them and brings them to liberation. The conduct of a Bodhisattva is difficult to extol.
None in the world can conceive of it; It universally eliminates all suffering And bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Having already attained the wisdom of Bodhi, He again takes pity on all sentient beings; His radiance illuminates the world, Delivering and liberating the entire multitude.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramatijñānarāja, who destroys all obstacles, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power,
surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, The name of the Buddha is difficult even to hear, How much more so to draw near to him?"

Having forever severed all doubts, the Tathāgata, the lamp of the world, has realized all dharmas and universally generates merit throughout the three periods of time, causing all beings to be completely purified.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is praised by all; for billions of kalpas one may gaze upon it, yet the mind never feels satiety.
If there are sons of the Buddha who contemplate the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body, they will surely abandon all attachments and turn toward the path of Bodhi.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body constantly emits a vast and expansive voice;
with unimpeded eloquence, it opens the gate of the Buddha’s Bodhi and brings all sentient beings to awakening.
Immeasurable and inconceivable, they cause others to enter the gateway of wisdom; They bestow the prediction of enlightenment.
The Tathāgata appears in the world as a great field of merit for the world; Universally guiding all sentient beings, he causes them to accumulate meritorious deeds.
If there are those who make offerings to the Buddha, They shall forever eliminate the fear of the evil realms.
Having extinguished all suffering and accomplished the body of wisdom, if one beholds the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings and can give rise to a vast and great mind,
that person will constantly encounter Buddhas and increase the power of their wisdom.
If one beholds the Supreme among Humans and resolutely directs the mind toward Bodhi, that person will be able to know for themselves.
"You shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Power of Vows, Wisdom, and Supernormal Knowledges of the Differentiations of the Dharma Realm, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
Śākyamuni, the Unsurpassed Honored One, endowed with all merits; Those who behold him find their minds purified.

He dedicates [merit] to great wisdom. The Tathāgata of great compassion appears in the world for the sake of all living beings, Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. For countless eons, the Tathāgata...
Toiling and suffering for the sake of sentient beings—how could those in the various worlds ever repay the Great Teacher’s kindness?
Rather than seeking liberation while forsaking the Tathāgata, one would endure all the sufferings of the evil realms throughout immeasurable eons;
rather than seeking escape alone, one would willingly take upon oneself all the sufferings of every sentient being.
One shall never abandon the Buddha in the pursuit of peace and happiness;
It would be better to remain in the various evil realms while constantly hearing the Buddha’s name, Than to wish for rebirth in the good paths where one might not hear the Buddha even for a moment.
It would be better to be born in the various hells for countless eons in each instance, Than ever to be far removed from the Buddha.
Why seek to escape the evil realms when one has already vowed to dwell long [in this world]?
Because by beholding the Tathāgata, all evil paths are transcended and wisdom is increased.
If one beholds the Buddha, all suffering is extinguished; one is able to enter the sphere of the great wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
If one is able to behold the Buddha, One abandons all obstacles. Nurturing inexhaustible merit, one accomplishes the path to enlightenment;
The Tathāgata is able to forever sever All doubts of sentient beings, And universally cause them to be fulfilled according to what their hearts desire.
The sixth major section: Bodhisattvas newly assembled from the ten directions recite verses in praise of the Buddha.
Each direction offers ten verses, collectively praising the various merits of the Tathāgata’s realm of samādhi and supernatural transformations.
The general manifestation that this assembly is sustained by his spiritual power has specific meanings for each case, which can be understood from the text itself.

Scroll Sixty-one Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;

Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Two: Entering the Dharmadhātu.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra universally surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas.
Section Seven, the Great Text: "At that time, Samantabhadra... and below, is the section on the "Development by Samantabhadra. As for what is meant by "development," it refers to the following:
Previously, when the assembly requested an explanation regarding the karmic functions within the fruit of enlightenment, the Tathāgata manifested signs in response.

His intention was to cause the great assembly to realize that all objects of contact are ultimately true, so that they might personally witness this and achieve a wondrous resonance with that which lies beyond words.
Yet, although the newly assembled Bodhisattvas from the ten directions spoke verses of praise, they merely provided a brief, peripheral glimpse of a single thread of the meaning.
The dharma-realm manifested by this samādhi is presided over by Samantabhadra; it is one who has already realized and entered it.

If he does not personally reveal and manifest it, then although observers may perceive its general characteristics, they will be unable to exhaustively fathom the profound and subtle realm of entry, nor will they know the skillful means for entering it. Therefore, this...
Observing the entire assembly, he saw that their longing for the Dharma was profound; therefore, he specifically revealed the skillful means for entering and the realms to be entered.

Each and every dharma-gate was taught not only so that those present at this assembly might realize and enter them instantaneously, but also so that future seekers of the Dharma-realm would fully obtain these gateways. This constitutes the beginning and end of this single assembly of the Avataṃsaka.
It is the ultimate entry into the pinnacle of the ocean of fruition. Therefore, the meaning of realization and entry is entirely contained within this single chapter of the primary assembly;
it constitutes the final destination of the Great Dharma of the orthodox teaching. Consequently, what follows is the section on dissemination (*pravacana*).
For any of us who study the Buddha-dharma, being able to enter this gate may be called the true seed for attaining Buddhahood. Thus, the commentary judges [the structure].
This portion has a specific destination.

It is through the skillful means that equalizes the dharma-realm, the skillful means that equalizes the realm of empty space, the skillful means that equalizes the realm of sentient beings, and by equalizing the three periods of time, all kalpas, the karma of all sentient beings, and the inclinations of all sentient beings. All [these are equalized].

This is for the understanding of sentient beings. It is equal to the faculties of all sentient beings, equal to the time for the maturation of all sentient beings, and equal to the skillful means of the light and shadows of all dharmas.

For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he uses ten phrases of Dharma to open up, reveal, illuminate, and expound this Lion’s Yawn Samādhi. What are these ten? They are as follows: expounding that which can manifest...

The Dharma-phrase that expounds the sequence of the appearance of all Buddhas within atoms of all Buddha-fields equal to the dharma-realm, and the sequence of the formation and destruction of those fields;
the Dharma-phrase that expounds the sounds of praising the Tathāgata’s merits throughout all future kalpas within all Buddha-fields equal to the realm of empty space;
and the Dharma-phrase that expounds the manifestation of [the Tathāgata] equal to empty space.
The Dharma-phrase of the infinite and boundless gates of the Tathāgatas’ appearance in the world and their attainment of perfect enlightenment within all Buddha-fields throughout the realms;
the Dharma-phrase that expounds and manifests the Buddhas sitting at the site of enlightenment amidst assemblies of Bodhisattvas in all Buddha-fields equal to the realm of empty space;
and the Dharma-phrase that expounds the manifestation from every pore, moment by moment, of all that exists throughout the three periods of time.

The Dharma phrase that causes the transformation bodies of the Buddhas to fill the dharma-realm; the Dharma phrase that proclaims the ability to cause all to appear equally throughout the oceans of lands in the ten directions;
the Dharma phrase that proclaims the ability to universally manifest the spiritual transformations of the Buddhas of the three periods of time within all realms;
the Dharma phrase that [proclaims the ability to enter] every atom of all Buddha-lands...

He expounds the Dharma-phrases that universally manifest throughout the middle [world-system] the various spiritual transformations of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-lands of the three periods of time, continuing through immeasurable eons;

he expounds the Dharma-phrases that can cause every pore to produce the ocean-like sounds of the great vows of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, developing and guiding all Bodhisattvas until the end of the future; he expounds the Dharma-phrases that can... [and so forth].

He causes the lion throne of the Buddha to be equal in measure to the dharma-realm, and the adornments of the assembly of bodhisattvas and the site of enlightenment to be likewise without distinction;
throughout kalpas as numerous as those yet to come, he turns various subtle and wondrous wheels of the Dharma through these phrases of the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha, with these ten as the foremost, there are phrases of the Dharma as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, all of which are the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, observed the Tathāgata;
he observed the assembly; he observed the inconceivable realms of all Buddhas; he observed the boundless samādhis of all Buddhas;
he observed the inconceivable oceans of worlds; and he observed the inconceivable wisdom of dharmas that are like illusions. He observed...
He observed that the inconceivable Buddhas of the three periods of time are all entirely equal.
He contemplated all the infinite and boundless dharmas of verbal expression and spoke in verse:

Within each and every pore, there are oceans of lands as numerous as atoms, all of which contain Tathāgatas seated amidst assemblies of bodhisattvas. Within each and every pore, immeasurable oceans of lands have Buddhas sitting upon the seat of enlightenment;
thus it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, within each and every pore.
Buddhas as numerous as atoms in all lands, surrounded by assemblies of bodhisattvas, expound the conduct of Samantabhadra.
A single Buddha sits within one land, yet fills the realms of the ten directions.
Clouds of immeasurable bodhisattvas all gather at his abode—bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in billions of lands, an ocean of their meritorious virtues.
Rising together from within the assembly, they pervade the realms of the ten directions; all abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra, they roam the ocean of the Dharma-realm.
Universally manifesting in all lands, they enter equally into the assemblies of all Buddhas;
dwelling securely in all lands, they listen to and hear all dharmas within each and every realm.
Having cultivated all practices for billions of eons—those very practices performed by Bodhisattvas—they universally enter the ocean of Dharma and the ocean of great vows.
Abiding on the stage of the Buddha-realm, they thoroughly master the conduct of Samantabhadra and give rise to all Buddha-dharmas.
Possessing the ocean of a Buddha’s merits, they extensively manifest miraculous powers.
Bodies as numerous as atoms, filling all lands, universally raining down the nectar of the Dharma so that all beings may abide in the Buddha-way.
(2) The second [section], beginning with "Equal to the Dharma-realm," clarifies the skillful means capable of opening [the path]. There are eleven phrases; this is the first phrase.
This serves as the general heading. The single character "yi" (以) at the beginning of the first line runs through the following ten phrases.
This means that the karmic function of the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* is profound and vast; it can only be revealed and manifested by means of these ten boundless expedient means (*upāya*).

Next, there is one line of scripture for the various bodhisattvas, which states: "By means of ten dharma-phrases. This passage explicitly clarifies the act of revelation; therefore, it points to what is being... [revealed].
That which is revealed is precisely the objective realm manifested by the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*. The fourteen lines of sutra text following "What next...
separately enumerate ten dharma-phrases. These ten dharma-phrases, in relation to the preceding ten skillful means, are that which is employed;
in relation to the objective realm of the samādhi, they are that which reveals. Therefore, these ten dharma-phrases...
Each one employs the ten previous kinds of skillful means, and each skillful means expounds these ten phrases.
Now, that which is opened by these ten dharma-phrases is precisely the ten phrases for requesting the fruit of the previous thought-moment;
it is also the realm manifested by samādhi. However, because this realm is profoundly deep, subtle, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter, although—
These ten skillful means (upāya) and their phrases mutually illuminate one another; however, only a small portion has been briefly cited, for in reality they are inconceivable.

Therefore, the conclusion states: "With these ten as the foremost, there are dharma-phrases as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, all of which are the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Their inconceivable meaning is fully contained therein.
In the verses, at that subsequent time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra reiterated this meaning and spoke these stanzas.

There are ten stanzas, which eulogize ten dharma-terms. Each one fully reveals how infinite oceans of lands within a single pore are mutually fused and encompassed—endlessly, inexhaustibly, and inconceivably—all being matters manifested within the sphere of samādhi.
Through the six aspects and ten mysteries, one perceives the wondrousness of perfect interfusion.

At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s Great Lion-Stretch Samādhi, emitted a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows. That light was named "Universally Illuminating the Dharmas of the Three Times."

Regarding the gateway of the realms: with as many rays of light as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields serving as their retinue, they universally illumine all the oceans of worlds and Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas in the Jeta Grove saw every single Buddha-field within the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the space-realm; within each and every atom, there was one...
In as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in all Buddha-lands— possessing various names, various colors, various purities, various abodes, and various forms— in all such lands,
there were great Bodhisattvas seated upon lion thrones at sites of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, surrounded before and behind by assemblies of Bodhisattvas.

They circumambulated him and made offerings to the Lords of all worlds. Or they saw him within great assemblies as vast as unspeakable Buddha-fields, emitting sublime sounds that filled the Dharma-realm as he turned the wheel of the True Dharma.
Or they saw him in the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, the palaces of the yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
Within the palaces of the *gandharvas*, humans, non-humans, and others, or in human realms such as villages,
towns, settlements, royal capitals, and great cities, he manifests various lineages, various names, various bodies, various marks, and various radiances.
Abiding in various modes of deportment, entering various samādhis, and manifesting various supernatural transformations, he sometimes uses various voices himself,
or causes various bodhisattvas within various great assemblies to preach various teachings using various expressions.
Thus, the great assembly of bodhisattvas in this gathering beholds these [manifestations].
The Buddha-Tathāgata’s profound samādhi and great supernormal powers abide throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—

in all directions of east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below— within the oceans of all quarters, dwelling in accordance with the mental conceptions of sentient beings.
From the beginningless past until the present, throughout all lands, all bodies of sentient beings, and all paths of empty space—
within every single location the size of a hair-tip, there are as many worlds as atoms,
each abiding in a sequence arising from various karmas; in each, there is a site of enlightenment with assemblies of bodhisattvas, and all see them in this very same way.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, which neither destroys the three periods of time nor destroys the world, he manifests his image within the minds of all sentient beings.
According to the inclinations of the hearts of all sentient beings, he utters sublime sounds and voices, universally entering into all assemblies.
He manifests universally before all sentient beings; while his physical forms differ, his wisdom is without distinction.
He reveals the Buddha-dharma according to what is appropriate for each, teaching, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings without ever resting.
Those who behold this buddha-power have all been gathered by the roots of goodness of Vairocana Tathāgata in former times. Or...
In the past, they were gathered through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); or they were matured through seeing, hearing, remembering, or associating with [the Buddha];
or in the past, he taught them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
or in the past, they planted roots of goodness together with various Buddhas; or in the past, by means of the skillful methods of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

They then teach and bring them to maturity. For this reason, they all attain entry into the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and profound samādhi, the great supernormal power that pervades the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. Some enter the dharma-body; some enter the form-body;
some enter the practices accomplished in the past; some enter the fulfillment of the various pāramitās; or some enter the adornments of purity.
The wheel of pure conduct. Whether entering the various stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva, or entering the power of perfect enlightenment,
or entering the great miraculous transformations of the non-differentiated samādhis in which Buddhas abide, or entering the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and wisdoms,
or entering the ocean of the Buddha’s unimpeded eloquence— those bodhisattvas, by means of various understandings, various paths, various gateways, and various...
They enter into various principles, various conformities, various wisdoms, various aids to the path, various skillful means, and various samādhis.
They enter such oceans of the spiritual transformations of Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, through these doors of skillful means.
What are the various samādhis? They are, namely, the Samādhi of Universally Adorning the Dharma Realm.
The samādhi of universally illuminating the unimpeded realm of all three periods of time; the samādhi of the light of wisdom that is non-differentiated from the dharma-realm;
the samādhi of entering the realm of the Tathāgata without wavering or turning back; and the samādhi of universally illuminating the boundless void.
They entered the Tathāgata Power Samādhi; the Buddha’s Fearless, Valiant, and Swift Adornment Samādhi; the All-Dharmadhātu Revolving Treasury Samādhi;
the Moon-like Universal Manifestation in All Dharmadhātus through the Great Expounding of Unobstructed Sound Samādhi;
the Universally Pure Dharma-Light Samādhi; and the Unobstructed Silk Banner of the Dharma King Samādhi. One.
The samādhi of seeing the ocean of all Buddhas within a single sphere of experience; the samādhi of manifesting the body in all worlds;
the samādhi of entering the realm of the Tathāgata’s undifferentiated body; the samādhi of the treasury of great compassion that revolves according to all worlds;
the samādhi of knowing that all phenomena leave no trace; and the samādhi of knowing the ultimate nature of all phenomena.
The samādhi of quiescent extinction; the samādhi of manifesting throughout the world through transformations despite having nothing to attain;
the samādhi of universally entering all lands; the samādhi of adorning all Buddha-lands and attaining perfect enlightenment;
the samādhi of contemplating the distinctions in the physical marks of the lords of all worlds; and the samādhi of contemplating the realms of all sentient beings without obstruction.
The samādhi that can give birth to the mothers of all Tathāgatas; the samādhi that can practice and enter the path of merit of the ocean of all Buddhas;
the samādhi that manifests spiritual transformations within each and every realm until the end of the future;
the samādhi that enters the ocean of the original deeds of all Tathāgatas; and the samādhi that protects and sustains the lineage of all Tathāgatas until the end of the future.
The samādhi that, through the power of resolute understanding, purifies all oceans of Buddha-fields in the ten directions of the present;
the samādhi that universally illumines all abodes of Buddhas in a single thought-moment; the samādhi that enters the unobstructed limit of all realms;
the samādhi that causes all worlds to become a single Buddha-field; and the samādhi that manifests the transformations of all Buddhas.
The samādhi of the transformation body; the samādhi of knowing the ocean of all faculties through the wisdom of the Vajra King;

the samādhi of knowing that all Tathāgatas are of one and the same body; the samādhi of knowing that all that is established within the dharma-realm dwells entirely within the limit of mental recollection;
and the samādhi of manifesting parinirvāṇa within the vast lands of all dharma-realms, causing [beings] to abide therein.
The samādhi of the supreme state; the samādhi that manifests the various distinct bodies of sentient beings in all Buddha-fields;
the samādhi that universally enters the wisdom of all Buddhas; the samādhi that knows the nature and characteristics of all phenomena;

the samādhi that universally knows the phenomena of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment; and the samādhi that universally manifests the body of the Dharma-realm in every thought-moment—by means of the lion-like courage...
The Samādhi of Fierce Wisdom Knowing the Successive Arisings of All Tathāgatas; the Samādhi of the Perfect Eye of Wisdom Regarding the Realm of All Dharmadhātus;
the Samādhi of Valiantly Advancing Toward the Ten Powers; the Samādhi of Emitting the Radiance of the Perfection of All Merits to Universally Illuminate the World;
the Samādhi of the Immovable Treasury; and the Samādhi of Explaining a Single Dharma that Universally Enters One.
The samādhi of all phenomena; the samādhi of explaining a single phenomenon through the differentiation of all vocal expressions;
the samādhi of expounding the non-dual dharma of all Buddhas; the samādhi of knowing the unimpeded limit of the three periods of time;
the samādhi of knowing that all kalpas are without distinction; the samādhi of entering the subtle skillful means of the ten powers; and the accomplishment [of these] throughout all kalpas.
The Samādhi of the Uninterrupted Practice of All Bodhisattvas; the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Bodies Throughout the Ten Directions;
the Samādhi of Attaining Perfect Enlightenment with Sovereignty over the Dharma Realm; the Samādhi of Producing All Peaceful Experiences;
the Samādhi of Adorning the Realm of Space with All Ornamental Implements; and from every thought-moment, the manifestation of clouds of transformation bodies as numerous as all sentient beings.
The Samādhi; the Tathāgata’s Pure Empty Moonlight Samādhi; the Samādhi of Constantly Beholding All Tathāgatas Abiding in Space;
the Samādhi that Reveals the Adornments of All Buddhas; and the Samādhi that Illuminates the Lamp of the Meaning of All Dharmas.
The Samādhi of Illuminating the Realm of the Ten Powers; the Samādhi of the Banner-Phenomena of All Buddhas of the Three Times;
the Samādhi of the Single Secret Treasury of All Buddhas; the Samādhi of Bringing All Deeds to Ultimate Completion in Every Thought-Moment;

the Samādhi of the Exhaustless Treasury of Merit; the Samādhi of Beholding the Boundless Realms of the Buddhas; the Samādhi of Firmly Abiding in All Dharmas; and the Samādhi of Manifesting All Suchnesses.
The Samādhi of Manifesting Transformations so that All May Know and See; the Samādhi of the Sun of the Buddhas Constantly Appearing in Every Thought-moment;
the Samādhi of Fully Knowing All Dharmas of the Three Times within a Single Day; the Samādhi of Universally Proclaiming the Quiescence of the Nature of All Dharmas;
the Samādhi of Beholding the Sovereign Power of All Buddhas; and the Samādhi of the Lotus Flower Blooming in the Dharma-realm.
The samādhi of contemplating all phenomena as being like space, having no place of abiding; the samādhi of universally entering one direction within the ocean of the ten directions;
the samādhi of entering the sourceless and bottomless dharma-realm; the samādhi of the ocean of all phenomena; the samādhi of emitting all light from a body of quiescence;
and the samādhi of manifesting all supernatural powers and great vows within a single thought-moment. One.
The Samādhi of Attaining Perfect Enlightenment at All Times and in All Places; the Samādhi of Entering All Dharma Realms through a Single Ornament;
the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Bodies of All Buddhas; the Samādhi of Knowing the Vast and Exalted Supernatural Powers and Wisdom of All Sentient Beings;
the Samādhi of One’s Body Pervading the Dharma Realm in a Single Thought-moment; and the Manifestation of the Pure Dharma Realm of the One Vehicle.
The Samādhi of Entering the Universal Gateway Dharma-realm to Manifest Great Adornment;
the Samādhi of Sustaining the Dharma-wheels of all Buddhas; the Samādhi of Adorning a Single Dharma-gateway with All Dharma-gateways;
the Samādhi of Gathering All Realms of Sentient Beings through Vows and Practices like Indra’s Net; the Samādhi of Discerning the Gateways to All Worlds; and the Vehicle...
The samādhi of the Lotus Sovereign’s Gait; the samādhi of the wisdom of supernatural powers that knows the various distinctions among all sentient beings;
the samādhi that causes one's body to constantly appear before all sentient beings;
the samādhi that knows the ocean of the various voices and languages of all sentient beings; and the samādhi of the supernatural powers of the various wisdoms of all sentient beings.
The Samādhi of the Treasury of Equal Great Compassion; the Samādhi of All Buddhas Entering the Boundary of the Tathāgata;
and the Samādhi of the Lion’s Stretching that Observes the Sphere of Liberation of All Tathāgatas.
By means of such samādhis, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-lands, the Bodhisattva enters into Vairocana Tathāgata, who in every thought-moment pervades all things.
In this ocean of miraculous transformations of the *dharmadhātu-samādhi*, all those bodhisattvas are fully endowed with great wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Being sharp, keen, and sovereign, they abide in the various stages (*bhūmi*). With vast wisdom, they universally contemplate all things;

born from the lineage of all wisdoms, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is ever present before them. Having attained the pure eye of wisdom free from the cataracts of delusion, they act as...
Acting as a teacher and guide for all sentient beings, they abide in the equanimity of a Buddha, remaining free from discrimination regarding all phenomena.
Having thoroughly realized the nature of their spheres of experience, they know that the nature of all worlds is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of any place of dependence.
They travel universally to all buddha-fields without attachment, and are able to observe all phenomena while remaining non-abiding. Pervading...
Entering the palaces of all sublime dharmas, they come from nowhere. They teach and transform all worlds, universally manifesting places of peace and security for all sentient beings.
Wisdom and liberation constitute their conduct; they constantly abide in the body of wisdom at the limit of detachment from desire.
Transcending the ocean of all realms of existence, they reveal the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). With the perfection of the light of wisdom, they see all phenomena universally, abiding in...
Firmly established and unshakable in samādhi, they constantly give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
They know that all dharma-gates are entirely like illusions; all sentient beings are entirely like dreams; all Tathāgatas are entirely like shadows;
all sounds and voices are entirely like echoes; and all dharmas are entirely like transformations. They are skillfully able to accumulate and perfect the sublime...
Supreme in conduct and vows, with wisdom perfected, pure, and skillful; his mind is profoundly tranquil, and he has skillfully entered the realm of all dhāraṇīs.
Possessing the power of samādhi, he is courageous and fearless; having attained the eye of clear wisdom, he dwells at the limit of the dharma-realm.
Having reached the state where all phenomena are non-apprehendable, he cultivates the boundless great ocean of wisdom and arrives at the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā).
Having reached the ultimate further shore, they are sustained by the *prajñāpāramitā*. Through the *abhijñāpāramitā*, they enter universally into the world;
through the *samādhipāramitā*, they attain mastery over the mind. By means of non-erroneous wisdom, they know all meanings;
by means of skillful analytical wisdom, they reveal the treasury of the Dharma; and by means of manifesting wisdom, they explain and interpret words and phrases.
Through the power of great vows, he preaches the Dharma inexhaustibly; with fearless, great lion-like roars, he constantly delights in observing the dharma that has no point of reliance.
With the pure eye of Dharma, he universally observes all things; with the moon of pure wisdom, he illuminates the formation and destruction of the world.
With the light of wisdom, one illuminates the true reality; merit and wisdom are like a mountain of adamant, beyond the reach of any analogy.
Skillfully contemplating all phenomena, the faculty of wisdom increases; through courageous diligence, one subdues all Māras.
His immeasurable wisdom and majestic radiance blaze intensely; his body transcends all worlds.

He has attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena and is well able to realize the limit of the exhausted and the inexhaustible. Abiding at the universal limit, he enters the true reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The wisdom of the contemplation of signlessness is constantly present before them. They skillfully accomplish all bodhisattva practices.
With non-dual wisdom, they know all objective realms; they universally behold all the various destinies within all worlds and travel everywhere to all buddha-lands.
The lamp of wisdom is perfected, free from all darkness and obscurations regarding all phenomena.
It radiates the pure light of the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions, serving as a true field of merit for all the world. Whether seen or heard, all aspirations are fulfilled.
His merit is vast and lofty, surpassing all the world; he is courageous and fearless, subduing all non-Buddhists. He proclaims the subtle and wondrous sound throughout all lands.
He beholds all Buddhas everywhere without ever feeling weary or satisfied. Having attained mastery over the Buddha’s Dharma-body, he manifests bodies according to those who are to be transformed.
A single body fills all Buddha-fields; he has attained mastery over pure supernormal powers.
Riding upon the great vessel of wisdom, they abide without obstruction; their wisdom is perfected and pervades the entire dharma-realm.

Like the rising sun that universally illuminates the world, they manifest their forms and images according to the minds of sentient beings, knowing the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all beings.

They enter the realm of non-contention regarding all phenomena; they know that the nature of all phenomena is without birth or arising, enabling the small and the great to enter one another with sovereign mastery.
They definitively comprehend the profound course of the Buddha-ground and expound its profound meaning through inexhaustible phrases.
Within a single phrase, they expound upon the ocean of all sūtras. Having attained the great wisdom dhāraṇī-body, whatever they receive and uphold is never forgotten.
In a single thought-moment, they can remember the events of immeasurable kalpas;
in a single thought-moment, they fully know the wisdom of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. They constantly expound the infinite through all the gates of dhāraṇī.
The ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma constantly turns the non-retrogressive, pure wheel of the Dharma, causing all sentient beings to give rise to wisdom.
They attain the light of wisdom of the Buddha-realm and enter the profound Samādhi of Excellent Vision.
They enter the unobstructed limit of all phenomena and achieve sovereign mastery over the supreme wisdom of all phenomena. All realms are pure and magnificently adorned.
They enter universally into all dharma-realms of the ten directions, reaching every single location without exception.

Within each and every atom, they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment; within the nature of formlessness, they manifest all forms. By means of all directions, they universally enter into a single direction.
These bodhisattvas possess such boundless treasuries of merit, wisdom, and virtue that they are constantly praised by all Buddhas;
though one were to describe their virtues with various words and phrases, one could never exhaust them.
There was not one who was not present within the Jeta Grove, having deeply entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s virtues and beholding the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas, having attained the light of the inconceivable true Dharma, felt great joy in their hearts. Within their own bodies,
the various ornaments of the pavilions, the lion thrones upon which they sat, and indeed within every object throughout the entire Jeta Grove,
they manifested clouds of various great adornments that filled the ten directions of space.
The realm: that is to say, within every moment of thought, they emit great clouds of light that fill the ten directions, fully awakening all sentient beings;

they produce clouds of all kinds of mani-jewel bells that fill the ten directions, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds that extol and praise all the merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; they produce clouds of all kinds of musical instruments that fill [the ten directions].

as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
The Eighth Major Section: At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from below his brow; this is the section on the benefit of the subsequent division.

It causes them to seek the light of wisdom as the means of realization. The intent is that although it was Samantabhadra who initiated the discourse with words, the assembly in the ocean-like multitude already understood its purport.
If one wishes to realize this through actual experience, even if it were not for the universally luminous wisdom (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*) of the *dharmadhātu*, one could not truly obtain its benefit.

This is called the "white tuft between the eyebrows" (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which symbolizes the fruit-wisdom of the Middle Way. Because the Buddha desires the great assembly to realize this through actual experience, he emits this light of fruition.
It is essential to rely upon this very light of the wisdom of the Middle Way within the *dharmadhātu* as the causal condition for direct realization.
Only then can one realize the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that has previously manifested. This is also like the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to assist in its awakening;
thus, this single ray of light serves as the gateway for entering the dharma-realm.
Because the realm of samādhi is inconceivable, the wisdom-light capable of entering it has a retinue numbering the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields, each of which is universally...
