He can bring forth the causes and conditions for vast roots of goodness. Noble son, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha shall cause you to enter the stage of the vast aids to enlightenment.
I shall cause you to give birth to the power of vast roots of goodness; I shall explain to you the causes for generating the bodhicitta;
I shall cause you to give birth to the light of the Great Vehicle; I shall cause you to cultivate the vast pāramitās;
I shall cause you to enter the ocean of vast practices; I shall cause you to fulfill the wheel of vast vows; I shall cause you to purify the vast [field].
"The Gate of Adornment shall cause you to give birth to the power of vast compassion.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, circumambulated him to the right, gazed upon him, took his leave, and departed.
The second major section, "Proceeding toward the Land of Supreme Bliss," contains ten spiritual friends who correspond to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This is divided into ten segments, each consisting of six subsections: (1) seeking according to the instructions; (2) seeing, paying respect, and inquiring;

(3) declaring one’s own resolve for enlightenment; (4) praising and bestowing the Dharma; (5) humbling oneself and deferring to the superior; and (6) pointing out the subsequent friend. Now, the first [segment].
Turning toward the Land of Supreme Bliss, one proceeds in accordance with the teachings. Because the mind ascends to its proper station, it is called "ascending the mountain.

Discerning the stages of practice through wisdom is "observation. The seven factors of enlightenment that aid the path constitute the "seven days. Because one forgets the specific location where one dwells, one sees oneself on a separate mountain.
The simultaneous movement of concentration and wisdom is "strolling slowly. Having completed this cultivation, one practices the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*.
Having seen [him], he prostrated and immediately paid his respects, making this request:

"I have recited one line of the sutra concerning the initial generation of the mind of awakening, yet I do not yet know the one and a half lines of the bodhisattva’s discourse that properly set forth what was asked.
There should have been eleven preceding questions; that only the beginning and end are cited here is due to the omissions of the translator. "Thus have I heard from the Noble One... [one line].

The first half of the sutra consists of the praise of virtues and the request for the teaching; the latter half consists of Meghashri’s response of praise and the bestowal of the Dharma, through which he immediately enters the Dharmadhātu.
First, he praises the difficulty of generating the bodhicitta; next, from the words "That which is called... onwards, he specifically restates the previous questions in eleven phrases.
Next, the two lines of sutra beginning with "Good son" constitute the formal demonstration of the Dharmadhātu, which is the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Within this:
The power of decisive understanding (*niścaya-vijñapti-bala*). This is the method for entering the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) through the correct teaching.

It universally contemplates the objective realm to explain the purification of the eye of superior faith. That is to say, faith is the primary requirement for the *nien-fo samādhi*; it is the internal cause.
The four lines beginning with "Going to the ten directions" provide the external conditions. The two lines below, "Constantly recollecting all Buddhas," constitute the actual [practice].
It teaches the mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) by means of non-mindfulness.

The following eight lines of scripture, beginning with "Constantly see all Buddhas of the ten directions," clarify the efficacy of mindfulness of the Buddha: because the mind accords with the Buddha's mind, one is able to see many Buddhas.
Next, the three and a half lines of scripture within each direction clarify the distinct phenomenal characteristics of what is seen. Thus, [the ten...]
The many Buddhas and various realms all manifest from within the mind that recollects the Buddha; this is the perfection of such mindfulness of the Buddha.
Now, the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī is entrusted with the first stage, called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), which is the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
One knows that all phenomena are the self-nature of the mind and achieves the body of wisdom (*jñāna-kāya*) without depending on others.

Awakening. Because one first perceives the Dharmakāya at this stage, one knows that through the opening of wisdom, the teaching of the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo) dharma-gate immediately enables one to see the many Buddhas of the ten directions.
From this point until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), one never departs from this realm of the Buddha being remembered;
rather, as one progresses through the stages, it gradually becomes all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, becoming perfectly integrated and sovereign, thereby reaching the ultimate Dharma.

Regarding the measure of the realms: it is known that what is cultivated by the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood is, in its entirety, not apart from the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance;
therefore, it is called the Samādhi of One Practice. That people nowadays falsely disparage this as an inferior practice—is it not lamentable?
Furthermore, good son, I have only attained this "Wisdom Light Universally Perceiving the Realm of All Buddhas through Recollection."
[This concludes] the section on the gate. This is merely a humble summary of my own limited understanding;

the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is in fact as vast and profound as this. Therefore, it is said below: "How could one possibly comprehend the boundless wisdom and pure practices of the great Bodhisattvas?
These words indicate that which one cannot achieve oneself; furthermore, one should also defer to superior companions. For now, let us simply practice Buddha-recitation.
One attains the purity of boundless wisdom. Furthermore, how could one possibly compare the superiority or inferiority of those who practice Chan meditation?

It simply depends on the state of one's mindfulness. Therefore, the twenty-one methods of mindfulness of the Buddha mentioned in the subsequent text are intended to reveal that the three bodies (trikāya) are not separate from a single thought-moment, the three lands (triloka) reside within a single mind, and the three Buddhas are inseparable [from that same source].
At present, the three lands are directly beneath one's feet; the infinite, wondrous purport is entirely contained within this school.
Thus, when Deven said that which he did not know, it was precisely for this reason. Therefore, he said: "How could I possibly know or speak of those meritorious practices?
Consequently, the Commentary provides a detailed explanation through many approaches, each approach containing manifold meanings, intended to cause the practitioner to set their will [upon them].
There is a place of refuge. Next, the *Sūtra on the Two Practices* states that in the south there is a country where the youth Sudhana is directed toward his next spiritual friend.
The five lines of the *Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha* praise the superior virtues of this friend and prefigure what is to be said later. Then, the youth Sudhana takes his leave and departs;
longing for [the teacher’s] virtue, he bows and bids farewell. This concludes the section on Sāgaramegha, which corresponds to the second stage, the Dwelling of Purification (*vimalā-vihāra*).

It is also a "friend. As for the country of Samudramukha (Sea Gate), because that country is situated precisely at the mouth of the Southern Sea, it symbolizes the profound and vast ocean of the contemplative mind (*citta*) as the gateway for cultivating the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).
The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha (Ocean Cloud) takes the contemplation of the ocean as his dharma-gate, for he moistens all things through the dharma-gate of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*).
This symbolizes the ten kinds of minds arising within the cultivation of the grounds, which are profound and vast.

Because of the clouds of compassion: by means of the aforementioned Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, one contemplates the ocean of the mind as deep and vast, giving rise to clouds of great compassion that moisten and cover all things;
this is the sublime practice for cultivating the ground of the mind.
At that time, the youth Sudhana single-mindedly contemplated the instructions of the spiritual friends. With right mindfulness, he observed the gateways of the light of wisdom;
with right mindfulness, he observed the gateways of the bodhisattvas' liberation; with right mindfulness, he observed the gateways of the bodhisattvas' samādhis;
with right mindfulness, he observed the gateways of the bodhisattvas' great oceans; with right mindfulness, he observed the gateways of the manifestation of all Buddhas before him. Thus...
He practiced the gate of mindfulness that observes the locations of all Buddhas; the gate of right mindfulness that observes the modes of conduct of all Buddhas;
the gate of right mindfulness that observes all Buddhas as being equal to the realm of empty space; the gate of right mindfulness that observes the sequential order of the appearance of all Buddhas;
and the gate of right mindfulness that observes the skillful means by which all Buddhas enter [the world]. Proceeding gradually toward the south, he arrived at the country of Samudramukha.
Having received instruction on the Dharma-gate, Sudhana proceeded to visit Samudramegha; thus, while on the road, he contemplated the teachings of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This "correct mindfulness and observation" is precisely contemplation following what has been heard. Since contemplation is itself cultivation, he was able to enter through the gate accordingly.
This correct mindfulness and observation is the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā*), which refers to the simultaneous flow of alertness and tranquility, and the balancing of sinking and excitation.
The two abandonments constitute the correct practice for entering [the path]. There are five sūtras that describe the practice of contemplation as the skillful means for entry.
By proceeding southward through these stages, one arrives at the kingdom of Samudramukha.
He prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, circumambulated him to the right, and with palms joined before him, spoke these words:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, desiring to enter the ocean of all unsurpassed wisdom;
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva can renounce worldly family life and become a Tathāgata."
Householder, how can one cross the ocean of birth and death and enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom? How can one leave the stage of ordinary beings and enter the stage of the Tathāgata?
How can one sever the stream of birth and death and flow into the stream of bodhisattva practice?
How can one shatter the wheel of birth and death and perfect the wheel of a bodhisattva’s vows? How can one extinguish the realm of Māra and manifest the realm of the Buddha? How...
How can one exhaust the ocean of craving and expand the ocean of great compassion? How can one close the gates to the various difficulties and evil destinies and open the gates to all great nirvāṇas?
How can one emerge from the city of the triple world and enter the city of omniscience?
How can one renounce all cherished objects and use them entirely for the benefit of all sentient beings?

Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Samudramegha, paid his respects, and requested instruction; he declared that he had already resolved upon bodhicitta, yet remained unaware of the essential points of the Dharma contained in the following six lines of scripture.
These do not go beyond the two gateways of wisdom and compassion; however, as for what he requested:

They also progress according to their respective stages; however, they merely state what they themselves do not know, answering by means of a single dharma-gate realized by themselves from among the teachings bestowed by their spiritual friends, in accordance with the depth or shallowness of Sudhana’s own realization.
The sequence of stages established here according to principle, based on the cultivation of various dharma-gates, is by no means the same as Sudhana’s sequential questioning.
Nevertheless, each of his questions encompasses both cause and effect; thus it is said that he "enters the ocean of unsurpassed wisdom.

Furthermore, the answers likewise constitute a perfectly integrated system of practice. One should understand that these elements interpenetrate from beginning to end; they must not be treated as [merely linear or sequential].
This is the sequential explanation. Therefore, the Commentary states that this is the formal demonstration of the *dharmadhātu*.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha addressed Sudhana, saying: "O son of good family, have you already resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Sudhana replied: "Yes; I have already previously resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Third, the Bodhicitta. Sāgaramegha said: "Good son, if sentient beings do not plant roots of goodness, they cannot give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One must obtain the light of the universal gate of roots of goodness."
Possessing the light of wisdom from the samādhi of the true path, they give rise to various vast oceans of merit.
They cultivate pure dharmas without weariness or rest; they serve spiritual friends without ever becoming weary; and they disregard their own bodies and lives, possessing no hoarded stores.
With a mind as even as the earth, free from high and low, their nature is one of constant compassion for all sentient beings;

they remain single-mindedly mindful of them without forsaking them throughout all realms of existence, and they always delight in contemplating the sphere of the Tathāgata. Only in this way can they give rise to the bodhicitta.
To generate the bodhicitta means: to generate the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), in order to universally rescue all sentient beings;

to generate the mind of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), in order to equally benefit all worlds; to generate the mind of peace and happiness, in order to cause all sentient beings to extinguish all sufferings;
to generate the mind of benefit, in order to cause all sentient beings to depart from unwholesome dharmas; and to generate the mind of pity...
Because they protect all who are afraid; because they give rise to an unimpeded mind that abandons all obstacles;
because they give rise to a vast mind that pervades the entire dharma-realm; because they give rise to a boundless mind that reaches everywhere, equal to the realm of empty space;
because they give rise to a broad and expansive mind that beholds all Tathāgatas; because they give rise to a pure mind regarding...
Because the knowledge of the dharmas of the three periods of time is without contradiction; because it gives rise to the mind of wisdom that universally enters the ocean of all wisdom.
Good son, I have dwelt in this country of Sāgaradvāra for twelve years, constantly taking the great ocean as my sphere of activity.
That is to say: contemplating that the great ocean is vast and immeasurable; contemplating that the great ocean is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom;
contemplating that the great ocean becomes gradually deeper and wider; contemplating that the great ocean is wonderfully adorned with immeasurable and marvelous jewels;
contemplating that the great ocean accumulates immeasurable waters; and contemplating that the colors of the waters in the great ocean are diverse and inconceivable. Contemplating...
The great ocean is the dwelling place of immeasurable sentient beings. One contemplates how the great ocean accommodates various beings of immense bodies;
one contemplates how the great ocean can receive the rain poured down by great clouds; one contemplates that the great ocean neither increases nor decreases.
Son of good family, while I was contemplating, I further thought: "Is there anything in this world that is as vast..."
"Is there anything that surpasses this ocean? Is there anything immeasurable that surpasses this ocean? Is there anything profoundly deep that surpasses this ocean?

Is there anything exceptionally sublime that surpasses this ocean? Son of good family, while I was reflecting thus, a great lotus flower suddenly appeared beneath this ocean, made of the Indranīla jewel known as 'Invincible'."
Its stem was made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel; its flowers were of *jāmbūnada* gold; its leaves were of agallochum; its calyx was of *musāragalva*;
and its filaments were of *aśmagarbha*. It bloomed profusely, spreading and covering the great ocean. A million asura kings grasped its stem;
a million nets adorned with *maṇi* jewels covered it from above; and a million naga kings rained down fragrant water upon it. A hundred...
Ten thousand *garuḍa* kings held various necklaces and precious silk ribbons that hung down all around;
one million *rākṣasa* kings observed with a compassionate heart; one million *yakṣa* kings paid homage with reverence;
one million *gandharva* kings offered praise and worship with various kinds of music; and one million heavenly kings rained down celestial flowers, celestial garlands, and celestial...
The gods of incense, the gods of burning incense, the gods of ointment, the gods of powdered incense, and the gods of exquisite garments;
a million Brahma kings prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet in reverence; a million gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens joined their palms in salutation;
a million wheel-turning monarchs each made offerings adorned with the seven treasures; and a million ocean deities simultaneously appeared to pay homage and prostrate themselves with their heads.
A hundred thousand *rasmi-prabhāsa-maṇi* jewels radiate light everywhere; a hundred thousand *viśuddha-puṇya-maṇi* jewels serve as adornments;
a hundred thousand *samanta-prabhāsa-maṇi* jewels constitute a pure treasury; a hundred thousand *viśeṣa-maṇi* jewels possess a brilliant and blazing luster;
a hundred thousand *sūkṣma-kośa-maṇi* jewels illuminate boundlessly; and there are a hundred thousand *jambū-dhvaja* [jewels].
The mani jewels were arranged in successive rows. There were one million indestructible and pure vajra-lion mani jewels;
one million sun-treasury (sūryagarbha) mani jewels, vast and pure; one million delightful (priya) mani jewels, possessing various colors;
and one million wish-fulfilling (cintāmaṇi) mani jewels, adorned with inexhaustible radiance.
O Radiant One! This great lotus flower arises from the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.

All bodhisattvas give rise to faith and joy. It manifests before all in the worlds of the ten directions. It is born from dharmas that are like illusions; it is born from dharmas that are like dreams; it is born from pure karma.
It is adorned by the dharma-gate of non-contention. It enters the seal of the unconditioned and abides in the gate of non-obstruction, filling [all space].

In all the lands of the ten directions, one could never exhaustively praise the merits of the profound realm of the Buddhas even throughout countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas. At that time, I saw upon that lotus flower a Tathāgata sitting cross-legged;
his body extended from there upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and his precious lotus throne was inconceivable.
The assembly at the site of enlightenment is inconceivable. The perfection of the primary marks is inconceivable. The fulfillment of the secondary characteristics is inconceivable.
The miraculous transformations of supernormal powers are inconceivable. The purity of physical form is inconceivable.
The mark of the invisible crown of the head is inconceivable; the mark of the broad and long tongue is inconceivable;
skillful speech is inconceivable; the perfect voice is inconceivable; and boundless power is inconceivable.
His purity and fearlessness are inconceivable; his vast eloquence is inconceivable.

Furthermore, one reflects upon that Buddha’s past cultivation of various practices as inconceivable, his attainment of the Way through mastery as inconceivable, his proclamation of the Dharma with sublime voice as inconceivable, and his universal manifestation of various adornments as inconceivable. Following him on either side...
The various distinctions [of these realms] were inconceivable; that all benefits were brought to complete fulfillment was inconceivable.
At that time, this Tathāgata extended his right hand and stroked my head, expounding for me the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye.

It reveals the realm of all Tathāgatas, manifests all the practices of Bodhisattvas, and elucidates all the sublime dharmas and all wheels of Dharma of all Buddhas, such that they are entirely contained within it; it is able to purify all Buddha-lands.
It can destroy all heterodox paths and false doctrines; it can extinguish all the hosts of Māra;
it can cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy; it can illuminate the mental activities of all sentient beings;
and it can comprehend the faculties of all sentient beings, causing them all to attain awakening according to their minds. I heard this Dharma-gate from that Tathāgata.

One should uphold, recite, remember, and contemplate it. Suppose there were a person who used ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as Mount Sumeru to transcribe even a single chapter of this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, a single section within that chapter, a single teaching within that section, a single meaning within that teaching, or a single phrase within that meaning—they would not be able to record even a small fraction, let alone the whole. Good son!
For twelve hundred years in the presence of that Buddha, I upheld this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye.

Day after day, by means of the light of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, I received countless chapters; by means of the light of the *dhāraṇī* of the gate of tranquility, I entered into countless chapters;
and by means of the light of the *dhāraṇī* of infinite revolution, I universally penetrated them all.
There are countless chapters on the observation of *dhāraṇī* light according to the stages;
countless chapters on the universal gathering through the power of *dhāraṇī* light; countless chapters on the elicitation through the lotus-adornment *dhāraṇī* light;
and countless chapters on the exposition through the pure vocal resonance *dhāraṇī* light.
By means of the light of the Gaganagañja-dhāraṇī, it reveals countless chapters;
by means of the light of the Raśmisaṃcayā-dhāraṇī, it expands countless chapters; by means of the light of the Sāgaragarbha-dhāraṇī, it analyzes and elucidates countless chapters.
If there are sentient beings coming from the ten directions— whether they be devas or deva-kings,
nāgas or nāga-kings, yakṣas or yakṣa-kings, gandharvas or gandharva-kings,
asuras or asura-kings, garuḍas or garuḍa-kings, or kiṃnaras or kiṃnara-kings...
O King, whether it be a mahoraga or a mahoraga king, a human or a human king, a Brahmā or a Brahmā king—
whenever any such beings come to me, I explain, interpret, extol, and praise [this teaching] for them all,
causing them to love, delight in, enter, and abide in this Universal Eye of Light of the practices of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Dharma-door. Good son, I know only this Universal Eye Dharma-door.

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have deeply entered the ocean of all bodhisattva practices, they do so by practicing in accordance with the power of their vows; thus they enter the great ocean of vows.
Because they abide in the world for immeasurable eons; because they enter the ocean of all sentient beings to extensively benefit them according to their mental inclinations;
because they enter the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings to produce the light of unimpeded wisdom of the ten powers;

because they enter the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings to teach and transform them at the appropriate time, causing them all to be tamed; and because they enter the ocean of all lands to bring them to completion...
In order to fulfill their original vows and adorn and purify Buddha-fields; to enter the ocean of all Buddhas and constantly make offerings to all Tathāgatas;
to enter the ocean of all dharmas and be able to awaken to and penetrate them all through wisdom;
to enter the ocean of all merits and cultivate each one until they are fully perfected; and to enter the ocean of the speech and languages of all sentient beings in all lands.
Because he has turned the wheel of the true Dharma, how could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
Good son, from here go south for six thousand yojanas; along the way to Laṅkā, there is a village called Seaport (Sāgaratīra).
"There is a bhikṣu there named Supratiṣṭhita. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva purifies the bodhisattva conduct.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Sāgaramegha, circumambulated him to the right, gazed up at him with reverence, and took his leave to depart.
When Samudrareṇu first met Sudhana, he first inquired to ascertain whether he had truly resolved his mind [to enlightenment], because he recognized the difficulty of generating the bodhicitta.
When Sudhana replied that he had indeed generated it and declared with certainty that it was not false, [Samudrareṇu] knew him to be a vessel for the Dharma;
therefore, in the five lines and a half of scripture that follow, he praises the one capable of generating the mind, speaking profoundly of his great roots of goodness. Thus...
"One is able to give rise to the bodhicitta. The seven lines of scripture following "after giving rise to the bodhicitta" reveal the characteristics of generating the mind.
"Taking great compassion as the foremost" and "entering the ocean of all wisdom as the practice" [are the characteristics].

The six lines of scripture following "Furthermore, son of good family, I abide here" correctly demonstrate the essential points of the Dharma. The statement "contemplating the great ocean" refers to contemplating the Dharma.
It is the ocean. This means that by means of the aforementioned mindfulness of the Buddha, one enters deeply into the ocean of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

Thus, this profound contemplation of the ocean of dharmas flows and moistens, giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For it is by relying on the ocean of wisdom that the ocean of compassion arises; therefore, the great ocean is taken as the object of contemplation.
To enter deeply into the dharma-nature and benefit sentient beings through great compassion is precisely what constitutes the vast propagation of the Dharma transformation. Sentient beings...
The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is itself bodhi. Therefore, the latter two lines of the sutra ask: "Is there any excellence that surpasses this ocean?

Thus, by means of the ocean of sentient beings, one enters the ocean of wisdom. Consequently, it is clarified that one immediately attains the vision of the Buddha and hears the Dharma, and immediately attains the upholding of the inexhaustible dharma-gates, even to the point of transforming sentient beings. Such is [the case].
It is the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, because it universally perceives that the *dharmatā* of sentient beings is equal and unimpeded.
The subsequent passage of three lines beginning with "I had this thought" expresses the signs of self-realization through the power of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*).
The following fourteen lines beginning with "One million asuras" manifest that upon the awakening of the mind, one immediately attains [realization].
The marks of external adornment; these four lines and a half of the sutra from "This great lotus flower" below illustrate the mark of manifesting excellence by citing its cause.
The nine lines and a half of the sutra from "At that time I saw him" below clarify the mark of seeing the Buddha’s primary retribution (*vipāka*).

The passage from "At that time this Tathāgata" below clarifies the hearing of the Dharma. The mention of preaching the Dharma within the ocean signifies that it flows forth from the ocean of compassion and wisdom.
Therefore, if there are sentient beings who practice the six lines of the sutra below, it clarifies that they transform and transmit the Dharma to teach and convert sentient beings.
This aforementioned self-benefit and benefit for others all arise from contemplating the ocean of the nature of sentient beings and thereby entering the ocean of wisdom and the ocean of compassion;

this is the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, the commentary clarifies that the first "good friend" refers to the Buddha, while this [passage] clarifies the Dharma. As for the subsequent "I"...
In this *Puyan* Dharma-gate, the first eight lines and a half of the sutra show the initial humility of not knowing [the path] oneself;
the subsequent two lines of the sutra, beginning with "From here, travel south," indicate the later companion who leads one six thousand *yojanas* to the seashore.

He manifested the cultivation of the six perfections and the purification of the six sense faculties, for he was able to reach the very limits of the ocean of Dharma. Thus, Sudhana took his leave and departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana focused his mind exclusively on the instructions of the spiritual friends, focused his mind exclusively on the "Universal Eye" Dharma-door, and focused his mind exclusively...

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he focused on upholding the clouds of Dharma-phrases, focused on entering the gates of the ocean of Dharma, focused on contemplating the distinctions of the Dharma, deeply entered the eddies of the Dharma, universally entered the void of the Dharma, purely maintained the obscurations of the Dharma, and observed the abodes of the Dharma-treasures.
Gradually traveling south, he reached the coastal village at the edge of Laṅkā Road. There he surveyed the ten directions in search of Sudhana and saw him.
This bhikṣu came and went, walking back and forth in mid-air, surrounded by countless devas who paid him homage.
They scattered celestial flowers and performed divine music; banners, pennants, and silken streamers, all innumerable, filled the void as an offering.
Great nāga kings raised inconceivable clouds of agallochum incense in the sky, shaking...
The King of the *Kinnaras* played various musical instruments and offered praise according to the Dharma as an act of worship.

The King of the *Mahoragas*, with inconceivable and most subtle garments, spread them throughout the void and offered worship with a heart full of joy. The King of the *Asuras* produced inconceivable...
Clouds of mani-jewels with immeasurable radiance and various adornments filled the entirety of space as an offering.
The Garuḍa Kings, appearing in the form of youths and surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens, had attained ultimate accomplishment in the mind free from the intent to harm;
they joined their palms in the midst of the sky to pay homage. There were also inconceivable numbers of Rākṣasa Kings.
Surrounded by immeasurable rākṣasas whose forms were tall and vast and most terrifying, they saw the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita with his mind of loving-kindness sovereign;
they bowed their bodies, joined their palms, and gazed up at him in worship.
An inconceivable number of yakṣa kings, each surrounded by their own retinues, stood on all four sides, encircling him to pay respect and provide protection. Inconceivable...
Countless Brahma kings in the void bowed their bodies and joined their palms, extolling and praising him according to human conventions.
Inconceivable numbers of Śuddhāvāsa devas in the void, together with their palaces, respectfully joined their palms and made great vows.
When the youth Sudhana saw these things, his heart was filled with joy, and he joined his palms.
He paid homage and spoke these words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should practice the Buddha-dharma, how they should accumulate the Buddha-dharma,
how they should fully equip themselves with the Buddha-dharma, how they should perfuse the Buddha-dharma, how they should cause the Buddha-dharma to increase, and how they should [summarize] it..."
The Compendium of the Buddha-Dharmas. What is the ultimate Buddha-dharma? What is the purified Buddha-dharma? What is the profoundly pure Buddha-dharma? What is the thoroughly realized Buddha-dharma?
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I only pray that, out of compassion, you will explain this for me.
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the vision of the Buddha, but constantly and diligently practice in his presence? Bodhisattva...
How does a bodhisattva not abandon other bodhisattvas, sharing the same roots of goodness as them?

How does a bodhisattva not abandon the Buddha-dharma, attaining clear realization through wisdom? How does a bodhisattva not abandon their great vows, being able to universally benefit all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva not abandon various practices, dwelling throughout all kalpas with a steadfast mind?
Without weariness. How does a bodhisattva not abandon the buddha-fields while being able to universally adorn and purify all worlds?
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the power of the Buddha while being able to fully know and see the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata?
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) yet likewise not dwell within it, appearing throughout all realms of existence like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*)?
Undergoing birth and death, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices. How does a bodhisattva not abandon hearing the Dharma, being able to fully receive and retain the true teachings of all Buddhas?
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the light of wisdom, universally entering the sphere of activity of the wisdom of the three periods of time?
Third, Sudhana visits the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita, who represents the stage of "Abiding in Practice. First, he proceeds according to the instructions;

initially, he recollects the teachings of his previous friend. This consists of four sections of the sūtra: recollecting the former instruction to hear the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, reflecting on entering the ocean to observe phenomena, and the contemplative cultivation that encompasses all dharmas. Proceeding gradually in this manner, he arrives at a village by the seashore.
Seeking out "Abiding Well" (*Susthitamati*), he next saw this bhikṣu coming and going in walking meditation within the void.
Below this is fourteen and a half lines of scripture concerning the vision, veneration, and inquiry. Seeing him first walking in the sky represents the cultivation of non-abiding practice.
Next, the passage beginning with "He spoke these words" consists of five lines of scripture; it first describes his own initial aspiration, and then correctly...
Cen asked a question. Next, there are five lines and a half of scripture regarding how a bodhisattva acts in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu Suvihita addressed Sudhana, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you have already previously resolved [upon enlightenment]."

The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Now, once again, I have resolved my mind to seek and inquire about the Buddha-dharma, the dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the dharma of spontaneity (*svayambhū*).
Son of good family, I have already accomplished the bodhisattva’s gate of liberation of unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid-vimokṣamukha*).
Whether coming or going, whether walking or staying, one contemplates, cultivates, and observes in accordance with [the teachings].
At that very moment, one attains the light of wisdom called "Ultimate Unobstructedness.

Because one has attained this light of wisdom, one knows the mental activities of all sentient beings without obstruction; one knows the deaths and births of all sentient beings without obstruction; one knows the...
They know the past lives of all sentient beings without obstruction. They know the events of future kalpas for all sentient beings without obstruction.
They know the affairs of the present world for all sentient beings without obstruction.
They know the various distinctions of the languages and voices of all sentient beings without obstruction. They resolve all the doubts of all sentient beings.
Questioning without obstruction: knowing the faculties of all sentient beings without obstruction;
being able to go forth to meet all sentient beings at the appropriate time for their transformation without obstruction;

knowing the succession of all moments—kṣaṇas, lava-s, muhūrta-s, days, nights, and divisions of time—without obstruction; and knowing the sequential flow of the ocean of the three periods of time without obstruction.
There is no obstruction. One is able to travel throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions with one’s body without obstruction.
Why is this? Because one has attained the power of supernatural faculties that are non-abiding and effortless.
Son of good family, because I have attained this power of supernatural faculties, I may walk, stand, sit, or lie down in the midst of empty space; I may become invisible or manifest myself; or...
He manifests a single body or many bodies; he passes through walls as if through empty space.
He sits cross-legged in mid-air and moves about with ease like a bird. He enters the earth as if it were water and treads upon water as if it were solid ground.
From every part of his body, above and below, smoke and flames issue forth everywhere like a great mass of fire. At times, he causes the entire great earth to tremble. Or...
At that time, he touched the sun and moon with his hand; or he manifested his body reaching as high as the Brahma palace;
or he manifested clouds of burning incense, clouds of jewel-flames, clouds of transformations, or clouds of light-nets, all of which were vast and expansive, covering the ten directions.
Or, in a single thought-moment, he passed beyond one world, two worlds, or a hundred worlds to the east.
In a thousand worlds, a hundred thousand worlds, even unto immeasurable worlds, even unto unspeakably unspeakable worlds;
or worlds exceeding the number of dust motes in Jambudvīpa, or worlds exceeding the number of dust motes in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields—
in all those Buddha-lands, before the presence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
While listening to the preaching of the Dharma, at each and every Buddha’s presence, he manifested bodies as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable Buddha-fields. From each body,
he rained down clouds of offerings as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable Buddha-fields— namely, clouds of all kinds of flowers, clouds of all kinds of incense, clouds of all kinds of garlands,
clouds of all kinds of powdered incense, clouds of all kinds of unguents, and clouds of all kinds of parasols.
With clouds of all garments, clouds of all banners, clouds of all flags, and clouds of all canopies, and with clouds of all bodies, I make offerings.
I receive and uphold everything proclaimed by each and every Tathāgata; I remember all the adornments of each and every land.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above.
The same applies to those below. In all such worlds, whatever sentient beings see my form shall all certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I clearly perceive all sentient beings in those worlds;
according to their size, their superior or inferior status, and their suffering or joy, I manifest in forms identical to theirs to teach and transform them.
Accomplishment. If there are sentient beings who draw near to me, I cause them all to dwell securely in this Dharma-gate.
Good son, I know only this unimpeded liberation gate of universally and swiftly making offerings to all Buddhas and accomplishing sentient beings.
As for the bodhisattvas who uphold the precepts of great compassion, the precepts of the pāramitās, and the precepts of the Mahāyāna—the characteristics of the bodhisattva path—[I do not know them].

It should be the precept of restraint; the precept of non-obstruction; the precept of non-retrogression; the precept of not abandoning the bodhicitta; the precept of always taking the Buddha-dharma as its object of focus;
the precept of constant mental attention toward omniscience; the precept like space; the precept that has no dependence on any world;
the precept without loss; the precept without impairment; the precept without deficiency; the precept without admixture; the precept without turbidity; the precept without...
The precept of repentance, the pure precept, the precept free from dust, and the precept free from defilement—how could I possibly know or speak of such virtues?
Son of good family, to the south of here there is a land named Darbhika and a city named Vaśavartin.
In it dwells a man named Megha. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva path.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, gazed up at him with reverence, and took his leave to depart.
[The section on] "Susthitamati’s Praise and Bestowal of the Dharma" first offers praise, then restates the dharma he had asked about, followed by the passage beginning with "I have... and so forth.
The essential points of the Dharma are correctly bestowed; that which he has personally realized is solely the gate of unimpeded liberation.
The passage from "Whether coming or going" for one and a half lines of scripture correctly demonstrates the method of cultivation.

The passage from "Attaining this light of wisdom" for eight and a half lines of scripture clearly and specifically shows the characteristics of the function of manifesting the Dharma. However, as for that which is realized, it is precisely the attainment of the six [supernormal powers].
Because of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). The subsequent commentary and explanation states: "Because one has attained the power of non-abiding and non-acting supernatural powers;

by not abiding and not acting, one attains unimpededness. Next, the six lines and a half of scripture beginning with "I have already attained this" specifically clarify the characteristics of the eighteen transformations of supernatural power.
Next, the thirteen lines and a half of scripture beginning with "Or in a single thought-moment" clarify that [these arise] from...
This supernormal power enables one to reach all worlds in the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas, and it also allows one to manifest forms to benefit sentient beings.
It concludes by saying: "If there are sentient beings who draw near to me, I shall cause them all to abide securely in this Dharma-gate.
This fully demonstrates the gate of unimpeded understanding; therefore, it concludes: "I know only this gate of liberation," and so forth.
This is all there is. Therefore, next, in the passage beginning with "As for those Bodhisattvas," he humbles himself regarding what he does not know and defers to his superior companions.

However, the fact that everything he says he does not know concerns the precepts (śīla) is intended to reveal that both the unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and liberation (vimukti) are fundamentally rooted in the observance of the Pratimokṣa precepts;
for without the precepts, one cannot cultivate and purify the mind. Next, from this point, "to the south... [is as follows].
He was instructed regarding his next companion, named Megha, who resided in a noble dwelling. Sudhana prostrated himself in farewell and departed.
*The Compendium of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-Two.
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Scroll Sixty-Three Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda,
a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Monastery
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Hanshan at Fayun Monastery on Mount Kuang in Ming China.
Excerpted from the *Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter*, Part 39.4.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded right mindfulness, deeply believed in and entered the Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Dharma, focusing exclusively upon it.

He maintains mindfulness of the Buddha so as not to sever the Three Jewels; he extols the nature of detachment from desire and remains mindful of spiritual friends. He universally illumines the three periods of time and recollects all great vows.

He universally rescues sentient beings without becoming attached to conditioned phenomena. He thoroughly contemplates the intrinsic nature of all dharmas and is fully able to adorn and purify all worlds.
Within the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas, his mind is free from attachment. Gradually...
Then, traveling south, he went to the city of Vaśavartī to seek out Megha.

There he saw the man seated upon a lion throne for preaching the Dharma in the midst of a marketplace, surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand people, teaching the Dharma-door of the Adornment of the Wheel-Syllable.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood before him with palms joined.
He spoke these words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path,
how they should pass through the various realms of existence without ever forgetting the mind of awakening, and how they may attain firmness in the impartial intention."
How is it that one remains steadfastly unmoving? How does one attain a pure mind that cannot be thwarted or destroyed?
How does one give rise to the power of great compassion that is never weary or exhausted? How does one enter the *dhāraṇī* and universally attain purity?

How does one generate the vast radiance of wisdom regarding all phenomena, remaining free from all obscurations of darkness? How does one possess the eloquence of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*)?
How does one use the power of resolve to penetrate the treasury of all profound meanings? How does one obtain the power of right mindfulness to retain all the various wheels of Dharma?
How does one obtain the power of pure destinies to universally expound all dharmas across all realms of existence?
How does one obtain the power of wisdom to definitively discern the meaning of all dharmas?

The fourth is the stage of Abiding in Noble Birth (*jātipratibaddha-vihāra*). "Noble birth" refers to being born into the family of the Buddha-dharma, also called being born into the family of the bodhicitta, because one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is noble.
This signifies that Sudhana, by hearing the gateway of the light of the aforementioned Dharma and entering into it with deep faith, has attained birth in the Buddha-family.
The first four lines of the sutra clarify the practice of initiating contemplation (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*). Gradually...
Next, he traveled southward to seek his subsequent friend. He then saw that person preaching the Dharma in a marketplace. Sudhana prostrated himself in reverence;

next, he set forth his own resolve for enlightenment. Then, from the words "But I do not yet know" (我而未知) down to seven and a half lines of scripture, he formally presents his inquiry, which concerns the characteristics of cultivation and realization.
At that time, Megha said to Sudhana, "Noble son, have you already resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Sudhana replied, "Yes; I have already previously resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Megha immediately descended from his lion throne and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before Sudhana, scattering...
With gold, silver, priceless jewels, and exquisite powdered sandalwood, he covered it with immeasurable varieties of garments.
He further scattered immeasurable kinds of incense and flowers, using various ritual implements as offerings.
Thereupon, he rose and uttered this praise: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you are truly able to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

[They] generate the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Good son, if there is anyone who can generate the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they thereby do not sever the lineage of all Buddhas, and they thereby adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
This constitutes the maturation of all sentient beings; it constitutes the thorough penetration of the nature of all phenomena;
it constitutes the awakening to and understanding of all karmic seeds; it constitutes the fulfillment of all practices; and it constitutes the non-interruption of all great vows.
Then, one will understand and become detached from the seeds of craving as they truly are; one will clearly perceive the distinctions of the three periods of time;
one’s faith and understanding will become forever firm; one will be sustained by all Tathāgatas; and one will be remembered by all Buddhas.
Then one will be equal to all bodhisattvas; then one will be praised and rejoiced in by all worthies and sages;
then one will be venerated and visited by all Brahma kings; then one will be offered worship by all celestial lords; and then one will be protected by all yakṣas.
Then all rākṣasa kings will serve as their guardians; all nāga kings will welcome them;
all kiṃnara kings will sing praises of them; and all the lords of the world will extol and rejoice in them.
It causes all realms of sentient beings to attain complete peace and security;
that is to say, it causes them to abandon the evil destinies, to emerge from places of hardship, to sever the root of all poverty, and to give rise to the happiness of all devas and humans.

Because of encountering and drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); because of hearing, receiving, and upholding the vast Dharma; because of generating the bodhicitta; because of purifying the bodhicitta;
because of illuminating the bodhisattva path; because of entering the wisdom of a bodhisattva; and because of dwelling in the bodhisattva stages.

Good son, you should know that what a bodhisattva accomplishes is exceedingly difficult; it is difficult to emerge from and difficult to encounter. Those who see a bodhisattva do so all the more [rarely].
It is rare for a bodhisattva to serve as a source of reliance for all sentient beings, so that they may grow, develop, and reach fulfillment;
to act as a savior for all sentient beings, so that they may be extracted from all suffering and hardship; and to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings, so that they may protect the world.
For the sake of protecting all sentient beings and causing them to be free from fear; because, like a wind-wheel, the Bodhisattva sustains all worlds so that they do not fall into the evil destinies;
because, like the great earth, he causes the roots of goodness in sentient beings to grow;
because, like the great ocean, his merit is full and inexhaustible; because, like the pure sun, the light of his wisdom shines everywhere; like the [Sumeru]...
Because his roots of goodness are loftily exalted; because the light of his moon-like wisdom has appeared; because he is like a valiant general who crushes and subdues the armies of Māra;

because he has attained sovereignty within the city of the Buddha-Dharma as a sovereign lord; because he is like a fierce fire that utterly consumes the self-cherishing and craving of sentient beings;
because he is like a great cloud that pours down the rain of immeasurable sublime Dharma; and because he is like the timely rain that causes all things to grow.
Because they are the sprouts of all roots of faith; because they are like a pilot who points out the crossing places and ferries across the ocean of the Dharma;
and because they are like a bridge that enables one to cross the sea of birth and death.
Third, at that time, Megha’s subsequent praise and bestowal of the Dharma begins with the initial examination and determination of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Next, Megha suddenly descends from his lion throne; he first pays homage to Sudhana and only thereafter transmits the Dharma.

The intention behind this is to reveal that the Dharma previously inquired about by Sudhana is based on the cultivation of practice according to phenomena (*vastu*), and is intended to clarify conduct that gathers in the secular world; therefore, [he acts] first...
One bestows the Dharma only after paying homage; this also demonstrates that the bodhicitta is the most supreme and honored state of mind, and thus must certainly be revered.

After [the disciple] has bowed, the teacher then rises and extensively praises the causal mind of bodhicitta as being profound and vast, saying: "The initial resolve and the ultimate attainment are fundamentally no different;
of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult to achieve. It is because of this that one gains the respect and protection of the ten kings.
To extensively benefit sentient beings, the text concludes below by pointing out: "One should know that what the Bodhisattva accomplishes is extremely difficult.

For it is difficult for a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to appear and difficult to encounter; yet to find a vessel capable of receiving the Dharma, where teacher and disciple are harmoniously matched—this is the difficulty of difficulties."
The reason for speaking so extensively of its difficulty is precisely to strengthen the resolve for progress.

Next, the nine lines of scripture following "the Bodhisattva for the sake of all sentient beings" specifically praise the great benefit of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and explain the reasons why such a person is difficult to encounter.
The text contains ten similes that extol the great advantage of the spiritual friend to the utmost.

After Megha had thus praised Sudhana and caused all the bodhisattvas to rejoice, various rays of light issued from his face, universally illuminating the trichiliocosm. All sentient beings within it who encountered this light—
All the nāgas, devas, and others, up to the Brahmā heavens, came to the place where Megha was.
The Mahāsattva Megha then, by means of skillful expedients, revealed, expounded, analyzed, and explained for them the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of the Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables.
When those sentient beings had heard this Dharma, they all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Megha then rose from his seat and addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son, I have attained the *dhāraṇī* of Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣavatī*), by which I am able to discern and know all the devas within the great trichiliocosm."
The languages of all nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all the Brahmā devas; likewise, throughout this trichiliocosm and in the ten directions,
in countless worlds even unto those that are unspeakably unspeakable, it is exactly the same.
Good son, I only know this Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Bodhisattva’s Wondrous Sound Dhāraṇī.

As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to universally enter the various oceans of conceptions of all sentient beings, the various oceans of designations, the various oceans of names and titles, and the various oceans of languages; who are able to universally enter the exposition of all profound and secret teachings—[how they do so, I do not know].

The ocean of phrases: expounding the ocean of phrases of all ultimate dharmas; expounding the ocean of phrases of all objects of focus throughout the three periods of time contained within all objects of focus;
expounding the ocean of supreme phrases; expounding the ocean of most supreme phrases; expounding the ocean of differentiated phrases;
expounding the ocean of all differentiated phrases; and being able to universally enter all worldly incantations and arts.
O Sea! Regarding the wheel of adornment of all sounds and the limit of the wheel of all distinct syllables—how could I now possibly know or describe such virtues?
Son of good family, if you travel south from here, there is a village named Vana-vāsin.
There lives an elder named Vimukti. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should cultivate awakening.
The Practice of the Bodhisattva. How does a bodhisattva accomplish the bodhisattva practice? How does a bodhisattva gather the bodhisattva practice?
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the bodhisattva practice? At that time, because of his spiritual friend, the youth Sudhana conceived a profound sense of reverence for the dharma of omniscience;
he planted deep roots of pure faith and greatly increased his own merit. He prostrated at the feet of Megha and shed tears from his eyes and nose.
Weeping with grief, they circumambulated him countless times; longing and gazing up at him in reverence, they took their leave and departed.
After the second Maitreya had thus offered praise, he bestowed upon them his own Dharma-gate, beginning with the *Pañcagatika-sūtra*.

From the opening of his face, he emitted various kinds of light, manifesting supernatural powers to benefit sentient beings. Within that light, he expounded the "Chapter on the Wheel-Syllable" (*Cakrākṣara-parivarta*).

The "Adornment of the Dharma Gate" is that which Megha has realized. As for the "Chapter on the Syllable *A*," it refers to revolving unimpededly through the sounds of the phonemes to enter the ocean of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is primarily intended to reveal the *dhāraṇī* dharma gate by means of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of letters.
Having completed his manifestation of supernatural powers, Megha returned to his original seat and addressed Sudhana.
Vasudhara said: "I have merely attained the *dhāraṇī* of Wondrous Sound and the Samādhi of Discerning Languages.
Within this trichiliocosm, all the languages and sounds of gods and humans are each and every one a gateway into the Dharma-realm.
This signifies that by entering this Dharma-gateway, all things—whether good or evil—"
All sounds, whether coarse or subtle, are the voices of the Dharma; there is not a single word or sound that is not a gateway for entering into principle.
If one wishes to enter the "Dharma-Gate of Radiance for Cultivating Progress" as asked by the noble Sudhana, one does so precisely through this samādhi of sound.
Therefore, when Megha answered Sudhana, he merely emitted this single light, which manifested his entire being.
This indicates that there is no further room for words; it is precisely through direct perception that the Way is preserved.
Therefore, Megha immediately told Sudhana: "I know only this Bodhisattva Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Wondrous Sound Dhāraṇī."
If bodhisattvas are able to universally enter the ocean of perceptions of all sentient beings,
up to the wheel of adornment of all sounds and the wheel of all distinctions, that is beyond my knowledge. However,
the fact that what is unknown begins with the raising of various perceptions and concludes with the differentiation of all sounds is intended to reveal the entirety of all speech.
All sounds arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Because sentient beings possess various kinds of conceptual constructions, there are various kinds of speech and sounds.
If one realizes that conceptual construction is fundamentally empty, then sounds have no inherent substance.
In this way, all speech enters the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, this is the *dhāraṇī* of letters.
This is the gateway. Since the former [teacher] was already humble regarding his own inability, he pointed out the name of his subsequent friend, the Elder Vimokṣa.
Sudhana, following these instructions, took his leave and departed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated the gate of the light-adornment of the *dhāraṇī* of the unimpeded analytical knowledge of all bodhisattvas;
he entered deeply into the ocean-gate of the speech of all bodhisattvas; he recollected the gate of the subtle skillful means of all bodhisattvas in knowing all sentient beings;
he observed the gate of the pure mind of all bodhisattvas; and he accomplished the [qualities] of all bodhisattvas.
The gateway of the radiance of roots of goodness; the gateway of purifying all bodhisattvas’ methods for teaching and transforming sentient beings;

the gateway of the sharp and keen wisdom of all bodhisattvas for gathering in sentient beings; the gateway of the firm and stable vast aspirations of all bodhisattvas; the gateway of sustaining the supreme aspirations of all bodhisattvas;
the gateway of purifying the various types of faith and understanding of all bodhisattvas; and the gateway of the contemplation of all bodhisattvas.
Through the gate of immeasurable virtuous minds, they maintain firm vows with hearts free from weariness.
Adorned with all manner of armor, their profound resolve for diligence is irreversible, and they possess indestructible faith.
Their minds are as firm as vajra and Nārāyaṇa, such that none can destroy them. They uphold the instructions of all spiritual friends regarding all objects of perception.

They attain the wisdom that does not destroy the realms (*dhātu*). Their conduct, purified through the universal gate, is unimpeded. The light of their wisdom is perfected, universally illuminating all things.
They are endowed with the light of the *dhāraṇīs* of all stages (*bhūmi*) and thoroughly understand the various distinctions within the *dharmadhātu*.
Being without dependence or abiding, they are equal and non-dual; though their intrinsic nature is pure, they are universally adorned. In all their practices, they have attained ultimate mastery.
It was concluded. Their wisdom was pure and free from all attachments; they possessed unobstructed knowledge of the distinct dharmas throughout the ten directions.

Their bodies traveled to the various locations throughout the ten directions without weariness or fatigue. They attained clear comprehension of the diverse karmic activities throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the Buddhas of the distinct regions throughout the ten directions, there were none they did not perceive directly. They were able to penetrate deeply into the distinct times throughout the ten directions. Pure...
The pure and wondrous Dharma fills their minds. The illumination of the Samādhi of Universal Wisdom shines upon their minds. Their minds constantly and universally enter the realm of equality.
They are touched by the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. The stream of all-knowledge flows on in uninterrupted succession.
Whether in body or mind, they are never separated from the Buddha-Dharma. They are empowered by the spiritual power of all Buddhas and the light of all Tathāgatas.
Illuminating all that is to be known, he fulfilled his great vows. His vow-body pervaded the entire network of all lands, and his body universally entered the entirety of the dharma-realm.
He traveled by stages for twelve years until he reached the city of Vana-vāsin, where he sought everywhere for the elder Vimokṣaka.
Having found him, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, rose, joined his palms, and said: "Noble One, I..."
Now that I have been able to meet with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), I have obtained vast and great benefit.

Why is this? A spiritual friend is difficult to see, difficult to hear of, difficult to appear before, difficult to serve, difficult to approach, difficult to receive as a guide, difficult to encounter, difficult to dwell with, difficult to please, and difficult to find.
I have followed you. Now that I have encountered you, I have gained a sublime benefit.
Noble One, I have already previously resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, desiring to serve all Buddhas and desiring to meet with all Buddhas.
It is because they desire to see all buddhas; because they desire to contemplate all buddhas; because they desire to know all buddhas;
because they desire to realize the equality of all buddhas; because they desire to give rise to the great vows of all buddhas;
because they desire to fulfill the great vows of all buddhas; because they desire to be endowed with the light of wisdom of all buddhas; and because they desire to accomplish...
Because they practice all the deeds of all Buddhas; because they desire to attain the supernormal powers of all Buddhas;
because they desire to be endowed with the various powers of all Buddhas; because they desire to obtain the fearlessnesses of all Buddhas;
because they desire to hear all Buddha-dharmas; because they desire to receive all Buddha-dharmas; because they desire to uphold all Buddha-dharmas; because they desire to understand...
Because it is all the Buddha-dharmas; because one wishes to protect all the Buddha-dharmas;
because one wishes to become of one essence with the entire assembly of bodhisattvas; because one wishes to be equal and no different from the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas;
because one wishes to fulfill all the bodhisattva pāramitās; because one wishes to accomplish all that is to be accomplished by bodhisattvas...
Because of their practice; because they desire to bring forth all the pure vows of bodhisattvas;
because they desire to obtain the treasury of the majestic spiritual power of all buddhas and bodhisattvas;

because they desire to obtain the great light of inexhaustible wisdom, the treasury of all bodhisattva dharmas; because they desire to obtain the vast treasury of all bodhisattva samādhis; because they desire—
Because they have accomplished the treasury of all bodhisattvas' immeasurable and innumerable supernormal powers;
because they desire to teach and discipline all sentient beings through the treasury of great compassion, causing them all to ultimately reach the furthest limit;
because they desire to manifest the treasury of spiritual transformations; and because they have attained mastery over all treasuries of sovereignty through their own minds.
Desiring to enter the treasury of purity, which is adorned with all marks, O Noble One,
I now approach you with such a mind, such an intention, such joy, such desire, such aspiration,
such reflection, such reverence, such skillful means, such ultimate resolve, and such humility. O Noble One, [I come] to you.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to instruct and guide the assembly of bodhisattvas;

that he can, through skillful means, elucidate what has been attained, show them the path, provide them with a bridge, and bestow upon them the Dharma-gates, so as to cause them to remove the obstacles of delusion and inversion, extract the arrows of hesitation, sever the net of doubt, illuminate the dense forest of the mind, wash away the turbidity of mental defilements, and make the mind pure and white. Please... [make the mind...]
Purify it. Rectify the mind from its crookedness; sever the mind from birth and death; still the mind from unwholesomeness; liberate the mind from attachment.
Cause the mind to be liberated from the locus of attachment; cause the mind to turn away from the locus of defiled craving. Cause it to swiftly enter the realm of all-knowledge;
cause it to quickly reach the unsurpassed city of Dharma. Cause it to abide in great compassion; cause it to cultivate great loving-kindness; cause it to enter...

The Bodhisattva practice causes one to cultivate the gateways of samādhi, causes one to enter and realize the stages of attainment, causes one to contemplate the mind of phenomena, causes the power of practice to increase, and causes the cultivation of conduct.
Toward all things, the mind is universally equanimous. I pray that the Noble One will expound this for me.
How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path so that, through whatever they practice, they quickly attain purity and quickly attain clarity?
This is the fifth liberation, the dwelling of the householder Gṛhapati Upāyasaṃpanna (Endowed with Skillful Means). Now, as for being "endowed with skillful means," it is precisely...

This clarifies that while maintaining the truth, one follows worldly conventions; it is the practice of cultivating immeasurable skillful means to transform sentient beings through non-abiding conduct.
Because one has attained entry into the *dhāraṇī* gate of the Supreme Sublime Sound, one is able to enter the world to benefit sentient beings without abiding.

Therefore, Sudhana, following the instructions, proceeds to seek [the teacher], first recollecting the previous teachings and entering into realization through each point of reflection. There are six lines of verse.

The eleven phrases are all dharma-gates that are objects of contemplation. Next, from "the vow is firm" (*śīlaṃ dṛḍhaṃ*) downward, twelve and a half lines of scripture reveal the benefits of cultivation.
He traveled gradually for twelve years, searching everywhere for the Elder Liberation (*Mokṣa-gṛhapati*).

This signifies that he profoundly investigated the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), thereby causing the twelve bases of sense-faculties and their objects (*āyatana*) to pervade the Dharma.
Each of these realms is a gate of liberation. Only after this does one see them;

having seen them, Sudhana spoke in extreme terms of how difficult it is to see, hear, emerge from, serve, approach, attend, encounter, associate with, please, or follow a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These ten "difficulties" expressed in such profound words arise because his entry into the Dharma has become so deep that he feels profound gratitude.
His reverence grew ever more profound, and his earnest seeking for instruction became increasingly intense; thus, his resolve for the sake of the Dharma deepened further.
Therefore, he rejoiced in such a rare opportunity, having fortunately been able to meet [the Master] after hoping for it for many years. First, he expressed his respectful greetings;
thereafter, he requested instruction. He first set forth his own initial aspiration, and subsequently, for the sake of all Buddhas, he specifically detailed his resolve.
There are three aspects [to this]. First, the first five lines of the sutra describe the desire to ascend and exhaustively reach the realm of the Buddhas.

Second, the following two lines of the sutra describe the desire to descend and exhaust the source of the Dharma. Finally, the last nine lines of the sutra describe the desire to equalize the practices of all Bodhisattvas;
these also constitute the Sangha Jewel. Because Sudhana’s entry into the Dharma is already profound, his inquiries likewise [reflect this depth].
Introduction. For this reason, he specifically poses questions regarding the Three Jewels, desiring to manifest his own vow to bear the burden [of the Dharma].
Next, the passage beginning with "Venerable One, I now with such a mind" summarizes the characteristics of the previously aroused resolve as the opening for his inquiry.
Following that, the nine lines of scripture beginning with "I have heard, Venerable One," praise the ability to provide guidance and instruction; thus, he requests a resolution of his doubts.
At that time, by the power of the householder Vimukta’s past roots of goodness, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
and the power of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s mindfulness, he immediately entered the bodhisattva samādhi-gate called "The Boundless Revolving Dhāraṇī that Universally Encompasses All Buddha-fields.
Having entered this samādhi, he attained a pure body, within which [all things] were manifested.
In each of the ten directions, there appeared Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, along with their assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

There were also various manifestations of light and diverse ornaments. Furthermore, there appeared the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers practiced by those Buddhas in the past, all the dharmas that assist the path through their great vows, and the pure adornments of their practices for transcendence. One also beheld those Buddhas attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
The Perfectly Awakened One turns the sublime wheel of Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.

All such things appear within his body without any obstruction; their various forms and various sequences abide as they originally were, without being confused or disordered—namely, various lands, various assemblies, various sites of enlightenment, and various adornments.
Within them, the various Buddhas manifest all manner of spiritual powers, establish various vehicles and paths, and demonstrate various gates of vows.
In some worlds, they perform buddha-work while residing in the Tuṣita Heaven; in other worlds, they perform buddha-work after passing away from the Tuṣita Heaven.
Likewise, there are those who dwell in the womb, or are born, or reside within the palace, or...
Furthermore, they manifest renunciation; or entering a place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*); or defeating the armies of Māra; or being respectfully surrounded by devas and nāgas;
or being entreated by the lords of the world to preach the Dharma; or turning the wheel of Dharma; or entering parinirvāṇa; or distributing the relics; or erecting stūpas and temples.
These Tathāgatas appear within various assemblies, various worlds, and various realms of rebirth.
Among all sentient beings— with their various lineages, various desires and pleasures, various karmic actions, various languages,
various faculties and natures, and various afflictions, latent tendencies, and habitual propensities— he may dwell in a subtle place of enlightenment, or in a vast place of enlightenment,
or in a place of enlightenment measuring one yojana, or in a place of enlightenment measuring ten yojanas.
In some places, they occupy a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) measuring as many yojanas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
By means of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), various modes of speech, various sounds, various Dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*), and various doors of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇīmukha*).

Through various gateways of eloquence, by means of various oceans of noble truths, with various fearless lion’s roars of great masters, they spoke of the various roots of goodness of all sentient beings, their various recollections, bestowed various predictions of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas, and expounded various teachings of the Buddhas.
Sudhana was able to hear and receive all the words spoken by those Tathāgatas. Furthermore—
He beheld the inconceivable samādhi and miraculous transformations of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the householder Vimokṣa arose from his samādhi and addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:
"Good son, I have entered and emerged from the Tathāgata’s liberation door of unimpeded adornment. Good son, when I enter and emerge from this liberation door, I immediately behold..."
In the east, in the world-system of Jāmbūnada-gold Radiance, there was the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Nāgeśvararāja,
surrounded by a great assembly at his site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Vairocanagarbha as the foremost. Furthermore, in the south, in the world-system of Swift Power,
there was the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantagandha, surrounded by a great assembly at his site of enlightenment.
surrounded by [a host of bodhisattvas], with the Bodhisattva Mind-King (*Cittarāja*) as their leader.

Furthermore, I saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sumerupradīparāja in the western world-realm of Gandhaprabhāsa, surrounded by an assembly at his site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), with the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind (*Asaṅgacitta*) as their leader.
Furthermore, I saw [the Tathāgata] Invincible Gold in the northern world-realm of Kāṣāyadhvaja...
He saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vajra, surrounded by an assembly at the site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Vajrapadavikrama as his chief.

Furthermore, he saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anupalambhagocaracakṣus in the northeastern direction, in the world-system Sarvottamavararatna, surrounded by an assembly at the site of enlightenment. He saw [the Tathāgata] Anupala... [the text continues].

He saw the Bodhisattva Skillful Transformation as the leader. Furthermore, he saw in the southeastern direction, in the world-system Fragrant Flame Radiance, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Incense Lamp, surrounded by an assembly at his place of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Diamond Flame Wisdom as the leader.
Moreover, he saw in the southwestern direction, in the world-system Universal Radiance of the Sun of Wisdom...
I saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dharmadhātucakraketu, surrounded by an assembly at his site of enlightenment,
with the Bodhisattva Sarvavikurvāṇaketu as his chief. Furthermore, I saw in the northwest direction,
in the world-system Viśuddhasarva, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvabuddharatnaviśeṣaketu, surrounded by an assembly at his site of enlightenment.
With the Bodhisattva Dharma-Dhvaja-Rāja as their leader, they were circumambulating him.

Furthermore, they saw above, in the world-systems of the ten directions that appear in succession and are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ananta-jñāna-raśmi-paripūrṇa-dhvaja, surrounded by a great assembly at his site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Dharmadhātu-mukha-dhvaja-rāja as their leader. Moreover, they saw below...
In the world-system Buddha-radiance, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Unobstructed Wisdom Banner was surrounded by an assembly at the site of enlightenment,
with the Bodhisattva Universal World-realm Banner King as their leader.

The third section, "Liberation of the Lower [Vehicle]," correctly demonstrates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Initially, he enters meditative absorption and indicates it through silence; subsequently, emerging from concentration, he answers with words.
Regarding the phrase "immediately entering the Samādhi of the Infinite Revolving Dhāraṇī that Universally Encompasses All Buddha-fields":

this means that all Buddha-fields of the ten directions are universally gathered within one's own body by means of the wisdom of mind-only, which is a dhāraṇī in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
It is named as such because it causes the essence and its functions to revolve without obstruction.

This reveals that when the contemplation of Mind-Only is perfected, one universally encompasses the boundless and differentiated realms of all Buddhas and enters instantaneously into the equal Dharma-realm.
