Therefore, the twenty-one lines of scripture following the phrase "having entered this samādhi" below all demonstrate the objects encompassed within this samādhi.
The entire realm manifested within the body of the elder. Within that manifested realm, all the Buddhas preached the Dharma;

all their speech, as well as their ineffable samādhis and miraculous transformations—this is what is called "the Dharma-body of all Buddhas entering my own nature, and my body merging with that of the Tathāgata.
All of this was made for Sudhana to hear personally and see directly. Immediately...
This samādhi has already manifested the inexhaustible dharma-realm of the inexhaustible, thereby clarifying the functional activity of meditative concentration;
it serves as a silent indication of that which Sudhana has inquired about. Thereafter, at that time, the Elder Vimokṣa arose from his samādhi.
He then replied with these words: "I have entered the Tathāgata’s liberation-gate of unimpeded adornment (*anāvaraṇa-vyūha*).
There are five general meanings for the exegesis of this liberation: first, that each and every Tathāgata possesses all unimpeded adornments;
second, that each and every Tathāgata is mutually pervasive and unimpeded; third, that all Tathāgatas..."
The adornments all entered the body of the elder. Fourth, the elder perceived the oceans of Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
Fifth, the elder maintained them with wisdom without obstruction. This is precisely what is meant by "first moving through concentration and subsequently uprooting [delusions] through wisdom.
Next, from "I enter and exit" below, there are twenty lines of scripture that describe seeing the assemblies of Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) entirely enters the body of the elder. This clearly elucidates the functional activity of meditative concentration;
that is, within this samādhi, the entire realm manifests throughout the whole body as the gateway for entering the Dharma-realm.
"Good son, I see Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions.

Those Tathāgatas do not come here, nor do I go there. If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Land of Peace and Bliss, I see him immediately at will. If I wish to see [the Tathāgata] Vajraprabhāsa of the Sandalwood World,"
The Tathāgata [of this world]; the Tathāgata Jewel Radiance in the World of Exquisite Fragrance; the Tathāgata Jewel Lotus Radiance in the World of Lotuses;
the Tathāgata Tranquil Light in the World of Exquisite Gold; the Tathāgata Acala in the World of Sukhāvatī; the Tathāgata Siṃha in the World of Excellent Abiding;
the Tathāgata Moon Awakening in the World of Mirror Radiance; and the Tathāgata Jewel Lion Ornament...
He saw all such things as the world-system of Vairocana Tathāgata;
yet that Tathāgata did not come here, nor did he go there to that place. He knew that all Buddhas and his own mind were entirely like a dream;
he knew that all Buddhas were like reflections and his own mind was like water; he knew all...
All the physical forms and characteristics of the Buddhas, as well as one's own mind, are entirely like an illusion.
One knows that all Buddhas and one’s own mind are entirely like echoes. Thus do I know; thus do I recollect: that all the Buddhas seen arise from one’s own mind.
Son of good family, you should know that the Bodhisattva cultivates all Buddha-dharmas, purifies all Buddha-fields, and accumulates sublime practices.
They tame sentient beings, give rise to great vows to enter all-knowledge, sport with mastery in the inconceivable gates of liberation,
attain the bodhi of the Buddhas, manifest great supernatural powers, and dwell pervasively throughout the dharma-realms of the ten directions.
By means of subtle wisdom, one universally enters all kalpas; all such things arise entirely from one's own mind.
Therefore, noble son, you should support your own mind with wholesome dharmas; you should moisten your own mind with the water of the Dharma;
you should purify your own mind regarding sensory objects; you should fortify your own mind with diligence; and you should broaden your own mind with patience.
Mind. One should realize one’s own mind through wisdom; one should clarify one’s own mind with sharp and keen wisdom;
one should develop one’s own mind through the sovereign power of the Buddha; one should broaden one’s own mind through the equanimity of the Buddha;
one should examine one’s own mind with the ten powers of the Buddha. Good son, I know only this liberation door of the Tathāgata’s unimpeded adornment.
Thus they attain the ability to enter and emerge [from samādhi]. Like all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they have attained unimpeded wisdom and abide in unimpeded conduct.
They have attained the samādhi of constantly seeing all Buddhas and the samādhi of not abiding in the limit of nirvāṇa. They have thoroughly mastered the universal-gate realm of samādhi;
they are entirely equal regarding the dharmas of the three periods of time; and they are able to skillfully manifest emanated bodies throughout all lands, dwelling therein.
Within the impartial realm of all Buddhas, the realms of the ten directions appear before them entirely; they observe with wisdom such that nothing is not clearly understood.
Within their own bodies, they manifest the formation and destruction of all worlds, yet they do not give rise to dualistic notions regarding their own bodies or those worlds.
How could I possibly know or describe such wondrous conduct? Good [son/daughter]...
"Good man, from here travel south to the edge of Jambudvīpa; there is a land named Mālikāra.
There dwells a bhikṣu named Sāgaradhvaja. Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the elder Vimokṣa, circumambulated him to the right, and gazed upon him.
They praise and extol them; they contemplate, yearn for, and look up to them with tears of grief flowing.

With single-minded recollection, they rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), serve spiritual friends, and revere spiritual friends. Through spiritual friends, they perceive all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
they do not give rise to opposition toward spiritual friends; their minds have no flattery or deception toward spiritual friends; and their minds always accord with spiritual friends.
One should conceive of the spiritual friend as a compassionate mother, because they cause one to abandon all unbeneficial dharmas;
one should conceive of the spiritual friend as a compassionate father, because they give birth to all wholesome dharmas. Having spoken thus, he withdrew and departed.
"Good sons, I see thus... and so forth below indicates the essential characteristics of meditative concentration; this is the gateway of the contemplation of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*).

This clarifies the practice of engaging with the world to benefit sentient beings. Showing the contemplation of Mind-Only immediately following the preceding dharma-gate precisely reveals the essential point of benefiting sentient beings:
first, one must thoroughly comprehend that the boundless realms of sentient beings are all manifestations of Mind-Only, thereby making this clear.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction, for they enter the equal Dharma-realm. Next, the gate of contemplation on Mind-Only is shown:
because the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear equally, one sees that those Tathāgatas of the ten directions do not come here, nor does one go there.
Next, the *Wuxing jing* (Sūtra of the Five Practices) extensively clarifies seeing the Buddha according to the mind; first, it explains:

"If one wishes to see [the Buddha], one sees him immediately. Following this, the passage beginning with "Then that Tathāgata... correctly reveals the essence of the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha as mind-only (*cittamātra*).
Its intent is to ask: what is the reason for seeing the Buddha as having no characteristics of coming or going?
It is because one knows that all Buddhas and one's own mind are entirely like a dream; all Buddhas are like reflections, appearing when water is clear or a mirror is bright.
The image manifests; one realizes that one's own mind is like an illusion and understands that all Buddhas and one's own mind are entirely like echoes.
By means of these five modes of contemplation, one knows that such mindfulness of the Buddha arises entirely from one's own mind. How magnificent is the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha!
It is the foremost sublime practice for engaging with the world to benefit sentient beings; therefore, it was specifically revealed to the Elder.
Nevertheless, for the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), taking the mind alone as the essential is paramount; thus, it was demonstrated through the direct realization of the Elder. Alas!
How can people of today, who disparage *nien-fo* and fail to practice it, know that the vast and unimpeded Dharma-realm of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zong*) must necessarily be realized gradually?
For this purpose, one should take *nien-fo* as the foremost practice. Therefore, Sudhana first visited the Venerable...
Yun then revealed and taught the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recollection). Now, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he specifically entrusts this exposition on the samādhi of *nianfo*.
How could those among the monastic and lay communities who possess aspiration during the Dharma-ending age not revere it? Therefore, he subsequently extensively praises the Dharma-gate of Mind-Only;
this is not merely the single gate of *nianfo*, for the mind encompasses all phenomena, including the essence and function of the Buddha-fruition and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas.

All are established based upon the single mind; therefore, it subsequently indicates that one should know that when Bodhisattvas cultivate all Buddha-dharmas and so forth, they all arise from their own minds.
Thus, it concludes by showing ten methods for treating the mind as the essential gateway for entering the practice of contemplation.

Regarding the practices for the dual benefit [of self and others], there is no analogy that surpasses the gateway of the "mind-only" contemplation; hence, the Elder [Vimalakīrti] later expresses his humility.
He said, "I have only attained entry into and emergence from this liberation door of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Array;
as for [the practices] of the bodhisattvas below this level, they are all beyond my capacity. Thus, he deferred to his superior companion.
From here, traveling south, he reached the shore of Jambudvīpa, where there was a bhikṣu named Sāgaramegha. "One should go to him and inquire," said Sudhana.
Having paid respects to the elder, he wept with longing and sorrow, then departed as instructed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded right mindfulness, contemplated the elder’s instruction and observed the elder’s instruction.
I call to mind that inconceivable gate of liberation of the bodhisattvas; I contemplate that inconceivable radiance of the wisdom of the bodhisattvas;
I enter deeply into that inconceivable gate of the dharma-realm; I proceed toward that inconceivable universal entrance of the bodhisattvas;
I clearly behold those inconceivable supernatural powers of the Tathāgatas; and I comprehend that inconceivable universal entry.
Buddha-fields. One discerns those inconceivable adornments of the Buddha’s power; contemplates those inconceivable stages of the bodhisattva’s samādhis and liberations;
thoroughly understands those inconceivable distinctions among worlds as ultimately unimpeded;
cultivates those inconceivable, firm, and profound bodhisattva intentions; and gives rise to those inconceivable...
The Bodhisattva’s great vow and pure karma led him to travel south by stages until he reached the village of Mālī on the borders of Jambudvīpa.
There he searched everywhere for the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja and saw him sitting cross-legged in the samādhi on the side of a walking path.
He was free from inhalation and exhalation, devoid of discursive thought or perception, his body peaceful and unmoving. From beneath his feet there issued forth...
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of elders, householders, and brahmins all adorned their bodies with various ornaments;
they all wore jeweled crowns with bright pearls fastened at the crown of their heads and traveled throughout all worlds in the ten directions,
raining down all manner of jewels, necklaces, garments, and food and drink as supreme offerings in accordance with the Dharma.
They provide all flavors, all garlands, all incenses, all ointments, and all requisites for desire and livelihood.
In all places, they rescue and sustain all impoverished sentient beings;
they console all suffering and distressed beings, causing them all to rejoice with pure minds and to achieve the path to unsurpassed bodhi. From that...
From his two knees emerged countless hundreds of thousands of billions of kṣatriyas and brahmins, all of whom were wise and intelligent.
They possessed various complexions, various physical forms, and various garments, adorned with the most exquisite ornaments.
They pervaded all worlds throughout the ten directions, gathering in sentient beings through kind speech and shared activities—namely, by providing for the poor and healing the sick.
He heals the sick; he brings safety to those in peril and stills the fears of those who are terrified. He causes all who suffer from grief and pain to experience joy and happiness.
Furthermore, through skillful means, he exhorts and guides them, causing them all to abandon evil and abide securely in wholesome dharmas.

From his waist, he produces immeasurable sages, equal in number to all sentient beings—some wearing garments of grass, others wearing garments of tree bark—all holding water-pots and maintaining majestic deportment.
In tranquility, they traverse and dwell throughout the worlds of the ten directions. From within the void, they praise the Tathāgata with the sublime voice of a Buddha and expound all dharmas.
Sometimes they speak of the path of pure brahmacarya, causing others to practice it and subdue their sense faculties.
Sometimes they speak of how all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, causing others to contemplate this and give rise to wisdom. Or they speak...

He reveals the conventions of worldly discourse, or else demonstrates the skillful means for the essential departure toward the wisdom of all-knowledge, causing them to cultivate their respective tasks in successive order.
From his two flanks emerge inconceivable nāgas and inconceivable nāga-girls.
They manifested inconceivable supernatural transformations of the nāgas, namely: inconceivable clouds of incense,
inconceivable clouds of flowers, inconceivable clouds of garlands, inconceivable clouds of precious parasols, inconceivable clouds of precious banners,
inconceivable clouds of exquisite jewel ornaments, inconceivable clouds of great maṇi jewels, and inconceivable clouds of jewels.
Clouds of necklaces, clouds of inconceivable jewel thrones, clouds of inconceivable jewel palaces,
clouds of inconceivable jewel lotuses, clouds of inconceivable jewel crowns, clouds of inconceivable celestial bodies,
and clouds of inconceivable handmaidens— all pervaded the void as adornments, filling the paths of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
They established this site as an offering, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.

From the *svastika* on his chest, he manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of *asura* kings, all of whom displayed inconceivable and sovereign illusory powers, causing a hundred worlds to tremble violently.
All the waters of the oceans spontaneously surged and boiled, and all the mountains...
The kings struck one another. The palaces of the devas shook without exception. The radiance of the māras was obscured without exception.

The hosts of the māra-armies were subdued without exception. They caused all sentient beings to abandon pride and arrogance, eliminate thoughts of anger and malice, shatter the mountains of affliction (*kleśa*), and stifle all unwholesome dharmas.
They caused long-term freedom from strife and eternal harmony. Furthermore, by means of illusion...
By their power, they awaken sentient beings; they cause them to extinguish evil and sin; they cause them to fear birth and death;

they cause them to emerge from the various realms of existence; they cause them to leave behind defiled attachments; they cause them to abide in the mind of unsurpassed bodhicitta; they cause them to cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva;
they cause them to abide in all the *pāramitās*; they cause them to enter all the bodhisattva stages; and they cause them to contemplate all subtle and wondrous dharmas.
This gate causes one to know the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas. Such actions pervade the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
From his back, for those who are to be delivered by means of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), he brings forth countless hundreds of thousands of billions of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
For those attached to a self, he teaches that there is no self. For those who cling to permanence, he teaches that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.

For those whose temperament is dominated by greed, he teaches the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). For those whose temperament is dominated by hatred, he teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*).

For those whose temperament is dominated by delusion, he teaches the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*). For those with equal proportions of the afflictions, he teaches the dharmas of the sphere that correspond to wisdom. For those who delight in...
For those attached to sensory objects, he teaches the Dharma of non-existence.
For those who delight in dwelling in places of tranquility, he teaches the Dharma of making great vows to universally benefit all sentient beings. Such deeds pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
From his two shoulders emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of various yakṣas and rākṣasas, with diverse forms and various colors.

Their forms may be tall or short, all of them terrifying. They surround themselves with immeasurable retinues to protect all sentient beings who practice virtue, as well as the assemblies of noble ones and bodhisattvas, whether they are abiding in the right way or those who are already correctly established.
At times, they manifest as Vajrapāṇi deities to protect the Buddhas and their dwelling places, or they guard everywhere.
He protects all the worlds. To those who have fear, he grants peace and security; to those with illness, he brings recovery;
to those with suffering and affliction, he enables their liberation; to those with transgressions and evils, he causes them to feel weary of them and repent;
to those with calamities and misfortunes, he causes them to be extinguished. Thus benefiting all sentient beings, he causes them all to abandon birth and death.
He turned the wheel of the True Dharma. From his belly emerged countless hundreds of thousands of billions of kinnara kings, each surrounded before and behind by countless kinnara maidens.

Furthermore, there emerged countless hundreds of thousands of billions of gandharva kings, each surrounded before and behind by countless gandharva maidens, all playing countless hundreds of thousands of celestial instruments.
They joyfully sing praises of the true nature of all phenomena; they joyfully sing praises of all Buddhas; they joyfully sing praises of the arousal of the bodhicitta;
they joyfully sing praises of the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices; they joyfully sing praises of the gateway through which all Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment;
they joyfully sing praises of the gateway through which all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma; they joyfully sing praises...
He praised the gate of all Buddhas manifesting spiritual transformations; he revealed and expounded the gate of the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas;
he revealed and expounded the gate of protecting and upholding the teachings of all Buddhas;
he revealed and expounded the gate of causing all sentient beings to rejoice; he revealed and expounded the gate of adorning and purifying all Buddha-fields. He revealed...
He expounds and reveals all subtle Dharma-gates; he elucidates and proclaims the gate of relinquishing all obstacles;
he elucidates and proclaims the gate of generating all roots of goodness.

Thus pervading the dharma-realm of the ten directions, from his face there emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of universal monarchs (cakravartin), fully endowed with the seven treasures.
Surrounded by the fourfold army, he radiated the light of great renunciation and rained down immeasurable jewels, causing all who were destitute to be fully satisfied.

He caused them to forever sever the practice of taking what is not given. With hundreds of thousands of beautiful maidens, he bestowed them all as gifts with a mind free from attachment, causing them to forever sever the practice of sexual misconduct. He caused them to give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and never to take life.
They cause him to ultimately always speak truthful words, refraining from false, deceptive, or useless speech;
they cause him to employ unifying speech, never practicing divisiveness; they cause him to use gentle and soft speech, free from harshness or malice;

they cause him to constantly expound upon profound, definitive, and clear meanings, rather than engaging in meaningless, ornate rhetoric; and for the sake of teaching few desires, they cause him to eliminate craving and attachment.
Their minds are free from blemish and defilement. For them, he preaches great compassion so that they may eliminate anger and their minds attain purity.
For them, he preaches the true meaning so that they may contemplate all phenomena, deeply penetrate dependent origination, and clearly illuminate the principles of the truths.
He extracts the thorns of false views, shatters the mountains of doubt, and causes all obstacles to be utterly extinguished. Such deeds as these fill the entire Dharma-realm.

From his two eyes, he emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of suns, which universally illuminated all the great hells and evil realms, causing them all to be freed from suffering. Furthermore, they shone upon the intervals between all worlds, dispelling the darkness.
Furthermore, it illuminates all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, causing them all to abandon the cataracts of ignorance and delusion.
It emits pure light upon defiled lands; it emits golden light upon lands of white silver; it emits white silver light upon lands of gold;
it emits crystal-colored light upon lands of lapis lazuli; and it emits lapis lazuli-colored light upon lands of crystal.
In the Śaṅkha realm, light of the color of agate is emitted; in the agate realm, light of the color of śaṅkha is emitted.
In the Indranīla realm, light of the color of the Sūryagarbha-maṇi-rāja is emitted; in the Sūryagarbha-maṇi-rāja realm, light of the color of indranīla is emitted.
In the red pearl realm, light of the color of the Candrābhā-jāla-garbha-maṇi-rāja is emitted. [In the] moonlight...
The realm of the net-stored maṇi-kings emits light the color of red pearls;
realms formed of a single jewel emit light of various jewel colors; and realms formed of various jewels emit light of the color of a single jewel.
These lights illuminate the dense forest of the minds of all sentient beings, accomplish the immeasurable tasks of all sentient beings, and adorn all worldly environments.
Throughout the realms, they cause the minds of all sentient beings to attain cool serenity and give rise to great joy. Such deeds fill the entire Dharma-realm.
From the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows, there emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Śakras, all of whom have attained mastery over their spheres of activity.
Jeweled *maṇi* gems are bound upon their heads, their light illuminating all the celestial palaces.
O Lord, it shook all the kings of Mount Sumeru, awakening the great assemblies of all the devas.

It extolled the power of merit, expounded the power of wisdom, gave rise to the power of joy, sustained the power of resolve, purified the power of mindfulness, and strengthened the power of the bodhicitta they had generated.
It praised the joy of seeing the Buddha to eliminate worldly desires, and praised the joy of hearing the Dharma to bring about weariness with the world.
Regarding the objective realm: he praises the wisdom of contemplation to sever worldly defilements; he halts the battle of the asuras and cuts off the strife of afflictions;
he extinguishes the fear of death and resolves to subdue Māra; he establishes the Sumeru King of Mountains of the True Dharma;

and he accomplishes all the activities of sentient beings—thus his deeds pervade the entire Dharma-realm. From the crown of his forehead, there emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Brahmās.
O Deva! Your physical form is upright and majestic, peerless in the world; your deportment is tranquil and your voice is exquisite.
You exhort the Buddha to preach the Dharma and extol the Buddha’s merits, causing all Bodhisattvas to rejoice.

You are able to accomplish immeasurable deeds for sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions. From the crown of your head, you emit as many rays of light as there are atoms in immeasurable Buddha-fields.
The multitude of bodhisattvas was incalculable. All had their bodies adorned with the primary and secondary marks, emitting boundless light as they expounded various practices.
That is to say, they praised giving so as to cause the abandonment of stinginess and greed, thereby attaining various wonderful jewels to adorn the world;
they extolled the merit of upholding the precepts, causing all sentient beings to forever sever all evils and abide in the Great [Vehicle] of the Bodhisattvas.
The precept of compassion: it teaches that all existing phenomena are entirely like dreams; it teaches that all sensual pleasures lack any true flavor;
it causes all sentient beings to be freed from the bonds of affliction; it speaks of the power of patience, causing the mind to attain mastery over all dharmas;
it praises the golden body, causing sentient beings to leave behind the defilement of anger; and it inspires the practice of remedies to sever the path of the animal realm. It extols...
They practice with vigor, causing them to remain far removed from worldly negligence and to diligently cultivate all immeasurable, sublime dharmas.
Furthermore, they praise the dhyāna-pāramitā, causing their minds to attain mastery over all things.
Moreover, they expound the prajñā-pāramitā and reveal right view, so that all sentient beings may delight in sovereign wisdom and extract the poison of all views.

Furthermore, he expounds upon various worldly activities in accordance with the world, enabling all sentient beings to take birth at will within the various realms of existence even while remaining free from birth and death.

Moreover, he manifests supernatural powers and transformations to teach mastery over lifespan, causing all sentient beings to give rise to great vows. Furthermore, he expounds upon the accomplishment of the power of *dhāraṇī* to bring forth...
The power of great vows; the power of purifying samādhis; the power of sovereign rebirth.

Furthermore, for the purpose of expounding various forms of knowledge—namely, the knowledge that universally knows the faculties of all sentient beings, the knowledge that universally knows all mental activities, the knowledge that universally knows the ten directions of the Tathāgatas, and the knowledge that universally knows the sovereign powers of all Buddhas—he performs such deeds pervading the entire Dharma-realm. From...
From the crown of his head, there issued forth hundreds of thousands of billions of Tathāgata bodies. Their forms were peerless, adorned with the pure major and minor marks;
their majestic radiance blazed like a mountain of pure gold, and immeasurable light shone universally throughout the ten directions.
They emit sublime sounds that fill the Dharma-realm and manifest immeasurable great supernormal powers.

For all worlds, they universally rain down the rain of Dharma; that is to say, for the bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they rain down the Dharma-rain of universal knowledge and equality;
for the bodhisattvas at the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), they rain down the Dharma-rain of entering the universal gate; and for the Dharma-princes...
For bodhisattvas at the stage of the ranks, he rains down the Dharma rain of Universal Adornment; for bodhisattvas at the stage of the youth, he rains down the Dharma rain of the Solid Mountain;
for bodhisattvas at the stage of non-retrogression, he rains down the Dharma rain of the Ocean Treasury;
for bodhisattvas at the stage of accomplishing the right mind, he rains down the Dharma rain of Universal Realms; and for bodhisattvas at the stage of perfecting skillful means, he rains down...
The rain of the Dharma from the gate of intrinsic nature; for bodhisattvas in the stage of noble birth, it rains the Dharma that accords with the world;
for bodhisattvas in the stage of practice, it rains the Dharma of universal compassion; for newly initiated bodhisattvas, it rains the Dharma of the accumulation of treasuries;
for bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, it rains the Dharma of gathering sentient beings; for those of faith and understanding...
The Bodhisattvas rain down the Dharma-rain of the universally manifest realm of inexhaustibility. For the sentient beings of the form realm, they rain down the Dharma-rain of the universal gate.
For the Brahmā deities, they rain down the Dharma-rain of the universal treasury. For the Vaśavartin deities, they rain down the Dharma-rain that generates power.
For the hosts of Māras, they rain down the Dharma-rain of the banner of the mind. For the Nirmanarati deities, they rain down the Dharma-rain of pure mindfulness.
The Rain of Dharma: for the Tuṣita devas, he rains the Dharma-rain that gives rise to the intent for awakening; for the Yāma devas, he rains the Dharma-rain of joy;
for the Trāyastriṃśa devas, he rains the Dharma-rain that swiftly adorns the realm of space;
for the yakṣa kings, he rains the Dharma-rain of joy; for the gandharva kings, he rains the Dharma-rain of the vajra-wheel; for all...
The Asura Kings rain down the Dharma-rain of the Great Realm; for the Garuḍa Kings, they rain down the Dharma-rain of Boundless Radiance;
for the Kiṃnara Kings, they rain down the Dharma-rain of Supreme Wisdom of All Worlds;
for the Human Kings, they rain down the Dharma-rain of Non-Attachment to Pleasure; for the Nāga Kings, they rain down the Dharma-rain of the Banner of Joy. For...
The various mahoraga kings rain down the great dharma-rain of rest; for the sake of sentient beings in the hells, they rain down the dharma-rain adorned with right mindfulness;

for the sake of those in the animal realm, they rain down the dharma-rain of the treasury of wisdom; for the sake of sentient beings in the realm of King Yama, they rain down the dharma-rain of fearlessness;
and for the sake of sentient beings in places of calamity and distress, they rain down the dharma-rain of universal consolation.
He caused them all to enter the assembly of noble sages. Such deeds of his filled the entire Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, from every single pore of his body, the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja emitted nets of light, as numerous as the atoms within incalculable Buddha-fields.
Each net of light possessed incalculable colors and forms, and was adorned with incalculable ornaments.
The realm of the *saṃkhyeya* was filled with *asaṃkhyeya* activities throughout all the dharma-realms of the ten directions.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded attention, observed the bhikṣu Sāgaradatta and gave rise to profound yearning.
He recollected that samādhi-liberation, contemplated that inconceivable bodhisattva-samādhi, and reflected upon those inconceivable benefits.
The ocean of skillful means of sentient beings: contemplating that inconceivable gate of universal adornment through non-action;
contemplating that pure wisdom which adorns the dharma-realm; contemplating that wisdom which receives the empowerment of the Buddhas;
contemplating that birth of the sovereign power of Bodhisattvas; contemplating that firm power of the great vows of Bodhisattvas; contemplating that increase...
He expanded the power of the various practices of the bodhisattvas. Thus he remained standing, contemplating and observing for one day and one night, and even for seven days and seven nights;
for a fortnight, a month, and even six months; and further for six more days.
After this had passed, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha emerged from samādhi. Sudhana praised him, saying, "O Noble One, how rare!"
It is marvelous! This samādhi is most profound; this samādhi is most vast; the sphere of this samādhi is immeasurable;
the supernatural power of this samādhi is inconceivable; the radiance of this samādhi is peerless;
the adornments of this samādhi are innumerable; the majesty of this samādhi is irresistible. As...
The realm of this samādhi is impartial. This samādhi shines universally throughout the ten directions.
This samādhi brings infinite benefit, for it is able to extinguish the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings;
that is to say, it enables all sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of poverty, emerge from the hells, escape the animal realm, and close the gates to all states of adversity.
Because it opens the way to the realms of humans and devas; because it causes beings among humans and devas to experience joy and happiness;

because it causes them to cherish and delight in the sphere of dhyāna; because it can cause the increase of conditioned bliss; because it can manifest the bliss of transcending existence; because it can induce the arousal of the bodhicitta;
because it can cause the growth of the practices of merit and wisdom; and because it can cause the increase of the mind of great compassion.
Therefore, it is able to cause the arising of the power of great vows; it is able to cause the clear understanding of the bodhisattva path;

it is able to cause the adornment of ultimate wisdom; it is able to cause the entry into the realm of the Mahāyāna; it is able to cause the illumination and comprehension of the conduct of Samantabhadra;
it is able to cause the realization of the light of wisdom of all the bodhisattva stages; and it is able to cause the accomplishment of all enlightenment.
Because it fulfills all vows and practices, and because it enables one to dwell securely within the sphere of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), the noble one asked:
"What is the name of this samādhi? The bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja replied: "Good son, this samādhi is named 'The Universal Eye of Renunciation and Attainment.
It is also named 'The Pure Radiance of the Sphere of Prajñāpāramitā,' and it is also named 'Universal Adornment.'"

[He] entered the gate of pure adornment. "Good son, because I have practiced the *prajñāpāramitā*, I have attained this Samādhi of Universal Adornment and Purity, as well as one million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, is the ultimate limit of the realm of this samādhi only this much? Sāgaradhvaja said, "Good son, upon entering this..."
While in samādhi, they understand all worlds without obstruction; they travel to all worlds without obstruction;
they transcend all worlds without obstruction; they adorn all worlds without obstruction;
they cultivate and refine all worlds without obstruction; and they purify all worlds without obstruction.
Unobstructed in what is hindered; unobstructed in seeing all Buddhas; unobstructed in contemplating the vast majesty and power of all Buddhas;
unobstructed in knowing the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas; unobstructed in realizing the various great powers of all Buddhas;
unobstructed in entering the ocean of all the merits of all Buddhas; receiving...
They are unimpeded regarding the infinite, wondrous teachings of all Buddhas. They are unimpeded in practicing sublime conduct within the teachings of all Buddhas.
They are unimpeded in realizing the equal wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
They are unimpeded in entering the ocean-like assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas. They are unimpeded in contemplating the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions.
Unimpeded. Great compassion embraces the sentient beings of the ten directions without obstruction. Constantly giving rise to great kindness that fills the ten directions without obstruction.
Seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions with a mind of no weariness or satiety without obstruction.
Entering the ocean of all sentient beings without obstruction. Knowing the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings without obstruction. Knowing...
I possess unimpeded knowledge regarding the differences in the faculties of all sentient beings. Good son, I know only this Samādhi-Light of the Prajñāpāramitā.

As for those Bodhisattvas who enter the ocean of wisdom and the realm of the pure Dharma-dhātu, who reach all destinies and pervade immeasurable lands, who possess mastery over dhāraṇīs and the purity of samādhi, and who [exercise] supernatural powers—[how could I know their conduct?]
His vast eloquence is inexhaustible; he skillfully expounds the various stages as a refuge for sentient beings.

How could I possibly know his wondrous conduct, discern his merits, understand his practices, clarify his spheres of experience, investigate the power of his vows, enter his essential gateways, realize his attainments, explain his path-factors, abide in his samādhis, perceive his mental objects, or grasp his...?
"Son of good family, all this is the wisdom of equality. From here, traveling south, there is a dwelling place called Sāgaratīra.
There is a grove there named Samantavyūha, and within that grove dwells an upāsikā named Śreṣṭhadattā.
Go to her and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? At that time, Sudhana...
The youth, having received a firm body from the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, attained the wealth of the sublime Dharma and entered the profound realm.
His wisdom was clear and penetrating, his samādhi radiant, and he dwelt in pure understanding, perceiving the most profound Dharma. His mind abided securely in all gates of purity;
the light of his wisdom filled every direction, and his heart gave rise to immeasurable joy and exultation.

Prostrating with his five limbs to the ground, he paid homage at the Buddha's feet. He circumambulated him countless times, gazing upon him with reverence, reflecting and contemplating with sighs of admiration and longing.
He held fast to the name of the Buddha, visualized his deportment, recollected his voice, and contemplated his samādhi.
Having received the pure radiance of wisdom regarding that great vow and its sphere of practice, he took his leave and departed.
The sixth bhikṣu, Sāgaradhvaja, was entrusted with the stage of "Abiding in Rectitude. He first followed the elder’s instruction to observe and contemplate.
Following those who had attained realization, he traveled south by stages until he reached the shore of Jambudvīpa.
Searching everywhere for the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, he finally saw him sitting cross-legged in the samādhi on the side of a walking path.
Because the bhikṣu was in meditative absorption, he had not yet been able to question him; instead, he beheld the manifestations of karmic activity within that samādhi. From...

From the feet to the crown, fourteen locations manifest: humans, devas, the eight classes of beings, asuras, Śakra, Brahmā kings, and even śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, up to the Buddhas—all appear within a single body. The scripture consists of fourteen sections;
subsequently, from the Buddha appearing upon the crown of the head, a wondrous sound issues forth, universally raining down the rain of Dharma. Therein...
There are thirty-two kinds of Dharma-rain. The first twelve kinds of Dharma-rain are specifically for Bodhisattvas;
the latter twenty kinds of Dharma-rain are universally extended to humans, devas, and various classes of beings.

From the Brahma-heaven at the summit of the Form Realm down to the three miserable paths of hell, there are none who are not fully satisfied. Such deeds fill the entire Dharma-realm. Furthermore, within a single body...
From every pore, there issued forth nets of light rays as numerous as the atoms within incalculable Buddha-fields (*asaṃkhyeya-buddhakṣetra-paramāṇu-rajas*).
Each net of light rays was endowed with the adornments, realms, and activities of incalculable colors and forms. Thus they filled the entirety of the ten directions and all *dharmadhātus*.
Within his meditative concentration, the Bhikṣu manifested such signs and functions simultaneously. Having seen this, Sudhana...
With single-minded observation, he gave rise to deep yearning and longing. He recollected that samādhi and liberation, contemplating that inconceivable realm.
Abiding thus in contemplation and observation, he continued day and night without ceasing until the sixth day of the sixth month, never for a moment relinquishing his practice.
After this period had passed, the bhikṣu then arose from samādhi. Well done!
Dhana then paid homage and spoke words of praise: "O Noble One, how rare and extraordinary! Such a samādhi is profoundly deep, vast, and of such great benefit.
There are thirteen lines of sūtra for this praise. Having finished praising him, he then asked the Noble One, "What is the name of this samādhi?
The bhikṣu replied, "This samādhi is named 'The Universal Eye of Renunciation and Attainment,' and it is also called..."
The *Prajñāpāramitā-viṣaya-viśuddha-prabhā* (Pure Radiance of the Realm of Prajñāpāramitā), also known as the *Samantavyūha-viśuddha-mukha* (Gate of Universal Adornment and Purity).
By practicing *prajñāpāramitā*, one attains this samādhi. Within it are a million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis.
As for the samādhi named *Samanta-cakṣu-tyāga-lābha* (Universal Eye’s Relinquishing and Attaining), it refers to the perfect illumination of the *dharmadhātu* by means of *prajñā*-wisdom.
Therefore, it is named the "Universal Eye. The essence of Prajñā is pure and luminous; since not a single dharma is grasped, it is called "abandoning and attaining.

By means of this Prajñā, the equality of Buddhas and ordinary beings arises, such that the holy and the mundane share a single boundary. Thus, the phenomena and appearances of the entire Dharma-realm are perfectly manifested.
This precisely reveals the essence and function of the previously mentioned gate of the contemplation of Mind-only; it need not be restricted to [that specific context].

This refers to the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Once the youth Sudhana had heard the name of this samādhi, he asked how its ultimate sphere of experience (*gocara*) was.
This question concerns its actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The bhikṣu replied: "When one enters this samādhi, then [one perceives] these three worlds:
the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), the world of the vessel (*bhājanaloka*), and the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom (*jñānasambuddhaloka*)."
The world is of one and the same limit, equal and pervasive; each and every thing is interfused without any obstruction—such is the extent of it.
This is the direct pointing to the gate of contemplation on Mind-Only, the ultimate reality. Therefore, the Bhikṣu said to Sudhana:
"I know only this Samādhi of the Light of the Prajñāpāramitā; as for the Bodhisattvas..."
Entering the ocean of wisdom and purifying the realm of the *dharmadhātu*, up to the level of equalizing wisdom, is not within my knowledge.
He then directed Sudhana to a companion, saying: "From here, travel south to a dwelling place called Sāgaratīra.
There dwells a laywoman named Śrīprabhā; you should go there and ask her. At that time, the youth Sudhana [departed from] the monk Sāgaradhvaja...
Having attained various Dharma-gates such as the "Durable Body" (Sthira-kāya) through the place where the Buddha resided, he felt gratitude and longing.
He maintained the name of the Buddha, contemplated his deportment, recollected his voice, reflected upon his samādhi, received his wisdom, and attained pure radiance;
thus he achieved profound realization within these Dharma-gates. Then, he took his leave and departed.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Scroll Sixty-three;
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Scroll Sixty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery;
Extracted and Annotated by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Huishan Fayun Monastery.
Chapter Thirty-Nine: Entering the Dharma Realm, Part Five.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, empowered by the strength of his spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), relying upon the instructions of his spiritual friends, and reflecting upon the words of his spiritual friends, felt deep love and joy for them. He thought to himself:

"It is because of my spiritual friends that I have been able to see the Buddhas; it is because of my spiritual friends that I have been able to hear the Dharma. Spiritual friends are my teachers and guides."
Because of my various Buddha-dharmas, spiritual friends are my eyes, enabling me to see the Buddhas as being like space.
Spiritual friends are my ferry, enabling me to enter the lotus ponds of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Gradually traveling south, he arrived at the place where the ocean tide meets the shore and saw the Universally Adorned Garden, surrounded on all sides by walls made of various jewels.
It was surrounded by rows of all kinds of jewel trees, magnificently adorned. All the jewel-flower trees rained down various exquisite flowers, scattering them over the ground.
All the jewel-incense trees emitted fragrant vapors that universally perfumed the ten directions.
All the jewel-garland trees rained down great jewel garlands, hanging down everywhere. All the kingly *maṇi* jewel trees rained down great *maṇi* jewels.
Jewels are spread everywhere in abundance. Trees of all kinds of precious garments rain down robes of various colors, which are draped all around according to what is appropriate.
Trees of all musical instruments produce sounds when moved by the wind; these sounds are exquisite and surpass even the music of the devas.
All the trees of various ornaments each rained down rare and wondrous treasures, distributed everywhere as adornments.
The ground was pure and level, free from elevations or depressions.
Within it were one million palaces composed of great maṇi jewels, and one million towers and pavilions covered with Jāmbūnada gold. One million...
The palace was adorned with an interlacing array of Vairocana-maṇi jewels.

Ten thousand bathing pools were composed of various precious gems, surrounded on all sides by railings made of the seven treasures. Stairways of the seven treasures were distributed across the four directions.
The water of eight meritorious qualities was clear and overflowing; its fragrance was like celestial sandalwood, and golden sand was spread upon the bottom. The water was pure and radiant.
Jewels were interspersed throughout in every direction. Ducks, geese, peacocks, and *kīra* birds frolicked therein, producing harmonious and elegant sounds.
Rows of precious *tāla* trees stood encircling it, covered by jeweled nets from which golden bells hung; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they constantly produced beautiful music.
Great jeweled canopies were spread above, surrounded by precious trees, where countless *maṇi* jewels were erected.

The banner shines with light that universally illuminates hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*. Within it, there are further ten million ponds, their bottoms covered with layers of black sandalwood mud.
All manner of exquisite jewels form lotus flowers spread across the water's surface, while great *maṇi* flowers radiate brilliant light and color.
Within the garden, there is also a vast palace named Adorned Banner (*Vyūha-dhvaja*), a wondrous treasure from the ocean depths.
Its ground is made of jewels; its pillars are of lapis lazuli; it is covered above with Jambūnada gold;
it is adorned with light-treasury maṇi-jewels. Countless jewel-kings blaze with radiant flames, and the multi-storied pavilions and side-galleries are variously decorated.
The Aruṇa-fragrance king and the Awakening-fragrance king both emit wondrous scents that permeate everywhere.
In all of them, within the palaces, there were further immeasurable jewel lotus thrones arranged in rows all around.
These included the mani-jewel lotus thrones that illuminate the ten directions and the Vairocana-mani-jewel lotus thrones.
The mani-jewel lotus throne that illuminates the world; the mani-jewel lotus throne of the wondrous treasury;
the mani-jewel lotus throne of the lion treasury; the mani-jewel lotus throne of the stainless treasury;
the mani-jewel lotus throne of universal gates; the mani-jewel lotus throne of radiant adornment; and the pure mani-jewel lotus throne abiding in the great ocean treasury.
The Queen of Nis had a precious lotus throne; the Vajrasimha had a mani-jewel lotus throne. Within the garden there were furthermore ten million kinds of canopies, namely:

canopies of garments, canopies of garlands, canopies of incense, canopies of flowers, canopies of branches, canopies of mani-jewels, canopies of pure gold, canopies of ornaments, canopies of music, canopies of the miraculous transformations of the Elephant King, canopies of the miraculous transformations of the Horse King, and canopies of Indra.
He removed the mani-jewel canopies he had worn; there were millions of such as these.
A million great jewel nets covered them from above, namely: nets of jewel bells, nets of jewel parasols, nets of jewel bodies, and nets of sea-treasury pearls.

There were nets of sapphire-maṇi jewels, nets of lion-maṇi jewels, nets of moonlight-maṇi jewels, nets of various forms and fragrances, nets of jeweled crowns, and nets of jeweled necklaces; such as these numbered in the millions.
They were illuminated by ten million great radiances, namely the radiance of the flame-light maṇi jewels and the sun-treasury maṇi...
The light of the jewel *nirbhāsa*; the light of the moon-bannered *maṇi* jewel; the light of the incense-flame *maṇi* jewel;
the light of the supreme-treasury *maṇi* jewel; the light of the lotus-treasury *maṇi* jewel; and the light of the flame-bannered *maṇi* jewel.
The radiance of the great lamp maṇi-jewel; the radiance of the maṇi-jewels that universally illumine the ten directions;
the radiance of the fragrant-light maṇi-jewel—of such kinds as these, numbering in the millions, there constantly rains down millions of ornaments.
From millions of black sandalwood incense, wondrous sounds emerge; and millions of *mandārava* flowers, surpassing those of the devas, are scattered.
One million [ornaments] surpassing those of the devas served as necklaces for adornment;
one million surpassing those of the devas were exquisite jewel-garlands and sashes hanging down everywhere; one million surpassing those of the devas were exquisite robes of various colors;
one million multicolored mani-jewels emitted a wondrous light that shone everywhere; and one million sons of gods joyfully gazed upon it, bowing their heads in prostration.
A million handmaidens descended from the void, casting themselves down. A million bodhisattvas approached with reverence and constant delight to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the laywoman Śreṣṭhī sat upon a throne of pure gold, wearing a crown of ocean-treasury pearls, adorned with golden armlets surpassing those of the devas, her deep blue-black hair hanging down, and arrayed in a great net of maṇi jewels.
His head was adorned with lion-mouthed *maṇi* jewels as ear-ornaments, and he wore necklaces made of the sovereign *maṇi* jewel that grants all wishes.
A net of every kind of jewel hung down, covering his body. Hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of sentient beings bowed their heads in reverent respect.
From the east, immeasurable sentient beings came to his presence, namely the Brahmā gods and the Brahmakāyika gods.

The Great Brahmā Heaven, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven, the Īśvara Heaven, and so on, down to all humans and non-humans—in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—it is likewise everywhere. All who behold this upāsikā have all their suffering and illness completely eliminated;
they are freed from the defilements of affliction, uproot the thorns of false views, shatter the mountains of obstacles, and enter into the state of no-...
They remove obstacles to the pure realm; they increase and clarify all roots of goodness; they nourish the faculties;

they enter the gates of all wisdom, the gates of all dhāraṇīs, the gates of all samādhis, the gates of all great vows, the gates of all sublime practices, and the gates of all merits, such that these all appear before them. Their minds are vast and endowed with spiritual power.
Pervasive; his body was without obstruction, reaching all places. At that time, the youth Sudhana entered the Universal Adornment Garden and surveyed it thoroughly.
He saw the laywoman Śreṣṭhadattā seated upon a sublime throne.
He approached her, prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her countless times, and said: "Noble Lady, I have already set my mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I have awakened the mind of supreme enlightenment, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. Śūradatta replied: "Good son,..."
I have attained but a single door of liberation for bodhisattvas. If there are those who see, hear, or remember me, or those who dwell with me and provide for me, none of this shall be in vain.

Good son, if there are sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, who have not been embraced by virtuous friends, and who are not protected and remembered by the Buddhas, such persons will ultimately never—
"You shall behold me, son of good family. Any sentient beings who behold me shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, the Buddhas of the eastern direction constantly come here, take their seats upon jeweled thrones, and preach the Dharma for me.
[Likewise do] those of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—all [the Buddhas]."
The Buddhas all come here and, seated upon jeweled thrones, preach the Dharma for me.

Son of good family, I am never separated from seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and dwelling together with the bodhisattvas. Son of good family, this great assembly of mine consists of eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* beings;
they all reside in this garden, practicing in accordance with me, and are all [destined] for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, all other sentient beings who dwell in this grove shall likewise universally enter the stage of non-retrogression.
The seventh, the laywoman Śrīprabhā, dwells in the stage of Non-retrogression.

Because Sudhana has received the power of the spiritual friend, his mind does not retreat from the Dharma-gates he enters; he realizes them through mindfulness and pursues them according to the instructions.
Arriving at the place by the ocean tide, he seeks the laywoman but does not yet see her; first, however, he beholds the park that adorns her dwelling and its surrounding environment.
This sublime realm is adorned with ten features: first, it is encircled by jeweled walls; second, rows of forest trees;
third, lofty and magnificent halls and pavilions; fourth, bathing pools of clear and fragrant water; fifth, ponds and streams reflecting one another; sixth, gardens laid out with palace seats;
seventh, draped with canopies and nets; eighth, illuminated by radiant light; ninth, showered with various ornaments; and tenth, inhabited by both ordinary beings and sages.
With joy and reverence, he next beheld her primary body (the *sambhogakāya*), which was upright, majestic, and exquisitely beautiful.
She was surrounded by a gathering of ten directions of *nayuta* numbers of devas and humans; all who saw her attained benefit, for her karmic activity was unfathomable.
At that time, having entered, Sudhana saw the laywoman (*upāsikā*) seated upon a wondrous throne. Sudhana approached her and prostrated himself at her feet.
He circumambulated her countless times. Having completed his acts of reverence, he inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
Once he had made this request and resolved his mind, he asked her to explain the practice of the bodhisattva path. Upon seeing Sudhana, the upāsikā offered no further words of praise;
she immediately revealed the dharma-realm, saying directly: "I have attained but a single door of liberation of a bodhisattva. If anyone sees me and recollects..."

All those who associate with me and provide for my needs do so without their efforts being in vain. Therefore, if sentient beings lack profound and deep roots of goodness, they will certainly not be able to see me.
If there are those who do manage to see me, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression on the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Although I have not yet praised Sudhana previously, this very fact of his being able to see me serves as proof of that.
Thus, Sudhana may be said to have deeply planted roots of goodness. Merely by seeing me, he need not further inquire as to the nature of the Dharma-gate;
he has already ascended to the stage of non-retrogression.
The reason for such great benefit upon seeing me is that the Buddhas of the ten directions come at all times to preach the Dharma for me, and because I am never separated from them.
The Buddha-dharma dwells together with all the bodhisattvas, because I am never separated from the Three Jewels.
Therefore, within this garden, eighty-four thousand nayutas of sentient beings have all universally entered the stage of non-retrogression.
This demonstrates that by attaining the light of the *prajñā-samādhi* as described above, one manifests skillful means for entering the mundane world. Thus:
The eighty-four thousand afflictions all become gates to the *pāramitās*. This has already been a direct revelation by Sudhana of the gate to the *dharmadhātu*.
The above comprises sixty-seven lines of scripture, which directly recount the matters of the dharma-gates.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, how long has it been since you first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

He replied, "Good son, I remember that in the past, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), paid respectful homage and made offerings, and heard and upheld the Dharma.
Prior to that, at the place of Vimalacandra Buddha, I left the household life to study the Way and upheld [the teachings]."
The True Dharma. Prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Subhaketu; prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Jayasumeru;
prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Padmaguṇakośa; prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Vairocana; prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Samantacakṣus;
prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Brahmāyuṣ; prior to that, at the place of the Buddha Vajranābhi; prior to that...

"At the abode of the Buddha Vairocana, O son of good family, I recall that in the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas and immeasurable births, I served, honored, and made offerings to thirty-six Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in successive order.
There I heard the Dharma, received and upheld it, and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring. Beyond this, it is known by the wisdom of the Buddhas, not by my own."
"Measuring one, son of good family: the initial resolve of a bodhisattva is immeasurable, for it fills the entire dharma-realm;
the gate of a bodhisattva’s great compassion is immeasurable, for it universally enters all worlds;

the gate of a bodhisattva’s great vows is immeasurable, for they reach the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm in the ten directions; the gate of a bodhisattva’s great kindness is immeasurable, for it universally covers all..."
Because it concerns all sentient beings; because the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, as they are practiced throughout all lands and throughout all eons;
because the power of Bodhisattva samādhi is immeasurable, causing them never to retreat from the Bodhisattva path;
because the power of Bodhisattva dhāraṇī is immeasurable, enabling them to sustain all worlds; because the power of the light of Bodhisattva wisdom is immeasurable...
The power of their measure is immeasurable, for they are able to universally realize and enter the three periods of time;

the power of the bodhisattvas' supernormal knowledges is immeasurable, for they universally manifest throughout all networks of lands; the power of the bodhisattvas' eloquence is immeasurable, for with a single sound they are understood by all;
the purity of the bodhisattvas' bodies is immeasurable, for they pervade all buddha-fields.
Below this, Sudhana perceives such great benefit from the laywoman (upāsikā) and thus asks whether it has been long or short since he first resolved his mind on Bodhi.
Consequently, the laywoman answers that from the time she practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) under the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
tracing back further still, she has successively served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers.
Under each and every Buddha, he diligently cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
As for the Buddhas he served in the past beyond this point, they are no longer within my comprehension; only the wisdom of a Buddha can know them.

Thus, by declaring that his resolve to serve the Buddhas over such a vast eon has remained undeterred until now, he has fully revealed the dharma-gate of non-retrogression for Sudhana. Therefore, the teaching states:
Sudhana said: "The initial aspiration of a Bodhisattva should be immeasurable and equal to the Dharma-realm;

thus, every practice cultivated is equal to the Dharma-realm. Being without beginning in the past and without end in the future, that which is generated is nothing other than the eternally abiding true mind of the Dharma-realm.
Above this, there are seventeen lines of scripture that fully reveal [this point].
The cause of the mind is profound.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, how long will it take before one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
He replied, "Son of good family, a bodhisattva does not set forth for the sake of teaching and taming even a single sentient being."
The mind does not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and taming even a hundred sentient beings;
nor does it resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and taming even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of times more sentient beings.

It does not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of teaching the sentient beings of a single world-system; nor does it resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of teaching even unspeakably... [many world-systems].
One does not generate the bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and transforming the sentient beings of unspeakably many worlds.
One does not generate the bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms of Jambudvīpa.

One does not generate the bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms of a trichiliocosm. And so on, until one does not [generate it] for the sake of teaching and transforming...
They resolve upon the mind of enlightenment not for the sake of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable multiples of trichiliocosms;

they do not resolve upon the mind of enlightenment for the sake of making offerings to a single Tathāgata, nor even for the sake of making offerings to unspeakably unspeakable multiples of Tathāgatas. They do not [resolve upon it] for the sake of...
They resolve upon the mind of enlightenment in order to serve the successive Tathāgatas appearing in a single world-system;
even unto not doing so merely for the sake of serving the successive Tathāgatas appearing in worlds as numerous as the unspeakably unspeakable number of revolutions of worlds;
nor for the sake of serving the Tathāgatas in worlds as numerous as the atoms within a single trichiliocosm.
They resolve upon the mind of enlightenment for the sake of the Tathāgatas who appear in succession throughout the realms;

even to the point of not resolving upon the mind of enlightenment merely for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgatas who appear in succession throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
They do not resolve upon the mind of enlightenment for the sake of adorning and purifying a single world. Nor...
They resolve upon bodhicitta not for the sake of purifying unspeakably unspeakable multiples of worlds,
nor do they resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of purifying as many worlds as there are atoms in a single trichiliocosm.
Nor do they generate the bodhicitta for the sake of adorning and purifying worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable multiples of trichiliocosms.
Nor do they generate the bodhicitta for the sake of maintaining the legacy of a single Tathāgata.
Nor, even, do they generate the bodhicitta for the sake of maintaining the legacies of unspeakably unspeakable multiples of Tathāgatas.
Therefore, they resolve upon bodhicitta. They do not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of upholding the bequeathed Dharma of a Tathāgata in a single world-system;
nor even for the sake of upholding the bequeathed Dharma of a Tathāgata in worlds as numerous as the unspeakably unspeakable number of revolutions;
nor for the sake of upholding [the bequeathed Dharma of a Tathāgata] in worlds as numerous as the atoms within a single Jambudvīpa.
They resolve their minds on enlightenment for the sake of preserving the legacy of the Dharma;

even to the extent that they do not resolve their minds on enlightenment merely for the sake of maintaining the legacy of the Dharma of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Thus, in brief, it is not for the sake of fulfilling the vows of a single Buddha, nor for the sake of going to a single Buddha-land, nor for the sake of entering a single...
It is not for the sake of the assembly of a Buddha; it is not for the sake of upholding the single Buddha-eye of Dharma; it is not for the sake of turning the single wheel of Dharma of a Buddha;
it is not for the sake of knowing the succession of kalpas within a single world-system; it is not for the sake of knowing the ocean of the minds of a single sentient being;
it is not for the sake of knowing the ocean of the faculties of a single sentient being; it is not for the sake of knowing the ocean of the karma of a single sentient being; it is not...
It is for the sake of knowing the ocean of the conduct of a single sentient being; it is not for the sake of knowing the ocean of the afflictions of a single sentient being;

it is not for the sake of knowing the ocean of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of a single sentient being; and so on, up to not for the sake of knowing the oceans of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable multiples of Buddha-fields that one awakens the mind of enlightenment. It is because one desires to transform and guide them.

They resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to tame all sentient beings without exception; they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to serve and make offerings to all Buddhas without exception;
they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields without exception;
and they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to protect and uphold the true teaching of all Buddhas without exception.
Therefore, they resolve upon the bodhicitta, because they wish to fulfill the vows of all Tathāgatas without exception;
they resolve upon the bodhicitta, because they wish to travel to all Buddha-fields without exception;
they resolve upon the bodhicitta, because they wish to enter all assemblies of Buddhas without exception; they resolve upon the bodhicitta, because they wish to know all worlds.
They resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to know, without exception, the sequence of all intermediate kalpas;

they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to know, without exception, the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings; they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to know, without exception, the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings;
they resolve upon the bodhicitta because they wish to know, without exception, the ocean of the karma of all sentient beings.
Mind. One generates the bodhicitta because one wishes to know the ocean of the conduct of all sentient beings without exception.
One generates the bodhicitta because one wishes to extinguish the ocean of all afflictions of all sentient beings without exception.
One generates the bodhicitta because one wishes to uproot the ocean of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions of all sentient beings without exception. Good son, to speak of it in brief:
It is by means of such hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* skillful practices that a bodhisattva gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Good son, because a bodhisattva practices so as to universally enter and realize all dharmas, and universally enters and purifies all lands;
therefore, good son, my vow shall only end when the purification of all worlds is complete. [I shall] uproot...
"When the afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings are exhausted, my vow will be fulfilled.
Below this, Sudhana, already knowing that the causal mind is immeasurable, asks about the duration—whether long or short—of attaining the fruit in the future.
The junior upāsikā replied: "The resolve of a bodhisattva is beyond measure.
From the very beginning, they do not generate the mind of enlightenment merely for the sake of subduing sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm."

Nor do they resolve their minds on enlightenment merely for the sake of making offerings to that many Buddhas, purifying that many Buddha-fields, or upholding the bequeathed Dharma of that many Buddhas;

rather, they resolve their minds on enlightenment even for the sake of knowing the afflictions and habitual tendencies of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable multiples of Buddha-fields. This [section] above is an inverse illustration of the mind.

There are no limits. The subsequent formal explanation states: "One simply desires that until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, until the offerings to the Buddhas are exhausted, until the upholding of the Dharma is exhausted, and even until the ocean of sentient beings' afflictions and habitual tendencies is exhausted, one shall resolve upon Bodhicitta.
To summarize: "My vow shall only end when I have completely adorned and purified all worlds and have extracted [all sentient beings from suffering]."
"When the habitual tendencies of afflictions are exhausted, my vow shall be fulfilled. By thus generating the mind of enlightenment, how could there be any thought of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood?
This has already fully demonstrated Sudhana’s inexhaustible and non-regressive practice that accords with the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, what other dharmas are there? Above this, there are forty-eight lines of scripture.

Sudhana said, "Noble One, what is the name of this liberation? He replied, "Good son, this liberation is named 'The Banner of Peaceful Security Free from Sorrow. Good son, I know only this single door of liberation. As...
The minds of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like the ocean, for they are able to contain and receive all Buddha-dharmas.
Like Mount Sumeru, their resolve is firm and unshakable. Like the *sudarśana* medicine, they can eliminate the grave illnesses of afflictions in sentient beings.
Like the bright and pure sun, they can shatter the dark obstructions of ignorance in sentient beings. Just as the great earth can provide support...
The locus upon which all sentient beings rely is like a fine wind that can accomplish the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings;
like a bright lamp that can produce the light of wisdom for sentient beings; like a great cloud that can rain down the dharma of nirvana for sentient beings;
like a pure moon that can radiate the light of merit for sentient beings; and like Śakra, who is able to [fulfill all needs].
They protect all sentient beings. How then could I know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Son of good family, to the south of here, at the edge of the ocean tide, there is a land named Nalasū.
Therein dwells a seer named Vimalacitra. Go to him and ask: how should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazed up at him with earnest devotion, weeping tears of sorrow as he reflected:
"To attain Bodhi is difficult; to approach a spiritual friend is difficult; to encounter a spiritual friend is difficult;
to obtain the faculties of a bodhisattva is difficult; to purify the faculties of a bodhisattva is difficult; and to meet a spiritual friend who is a fellow practitioner is difficult."

It is difficult to investigate according to the principle; it is difficult to practice in reliance upon the teaching; it is difficult to encounter the skillful means that give rise to a virtuous mind;
and it is difficult to encounter the light of the Dharma that increases all-knowledge. Having formed this thought, he took his leave and departed.
Having already received these superior Dharma-gates, this youth Sudhana asked, "What is the name of this liberation-gate?
He replied, "This liberation is named 'The Banner of Peaceful Security Free from Sorrow.

As for being 'free from sorrow,' it is because one possesses such a vast, immeasurable, and non-retrogressive mind; how then could one worry that sentient beings are difficult to deliver? For [it is not so]..."
One seeks the fruit of Buddhahood; why then worry that the path to Buddhahood is difficult to accomplish?
Because one does not abandon the realm of sentient beings, why worry that the suffering of birth and death can cause disturbance? What, then, is there that is not secure?
Simply by means of this mind that neither loathes nor seeks, one perceives no nirvana above and perceives no birth and death below. Therefore—
Since both [types of] views have been utterly crushed and exhausted, it is named after a banner. Thus, the conclusion states:
"I know only this single gate of liberation. As for the Bodhisattvas, their minds are like the ocean, able to contain all Buddha-dharmas;
their resolve is as firm as Mount Sumeru, unshakable, and so forth—all such qualities are beyond my reach.
"It is possible. Therefore, I shall direct you to a later friend. In the country of Nalasa, there is the seer Vimalacandra who will be able to explain it to you.
At that time, having heard this superior instruction on the Dharma-gate of non-retrogression, Sudhana’s sense of reverence increased even further.
He reflected upon the difficulty of attaining Bodhi, the difficulty of approaching spiritual friends, and the difficulty of encountering spiritual friends.
It is difficult to attain the faculties of a bodhisattva; it is difficult to purify the faculties of a bodhisattva; it is difficult to encounter virtuous friends who practice together;
it is difficult to engage in investigation according to reality; it is difficult to practice in accordance with the teachings; it is difficult to give rise to the skillful means of a virtuous mind;
and it is difficult to increase the radiance of omniscience. Because these ten kinds of thoughts regarding what is difficult to encounter exist, one should thus advance with diligent seeking.
Having formed this thought, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, reflecting in accordance with the true teaching of the Bodhisattvas and reflecting in accordance with the pure conduct of the Bodhisattvas,
gave rise to a mind that increases the power of a Bodhisattva’s merit, a mind that clearly perceives all Buddhas, and a mind that gives rise to...

It gives birth to the mind that produces all Buddhas; it gives birth to the mind that increases all great vows; it gives birth to the mind that universally perceives all phenomena throughout the ten directions;
it gives birth to the mind that clearly illuminates the true nature of all phenomena; it gives birth to the mind that universally disperses all obstacles;

it gives birth to the mind that observes the dharma-realm without darkness; it gives birth to the mind adorned with the jewel of pure intention; it gives birth to the mind that subdues and overcomes all [adversaries].
With a demonic mind, he gradually traveled until he reached the kingdom of Nalasura.
He searched everywhere for Vimalakṣa and saw a great forest adorned with incalculable trees: namely, various leafy trees spreading their branches in profusion;
various flowering trees in full, brilliant bloom; various fruit trees ripening in succession; and various precious...
Trees rain down mani-fruit; great sandalwood trees stand in rows everywhere; various aloeswood trees constantly emit exquisite fragrances;
delightful fragrance-trees are adorned with wondrous scents; pāṭala trees surround it on all four sides; nyagrodha trees tower high;
jambūnada trees constantly rain down sweet fruit; and there are utpala and padma lotuses.
The flowers adorned the ponds and pools. At that time, the youth Sudhana saw the seer sitting on a layer of grass beneath a sandalwood tree, surrounded by ten thousand disciples.
Some wore deer skins, some wore tree bark, and others had woven grass for clothing;
their topknots and earrings hung down, framing their faces from front and back. Having seen this, Sudhana went to where he was. Five.
Prostrating himself on the ground, he spoke these words: "I have now encountered a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
A spiritual friend is the gateway leading toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), for they enable me to enter the path of reality.
