A spiritual friend is the vehicle leading toward all-knowledge, for they enable me to reach the stage of a Tathāgata. A spiritual friend is..."
A spiritual friend is a ship for proceeding toward omniscience, for it enables me to reach the island of the jewels of wisdom.
A spiritual friend is a torch for proceeding toward omniscience, for it enables me to give birth to the light of the ten powers.
A spiritual friend is a path for proceeding toward omniscience, for it enables me to enter the city of nirvāṇa. A spiritual friend is...
A spiritual friend is a lamp leading toward omniscience, for they enable me to see the even and uneven paths.
A spiritual friend is a bridge leading toward omniscience, for they enable me to cross over dangerous and evil places.
A spiritual friend is a parasol leading toward omniscience, for they enable me to give rise to the coolness of great compassion. A spiritual friend is...
"This is because it leads toward the eye of omniscience, enabling me to perceive the gateway to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is one who leads toward the tide of omniscience, enabling me to fulfill the waters of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Having spoken these words, he rose from the ground, circumambulated [the teacher] countless times, and standing before him with palms joined, said: "Noble One, I have already previously resolved upon [enlightenment]..."
"...the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet he does not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices or how he should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
Then Vimalakṣa looked toward his assembly and said: "Good son, this youth has already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Good son, this youth universally bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
this youth universally grants benefit to all sentient beings; this youth constantly contemplates the ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas;
this youth desires to drink the nectar of the rain of Dharma from all [sources]; this youth desires...
He fathoms the vast ocean of all dharmas. This youth desires to cause sentient beings to dwell within the ocean of wisdom.
This youth desires to universally give rise to the vast clouds of compassion. This youth desires to universally rain down the vast rain of Dharma.
"This youth wishes to universally illuminate the world with the moon of wisdom. This youth wishes to extinguish the poisonous heat of the afflictions of the world.
This youth wishes to cause all roots of goodness in sentient beings to grow.
When the assembly of sages heard these words, each scattered various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers upon Sudhana, prostrated themselves in worship, and circumambulated him with reverence.
With reverence, they spoke these words: "This youth shall surely protect and deliver all sentient beings;
he shall surely extinguish the sufferings of the various hells; he shall surely sever forever the paths of the animal realm; he shall surely cause the realm of King Yama to be overturned;
he shall surely close the gates to all places of peril; he shall surely dry up the ocean of craving and desire; he shall surely cause the multitude..."

They shall give rise to the eternal extinction of the aggregate of suffering. They shall surely and eternally shatter the darkness of ignorance. They shall surely and eternally sever the fetters of craving and attachment.
They shall surely encircle the world with the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains of merit. They shall surely manifest the world with the Great Jewel Mount Sumeru of wisdom.
They shall surely cause the sun of pure knowledge to appear. They shall surely reveal the dharmas of the roots of goodness.
[The Buddha] concealed [the path]. He ensured that those in the world would clearly recognize the treacherous and the easy. At that time, Vimuṣṭi addressed the assembly of sages, saying:
"O sons of noble family, if there are those who can resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will surely accomplish the path to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This son of noble family has already resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He shall..."
[He] purifies the ground of all Buddhas’ merits. Then, Vimalacakra addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:

"Noble son, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation called 'The Banner of Invincibility' (*anabhibhūta-dhvaja*. Sudhana asked: "Noble One, what is the sphere of this liberation, the Banner of Invincibility?
Thereupon, the Rishi Vimalacakra extended his right hand, stroked Sudhana’s head, and took hold of him.

Sudhana. At that moment, Sudhana saw his own body go to worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields in the ten directions, arriving at the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, and beholding those buddha-fields and their assemblies.

he thoroughly mastered every word and phrase, upholding each one distinctly without any confusion.
He also knows how that Buddha purified all his vows through various modes of understanding; he also knows how that Buddha accomplished all the powers through pure vows;
he also sees the physical forms manifested by that Buddha according to the minds of sentient beings;
he also sees the various colors of that Buddha’s great net of light, which are pure and perfect; and he also knows that Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom.
By the power of great radiance, they further see themselves at the abodes of various Buddhas for the duration of one day and night,

At that moment, the rishi released Sudhana’s hand, and Sudhana the youth immediately saw his own body returned to its original place.
Then the rishi said to Sudhana, "Noble son, do you remember? Sudhana replied, "Yes; this is it."
"Noble one, this is the power of a spiritual friend. The ṛṣi said, "Son of good family, I know only this bodhisattva liberation called 'Incomparable Banner.

As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished all supreme samādhis and attained mastery at all times, who in a single thought-moment give birth to the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas—by means of that Buddha..."
Adorned with the lamp of wisdom, they illuminate the world universally. In a single thought-moment, they enter the realms of the three periods of time.

They manifest diverse forms, traveling everywhere to the lands of the ten directions. Their bodies of wisdom pervade all dharma-realms, appearing before sentient beings in accordance with their minds.
Observing their faculties and conduct, they bring them benefit. They radiate pure light that is most lovely and delightful. And I—
How can one know and speak of his meritorious conduct, his sublime vows, his adornment of the buddha-field,

the distinctions of his physical marks, the purity of his voice, and the radiance of his wisdom? Son of good family, in this southern direction there is...

"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana, filled with joy and exultation, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with deep reverence, and taking his leave, traveled south.
The eighth, the Rishi Vimala, dwells in the stage of Youthful Purity (*kumārabhūmi*).
Sudhana, following and reflecting upon the instructions of his previous spiritual friends, increased his various kinds of non-retrogressive resolve.
Gradually proceeding to the country of Nalasa, he sought out the Rishi Vimalakusuma. There he saw a great forest, adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) trees. Sudhana—
He saw that seer sitting upon grass spread beneath a sandalwood tree, surrounded before and behind by ten thousand groups of seers.
Upon seeing him, Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and paid homage with praise.
He praised the true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in twelve ways, likening them to a vehicle, a ship, a torch, a bridge, and so forth. This is why [it is said]:

This praise was offered because of the aforementioned difficulty of encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Having finished praising him, he prostrated and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
At that time, the seer Gopaka looked upon his assembly of disciples and praised Sudhana for possessing eleven kinds of merit.
Upon hearing this, the various seers each made offerings and likewise praised Sudhana for possessing thirteen kinds [of merit].
He will obtain great benefit. At the end, the ṛṣi praised Sudhana in general, saying, "You shall purify all the merits of the Buddhas.
Seeing clearly that he was a vessel for the Dharma, he then said, "I have attained the bodhisattva liberation called 'Incomparable Banner' (Anabhibhū-dhvaja).
Sudhana asked, "What is the sphere of this 'Incomparable Banner' liberation? Such was the reason for his inquiry.
Because the questioner desired direct realization, Vimalanetra Rishi then took Sudhana by the hand; at that very moment,
Sudhana saw his own body traveling to as many worlds in the ten directions as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields, seeing the physical marks and signs of those Buddhas and their assemblies,
and how they taught various dharmas according to the minds of sentient beings, with every single phrase and every single syllable.

He attained thorough penetration, even unto various realms of experience. Furthermore, he saw his own body at the presence of those Buddhas, having already passed through as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields during this single moment of grasping hands; yet, in that very instant, his body had already pervaded the ten directions.

To have approached many Buddhas, traversed many dharma-gates, and passed through numerous kalpas—this is precisely the unimpeded harmony of the vast and the narrow, where extension and brevity are simultaneous, and kalpas and moments are perfectly interfused.
This is the Great Gate of Liberation of the Perfectly Interfused and Unimpeded Dharmadhātu.
That one is able to be thus is entirely due to the indestructible banner of liberation-wisdom of the Rishi Vimala.
By the power of that radiance, Sudhana also suddenly realized various samādhis of light; this was due to the power of sudden realization in a single thought-moment.
Thus, when the seer released Sudhana’s hand, Sudhana immediately saw his own body back in its original place.
The seer asked, "Do you remember? This did not require any verbal explanation, but...
They merely grasped hands. Thus, one can clearly see the empowerment of the power of the Dharma. Therefore, Sudhana said, "This is the power of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
His intention was that this was specifically a dharma-gate of dreams and illusions, not his own actual realization. Below, he humbles himself and defers to the superior;

Because [the knowledge] of samādhi is vast, he briefly cited twenty kinds of things he did not know, pointing out that the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa in the village of Īśāna would explain them for him. With joy, Sudhana took his leave and traveled south.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, illuminated by the Bodhisattva liberation of the Invincible Banner, dwelt within the inconceivable spiritual powers of all Buddhas;

he realized the inconceivable wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s liberations and supernormal knowledges, attained the light of wisdom of the inconceivable Bodhisattva samādhis, and attained the light of wisdom of the samādhis cultivated at all times. He attained...
They possess the light of wisdom of the samādhi that knows all objective realms abide solely in conceptualization. They attain the light of wisdom that is supreme among all worlds.
They manifest their bodies in all places. With ultimate wisdom, they preach the dharma of non-duality, non-conceptualization, and equality.
With clear and pure wisdom, they universally illumine all objective realms. Whatever teachings they hear, they are able to...
They endure with patience and possess pure faith and understanding. They have definitive clarity regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).

Adorned with all boundless great vows already purified, they know the net of boundless worlds through inexhaustible wisdom;

The subtle realm of infinite worlds; knowing the various names of infinite worlds; knowing the various expressions of infinite worlds;

Jñānaprabha traveled by stages until he reached the village of Īśāna, where he saw the ascetic Ugra practicing various austerities in his quest for omniscience.
On all four sides were masses of fire like great mountains, and in their midst stood a mountain of blades, towering and boundless in height.

"Noble One, you are well-able to instruct and guide; I pray that you will speak for me.

Is this not the work of Māra or one sent by Māra? Is this not a member of Māra’s treacherous and evil faction falsely manifesting as a Bodhisattva who possesses skillful knowledge?
They perceive the characteristics of consciousness and seek to create obstacles for me regarding my roots of goodness and my lifespan;

When he was thinking this, ten thousand Brahmā gods spoke these words from the midst of the sky: "O son of good family, do not do this."
Do not have such a thought; do not entertain this notion. This noble one has attained the radiance of the Vajrajvālā-samādhi.
He has aroused great vigor to deliver all sentient beings with a mind that never regresses.
He desires to drain the ocean of all craving, to sever the net of all false views, to burn the fuel of all afflictions, to illuminate the dense forest of all delusions, and to cut them off...
To overcome all fear of old age and death; to destroy all obstacles of the three periods of time; and to radiate the light of all dharmas.
Good son, many of my Brahmā-devas are deeply attached to false views; they all consider themselves to be autonomous and creators, thinking, "In this world, I am the most supreme.
Seeing a Brahmin performing the austerity of the five fires, they [regard themselves]... regarding themselves—
Finding no pleasure in the palaces and finding no flavor in the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), they all came together to the place where the brahmin was.
At that time, the brahmin, by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), manifested great ascetic practices and preached the Dharma for them,
enabling us to extinguish all views, eliminate all pride, abide in great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), practice great compassion (*karuṇā*), and give rise to vast [resolve].
With a great resolve, he gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). He constantly beheld all Buddhas and perpetually heard the sublime Dharma;

They attained non-retrogression from *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, ten thousand kings of the *Īśvara* devas scattered celestial flowers in the void and spoke these words:

"O Mañjuśrī, cause me not to give rise to attachment therein. Immediately, together with my retinue, I went to his place.

This Brahmin preached the Dharma for me, causing me to attain mastery over my mind, mastery over the afflictions, mastery over rebirth, mastery over all karmic obstructions, and mastery over all the three [realms]...
They attained mastery over obscurity; they attained mastery over ornaments; they attained mastery over the span of life;

When this brahmin was performing the austerity of being scorched by the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated my palace, its various ornaments, and all the court ladies.
It caused us to no longer experience sensual pleasure and to cease seeking it; our bodies and minds became supple and gentle.
Thereupon, we went together with the assembly to where he was. At that time, the brahmin preached the Dharma for me, which was able to cause me—
Their minds attain purity; their minds become bright and clean; their minds become purely wholesome; their minds become supple; their minds give rise to joy.

The Dharma they hear being taught enables us to become free from craving for sense objects, to have few desires and be content, to give rise to joy in the heart and a mind of fulfillment,

there were ten thousand gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, along with their retinues of devaputras and devakanyās, preceding and following [them].

The Dharma is impermanent and subject to decay; it causes me to renounce all sensual pleasures, causes me to sever arrogance and heedlessness, and causes me to love and delight in unsurpassed bodhi.

He remained unmoving. Furthermore, ten thousand nāga kings—namely, the nāga king Elāpattra, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, and others—rained black sandalwood from the midst of the sky.

When this brahmin performed the austerity of being scorched by the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated all the palaces of the nāgas.

It caused the hosts of nāgas to be freed from the fear of hot sand and the fear of the garuḍas; it extinguished their malice, so that their bodies attained coolness and their minds became free from defilement.

Obstacles... up until the arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abiding in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

At that time, I and my retinue all gave rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings. All the rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others likewise gave rise to a compassionate mind.

Neither I nor they conceived any attachment to our own palaces; we immediately went together to visit [the Buddha].
At that time, the Brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us as was appropriate, and we all attained peace and happiness of body and mind.
Furthermore, he caused immeasurable yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta.
Additionally, ten thousand gandharva kings spoke these words from the midst of the sky: "O noble sons..."

"Son, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated our palaces, causing us all to experience inconceivable and immeasurable bliss. For this reason, we came to his presence.

They attained non-retrogression. Furthermore, ten thousand asura kings emerged from the great ocean and, standing in the air with their right knees touching the ground, joined their palms in prostration before him and spoke these words:
"O son of good family, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, all our asuras' palaces, the great ocean, and the great earth shook violently."
"May we cause ourselves to abandon arrogance and heedlessness; for this reason, we have come to his presence.
Having heard the Dharma from him, we shall abandon flattery and deception, abide securely on the stage of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi) immovably, and fulfill the ten powers.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand garuḍa kings, with the king Valavanta as their leader, who transformed themselves into the forms of non-Buddhist youths.
In the midst of the void, they proclaimed these words: "O noble son, when this brahmin scorched himself with the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated my palace;
everything shook and we were all struck with terror. For this reason, we came to his presence.
Then the brahmin preached the Dharma to us according to our needs, causing us to practice the Great [Vehicle]."
They praised Great Compassion, which delivers beings from the ocean of birth and death and rescues them from the mire of desire;
they extolled the bodhicitta that gives rise to the wisdom of skillful means, taming sentient beings according to what is appropriate for each.
Furthermore, ten thousand kinnara kings proclaimed these words in the sky: "O noble son, this brahmin is performing the ascetic practice of being scorched by the five fires."
At that time, from the many *tāla* trees, jeweled bell-nets, and precious silk streamers within the palaces where we dwell,
as well as from the musical trees, the exquisite jewel-trees, and the various musical instruments, there spontaneously issued forth the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma,
the sound of the assembly of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and the sound of those aspiring for unsurpassed bodhi, saying: "In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land..."

There is a certain bodhisattva who has resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, there is a certain bodhisattva practicing austerities, able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, up to and including the purification of all-knowledge conduct (*sarvajñatā-caryā*). In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, there is a certain bodhisattva proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Up to and including: in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, a certain Tathāgata, having performed the work of a Buddha, enters *parinirvāṇa*.
Nirvāṇa. Good son, suppose there were a person who reduced all the grasses and trees of Jambudvīpa into fine dust;

the limit of the number of those dust motes could be known. We came to know its limits. Good son, having heard the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, we were filled with great joy and went to that place. At that time, the brahmin preached the Dharma to us according to our needs.
"May I and immeasurable other sentient beings attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The light shines upon all hells, such as Avīci, causing all sufferings therein to cease entirely.

Out of gratitude, we have come to this place, gazing with reverence and never tiring of our adoration. At that time, the Bhagavān...
The Brahmin preached the Dharma for me, causing immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, hearing such a teaching, was filled with great joy;

he conceived a heart of true spiritual friendship (*kalyāṇamitra*) toward the Brahmin, prostrated himself with his head at his feet, and uttered these words: "I have given rise to [faith] toward the Great Sage, the Spiritual Friend..."
With a virtuous mind, he said: "I only pray that the Noble One will grant me forgiveness for my transgression. Then the brahmin spoke these verses to Sudhana:
"If there are bodhisattvas who follow the instructions of spiritual friends, they shall have no doubt or fear whatsoever."
"One who dwells with a mind unmoving—know that such a person will surely obtain vast benefit;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, they shall achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, the youth Sudhana immediately ascended the mountain of blades and threw himself into the mass of fire; before he had even reached the middle, he attained [realization].
The Bodhisattva dwells well in samādhi; as soon as he touches the flames, he further attains the Bodhisattva samādhi of the supernatural power of tranquil bliss.
Sudhana said, "How marvelous, O Noble One! When my body touches such a mountain of blades and this great mass of fire, it is peaceful and joyful.
Then the Brahmin said to Sudhana, "Good son, I have only attained this much."
The Bodhisattva’s liberation of the inexhaustible wheel is like the great blaze of merit of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
which is able to incinerate all the afflictions of views among sentient beings until none remain, ensuring they never regress. With a mind that is inexhaustible,
free from indolence, and free from cowardice, they give rise to a mind like the Vajra-treasury and Nārāyaṇa, swiftly cultivating all practices.
With a mind of steadfastness, may all your great vows of diligence be universally sustained like the wind-circle, never to regress.
How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? Son of good family, to the south there is a city named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā.
Within it dwells a maiden named Maitrāyaṇī. Go to her and ask how a bodhisattva...
"How does one study the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, took his leave, and departed.
Below this, the ninth section concerns the Brahmin Jvalanāgra residing with the prince.
Because Sudhana was illuminated by the light of the "Invincible" liberation (*anabhibhūta-vimokṣa*), he suddenly realized the inconceivable spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
thus, he attained the wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation, supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and various samādhis. He sought...
The omniscient one never regresses. This continues until the passage describing the perception of the diverse thoughts of infinite sentient beings;
there are thirteen lines and a half of scripture, all of which describe the benefits of entering the dharma-gate through realization.
Following the teachings to seek it out, he gradually arrives at the village of Īśāna and sees the brahmin Jyotipāla performing various ascetic practices, with masses of fire on all four sides.

Having seen this, Sudhana paid his respects and inquired about the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, saying, "I pray that you will explain them to me.

The brahmin said, "If you can now ascend this mountain of swords and cast yourself into the mass of fire, all the bodhisattva practices will become completely pure. [The mountain of swords and the fire...]

This is the "Cluster," which is the Dharma-gate of the Matured Brahman. Therefore, he uses the Dharma-realm realized by himself to instruct Sudhana, thereby demonstrating the Dharma and exhorting him to practice.
The commentary states: "The mountain of knives cannot be grasped; the mass of fire cannot be taken. Thus, Prajñā is like a great mass of fire;
one cannot enter it from any of the four directions. Yet, one can also enter from all four directions. If one grasps it or takes hold of it...
If one clings to them, the four perversions are formed; if one neither clings nor grasps, they become the four gates of liberation.

Furthermore, he suspected that it was Māra creating obstacles to his path, and thus he reflected upon the thirteen difficulties, which led him to harbor further doubts.
Terrified, he did not dare to enter. While he was in this state of doubt and difficulty, the Brahmās of the ten directions exhorted him;
furthermore, the Māra kings and all the deities of the six heavens of desire—thirteen classes in total—united their voices to exhort Sudhana together.
He caused him to believe with certainty and not doubt, urging him to enter truly according to the teaching. Thereupon, Sudhana was filled with great joy;

At that moment, Sudhana dared to ascend the mountain of blades and cast himself into the mass of fire; before he had even reached the middle, while still in mid-air—

He then exclaimed, "How extraordinary! Though such a mountain of knives and mass of fire, when my body touches it, I experience peace and joy.

Having gathered [the accumulations] and personally realized the bliss of liberation that is tranquility, one realizes that the Dharma-gates previously encountered through spiritual mentors were merely attained by relying on the power of others and were not one's own actual realization.

therefore, entering this gate of liberation constitutes the stage of the Dharma Prince.

By training in the methods of writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals (*mudrā*), one immediately attains entry into the dharma-gate of the wisdom of all arts and supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Regarding this precept, the statement that one studies writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals is explained in the commentary as being because wisdom can protect the precepts;

since one receives instructions on what to abstain from and what to practice from Mañjuśrī, it is called "studying writing," which serves to examine and restrain the three karmas and the four grave offenses.

Because there are ten grave offenses, three thousand modes of dignified conduct, and eighty thousand subtle practices; those who study calculation weigh and measure each cause that can induce its corresponding fruit.
As for "seals" (*mudrā*), it refers to the certainty with which the transgression or observance of precepts—whether good or evil—induces its fruit.

Although the intent encompasses the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), they are all explained here in relation to the precepts. Subsequently, the youth himself declares the Dharma-gate he has realized, by means of this calculation.
The single vidyā encompasses all five vidyās; therefore, by citing matters such as medical prescriptions, it establishes ultimate purity.
Furthermore, it extensively sets forth the numerical figures of that which calculates and that which is calculated, consisting of twenty-one lines of sūtra.

Indeed! Her mind dwells in discipline; her mind is free from craving and seeking. Those who hear her voice leap with joy, and those who behold her form are entirely freed from defiled attachment.

Within a small vessel, according to the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings, it produces all kinds of delicious food and drink,
filling them all completely. Even if there be a hundred sentient beings, a thousand sentient beings, a hundred thousand sentient beings, a billion sentient beings, ten billion sentient beings,
a hundred billion sentient beings, a hundred thousand billion nayuta sentient beings, or even up to an unspeakable number of sentient beings— [it fills them all].

One may speak of sentient beings. Suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; as many sentient beings as there are atoms in one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*);
sentient beings in a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, and a great trichiliocosm;
even up to as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; or suppose there were all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
According to their desires and inclinations, he causes them all to be fully satisfied; yet that food and drink is neither exhausted nor diminished.

Such food and drink, as well as various superior flavors, various seats, various garments, various bedding, various vehicles, various flowers, various garlands, various incenses, and various ointments—[all these are provided].
Various kinds of incense, various kinds of powdered incense, various kinds of precious jewels, various kinds of necklaces, various kinds of banners, various kinds of flags, various kinds of parasols,
and various kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of daily life— all these were made fully available according to their wishes and inclinations.
Furthermore, son of good family, suppose that in a single world-system in the eastern direction, all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having eaten my food,
were to realize the fruits of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha and abide in their final bodies. As it is in one world-system, so it is in a hundred world-systems,
a thousand world-systems, a hundred-thousand world-systems, a billion world-systems, ten billion world-systems, and a hundred billion world-systems.
Worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions; worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas; worlds as numerous as the atoms in Jambudvīpa;
worlds as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent world system; worlds as numerous as the atoms in a small thousandfold world system;
worlds as numerous as the atoms in a medium thousandfold world system; and worlds as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm. Thus...

Throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have partaken of my food have all realized the fruits of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha stages and abide in their final bodies.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. Furthermore, O son of good family, in the east...
Throughout a single world-system, and even throughout as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
all those bodhisattvas bound by only one more birth who have eaten my food shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment and,
having subdued the armies of Māra, attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment. As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, [and north].
It is likewise in the north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. "Good son, have you seen these ten thousand maidens who are my retinue?

He replied, "I have seen them. The upāsikā said, "Good son, with these ten thousand maidens as their leaders, there is a retinue of one million asaṃkhyeya [beings], all of whom practice together with me."

They share the same aspiration; they share the same roots of goodness; they share the same path of renunciation; they share the same pure understanding; they share the same pure mindfulness; they share the same pure destination;
they share the same immeasurable awakening; they share the same attainment of the faculties; they share the same vast mind; they share the same sphere of activity;

they share the same principle; they share the same meaning; they share the same clear comprehension of the Dharma; they share the same pure physical form; they share the same immeasurable power; they share the same supreme diligence; and they share the same True Dharma.
Their voices are identical to the sounds that accord with all species; identical to the foremost pure sound; identical in praising immeasurable pure merits;
identical in pure karma; identical in pure retribution; identical in great kindness that universally protects and delivers all;

identical in great compassion that universally brings sentient beings to maturity; and identical in pure physical action that arises in accordance with conditions, causing all who see it to rejoice. Identical...
Purifying their verbal karma, they proclaim the transformation of the Dharma through worldly speech;
they go together to the assemblies and places of enlightenment of all Buddhas; they go together to all Buddha-fields to make offerings to all Buddhas;
they are able together to manifest and behold all Dharma-gates; and they dwell together on the stages of pure bodhisattva conduct. Good son, these ten thousand maidens are able to...
This vessel takes up the food and drink from above and, in a single kṣaṇa, reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions.

It makes offerings to all the bodhisattvas in their final births, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas, extending even to all those in the realm of hungry ghosts, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Good son, these ten thousand women, by means of this vessel of mine, can provide sufficient celestial food among the devas, and likewise for humans.
"It is sufficient for the food of all people. Good son, wait but a moment and you shall see for yourself.
As she spoke these words, Sudhana saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates; they were all those invited by the original vows of the laywoman.
Once they had assembled, she prepared seats for them to sit upon. She provided them with whatever food and drink they required, ensuring that everyone was fully satisfied.
Then she addressed Sudhana, saying: "Noble son, I know only this liberation-door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, all their virtues are like the great ocean—profound and inexhaustible. Like...
Vast and boundless as space, like a wish-fulfilling jewel that fulfills the vows of sentient beings; like a great settlement where all that is sought is obtained;
like Mount Sumeru where all manner of treasures are gathered; like a profound treasury constantly storing the wealth of the Dharma;
like a bright lamp that destroys all darkness; like a lofty parasol that universally shades all living beings—how could I possibly know [this]?
"He can explain those meritorious practices. Son of good family, to the south there is a city named Mahodaya.
There dwells a householder named Prajñākūṭa. Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva practice? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?
" Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazed upon him without weariness before taking his leave.
And she departed.
This section below is the third, concerning the upāsikā Guṇavatī, who is entrusted with the practice of non-opposition. This refers to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Patience accords with the nature of things; thus it is called "non-opposition. The city is named Sāgaravatī because it is situated near the sea. She dwells securely therein.

Regarding patience (*kṣānti*): it is like the ocean because it contains all things; she is named "Endowed" (*Samantaguptā*) because within her single vessel there is nothing that is not complete, for patience universally accommodates all virtues. Because patience is gentle and supple, she is represented by a woman.
Having heard the instructions of his previous friend, Sudhana reflected and contemplated that the teachings of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) bring manifold benefits. Thus...
Having extolled these ten kinds of great benefits, he gradually traveled south until he reached the city of Samudrapratisthāna.
There he sought out this upāsikā, and the people told him, "This upāsikā resides within her home in this very city.
Upon hearing this, Sudhana went immediately to her gate and saw that her residence was vast and adorned with many jewels; having entered, Sudhana...
He saw the upāsikā, in the prime of her youth and of exquisite beauty, whose majestic virtue and radiant light were such that none could equal them except for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Within her residence, he saw ten billion seats spread out as if someone were waiting there; yet everything else was entirely empty and devoid of anything.
Only before those seats was placed a single small vessel, and she was surrounded by ten thousand young maidens.
Sudhana paid his respects, offered salutations, and inquired: "How does one cultivate the path of a bodhisattva? He replied:

"I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door called 'the inexhaustible treasury of merit. Within this single small vessel, I can produce all kinds of delicious food and drink, filling them completely.
Even if hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings were to arrive..."
Throughout a thousand great trichiliocosms, and even unto as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields,
they are all fully satisfied according to their desires, yet without diminishing; just as with food and drink, so too with various garments,
bedding, exquisite ornaments, and articles of livelihood— whatever they delight in, all are made to be filled.
This correctly demonstrates that the Dharma-realm is an inexhaustible treasury, all of which is produced based upon the practice of a single patience (*kṣānti*).
However, because the practice of patience is the most foundational, it is symbolized by a small vessel; yet, because it encompasses everything without exception, it yields inexhaustibly.
This means that it not only fulfills the desires and joys of sentient beings, but even within worlds as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions...

"Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and even bodhisattvas bound to one more birth—whoever eats the food from my vessel—all sit at the site of enlightenment and realize the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi; this is the ultimate fulfillment of the great function of the practice of patience.
The upāsikā spoke again: "Good son, the food from my vessel not only provides external benefit,"

In the ten directions, there are ten thousand young maidens who practice together with me in my own home, headed by the foremost among them, and even including a retinue of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* followers;
when they eat this food, they reach throughout the ten directions in a single kṣaṇa.
She performed great buddha-work, even to the point that those in the hells and the hungry ghost realms were all brought to full satisfaction. "Good son, wait but a moment;

you shall see it for yourself. Then Sudhana saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates, and she caused them all to be fully satisfied according to their needs. Having performed this deed, the upāsikā said to Sudhana: "I..."
"I know only this liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

As for the ocean of merits of the bodhisattvas—its profound depth and inexhaustibility, and their various sublime practices—these are not within my knowledge. Thus, he humbled himself and deferred to the excellence of the next friend, pointing out to him:
"To the south there is a city named Mahābhiṣa; there dwells a householder named Prajñāmati. You should go to him."
He went to inquire after her; Sudhana prostrated himself and withdrew.

At that time, having attained the light of liberation known as the Treasury of Inexhaustible Adornments of Merit, the youth Sudhana contemplated that ocean of merit, observed that space of merit, and proceeded toward that mass of merit. He ascended it...
Mounting the mountain of merit, he gathered that treasury of merit, entered that abyss of merit, roamed that pool of merit,
purified that wheel of merit, beheld that storehouse of merit, entered that gate of merit, traversed that path of merit, and cultivated those seeds of merit. Proceeding by these stages,
he arrived at the city of Mahāvyūha (Great Prosperity) and searched everywhere for the wise householder.
The mind of the spiritual friend gives rise to yearning; his mind is perfumed by the spiritual friend; his resolve toward the spiritual friend is firm and steadfast;
through skillful means he seeks to see all spiritual friends with a mind that never regresses; he vows to serve all spiritual friends with a mind free from weariness;
and he knows that it is by relying upon spiritual friends that one can fulfill all virtues. He knows...
By relying upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one is able to generate manifold merits. One knows that by relying upon spiritual friends, one is able to increase manifold practices.
One knows that by relying upon spiritual friends, one is able to personally serve all virtuous friends without being taught by others.
When reflecting in this way, one causes one's roots of goodness to grow, purifies one's profound mind, and increases one's spiritual faculties.
He increased the root of his virtue, augmented his great vows, expanded his great compassion, drew near to all-knowledge, and perfected the path of Samantabhadra.
He illuminated the true Dharma of all Buddhas and increased the radiance of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
At that time, Sudhana saw the householder within the city, at the crossroads of the marketplace, upon a terrace of the seven precious gems, seated amidst countless jewels.
It was a magnificently adorned seat, exquisite and pure, with a body made of mani-jewels and legs of diamond-blue sapphire.
It was entwined with jeweled cords and embellished with five hundred wonderful gems; celestial jewel-cloths were spread upon it.
They erected celestial banners and streamers, spread great jeweled nets, and hung great jeweled canopies.
A cover made of Jāmbūnada gold was fashioned with a shaft of Vaiḍūrya beryl, which people were made to hold so as to shield it from above.

The pure and immaculate plumage of the king of geese served as its fans. They burned various exquisite incenses and rained down various celestial flowers, while music was constantly played on both sides.

There were five hundred musical instruments, whose sounds were more exquisite and beautiful than those of the celestial musicians. Among sentient beings, there was none who did not feel joy upon hearing them.
Ten thousand attendants surrounded him from before and behind; his physical appearance was upright and majestic, pleasing for all to behold.
Adorned with celestial ornaments, he was peerless and most excellent among gods and humans. He had already fully accomplished the aspirations and vows of a bodhisattva.
All these householders shared the same roots of goodness from the past as he; they stood in attendance before him, gazing upon him and receiving his instructions.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying:
"Noble One, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from all sufferings and difficulties, for the sake of causing all..."
For the sake of the ultimate peace and happiness of all sentient beings; to cause all sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
to cause all sentient beings to abide upon the island of the Dharma-treasure; and to cause all sentient beings to dry up the river of craving.
In order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to great compassion; in order to cause all sentient beings to abandon and leave behind desire and attachment;
in order to cause all sentient beings to thirst for and long for the Buddha’s wisdom; in order to cause all sentient beings to emerge from the wilderness of birth and death;
in order to cause all sentient beings to delight in the merits of all Buddhas; in order to cause one—
In order to cause all sentient beings to exit the city of the three realms, and to cause all sentient beings to enter the city of omniscience,
he has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet, he does not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path, so as to be able to serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings, O Householder.

He addressed him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—son of good family, such a person who resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is difficult to find.
If one can resolve their mind thus, that person will be able to seek the bodhisattva practices and will constantly encounter spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)."
They are never satiated; they draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) without ever becoming weary; they serve spiritual friends without ever growing indolent;
they attend upon spiritual friends without giving rise to sorrow or distress; they seek out spiritual friends without ever turning back;
they cherish spiritual friends without ever abandoning them; they attend to spiritual friends without even a moment’s rest; they gaze up at spiritual friends...
Consciousness never rests; he has never been indolent in following the instructions of spiritual friends, and his mind has never erred in receiving the teachings of spiritual friends.
"Good son, do you see this assembly of people before me? Sudhana replied, "Yes, I see them.
The householder said, "Good son, I have already caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
The bodhicitta gives birth to the family of the Tathāgatas and increases the white dharmas (*śukladharma*). It abides in the immeasurable *pāramitās* and trains in the ten powers of the Buddha.
It leaves behind the worldly lineage and dwells in the lineage of the Tathāgatas; it abandons the wheel of saṃsāra and turns the wheel of the true Dharma.
It extinguishes the three evil destinies and dwells in the path of the true Dharma. Like all Bodhisattvas, it is fully capable of protecting and rescuing all sentient beings. Well...
"Good man, I have attained the liberation door called 'the treasury of merit produced at will.
Whatever is required, all such wishes are fulfilled—namely, clothing and ornaments; elephants, horses, and carriages; flowers, incense, banners, and canopies; food, drink, and medicinal elixirs."

Dwellings and houses, couches and seats, lamps and torches, male and female servants, oxen and sheep, as well as all various attendants—may all such articles of livelihood and whatever else is required be fully provided. Furthermore, for their sake, he shall preach the true and wondrous Dharma.
"Good son, wait but a moment and you shall see for yourself. As these words were spoken,
immeasurable sentient beings from various locations, various worlds, various lands, and various cities—
each with distinct physical forms and differing desires— all gathered together in an infinite number by virtue of the Bodhisattva’s past vows.
Each person made their requests according to their own desires. At that time, the householder, as the entire assembly had gathered, focused his mind for a moment and looked up into the void;
everything they required descended from the sky, and the entire multitude was fully satisfied.

Thereafter, he further expounded various teachings for them. That is to say, for those who seek to obtain and be satisfied with fine food, he taught various practices for accumulating merit, practices for departing from poverty, and practices for knowing all dharmas.

He taught the practice of attaining the food of dharma-joy and the bliss of dhyāna, the practice of cultivating and perfecting the primary and secondary marks, and the practice of increasing and accomplishing that which is difficult to subdue. He was well able to...
To those who have fully realized the practice of the unsurpassed food and have accomplished the practice of subduing demonic adversaries through inexhaustible great majestic power;
for those who desire to obtain excellent drink and be fully satisfied, he preaches the Dharma to them, causing them to abandon attachment to birth and death and enter the flavor of the Buddha-dharma.
For those who desire to obtain various kinds of supreme flavors, he preaches the Dharma to them, causing them all to attain the [flavors] of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata’s mark of supreme flavor is such that for those who seek fulfillment through vehicles, he proclaims various Dharma gates so that they may all board the Mahāyāna vehicle;

for those who seek fulfillment through clothing, he preaches the Dharma so that they may obtain the raiment of pure shame and dread, up to and including the Tathāgata’s own pure and wondrous physical form. Thus it is.
There was nothing that was not provided for them. Thereafter, he preached the Dharma to them all according to their needs. Having heard the Dharma, they returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, after the householder had manifested for the youth Sudhana the inconceivable realm of liberation of a bodhisattva, he said:
"Good son, I know only this treasury of merit that arises according to one's wishes."
This is the gate of liberation. Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the "Jewel Hand," which completely covers all lands throughout the ten directions and,
by the power of their mastery, universally rains down all requisites for life— namely, various kinds of colored jewels,
various kinds of colored necklaces, various kinds of colored crowns, various kinds of colored garments, and various kinds of sounds.
There were various colors of flowers, various colors of incense, various colors of powdered incense, various colors of burning incense, various colors of jeweled canopies,
and various colors of banners and streamers, filling all the dwellings of sentient beings as well as the assembly grounds and *bodhimaṇḍas* of all Tathāgatas.
Some were for the purpose of maturing all sentient beings, while others were for the purpose of making offerings to all the Buddhas.
"Buddha, how could I possibly know or describe those various merits and sovereign spiritual powers?
Good son, to the south of here there is a great city named Siṃhala. Therein dwells an elder named Dharmaratnaśikhin."
"You should go and ask the Bodhisattva how one studies the conduct of a Bodhisattva and cultivates the path of a Bodhisattva.
At that time, the youth Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with reverence and respect, he paid homage as a disciple would and thought to himself:
"It is because this householder has taken me under his care that I have been able to see the path to omniscience, and my love and remembrance for spiritual friends shall never cease."
Having seen [the spiritual friend], he did not allow his mind of reverence for the spiritual friend to be impaired.

He was always able to comply with the instructions of the spiritual friend, possessed resolute and deep faith in the words of the spiritual friend, and constantly gave rise to a profound heart of service toward the spiritual friend.
He prostrated at the spiritual friend’s feet, circumambulated them countless times, gazed upon them with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

Below this is the fourth section concerning the wise householder [Megha], who relies on unyielding conduct. Regarding the stage of progress, "unyielding" means that his diligence is free from indolence or retreat.
Sudhana, following the instructions, proceeds to seek him; relying on his previous cultivation and purification, he gradually advances in his quest.

The city is named Mahāsaṃbhava because it arises from great diligence (*mahāvīrya*). The friend is named Prajñākūṭa because progress toward the goal must necessarily be guided by the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

Sudhana saw that merchant within the city, at the crossroads of the marketplace, seated upon a throne of the seven precious gems, adorned with various jewels, and surrounded by ten thousand attendants. Having seen him, Sudhana paid his respects.
He inquired, saying: "Noble One, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have fully described the characteristics of generating the resolve [for awakening].
Now I ask about the practice of the bodhisattva path. The elder replied: "Excellent, excellent!
You have extensively praised the supreme power of generating the resolve. He then asked: "Do you see this assembly of mine? All of these are those whom I have transformed."

Regarding the retinue who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment]: having already been born into the family of the Tathāgata, he first demonstrates this before teaching the Dharma-gate, because he perceives that those to be converted are not in vain. Thereafter, he correctly reveals the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), declaring:
"O sons of good family, I have attained the liberation-door called 'The Treasury of Merit Produced According to One’s Wishes. Whatever is required, all such wishes are fulfilled. And so forth.
"Wait a moment; you shall see for yourself. As these words were spoken, immeasurable sentient beings arrived from various directions, each with their own needs.
At that time, the householder looked up into the sky, and whatever they required descended from the air.
The entire assembly was fully satisfied. First he bestowed material gifts, and thereafter...

They preach the Dharma for them and provide the gift of Dharma, such that there is nothing that does not satisfy their joy in the Dharma and their delight in meditation. Each returns to their original place.

This is because it is thought that wealth and the Dharma are stored within space and are bestowed according to one's wishes; therefore, it is called the "Treasury of Merit that Produces Whatever is Desired.
However, regarding the two gifts of wealth and Dharma mentioned here in the context of progressive practice, these two gifts are [performed] with a mind that is... [without attachment].
To be free from weariness is great diligence; that is to say, the meaning of *dāna* (generosity) subsumes all six perfections.

The phrase "contained within emptiness" intends to reveal that [these perfections] are born from the wondrous emptiness of *prajñā* (wisdom). At that time, the householder [Vasu] was for the youth Sudhana...
Manifesting an inconceivable realm, he addressed Sudhana, saying: "I know only this liberation door of the treasury of merit that arises according to one's wishes.
As for the various and supreme virtues of the bodhisattvas, they are beyond my knowledge.
You should therefore go to the elder Ratnacūḍa in the city of Siṃhapura and inquire of him."
Sudhana was filled with joy and, moved by his earnest devotion, prostrated at his feet and took his leave to depart.
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-five;
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
commentary on the meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dabaoji Huayan Monastery;
edited and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fayun Monastery on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty.
Entering the Dharma Realm, Chapter Thirty-nine,
Part Seven. At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard this liberation from the householder Sumati, traveled through that ocean of merit,
cultivated that field of merit, gazed upon that mountain of merit, proceeded toward that ford of merit, and opened that [gate] of merit.
O Guṇagañja, contemplating those dharmas of merit, purifying that wheel of merit, savoring that mass of merit,
generating that power of merit, and increasing that momentum of merit, he proceeded by stages toward the city of Siṃhapura. He searched everywhere for the elder Ratnaśikhin and,
seeing this elder in the marketplace, he immediately approached him, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him.

Having circumambulated him countless times, he stood with palms joined and said: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva cultivates the bodhisattva path.
It would be well, Noble One, if you would explain to me the path of all bodhisattvas; by means of this path, I shall proceed toward [enlightenment]."
"O Sarvajña! At that time, the elder took Sudhana by the hand and led him to his residence, showing him the house and saying these words: 'Noble son, look now at my home.
Then Sudhana beheld that residence, pure and radiant, constructed of genuine gold, with walls of white silver, a palace of crystal, and towers made of deep-blue lapis lazuli."
The pavilion has pillars made of exquisite *śaṅkhaśilā* gems, adorned throughout with hundreds of thousands of varieties of jewels.
A lion throne is fashioned from red *maṇi* pearls, with a canopy of *maṇi* and a net of pearls draped above it.
A pool of *musāragalva* gems is filled with fragrant water, and immeasurable jewel trees stand in rows all around. This residence is vast and expansive, consisting of eight stories.
Having entered through the gate, Sudhana observed them in succession. He saw that on the lowest level, various foods and drinks were being given;
on the second level, various precious garments; on the third level, all manner of precious ornaments;
on the fourth level, various court ladies as well as all kinds of exquisite and rare jewels; and on the fifth level... up to five [levels].
Bodhisattvas from the various stages gathered like clouds, expounding all dharmas to benefit the world.
They had accomplished all *dhāraṇī* gates, all seals of samādhi, and the practices of samādhi, as well as the light of wisdom.

Upon seeing the sixth tier, they beheld bodhisattvas who had all already perfected profound wisdom; they clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated the nature of all dharmas, having achieved vast [realization].
The Great Dhāraṇī Samādhi, the Gate of Non-obstruction, whose practice is unimpeded and does not dwell in dualistic dharmas,
gathered together within the unspeakably wondrously adorned site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to analyze and reveal the gates of the Prajñāpāramitā.
These include, for example, the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Quiescent Treasury and the gate of the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all sentient beings.
The gate of the perfections: the gate of the perfection of wisdom that is immovable; the gate of the perfection of wisdom that is the radiance of detachment;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom that is the treasury of the unconquerable; the gate of the perfection of wisdom that illuminates the wheel of sentient beings;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom that is the ocean-treasury; the gate of the perfection of wisdom that is the universal eye’s relinquishment and attainment.
The gate of the *pāramitās*. The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* that enters the inexhaustible treasury.
The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* that is the ocean of all skillful means. The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* that enters the ocean of all worlds.
The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of unimpeded eloquence. The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* that accords with sentient beings. The gate of unimpeded light.
The gate of Prajñāpāramitā that illuminates [reality]; the gate of Prajñāpāramitā that constantly contemplates past conditions and spreads the clouds of Dharma;

he expounded such gates of Prajñāpāramitā numbering one million asaṃkhyeyas. He saw on the seventh level various bodhisattvas who had attained the patience like an echo (*pratiśrutkā-samādhi*), and through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), they discerned and observed [all phenomena] to achieve liberation.

They are all able to hear and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas. Upon seeing the eighth tier, they behold immeasurable bodhisattvas gathered therein, all of whom have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and are free from regression.
They are able to use a single voice to pervade the lands of the ten directions;

their bodies appear universally in all places of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), reaching everywhere throughout the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). They enter universally into the realms of the Buddhas and perceive universally the bodies of the Buddhas.
He acted as the foremost among all the assemblies of Buddhas, expounding the Dharma.
He saw the bodhisattvas bound to one more birth gathered in the ninth tier;

he saw the tenth tier filled with all Tathāgatas, who, from their initial resolve, had cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, transcended birth and death, and brought their great vows to fulfillment.
As well as his supernormal powers; he purified buddha-fields, assemblies at sites of enlightenment, and turned the wheel of the true Dharma to subdue sentient beings.
All such things he caused [the youth] to see clearly. At that time, having seen these matters, Sudhana said: "O Noble One!"
"For what reason has this pure assembly been brought about? What roots of goodness were planted to obtain such a reward?
The elder replied, "Good son, I recall that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there was a world named Perfectly Adorned.
The Buddha’s name was King of Universal Adornment of the Dharma Realm with Boundless Light, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The ten titles [of the Buddha] were perfected. When that Buddha entered the city, I played musical instruments and burned a single pellet of incense as an offering.
I dedicated this merit toward three goals: namely, to be forever free from all poverty and suffering; to always behold the Buddhas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
and to constantly hear the True Dharma. It is because of this that I have obtained this retribution. Son of good family, I know only this.
This is the liberation door of the immeasurable treasure-store of merit of this bodhisattva. Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the inconceivable treasure-store of merit,
enter the ocean of the non-conceptual body of the Tathāgata, receive the non-conceptual, unsurpassed cloud of Dharma,
cultivate the non-conceptual implements of merit, and give rise to the non-conceptual net of Samantabhadra’s practices, so too does he enter.
The realm of non-conceptual samādhi; the roots of goodness of Bodhisattvas who are equal to the non-conceptual;
abiding where Tathāgatas abide in non-conceptuality; realizing the non-conceptual equality of the three periods of time; abiding in the realm of the Universal Eye in non-conceptuality;
and abiding through all kalpas without weariness or fatigue—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good [son].
"Good man, to the south of here there is a land called Veṇuvana. In that land there is a city named Samantamukha, and within it dwells an elder named Samantanetra.
Go to him and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and with deep reverence..."
He gazed up at him with diligence, took his leave, and departed.

This concludes the fifth section concerning the Elder Ratnacūḍa, who exemplifies the practice of being free from delusion and confusion. In terms of the perfection of dhyāna, he uses wisdom to support meditative concentration;
thus, when still, there is no lack of illumination, and when moving, he does not depart from tranquility—this is called being "free from delusion and confusion. By means of this, the youth Sudhana...

Having heard from the householder Prajñādhara the liberation door called "The Treasury of Merit," he practiced and realized it according to the Dharma, thereby attaining ten kinds of oceans of merit and other qualities.
Following these instructions, he traveled southward by stages toward the city of Siṃhapura.
Searching everywhere for the Elder Ratnacūḍa, he saw the elder in the marketplace.

Now, being in the marketplace signifies abiding amidst bustle with a mind free from attachment; remaining constantly in samādhi amidst disorder, he is still while moving, and thus is free from delusion and distraction.
Having seen him, Sudhana approached and inquired about the Dharma-gate. At that time, the elder was precisely demonstrating it.
The Dharma-realm [Lord] then took Sudhana by the hand and led him to his residence, showing him the house, saying, "Behold my home.
This was intended for Sudhana to achieve sudden realization through direct perception.
As for the detailed observation of the house—its pure radiance and adornments—it specifically demonstrates entry via skillful means. The house has ten stories and eight gates.
It is like an octagonal stupa, the great palace of a Western King; such is its general outline.

However, it has symbolic significance, using the Eightfold Noble Path as the gateway for entering the wondrous. Within each of the ten stories, specific arrangements are made to represent the many meanings contained within the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is said that these need not necessarily be represented; rather, this Bodhisattva proceeds by means of practice.
The capacity [of this stage] manifests as currently abiding in superior retribution, gradually becoming ever more exalted and supreme, as ten aspects reveal its inexhaustibility.

Now, the wealth accumulated on the lower four tiers is given as the gift of material sustenance (*āmiṣadāna*). Next, on the fifth and sixth tiers, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, which constitutes the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Finally, the dharmas such as cause, effect, practice, and stages revealed on the upper four tiers collectively demonstrate that the Bodhisattva of this stage is fully endowed with these qualities.

The virtues accumulated by his feet were thus gathered within his residence. When Sudhana saw this, he asked, "From what causes and conditions was this sublime karmic fruit obtained? The elder explained the causes and conditions to him:
"I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are atoms, a Buddha appeared in the world named King of Universal Adornment (Samantavyūharāja) Tathāgata. That Buddha entered the city."
I burned a single pellet of incense as an offering. Although my offering was minute, because I dedicated it toward three realms, I have obtained this retribution.
This single pellet of incense symbolizes how *prajñā* blends and integrates all practices;

thus, even a single subtle act possesses inexhaustible merit and accords with practice that pervades the Dharma-realm. Therefore, the resulting retribution is so sublime. This, then, is what constitutes a "great elder."
Go! Therefore, I call you "son of good family. I know only this Bodhisattva liberation door of the inexhaustible treasure-store of merit.
As for the various dharma-doors, such as the inconceivable treasure-stores of merit of all Bodhisattvas, these are not within my knowledge;
therefore, I point you toward a later friend. To the south of here, there is a country called Vītaṃsaka.
"In the city of Samantamukha, there is an elder named Samantanetra who will explain it for you; you should go and inquire of him.
Sudhana prostrated himself, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, having heard this liberation from the elder Ratnaśikhin, the youth Sudhana deeply entered the immeasurable knowledge and vision of all Buddhas;
he dwelt securely in the immeasurable supreme practices of Bodhisattvas; he thoroughly understood the immeasurable skillful means of Bodhisattvas;
he sought after the immeasurable Dharma-gates of Bodhisattvas; he purified the immeasurable faith and understanding of Bodhisattvas; and he made the wisdom of Bodhisattvas sharp and keen.
Possessing immeasurable faculties, he accomplished the immeasurable aspirations of a bodhisattva, mastered the immeasurable gateways of bodhisattva practice,
increased the immeasurable power of his vows, established the invincible banner of a bodhisattva, gave rise to bodhisattva wisdom,
and illuminated the bodhisattva teachings. Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Veṇuvana and inquired about and sought out that city.

While on the way, though he encountered hardships, he did not shrink from toil and suffering; he maintained only right mindfulness of the instructions of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), vowing to always remain close to him, serve and make offerings to him, thoroughly restraining all his faculties, and remaining free from all negligence.

Only then did he see the City of Universal Gates (*Samantamukha-pura*), surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of villages and settlements, with its high and steep battlements and wide, level thoroughfares. There he saw that long...
He went to where he was, prostrated before him with palms joined, and stood there, saying:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. The elder replied: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you..."
Having already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, O son of good family, I know all the ailments of all sentient beings:
those caused by wind, bile, phlegm, or heat; by malevolent spirits, demons, or poisons; and even those injuries inflicted by water or fire.
All such various ailments that may arise, I am able to cure and treat through skillful means.
Good son, all sentient beings from the ten directions who are ill come to my place; I treat them all so that they may recover.
Furthermore, I bathe their bodies with fragrant water and adorn them with fragrant flowers, necklaces, famous garments, and superior robes, providing all manner of ornaments.
He causes all food, drink, and wealth to be fully provided so that there is no lack or deficiency whatsoever. Thereafter, he preaches the Dharma to each according to their needs:
for those with excessive desire, he teaches the contemplation of impurity; for those with excessive hatred, he teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those with a predominance of delusion, he teaches them to discern the various characteristics of phenomena;
for those with equal proportions of the afflictions, he reveals to them the sublime gateways of the Dharma. Desiring to cause them to generate the bodhicitta, he extols the merits of all Buddhas.
In order to cause them to give rise to the mind of great compassion, he reveals the immeasurable suffering and affliction of birth and death;
in order to cause their merit to increase, he praises the cultivation of immeasurable merit and wisdom; and in order to cause them to make great vows.
He praised the taming of all sentient beings, desiring to cause them to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra;
he spoke of how Bodhisattvas dwell in all lands throughout all eons to cultivate the web of all practices, desiring to cause them to be endowed with the marks and signs of a Buddha.
They praise and extol the dāna-pāramitā, desiring that they may attain the Buddha’s pure body, which is able to reach all places.
They praise and extol the śīla-pāramitā, desiring that they may attain the Buddha’s pure and inconceivable body.
They praise and extol the kṣānti-pāramitā, desiring that they may obtain the state of a Tathāgata.
He extols and praises the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) because he desires them to attain a body that is invincible.
He extols and praises the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) because he desires them to manifest the pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of a Tathāgata.
He extols and praises the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) because he desires them to manifest the Buddha.

The World-Honored One’s pure form-body extols and praises the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) because he wishes to cause [beings] to abide for all eons for the sake of all sentient beings;

he extols and praises the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) because he wishes to cause [them] to manifest pure bodies that completely surpass all Buddha-fields; he extols and praises the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) because...
I desire to cause them to manifest pure bodies that bring joy to all sentient beings according to their respective minds.

I praise and extol the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*). Desiring to cause them to attain an ultimately pure and wondrous body, I praise and extol the eternal departure from all unwholesome dharmas.
Having bestowed such gifts, I bid each of them to return. Furthermore, O son of good family, I...
He was well-versed in the essential methods for compounding all types of incense, namely:

the peerless incense (*asama-gandha*), the Sindhuvara incense, the unsurpassed incense (*anabhibhūta-gandha*), the awakening incense (*bodhana-gandha*), the Aruṇavati incense, the firm black sandalwood incense (*kālāguru-candana-gandha*), the uraga-sandalwood incense, the aloeswood incense (*agaru-gandha*), and the incense that stabilizes the faculties (*akṣobhya-indriya-gandha*). He knew how to prepare and blend all such incenses.
The Method of Conjunction. Furthermore, good son, when I hold this incense as an offering, all the vows made before all the Buddhas are universally fulfilled.
These are: the vow to rescue and protect all sentient beings; the vow to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields;
and the vow to make offerings to all Tathāgatas. Furthermore, good son, when this incense is burned, from each and every piece of incense there emerge [innumerable...]
The fragrance pervaded all Buddha-assemblies and sites of enlightenment throughout the entire dharma-realm of the ten directions.
It manifested as fragrant palaces, fragrant halls, and likewise as fragrant railings, fragrant walls, fragrant parapets, and fragrant windows and doors.

There were fragrant multi-storied pavilions, fragrant crescents, fragrant canopies, fragrant banners, fragrant pennants, fragrant curtains, fragrant nets, fragrant images, fragrant ornaments, fragrant radiance, and fragrant clouds and rains, filling every place as a magnificent adornment.
"Good son, I know only this Dharma-door of causing all sentient beings everywhere to see all Buddhas and rejoice. As for those [who possess it]..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like great medicinal kings; whether seen, heard, or remembered;
whether dwelling together with, following in the footsteps of, or merely calling upon their names—all obtain benefit, and none do so in vain.

If any sentient beings encounter them even for a moment, they will surely cause all afflictions to be extinguished, lead them into the Buddha-dharma, and bring them forever away from the aggregates of suffering.
Having stilled all fears of birth and death, they have reached the state of fearlessness and the realm of omniscience.
Having shattered the great mountain of old age and death, they abide in the bliss of equanimity and cessation.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good son, to the south of here there is a great city named Tālaketu. Within it...
There is a king named Analaṃkāra (No-Satiety). Go to him and ask: "How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Samantacakṣus, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and took his leave.
The sixth is the Elder Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*), who is associated with the stage of Good Manifestation (*Sudarśana*) and pertains to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Wisdom is able to manifest the principles of the three truths because *prajñā* is present before one.

After the youth Sudhana heard this liberation from the Elder Jewel Topknot (*Ratnaśikhin*), he deeply entered twelve kinds of dharmas, such as the various virtues and immeasurable knowledge and vision, proceeding gradually.
Traveling south, he arrived at the kingdom of Tenggen (Wisteria Root). As for why the kingdom is named Tenggen: wisteria roots penetrate deep into the earth and send forth flowers and sprouts above;
this symbolizes that the profound realization of the practice of *prajñā-pāramitā* gives rise to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Because this subsequently attained wisdom functions in accordance with sentient beings, it is likened to the wisteria. The city is named Pumen (Universal Gate) because the *prajñā-pāramitā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is without... [omission].
Because it is not obstructed. The elder named Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) is so called because the *prajñā* of contemplative observation sees all things.

Sudhana first follows the instructions to seek him out, searching everywhere until he finally beholds the city of Universal Gate (Samantamukha), which is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of villages;
this symbolizes that the *prajñā* of the retinue assists and supports the *dharmatā* of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Having seen him...
The elder paid his respects and inquired, "How does one learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
The elder first praised the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment, and then correctly demonstrated the Dharma-realm, saying:

"I know all the ailments of sentient beings—such as diseases of wind, bile, phlegm, heat, spirits, and poisons—and am able to cure them all. I am able to heal the various illnesses of sentient beings throughout the ten directions."
Once their illness has been treated, he subsequently provides them with all kinds of superior food, drink, clothing, and wealth until they are fully satisfied;

this is the gift of material requisites (*āmiṣadāna*).
