Having healed their physical ailments, he then expounds various sublime teachings (*dharmadeśanā*) to treat their mental illnesses, not only causing them to sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), but also inspiring them to generate the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). He praises this extensively.
The six perfections are taught so that they may practice this Dharma-giving. Having thus given, he causes each to return;
this is the practice of exalting oneself and transforming sentient beings. Furthermore, I am able to blend various incenses and offer the blended incense to all Buddhas;
this is the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas. When burning this incense, immeasurable [fragrances] emerge from within it.
The fragrance fills the Dharma-realm of the ten directions, forming various adornments that pervade every place.
This symbolizes how Prajñāpāramitā integrates all practices to adorn the Dharmakāya as sublime conduct;
this is why it is called "present practice. Having shown the Dharma-realm, the Elder said: "I know only this which causes all beings..."
This gives rise to the Dharma-gate of Universally Beholding All Buddhas with Joy. That is to say, when the ailments of body and mind are eliminated, one attains happiness in both worlds;
therefore, all rejoice. By universally making offerings with incense, one attains the ten bodies of a Buddha, whereby what Buddha would not be seen? Such is the nature of the realization.
Just as the Bodhisattvas are like great medicinal kings, for all who see, hear, remember, or call their names, there is no [suffering that remains].

"One does not fail to gain benefit; none shall pass by in vain. Such sublime practice is not within my knowledge," he said, thus humbling himself and deferring to the superior one to point the way for his future companion.
"In this southern direction, there is a city called Tāladhvaja where a king named Anala resides.
You should go there and inquire. Then Sudhana paid his respects, gazed upon him with longing, and took his leave to depart.
At that time, the youth Sudhana recollected and contemplated the instructions of his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He reflected that these spiritual friends were able to sustain him and protect him, ensuring that he would never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thinking thus, he gave rise to a heart of joy, a heart of pure faith, a vast heart, and a heart of serene gladness; he leaped up with exultation.
A leaping mind; a joyful and celebratory mind; a sublime and wondrous mind; a tranquil mind; an adorned mind; an unattached mind; an unimpeded mind;

an equanimous mind; a sovereign mind; a mind dwelling in the Dharma; a mind that travels everywhere to Buddha-fields; a mind beholding the adornments of the Buddhas; and a mind that never abandons the ten powers.
Proceeding gradually, he passed through kingdoms, villages, towns, and settlements, until he reached Tāladhvaja.
The city official asked where King Anala was. The people replied, "This king is currently seated upon the lion throne in the main hall, proclaiming the Dharma and transforming sentient beings:
those who should be disciplined, he disciplines; those who should be gathered, he gathers;
he punishes their evils and adjudicates their disputes; he comforts the orphaned and the weak, causing them all to forever sever the ways of killing and stealing."
sexual misconduct; he also caused them to refrain from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
Furthermore, he led them to distance themselves from greed, hatred, and wrong views. At that time, following the words of the multitude, Sudhana went to visit him.
From afar, he saw the king seated upon a Nārāyaṇa-vajra throne, whose legs were made of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels and adorned with immeasurable jeweled images.
For the sake of adornment, a net of golden cords completely covers its surface. A *cintāmaṇi* jewel serves as a crown to adorn his head.
A crescent moon made of Jambūnada gold adorns his forehead. An *indranīla* jewel serves as an earring, hanging down from both sides.
Priceless *maṇi* jewels serve as a necklace to adorn his neck. [The gods...]
His arms were adorned with bracelets made of exquisite maṇi jewels. A canopy was fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold, and its spokes were interspersed with various precious gems.
Its shaft was made of great lapis lazuli, and its hub was composed of light-flavored maṇi jewels.
Bells made of assorted gems constantly emitted sublime sounds, radiating great light that pervaded the ten directions. As...
A precious canopy covered its summit. King Anala possessed great power and might; he could subdue other hosts and none could oppose him.
A fillet of stainless silk was bound upon his head. Ten thousand ministers surrounded him before and behind, jointly managing the affairs of state.
Furthermore, in front of him were one hundred thousand fierce soldiers, their appearances hideous and their clothing coarse and shabby, holding—
Wielding weapons, with arms bared and eyes glaring in rage, all sentient beings who saw them were struck with terror. Immeasurable numbers of sentient beings violated the king’s commands;

some stole the property of others, some took the lives of others, some violated the wives of others, some gave rise to false views, some harbored hatred and resentment, and some conceived greed and envy.
Having committed such various evil deeds, they were bound in fivefold fetters and led away.
They were brought before the king, who punished them according to their offenses: some had their hands and feet cut off;
some had their ears and noses sliced off; some had their eyes gouged out; some had their heads severed; some had their skin flayed; some had their bodies dismembered;
some were boiled in boiling water; some were burned with fire; and some were driven up high mountains and pushed over to fall. There were such immeasurable tortures as these.
He let out a cry of lamentation, like those in the Saṃghāta Great Hell. Having seen this, Sudhana thought to himself:
"For the benefit of all sentient beings, I seek the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva;
yet now this king destroys all wholesome dharmas and commits great sinful karma, oppressing and tormenting sentient beings even unto taking their lives, without ever feeling dread or remorse."
Regarding the evil realms of the future, how can one seek the Dharma therein and give rise to a heart of great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings?
While he was reflecting thus, a deva in the sky addressed him, saying:
"Good son, you should remember the instructions of the spiritual friend, the Elder Universal Eye. Sudhana looked up and said to him: "I constantly remember from the beginning..."
"I dare not forget. The Deity said, "Good son, do not feel weary of or distance yourself from the words of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
A spiritual friend can lead you to a place of safety free from all dangers. Good son, the wisdom of a bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is inconceivable;
the wisdom that gathers in sentient beings is inconceivable; and the wisdom that protects and mindfully attends to sentient beings is inconceivable."
Inconceivable is the wisdom that matures sentient beings; inconceivable is the wisdom that protects sentient beings;
inconceivable is the wisdom that liberates sentient beings; inconceivable is the wisdom that disciplines sentient beings.
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Sudhana went immediately to the king’s place, prostrated at his feet, and said:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction."
"Please speak for me. Then King Anala, having attended to his royal duties, took Sudhana by the hand and led him into the palace, bidding him sit beside him.
He said, "Noble son, you should observe the palace in which I dwell.
At these words, Sudhana looked all around and beheld that the palace was incomparably vast, adorned entirely with exquisite jewels.

It was constructed with walls made of the seven precious jewels, encircling it on all sides. There were pavilions made of hundreds of thousands of various jewels, all exquisitely adorned and most wonderful.
An inconceivable net of mani-jewels covered its summit. Ten billion handmaidens were of peerless beauty;
their deportment and every movement were worthy of admiration, and everything they did was nothing but skillful.
"Excellent! You first rise and later lie down, serving my will with a gentle mind. Then King Anala said to Sudhana:

"Good son, what do you think? If I had truly committed such evil deeds, how could I have obtained such a retribution as this—a body such as this, such a retinue, such wealth and abundance, and such sovereignty? Good son.

I have attained the bodhisattva liberation of being like an illusion. Good son, all the sentient beings in this land of mine mostly practice killing, stealing, and even wrong views; no other skillful means can cause them to abandon their evil karma.
Good son, for the sake of subduing those sentient beings, I manifest as an evildoer who commits various sinful acts and undergoes various forms of suffering.

Various sufferings. When all those sentient beings who commit evil see these things, their hearts give rise to terror, their hearts give rise to weary detachment, and their hearts give rise to timidity;
they sever all the evil karma they have created and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, it is by means of such skillful expedients that I cause all sentient beings—
Abandoning the ten unwholesome actions, one dwells in the ten paths of wholesome conduct, attaining ultimate happiness, ultimate peace, and ultimately abiding in the ground of omniscience.
Good son, throughout my body, speech, and mind, I have never harmed even a single sentient being.
Good son, as for my heart, I would rather undergo the sufferings of the Avīci Hell in the future than ever give rise to a single thought [of malice].
...this intention is no different from performing a painful task for a single mosquito or ant; how much more so for a human being?
A human is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), for they are able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas. Good son, I have attained only this liberation like an illusion (*māyopama-vimokṣa*).

As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they know that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions. [The Bodhisattvas...]
All practices are entirely like transformations; all worlds are entirely like shadows; all phenomena are entirely like dreams.
Entering the unimpeded dharma-gate of the true mark, one cultivates all practices of the Indra-net.
With unimpeded wisdom, one acts within the spheres of experience and universally enters all samādhis of equality, having already attained mastery over dhāraṇīs.
"Being thus, how could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Jyotiṣprabhā and a king named Mahāprabha.
Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the king's feet, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave."
He departed.

Below this is King Anala (No-Yan-Zu), who entrusts himself to the practice of non-attachment (*asaṅga*) by means of skillful means (*upāya*). Through skillful means, he engages with phenomenal existence (*saṃsāra*) without being deluded regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
because his engagement with phenomena and principles is unhindered, and because he neither abandons nor grasps, he is named "Non-Attached. Upon hearing the preceding [account], Sudhana...
Following the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he reflects upon and contemplates them, entering into realization with a profound mind.
He gives rise to seventeen kinds of mental states, such as the mind of joy. Relying on these instructions, he seeks his goal and gradually travels south until he reaches the city of Tālāvatī.

*Tālā* means "clear and pure" (*viśuddha*), and *vatī* means "established" (*vyavasthita*); this signifies that one establishes superior practice by relying on Prajñāpāramitā, through skillful means (*upāya*) that are like an illusion.
Therefore, he never grew weary. For this reason, he was known by the name of King. Sudhana asked where the king was;
the people replied, "The king is seated upon the lion throne in the main hall, proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Dharma and guiding sentient beings.

Those who can be disciplined, he disciplines; those who can be gathered, he gathers. He causes them to abandon the ten non-virtues and sever greed, anger, and ignorance. Sudhana immediately went there and saw him from afar.
That king sat upon the Nārāyaṇa-vajra throne, adorned with immeasurable precious jewels. Ten thousand ministers surrounded him before and behind, collectively managing the affairs of state.

They manifested *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means) and *prajñā* (wisdom), engaging with the mundane world through expedient means and guiding all beings through the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*) to adorn the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, ten thousand fierce guards of hideous appearance... held [their weapons].
Those who wield weapons to punish offenders demonstrate the practice of using reverse methods to subdue sentient beings;
thus, they manifest various forms of torment and suffering. When Sudhana saw this, fear and doubt arose in his heart, whereupon a deity in the sky exhorted him.
First, he caused [Sudhana] to recall his previous teacher’s instructions without error, so that no doubt might arise;
thereafter, he revealed to him the skillful means of manifestation, saying, "You should enter this with faith: the wisdom of a bodhisattva for taming sentient beings is inconceivable.
Having heard this, Sudhana then ventured to respectfully inquire about the practice of the bodhisattva path. At that time, Anala—
The King took Sudhana by the hand and entered the royal palace, inviting him to sit beside him. He addressed him, saying, "Son of good family, you should observe the palace in which I dwell.
This was the King’s direct demonstration of the *dharmadhātu* to bring about realization in accordance with it.
Sudhana surveyed the entire palace, its vast and magnificent adornments, and the exquisite beauty of his retinue and attendants. This...

He brought forth the karmic retribution to make known his past causes. The king then said, "Virtuous man, if I truly committed such evil deeds, how could I have obtained such a karmic retribution as this—such a physical body, such a retinue, and such abundant wealth and sovereignty?
He then pointed directly to the actual proof, saying, "I have attained the Bodhisattva’s illusory-like understanding."

“Released! Because the sentient beings of my land have committed many evil deeds, I employ the illusory dharma-gate to transform these illusory sentient beings, desiring only that they reach the ultimate stage of omniscience.
How could I perform evil acts with real dharmas? Furthermore, my actions of body, speech, and mind have never from the beginning caused harm or affliction to others.”
"Regarding even a single sentient being, down to a mosquito or an ant, I have never performed a single act of harm; how much less so for a human?
For humans are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) capable of giving rise to all wholesome dharmas; how could I ever harm them?
This fully demonstrates that within the sovereign, illusion-like activities of compassion, it is said: 'Good son, I have attained only this liberation that is like an illusion.'"

It is merely a gateway. Just as the various bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) know that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions, like transformations, like shadows, and like dreams—this unimpeded dharma-gateway is not something I can know.

Thus, he humbled himself and deferred to a superior, pointing out that to the south there is a city named *Prabhāsa* where there is a king named *Mahāprabha*; "You should go there and inquire and learn."
The Bodhisattva Path. Having heard this, Sudhana prostrated himself, gazed up with reverence, and took his leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded right mindfulness, contemplated the Dharma-gate of illusory wisdom attained by that king;

he reflected upon that king’s liberation as being like an illusion and observed that king’s illusory nature of phenomena (dharmatā), making vows like an illusion and purifying [them] like an illusion.
Regarding the illusory nature of phenomena: throughout all three times which are universally like an illusion, he gives rise to various illusory transformations.

Contemplating in this manner, he travels by stages, whether reaching human cities, towns, and villages, or passing through wildernesses, rocky gorges, and perilous difficulties, without weariness or fatigue and never resting; thereafter, he eventually arrives at the great city of Prabhāketu and inquires.
People asked, "Where is the great city of Prabhāpurī? Everyone replied, "This very city is the city of Prabhāpurī;
it is the dwelling place of King Mahāprabha. At that time, the youth Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to himself:
"My spiritual friend is within this city; I shall now certainly behold him in person. Thus he heard.
The practices performed by all bodhisattvas; hearing the gateways to liberation of all bodhisattvas; hearing the dharmas realized by all bodhisattvas;
hearing the inconceivable merits of all bodhisattvas; hearing the inconceivable sovereignty of all bodhisattvas;
hearing the inconceivable equanimity of all bodhisattvas; hearing the inconceivable valor of all bodhisattvas; hearing...
The inconceivable realm of all bodhisattvas is vast and pure. Having formed this thought, he entered the City of Sublime Light (*Prabhāvyūha*).
He saw that this great city was composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, conch-shell, and agate.
It was surrounded by seven tiers of deep moats made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight virtues, and its floor was spread with gold.
Sands, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers were spread all over its surface.
Seven rows of precious *tāla* trees stood in formation, and sevenfold walls of vajra surrounded it on every side.
These were the Vajra Wall of Lion Radiance, the Vajra Wall of Insuperable Excellence, and the Vajra Wall that Cannot Be Repelled.

It had adamantine walls that were indestructible, adamantine walls that could not be breached, adamantine walls that were firm and unimpeded, adamantine walls with exquisite jewel-lattices, and adamantine walls pure and free from dust;
all were adorned with the interlacing of countless wonderful mani-jewels, and their battlements were made of various kinds of precious gems. The city was ten yojanas in length and breadth.
Surrounded on all eight sides, it has eight gates, all of which are extensively adorned with the seven treasures.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, and its various ornaments are most delightful. Within the city, there are ten billion streets.
Between each and every path, there dwell immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings.
There are countless Jambūnada-gold pavilions, covered above by nets of *vaiḍūrya* mani-jewels;
countless silver pavilions, covered above by nets of red pearl manis; and countless *vaiḍūrya* pavilions, [covered] by nets of the *sudarśana* (wondrous store) mani.
It was covered above by a net of lapis lazuli; it was covered above by a net of stainless-treasury *maṇi*-king jewels;
it was covered above by a net of countless world-illuminating *maṇi*-jewel pavilions; it was covered above by a net of *maṇi*-king sun-treasury jewels;
it was covered above by a net of countless indranīla *maṇi*-jewel pavilions; and it was covered above by a net of exquisite-light *maṇi*-king jewels.
Above it was covered by a sea of countless *maṇi-rāja* pavilions of sentient beings; above that, it was covered by a net of *maṇi-rāja* of blazing light.
Above it were countless pavilions of diamond jewels; above those, it was covered by a net of *maṇi-rāja* of invincible banners.
Above it were countless pavilions of black sandalwood; above those, it was covered by a net of celestial *mandārava* flowers.
There were countless peerless pavilions made of the king of incenses, their surfaces covered by various nets of flowers.
Furthermore, that city possessed countless nets of mani-jewels, countless nets of precious bells, countless nets of celestial incense, and countless nets of celestial flowers.

It was completely covered by countless nets of precious images, countless canopies of precious garments, countless canopies of precious parasols, countless canopies of precious pavilions, and countless canopies of precious flower garlands; everywhere were erected precious parasols, banners, and flags.
Within this city, there was a tower named the Treasury of the True Dharma (*Saddharmakośa*).
It was adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, its radiance blazing and magnificent, supreme and beyond compare. Sentient beings who beheld it could never tire of it.
King Mahāprabha constantly resided therein. At that time, the youth Sudhana [beheld] all these rare treasures and exquisite objects, and even...
Neither men nor women, nor the objects of the six sense-fields, evoked any attachment in him.
He reflected correctly upon the ultimate Dharma and, with single-minded aspiration, sought to see a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
As he traveled by stages, he saw King Mahāprabha not far from his residence, seated in the middle of a crossroads upon a vast and magnificent throne of a wish-fulfilling maṇi-jewel lotus treasury.
His throne had feet made of deep-blue lapis lazuli gems, a canopy of golden silk, and a net of various jewels;
with exquisite celestial garments serving as a mattress and coverlet, the king sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
His body was adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a great man and eighty secondary signs, possessing a radiant brilliance like that of a mountain of pure gold. As if...
The majestic radiance of his pure, empty sun blazes forth; like the full moon, those who behold him feel refreshed and cool.
Like the Brahmā King dwelling amidst the Brahmā assembly, he is also like the great ocean, whose jewels of merit and Dharma are boundless.
Like the Snowy Mountains, he is adorned with the forest of his primary and secondary marks; like a great cloud, he can thunder the Dharma’s roar to awaken all classes of beings. Furthermore—
Like space, it manifests various dharma-gates as constellations; like Mount Sumeru, its four colors appear universally within the ocean of sentient beings' minds;
and like a jewel island, it is filled with the various treasures of wisdom.
Before the royal throne, there were heaps of precious jewels, including gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mani-gems, pearls, coral, amber, conch shells, and jade.
There were immeasurable and boundless varieties of clothing, necklaces, and food and drink, filling [the place] completely.

Furthermore, one saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite jeweled chariots; hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial musical performances; hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial, wonderful incenses;
and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of medicinal decoctions and requisites for the sick. All such things as these were present.
All were exquisitely beautiful. Their countless, variegated cow-hooves and horns were golden in color.

Countless billions of upright women anointed their bodies with the most sublime *candana* sandalwood paste. Adorned with celestial garments and various necklaces, they were thoroughly proficient in all sixty-four arts.
They were well-versed in all worldly customs and etiquette, bestowing gifts upon sentient beings in accordance with their inclinations.
In cities, villages, and at the crossroads, they placed all manner of requisites for life. Along every path,
there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who bestowed these various goods upon sentient beings, desiring to universally gather them in,
to cause them to rejoice, to cause them to leap with joy, and to cause them to...
Because the mind is pure; in order to bring coolness to sentient beings; in order to extinguish the afflictions of sentient beings;
in order to cause sentient beings to know all principles and meanings; in order to cause sentient beings to enter the path of omniscience;
in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the mind of enmity; in order to cause sentient beings to depart from evil of body and speech; in order to cause sentient beings to uproot...

Because of various false views, and in order to cause sentient beings to purify their paths of action, the youth Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the [sage’s] feet.
He reverently circumambulated him to the right for immeasurable times, then stood with palms joined and said:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know..."
"How does one learn the bodhisattva conduct? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will explain this to me. At that time, the King replied, "Noble son, I purely cultivate the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion.
I fulfill the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion. Noble son, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions..."
At the abodes of hundreds of millions, up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, I have questioned them regarding this Dharma, contemplated and observed it, and cultivated its adornments.
Good son, I take this Dharma as my sovereignty; I issue commands by means of this Dharma; I gather and sustain beings through this Dharma;
I follow along with the world by means of this Dharma; I guide sentient beings by means of this Dharma; and I cause [them] to...
Sentient beings practice; by means of this Dharma they are caused to enter, by means of this Dharma they are provided with skillful means,
by means of this Dharma they are caused to cultivate, by means of this Dharma they are caused to initiate practice,
by means of this Dharma they are caused to dwell in contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and by means of this Dharma they are caused to dwell in a mind of loving-kindness.
Taking loving-kindness as primary and being fully endowed with the power of loving-kindness, one thus causes [the mind] to abide in a heart of benefit,

a heart of peace and happiness, a heart of compassion, a heart of gathering-in, a heart that protects sentient beings without abandoning them, and a heart that uproots the suffering of sentient beings without ceasing.
By means of this Dharma, I cause all sentient beings to attain ultimate happiness. May they always be joyful themselves, free from all physical suffering, and may their minds attain cool clarity.
May they sever the craving for birth and death and delight in the joy of the True Dharma. May they wash away the defilements of affliction and shatter the obstructions of evil karma.
May they cut off the flow into the cycle of birth and death and enter the true ocean of Dharma. May they sever all realms of existence and seek after omniscience, purifying all their minds.

Sāgarabuddhi-akṣayaprasāda. "O son of good family, I have already dwelled in this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrīdhvaja*), and am able to transform the world through the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
O son of good family, all sentient beings within my land have no fear toward me.
O son of good family, if there are sentient beings who are poor, destitute, and in need, and they come to me..."
They sought and searched for it. I opened my storehouses and allowed them to take whatever they desired, and I spoke to them, saying:
"Commit no evil. Do not harm sentient beings. Do not give rise to various views. Do not produce attachments. You are poor and destitute;

if you have anything you require, come to me or to the crossroads where all manner of things are fully provided. Take as much as you wish according to your desire; do not harbor [fear or hesitation]."
Question: "Virtuous son, the sentient beings dwelling in this City of Sublime Light are all bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
According to their respective inclinations, what they perceive differs: some see this city as being small in scale, while others see it as vast;
some see its ground as composed of earth and sand, while others see it adorned with various jewels."
Some see walls made of piled earth; some see precious walls surrounding them on all sides. Some see the ground covered with many tiles and stones, uneven and undulating;
some see it adorned with countless great maṇi jewels interspersed here and there, as level as the palm of a hand.
Some see houses constructed of wood and earth; some see palaces and various multi-storied towers.

The pavilions, stairways, courtyards, windows, gates, balconies, railings, doors, and casements— all such things as these were nothing but exquisite jewels. Good son, if there are sentient beings whose minds are pure,
who have planted roots of goodness by making offerings to the Buddhas, who have resolved their minds to follow the path to omniscience,
and who take omniscience as their ultimate goal— as well as those who, in my past time, cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva— [they shall behold this].
Those whom I had previously taken under my care saw this city as adorned and purified with various jewels, while all others saw it as defiled.

Good son, when all sentient beings within this land were during the age of the five corruptions and delighted in committing various evils, I felt compassion for them and desired to rescue and protect them;
thus, I entered the gate of the Bodhisattva samādhi headed by great loving-kindness that accords with the world. I entered.
At the time of this samādhi, all the minds of those sentient beings—whether they be minds of fear, of malice, of enmity, or of contention—all naturally vanish and are extinguished.

Why is this? Because the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi, which takes great compassion as its foremost principle and accords with the world, is such as this. Good son, wait but a moment and you shall see it for yourself.
At that time, King Mahāprabha entered this samādhi. The city, both inside and out, shook in six ways.

All the jeweled grounds, jeweled walls, jeweled halls, jeweled palaces, terraces, pavilions, towers, balconies, steps, and windows—all such things as these—emitted wondrous sounds and bowed in respectful salutation toward the king.
Among all the inhabitants dwelling within the city of Suprabhā, there was none who did not likewise [rejoice].
At that time, filled with joy and exultation, they all approached the king and prostrated themselves with their entire bodies upon the ground.

All the people from the villages, camps, and cities came to see the king, greeting him with joy and reverence. Even the birds and beasts dwelling near the king looked at one another and gave rise to hearts of compassion;
they all turned before the king and paid him respectful homage. All the mountains, plains, and various grasses...
The trees all turned toward the king in homage and reverence. The ponds, pools, springs, wells, rivers, and oceans all surged and overflowed, flowing and pouring before the king.
Ten thousand dragon kings raised great clouds of fragrance, flashing lightning, rolling thunder, and pouring down a fine rain.
There were ten thousand celestial kings, namely the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the King of the Yāma Heaven, and the Tuṣita Heaven.
The King of the Heaven of Good Transformations, the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations, and others such as these were the leaders;
in the midst of the void, they performed various musical performances, while countless celestial maidens sang praises and rained down clouds of countless flowers.
Countless clouds of incense, countless clouds of jewel-garlands, countless clouds of precious robes, countless clouds of precious parasols,
countless clouds of precious banners, and countless clouds of precious streamers adorned the void as offerings to the king.
By the sovereign power of the great elephant king Airāvaṇa, he spread these countless [clouds] throughout the sky.
The great precious lotus flower was adorned with countless precious necklaces, countless precious silk ribbons, countless precious garlands,
countless precious ornaments, countless precious flowers, and countless precious incenses— various wondrous and marvelous things serving as its embellishments.

Countless court ladies offered various songs of praise. Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rākṣasa kings, yakṣa kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, and piśāca kings, some of whom dwelt in the great ocean.

Some dwell on land, drinking blood and eating flesh while harming sentient beings; yet they all give rise to a mind of compassion, vowing to practice what is beneficial, clearly recognizing the afterlife and refraining from all evil deeds.
With reverence and palms joined, they prostrate themselves before the King, just as those in Jambudvīpa do.

The same applies to all other three continents, up to the trichiliocosm, and even throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions—every single poisonous and evil sentient being therein is likewise.
Then, King Mahāprabha arose from samādhi and said to Sudhana: "Good son, I know only this Bodhisattva Great..."

The samādhi gate of "Compassion as the Foremost Accordance with the World": It is like a high canopy for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, because the heart of compassion universally shades all sentient beings;
it is a practice, because it performs the lower, middle, and upper stages with equal conduct;
it is the great earth, because it can sustain all sentient beings through the heart of compassion; it is the full moon, because its light of merit...
Because it manifests with equality within the world, it is a pure sun; because it illuminates all objects of knowledge with the light of wisdom, it is a bright lamp;
because it can destroy all darkness within the minds of sentient beings, it is a water-purifying jewel;
because it can clear away the turbidity of flattery and deception within the minds of all sentient beings, it is a wish-fulfilling gem. It is entirely...
Because they can satisfy the heart's desires of all sentient beings, they act as great winds;
because they cause sentient beings to swiftly practice samādhi and enter the great city of omniscience, how could I possibly know their conduct,
describe their virtues, weigh that mountain of merit, gaze upon those stars of excellence, or observe them?
Examine that wind-wheel of great vows, which can lead one into those profound gateways of the Dharma,
can manifest that ocean of adornments, can elucidate those gateways of Samantabhadra’s conduct, can reveal those caves of various samādhis,
and can praise those clouds of great compassion. Noble son, to the south of here there is a royal capital named Anala.
There dwells a laywoman named Acalā. Go to her and ask: "How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, Sudhana the youth prostrated at the king's feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave.

Below this is the eighth, King Mahāprabha, who represents the practice that is difficult to attain (*durlabha-caryā*). This is categorized according to the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*);

it is called "difficult to attain" because it can only be achieved through the power of unobstructed aspiration. Sudhana contemplates the dharma-gate of the illusory nature (*māyopama-dharmamukha*) and, following the instructions, proceeds to seek it.

Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city named Suprabha. It is called Suprabha because, whereas in his previous stage his compassion was predominant, he has now attained non-abiding sublime wisdom to guide sentient beings.
The king is named Mahāprabha because the wisdom of his compassionate concentration encompasses all things without exception, and because it shines through everything within his vast vows.
At that time, the youth Sudhana rejoiced, thinking that his own benefit would surely increase.
Having resolved that he must hear of the inconceivable, vast, and pure realms of the bodhisattvas, he entered the City of Sublime Light (*Prabhāvyūhā*).
He beheld this great city adorned with immeasurable treasures, ten *yojanas* in length and breadth, with eight gates on its eight sides.
Within the city were ten billion thoroughfares, where immeasurable sentient beings dwelt.
It was situated there, with various kinds of exquisite pavilions adorned with diverse, subtle ornaments that radiated brilliant light, most excellent and peerless.
Upon seeing all this, Sudhana felt no attachment; with a single-minded aspiration, he longed only to see the spiritual friend.

However, as for this spiritual friend’s environment and its adornments being so exceptionally sublime, it is because all the various practices previously cultivated have been concentrated here, as his stage is about to be fulfilled.
When Sudhana saw King Mahāprabha, he was not far from the tower where [the king] resided;
the king sat upon a lion throne of lotus-treasury at a crossroads. As for the "four crossroads," they symbolize the four...

Because he gathers immeasurable sentient beings, the king’s primary retribution consists of twenty-eight marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) that adorn his body.
As for the reason there are twenty-eight marks, it is because they have not yet reached full completion.
Like the color of pure gold, his radiance is intensely blazing, like the sun in the sky. Before the king’s throne, there are immeasurable wonders.
He bestowed robes, food, and drink adorned with jewels, as well as women, as gifts. Along every path, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who gave these various things to sentient beings;
this represents the vow to deliver others, encompassing all the perfections (pāramitās) to fulfill the Great Vow.
Upon seeing this, Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and respectfully inquired about the cultivation of the bodhisattva [path].
At that time, the King was formally bestowing the Dharma-realm. First, he generally indicated the Dharma-gate, declaring:
"I have purely cultivated the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion; I have fulfilled the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion.

He first showed this practice because it is preeminent, being free from defilement and perfectly complete. Subsequently, he spoke of the causes and conditions for attaining this Dharma, saying: "I, at..."
I have questioned this Dharma before immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, contemplating and examining it, and cultivating its adornments;
these words enter through the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Therefore, by means of this Dharma-gate of great compassion, I teach and gather in all sentient beings, causing each of them to practice and cultivate so as to seek all-encompassing wisdom.
I abide in this practice of the Great Compassion Banner, and am able to transform the world through the True Dharma.
With the twelve lines of sūtra that follow, I speak of the matter of transforming sentient beings; this constitutes the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, if there are impoverished sentient beings who come to me seeking [aid], I open my treasuries so that they may take as much as they desire. There are four lines of sūtra which state:
Regarding that gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*): the preceding passage spoke of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) through the two gifts of material wealth and the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Because [beings] act according to their own inclinations, the resulting retributions (*vipākaphala*) they experience also differ accordingly. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that each perceives this city differently—some as pure and others as impure—and that this is brought about by the power of the "Samādhi of Great Compassion Accordant with the World" (*mahāmaitrī-lokānuvartana-samādhi*). The *Pañcavimśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* likewise speaks of this.
Regarding this matter of samādhi, King Mahāprabha then entered this concentration for the sake of Sudhana to manifest its characteristics.
When the king entered this samādhi, the city, both inside and out, shook in six ways;
from within all the towers, pavilions, doors, and windows, wondrous sounds issued forth; and all the mountains, plains, grasses, trees, and forests turned toward him.
The King bowed his head. All rivers, marshes, ponds, wells, and springs flowed toward the King.
Various devas, nāga kings, and the eight classes of beings each presented whatever subtle and wondrous offerings they possessed, filling the air.
Thus there are twenty-one sections of sutra describing the realms manifested within meditative concentration, which serve to manifest the Great Compassion.
Regarding the functional activity of this profound state: it is solely through the Samādhi of Great Compassion that King Mahāprabha gathers and transforms sentient beings.

Now, he directly reveals this realm of samādhi to Sudhana. That when entering meditative absorption, both the animate and the inanimate are moved and turn toward him, signifies his great compassion of shared essence; since all things and the self are one body, they all follow the samādhi in its return.
It is a transformation. How magnificent is the practice of loving-kindness! Because the practice of loving-kindness is so great, the power of one's vows becomes increasingly vast;
thus it is brought to fulfillment. This is why it is so difficult to attain. At that time, the Great King arose from samādhi and addressed Sudhana, saying:
"I know only this samādhi-door of the Bodhisattva's great compassion as the foremost, which accords with the world; it is merely this.
Such things as the high canopy of the Bodhisattvas' compassionate heart, which universally shelters all sentient beings like various clouds of great compassion—these are not within my knowledge.
Thus, he humbled himself and deferred to the superior, saying, "To the south, there is a royal capital..."
Her name is Anvaya (Abiding). There is an upāsikā named Acalā (Immovable). You should go and question her.
Then, Sudhana the youth prostrated himself, gazed up at her with reverence, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana emerged from the city of Suprabha and traveled along the road, mindfully reflecting upon the instructions of King Mahāprabha;
he recollected the bodhisattva practice-gate of the Banner of Great Compassion, contemplated the bodhisattva samādhi-gate of the Radiance of Accordance with the World,
and increased his inconceivable power of merit and mastery over vows, strengthening that [resolve].
One contemplates the wisdom that matures sentient beings; one observes his inconceivable and uncommon enjoyment of great majesty;
one recollects his inconceivable variety of marks; one contemplates his inconceivable pure retinue;
and one contemplates his inconceivable activities. Thus, one gives rise to a heart of joy, a heart of pure faith, and a heart of intense vigor.
He gave rise to a heart of joy; he gave rise to a heart of exultation; he gave rise to a heart of felicitation; he gave rise to a heart free from turbidity;
he gave rise to a pure heart; he gave rise to a firm heart; he gave rise to a vast heart; he gave rise to an inexhaustible heart. Reflecting in this way, he wept and shed tears.

One should reflect that a spiritual friend is truly rare; they are the source from which all merits arise, the source from which all bodhisattva practices arise, the source from which all pure mindfulness of bodhisattvas arises, and the source from which all wheels of dhāraṇī arise.
It gives birth to the radiance of all samādhis; it gives birth to the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas;
it universally rains down the Dharma-rain of all Buddhas; it reveals the gateways of the vows of all Bodhisattvas; and it gives birth to the inconceivable radiance of wisdom.
It causes all the roots and sprouts of bodhisattvas to grow. Furthermore, one should think: "A spiritual friend is able to universally rescue and protect from all evil paths;
is able to universally expound all dharmas of equality; and is able to universally reveal all even and uneven paths."

It is able to universally expound the profound meanings of the Mahāyāna; it is able to universally exhort and inspire all practices of Samantabhadra; it is able to universally lead one to the city of omniscience;
it is able to universally cause one to enter the great ocean of the Dharma-realm; and it is able to universally cause one to behold the ocean of phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
It is able to universally bestow the site of enlightenment upon all noble ones; it is able to universally increase all pure dharmas.

Sudhana, while he was thus reflecting with such compassion, the Bodhisattva Ever-Attendant-Awakening, acting as a messenger of the Tathāgata, spoke from the midst of the sky, saying: "Noble son, those who practice the teachings of a spiritual friend..."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was entirely pleased. Those who follow the words of spiritual friends will draw near to the stage of omniscience.
Those who are able to have no doubt regarding the words of spiritual friends will constantly encounter all virtuous friends.
Those who resolve their minds to never be separated from spiritual friends will attain perfection in one [quality].
"All purposes and benefits. "Noble son, you should go to the royal capital of Anālaya;

The answer below praises and confers the Dharma. It states: "Having already dwelt in the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places, one has already accomplished the Samādhi of Universally Contemplating the World.

Regarding "the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) that is without dependence or effort," it is because of this supernormal power that one is able to reach all places of transformation, and because of the *prajñā* of the universal gate (*samantamukha*), one is able to universally observe while remaining in concentration.

Furthermore, he thoroughly understands the various fragrances of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Moreover, he skillfully distinguishes the fragrances that treat various diseases and the fragrances that sever all evils.
The fragrance that gives rise to joy; the fragrance that increases afflictions; the fragrance that extinguishes afflictions; the fragrance that causes attachment to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
the fragrance that causes weariness with and detachment from the conditioned; the fragrance that abandons all pride and negligence; the fragrance that inspires the mind to recollect the Buddha;
the fragrance that realizes and understands the Dharma-gates; the fragrance enjoyed by the noble ones; the various fragrances of all bodhisattvas; and the fragrances of all bodhisattva stages.
The locus of fragrance. In this way, the forms and characteristics of such fragrances arise, manifest, and are accomplished.
I have fully realized all such things—the realm of pure and peaceful skillful means, their majestic power, their functional applications, and their fundamental source.

Good son, in the human world there is a fragrance called "Elephant Treasury" (*gajagarbha*), which is produced by the fighting of dragons; if one pellet is burned, it immediately gives rise to a great [fragrance].

Free from all illnesses, they do not harm one another and are liberated from all sorrow and suffering. Without alarm, without fear, without distraction, and without anger, they face one another with hearts of loving-kindness and pure intentions.
Having understood this, I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to resolutely resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son, the sandalwood incense originates from Mount Malaya.
It is named "Ox-Head. If one anoints the body with it, even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn them.

The name of this incense is Padmagarbha. A single pellet of this incense is as large as a sesame seed; if it is burned, its fragrance will pervade the entire realm of Jambudvīpa.
Any sentient beings who smell it shall be freed from all transgressions, and their aggregate of precepts will become pure. Good son!
On the Snowy Mountains there is a fragrance named Aruṇa. If any sentient being smells this fragrance, their mind will certainly become free from all defiled attachments.
When I preach the Dharma for them, there are none who do not attain the Stainless Samādhi.

They nourish all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Good son, among the gods of Skillful Transformation there is an incense called "Captivating the Mind.

This concludes the fourth major section below. Regarding the ten virtuous friends who embody the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*):
this means that the distinct ten perfections (*pāramitā*) cultivated through the preceding ten practices are fused into a single flavor and collectively dedicated toward three objects.
These are: dedication to sentient beings, which is the vast mind; dedication to bodhi, which is the foremost mind; and dedication to reality...
The limit is the constant mind. By means of these three minds, one converges upon the single mind of the Middle Way within the Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is symbolized by the fragrance of the vast land. As for the phrase "one who sells incense," "sells" means to trade. Whether buying or selling, both obtain the fragrance;
this signifies that the roots of goodness of both self and others can all be dedicated. Although the substance of the incense is subtle, its fragrance...
It pervades and fills everywhere to signify that even minute causes and small virtues, when each is dedicated in a manner equal to the Dharma-realm, become vast.
As for the elder named Utpalaka (Blue Lotus): just as a lotus emerges from the mud yet remains unstained, so too does he protect sentient beings while remaining free from attachment to signs.
Furthermore, the blue lotus is the most excellent among aquatic flowers; likewise, the act of saving and protecting is the most honored among those who enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, this is used to represent it. It is entrusted to ten virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), with the Elder Blue Lotus (*Nīlotpala*) placed first.

This is the dedication of merit that rescues and protects sentient beings while remaining free from the characteristics of sentient beings. Thus, because of the instructions of his previous spiritual mentors, the youth Sudhana disregards his own body and life;
he does so by giving rise to the eleven kinds of great [vows], such as the transformation and liberation of all sentient beings.
Vowing to single-mindedly seek all such merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he traveled by stages until he reached a vast kingdom.

Praise. This is the formal transmission of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). It simply states: "I am well able to distinguish all fragrances, and I also know the methods for blending all fragrances.

To say that one "knows fragrance" means that by means of the perfumes of morality (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), compassion (karuṇā), and so forth, one cultivates wholesome tendencies and extinguishes the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of evil;
thus, it refers to the practice of discerning the distinctions between fragrances. Furthermore, it refers to knowing how to harmonize and blend fragrances.

This refers to the unimpeded penetration of fusion. One shatters [all things] with the vajra-pestle; through the harmonization of the *prajñāpāramitā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one causes the pure and the mixed to be without obstruction.
Because compassion and wisdom are perfectly fused, they accomplish the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). Next, regarding "all fragrances," there are three aspects:

first, knowing the difference in the essence of fragrance; second, distinguishing differences according to number; third, knowing the difference in their power and function. Regarding "in this way" and so forth...

That is to say, he observed whether the roads were high or low, whether they were level or rugged, whether they were pure or defiled, and whether they were winding or straight. As he proceeded gradually along his journey, he reflected:

The causal basis for the path. It is the causal basis for accomplishing the practice of the *pāramitās*. It is the causal basis for accomplishing the practice of gathering in sentient beings.
It is the causal basis for accomplishing the practice of universally entering the *dharmadhātu* without obstruction.
It is the causal basis for accomplishing the practice of causing all sentient beings to eliminate false wisdom. It is the causal basis for accomplishing the practice of causing all sentient beings...

it is the cause for accomplishing the practice that causes all sentient beings to relinquish all views;
it is the cause for accomplishing the practice that causes all sentient beings to extract all thorns of evil; it is the cause for accomplishing the practice that causes one—
The cause for all sentient beings to reach the city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-pura*). Why is this?
Because it is from the presence of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that one obtains all wholesome dharmas, and by the power of the spiritual friend, one attains the path to omniscience.
Thinking thus—that a spiritual friend is difficult to see and difficult to encounter—he gradually traveled on. Having reached that city, he saw the boatman there.

Riding upon the vehicle of fear regarding birth and death, they abide in the causes of the whirlpools of all tranquil samādhis.

Adorned with the conduct of a bodhisattva, they possess the cause for the pure path of indestructible wisdom. They universally contemplate all phenomena throughout the ten directions as being entirely without obstruction.
It is an obstacle to the causes for the path of purification; it is a cause for swiftly entering the pure path of the ocean of all-knowledge.
Son of good family, here on this city’s seashore road, I have purely cultivated the bodhisattva practice of the banner of great compassion.
Son of good family, observing the impoverished sentient beings within Jambudvīpa, I have practiced various ascetic austerities for their benefit, according to their [needs].
May all these be fully satisfied. First, may their desires be fulfilled with worldly things; then, by bestowing the wealth of the Dharma, may they be made to rejoice.

May they be led to cultivate meritorious deeds, to give rise to the path of wisdom, to increase the power of their roots of goodness, to awaken the bodhicitta, to purify their bodhisattva vows, to strengthen the power of great compassion, to cultivate the path that extinguishes birth and death, and to never grow weary of it.
The practice of birth and death causes one to gather the ocean of all sentient beings, to cultivate the ocean of all merits,

"Born! Son of good family, I know all the jewel islands, all the jewel sites, all the categories of jewels, and all the species of jewels within the ocean.

I count the days and nights, the morning and evening, and the lengthening or shortening of the shadows and water-drops.

I also know whether the iron and wood of the ship are firm or brittle, whether its mechanisms are stiff or smooth, the volume of the waters, and whether the winds are headwinds or tailwinds. Regarding all such signs of safety and peril, there is nothing I do not clearly understand.
When it is time to proceed, I proceed; when it is time to stop, I stop. Good son, it is by having accomplished such wisdom that I am thus able.
I am always able to benefit all sentient beings. Good son, I use excellent ships to transport various merchants along safe paths;

Coming and going, I have never allowed even one of them to suffer damage or destruction. If there are sentient beings who see my body or hear my Dharma, I cause them to never again fear the ocean of birth and death;

they shall surely enter the ocean of all-knowledge, they shall surely be able to exhaust the ocean of all craving and desire, they shall be able to illuminate the ocean of the three periods of time with the light of wisdom, and they shall be able to bring all sentient beings to their end [of suffering].

The ocean of suffering. It can purify the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings; it can swiftly adorn and purify the ocean of all buddha-lands; it can universally travel to the great oceans of the ten directions;

If there are those who see me, hear of me, dwell with me, or remember me, all such acts shall not be in vain.
Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are skillfully able to traverse the great ocean of saṃsāra, remaining unstained by the ocean of all afflictions (*kleśa*),
being able to relinquish the ocean of all false views, and being able to contemplate the ocean of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

They are able to gather the ocean of sentient beings through the four means of integration; they are already well-established in the ocean of omniscience; they are able to extinguish the ocean of attachments of all sentient beings;
they are able to dwell with equanimity throughout the ocean of all times; and they are able to deliver the ocean of sentient beings by means of their supernormal powers.
They are able to discipline the ocean of sentient beings according to the proper time. How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?

With firm diligence as their ramparts and moats, and profound samādhi as their garden, they shatter the darkness of ignorance with the sunlight of wisdom, employing skillful means.

Freed from all defilements, they acquired the power of pure faith; they constantly delighted in seeing the Buddha, upheld the Buddha-dharma, and gave birth to the bodhicitta.
[He] exerts power, initiates the bodhisattva practice, enters the bodhisattva samādhi, attains bodhisattva wisdom, abides in bodhisattva right mindfulness, and increases bodhisattva aspiration.

they are always able to manifest before and behold all Buddhas; they constantly obtain to hear all Buddha-dharmas; they are always able to uphold and maintain all Buddha-dharmas;
they are always able to enter all Dharma-gates; and they enter all lands to study the bodhisattva practices.

Abiding through all kalpas to cultivate the bodhisattva path, he is able to know the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas, receive the protective mindfulness of all Tathāgatas, and attain the wisdom of all Tathāgatas. At that time, the elder addressed Sudhana, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have already been able to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, I have accomplished the power of the bodhisattva’s gateway of practice that reaches all places—a supernormal power that is non-reliant and non-constructive.
Son of good family, what is this bodhisattva’s gateway of practice that reaches all places? Son of good family:
Within this trichiliocosm, among all sentient beings of the desire realm— namely, all those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
all in the Yāma Heaven, all in the Tuṣita Heaven, all in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven,
all in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, all in the Māra heavens, and all other devas, nāgas, and so forth— [I am the foremost].
To yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—
in all dwellings such as villages, camps, cities, and towns— he preached the Dharma among all sentient beings,
causing them to abandon what is contrary to the Dharma, to cease disputes, to eliminate warfare, and to put an end to anger and contention.
May they cause the breaking of karmic enmities; may they cause the loosening of fetters; may they cause the emergence from prisons; may they cause the avoidance of terrors.
May they cause all unwholesome deeds and improper actions—from killing to wrong views—to be severed and strictly prohibited.
May they cause them to practice all wholesome dharmas in accordance with the Dharma; may they cause them to study and master all arts and crafts, thereby bringing benefit to all the world.
For their sake, I analyze various treatises to inspire joy in them and bring them gradually to maturity.
Following the ways of non-Buddhists, I teach them superior wisdom to cause them to sever all views and enter the Buddha-dharma;
even for all the Brahmās of the form realm, I likewise teach the transcendent and supreme Dharma. Just as I do in this trichiliocosm, so too [do I do] up to the tenth...

Throughout world-systems as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, I have everywhere expounded the Buddha-dharma, the Bodhisattva-dharma, the Śrāvaka-dharma, and the Pratyekabuddha-dharma;

I have spoken of the hells, of the sentient beings in the hells, and of the paths leading to the hells; I have spoken of animals, of the various distinctions among animals, and of the sufferings endured by animals.
He speaks of the realm of animals; he speaks of the world of King Yama; he speaks of the suffering in the world of King Yama; he speaks of the path leading to the world of King Yama.
He speaks of the world of devas; he speaks of the bliss in the world of devas; he speaks of the path leading to the world of devas. He speaks of the world of humans;
he speaks of the suffering and bliss in the world of humans; he speaks of the path leading to the world of humans. This is for the purpose of opening [the way].
To manifest the virtues of a bodhisattva; to cause the abandonment of the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra;

to cause the knowledge and vision of the sublime virtues of those who possess all-knowledge (sarvajña); to cause the knowledge that beings within the various realms of existence suffer due to delusion;
to cause the knowledge and vision of the unobstructed Dharma; to manifest the causes for the arising of all worlds; and to manifest...

I demonstrate to all the world that quiescence is bliss; I do so to cause sentient beings to abandon all conceptual attachments, to cause them to realize the Buddha’s dharma that is free from reliance, to cause them to forever extinguish the wheel of afflictions, and to enable them to turn the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma.
For the sake of sentient beings, I preach such a teaching. Good son, I know only this "Pervading All Places" Samādhi.
The Dharma-gate of the pure practice of the bodhisattva path; the power of spiritual penetrations that are non-reliant and non-constructive;
like all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with all sovereign spiritual penetrations, they are able to travel everywhere to all buddha-fields;
having attained the stage of the Universal Eye, they hear all sounds and speech; they universally enter into all dharmas with mastery of wisdom. Without...
He is free from conflict and possesses incomparable courage and vigor. With his broad and long tongue, he utters a voice of universal equality.
His body is wondrously beautiful, identical to that of all bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas; ultimately, they are non-dual and without distinction.
His wisdom-body is vast and expansive, universally entering the three periods of time; its realm is boundless, equal to empty space. How could I possibly know or describe him?
"Virtuous Conduct. Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Sūna.
In that land there is a city named Kaliṅgavana, where there is a bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā. Go to her and ask:
how does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated himself before her...
He circumambulated [the Buddha] immeasurable times, gazing upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.
As for the third, the householder Anuttaravijaya, he dedicated [his merit] equally to all Buddhas;

because he had attained superior supernormal powers that surpassed others, he was equal to all Buddhas, for there was nothing more excellent than them. Regarding his being in the land of Sukhāvatī, it is due to his equality with the Buddhas.

Dedication. Because he does not perceive beauty or ugliness, as all things are pure, joyful, and blissful, Sudhana, having received the instructions of his previous spiritual friends, gave rise to a mind of great compassion that is all-pervasive, and so forth, along with supreme wisdom and vows;
proceeding by stages, he arrived within that city and saw Anūpamaśreṣṭhin in the Great Adorned Banner无忧林 (Aśoka) Grove to the east of the city. Without...
Surrounded by a multitude of merchants, he adjudicated various human affairs and expounded the Dharma.
Sudhana beheld that elder, prostrated at his feet, and said: "O Victorious One, I am Sudhana.
I am single-mindedly seeking the path of the Bodhisattvas; I pray that you will speak for me. Then, that elder praised his resolve in various ways.
This correctly demonstrates the Dharma-realm. It says: "I shall proceed to all places through the gate of bodhisattva practice;
by the power of spiritual penetrations that are non-reliant and non-conditioned, because they are non-conditioned and non-reliant, I am able to reach everywhere. Later it asks:
"What is the gate of bodhisattva practice for reaching all places? It means: "In this trichiliocosm, I act for the sake of the six realms of existence..."
For sentient beings, I preach the Dharma according to their respective capacities, even up to the four supramundane noble dharmas;

I also preach them so that they may realize the Buddha’s dharma of non-reliance. There are twenty-two and a half lines of sūtra that investigate and explain its functional activity, clarifying how it reaches all places by extensively preaching the Dharma.
Following this, he expresses humility regarding himself and defers to the excellence [of the teaching], saying:
I know only this Dharma-door of purifying the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places, and this Dharma-door of the power of supernatural penetrations that is non-reliant and non-constructive.

As for those Bodhisattvas who are fully endowed with all supernatural penetrations and all cool Dharma-doors, these are not within my knowledge; thus, he humbles himself and defers to the superior, pointing the way.
Later, a friend said, "In the south there is a city in the country of Śūrpāraka called Kaliṅgavana.
There is a bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhahanu; you should go and ask her, and she will explain it for you. Sudhana prostrated himself, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages until he reached that royal city, where he searched everywhere for this bhikṣuṇī.

Countless people all told him: "Noble son, this bhikṣuṇī is teaching the Dharma and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings within the Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna) bestowed upon her by King Prasenajit. Then Sudhana—

The youth then went to that garden and surveyed it thoroughly. Within the garden, he saw a great tree named Pūrṇacandra (Full Moon), shaped like a multi-storied pavilion, emitting a great radiance that illuminated one yojana.
