The Flower Treasury [World-System] is as vast and lofty in form as the King of Snow Mountains.
It rains down various exquisite flowers without end, like the Pārijātaka tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, one sees a tree of nectar-fruit, shaped like a mountain of gold, constantly emitting radiance and fully endowed with all kinds of fruits. Moreover, one sees a mani-jewel.
There is a tree named Vairocana-garbha; its form is incomparable. At its summit is a heart-king maṇi-jewel, and it is universally adorned with maṇi-jewels of incalculable colors and forms.
Furthermore, there are clothing trees named "Pure," from which various colored garments hang down as ornaments. There are also musical instrument trees named "Joy," whose sounds are exquisite.

It surpasses the pleasures of all the devas in its excellence. Furthermore, there are fragrance trees named Universal Adornment (*Samalaṃkāra*), which constantly emit sublime fragrances that pervade the ten directions without obstruction.
Within the garden, there are also springs, streams, and ponds, all adorned with the seven precious gems.
Black sandalwood mud accumulates within them, and exquisite golden sand covers their bottoms. They possess the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa*).
The waters were perfectly full and overflowing, their surfaces entirely covered with blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*),
and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*). Countless jewel trees stood in rows all around,

and beneath each of these jewel trees were spread lion thrones, adorned with various exquisite jewels, draped with celestial garments, perfumed with sublime fragrances, and hung with precious ornaments.
Silken canopies were spread, with nets of Jambu-river gold covering them above. Precious bells swayed gently, emitting wondrous sounds.
Beneath some trees were spread lion thrones of the Lotus-Treasury;
beneath others, lion thrones of the Fragrance-King Mani-Treasury; and beneath others, lion thrones of the Dragon-Adorned Mani-King Treasury.
As for the seats of the sons [of the Buddha]: beneath some trees were spread lion-thrones of the treasury of the *maṇi*-king of jewel-lions;
beneath some trees were spread lion-thrones of the treasury of the *maṇi*-king Vairocana;
and beneath some trees were spread lion-thrones of the treasury of the *maṇi*-kings Vairocana of the ten directions. Each and every one of these thrones...
Each was surrounded by one hundred thousand precious lion-thrones, every one of which was endowed with immeasurable adornments.
This great garden was filled everywhere with various jewels, like a treasure island in the great ocean. Kāliṅga cloth was spread upon its ground;
it was soft, exquisite, and produced a pleasant tactile sensation. When stepped upon, it sank to the ankle; when lifted, it returned to its original state.
Innumerable birds emit harmonious and elegant sounds. The precious sandalwood groves are exquisitely adorned.
Various wondrous flowers fall perpetually in an inexhaustible rain, like Śakra’s Garden of Miscellaneous Flowers. An incomparable king of perfumes pervasively scents all things.
It was like Śakra’s Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), where musical trees, precious *tāla* trees,
and nets of various jeweled bells produced exquisite sounds, like the songs sung by the celestial maidens of the Heaven of Sovereign Power (*Īśvara*).
It was adorned with various wonderful garments hanging from wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and it possessed hundreds of thousands of pavilions, as varied in color as the great ocean.
Adorned with various jewels, it was like the Great City of Sudarśana in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
its jeweled canopy spread far and wide like the peak of Mount Sumeru, and its radiance shone everywhere like the palace of Brahmā.

At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld this great garden, adorned with immeasurable merit and manifold ornaments—all of which were the fruition of the bodhisattva’s karmic retribution and his supramundane roots of goodness.
This arising is the outflow of the merit of making offerings to all Buddhas; it is peerless among all the worlds.
All of this was accomplished by the Bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā through her realization that all phenomena are like illusions, and by the accumulation of vast, pure, and virtuous karmic merit.
It was witnessed by the immeasurable multitudes of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings throughout the trichiliocosm.
All those born there enter this garden without it becoming cramped. Why is this? It is because of the inconceivable power of the bhikṣuṇī’s majestic spiritual authority.
At that time, Sudhana saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated upon great lion thrones beneath all the jewel trees;
her physical form was upright and dignified, her deportment was tranquil, and her faculties were perfectly disciplined.
Like a great elephant king, his mind is free from defilement and turbidity, like a pure pool. He universally fulfills all requests, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Unstained by worldly dharmas, he is like a lotus flower. His mind is fearless, like a lion king.
He upholds the pure precepts, immovable as Mount Sumeru. He can cause those who behold him to attain mental coolness, like a sovereign of exquisite fragrance.
He can remove the heat of the afflictions of sentient beings like the exquisite sandalwood from the Snowy Mountains;
those who see him have their various sufferings extinguished like the King of Medicines, Sudarśana; seeing him is never in vain, like the deity Varuṇa;
he can cause the sprouts of all roots of goodness to grow like a fertile and rich field. In each and every assembly, though the congregations differ, that which he teaches remains the same.
The Dharma-gates are likewise each distinct. In some instances, he saw her seated on a throne, surrounded by a host of Śuddhāvāsa devas, with the son of Maheśvara as their leader;
for these bhikṣuṇīs, she was preaching a Dharma-gate named "Inexhaustible Liberation."
In some places she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of Brahmā deities, with the Brahmā King Priyadarśana as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī was preaching for them a Dharma-gate called the "Pure Wheel of Vocalization with Universal Gate Distinctions.
In other places she was seen seated, surrounded by sons and daughters of the gods from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, with the Lord of that Heaven as their leader.
She acts as their leader. This bhikṣuṇī teaches them a Dharma-gate called "The Pure Mind of a Bodhisattva.
Or, one may see her seated, surrounded by devaputras and devakanyās of the Sunirmita Heaven, with the King of the Sunirmitas acting as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī teaches them a Dharma-gate called "The Excellent Adornment of All Dharmas. Or, one may see her seated.

Surrounded by the sons and daughters of the Tuṣita Heaven, with the King of the Tuṣita Heaven as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī expounds for them a Dharma-gate called the "Revolution of the Heart-Treasury.
Or, one may see her seated, surrounded by the sons and daughters of the Suyāma Heaven, with the King of the Suyāma Heaven as their leader; this bhikṣuṇī...

She was preaching a dharma-gate called "Boundless Adornment. Or she was seen seated, surrounded by the sons and daughters of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, with Śakra-devendra as their leader; this bhikṣuṇī was preaching a dharma-gate called "The Gate of Disenchantment.
Or she was seen seated with the Nāga King Hundred Radiances, the Nāga King Nanda, and the Nāga King Upananda.
Surrounded by Nanda the Naga King, Manasvin the Naga King, Elapatra the Naga King,
Anavatapta the Naga King, and others, as well as naga sons and naga daughters— with Sagara the Naga King as their leader—
this bhikṣuṇī expounded for them a Dharma gate called "The Radiant Adornment of the Buddha’s Sphere of Supernatural Power. Or...
She was seen seated, surrounded by a host of yakṣas, with the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī was preaching for them a dharma-gate called "The Treasury that Protects and Saves All Sentient Beings.
Or she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of gandharvas, with the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra as their leader; this bhikṣuṇī...
She was preaching a Dharma-gate called "Inexhaustible Joy. Or she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of asuras, with the asura king Rāhu at their head;
for them, this bhikṣuṇī was preaching a Dharma-gate called "The Gateway of Wisdom for Swiftly Adorning the Dharmadhātu. Or she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of garuḍas, [with] Jaitra...
With the Garuḍa King as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma-gate called "Terrorizing the Ocean of All Existences.
Or she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of Kiṃnaras, with the Great Tree Kiṃnara King as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma-gate called "The Radiance of the Buddha’s Conduct. Or she was seen...
Seated there, surrounded by a host of mahoragas, with the mahoraga king Āmra as their leader,
this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma gate called "Arousing the Mind of Joy in the Buddha. Or, seeing her seated there,
surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of men and women, this bhikṣuṇī taught the Dharma.

The gate is named "All Supreme Practices. Alternatively, one may see her seated, surrounded by a host of rākṣasas, headed by the Great Tree Rākṣasa King who constantly robs [beings] of their vital essence;
this bhikṣuṇī preaches for them a dharma-gate named "Generating a Mind of Compassion.
Or, one may see her seated, surrounded by sentient beings who have faith in and delight in the Śrāvaka Vehicle. This...
He saw a bhikṣuṇī seated on a throne, teaching a dharma-gate called "Victorious Wisdom Radiance," surrounded by sentient beings who take faith and delight in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Or he saw her seated on a throne, teaching a dharma-gate called "Vast Radiance of the Buddha’s Merits," surrounded by sentient beings who take faith and delight in the Mahāyāna. This bhikṣuṇī...

He saw the bhikṣuṇī seated on a throne, teaching a dharma-gate called the "Light of Wisdom of the Universal Gate Samādhi," surrounded by bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
Or he saw her seated on a throne, teaching a dharma-gate called the "Gathering of the Vows of All Buddhas," surrounded by bodhisattvas of the second stage. This bhikṣuṇī...
He saw her seated, teaching a Dharma-door named "The Stainless Wheel" to a retinue of Bodhisattvas of the third stage.
Or he saw her seated, teaching a Dharma-door named "Tranquil Adornment" to a retinue of Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage. Or he saw her seated, teaching a Dharma-door named "Arising as One."
The sphere of omniscience. Or he saw her seated, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the fifth stage, as this bhikṣuṇī was preaching the dharma-gate named "Exquisite Flower Treasury.
Or he saw her seated, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the sixth stage, as this bhikṣuṇī was preaching the dharma-gate named "Vairocana Treasury. Or he saw...
Seated upon a throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, this bhikṣuṇī was preaching a dharma-gate called "The Stage of Universal Adornment.

Or, he saw her seated upon a throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, this bhikṣuṇī preaching a dharma-gate called "The Body of the Sphere of the Entire Dharmadhātu. Or, he saw her seated upon a throne, [surrounded by bodhisattvas] of the ninth [stage].
Surrounded by bodhisattvas of the various stages, this bhikṣuṇī was teaching a dharma-gate called "Adornment of the Power of Non-Apprehension.
Or, he saw her seated, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, this bhikṣuṇī teaching a dharma-gate called "The Unobstructed Wheel. Or, he saw her seated, surrounded by Vajrapāṇi deities.
They circumambulated him. This bhikṣuṇī was preaching a Dharma-gate called "Vajra-Wisdom Nārāyaṇa Adornment.

Sudhana saw all the sentient beings in all such realms of existence who were already matured, already tamed, and capable of being vessels for the Dharma, all entering this garden and sitting in a circle beneath their respective seats around the Lion.

The bhikṣuṇī Bhṛkuṭī expounded the Dharma according to the differences in their inclinations, understandings, superiorities, and inferiorities, causing them to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because this bhikṣuṇī has entered the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Universal Eye: Abandonment and Attainment," which explains the *prajñāpāramitā* of all Buddha-dharmas.
The gate of the differentiation of the dharma-realm; the gate of the perfection of wisdom that shatters all wheels of obstruction;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom that gives birth to the virtuous minds of all sentient beings;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom of sublime adornment; the gate of the perfection of wisdom of the unobstructed treasury of reality; the dharma-realm...
The gate of the perfection of wisdom of fulfillment; the gate of the perfection of wisdom of the heart-treasury;

the gate of the perfection of wisdom of the universal source-treasury. With these ten gates of the perfection of wisdom as the foremost, they enter into countless millions of such gates of the perfection of wisdom. All the bodhisattvas within this Sunlight Garden and...
All these sentient beings were first inspired to resolve their minds on enlightenment by the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā;
they have upheld the True Dharma, contemplated and cultivated it, and attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā’s grove, her seat, and so forth.
This was her walking meditation. Such was the assembly, such the supernormal power, and such the eloquence.
Furthermore, she heard an inconceivable Dharma-gate, and the vast cloud of Dharma moistened her heart. She then formed this thought:

"I shall circumambulate [the Buddha] to the right for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of times. At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī emitted a great radiance, which universally illuminated the park and the majesty of the assembly.
The youth Sudhana immediately saw his own body and all the trees within the grove circumambulating this bhikṣuṇī to the right for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Having completed the circumambulation, Sudhana stood with palms joined and said: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He focused his mind, yet he did not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.

The bhikṣuṇī said, "Noble son, I have attained liberation called 'Accomplishment of All-Knowledge' (Sarvajñatā-saṃpatti). Sudhana asked, "Noble One, for what reason is it called 'Accomplishment of All-Knowledge'?"
"Omniscience. The bhikṣuṇī said, "Noble son, this light of wisdom universally illumines all phenomena of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, what is the scope of this light of wisdom?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "Noble son, having entered this gate of the light of wisdom, I have attained the birth of all phenomena."

O King, by means of this samādhi, one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and travels to all worlds throughout the ten directions, to the Tuṣita heaven palaces, to the presence of Bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).

Before each and every Bodhisattva, one manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Each body performs acts of worship as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields, namely:
Manifesting in the forms of celestial kings, up to and including human kings, I hold clouds of flowers, clouds of garlands, burning incense, unguents, and powdered incense;

robes, necklaces, banners, pennants, silken canopies, jeweled nets, jeweled curtains, jeweled treasuries, and jeweled lamps—all such ornaments as these I hold and offer in worship. As when dwelling...

Just as the Bodhisattvas in the Tuṣita palace [manifest their deeds], so too do they manifest dwelling in the womb, birth from the womb, life as a householder, renunciation of the household life, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma, and entering into nirvāṇa.

Likewise, during the interval between these, they may dwell in celestial palaces, or dwell in the palaces of nāgas, or even dwell in the palaces of humans; regarding each and every one of those Tathāgatas—

In all such places, I have made offerings in this manner. If there are sentient beings who know that I thus make offerings to the Buddhas, they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there are sentient beings who come to my presence, I immediately preach the *prajñāpāramitā* for them. Good son, I see all...
Sentient beings do not conceptualize the marks of sentient beings, because their wisdom is limited by clear vision.
They hear all speech without conceptualizing the marks of speech, because their minds have no attachments. They see all Tathāgatas without conceptualizing the marks of the Tathāgatas.
Because they have fully realized the Dharma-body, they maintain all wheels of Dharma without discriminating the characteristics of those wheels.

Because they have awakened to the self-nature of phenomena, they know all phenomena universally in a single thought-moment without discriminating the characteristics of those phenomena. This is because they know that phenomena are like illusions.
"Good son, I only know this liberation that accomplishes all-knowledge. As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, their minds are free from discrimination and they universally know all dharmas.
Sitting upright in a single body, they fill the Dharma-realm; within their own bodies they manifest all lands;
in a single thought-moment they go to the abodes of all Buddhas; and within their own bodies they universally manifest a single..."
By means of the spiritual power of all Buddhas, they lift up unspeakably many Buddha-worlds with a single hair.
Within a single pore of their own body, they manifest the formation and destruction of unspeakable worlds.
In a single thought-moment, they dwell together with unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings. In a single thought-moment, they enter into unspeakably unspeakable [realms].
Throughout all kalpas, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Son of good family, to the south of here there is a land called Durga. In that land there is a city named Ratnavyuha-alamkara.
Within it dwells a woman named Vasumitra. Go to her and ask: "How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct?"
While practicing the bodhisattva path, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion,
and then took his leave and departed.
The fourth is the dedication reaching all places (*sarvatragatā-pariṇāmanā*). It is associated with the name of the spiritual friend Siṃha-praśarita.
*Praśarita* means to extend or unfold with mastery; because he travels without fear, there is nowhere he does not reach.
The term "bhikṣuṇī" refers to pure compassion, which causes goodness to pervade everywhere. The country is named Śūna, which here means "valiant. Valiant...

It is the power of vigor (*vīrya*), for it enables the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to reach everywhere. Furthermore, according to the meaning clarified by the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), this corresponds to diligence (*vīrya*).
As for the city named Kaliṅgavana, translated according to its meaning as "the time of mutual combat," it refers to the establishment of a city based on victory in battle;
this symbolizes this dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which, through the great power of faith and understanding, is vast.
Because great wisdom is unobstructed, its meaning corresponds to the time of battle. Initially, one relies on the teachings to seek it out.

As for the term "Grove of Victorious Light" (Jetavana), it symbolizes that through the victorious light of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), one causes those roots of goodness to pervade the garden of the Dharma-realm.
At that time, the youth Sudhana went to that garden, descended, and paid his respects and inquiries.
First, there were six kinds of external environments (*niśraya-vipāka*) he beheld, which the Sūtra divides into six sections: 1. He beheld the groves of trees within the garden;

this consists of ten lines of sūtra, which symbolize the forest of untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities, for they are established based upon the practice of the untainted dharmas. 2. He beheld the springs, streams, and ponds below.
1. The three lines of the sūtra represent the spring of the eight liberations, from which flow the waters of the eight meritorious qualities. 2.

Beneath the three precious trees of the immeasurables, there are eight lines and a half of the sūtra, representing the spreading of the Dharma-jewel throne, adorned according to the Dharma; this differs from the four [preceding sections]. 3.
Within this great garden, beneath it, there are eight lines of the sūtra that variously clarify the adornments, representing that the myriad practices are not of one kind. 4. At that time, Sudhana...
Below, there are four lines of sūtra that set forth their causes. The six [lines] and two lines of sūtra below the "three thousand" clarify the sovereign function of the fruit.
Next, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, it clarifies the vision of the primary retribution. The first eight lines of sūtra clarify the pervasive manifestation of supreme virtues throughout.
Next, from the section on seeing the place and the seat, there are thirty lines of sūtra that specifically clarify what is pervaded; this is the exposition.
The dharmas each differ. There are thirty locations in total, divided into three parts. First, the initial sixteen locations pertain to the eight classes of beings, including humans and devas.
Next, the passage of three lines following "or seen" clarifies the universal presence among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Next, the passage of sixteen lines following "or seen" clarifies the universal presence among the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten stages up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment. Next...
The passage beginning with "In this way" below summarizes the various types who hear the Dharma and resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" below generally reveals the underlying causes and explains the attainment of mastery; it consists of nine lines of scripture.

The first ten [lines] regarding Prajñā represent the transformer (the teacher), while the subsequent section beginning with "In this Garden of Day-Blooming Flowers" represents those being transformed, as their faculties have already matured. The above collectively clarifies the identity of this bhikṣu.
The Bhikṣuṇī, by means of her very body, sat throughout nine locations within this single garden and preached the Dharma.
This was because she taught the Dharma for the sake of transforming sentient beings of the nine realms; thus, it symbolizes the dedication of merit to reaching all places.
That which is dedicated is entirely this practice of the Dharma. Below, the youth Sudhana sees the Bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā in this manner.
Because it was so supremely wonderful, he further gave rise to a superior resolve. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī first emitted light to receive Sudhana and extend her respect.
After he had paid his respects and given rise to the resolve, he inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. Below, the Dharma-realm is correctly revealed. The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I have only attained the accomplishment of the liberation of 'all-knowledge' (sarvajñā). 'All-knowledge' is so called because it is identical to the wisdom of the Buddha. Next...

Sudhana inquired about its essence, to which it was replied: "Because a single thought universally illumines all. Subsequently, Sudhana again asked about its sphere of activity (*viṣaya*), whereupon the function of its operation was explained.
Next, the bhikṣu answered: "I have entered this gate of the light of wisdom and attained the King of Samādhis that gives birth to all dharmas;
therefore, I have obtained the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*). This first clarifies the basis upon which all [dharmas] rely.
Because of this wisdom, she is able to enter the King Samādhi (Rājasamādhi). As for the "King Samādhi," it is so called because all other samādhis enter into it.
Next, there are fifteen lines of scripture following the passage on the ten directions, which clarify the wisdom of functional application based upon that [samādhi].
That is to say, the bhikṣuṇī ascends to preach the Dharma for the six realms and the three vehicles; all of these are the functional application and the wisdom of application of this samādhi.
Therefore, this has already demonstrated the essence and function of the dedication that reaches all places.
Thus, [the text] below expresses humility and defers to the superior, saying: "I know only this gate of liberation of omniscience;
as for the gates of the Dharma such as those where Bodhisattvas universally know all phenomena, filling the Dharma-realm while sitting upright in a single body, and so forth—I do not know them."
How is this known? Therefore, the latter friend pointed the way, saying:
"To the south of here, in the city of Ratnavyūha in the kingdom of Durgama, there is a woman named Vasumitrā. You should go and inquire of her;
she will explain it to you. Then Sudhana paid his respects and departed.

Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Nine: Entering the Dharmadhātu.
At that time, the light of great wisdom illuminated and opened the mind of the youth Sudhana. He contemplated and observed, seeing the nature of all phenomena.
He attained the dhāraṇī-door of comprehending all sounds and voices; he attained the dhāraṇī-door of upholding all wheels of Dharma;
he attained the power of great compassion that serves as a refuge for all sentient beings; and he attained the power of observation.

The gateway of the light of the principles and meanings of all dharmas; the attainment of pure vows that fill the dharma-realm and universally illumine the light of wisdom regarding all dharmas in the ten directions; the attainment of sovereign power to universally adorn all worlds;
and the attainment of the vow to universally initiate the complete fulfillment of all bodhisattva activities. Proceeding gradually on his journey, he arrived at the perilous land of Ratnavyūha.
In the city of Śroṇāparāntaka, people searched everywhere for the maiden Puṣpamitrā. There were those in the city who did not know of this girl’s merit and wisdom;
they thought to themselves: "This youth has tranquil faculties and clear wisdom. He is neither deluded nor distracted, gazing steadily at a distance of one fathom.
He is without weariness or indolence, and is free from all grasping and attachment. His eyes do not blink, and his mind..."
It is unmoving, profound and vast like the great ocean. One should not harbor thoughts of craving or attachment toward this woman Vāsudhārā;
one should not harbor perverted thoughts, nor give rise to perceptions of purity or perceptions of desire. One should not be captivated by the beauty of this woman.
This youth does not practice the ways of Māra, does not enter the realm of Māra, and does not sink into the mire of desire.
Bound by Māra, she refrains from engaging in what should not be done. With what intention do you seek this woman?
Among them was one who already knew that this woman possessed wisdom; he said to Sudhana, "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, it is well that you are now able to investigate and search for the lady Vasumitrā. You have already attained the vast..."
Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You should resolutely seek the state of Buddhahood; you should resolutely desire to act as a refuge for all sentient beings;
you should resolutely desire to extract the poisonous arrows of craving from all sentient beings;
you should resolutely desire to shatter all notions of purity regarding female form held by all sentient beings. Son of good family, the woman Vasumitrā—
He resided in his own home to the north of the marketplace within this city.
When the youth Sudhana heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as he went to her gate.
He beheld her residence, vast and magnificent, with jeweled walls, jeweled trees, and jeweled moats, each surrounded by tenfold enclosures. Within those jeweled moats, fragrant water overflowed.
The ground was covered with a layer of golden sand. Various celestial jewel flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—completely overspread the surface of the water.
Palaces and towers were distributed everywhere; gates, portals, windows, and casements faced one another in orderly rows.
All were provided with jeweled nets and bells, and banners and streamers were set out throughout, adorned with immeasurable rare treasures.
Adorned with lapis lazuli as its ground, interspersed with various jewels, it was perfumed with burning aloeswood and anointed with sandalwood.
Suspended jeweled bells produced melodic sounds when stirred by the wind, and celestial flowers were scattered, covering the entire ground. Its manifold splendor and beauty are beyond description;
hundreds of thousands of treasuries of rare gems and ten great groves served as its adornments. At that time, the virtuous...
Dhana beheld this woman’s countenance as upright and majestic, her physical marks perfect and complete, her skin golden, and her eyes and hair deep blue.
She was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate; among the humans and devas of the desire realm, none could compare to her.
Her voice was exquisite and transcended all the Brahma worlds, fully possessing every variety of sentient beings’ distinct speech and sounds, such that there was nothing she could not understand.
He has attained full realization and profoundly mastered the meaning of words, being skillful in discourse. Having attained the wisdom of illusion, he enters the gateway of skillful means;
his body is adorned with various ornaments and necklaces of many jewels. A wish-fulfilling *maṇi* serves as a jeweled crown upon his head.
Furthermore, he is surrounded by immeasurable retinues, all of whom share the same roots of goodness, identical practices, and vows, and possess great merit.

The treasury was fully endowed and inexhaustible. At that time, the woman Vasumitrā emitted from her body a vast radiance that illuminated all the palaces within the residence. Those who encountered this light found their bodies cooled and refreshed.
Then, Sudhana went before her, prostrated at her feet, and stood with palms joined, saying: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon [enlightenment]..."
"I have generated the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.
He then replied: "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'The Limit Beyond Greed. In accordance with one's inclinations..."
And I manifest my body for them. If a deva sees me, I appear in the form of a celestial maiden with a radiance and excellence beyond compare.
Likewise, even if humans, non-humans, or others see me, I immediately manifest as a human or non-human female for them.
I cause all to see me according to their inclinations and desires. If there are sentient beings who, being entangled by the mind of desire, come to where I am, I preach the Dharma for them;
having heard the Dharma, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva samādhi of the unattached realm.
If there are sentient beings who see me even for a moment, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva samādhi of joy.
If there are sentient beings who briefly converse with me, they shall be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Unobstructed Sound.
If there are sentient beings who briefly take my hand, they shall be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Traveling to All Buddha-fields.
If there are sentient beings who briefly ascend my seat, they shall be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva [Samādhi of] Liberation...
The liberation of the Samādhi of Radiance: if there are sentient beings who even briefly gaze upon me, they shall be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Tranquil Adornment.

If there are sentient beings who see me stretching my limbs, they shall be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Subduing Non-Buddhists. If there are sentient beings who see me blink my eyes, they shall be freed from desire and attain...

The Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of the Buddha’s Realm: if there are sentient beings who embrace me, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Gathering and Never Abandoning All Sentient Beings.
If there are sentient beings who kiss my lips, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva [Samādhi] of Increasing the Treasury of Merit for All Sentient Beings.

...obscured. Whenever any sentient beings draw near to me, they all attain the state of being free from the limits of greed and enter the Bodhisattva stage of omniscience, manifesting the unimpeded liberation.
Sudhana said: "Noble One, what roots of goodness have you planted and what meritorious deeds have you cultivated to achieve such sovereign mastery? He replied: "Good son, I recall the past..."
In the past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Uccagāmin (High Conduct). The capital city of that king was called Suvilokitamukha (Exquisite Gate).
Good son, out of compassion for sentient beings, that Tathāgata Uccagāmin entered the royal city;
as he stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the entire city trembled and suddenly became vast and expansive, adorned with various jewels, with immeasurable lights reflecting one another.
[The ground] was thoroughly covered. Various kinds of precious flowers were strewn upon the earth, and the music of the devas played simultaneously.
All the devas filled the void. Good son, at that time, I was the wife of a householder, named Shanhui (Good Wisdom).

Upon witnessing the Buddha’s supernatural power, my mind attained awakening. I then went with my husband to the place where the Buddha was and made an offering of a single precious coin. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī was the Buddha’s attendant;
he taught me the Dharma so that I might resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son, this is all I know of this bodhi—

Sāriputra is liberated at the limit of freedom from greed. As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished boundless wisdom of skillful means, whose treasury is vast and whose sphere of activity is incomparable—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Śubhavyūha. Within it dwells a householder named Viśeṣamati.
"Ti-lo! He constantly makes offerings at the stūpa of the Buddha Candanāsana.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him countless times.
Gazing up at him with earnest devotion, he took his leave and departed.
Fifth is the good friend, the maiden Puṣpamitrā. She is entrusted with the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit;
by the power of this dedication, one is able to accomplish an immeasurable treasury of merit. Puṣpamitra is translated here as "World-Friend" (Shiyou) and is also called...

O celestial friend, because he transforms according to the skillful means of worldly humans and devas: the land is named "Perilous and Difficult" because those who follow the non-path of retrogression cannot proceed there;
the city is named "Jeweled Adornment" because it can produce inexhaustible treasuries of merit through both conforming to and opposing worldly conduct.
Because Sudhana heard the Light of All-Knowledge, he contemplated, cultivated, and entered it, thereby attaining [realization].

There are two kinds of benefit: by seeing the nature of all phenomena, one attains the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*); furthermore, by thoroughly knowing all that is inferior, one attains expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Because of the former, one exhaustively understands the distinctions of the three periods of time; because of attaining these two wisdoms, one is able to manifest逆行 (*pratiloma-caryā*, contrary conduct).
Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), each act of contrary conduct ultimately perfects the treasury of merit (*guṇa-kośa*). Therefore, by means of...
Vasudhārā resides in this station. Once Sudhana had obtained these benefits, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Ratnavyūha in the country of Durgama.
He sought Vasudhārā there. As for the name "Durgama" (Difficult to Traverse), it refers to the difficulty of entering desire through the path of reversal;
because she turns the reverse into the compliant, it becomes "Ratnavyūha" (Adorned with Jewels). Vasudhārā’s practice of the reverse path is intended...
In this regard, because he acts in a counter-intuitive manner that is difficult to fathom and cannot be understood through ordinary means, everyone who first encountered Sudhana gave rise to doubt;
it was not that they lacked the eye of wisdom, but rather [they did not recognize him]. Someone said, "He has attained vast and great benefit.

As for the statement that he is "in the city, in the northern marketplace," this means that while he practices dhyāna amidst desire, he remains constantly tranquil even in the midst of clamor. "Within his own home" refers to...
Only by abiding in ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) can one practice the "counter-flow" (*pratiloma*). Sudhana, following these instructions, went to visit him;
first he beheld the excellence of the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (the environment), for which there are seven lines of scripture describing the various adornments of the house.

This is because within ultimate emptiness, there is no virtue that is not fully present. Next, he beheld the majesty of the *sambhoga-kāya* (the primary manifestation), for which there are eight lines of scripture concerning the body of Vāsantī.

Regarding "there is a light that universally illumines the interior of the house": because one uses the light of primordial wisdom to illuminate ultimate emptiness, those who touch it find their bodies attain coolness;
this is precisely the attainment of the *vairāgya-samādhi* (samādhi of freedom from desire).
Sudhana respectfully inquired about the dharma-gate, and Vāsukī replied that she had attained the Bodhisattva liberation named "The Limit of Freedom from Greed. This is the formal transmission.

This is the "Dharmadhātu of Oneself. First, its name is indicated. Regarding the phrase "the limit of detachment from desire" (*vairāgya-koṭi*): ordinary beings are attached to desire, while those of the Two Vehicles detach from it.
The Bodhisattva, however, attains liberation without severing greed and desire, because through wisdom they realize that the nature of things is empty;
thus, desire itself is the Path. Therefore, abiding amidst defilement yet remaining unstained constitutes the ultimate limit of detachment from desire, for it is the reality itself.
Next, the specific functions and activities of the samādhi are revealed: manifesting various bodies and demonstrating various practices.

Fifteen lines of scripture fully illustrate how, according to one's desires and aptitudes, one attains profound samādhi. Subsequently, Sudhana said, inquiring into the causes and conditions for attaining this Dharma;
his intention was to practice in accordance with the teachings. Therefore, Vāsantī replied that in the past, by means of one...
He offered precious coins as an offering to the Tathāgata Uccagāmin. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī was the Buddha’s attendant;
he expounded the Dharma for me, causing me to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
This practice thus originated from fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), which is why the Buddha was named Uccagāmin. For this is the very root of samādhi. Nevertheless, a single coin is extremely minute.
One who is able to attain this profound samādhi regards jewels as their ultimate object of affection; though the objects are small, their attachment is intense.
Because they are able to relinquish what is so deeply cherished, it is fitting that they attain liberation at the limit of freedom from greed. Next, he humbles himself, saying:
"I have attained only this single dharma-gate. As for the Bodhisattvas who have accomplished boundless and vast spheres of experience, I am not [like them]."
"I know," he said, pointing toward his companion behind him. "In the south there is a city called Supāraga.
There dwells a householder named Vīśeṣagiri. You should go and inquire of him; he will explain it to you. Sudhana paid his respects and departed.
At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages until he reached the city of Supāraga.

He went to the house of the lay devotee, prostrated at his feet, and stood with palms joined, saying: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate it."
“Excellent! I have heard that the Noble One is skilled in providing instruction. I pray that you will explain this to me.
The householder replied, “Son of good family, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called ‘The Limit of Non-Nirvāṇa. Son of good family, I do not give rise to the thought:
‘Such a Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa,’ nor ‘Such a Tathāgata is currently entering parinirvāṇa,’ nor ‘Such a Tathāgata [will enter parinirvāṇa].’”
"When entering parinirvāṇa, I know that in all worlds throughout the ten directions, no Buddha-Tathāgata ever truly enters parinirvāṇa;
it is only for the sake of taming sentient beings that they manifest such an appearance.
Son of good family, when I opened the door of the Tathāgata Candanāsana’s stūpa, I attained a samādhi named ‘The Inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed. Son of good family..."
"In every thought-moment, I enter this samādhi; in every thought-moment, I come to know all immeasurable and supreme matters.
Sudhana said, "What is the scope of this samādhi? The householder replied, "Noble son, when I enter this samādhi, I see all the Buddhas of this world in their proper sequence, namely Kāśyapa..."
The Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Vipaśyin Buddha,
Tiṣya Buddha, Puṣya Buddha, Anuttarajaya Buddha, Anuttarapadma Buddha— these and others were the leaders.
In a single moment of thought, they see one hundred Buddhas; they see one thousand Buddhas; they see one hundred thousand Buddhas; they see ten million Buddhas;
a billion Buddhas; ten billion Buddhas; a hundred billion Buddhas; a hundred trillion Buddhas; a quadrillion Buddhas; nayuta-billions of Buddhas;
and even as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds. All such [Buddhas] are seen in this successive order.
I also saw that Buddha’s initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, his planting of various roots of goodness, his attainment of supreme supernormal powers, and his fulfillment of great vows.
I saw him practicing sublime conduct, perfecting the pāramitās, entering the bodhisattva stages, and attaining pure patience.
I saw him subduing the armies of Māra, achieving perfect enlightenment, purifying his buddha-field, being surrounded by assemblies, emitting great radiance, and turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma.
I am able to maintain, remember, observe, analyze, and manifest all the various distinctions of supernatural transformations.
This applies equally to all Buddhas of the future, such as Maitreya Buddha, and all Buddhas of the present, such as Vairocana Buddha.
It is likewise for all that exists in this world and in the worlds of the ten directions.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, as well as the assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, are all likewise.
Good son, I have attained only this bodhisattva liberation of the limit of non-nirvāṇa.
As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who with a single moment of wisdom universally know the three periods of time and in a single thought-moment enter all samādhis—[I do not know their practice].
The wisdom that has arrived enters and constantly illuminates the mind. It is without discrimination regarding any phenomena;
it realizes that all Buddhas are entirely equal. The Tathāgata, myself, and all sentient beings are identical and without duality.
Knowing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, it is free from thought and devoid of movement, yet it is able to universally enter all worlds. Free from...
All those who dwell in the seal of the Buddha-dharma through various forms of discernment are able to awaken all sentient beings within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good son, to the south of here there is a mountain named Potalaka.
There dwells a bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should train as a bodhisattva.
Practicing the Bodhisattva path, he then spoke these verses:
Upon a mountain in the sea dwell many sages and worthies; Composed of various jewels, it is exceedingly pure and serene.
Flowers, fruits, and groves of trees fill it everywhere, And springs, streams, ponds, and pools are all fully present.
The heroic man Avalokiteśvara dwells on this mountain for the benefit of sentient beings;
go there and inquire about all his virtues, and he shall show you the great skillful means.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest reverence, and took his leave.
And he departed.
The sixth good friend is Vessantara. He entrusts all roots of goodness in their equality to dedication.
As for why the good friend is named Vessantara, it means "enveloping" (*veṣṭana*); in meaning, it corresponds to "comprehensively encompassing. This refers to being enveloped within the stupa.
Because it encompasses all Buddhas—or as some say, "enters into" them—this elder makes offerings to the Buddha-stūpa. Now, the stūpa symbolizes the *dharmakāya* of quiescent extinction.
Since the *dharmakāya* gives rise to the equality of all Buddhas, it symbolizes the gathering of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), for they enter into the state of equality of the *dharmakāya*.
As for the city named "Good Friend" (*Suhṛd*), not a single root of goodness fails to reach ultimate perfection.

Because it is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), Sudhana followed the instructions to seek it out. Upon reaching the city of Supāraga, he went to the house of the lay devotee (gṛhapati), where he paid his respects and inquired.
The lay devotee said to him: "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'The Limit of Non-Parinirvāṇa' (*aparinirvāṇakoṭi*).
This is the formal bestowal of the name of the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the term "non-parinirvāṇa," *pari* means "to enter. It refers to exhausting all suchnesses (*tathatā*).
This is because [the Tathāgata] does not enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of *nirvāṇa*. That is to say, the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, quiescent, and forever at peace;
it is perpetually in *nirvāṇa*, so how could it enter again? Therefore, it is said that it "does not enter. Sandalwood incense represents the *dharmakāya*;
since its fragrance permeates everywhere, there is equality between the Buddha and sentient beings. Thus, whenever sentient beings possess roots of goodness, they are all the *dharmakāya*.
Because they flow forth [from the Dharma-realm], they are equal; because each and every one returns to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
Therefore, the Elder told Sudhana: "When I opened the door of the stūpa, I attained a samādhi named 'Inexhaustible Buddha-seed'.
This intends to reveal that all roots of goodness are the "Buddha-seed" because they rely upon the Dharma-body; thus, in every thought-moment, one enters this.
Samādhi. In every thought-moment, he attains knowledge of immeasurable and sublime matters;
because each and every matter accords with the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are called "sublime. Next, Sudhana asks about the sphere of this samādhi.
The elder informs him that when entering samādhi, one sequentially beholds all Buddhas. There are thirteen lines of scripture, all of which describe the sphere of samādhi.

The realm (*dhātu*) reveals the functional activity of samādhi; therefore, it concludes by stating that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are equal to all Buddhas of the three periods of time and equal to Vairocana. This concluding statement demonstrates the equality of the *dharmadhātu*.
Next, he humbled himself, saying: "I have attained only this single dharma-gate of liberation that does not enter parinirvāṇa.
Such supreme merits as those of the bodhisattvas—who universally know the three periods of time in a single thought-moment—are beyond my knowledge.
Thus, he deferred to his superior and pointed out the way for his companion, saying: "To the south of here, there is a mountain named Potalaka. There..."
The Bodhisattva is named Avalokiteśvara. You should go and question him, and he will explain it for you. Furthermore, he praised him with a verse, saying:
"There is a mountain upon the ocean" because, through great compassion, he enters the ocean of birth and death while dwelling upon the mountain of nirvāṇa.
This is the Southern Sea of South India. At that time, the youth Sudhana gazed up at him, took his leave, and departed.
This concludes the seventh major section: the dedication of merit in accordance with all sentient beings, entrusted to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

This means that by means of roots of goodness and so forth, the mind accords with all sentient beings. However, regarding Avalokiteśvara’s manifestation through the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), appearing in response to the perceptions of sentient beings' minds, this constitutes the sense of "equal accordance.

He is called "Avalokiteśvara," and is also called "Avalokitasvara. This is because in Sanskrit it is *avalokita*, which here means "observing" (*guan*), and *īśvara*, which here means... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source text].

"Self-Mastery" (*Svayambhū*). It is also called *Śabdavāda*, which means "Sound. Because he contemplates the profound *prajñā* as a Bodhisattva and perceives that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty, he is called "Self-Mastery.

If referring to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, because he attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he is called "Avalokita-śvara" (Perceiver of Sounds). Furthermore, his manifestation through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) is precisely this.
This is the meaning of the dedication that accords with all sentient beings.
At that time, the youth Sudhana reflected single-mindedly upon the instructions of that householder;

he entered the treasury of that bodhisattva’s liberation and attained the power of that bodhisattva’s ability to recollect, whereby he remembered the successive appearances of those Buddhas and kept them in mind.
He followed the succession of the Buddhas, maintained the sequence of those Buddhas' names, contemplated the sublime Dharma taught by those Buddhas,
understood the complete adornments of those Buddhas, beheld those Buddhas attaining perfect enlightenment,
and comprehended the inconceivable activities of those Buddhas. Proceeding gradually, he arrived at that mountain and searched everywhere for this Great [Vehicle].
The Bodhisattva saw that within the rocky valleys to the west, springs flowed with shimmering clarity and the forests were lush and verdant.
Fragrant grasses, soft and supple, were spread across the ground in a clockwise pattern.

There, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara sat in the full lotus posture upon a diamond-jewel throne, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas who sat upon jewel thrones in reverent attendance, as he proclaimed the Great Compassion.
The Dharma causes one to embrace all sentient beings. Upon seeing this, Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he joined his palms and gazed at him intently without blinking for even a moment, thinking: "A spiritual friend is the Tathāgata; a spiritual friend is the cloud of all Dharmas;
a spiritual friend is the treasury of all merits; a spiritual friend is difficult to encounter."
Encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the cause for the jewels of the ten powers; a spiritual friend is the inexhaustible torch of wisdom;
a spiritual friend is the sprout of the roots of merit; a spiritual friend is the gateway to all-knowledge; a spiritual friend is the guide across the ocean of wisdom;
a spiritual friend is the equipment for the path leading to all-knowledge. Thereupon, he immediately went to visit the Great Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara saw Sudhana from afar and said to him, "Welcome! You have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind to universally gather in all sentient beings;
you have given rise to a straightforward mind to single-mindedly seek the Buddha-dharma; your profound and heavy great compassion protects and delivers all;
the wondrous practices of Samantabhadra appear continuously before you; and your deep resolve for great vows is perfectly pure. You diligently seek the Buddha..."
They are able to receive and uphold all dharmas; they accumulate roots of goodness with constant insatiability; they follow spiritual friends and do not contravene their instructions;
they are born from the great ocean of the merit and wisdom of Mañjuśrī; their minds are matured and they have attained the power of the Buddhas;
they have already acquired the light of vast samādhis; they single-mindedly seek the profound and wondrous Dharma; they shall behold it.
All Buddhas experience great joy. Their wisdom is pure like space; having attained clarity themselves, they further explain it to others, abiding in the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, circumambulated him countless times, and standing with palms joined, addressed him, saying: "O Noble One, I have already set forth [upon the path]..."
“...the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
The Bodhisattva replied: “Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...”
Third is the bodhicitta. Good son, I have already accomplished the liberation door of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion.
Good son, by means of this Bodhisattva door of the practice of great compassion, I impartially teach and transform all sentient beings in an uninterrupted succession.
Good son, dwelling in this door of the practice of great compassion, I am always present with all Tathāgatas.
He appears universally before all sentient beings. He gathers in sentient beings through giving, or through kind speech, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation;
he gathers in sentient beings by manifesting a physical body, or by manifesting various inconceivable nets of pure light from his form, or by means of sound.

By means of sound; or by means of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*); or by preaching the Dharma; or by manifesting supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) to cause their minds to awaken and thereby bring them to maturity;
or by manifesting a form identical to their own kind and dwelling together with them to bring them to maturity. Good son!
I practice this gateway of great compassion. May I always rescue and protect all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings be free from the fear of perilous paths; free from the fear of burning affliction; free from the fear of confusion; free from the fear of bondage;

free from the fear of slaughter; free from the fear of poverty; free from the fear of being unable to survive; free from the fear of ill repute; free from the fear of death; and free from the fear of the great assembly.
Fear. Fear of the evil realms. Fear of darkness. Fear of transmigration. Fear of separation from loved ones. Fear of encountering enemies.
Fear of bodily affliction. Fear of mental affliction. Fear of sorrow and lamentation. Furthermore, they made this vow:
"May all sentient beings, whether they think of me, recite my name, or behold my body, all be liberated from these [fears]."

"O son of good family, having used these skillful means to cause all sentient beings to be free from fear, I further instruct them to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi so that they shall never again fall back. O son of good family..."
I have only attained this gate of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion.

As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have already purified all the vows of Samantabhadra, who have already dwelled in all the practices of Samantabhadra, who constantly practice all wholesome dharmas, who constantly enter all samādhis, who constantly abide throughout all boundless eons, and who constantly know all phenomena of the three periods of time—[they are far beyond me]. Constantly...

They visit all infinite lands; they constantly pacify the evils of all sentient beings, constantly increase the virtues of all sentient beings, and constantly sever the stream of birth and death for sentient beings. How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
At that time, there was a bodhisattva from the east named Samantagāmin, who came through the air to this Sahā world.
Standing upon the summit of the Cakravāḍa Mountains, he pressed the earth with his foot, causing the Sahā world-system to quake in six ways.
Everything became adorned with various jewels. The Bodhisattva Saṃpūrṇagāmin emitted a radiance from his body that eclipsed all the suns, moons, stars, and lightning;
the light of the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors was like a mass of ink. That light pervaded everywhere.

It illuminates all the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the hungry ghosts, and the abode of King Yama, causing all the sufferings of these evil destinies to be extinguished, so that afflictions do not arise and all grief and lamentation are entirely left behind.

Furthermore, throughout all the buddha-fields, it rains down universally all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, garments, banners, and canopies; with all such articles of adornment, it makes offerings to [the Buddhas].

The Buddha, furthermore, in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, manifested his body universally within all the palaces, causing all who saw him to rejoice. Thereafter, he proceeded to where Avalokiteśvara was.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said to Sudhana: "Noble son, do you see the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin coming to this assembly?"
He replied, "I have seen him. [The elder] said, "Good son, you should go and ask the Bodhisattva how one studies the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path.
First, the names [of the stages] were explained; hereafter, one proceeds according to the instructions to seek them out. Therefore, Sudhana reflected upon those instructions. Thus:
Entering that liberation, he realized it through contemplation and proceeded by stages until he reached the mountain.

There, on the western face within a rocky valley, he saw the Bodhisattva seated upon a diamond-jewel throne, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, proclaiming the Dharma of great compassion. Upon seeing this, Sudhana leaped for joy and gazed intently.
Reflecting on the benefits of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he went to where the Great Bodhisattva was. Upon seeing him, he paid homage and inquired after his well-being.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara saw Sudhana from afar and immediately welcomed him with praise.

Because his great compassion was profound and he sought to guide him through sympathetic resonance, there are seven lines of scripture, all of which consist of words of praise and reception. Sudhana prostrated himself and respectfully inquired about the Dharma.
Essential. First, the Bodhisattva carefully resolves the mind; next, the Dharma-realm is bestowed [upon him], saying:

"I have already accomplished the gate of liberation of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion. By means of this practice, I impartially teach and transform all sentient beings in an uninterrupted succession.
Next, while abiding in this gate of the practice of great compassion, I shall extensively manifest its functional activity. First, five lines and a half [are spoken].

The Sūtra reveals the activity and function [of the Buddha] by way of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). Through the eleven phrases beginning with the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), various manifestations have already been subsumed;
however, the thirty-two responses are fully and exhaustively contained within these two phrases: "manifesting here in bodily form" and "preaching the Dharma.
Next, there are eight lines of sūtra that reveal the activity and function by way of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). At the end...
This causes one to advance with the great resolve, never to regress. Next, one humbles oneself, saying: "I have attained only this gateway to the practice of great compassion;
such vast gateways of practice as those of the Bodhisattvas and the vows of Samantabhadra are beyond my knowledge."

At that time, he saw a bodhisattva from the east named Samantagāmin (Universal Progress) coming through the air to the Sahā world, manifesting great supernormal transformations. Then, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said to Sudhana:
"Do you see the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin coming to this assembly? He replied, "I have already seen him. Avalokiteśvara said, "You should go [to him]."
Question: Because he was present at that assembly, he omitted the formal salutation and departure.
At that time, the youth Sudhana respectfully received his instruction and immediately went to where that Bodhisattva was.
He prostrated at his feet, stood with palms joined, and said: "O Noble One, I have already previously resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
I have awakened the mind of enlightenment three times, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The Bodhisattva Samantagāmin said:
"Noble son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Universal Gateway Swift Movement'. Sudhana said: "In what way, Holy One..."
"Buddha, how far is that land from here where you obtained this Dharma-gate? How long has it been since you set out and arrived?
He replied, "Good son, this matter is difficult to know; it cannot be understood by any in the world—gods, humans, asuras, śramaṇas, or brahmins.
It can only be known by those bodhisattvas who are courageous, diligent, and free from retreat or fear."

He is embraced by all spiritual friends, is held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas, is fully endowed with roots of goodness, possesses pure aspirations, has attained the faculties of a bodhisattva, and has the eye of wisdom;
he is able to hear, retain, understand, and explain [the teachings]. Sudhana said: "Noble One!"
"Relying on the Buddha's spiritual power and the power of my spiritual friend, I am able to believe and accept it; I pray that you will explain it to me.

The Bodhisattva Samyaktvaniyata said, "Good son, I have come from the world-system called Wondrous Treasury (Prabhūtagarbha) in the eastern direction, from the presence of the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth (Samantavijayajanan).
I received this Dharma-gate from that Buddha, and since departing from there, an unspeakable number of eons have already passed."
For as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field that can be described, in each and every thought-moment,
I take steps numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable buddha-fields; with each step, I pass through as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds,
and into each and every one of those buddha-fields I enter everywhere, arriving at the presence of those Buddhas to present them with sublime offerings.

I made offerings. All these articles of offering were produced by the unsurpassed mind, sealed by the Dharma of non-action, approved by all Tathāgatas, and praised by all Bodhisattvas. Good son, I also universally beheld all sentient beings in that world;
I fully knew their minds and fully knew their faculties, manifesting my body and preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations and understandings. Or...
They emit rays of light; or they bestow wealth and treasures, employing various skillful means to teach and subdue beings without ceasing.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Good son, I have attained only this Bodhisattva liberation of "Universal Swift Movement," which enables one to swiftly reach all places, just as [all other] Bodhisattvas do.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions; his realm of wisdom is equal and without distinction.
He skillfully arrays his body so as to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, reaching all paths and entering all lands.
Knowing all phenomena and arriving at all worlds, he impartially expounds all Dharma-gates, simultaneously illuminating all sentient beings.
He does not give rise to discrimination regarding the Buddhas, and he is without obstruction in all places.
How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? Son of good family, to the south of here there is a city named Dravavatī.
Within it dwells a deity named Mahādeva. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should train in awakening.
While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivating the bodhisattva path, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times,
gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

The eighth is the Bodhisattva Samyaktvānugata’s dedication based on the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This means that because the roots of goodness are themselves suchness, they constitute the dedication.
Since all phenomena proceed toward True Suchness, he is named Samyaktvānugata (“One Who Proceeds Correctly”).

After Sudhana had related his own initial generation of the mind of awakening, he asked about the cultivation of the bodhisattva path. Samyaktvānugata replied, “I have attained the bodhisattva liberation [known as] ‘The Sphere of Non-differentiation.’”

He is named "Universal Gateway Swift Traveler. This is the formal transmission of the Dharma-realm. First, the name and essence are indicated: because it reaches the boundless ten directions, it is called "Universal Gateway";

because it transcends many [eons] in a single thought-moment, it is called "Swift Traveler. Since one relies on the practice of True Suchness (Tathatā), one suddenly realizes Bodhi in a single thought-moment;
therefore, the following section reveals the functional activity of this Dharma-gate. Thus, Sudhana asks: "From which Buddha..."
Having attained this dharma, Sudhana again asked: "From which land have you come? How far is it from here? How long has it been since you set out? Samantagambhīra replied:

"This matter is difficult to know, for those who lack great roots are incapable of receiving such instruction. Sudhana declared that he himself was capable through his own power. Samantagambhīra then said:
"I have come from the world-system called *Prasādagandhavatī* in the eastern direction, from the presence of the Buddha *Samantavijayottama*."

This Dharma-gate that has been attained has "emerged from that," which signifies that it originates from the Tathāgata-garbha realm of one's own unmoving fundamental wisdom, arising from the universal production of the ten thousand virtues of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). This answers the question of where it was obtained.

Because it transcends [all stages] instantaneously in a single thought-moment, it is said to have "emerged from that. Having passed through unspeakable eons—this answers the duration of time. Much time...
By walking, one knows its distance; yet as long as one does not depart from a single thought-moment, though it is distant, it is near, and thus it is swift.
In each and every Buddha-field traversed, sentient beings are tamed. As it is in one direction, so it is in all ten directions;
therefore, it is called the Universal Gate. Next, he humbled himself, saying: "I have only attained this bodhisattva liberation of universal and swift movement."
"Thus it is. The wisdom-sphere, equal and supreme meritorious conduct, and the universal reach of all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions—to these I cannot attain knowledge.
However, he pointed to a companion behind him and said: 'To the south there is a city named Dvāravatī.
Within it dwells a deity named Mahādeva. You should go and inquire of him; he will explain it for you.'"
At that time, the youth Sudhana gazed at him with earnest devotion, took his leave, and departed. Then,
as Sudhana entered into the vast conduct of a bodhisattva, sought the sphere of a bodhisattva’s wisdom, beheld the miraculous feats of a bodhisattva,
contemplated the supreme merits of a bodhisattva, gave rise to great joy as a bodhisattva, and established the firm resolve of a bodhisattva...
With diligence, he entered the inconceivable and sovereign liberation of a bodhisattva;

he traversed the ground of bodhisattva merit, contemplated the ground of bodhisattva samādhi, dwelt in the ground of bodhisattva dhāraṇī, entered the ground of bodhisattva great vows, attained the ground of bodhisattva eloquence, and perfected the ground of bodhisattva powers. Proceeding gradually, he arrived at that city and inquired after Mahādeva.
"Where is he now? People all replied, "He is within this city, manifesting a vast body to preach the Dharma for the multitude.
At that time, Sudhana went to where Mahādeva was, prostrated at his feet, joined his palms before him, and spoke these words:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will explain this to me. At that time, Mahādeva extended his four hands and took up the waters of the four great oceans to wash himself.
With his face turned toward him, he took various golden flowers and scattered them over Sudhana, addressing him thus:
"Noble son, all Bodhisattvas are difficult to behold and difficult to hear of; they rarely appear in the world. Among all beings, they are the most supreme;
among all men, they are the white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*). They are the refuge for sentient beings, the saviors of sentient beings, and for all the worlds..."
Acting as a place of peace and security, they provide great illumination for all the world. To those who are deluded, they show the secure and correct path;
as great guides, they lead all sentient beings into the gateway of the Buddha-dharma. As great Dharma generals, they are well able to protect the city of omniscience.
Thus, Bodhisattvas are difficult to encounter; they are such that their body, speech, and mind are free from fault.
Only then can one see his physical form and hear his eloquence, which are ever-present before one at all times.
"Good son, I have already attained the bodhisattva liberation called Cloud-Net.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, what is the sphere of the Cloud-Net liberation? At that time, Mahādeva manifested a golden image before Sudhana.
Heaps of silver; heaps of lapis lazuli; heaps of crystal; heaps of *śaṅkha* shell; heaps of agate;
heaps of great-flame jewels; heaps of stainless-treasury jewels; heaps of great-radiance jewels; heaps of jewels that universally manifest in the ten directions;

heaps of jeweled crowns; heaps of jeweled seals; heaps of jeweled necklaces; heaps of jeweled earrings; heaps of jeweled bracelets; heaps of jeweled chains; heaps of pearl nets; and various kinds of *maṇi* gems.
Noble ladies were like a mass of jewels; all manner of ornaments were like a mass of jewels; wish-fulfilling maṇi-gems were all like great mountains.

Furthermore, he manifested all flowers, all garlands, all perfumes, all incense, all ointments, all garments, all banners and flags, all music, and all implements for the enjoyment of the five desires.
They were piled up like mountains. Then, an immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of young maidens appeared. That Great Deva addressed Sudhana, saying:
"Good son, you may take these things to make offerings to the Tathāgata and cultivate various merits.
Furthermore, bestow them upon all beings to gather them in, causing them to practice and study the *dānapāramitā* so that they can relinquish what is difficult to relinquish. Good son...
"Son, just as I have manifested these objects for you and taught you to practice giving, I do exactly the same for all sentient beings.

I cause them all to perfume themselves with these roots of goodness by means of revering and making offerings to the Three Jewels and to spiritual friends, thereby increasing their wholesome dharmas and generating the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi. Good son, if there are any sentient beings..."
For those who give rise to craving and attachment for the five desires and indulge in self-indulgence,
he manifests impure objects for them. If there are sentient beings who harbor anger, pride, and engage in much contention, he manifests extremely terrifying forms,
such as rākṣasas drinking blood and devouring flesh, so that upon seeing them, they become struck with alarm and dread, their minds become gentle and supple, and they abandon their enmity.

[The] Binding: If there are sentient beings who are dull-witted and indolent, for their sake he manifests kings, thieves, water, fire, and various grave illnesses, so that upon seeing these, they give rise to fear and dread. Knowing that there is sorrow and suffering, they exert themselves.
By means of such various skillful methods, he causes them to abandon all unwholesome conduct and practice wholesome dharmas, causing them to eliminate [the afflictions].
The perfection of all perfections that removes obstacles to the *pāramitās* causes one to transcend all perilous paths of hindrance and reach the place of non-obstruction.

Good son, I know only this liberation of the Cloud-Net. As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they are like Śakra, having already been able to crush the entire army of the asuras of affliction; they are like great waters, universally...
It can extinguish the fires of all afflictions of all sentient beings; it is like a fierce fire that can universally dry up the waters of all craving and desire of all sentient beings;
it is like a great wind that can universally blow down the banners of all views and attachments of all sentient beings;
it is like a vajra that can completely shatter the mountains of the view of self of all sentient beings. And...

"How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good son, in this Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Magadha, within the Bodhimaṇḍa, there is a presiding earth goddess named Anala. Go to her and ask:
'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? " Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Mahādevī and circumambulated her.
Having circumambulated him countless times, he took his leave and departed.
The ninth is the Good Friend Mahādeva, who dedicates through liberation that is unbound and unattached.
This means he is not bound by signs and not attached to views, because his activity is sovereign. He is called the Good Friend Mahādeva because he manifests...
Because of his great body, he is without bondage and without attachment; because his wisdom is pure and sovereign, he is called a *deva* (heavenly being).
Because he universally responds in accordance with principle, he is called "Great" (*mahā*). Because his wondrous functions are difficult to fathom, he is called "Divine" (*divya*).
As for the city of Drāmapati, this is translated as "Gate of Existence," meaning that he serves as a Dharma-preacher for this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate. At that time, the youth Sudhana...
Son, by receiving the preceding instructions, you have gained entry into thirteen kinds of Dharma-gates, such as the vast conduct of a bodhisattva.
Proceeding gradually, you arrived at that city and heard Mahādeva manifesting a vast body to preach the Dharma to the assembly.

Because he occupies the rank of a Dharma Master of the Nine Realms and speaks in accordance with the Dharmadhātu, he manifests a great body to teach. Sudhana prostrated himself and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
At that time, Mahādeva extended his four hands and took up the waters of the four great oceans to wash his own face.
He held various golden flowers and scattered them over Sudhana; this was because he was about to bestow the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and thus first employed this expedient means.

Regarding the phrase "extended his [hands]," the commentary (*śūtra*) provides two meanings. In terms of the phenomenal event, it signifies that the arousal of the bodhicitta is difficult to encounter; one should observe it with pure eyes. As for "scattered,"...

He offers flowers as a symbolic gesture, extending his hands of the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to take up the Dharma-gates that correspond to the flow of the supreme *tathatā* he has realized.
First, he purifies his own *dharmakāya*; subsequently, for the sake of benefiting others, he scatters the flowers.
Mahādeva declared: "Good son, I have already accomplished the bodhisattva liberation named 'Cloud-Net' (*meghajāla*). This...
He formally bestowed the Dharma-realm. Sudhana asked, "What is the sphere of the liberation of the Cloud-Net?
Mahādeva immediately manifested before Sudhana a mass of various precious treasures, such as gold and silver, like a great mountain.
