Named Universal Wisdom Radiant Lamp. Good son, there were as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, the last of whom was named Wisdom Lamp of the Dharma-realm City. All appeared in the world during the eon called Stainless Radiance.
I honored, approached, and made offerings to them all; I listened to, received, and upheld the sublime Dharma they taught. Furthermore...

In the presence of all those Tathāgatas, he left the household life to study the Way, protected and upheld the teachings of the Dharma, and entered this Bodhisattva liberation of profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound.
Through various skillful means, he taught and transformed, bringing immeasurable sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
From that time until now, I have made offerings to all the Buddhas who appeared in the world throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, and I have practiced their teachings.
Good son, since then, I alone have awakened among sentient beings who were slumbering in the darkness of ignorance during the night of saṃsāra;
I have caused those sentient beings to guard the city of the mind and to abandon the three [poisons].
The City of the Realms. They dwell in the unsurpassed city of the Dharma of omniscience.

Good son, I know only this profound liberation of Sovereign Wondrous Sound, which causes all worlds to be free from discursive speech, to speak no dualistic words, to always speak truthful words, and to constantly speak pure words;
yet it is as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to know the intrinsic nature of all speech.
In every thought-moment, they spontaneously awaken all sentient beings; they enter the ocean of the speech and sounds of all sentient beings and are fully eloquent in all modes of expression;

they clearly perceive the ocean of all dharma-doors and have attained mastery over the dhāraṇīs that universally encompass all dharmas; according to the doubts in the minds of sentient beings, they act for their sake...
He expounds the Dharma, ultimately taming all sentient beings and being able to universally embrace all sentient beings.

He skillfully cultivates the various unsurpassed deeds of a bodhisattva, deeply enters the various subtle wisdoms of a bodhisattva, is able to skillfully examine the various bodhisattva-piṭakas, and is able to freely expound the various dharmas of a bodhisattva. Why is this? Because he has already attained the accomplishment of all dharmas.
Because of the *cakra-dhāraṇī*, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Son of good family, in this assembly of the Buddha there is a night goddess named Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamkusumitā. Go to her and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva train in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)? How should they establish all sentient beings in all-knowledge? Thus it was said.
Then the Night Goddess Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥ, wishing to reiterate the meaning of this liberation, spoke these verses for the sake of the youth Sudhana:
"The liberation of the Bodhisattvas is profound and difficult to see; it is like space, with the equal characteristic of suchness."
Universally beholding within the boundless realm of phenomena, All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time give rise to immeasurable,
supreme merit; Realizing and entering the inconceivable true nature of reality,
They increase all sovereign wisdoms and open the path to liberation throughout the three periods of time.
Passing through as many eons as there are atoms in a turning world-system,
at that time there was an eon named Pure Light in a world named Dharma-Flame Cloud; its city was called Jewel Flower Radiance,
wherein Buddhas arose in the world, as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable Mount Sumerus.
There was a Buddha named Dharma-Ocean Sound who first appeared within this eon,
continuing until the very last Buddha among them, named Dharma-Domain Flame-Lamp King;
to all such Tathāgatas as these, I have made offerings and listened to their teachings.

I beheld the Buddha Dharma-ocean Thunder-Sound, His body universally manifesting in true golden color, Adorned with all marks like a mountain of jewels; I made a vow to attain the state of a Tathāgata.
As soon as I briefly beheld those Tathāgatas, I immediately gave rise to the vast mind of Bodhi.
Vowing to diligently seek all-knowledge, whose nature is equal to the dharma-realm and space,
thereby universally beholding the Buddhas of the three times, as well as the assembly of all Bodhisattvas; furthermore,
seeing the oceans of lands and sentient beings, they universally take them as objects of focus and give rise to great compassion.
In accordance with the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, He manifests various infinite bodies, pervading all lands throughout the ten directions.
Shaking the earth and radiating light, he awakens all conscious beings;
They see a second Buddha and draw near to him, And likewise behold the Buddhas within the ocean of lands of the ten directions.
Until the very last Buddha appears, throughout as many eons as atoms in all lands—
equal in number to the atoms of Mount Sumeru— I have personally approached and venerated every Tathāgata,
the Lamp that Illumines the World; thus, this liberation has attained purity.

At that time, because the youth Sudhana had attained this bodhisattva liberation of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound, he entered the ocean of boundless samādhis and the ocean of vast dhāraṇīs;
he acquired the great supernormal powers of a bodhisattva and obtained the great eloquence of a bodhisattva.
With a heart full of great joy, he gazed upon the night goddess Sarvajagadrakṣāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhā and addressed her in verse:
The praise says:
Having traversed the vast ocean of sublime wisdom, Having crossed the boundless ocean of all existences, Your body is a treasury of long life, freedom from affliction, and knowledge;
With majestic power and radiant light, you abide here among this assembly.
Thoroughly realizing that the nature of phenomena is like space, they enter universally throughout the three periods of time without obstruction.
Though every thought-moment grasps at all objects, mind after mind forever severs all conceptual discrimination.
Thoroughly realizing that sentient beings have no inherent nature, they nevertheless give rise to great compassion for them.
Deeply entering the Tathāgata’s gate of liberation, Universally delivering immeasurable multitudes of deluded beings;
Observing and contemplating all phenomena, Thoroughly understanding and realizing the nature of all dharmas;
Thus practicing the Buddha’s wisdom, Universally transforming sentient beings to bring them to liberation.
The Deva is the teacher who tames sentient beings, Revealing the path of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
For all conscious beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm, He proclaims the practice that transcends all worldly fears.
Having already established himself upon the path of the Tathāgata’s vows, He has received the vast teaching of Bodhi.
Having cultivated all powers of universal application, and having seen the sovereign deities and Buddhas of the ten directions,
their minds are as pure as space; universally free from all afflictions,
they thoroughly understand the infinite lands of the three periods of time, as well as all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sentient beings.
The celestial deity understands all in a single thought; he also knows the oceans of days and nights, months, years, and eons.
He knows all classes of sentient beings, with their various names and characteristics, each distinct from the others;
he knows the places where the beings of the ten directions undergo birth and death—whether they possess form, lack form, have perception, or lack perception.
Comprehending all things in accordance with worldly convention, They lead others onto the path to enlightenment.
Having been born into the family of the Tathāgatas’ vows, And having entered the ocean of the Buddhas' merit, Their Dharma-body is pure and their minds are unimpeded;
According to the inclinations of sentient beings, they manifest in various forms.
When the youth Sudhana had spoken these verses, he prostrated at the feet of the night goddess, circumambulated her countless times, gazed upon her with profound reverence,
and then took his leave and departed.
The sixth is the Night Goddess who Protects All Cities, who is associated with the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
"Presence" means that by abiding in the wisdom of dependent origination, one causes the most excellent non-conceptual *prajñā* to manifest before oneself.
Having heard the instruction of the Goddess Silent Sound Ocean, Sudhana contemplated and examined the dharma-gate she had taught, not forgetting a single word or phrase.
His mind became vast, and having realized and entered this state, he remained therein.

He went to where the night goddess Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥketurnayanavikrāntarājā was, and saw her seated upon a lion throne of the king of *maṇi* jewels radiating all precious light, surrounded by countless night goddesses.
She manifested various bodies to discipline sentient beings. Upon seeing her, Sudhana rejoiced.
He joyfully prostrated himself, recounted his own initial resolve, and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, the night goddess praised Sudhana’s manner of generating the bodhicitta and formally bestowed upon him the Dharma-realm, saying: "I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation of 'Profound and Sovereign Wondrous Sound.
As for the term 'profound' and so forth: it is called profound because it accords with phenomena and eons; it is the non-obstruction of the provisional and the ultimate."

The inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*) within sublime eloquence is called mastery (*vaśitā*). Relying upon this to expound the Dharma in universal response to the capacities of all beings is termed "sublime voice.
This constitutes the essence [of the term]. Next, the twelve lines of scripture beginning with "As a great Dharma-preacher, unimpeded...
collectively manifest the functional activity of liberation and reveal the virtue of the gift of Dharma. Next, "By means of such light of the pure Dharma..."
Below "Illumination" (*vidyā*), there are twelve lines of sūtra that specifically reveal the function of karma to explain the meaning of profundity.
Next, from "I thus contemplate with right mindfulness" onwards, there are eight lines of sūtra that explain the meaning of mastery (*vaśitā*).

Next, from "Or for the sake of sentient beings, I preach the Dharma of the wisdom of hearing" onwards, there are twelve lines of sūtra that explain the meaning of wondrous sound (*svara*); these consist of twenty-three phrases, clarifying [the matter].
The phenomena and principle of the Dharma taught are non-dual; therefore, it is summarized by saying: "I have taught such inexpressible Dharma-gates for the sake of sentient beings.
Next, from the passage "I enter the Tathāgata’s gate of non-differentiated Dharma" onwards, the remaining three lines of the sutra summarize the benefits.
This collectively summarizes the mastery over profound and wondrous sounds to clarify the functional activity of liberation.
[The text continues with] "Furthermore. Next, the youth Sudhana asked the celestial deity: "This gate of liberation is so rare;
O Noble One, how long has it been since you realized it? This question regarding the duration since he attained the dharma-gate implicitly includes the timing of his initial resolve (*cittotpāda*).
Therefore, the Night Goddess recounted the causes and conditions of his resolve, saying: "In the remote past, beyond worlds..."
The *dhātu-parivarta* consists of a number of kalpas equal to the number of atoms [in a world-system]. Regarding the "turning of the world-system" (*loka-dhātu-parivarta*):
it means first that one world-system is crushed into atoms; these atoms serve as the count, with one atom representing one world-system.
Then, all those world-systems, numbering as many as those atoms, are again compressed into a single mass of atoms. Taking each of these atoms as one kalpa constitutes the past kalpas.
Far, far indeed! Within that great eon there is a world-system; within this world-system there are four continents as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru.
Among them is a single four-continent system named Wondrous Banner (*Cih-dhvaja*).
Within it is a royal capital, and not far from this royal capital is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Within this site, there are [beings] as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru...
The Tathāgata appeared therein; thus, the Buddhas who have appeared are already many. Tracing back to the very first Buddha to appear therein, his name was Dharmasāgaragarjitaprabhāsarāja.
When that Buddha appeared, there was a wheel-turning king named Viśuddhasūryaprabhāvaktra, who heard the Dharma from that Buddha, left the household life, and upheld the True Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma: when that Buddha-dharma was about to perish, a thousand different schools arose and preached various doctrines, thereby destroying the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, a king-monk used his supernormal powers to restore the Buddha-dharma once more. There was then a bhikṣuṇī named Dharmacakra-vibhūti-prabhā.
This daughter of the king, having heard her father’s words and witnessed the supernatural power of Dharmapāla, gave rise to the bodhicitta and never again regressed.

She beheld all the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata Dharmasāgaraprabha and immediately attained this profound liberation of Sovereign Wondrous Sound. That bhikṣu King of the Flourishing Final Dharma is now Samantabhadra...
The worthy Bodhisattva was he; the bhikṣuṇī Dharmacakrapravartanaprabhā was none other than myself.
This was the beginning of my resolve for enlightenment and the first moment I attained liberation. Thus, the duration of time since I first attained the Dharma has been answered.
Following my encounter with that initial Buddha, there subsequently arose another Buddha named Vimaladharmaprabha, who appeared in succession.
In succession, throughout the course of great kalpas, there were one hundred Buddhas who appeared in the world;

I served, attended upon, and made offerings to them all. Since that time, throughout as many kalpas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, for every Buddha who appeared in the world, I have served them all, causing all sentient beings to guard the city of their minds and to abandon the city of the triple world, so that they may attain [liberation].
"This is the unsurpassed city of the Dharma of omniscience; this is the reason for the name 'Guardian of All Cities.
Having said this, he humbled himself and deferred to others of superior merit, saying: "I know only this liberation of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound.
As for the bodhisattvas who know the intrinsic nature of all speech, and so forth, until they have attained..."
"Regarding this *Sarvadharmanirghoṣa-dhāraṇī*, how could I possibly know it? Look behind you;
in this assembly of the Buddha, there is a night goddess named Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamkusumitā. You should go and ask her; she will explain it to you.
Then, the night goddess Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥprabhā spoke again in verse, repeating the aforementioned teaching: [Verse follows]

It says: "The liberation of the Bodhisattva is profound and difficult to perceive; it is the mark of the equality of space and suchness. There are eleven verses beginning with this, which continue until:
"...causing this liberation to attain purity, etc. The first two verses praise the preceding essence and function;
the remainder praise the depth of the roots of the Dharma. At the point of departure, [the teacher] earnestly exhorted him to practice and study. At that time, Sudhana entered into this...
Through the Bodhisattva’s profound and sovereign liberation of wondrous sound, he immediately entered the ocean of boundless samādhis and the ocean of dhāraṇīs.
Attaining great supernormal powers and eloquence, his heart was filled with immense joy.

He spoke ten verses in praise of the Night Goddess’s virtues, extolling the transcendence of her merit and wisdom and the profundity of her samādhi, thereby manifesting the perfection of her qualities and her freedom from attachment.
[Obstruction]. Having spoken these verses, Sudhana gazed up at him, paid his respects, took his leave, and departed.

Entering the Dharma Realm, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Thirteen.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having entered the Bodhisattva liberation gate of the Profound and Sovereign Sublime Sound and having advanced in his practice, went to the place where the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasukhasaṃvāsā resided. He saw her body amidst a multitude of precious fragrances.
Within a tree-pavilion, upon a lion throne composed of exquisite jewels, he was surrounded by a hundred thousand night goddesses.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at her feet and, joining his palms before her, spoke these words: "Noble Lady," he said.

"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). I only pray that you will deign to show me compassion and explain this for me.
The night goddess said, "Noble son, in this Sahā world, the sunlight has already set and the lotuses have closed their petals."

When the various crowds have finished their excursions and sightseeing, they see all those beings—whether in mountains, waters, cities, or wildernesses—and they all resolve to return to their respective dwellings.

I secretly protect them all, enabling them to reach their destinations via the right path and ensuring they dwell in peace and happiness throughout the night. Son of good family, if there are beings who are in full vigor...
They are fond of fine colors, arrogant, heedless, and self-indulgent in the five desires.

For their sake, I manifest the signs of old age, sickness, and death to cause them to give rise to fear and abandon all evils. Furthermore, I praise various roots of goodness to lead them to practice them;
for those who are stingy, I extol generosity; for those who violate the precepts, I laud pure morality; and for those who harbor anger, I provide instruction.

Abiding in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), they cause those who harbor malice and harm to practice patience (*kṣānti*). If there are those who are indolent, they cause them to arouse diligence (*vīrya*).

If there are those who are distracted, they cause them to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). To those who abide in wrong wisdom, they cause them to study Prajñā. To those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), they cause them to abide in the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

To those who take pleasure in and are attached to the various realms of existence within the triple world, they cause them to abide in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of vows (*praṇidhānapāramitā*). If...

For those sentient beings whose merit and wisdom are weak and inferior, who are oppressed by various fetters and karmic actions, and who encounter many obstacles, I cause them to abide in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
For those sentient beings whose minds are dark and dull and who lack wisdom, I cause them to abide in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
Noble son, I have already accomplished the Bodhisattva’s birth of vastness.
The liberation door of the Radiance of Joy. Sudhana said, "O Great Sage, what is the scope of this liberation door?
The night goddess replied, "Noble son, by entering this liberation, one is able to know the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means that universally gathers in all sentient beings.
How does he gather them in? Noble son, whatever happiness all sentient beings experience is entirely due to the Tathāgata."
By the power of majestic virtue; by conforming to the Tathāgata’s teaching; by practicing the Tathāgata’s words; by training in the Tathāgata’s conduct;
by attaining the power of the Tathāgata’s protection; by cultivating the path sealed by the Tathāgata; and by planting the roots of goodness practiced by the Tathāgata.
It is because of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; because it is illuminated by the sun-like wisdom of the Tathāgata;
and because it is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata’s pure karma. How is this known?
Good son, having entered this liberation of the "Light of Vast Joy Arising," I recollect the past of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana.
He clearly perceives the entire ocean of bodhisattva practices he has cultivated.

Good son, in the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he saw all sentient beings clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," dwelling in the dark chamber of ignorance, and entering the dense forest of various views.

Bound by craving, destroyed by anger, distracted by ignorance, and entangled by stinginess and envy, they wander through the cycle of birth and death in poverty and suffering, failing to encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Having perceived this, one gives rise to great compassion to benefit sentient beings;
that is to say, one arouses the aspiration to gather in sentient beings by providing all manner of exquisite jewels and requisites.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the necessities of life and have no lack of heart; may they have hearts free from attachment toward all matters;
may they have hearts free from greedy defilement toward all sensory realms; may they have hearts free from stinginess regarding all possessions;
may they have hearts free from expectation regarding all karmic rewards; and may they have hearts free from envy toward all that is glorious and excellent.
A mind of longing; a mind free from delusion regarding all causes and conditions; a mind that gives rise to the observation of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
a mind that gives rise to the protection and salvation of all sentient beings; a mind that gives rise to deep entry into the whirlpools of all phenomena;

a mind that gives rise to abiding in impartial great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; and a mind that gives rise to the practice of skillful means and great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Arise as the great Dharma-canopy, universally covering the minds of all sentient beings. Arise with the vajra-pestle of great wisdom to shatter the mountain-like obstacles of affliction in the minds of all sentient beings.
Arise to cause all sentient beings to increase their hearts of joy and bliss. Arise with the aspiration that all sentient beings attain ultimate peace and happiness.
Arise to rain down all manner of wealth and treasures according to the desires of sentient beings.
The mind that arises through the skillful means of equality to bring all sentient beings to maturity;

the mind that arises to cause all sentient beings to be satisfied with the wealth of the noble ones; and the mind that arises with the vow that all sentient beings shall ultimately attain the fruit of omnidirectional wisdom.
Having given rise to such a mind, they attain the power of a bodhisattva and manifest great spiritual transformations throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
Before all sentient beings, they rain down all manner of necessities for life, fulfilling their every desire and bringing them universal joy.
Without regret or stinginess, and without interruption or cessation, they universally gather in and sustain all beings through these skillful means.

They are born [into the world] to teach and transform all beings, bringing them all to maturity so that they may escape the sufferings and hardships of birth and death, yet they do not seek any recompense for this.

They purify the jewel-like minds of all sentient beings, causing them to give rise to the same roots of goodness shared by all Buddhas, and increasing the great ocean of merit and virtue of omniscience.
In this way, the Bodhisattva matures all sentient beings in every thought-moment, and in every thought-moment adorns [the Buddha-fields].
They purify all Buddha-fields. In every thought-moment they universally enter all dharma-realms; in every thought-moment they pervade the entirety of the realm of empty space;
in every thought-moment they universally enter all three periods of time; in every thought-moment they accomplish the wisdom that tames all sentient beings;
in every thought-moment they constantly turn all wheels of Dharma; and in every thought-moment they constantly benefit sentient beings through the path of omniscience.

Birth: In every thought-moment, throughout all worlds, before all beings of various distinctions, one manifests the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas until the end of all future kalpas.

In every thought-moment, throughout all worlds and all kalpas, one universally cultivates the bodhisattva practices without giving rise to dualistic conceptions—namely, universally entering into all vast oceans of worlds.

Within all the various types of world-systems, there are worlds with diverse boundaries, worlds with diverse adornments, worlds with diverse essential natures, worlds with diverse shapes, and worlds with diverse distributions.
There are some worlds that are defiled yet mixed with purity; some worlds that are pure yet mixed with defilement; and some worlds...
Some realms are entirely defiled, while some worlds are entirely pure; they may be small or large, coarse or subtle, upright or tilted, inverted or face-up.

Throughout all such worlds, moment by moment, they practice the various bodhisattva deeds, enter the bodhisattva stage, manifest the power of a bodhisattva, and likewise manifest all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Body. He causes all sentient beings to universally know and see [him] according to their own minds.

Good son, in the past, when the Tathāgata Vairocana was thus practicing the bodhisattva path, he saw that sentient beings did not cultivate merit, lacked wisdom, were obscured by the cataracts of ignorance through attachment to self and what belongs to self, entered into various false views due to improper reflection, and were unaware.
Following the sequence of cause and effect, they fall into the perilous and deep pit of birth and death, undergoing all manner of immeasurable sufferings.
Arising with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they fully cultivate all practices of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

For the sake of all sentient beings, they extol and praise firm roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), causing them to dwell securely therein and remain far removed from the suffering of the poverty of birth and death. They diligently practice...
Regarding the dharmas that assist the path of merit and wisdom: for them, he expounds various gateways of cause and effect; he expounds how karmic retribution is never inconsistent;

he expounds the points of realization and entry into the Dharma; and he expounds the inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings, as well as all lands where they take birth, so as to ensure that the lineage of all Buddhas is never severed and that they are protected and maintained.
The Buddha-dharma causes them to abandon all evils. Furthermore, it praises the dharmas that assist the path toward omniscience, causing the hearts of all sentient beings to rejoice.

It causes them to practice the gift of Dharma so as to universally gather all beings, inspires them to initiate the conduct of omniscience, and leads them to study and train in the path of the pāramitās of the great bodhisattvas. It causes them...
He causes the ocean of all roots of goodness for omniscience to increase; he causes them to fulfill all noble riches; he causes them to enter the gate of the Buddha’s sovereignty;
he causes them to grasp immeasurable skillful means; he causes them to behold the majestic power of the Tathāgata;
and he causes them to dwell securely in the wisdom of a bodhisattva. Sudhana said: "Noble One, having set out for unexcelled..."
"How long has it been since you first gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The night goddess replied, "Good son, this matter is difficult to believe, difficult to know, difficult to understand, difficult to enter, and difficult to explain.

It cannot be known by anyone in all the worlds, nor by those of the two vehicles, except for those protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas, embraced by virtuous friends, who have accumulated supreme merit and possess the aspiration [for enlightenment]."
A mind that is pure and free from inferiority; a mind free from defilement; a mind free from deceit and crookedness; a mind that attains the light of wisdom that shines universally;
a mind that resolves to universally benefit all sentient beings; a mind that cannot be destroyed by any afflictions or maras;
a mind that sets out with the certainty of accomplishing all-knowledge; a mind that takes no pleasure in the joys of any cycle of birth and death; [and] a mind that delights in seeking...
The sublime bliss of all Buddhas, which can extinguish the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings; which can cultivate the ocean of all Buddha-merits;
which can contemplate the true nature of all phenomena; which can possess all pure faith and understanding;
which can arise amidst the turbulent flow of all birth and death; which can enter the ocean of wisdom of all Tathāgatas; and which can definitively reach the Unsurpassed.

The City of Dharma. Such a person is able to courageously enter the realm of the Tathāgatas, is able to swiftly proceed to the stages of all Buddhas, is able to immediately accomplish the power of all-knowledge, and is able to attain ultimate perfection in the ten powers.
Why is this? Because this is the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and for all Bodhisattvas...

Even I cannot know this, let alone other sentient beings. However, by the power of the Buddha, I now wish to cause the minds of those sentient beings who are ready for conversion to be swiftly purified;
I wish to cause the minds of those sentient beings who cultivate roots of goodness to attain mastery.
I shall explain it to you according to your questions. At that time, the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamaya... [wished] to...
To further clarify this meaning, he observes the three periods of time and, knowing the future realms, speaks these verses:

"O Son of the Buddha, regarding that which you have asked— The profound realm of the Buddhas, Inconceivable, even if explained for as many eons as there are atoms in a land, it could not be exhausted.
It is not something shrouded by greed, hatred, delusion, Or the confusion of pride."
Such sentient beings as these are able to know the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma;
they are not those who dwell with minds turbid with stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception, nor are they those covered by afflictions and karma.
They are able to know the Buddha’s realm, being unattached to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and free from those who hold views and perceptions inverted regarding the existence of a self.

One who can know that which the Buddha has awakened to—the tranquil realm of the Buddha, whose nature is pure, free from conceptualization, and unattached to any existence—such a person knows this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Born into the family of all Buddhas and protected by the Buddhas, they are the upholders of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas; such is the domain of the eye of wisdom.
Associating with spiritual friends, Delighting in pure and white dharmas, Diligently seeking the power of all Buddhas,
And hearing this Dharma with joy, The mind becomes pure and free from discrimination,
Like the vast empty sky; The lamp of wisdom destroys all darkness— Such is their sphere of experience, With a mind of great compassion.
Universally covering all worlds, they are entirely equal; this is their sphere of activity.
With a joyful mind free from attachment, they are able to relinquish everything; giving equally to all sentient beings is their sphere of activity.
Their minds are pure and free from all evils, ultimately without any regret.
To practice in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas is their sphere of activity;
To thoroughly understand the intrinsic nature of phenomena and the seeds of various karmas, And for their minds to remain unmoved and undisturbed—this is their sphere of activity.
With courageous and diligent exertion, Abiding with a mind that never regresses, they zealously cultivate omniscience.
This is their sphere of experience:

their minds dwell in tranquility within samādhi; having attained ultimate coolness and freedom from the fever of affliction, they have cultivated the causes for the ocean of all-knowledge—this is the liberation of those who have realized it.
Thoroughly knowing the true nature of all things, Entering deeply into the gates of the boundless Dharma-realm,
Universally delivering all living beings without exception— This is the liberation of the Lamp of Wisdom,
Who fully comprehends the true nature of sentient beings And remains unattached to the ocean of all existences.
Like reflections appearing universally in the waters of the mind,
this liberation of those on the true path arises from all Buddhas of the three periods of time through the seeds of skillful means and vows;
having practiced diligently throughout all kalpas and lands, this is the liberation of Samantabhadra.

Universally entering the gates of all dharma-realms, They see entirely the oceans of lands in the ten directions, And also see the kalpas of their formation and destruction therein; Yet their minds remain ultimately free from discrimination.
Within every single atom of the dharma-realm, They see the Tathāgata sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment.
Having accomplished enlightenment, you transform all classes of beings; this is the liberation of the Unobstructed Eye.

Throughout an ocean of immeasurable great eons, you have personally approached and made offerings to spiritual friends, seeking the True Dharma for the benefit of all living beings; having heard it, you remember it without any loss.
The vast realm of Vairocana, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable—
I shall now proclaim it for you by the power of the Buddha, so that your profound mind may become utterly pure.
Good son, in the distant past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, there was an ocean of worlds named...

The Mountain of Universal Radiance, True Gold and Mani Jewels. Within that ocean of worlds, there appeared a Buddha named King of Tranquil Majesty, the Wisdom Mountain Illumining the Entire Dharma Realm.
Good son, when that Buddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he purified that ocean of worlds.
Within that ocean of worlds, there were world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a world.
In each and every world-system, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms within a world; in each of these worlds, a Tathāgata appears in the world.

Each such Tathāgata proclaims as many sūtras as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, and in each sūtra, he bestows predictions of enlightenment upon as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, manifesting various supernormal powers and preaching the Dharma.

Through various Dharma-gates, they deliver immeasurable sentient beings. Good son, within that world-ocean of the True Gold Maṇi Mountain of Universal Radiance, there is a world-system named Banner of Universal Adornment.
Within this world-system, there is a world named Universal Radiance of All Jewel Colors, which manifests the reflections of all transformation Buddhas by means of a maṇi-king.

It constitutes the substance [of this world-system]. Its shape is like a celestial city. It has as its lower boundary a king of *maṇi* jewels that manifests the images of the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Tathāgatas.
It rests upon an ocean of all kinds of jewel-flowers, where the pure and the impure are intermingled.
Within this world-system, there are four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*) as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru. Among them, one four-continent system stands at the very center, named Sarva... (All).
Mount Ratnakūṭadhvaja. Each of its four continents is one hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and each contains ten thousand great cities.
Within Jambudvīpa, there is a royal capital named Dṛḍharatnavyūhadhvajapradīpa, which is surrounded on all sides by ten thousand great cities.
At a time when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa was ten thousand years, within it...
The king was named Sarvadharmasvaranirghoṣaparipūrṇakusumaketu. He had five hundred ministers, sixty thousand court ladies, and seven hundred princes.
All those princes were handsome, brave, and possessed of great majesty. At that time, the king’s sovereign power pervaded all of Jambudvīpa, and he had no enemies or adversaries.
Then, at the time when that world-system’s kalpa was nearing its end, there appeared...
The five corruptions arise. All people have short lifespans and meager resources; their physical forms are coarse and ugly, and they experience much suffering with little joy.

They do not cultivate the ten wholesome actions but instead devote themselves exclusively to evil deeds. They contend with one another in anger and mutually insult each other; they alienate others' kin and envy their prosperity.
Following their own whims, they give rise to biased views and greedily seek what is contrary to the Dharma. Due to these causes and conditions, the winds—
Rain does not fall at the proper time; the crops do not ripen. Gardens, forests, grasses, and trees all wither and dry up.
The people are destitute, and there are many pestilential diseases. They flee in all directions, finding no one to rely upon.

Countless, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of beings come together to surround the great capital city on all four sides, crying out at the top of their voices, some raising their hands, or...
They pressed their palms together; some struck their heads against the ground, some beat their breasts with their hands, some knelt and wailed aloud, and some leaped up and cried out.
Their hair was disheveled, their garments were tattered and filthy, their skin was cracked and split, and their faces were devoid of luster.
They spoke to the king, saying: "Great King, Great King! We are now impoverished, destitute, and exposed; we suffer from hunger, thirst, cold, and freezing. They were afflicted by disease.
We are frail and emaciated by illness, oppressed by manifold sufferings, and our lives will soon come to an end.
Having no refuge, no protector, and no one to whom we may appeal, we now come to take refuge in the Great King. We perceive in the Great King benevolence and wisdom;

toward the Great King, we conceive the thought of finding peace and happiness, the thought of finding what is dear, the thought of finding sustenance for life, the thought of being cared for, and the thought of finding a treasury of jewels.

He conceived the thought of encountering a bridge and ferry; the thought of meeting a road; the thought of finding a boat and raft; the thought of seeing a jewel island; the thought of obtaining wealth and profit;
and the thought of ascending to a celestial palace. At that time, having heard these words, the Great King attained a million *asaṃkhyeya* gates of great compassion.
With single-minded contemplation, he uttered ten kinds of words of great compassion. What are these ten? They are: "Alas! The multitudes..."
They have fallen into the bottomless great pit of saṃsāra; how shall I swiftly exert myself to rescue them and cause them to abide on the stage of omniscience?

Alas! Sentient beings are oppressed by all manner of afflictions; how shall I act as their protector and cause them to dwell securely in all wholesome deeds? Alas! Sentient beings [are afflicted by] birth, old age, and sickness...
“Toward that which is the terror of death, how shall I act as a refuge so that they may forever attain peace and stability of body and mind?
Alas! Sentient beings are constantly oppressed by the various fears of the world; how shall I provide them with aid so that they may dwell upon the path to omniscience?
Alas! Sentient beings lack the eye of wisdom and are constantly [afflicted] by their own bodies...”
Seeing them shrouded by the cataracts of doubt and false views, how shall I employ skillful means to enable them to extract these films?
Alas! Sentient beings are constantly deluded by the darkness of ignorance; how shall I act as a bright torch to cause them to behold the city of omniscience?
Alas! Sentient beings are constantly [afflicted] by stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception...
They are turbid. How shall I enlighten them so that they may realize the pure Dharma-body? Alas!
Sentient beings have long been adrift and submerged in the great ocean of birth and death.

How shall I universally transport and deliver them so that they may reach the further shore of supreme enlightenment? Alas! The faculties of sentient beings are rigid and difficult to subdue. How shall I...
"How shall I act as a charioteer to cause them to be fully endowed with the spiritual powers of all Buddhas? Alas!
Sentient beings are like those who are blind and sightless, unable to see the path. How shall I guide them so that they may enter the gateway of omniscience?
Having spoken these words, he beat the drum and issued a proclamation: "I now universally bestow [these gifts] upon all sentient beings, according to their needs."

He commanded that all be fully satisfied. Immediately, he issued a decree throughout the cities, large and small, and all the villages within Jambudvīpa, ordering that the treasuries be opened and various items be placed at the crossroads. These included gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *maṇi* gems, and other jewels;
clothing, food, drink, flowers, incense, and necklaces; as well as palaces, houses, couches, and bedding. He established them there.
Great luminous mani-jewel banners, whose light touches the body and renders it entirely peaceful and secure;
furthermore, providing medicinal decoctions for all causes of illness; various precious vessels filled with diverse jewels; vajra vessels filled with various fragrances;
precious incense vessels filled with various garments; palanquins, carriages, banners, flags, and silk canopies—all such requisites.
For all living beings, he opened his treasuries and bestowed their contents as gifts; he likewise gave away all villages, camps, cities, towns, mountains, marshes, forests, and thickets.

He surrendered his wife, children, kinsmen, and even his royal throne. He was able to relinquish everything internal and external—his head, eyes, ears, nose, lips, tongue, teeth, hands, feet, skin, flesh, heart, kidneys, liver, and lungs. Such was his steadfast and wondrous jewel.
On the eastern side of the city of Cloud-Lamp Adornment, there is a gate named Light of the Maṇi Mountain.
Outside that gate is a place for almsgiving assemblies; its ground is vast, pure, and level, free from pits, ravines, thorns, and gravel, all being composed of exquisite jewels.
It is strewn with various precious flowers, perfumed with various wonderful incenses, and illuminated by various jewel lamps. First.
Clouds of all manner of incense fill the void; immeasurable jewel trees stand in successive rows;
immeasurable nets of flowers and immeasurable nets of incense cover them from above; and hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of musical instruments constantly produce sublime sounds.
All such things are adorned with exquisite jewels; they are entirely the pure [abodes] of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the karmic fruits and retributions: within that assembly, lion thrones were established, with the ground made of ten kinds of jewels and railings of ten kinds of jewels.
Ten types of jewel-trees surrounded them on all sides, supported from below by diamond-jewel wheels, and held up together by images of nāgas and devas made of every kind of jewel.
Various precious objects served as adornments, with banners and streamers arranged in rows.
Above it was covered with a net, from which immeasurable precious incenses constantly emitted clouds of fragrance.
Various precious garments were distributed everywhere, and hundreds of thousands of kinds of music perpetually played beautiful melodies.

Furthermore, precious canopies were spread over it, constantly emitting the light of immeasurable precious flames, as brilliant and pure as Jāmbūnada gold. It was covered with a jeweled net from which various necklaces hung down. The *mo*... [text ends]
Jewel belts encircled the perimeter, and various jeweled bells constantly emitted sublime sounds, exhorting all sentient beings to practice virtuous deeds.
At that time, the Great King sat upon a lion throne; his appearance was upright and his physical marks were complete.
He wore a crown made of radiant, wondrous jewels, and his body, like that of Nārāyaṇa, was indestructible. Every single limb...
All were perfected. By nature, he was born into the lineage of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) and the King of Goodness; he attained mastery over both wealth and the Dharma.
His eloquence was unimpeded and his wisdom was clear and penetrating. He governed the country with such righteousness that none disobeyed his commands.
At that time, there were immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings throughout the various lands and diverse clans of Jambudvīpa.
Beings of various forms, various garments, various modes of speech, and various desires all came to this assembly to observe that king.
They all said, "This king is one of great wisdom; he is a Sumeru of merit; he is a moon of virtue;
he abides in the vows of a bodhisattva and practices vast generosity. At that time, when the king saw those who had come as supplicants, compassion arose within him.

The mind. One gives rise to a mind of joy; one gives rise to a mind of reverence; one gives rise to a mind of regarding [the teacher] as a virtuous friend; one gives rise to a vast mind; one gives rise to a continuous mind;
one gives rise to a mind of diligence; one gives rise to a non-retrogressive mind; one gives rise to a mind of relinquishment; one gives rise to a pervasive mind. Good son.
At that time, when the king saw those beggars, his heart was filled with great joy.

For even the pleasure experienced by the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the King of the Yāma Heaven, or the King of the Tuṣita Heaven throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas could not equal it;
nor could the pleasure experienced by the King of the Sunirmita Heaven over countless kalpas. From himself—
The bliss experienced by the King of Devas for immeasurable kalpas; the Brahma-bliss experienced by the Great Brahma King for boundless kalpas;
the celestial bliss experienced by the King of the Ābhāsvara Heaven for inconceivable kalpas; the celestial bliss experienced by the King of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven for inexhaustible kalpas;
and the bliss of dwelling in tranquility experienced by the Kings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens for unspeakable kalpas—all these were fully [attained].
It cannot be matched. Good son, it is like a person who is compassionate, filial, and fraternal, who encounters a world of calamity;
his parents, wife, children, brothers, and sisters are all lost. Suddenly, amidst the wilderness and on the roads, they encounter one another.
They gaze upon, honor, and console one another, their affection never reaching satiety. At that time, when the Great King sees those who have come seeking him, a thought arises in his mind...

Joy was likewise thus. Good son, at that time, because of his spiritual friend, the king’s aspiration for the Buddha’s bodhi increased, his faculties were perfected, his faith became pure, and his joy was fulfilled. Why was this?
This bodhisattva diligently cultivates all practices to seek omniscience. He vows to benefit all sentient beings;
he vows to attain the immeasurable, wondrous bliss of bodhi. He abandons all unwholesome states of mind and constantly delights in accumulating all roots of goodness.
He constantly vows to rescue and protect all sentient beings, and constantly delights in observing the path to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Constantly...
Delighting in the practice of the dharma of omniscience, fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings, entering the great ocean of the merits of all Buddhas,
shattering the mountains of the hindrances of all demonic activities and delusions, following in accordance with the teachings and practices of all Tathāgatas,
traversing the unobstructed path of omniscience, having already been able to enter deeply into the stream of omniscience, and the stream of all dharmas is ever...
Manifesting before them, their great vows are inexhaustible. As great beings, they abide in the dharma of great men.

They have accumulated the treasury of all universal gates of goodness. They are free from all attachments and remain unstained by any worldly realms. They know that the nature of all phenomena is like empty space.
Toward those who come to beg, they conceive the thought of them as their only son, the thought of them as their parents, and the thought of them as a field of merit. They conceive...

One should cultivate the perception of its rarity, the perception of the debt of gratitude for its benefits, and the perception of its firm stability. One should regard it as one's teacher and as the Buddha.
Without discriminating between place, without selecting based on lineage, and without choosing according to physical appearance, one should respond to whoever arrives as they desire.

With a mind of great compassion that is impartial and unimpeded, one should bestow everything universally so that all are fully satisfied. To those who seek food and drink, one gives food and drink. To those who seek... [text continues]
To those seeking clothing, he gives clothing; to those seeking incense and flowers, he gives incense and flowers; to those seeking garlands and parasols, he gives garlands and parasols.
He gives banners, pennants, necklaces, palaces, gardens, elephants, horses, chariots, seats, cushions, and bedding;
gold, silver, mani-jewels, and all manner of precious objects; all storehouses and treasuries; as well as his various retinues, cities, towns, and villages—all of these he gives away.
He bestowed all these things universally upon sentient beings. At that time, within this assembly, there was a daughter of a householder named Ratnaprabhā.
She was accompanied by sixty young maidens; she was upright and exquisite, a sight pleasing to all who beheld her.

Her skin was golden, her eyes and hair were deep blue, her body emitted a wondrous fragrance, and her mouth produced Brahma-sounds. She was adorned with most excellent precious garments and always maintained a sense of shame.
He felt shame. His right mindfulness was undisturbed. He was fully endowed with dignified deportment and showed reverence to his teachers and elders.

He constantly recollected and practiced the profound and wondrous conduct. He remembered and did not forget the Dharma he had heard. The roots of goodness from his past lives moistened his mind, making it pure and vast like space.
He brought peace equally to all sentient beings and constantly beheld the Buddhas, seeking all-encompassing wisdom. At that time, Ratnaprabha...
The woman approached the king from no great distance, joined her palms in homage, prostrated herself, and thought to herself: "I have gained a great benefit! I have gained a great benefit!

I have now encountered a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Toward this king, I conceive the notion of him as my great teacher, the notion of him as a spiritual friend, the notion of his being endowed with compassion, and the notion of his being able to provide me with protection. With a mind that was upright, she gave rise to great joy and cast off her body.

He offered the necklaces to that king and made this aspiration: "May this Great King now serve as a place of reliance for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings shrouded in ignorance. May I, in the future, likewise be so.

May I possess the same dharmas known by that Great King, the same vehicle he rides, the same path he cultivates, the same physical marks and characteristics he possesses, and all his wealth and property."
It gathers the assembly; it is boundless, inexhaustible, difficult to surpass, and indestructible.

May I, in the future, fully attain such as this, and wherever I am born, may I be reborn accordingly. At that time, the Great King, knowing that this maiden had conceived such a resolve, addressed her, saying:
"Maiden, whatever you desire, I shall grant it all to you; everything that I now possess—"

He renounced them so that all sentient beings might universally attain fulfillment. At that time, the girl Ratnaprabhā, her faith purified, gave rise to great joy and praised the king with these verses:
In the past, before this great king had appeared in this city, everything was utterly joyless, like the abode of hungry ghosts.
Sentient beings slaughtered one another; they engaged in theft, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, and untruthful words;
they spoke meaningless and harsh language, and they greedily coveted the wealth and possessions of others.
Those who harbor malice and poisonous intent, who hold wrong views and perform unwholesome deeds, fall into evil realms at the end of their lives.
Because such beings are shrouded by ignorance and abide in inverted views, the heavens do not send down rain;
due to the lack of timely showers, the hundred grains fail to grow.
The grasses and trees are all withered and parched, And the flowing springs have likewise run dry.
Before the Great King arose in this world, Rivers and ponds were all dried up; In the gardens and groves, there were many skeletons, Appearing from afar like a desolate wilderness.
Now that the Great King has ascended the precious throne, He extensively delivers all living beings; Like rising clouds, his bounty covers the eight directions.
A universal rain falls, satisfying all; the Great King attends to the common people.
All violent cruelties are severed, and the prisons are brought to rest; the orphaned and the solitary are all made secure.
In the past, sentient beings each harmed one another, drinking blood and eating flesh; now they have all given rise to a heart of compassion.
In the past, all sentient beings were poor and lacked clothing; they covered themselves with grass, emaciated by hunger like hungry ghosts.
Now that the Great King has appeared in the world, non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously and exquisite garments emerge from the trees.
Men and women are all adorned with finery; formerly, they vied for meager profits.

In times past, people committed evil acts, unlawfully usurping and plundering one another; they gave rise to improper greed and lust for others' wives and young maidens, violating and oppressing them in various ways.

Yet now, when seeing other women who are upright, beautiful, and finely adorned, everyone is instead fully satisfied. [This is the time when] all are now abundant and prosperous. It is as if one were wandering in the garden of Śakra. In former times, people committed evil deeds; they gave rise to improper greed and defilement, and in various ways they violated and coerced the wives of others and young maidens. Now, when seeing other women who are upright, exquisite, and beautifully adorned...
Yet his mind is free from attachment, like the gods of the Heaven of Contentment. In former times, sentient beings spoke falsely and untruthfully;
their speech was contrary to the Dharma and devoid of benefit, being crooked and intended only to win over others' minds.
Today, all classes of living beings have completely abandoned such evil speech, for their minds have become supple and gentle.

His speech is likewise harmonious and gentle. All sentient beings of former times who practiced various false dharmas—beings such as cattle, sheep, dogs, and swine—now join their palms in reverent salutation. Having heard the King’s True Dharma, they have awakened and abandoned their wrong views;
they now fully understand that the retribution of suffering and pleasure all arises from causes and conditions.
The Great King utters wondrous sounds, and all who hear them rejoice. The voices of Brahmā and Śakra, and all others alike, cannot equal his.
The Great King’s many precious canopies hang suspended in the midst of space;
supported by crystal poles and covered with nets of mani-jewels, golden bells naturally ring out from them.
With a harmonious and elegant voice, the Tathāgata proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma, extinguishing the delusions of sentient beings.
Furthermore, he extensively expounds upon all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions and within all kalpas;
he also speaks in successive order of the Tathāgatas and their retinues in the past lands of the ten directions.

And all the Tathāgatas within those lands likewise emit subtle and wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Jambudvīpa, extensively explaining the various distinctions of karma for humans, devas, and others.
Having heard this, sentient beings come to know their own storehouses of karma; they abandon evil and diligently engage in spiritual practice.
Dedicating this toward the Bodhi of the Buddha, The royal father was Pure Radiance, And the royal mother was Lotus Light.
When the five turbidities appeared, He occupied the throne and ruled the world.
At that time there was a vast garden, Within which were five hundred ponds; Each was surrounded by a thousand trees, With flowers covering them all.
Upon the banks of that pond, he erected a hall supported by a thousand pillars; its railings and other ornaments were all fully prepared without exception.
When evil dharmas arose in the final age, no rain fell for many years, and the ponds and streams were completely dried up;
grasses and trees all withered away seven days before the king was born.
First, auspicious signs appeared, which all who saw them took to heart; "The Savior of the World shall now emerge!
Then, at midnight, the great earth shook in six ways.
There was a jewel-lotus pond, its radiance like the rising sun, within which five hundred ponds were filled with water of merit.
Withered trees all sprout branches, Their flowers and leaves flourish and thrive.
The waters of the ponds, having filled to the brim, flow and spread everywhere, Pervading the land of Jambudvīpa;
There is nowhere they do not moisten and saturate— The medicinal herbs and various trees, The hundred grains, seedlings, and crops, Along with their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
All shall flourish and prosper; the ditches, pits, and mounds—every such place on the earth, whether high or low—shall all become level and even.
All thorns, gravel, pebbles, and every kind of impurity shall, in a single thought-moment, be transformed into various precious gems and jewels.
When sentient beings saw this, they rejoiced and offered praise, all saying:
"We have gained a great benefit, like a thirsty person drinking sweet water.
At that time, King Prabhāsa, together with his immeasurable retinue, prepared the royal carriage and traveled to observe the various gardens and within the five hundred ponds.
There is a pond named *Ānanda*; upon the pond is a Dharma hall where the father-king resides.
The former king said to his queen: "I recall that seven nights ago, at midnight, the earth shook and a light appeared here.
At that time, within that flower pond, a thousand-petaled lotus emerged."
The light is like that of seven suns, reaching upward to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
With a diamond for its stem and Jambu-river gold for its pedestal, it has various jewels for its petals and exquisite fragrance for its filaments.
The Medicine King is born upon that flower; with body upright, he sits in the full-lotus posture, adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Revered by the devas, the former kings were filled with great joy; entering the pond, he stroked the infant himself and took him to present to the Queen. "Your son should rejoice!
Treasure-treasuries all surge forth, and jeweled trees produce exquisite garments; celestial music plays beautiful sounds, filling the void of space."
All sentient beings were filled with great joy; With palms joined, they cried out, "How marvelous!

Sudhana’s heart of compassionate protection— At that time, the King emitted a bodily radiance That shone universally upon all things, Causing the darkness throughout the four continents to vanish And all illnesses to be extinguished, including those of yakṣas and piśācas.
Poisonous insects and various evil beasts that seek to harm others all hide away of their own accord;
ill repute and the loss of wholesome benefits, calamitous events, and the afflictions of disease—all such manifold sufferings are extinguished, and everyone rejoices.
All classes of sentient beings regard one another as their own parents.

Leaving behind evil, you give rise to a compassionate mind; Solely seeking all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), You close the gates to the miserable realms and reveal the path for humans and devas. Proclaiming omniscience (*sarvajña*), you deliver all living beings.
We, having seen the Great King, have universally obtained excellent benefit— We who were without refuge and without a guide.
"May all be at peace and happy.
At that time, the maiden Ratnaprabhā, having praised King Sarvadharmanirghoṣasamantavyūha with these verses, circumambulated him countless times.
With palms joined, she prostrated herself, bowed with deep reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side. Then, that great king—
He addressed the young woman, saying: "Excellent, young woman! That you are able to believe in and know the merits of others is truly rare.
Young woman, all sentient beings are unable to believe in and know the merits of others. Young woman, all sentient beings do not know how to repay kindness;
they lack wisdom, their minds are turbid and distracted, their natures are not clear, and they originally possess no resolve or strength."
Furthermore, there are those who regress from their practice. Such people do not believe in or understand the merits, supernatural powers, and wisdom possessed by Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas.
Girl, you now resolutely seek to attain Bodhi; you are able to know such merits of the Bodhisattvas.
Having been born now in this Jambudvīpa, you have developed a courageous mind to universally gather in all sentient beings—an achievement of no small merit.

It shall not be in vain; you too shall likewise achieve such merit. After the King had praised the girl, he personally bestowed priceless precious garments upon the maiden Ratnaprabhā and her retinue. Addressing each one individually, he said, "Put on these robes.
Then, the maidens knelt with both knees upon the ground, received them in their hands, placed them upon the crowns of their heads, and thereafter donned them. Once they had...
Having put on their garments, they circumambulated the king to the right. From within all those precious robes, the light of all the stars issued forth everywhere.
When the multitude saw this, they all said: "These women are all exceedingly beautiful; they are like the stars adorning a clear night sky.
Good son, who else could that King Sarvadharmanirghoṣaparipūrṇacchatra have been at that time? It was none other than [the Buddha].
Indeed, it is the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana. King Prabhāsa was King Śuddhodana;
Lady Padmaprabhā was Lady Māyā; and the maiden Ratnaprabhā was none other than my own self.
Those beings whom that king at that time gathered through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are precisely all those in this assembly.
These are bodhisattvas who have all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They dwell in stages ranging from the first to the tenth, possessing various great vows, accumulating various aids to the path, cultivating various sublime practices, being equipped with various adornments, attaining various supernormal powers, and abiding in various liberations; within this assembly, they are as follows:
Abiding within various palaces of sublime Dharma, at that time the Night Goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasukhasaṃvāsā,
wishing to reiterate the meaning of this liberation for the youth Sudhana, spoke these verses:
I possess vast eyes that see everywhere throughout the ten directions;

Within the ocean of all buddha-fields, I see those wandering through the cycle of the five destinies, And I also see all those Buddhas seated beneath the Bodhi tree, Their spiritual powers pervading the ten directions as they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. I possess pure ears.
I hear all sounds everywhere, and I also hear the Buddhas preaching the Dharma; with joy, I receive and uphold it.
I possess the knowledge of others' minds, which is non-dual and unimpeded; within a single thought-moment, I can fully comprehend the ocean of all minds.
I have attained the knowledge of past lives, by which I am able to know all kalpas.
I clearly understand the distinctions between myself and others; In a single thought-moment, I know the eons as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of lands.
I remember all those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, And the various classes of sentient beings within the five realms of existence.
I recall those Buddhas from the time they first resolved upon the aspiration for enlightenment, Until they cultivated all manner of practices.

Each and every one is perfectly fulfilled; they also know those Buddhas who, having accomplished the path to enlightenment through various skillful means, turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
They also know the ocean of all vehicles belonging to those Buddhas, as well as how long the True Dharma will endure and how many sentient beings will be delivered.
Throughout immeasurable eons, I have practiced this Dharma-gate; I shall now explain it for you.
O Son of the Buddha, you should study it!
O noble son, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation gate called "The Radiance of Vast Joy Born from [the Dharma]. As...
All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas draw near to and make offerings to all Buddhas; they enter the great ocean of vows for omniscience and fulfill the ocean of all the Buddhas' vows.
Attaining courageous wisdom, they universally enter the ocean of all bodhisattva stages from within a single bodhisattva stage.
Attaining pure vows, they universally enter all bodhisattva practices from within a single bodhisattva practice.
O Ocean of Conduct, you have attained the power of mastery; through a single gate of liberation of a bodhisattva, you universally enter the ocean of all gates of liberation of bodhisattvas.

How could I possibly know or describe those meritorious practices? Son of Good Family, within this site of enlightenment there is a night goddess named Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings. Go to her.
He asked the Bodhisattva: "How does one teach and transform sentient beings so that they may advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How does one adorn and purify all Buddha-fields? How does one serve all Tathāgatas? How does one practice all Buddha-dharmas?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and with great earnestness—
He gazed upon her with reverence, took his leave, and departed.
The seventh night goddess, Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamantāloka, represents the stage of *dūramgamā* (Far-Going).

"Far-Going" refers to reaching the very limit of the stage of effortful cultivation within the signless (*animitta*) state, thereby transcending the paths of the world and the two vehicles. At that time, Sudhana...

Having heard this liberation door of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous voice of the Bodhisattva, the youth was able to enter into its practice, progress therein, and seek it out according to the instructions.

He went to where the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamaya resided, and saw her seated upon a throne of exquisite jewels in the form of a lion, within a pavilion of various precious fragrant trees. Well...
Vasumitrā prostrated and, having expressed her resolve for awakening, inquired about the essential points of the Dharma.
The night goddess then bestowed upon her the Dharma-realm, first manifesting its efficacy by saying: "In this Sahā world, after the sun has set and amidst the darkness of night,"

Whenever I see sentient beings of various kinds from all places returning from distant travels, I secretly protect them all, ensuring they reach their destinations and dwell in peace and happiness throughout the night.

To those sentient beings in the prime of their youth who are addicted to beauty, indulgent in negligence, and self-indulgent in the five desires, I manifest the signs of old age, sickness, and death to terrify them, causing them to renounce desire and cultivate goodness. As for those of various kinds...
For sentient beings who are attached to desire, I teach the Dharma of the six pāramitās as individual remedies, causing them to abandon their obscurations and abide in the bodhisattva path.

This is the practice I myself follow; because Sudhana asked about the bodhisattva practice, I first informed him of this, and thereafter revealed the name of the dharma-gate, saying: "I have already accomplished the Bodhisattva Departure..."
[He attained] the liberation door of the light of vast, great joy. Sudhana asked, "What is the sphere of this liberation door?
This question concerns the scope of the activity and function of that liberation. The night goddess’s intended answer was:
"By entering this liberation, one can know the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means for universally gathering in sentient beings. This is the general statement of the answer, namely:
Taking the wisdom that knows how the Buddha gathers in sentient beings as the scope of its functional activity. Next, what is meant by "universally gathering"?
This refers to the fact that all the various joys experienced by all sentient beings are due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata. There are ten phrases in total.

This briefly reveals the aspect of universal inclusion. How is it known to be so? It is because the subsequent passage provides an interrogative explanation that extensively reveals the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
It says: "When I entered this liberation, I saw the Tathāgata—from cause to fruition—skillfully gathering sentient beings through great compassion.
Thus, one knows that joy arises from the Buddha. This is the general indication of its meaning. The following text first demonstrates the Tathāgata...
This is because, within the causes for [attaining] this state, one develops a mind of skillful means that universally encompasses all beings,
seeing that all sentient beings are attached to a self and what belongs to a self, dwelling in the dark chamber of ignorance, entering the dense forest of various views,
creating various karmas through manifold inversions, and thus transmigrating through birth and death in poverty and suffering, failing to encounter any Buddhas or Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is...
Confronting this pitiable state, he then gave rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to rescue beings from suffering and benefit all sentient beings.

This is what is meant by the aspiration that "may all sentient beings obtain all manner of exquisite jewels and requisites" to win over the hearts of beings. From this, twenty kinds of resolve are generated;
these are presented across fifteen lines of scripture to manifest the mind in which compassion and wisdom are practiced in union. Having thus given rise to the resolve to rescue those in suffering...
With a mind that universally encompasses all, one immediately practices the deed of rescuing those from suffering.
Having next given rise to such a mind, one attains the power of a bodhisattva and manifests great spiritual transformations throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
Before all sentient beings, one rains down all manner of necessities for life, fulfilling their every desire and intention so that they all rejoice.

Without regret and without parsimony, without interval and without interruption. Following the phrase "having given rise to such a mind," there are eighteen lines of scripture that fully clarify the practice of universal inclusion;
that is to say, in every thought-moment, one pervades the entire realm of sentient beings extensively and without limit.
Below this, it says: "Good son, in past ages, the Tathāgata Vairocana cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva."

At that time, there was not a single class of sentient beings who was not delivered; therefore, there was no single practice that was not cultivated. For this reason, he cultivated various miscellaneous practices.
Because the suffering of sentient beings is boundless, his practices were likewise immeasurable, causing the hearts of all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Below the passage on Vairocana, there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify these various practices in their entirety.
The above provides a general answer to the question concerning the realm of liberation.

Because one can know the Tathāgata’s skillful means and wisdom—which universally gathered in sentient beings throughout his past causal stages—as briefly explained above, this constitutes the realm of liberation.
The youth Sudhana asked, "Noble One, how long has it been since you first resolved your mind [for enlightenment]?

This question concerns the beginning of the night goddess’s resolve, intended to demonstrate the depth of her roots in the *dharmadhātu*. According to the subsequent answer, she resolved her mind at the same time as Vairocana;
therefore, the depth of what was investigated is vast and unfathomable. Thus, the night goddess replied: "In this place..."

It is difficult to believe and difficult to know; it is difficult to understand, difficult to enter, and difficult to explain. Because this mind of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-citta) is the cessation of objective conditions and is not an object of hearing, reflection, or cultivation, it is difficult to believe, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

Because the path of language is severed, it is difficult to explain. Because it is a realm that transcends emotion and leaves behind views, it is not known by worldly beings or those of the two vehicles. Furthermore...
This is not something known by bodhisattvas of provisional teaching.

As for those who are permitted to know it, only those protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas—who have eternally severed the afflictions and attained the realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—truly know it.
Because this Dharma-realm is the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it is not known by those of the Three Vehicles. (Above, eleven [sections]).
The preceding half of the sutra has clarified that it is permissible for those who are capable of understanding; yet, this Dharma-gate is inherently unspeakable.

Nevertheless, now, by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, I may also speak of it. Although those capable of understanding are difficult to find, because I wish to bring to harmony and transform those sentient beings who are ready for conversion, there are indeed those of the highest faculties who can believe and enter. Therefore, following [the Buddha’s intent] now...

"What you have asked may indeed be explained. At that time, the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamantadigvairocanā, observing the realm of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, reiterated the meaning of what is difficult to know and difficult to explain.
First, she spoke in verse to clarify its significance, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, as for what you have asked— The profound realm of the Buddhas is difficult..."
Even if one were to contemplate for as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, it could not be fully described.

The following twenty-one verses all reiterate the profound meaning that is difficult to comprehend. The preceding section has set forth the intent of the dharma-gate; the following section now directly answers the questions posed.
There are both prose and verse sections. First, it narrates the beginning of the arousal of the bodhicitta, stating:
"Good son, in the distant past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the atoms of an ocean of worlds. This single sentence alone is already inconceivable.
Regarding what is called an "ocean of worlds": suppose a single buddha-field were ground into atoms, and each atom were itself a field.
By gathering together as many such fields as there are atoms, they are combined to form a single ocean of worlds. Within this context, a metaphor is employed:
the ocean of worlds is further ground into dust, and each atom represents one kalpa. How could such kalpas ever be reached?
Is it conceivable? This refers to a time prior to kalpas as numerous as the atoms within this ocean of lands;
that was the very beginning of Vairocana’s generation of the bodhicitta. How could such a place be known?
It is said that prior to these atom-like kalpas, there was an ocean of worlds named Universal Radiance True Gold Maṇi Mountain. This refers to the most [distant]...
The name of the capital city of the first ocean of worlds is "Great Array of Lands. This collectively reveals the time and place of generating the bodhicitta.
There are seven lines of scripture that merely describe the events of a Buddha appearing in the world at that time, preaching the Dharma, and saving sentient beings.
Next, noble son, within that ocean of worlds called Universal Radiance, there is a world-system named Universal Adornment Banner.
This indicates that the aforementioned ocean of worlds called Universal Radiance is formed by the aggregation of many world-systems;
this world-system of Universal Adornment is one among those many within that ocean.
It is merely a world-system (*lokadhātu-jāti*). Next, it says: "Within this world-system, there is a world named Universal Radiance of All Jewel Colors.
This intends to show that many worlds are gathered together to form a single universally adorned world-system;
thus, this "world of all jewel colors" is but one world within that system. [This progression] moves from the broad to the narrow. From...
Within the ocean of infinite lands, the text describes reaching a single world-system to demonstrate that the Dharma-realm is immeasurable;
it indicates that one can know each and every such place. Below, it describes that within every world of various jewel colors there are four continents as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru;
this further proceeds from the description of many sets of four continents and contracts down to a single set of four continents.
Within this, one southern Jambudvīpa is precisely the place where Vairocana first resolved his mind.
