The preceding section on the world contains eight lines of scripture; next, the passage beginning with "In it there was a king" correctly narrates the primary narrative (nidāna).
It says that the King of Jambudvīpa was an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), named Sarvadharmanirghoṣasamantacchatra. This is precisely...
This is the very person of Vairocana’s initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Below, it describes how, at a time when that world and its eon were nearing their end and the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) had arisen, the Universal Monarch first generated the mind of enlightenment and practiced the conduct of gathering in sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "when the kalpa is about to end," this refers to how sentient beings, due to the five turbidities and evil karma, experience the suffering of the three calamities.
There is a passage of five lines that describes the sufferings within the kalpa; it continues by saying that [the calamities] all come together to surround the great capital city of the king.
This signifies that suffering sentient beings come to seek salvation from the king, which is precisely a pitiable state. There is a passage of eight and a half lines.
He describes the pitiable state [of sentient beings]. Next, at that time, having heard these words, the Great King attained one million *asaṃkhyeya* gates of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This means that the mind of great compassion seeking to rescue from suffering suddenly and all at once arose; how courageous it was!
Thus, he gave rise to ten kinds of great compassion, saying: "Alas! Sentient beings have fallen into bottomless birth and death."
"This great pit—how can I swiftly exert myself to rescue them and cause them to abide upon the ground of all-knowledge?
This is the first thought-moment generated by Vairocana Tathāgata. Contemplate this single phrase:
it not only completely uproots the suffering of sentient beings and bestows all happiness upon them, but also speaks of causing them to abide in all-knowledge."
The Ground (*bhūmi*). This means causing each and every being to ultimately attain Buddhahood and obtain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

How could this mind be known by those of the Two Vehicles or by Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings? Below this are ten "Alas for sentient beings," and those for whom there is compassion consist of three classes of beings:
namely, those who seek desire, those who seek existence, and those who seek a false holy life (*brahmacarya*) within the triple world.
The suffering of sentient beings is brought to rest by these three types [of compassion]. Thus, there are these ten forms of pity (*karuṇā*).

Desiring to rescue and deliver them all, the meaning of these ten forms of pity in the sutra is extremely profound. The commentary cites the text of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to explain it, whereby its subtlety becomes apparent.
Therefore, at the end of the section on the ten forms of pity, it says: "How shall I act as a guide so that they may enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?"
Therefore, as a disciple, one must not fail to know the original mind first generated by our Buddha when he cultivated the causes for kalpas past.
After these words were spoken, and after ten expressions of compassion had been uttered, he then struck the drum and issued a proclamation to inform and entreat the suffering beings, saying:
"I now universally bestow [myself] upon all sentient beings; according to their needs..."

He caused all necessities to be fully provided for. He then issued a decree throughout all the large and small cities under his dominion in Jambudvīpa to open their treasuries and distribute all manner of goods, bestowing them entirely upon sentient beings.
Below this, there are fifty-seven lines of scripture describing the extensive practice of great giving, the King’s heart of joy, and how, through this giving, he entered deeply into all things.
Regarding this Dharma-gate, it is said that one does not select locations, nor does one select species, nor does one choose physical appearances;
rather, to whoever comes, according to their desires, one bestows [the gift] upon all sentient beings universally with such great and impartial compassion.
Since even this very first thought of generating the mind and this single act performed are thus vast and unobstructed, how much more so...
Can this be conceived by thought? The above section narrates the beginning of Vairocana’s initial resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

The following section narrates the beginning of the night goddess Śaradāṃśusamudgatā’s initial resolve; since she was contemporaneous with Vairocana, it can be known that her arrival [in the world] was long ago.
Next, at that time, there was a daughter of a householder in this assembly named Ratnaprabhā.
[The Buddha] said, "This girl was the very person who, as a night goddess in the past, first resolved her mind [on enlightenment].
While the King was indeed presiding over the great assembly of offerings, the girl Ratnaprabhā, standing not far from the King, saw him practicing such vast generosity.

She then conceived the thought that such an opportunity was difficult to encounter; she removed the jeweled necklace from her own body and offered it to the King, making this aspiration: 'May I, in the future...'"
It was likewise so. This was the very first thought-moment of the night goddess’s initial resolve, which arose because of the king.
Because the girl Ratnaprabhā had resolved that all beings should be like the king, wherever she was born, she was always reborn there.
At that time, the great king, knowing that this young girl had conceived such a mind, addressed her:

He said: "O maiden, whatever you desire, I shall grant it all to you. Above this, there are fourteen and a half lines of sūtra text describing the maiden’s initial resolve and the past causes for her vision of the night goddess. Next, the maiden Ratnaprabhā spoke verses in praise of the king;
there are fifty-two verses in total, from the beginning up to the dedication toward the Buddha-bodhi, which constitutes the twenty-fifth [chapter].

The verse generally praises these two virtues. Following this, from "the father of the king, King Pure Radiance" and "the mother, Lotus Light" onwards, there are twenty-seven verses that reveal the original parents of the king.
The reason for recounting the king’s parents is to demonstrate that the present Śuddhodana and Māyā were both Vairocana’s very first generation of the bodhicitta in the past.
This is the origin from which [the Buddha's] parents came. The verses recount the king’s past lives (jātaka) to reveal the causal conditions for this single assembly.
At that time, after the maiden Ratnaprabhā had praised the king, she joined her palms in reverence and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, the great king deeply praised the young woman and further prophesied that she too would likewise achieve such [enlightenment].
Merit. He then took a precious robe and personally bestowed it upon the young girl, instructing her to put it on immediately.
Once the girl had put it on, the assembly saw that she was so upright and beautiful, like the stars adorning a clear night sky. From this point onward, there is the prophecy of this Night Goddess;
above this, there are thirteen lines of scripture describing the King’s praise of the young girl. These two [sections] above—
This major section sequentially recounts past causes to directly answer Sudhana’s question regarding how long it has been since he first resolved his mind upon enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Considering the inconceivability of each instance of his resolve and every one of his practices, as well as the vast length of the kalpas through which they have spanned, the Night Goddess initially stated that this matter is difficult to believe, difficult to understand, difficult to enter, difficult to know, and difficult to explain. Thus far, the account of the initial resolution of the mind has been narrated.
To begin with, he points to past causes; thus, he brings the present together with the past. He next says:
"Good son, was the King Universal Sound of All Dharmas at that time anyone other than the present Tathāgata Vairocana?"
King Prabhāsa was King Śuddhodana. Lady Padmaprabhā was Lady Māyā. The maiden Ratnaprabhā was none other than myself.
Those beings whom that king at that time gathered through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are precisely the bodhisattvas in this assembly;
they have all attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed enlightenment.
[The section on] "Transformation," or those who dwell from the first stage up to the tenth stage, consists of seven scriptural passages that synthesize the ancient and the modern.
At that time, the Night Goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamantāloka, for the sake of the youth Sudhana, further proclaimed the meaning of liberation and spoke these verses:
"I possess vast eyes, which universally behold the ten directions; all the oceans of lands..."
Regarding the cycle of the five destinies: hereafter follow ten verses in total, which describe the general characteristics of liberation to demonstrate one’s own realization.
The final verse says: "Throughout immeasurable eons, I have practiced this dharma-gate; I now speak it for you. O Son of the Buddha, you should study it.
Having thus concluded, he exhorts [the assembly] to practice and study within the *dharmadhātu*. Next follows the expression of humility.
He then humbled himself, saying: "I know only this Bodhisattva liberation door of the Radiance of Vast Joy Born of Birth;

as for those Bodhisattvas who attend upon and make offerings to all Buddhas, who enter the ocean of great vows of omniscience, and even universally enter the ocean of all liberations—how could I possibly know them? Thus he deferred to those who followed.
The friend said, "In this place of practice, there is a night goddess named Mahāpraṇidhānavīryaparākramasarvasattvatrāṇa.
You should go and ask her; she will explain it for you. Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at her feet, gazed up at her with earnest devotion, and took his leave to depart.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Fascicle Seventy-two;
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Fascicle Seventy-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Sī;
Excerpts and Clarifications by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Sī on Kuāngshān, Chapter Thirty-nine, Section Fourteen: Entering the Dharmadhātu.
At that time, the youth Sudhana went to the place of the night goddess Sarvajagadrakṣāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhā.
He saw that night goddess seated upon a lion throne of the king of mani-jewels that manifests all palaces, within a great assembly.
A net of mani-jewels manifesting all lands throughout the dharma-realm covered her above. She appeared like the sun...
The body that manifests as the reflections of the moon and the lunar mansions; the body that appears according to the minds of sentient beings so that all may universally behold it;
the body that manifests forms identical to those of all sentient beings; the body that manifests an infinite and vast ocean of colors and marks;

the body that manifests all modes of conduct; the body that manifests appearances throughout the ten directions; the body that universally tames all sentient beings; the body that manifests extensively...
He manifests a body of swift and rapid supernormal powers; he manifests a body that incessantly benefits sentient beings;

he manifests a body that constantly traverses space to benefit others; he manifests a body that pays homage at the feet of all Buddhas; he manifests a body that cultivates and practices all roots of goodness;

he manifests a body that upholds the Buddha-dharma without forgetfulness; he manifests a body that brings to fulfillment the great vows of Bodhisattvas; he manifests a body whose radiance fills the ten directions.

The body of the square form; the body that manifests the lamp of the Dharma to universally extinguish the darkness of the world; the body of pure wisdom that manifests the realization that all phenomena are like illusions;
the body of the nature of reality (dharmatā) that manifests as being far removed from the darkness of defilements; the body of clear comprehension of phenomena manifested by universal wisdom;

the body that manifests ultimate freedom from affliction and fever; the body of indestructible solidity; the body of the Buddha’s power that manifests as having no fixed abode; and the body that manifests as being without division.
He manifested a body distinct from the defiled body, revealing his original, pure *dharmatā*-body.

At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld such bodies, as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, and with single-minded devotion prostrated himself, casting his entire body to the ground. After a long while, he rose, joined his palms in reverence, and gazed up at him.
He gave rise to ten kinds of mind toward the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). What are these ten? Namely, toward the spiritual friend... [he gave rise to] a mind of... etc.

One should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind that produces knowledge identical to one’s own, so as to cause me to apply myself with diligence to the factors conducive to the path to all-knowledge.
One should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind regarding the pure fruits of one’s own karma, so as to cultivate roots of goodness through attending upon and making offerings to them.
One should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind that adorns the bodhisattva practices, so as to enable me to swiftly adorn all bodhisattva practices.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) the mind that accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas, because they instruct and guide me so that I may cultivate the Path.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend the mind that gives birth, because they can give birth to the unsurpassed Dharma within me.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend the mind of renunciation, because they cause me to practice the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and thereby achieve renunciation.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend a mind that possesses the ocean of all merit and wisdom, so that I may accumulate all pure dharmas.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend a mind of growth, so that I may increase all-encompassing knowledge.
One should conceive toward the spiritual friend a mind that possesses all roots of goodness, so that my aspirations may be fulfilled. One should conceive toward the spiritual friend...
It is the mind capable of accomplishing great benefit, because it enables me to dwell with mastery in all bodhisattva dharmas, to perfect the path to omniscience, and to attain all Buddha-dharmas.

These are the ten. Having generated this mind, one attains the same practices as that night goddess and as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field; that is to say, they share the same mindfulness, constantly recollecting in their hearts...
They share the same wisdom because they mindfully contemplate all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;

they share the same destination because they discern and resolve the various gateways of the ocean of all dharmas; they share the same awakening because they are able to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;

they share the same faculties because they universally enter all worlds of the three periods of time with wisdom equal to space; and they share the same roots because they have accomplished the pure light of Bodhisattvas.
They share the same faculty because they clarify the faculty of wisdom. They share the same object because they are well able to cultivate the adornment of unimpeded merit for all bodhisattva paths.
They share the same realization because they universally illumine the sphere of activity of all Buddhas.
They share the same meaning because they are able to comprehend the true nature of all phenomena through wisdom.
Therefore, they are identical in valor, for they are able to shatter all mountains of obstacles; identical in form-body, for they manifest bodies in accordance with the minds of sentient beings;
identical in power, for they do not regress in their quest for omniscience; identical in fearlessness, for their minds are as pure as space;
and identical in diligence, for they practice the bodhisattva path through immeasurable eons without weariness. They are identical in...

[They are] like eloquence, because they have attained the light of unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). They are like peerless equality, because their physical marks are pure and transcend the world.
They are like kind speech (*priyavāditā*), because they cause all sentient beings to rejoice. They are like wondrous voices, because they universally expound the ocean of all dharma-gates.
They are like full sounds, because all sentient beings understand according to their respective types. They are like pure virtue, because they cultivate...

Because they possess the pure merit of the Tathāgata, they are identical in the ground of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*). Because they receive the wheel of Dharma from all Buddhas, they are identical in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Because they dwell securely within the realm of all Buddhas, they are identical in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), for in every thought-moment they universally encompass the ocean of sentient beings in all lands.
Because they universally rain down the rain of Dharma to moisten and nourish all sentient beings, they are identical in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). They are identical in body.

They share the same karma of action, because they teach and transform all sentient beings through skillful means. They share the same karma of speech, because they expound all dharma-gates using sounds that accord with the various species of beings.
They share the same karma of mind, because they universally gather in sentient beings and establish them within the realm of omniscience.
They share the same adornment, because they purify and adorn all Buddha-fields. They share the same intimacy, because whenever a Buddha appears...
Because they all draw near to the world, they join in the exhortation, requesting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma;
because they always delight in making offerings to all Buddhas, they join in the offering; because they discipline and subdue all sentient beings, they join in the teaching and transformation;
because they illuminate all dharma-gates, they share the same radiance; because they universally know the minds of all sentient beings, they share the same samādhi.
They are identical in pervasiveness, for by the power of their mastery they fill all oceans of Buddha-fields while cultivating various practices.
They are identical in their place of dwelling, for they abide in the great supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas. They are identical in their retinue, for they dwell together with all bodhisattvas.
They are identical in their sphere of entry, for they universally enter the most subtle locations within worlds. They are identical in their mental intention, for they universally know all...
They are identical in their buddha-fields, for they universally enter the ocean of all buddha-fields. They are identical in their skillful means, for they manifest within all buddha-fields.

They are identical in their supreme excellence, for they are peerless among all buddha-fields. They are identical in their non-retrogression, for they universally enter the ten directions without obstruction.
They are identical in their destruction of darkness, for they have attained the great light of the wisdom of all Buddhas' attainment of bodhi.
They are identical in their clarity, for they enter the ocean-like assemblies of all Buddhas;
they are identical in their endurance of non-arising, for they universally pervade the networks of all Buddha-fields and reverently make offerings to the Tathāgatas of unspeakably many lands;

they are identical in their wisdom-realization, for they thoroughly understand the oceans of various Dharma-gates; they are identical in their practice, for they accord with and proceed through all Dharma-gates; they are identical in their aspiration, for—

Because of their deep aspiration for the pure Dharma, they are identical in purity. Because they adorn their body, speech, and mind by accumulating the merits of a Buddha, they are identical in wondrous intent.
Because their wisdom regarding all phenomena is clear and lucid, they are identical in diligence. Because they universally gather all roots of goodness, they are identical in pure conduct.
Because they bring all bodhisattva practices to fulfillment, they are identical in non-obstruction. [They are identical] in the realization of...

Because all phenomena are signless, they are identical in skillful means (*kauśalya*). Because there is mastery of wisdom regarding all phenomena, they are identical in accordance with inclination (*yathābhiprāya*).

Because they manifest objects according to the minds of sentient beings, they are identical in expedient means (*upāya*). Because they have well-practiced all that should be practiced, they are identical in protective mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇā*).

Because they have attained the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas, they are identical in entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Because they have attained entry into all bodhisattva stages, they are identical in their realization of the ground.
Therefore, they share the same dwelling, for they abide securely in all bodhisattva stages; they share the same prediction, for all Buddhas bestow predictions upon them;
they share the same samādhi, for in a single instant they universally enter all doors of samādhi;

they share the same establishment, for they manifest the various deeds of all Buddhas; and they share the same right mindfulness, for they maintain right mindfulness toward all doors of objective realms.

They share the same practice, for they cultivate all bodhisattva practices throughout all future kalpas. They share the same pure faith, for they take supreme delight in the immeasurable wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
They share the same renunciation, for they eliminate all obstacles. They share the same non-retrogressive wisdom, for their wisdom is equal to that of all Tathāgatas.
They share the same taking of birth, for they manifest in accordance with the needs of beings to bring them to maturity.
They share the same dwelling because they act for the sake of all sentient beings; they share the same objective sphere because they abide in the gateway of skillful means toward omniscience;
they share the same lack of dependence because they have forever severed all minds that rely on a basis; and they share the same teaching of the Dharma.

Because they have already entered the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena, they are identical in their diligent cultivation; because they are constantly protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, they are identical in their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
because they awaken sentient beings and cause them to cultivate all bodhisattva practices, they are identical in their spiritual might (*ṛddhi*);

because they are able to enter the oceans of worlds in the ten directions, they are identical in their *dhāraṇīs*; because they universally illumine the ocean of all total-retentions (*saṃdhāraṇī*), they are identical in their secrets.
It is identical to the Dharma, for it thoroughly understands the sublime gateways of the Dharma within all sūtras.
It is identical to the profound Dharma, for it realizes that all phenomena are like empty space. It is identical to radiance, for it universally illumines all worlds.

It is identical to joy, for it reveals the teachings according to the minds of sentient beings to bring them delight. It is identical to trembling, for it manifests spiritual powers for the sake of all sentient beings.

Because the power of their supernatural penetrations universally vibrates all lands throughout the ten directions, they are identical in being non-empty; because seeing, hearing, remembering, or thinking of them causes the minds of all beings to be tamed, they are identical in renunciation;
and because they fulfill the ocean of all great vows and accomplish the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, they are identical in liberation.
At that time, the youth Sudhana observed the power of great vows and diligence that protects and delivers all beings.
The night goddess Sarvasattvābhirucitadarśanā gave rise to ten kinds of pure minds and attained as many practices identical to those of bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
Having attained these, her mind became even more purified. She bared her right shoulder, prostrated at her feet, joined her palms with single-minded devotion, and praised her with these verses:
I have resolved with a firm mind, Vowing to seek supreme enlightenment. Now, regarding this spiritual friend, I shall give rise to the thought of him as myself;
By beholding the spiritual friend, I shall gather inexhaustible pure dharmas and eliminate all stains of sin, Thereby accomplishing the fruit of bodhi. Thus do I behold the spiritual friend.
With a mind adorned by merit, throughout all lands and eons until the end of the future, I diligently cultivate the path I have traveled.
I call to mind my spiritual friends who have gathered me in and benefited me;
for my sake, they have fully manifested the true Dharma of the correct teaching, closing off all evil realms and revealing the path to humans and devas.
They also demonstrate to all Tathāgatas the path to the attainment of omniscience. I recall that spiritual friends are the treasury of the Buddha’s merits;
moment by moment they are able to give birth to an ocean of space-like virtues, bestow upon me the pāramitās, increase my inconceivable merit, and grow my pure qualities.
May I wear the Buddha’s silken crown; may I keep in mind the spiritual friend who can fulfill the path of Buddha-wisdom.
May I always rely upon my vows and bring the pure, white dharmas to perfection.
By means of these things, may I be fully endowed with all merit, and for the sake of all sentient beings everywhere, may I preach the path of omniscience.
"The Noble One is my teacher; he has bestowed upon me the unsurpassed Dharma. Even throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, one could not repay his kindness.
At that time, after Sudhana had spoken these verses, he said: "O Great Sage, I pray that you will explain this door of liberation for me."
"What is its name? How long has it been since you first resolved your mind [for enlightenment]? After how much time will you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The night goddess replied: "Good son, this door of liberation is named 'Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings to Cause Them to Produce Roots of Goodness.
Because I have accomplished this liberation, I have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal."
Thus, they enter into the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Having realized the state of non-reliance, they abandon the world.

They fully know the distinctions between the characteristics of all phenomena, and are likewise able to comprehend that blue, yellow, red, and white are all by nature unreal and without distinction, yet they constantly manifest immeasurable physical bodies (*rūpakāya*), namely various physical bodies rather than a single physical body. There is no...
The physical body of the limits; the pure physical body; the physical body adorned with all ornaments; the universally seen physical body;
the physical body equal to all sentient beings; the physical body that appears before all sentient beings; the physical body whose radiance shines everywhere;
the physical body that one never tires of beholding; the physical body with pure marks and signs; and the physical body of light free from all evils—these he manifested.
The physical body of great valor; the physical body that is exceedingly difficult to encounter; the physical body that no one in all the worlds can eclipse;
the physical body universally praised by all the worlds as inexhaustible; the physical body that constantly observes in every thought-moment;
the physical body that manifests various clouds; the physical body of various shapes and manifest colors; the physical body that displays immeasurable powers of mastery.
The body of wondrous radiant light; the body of all-pure and exquisite adornments; the body that accords with and matures all sentient beings;
the body that appears before them to subdue them according to their inclinations; the body of unobstructed universal radiance;
the body that is pure and free from turbidity or defilement; the indestructible body fully endowed with adornments; the inconceivable...
The body of the radiance of skillful means of the Dharma; the body that cannot be eclipsed by any other form; the body that destroys all darkness and is free from all obscurity;
the body that gathers all pure and white dharmas; the body of the ocean of merit with great power.
The form-body born from the cause of past reverence; the form-body born from a mind as pure as space; the most supreme and vast form-body;
the form-body that is uninterrupted and inexhaustible; the form-body that is an ocean of radiance;
the form-body of equality that has no dependence upon any world; the form-body that pervades the ten directions without obstruction—these appear in every thought-moment.
The body of the ocean of various colors and forms; the body that increases the heart of joy in all sentient beings;
the body that gathers in the ocean of all sentient beings; the body that proclaims the ocean of merits of all Buddhas from within each and every pore;
the body that purifies the ocean of desires and understandings of all sentient beings; the body that definitively resolves the meaning of all dharmas; the body without...
The body that universally illuminates all obstructions; the body of pure radiance equal to space; the body that emits vast and pure light;
the body that manifests the stainless Dharma; the incomparable body; and the body adorned with diverse distinctions.
The form-body that universally illumines the ten directions; the form-body manifested according to the times to respond to sentient beings;
the tranquil form-body; the form-body that extinguishes all afflictions; the form-body that is a field of merit for all sentient beings;
the form-body that is not in vain for any sentient being who beholds it; the form-body of great wisdom and heroic power; the form-body that is unobstructed and universally pervasive; the sublime...

A body-cloud that appears everywhere throughout the world so that all may receive benefit; a form-body complete with an ocean of great compassion; a form-body like a king of jewel mountains of vast merit;
a form-body that emits light shining universally upon all realms of existence in the world; a form-body of great wisdom and purity;
a form-body that gives rise to the mind of right mindfulness in sentient beings; and a form-body of the radiance of all jewels.
The form-body of the treasury of universal radiance; the form-body manifesting various pure marks within the world; the form-body seeking the locus of all-knowledge;
the form-body manifesting smiles to cause sentient beings to give rise to pure faith; the form-body of light adorned with all jewels;
the form-body that neither grasps nor abandons any sentient being; the form-body that is neither determinate nor ultimate.
The body that manifests through the power of sovereign empowerment; the body that manifests all supernatural transformations and emanations;
the body born into the family of the Tathāgatas; the body that is free from all evils and pervades the ocean of the Dharma-realm;

the body that universally appears in the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas; the body endowed with an ocean of various multitudes of colors; and the body that flows forth from virtuous conduct.
He manifests a physical body according to those to be transformed; a physical body that all worlds never tire of beholding; a physical body of various pure radiances;
a physical body manifesting the ocean of all three periods of time; a physical body emitting an ocean of all radiances;
a physical body manifesting an ocean of infinite varieties of radiances; and a physical body of fragrant radiances that transcends all worlds.
The form-body manifests as clouds of sun-discs of ineffable radiance; it manifests as clouds of vast moon-discs;
it emits clouds of exquisite flowers from Mount Sumeru in infinite measure; it issues forth clouds of various garlands;
it manifests clouds of all kinds of precious lotuses; it raises clouds of all burning incense pervading the entire dharma-realm; it scatters all...
He manifests a body like the color of clouds from powdered incense; he manifests a body of the great vows of all Tathāgatas;
he manifests a body that expounds the ocean of Dharma through all languages and sounds; he manifests the form of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
In every thought-moment, he manifests such physical forms and appearances, filling the ten directions, so that all sentient beings may see them, remember them, or hear them.

They preach the Dharma; whether through close association, or by attaining awakening, or by seeing supernatural powers, or by witnessing transformations, they all tame beings according to their inclinations at the appropriate time.
These beings abandon unwholesome karma and abide in wholesome conduct.
Good son, you should know that this is due to the power of great vows, the power of the knowledge of all modes, the power of the bodhisattva’s liberation, and the power of great compassion.

It is through the power of great compassion that such deeds are performed. Good son, having entered this liberation, I thoroughly understand that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without differentiation, yet I am able to manifest immeasurable physical bodies (*rūpakāya*). Within each body, I manifest an ocean of immeasurable physical forms;
from each form, I emit clouds of immeasurable light; and within each ray of light, I manifest immeasurable Buddha-lands. One...
In a single land, immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world. Each Buddha manifests immeasurable supernormal powers to awaken the roots of goodness from past lives of sentient beings:
causing those who have not yet planted them to plant them; causing those who have already planted them to grow; and causing those who have already grown to reach maturity.
In every moment of thought, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to [attain] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He has attained non-retrogression. Good son, regarding your question as to how long ago he first resolved his mind on Bodhi and cultivated the practices of a Bodhisattva—this matter I shall now explain for you by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Good son, the wheel of wisdom of a Bodhisattva is far removed from all realms of conceptual discrimination; it cannot be defiled by the length or brevity of saṃsāra.
Thus, these various kalpas are distinguished and displayed according to their purity, vastness, narrowness, and quantity. Why is this? Because the wheel of wisdom of a bodhisattva is pure by nature;
it is free from the net of all conceptualization and transcends the mountains of all obstacles, shining universally upon those who are to be transformed according to their needs.
Son of good family, it is like the solar orb, which has no day or night; yet when it rises, it is called "day."
The time of disappearance is called night. The wisdom-wheel of the Bodhisattva is likewise: it is without discrimination and without the three periods of time;
yet, appearing in accordance with the minds [of beings], it teaches and transforms sentient beings. To speak of its abiding in past or future kalpas is merely a designation.
Good son, it is like the solar disc: though it dwells in the sky over Jambudvīpa, its reflection appears within all precious objects, as well as in rivers, seas, and all [other receptacles].
In clear water, all sentient beings behold it with their own eyes, yet that pure sun does not come here.
Likewise, the wheel of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom emerges from the ocean of existence and dwells in the tranquil sky of the Buddha’s true Dharma, free from any dependence.
Nevertheless, for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, he takes birth among the various realms of existence according to their respective types. Truly...
They do not undergo birth and death, nor are they stained by attachment. They have no conceptual discriminations regarding kalpas of long or short duration.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas have ultimately abandoned all perversions of thought, mind, and view, attaining true vision and seeing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
They know that all worlds are like dreams and illusions, and that there are no sentient beings; yet, solely through the power of great compassion and great vows, they manifest.

They teach, transform, and subdue sentient beings. Son of the Buddha, it is like a boatman who, with a great ship upon a river, relies neither on this shore nor clings to the opposite shore, nor does he dwell in midstream, yet he ferries sentient beings across without ceasing.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this; by means of the ship of the *pāramitās*, within the stream of birth and death...
They do not rely on this shore, they do not cling to the other shore, and they do not dwell in the middle of the stream; yet they ferry sentient beings across without ceasing.
Although they have practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons, they have never discriminated between the length or brevity of those eons. O Son of the Buddha, they are like the great void:
within it, all worlds are formed and destroyed, yet it remains free from discrimination, its fundamental nature pure and untainted.
Without confusion, without obstruction, and without weariness; neither long nor short, they sustain all lands throughout all future eons.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: with a vast and profound mind equal to the realm of empty space, they raise the wind-wheel of great vows to gather in all sentient beings, causing them to leave the evil realms and be born in the various good destinies, and leading them all to dwell securely in omniscience.
The Ground. Having extinguished the bonds of the suffering of all afflictions and birth-and-death, they possess no mind of sorrow, joy, weariness, or aversion.
Good son, it is like a person created by illusion who, though possessing all limbs, lacks the ten things—inhaling and exhaling, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, sorrow and joy, and birth and death.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this; by means of [the realization that all is] like an illusion...
Wisdom. The equal Dharma-body manifests various forms and appearances, dwelling for immeasurable eons within all realms of existence to transform sentient beings.
Amidst all circumstances within birth and death, it feels neither joy nor weariness;

it is without attachment or aversion, without suffering or pleasure, without grasping or relinquishing, and without tranquility or fear. O Son of the Buddha, although the wisdom of a bodhisattva is thus profound...

It is profound and difficult to fathom. I shall, by relying on the Buddha’s power of majestic spiritual authority, explain it for you, so that all bodhisattvas of future ages may fulfill their great vows and accomplish all powers.
Son of the Buddha, in the distant past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, there was an eon named Good Light and a world named Jewel Radiance. Within that eon, there was...

Ten thousand Buddhas appeared in the world. The first of these Buddhas was named Dharma-wheel Sound Void-Lamp King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with the ten titles fully perfected. In that Jambudvīpa, there was a royal capital named Ratnavyūha.
Not far to its east was a great forest called Subhāsa, within which was a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) named Ratna.
Flowers. Within that place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) was a lion throne consisting of a treasury of *maṇi* lotuses of universal radiance.
At that time, the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon this throne.

He remained seated in the place of enlightenment for a full hundred years, [teaching] for the sake of all bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and those in Jambudvīpa who had planted roots of goodness in the past.
For those already matured, he expounded the True Dharma. At that time, there was a king named Prasenajit.

The lifespan of the people of that age was ten thousand years. Among them, many committed killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, harsh words, greed, malice, and wrong views;
they were unfilial toward their parents and showed no respect for śramaṇas, brahmins, and others. At that time, the king, desiring...
In order to subdue them, he established prisons, stocks, and fetters for their confinement; therein, immeasurable sentient beings suffered various pains.
The king had a crown prince named Shanfu (Well-Subdued), who was exceptionally handsome and pleasing to behold, endowed with twenty-eight of the marks of a great man.
While in his palace, he heard from afar the sounds of the prisoners' agonizing cries and felt deep compassion in his heart.
From the palace, he entered the prison, where he saw various offenders bound together by shackles, fetters, and collars, placed in dark and secluded places;
some were being scorched with fire, some were being smoked with fumes, some were being subjected to flogging and caning, and some were undergoing castration and dismemberment.
Naked, with disheveled hair, emaciated by hunger and thirst, with tendons severed and bones exposed, they wailed in intense agony.
Upon seeing them, the Prince felt compassion in his heart and comforted them with a voice free from fear, saying: "Do not be distressed; do not grieve or be afraid."
"I shall cause you all to attain liberation. He then went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying, "The prisoners in the jail endure bitter suffering that is difficult to endure;
I pray that you will grant them clemency and bestow upon them fearlessness. At that time, the king immediately assembled five hundred ministers and asked them, "What do you say of this matter?
The ministers replied, "Those criminals have privately stolen the property of the state."
"He plotted to seize the royal throne and broke into the inner palace; his crimes deserve execution. Even those who pity him and seek to rescue him should likewise face the death penalty.
At that time, the crown prince’s compassion grew even more intense, and he said to the great minister: "If it must be as you say, then release this man.
You may punish me according to what is appropriate; for his sake, I am able to endure all manner of suffering."
I would not hesitate to sacrifice my body or lose my life, so that these sinners might all be freed from suffering. Why is this?
If I do not rescue these sentient beings, how can I possibly rescue those in the prison of the triple world who suffer?
All sentient beings within the triple world are bound by craving, obscured by ignorance, impoverished and lacking merit, and have fallen [into ruin].
In the various evil realms, their physical forms are base and ugly; their faculties are dissolute and their minds are deluded, seeking no way out.

They have lost the light of wisdom and take pleasure in attachment to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). They sever all merit and extinguish all wisdom; various afflictions (*kleśa*) turbidly agitate their minds.
Dwelling in the prison of suffering, they enter the snares and nets of Māra, subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, distress, and harm. Thus it is.
These beings are constantly oppressed by various sufferings; how may I bring them liberation? I ought to sacrifice my own body and life to rescue them.
At that time, the ministers went together to the king’s presence and, raising their hands, cried out in a loud voice:
"Great King, you should know that according to the Crown Prince's intent, he would destroy the royal law, and the calamity would reach ten thousand people. If Your Majesty cherishes him..."

"If the one who administers punishment is held accountable, the King’s precious throne will not endure for long. Upon hearing these words, the King was filled with a towering rage and ordered that the Crown Prince and the criminals be executed.
When the Queen heard this, she was overcome with grief and wailed aloud. She disfigured her appearance and cast off her finery, then hurried to the King's presence with a thousand court ladies.
Prostrating herself on the ground, she bowed at the King's feet and spoke thus to them all: "Only..."
"I pray that Your Majesty will spare the life of the crown prince. The king immediately turned to address the prince, saying, "Do not save this criminal.

If you save this criminal, I shall surely put you to death. At that time, because the prince desired to seek omniscience exclusively, because he desired to benefit all sentient beings, and because he wished to universally rescue and gather them through great compassion, his mind remained firm and unshakable.
Feeling discouraged, he again addressed the king, saying, "I pray you, forgive his offense; I shall take his place and suffer execution. The king said, "Do as you wish.
At that time, the queen said to the king, "Great King, I pray you grant the prince permission to practice giving for half a month and cultivate merit to his heart's content before he is punished.
The king immediately granted his consent. At that time, to the north of the capital city, there was a great garden named Sunlight (Sūryaprabha). This was...
In the past, at the site of the almsgiving, the Prince went there to establish a great assembly of offerings.

Food and drink, clothing, flower garlands and necklaces, scented ointments and powdered incense, banners, flags, precious parasols, and all manner of ornamental requisites were provided in full measure to everyone according to their requests.
After half a month had passed, on the final day, the king, ministers, elders, householders, and the people of the city and towns, as well as...

All the various non-Buddhists gathered together. At that time, the Tathāgata Dharmacakranirghoṣagaganapradīparāja, knowing that the time had come to discipline all sentient beings, was accompanied by a great assembly;
surrounded by celestial kings, honored by dragon kings, protected by yakṣa kings, praised by gandharva kings, and bowed down with heads touching his feet by asura kings and garuḍa kings.
With pure minds, they scattered various precious flowers. The Kinnara King joyfully invited him, and the Mahoraga King gazed upon him with single-minded devotion as he entered that assembly.

At that time, the Prince and the great multitude saw from afar the Buddha approaching, majestic and extraordinary, his faculties serene and composed like a well-trained elephant, his mind free from defilement and pure.
In the pond, he manifested great supernatural powers, displayed great mastery, and revealed great majestic virtue. His body was adorned with various marks and signs of excellence.
He emitted great radiance that shone universally upon the world. From every pore, clouds of fragrant flames issued forth, shaking immeasurable Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
Wherever they reached, they rained down all manner of ornaments. By the power of the Buddha...
[The Buddha’s] majestic demeanor was such that any sentient being who beheld him would have their mind purified and filled with joy, and their afflictions extinguished.
At that time, the Prince and the great assembly prostrated themselves before his feet, touching the ground with their five limbs. They prepared a seat for him, joined their palms, and said:
"Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! We pray that you will compassionately accept us and dwell here."
As for the seat: by the supernatural power of the Buddha, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens immediately transformed this seat into a seat of fragrant maṇi lotuses.
The Buddha sat upon it, and the assembly of bodhisattvas likewise took their seats, surrounding him on all sides.

At that time, all sentient beings within that assembly, having seen the Tathāgata, found their suffering extinguished and their obstacles removed, becoming capable of receiving the noble Dharma. Then the Tathāgata...

Knowing that they were ready to be transformed, he spoke the *sūtra* with a perfect voice, titled "The Universal Illumination Wheel of Causes," enabling all sentient beings to understand it according to their respective capacities.
At that time, eighty *nayuta* of sentient beings within the assembly distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
An immeasurable number of *nayuta* of sentient beings attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), and ten thousand [sentient beings]...
Having been born into the path of the Mahāyāna, he entered the conduct of Samantabhadra and fulfilled his great vows.
At that time, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a hundred Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions attained mastery over their minds through the Mahāyāna.
All sentient beings in immeasurable worlds were liberated from the evil realms and reborn in the heavens. It was at this very moment that Prince Sudānta—
I attained the Bodhisattva liberation door of teaching and transforming sentient beings to cause them to produce roots of goodness.

Good son, who else could that Prince have been at that time? It was I myself. Because I gave rise to great compassion in the past, I sacrificed my body, life, and wealth to rescue suffering sentient beings;
I opened my doors for great giving and made offerings to the Buddhas, thereby attaining this liberation. O Son of the Buddha, you should...
Know that at that time, I acted solely for the benefit of all sentient beings; I was unattached to the triple world, sought no karmic retribution, and did not crave fame.
I had no desire to praise myself or disparage others. Regarding all sensory objects, I was neither stained by craving nor overcome by fear;
I merely adorned the essential path of the Mahāyāna and constantly delighted in observing all things.
This is the gateway of wisdom. By practicing asceticism, one attains this liberation. Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Were those five hundred ministers who wished to harm me at that time anyone else? They were none other than the present followers of Devadatta, numbering five hundred.
All these people, having received the Buddha’s transformation through his teaching, shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding the three types of enlightenment: in a future age, after eons as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru have passed, there will be an eon named *Sūryaprabha* (Good Light) and a world named *Ratnaprabhā* (Jewel Light).

Within that world, he will attain Buddhahood; five hundred Buddhas will appear in succession in the world, the first Tathāgata being named Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion), the second named Lokānugrahakara (Benefiting the World), and the third named Mahākāruṇikaguru (Teacher of Great Compassion).
Son, the fourth was named Savior of Sentient Beings, and so on, until the last, who was named King of Physicians.
Although the great compassion of those Buddhas was equal, their lands, clans, parents, births, renunciations, and studies of the Way were not the same.
They proceeded to the site of enlightenment, turned the wheel of the true Dharma, and preached the sūtras.
Their speech and voices, their assemblies of light, their lifespans, the duration of the Dharma’s abiding, and their respective names were each distinct.

O Son of the Buddha, those sinful beings whom I have saved are none other than Krakucchanda and the other thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, as well as millions of asaṃkhyeyas of great bodhisattvas.
Sa. In the presence of the Tathāgata Amitavīryabalakīrtiguṇaprajña, he resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now, throughout the lands of the ten directions, he practices the bodhisattva path, cultivating and increasing it.

This Bodhisattva who taught and transformed sentient beings, causing them to give rise to roots of goodness and attain liberation, was at that time King Prasenajit, who is now the great master of debate, the Nirgrantha Sañjayin.
Those who were the king’s court ladies and various attendants at that time were these sixty thousand disciples of the Nirgrantha.
Together with their teacher, they came to erect the banner of great debate and engaged in discussion with the Buddha, whereupon they were all completely subdued.
This is the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. All these people shall become Buddhas;

their lands, adornments, eons, and names shall each be distinct. Son of the Buddha, at that time, after I had saved those whose offenses were to be expiated, my parents permitted me to renounce my kingdom, wife, children, and wealth, and [I proceeded] to the Sound of the Wheel of Dharma.
He left the household life to study the Way under the Buddha Ākāśapradīparāja. For five hundred years, he purely cultivated the brahma-faring.
Thereupon, he attained the accomplishment of one million dhāraṇīs, one million supernormal powers, and one million treasuries of Dharma.
He applied courageous and vigorous effort in seeking all-knowledge, purified one million gates of endurance, increased one million minds of contemplation, and achieved...
By means of the power of a million bodhisattvas, they enter a million gates of bodhisattva wisdom; they attain a million gates of the *prajñāpāramitā*;

they behold a million Buddhas of the ten directions; they give rise to a million great vows of a bodhisattva; in every thought-moment, they illuminate a million Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions;
and in every thought-moment, they recollect the past and future kalpas of the worlds in the ten directions.
Within every thought-moment, they know the ocean of transformations of ten million Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Within every thought-moment, they see all sentient beings in ten million worlds throughout the ten directions— those in their various realms of existence according to their karma,
at the time of birth and at the time of death, in good or evil destinies, with beautiful or ugly forms— and they perceive the various minds of those sentient beings.
He practiced. He clearly understood all their various desires and pleasures, various faculties and natures, various karmic habits, and various accomplishments.
Son of the Buddha, after my life ended at that time, I was reborn once again in that royal family and became a wheel-turning monarch.
Following the parinirvāṇa of that Tathāgata Dharmacakraghoṣagaganapradīpa-rāja, I immediately encountered him here.
He served and made offerings to the Tathāgata Dharmasūnya-rāja; next, he became Śakra.
In this very place of practice, he encountered the Tathāgata Devendragarbha, whom he approached and made offerings to; next, he became the King of the Yāma Heaven.
In this very world, he encountered the Tathāgata Mahāpṛthivībalaparvata, whom he approached and made offerings to; next, he became the King of the Tuṣita Heaven. In this very world...
He encountered and made offerings to the Tathāgata Dharmacakra-raśmi-ghoṣarāja.
Next, as the king of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, he encountered and made offerings to the Tathāgata Gaganajñānarāja in this very world.
Next, as the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, he encountered and made offerings to the Tathāgata Abhedyadhvaja in this very world.
Next, he became a king of the asuras; in this very world, he encountered the Tathāgata Sarvadharmanirghoṣarāja, whom he approached and made offerings to.
Next, he became a Brahmā king; in this very world, he encountered the Tathāgata Samantavyūhanirmāṇadharmaghoṣa, whom he approached and made offerings to.
O Son of the Buddha, within this Good Light eon in this Jewel Radiance world, there were ten thousand...
When Buddhas appeared in the world, I approached, served, and made offerings to them all.
Subsequently, there was an eon named Sunlight, during which sixty billion Buddhas appeared in the world. The first Tathāgata was named Mountain of Wondrous Features;
at that time, I was a king named Great Wisdom, and I served and made offerings to that Buddha. Following that, there was a Buddha named Appearance of Perfection.
Pūrṇaskandha. I served and made offerings to him as a householder. Next, there was a Buddha named Vimalaketu; I served and made offerings to him as a minister.
Next, there was a Buddha named Parākramadhara; I served and made offerings to him as an asura king.
Next, there was a Buddha named Merudhvaja; I served and made offerings to him as a tree deity.
Poṣa. Next there was a Buddha named Vimalabāhu; I served and made offerings to him as a caravan leader.
Next there was a Buddha named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin; I served and made offerings to him as a city deity. Next there was a Buddha named Ratnaśikhin;
I served and made offerings to him as Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King. Next there was a Buddha named Anuttara.
Dharmakīrti, I approached and made offerings to the Buddha named Gandharvarāja as a king of the gandharvas.
Next, there was a Buddha named Prabhāsa-mukuṭa; I approached and made offerings to him as a king of the kumbhāṇḍas.
During that kalpa, sixty billion Tathāgatas appeared in the world in this successive order. At each of these Buddhas' abodes, I constantly assumed various bodies.
They draw near to and make offerings to [the Buddhas], teaching and bringing to maturity immeasurable sentient beings. From each and every Buddha,
they obtain various gates of samādhi, various gates of dhāraṇī, various gates of supernatural powers, various gates of eloquence, various gates of all-knowledge,
various gates of the light of Dharma, and various gates of wisdom, which illuminate the various worlds of the ten directions.
Entering oceans of various Buddha-fields, one beholds oceans of various Buddhas, becoming purified, accomplished, increased, and expanded.
Just as one has approached and made offerings to that many Buddhas within this eon, so too, throughout all places in oceans of worlds for as many eons as there are atoms,
one approaches and makes offerings to all the Buddhas who appear in the world, and listens [to their teachings].
Hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith, upholding and protecting it was likewise so.
Thus, in the presence of all such Tathāgatas, they all cultivated this door of liberation and further attained immeasurable skillful means for liberation.
At that time, the Night Goddess Sarvasattvatrāṇaśaraṇadā, wishing to reiterate the meaning of this liberation, spoke these verses for Sudhana:
He said:
"With a heart of joy, faith, and delight, you ask about this inconceivable Dharma of liberation.
Relying on the power of the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, I shall proclaim it for you; you should listen and receive it."
In the past, throughout boundless and vast eons, exceeding in number the atoms within oceans of lands, there was a world named Jewel Light. Within it was an eon called Good Light;
during this Great Eon of Good Light, ten thousand Tathāgatas appeared in the world.
I have approached and made offerings to them all, and from them I studied this liberation. At that time,
there was a royal capital named Priyavyūha, vast, level, and exceedingly beautiful,
inhabited by beings of various karmas— some with pure minds and some who committed evil.
At that time there was a king named Jyotiṣprabha, who always governed all living beings with the True Dharma.
His crown prince was named Sudānta; his physical form was upright and he was endowed with all the marks of excellence.
At that time, there were immeasurable criminals whose bodies were bound in prison, destined for execution.
Upon seeing this, the Crown Prince gave rise to compassion and petitioned the King from above, requesting that he grant clemency.
At that time, the ministers together addressed the King: "Now this Crown Prince endangers the kingdom;
such a criminal ought to be executed. Why then do you seek to save them all and set them free?"
At that time, King Prasenajit said to the Crown Prince: "You must save him; you shall receive his retribution yourself.
The Prince’s compassionate thoughts grew even deeper, and he vowed to save all sentient beings without ever retreating or fearing.

Then the King’s consort, her attendants, and others all came to the King's presence and addressed him, saying: [The remainder of the verse is: "The King’s consort, her maidservants, and the rest, All came together to the King's side and spoke these words:"
"I pray that you release the Crown Prince for half a month, so that he may practice giving to sentient beings and cultivate merit.
Having heard this, the King immediately granted his permission. He established a great assembly of almsgiving to relieve the poor and destitute;
there were no sentient beings who did not arrive, and whatever they requested was all provided to them.
Thus, as the fifteen days of the fortnight drew to a close and the time for the Prince’s execution was approaching,
hundreds of thousands of millions of people gazed upon him simultaneously, all wailing in lamentation.
Knowing that the faculties of the assembly were about to ripen, that Buddha came to this gathering to transform the multitude of living beings.
Manifesting the great adornment of miraculous transformations, The Buddha,
through the skillful means of a single voice, Expounds the sutras that universally illuminate the lamp of Dharma;
The minds of immeasurable beings become supple and gentle, And all receive the prediction of their future enlightenment.
Prince Śubha-vinīta gave rise to great joy and resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
he vowed to serve the Tathāgata and become a refuge for all sentient beings.
He then immediately left the household life to dwell under the Buddha’s guidance, practicing the path to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, he immediately attained this liberation; With great compassion, he extensively saves all living beings.
Dwelling therein for oceans of kalpas, He contemplates the true nature of all phenomena.
Constantly rescuing sentient beings from the ocean of suffering, In this way he cultivates the path to enlightenment.
All the Buddhas who appear throughout the kalpas, I serve them all without exception,
With a mind of pure faith and understanding, Listening to, upholding, and protecting the Dharma they teach. Furthermore,
for as many oceans of immeasurable and boundless kalpas As there are atoms within a Buddha-field, [I shall practice].
I shall make offerings to every single Buddha appearing in the world,
just as I have done; I recall how in the past, when I was a crown prince, seeing sentient beings in prison,
I vowed to sacrifice my own body to rescue and protect them, thereby realizing this gate of liberation.
Throughout an ocean of vast eons, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields, I have constantly practiced and cultivated this,
causing it to increase in every thought-moment; furthermore, I have attained boundless skillful means,
through which I have been able to see all the Tathāgatas therein and receive their awakening.
May I increase and clarify this liberation, And through various powers of skillful means, Throughout immeasurable billions of eons, I shall study this inconceivable gate of liberation.
The ocean of all Buddhas' teachings is boundless; I am able to drink it all at once in its entirety.
All lands throughout the ten directions—his body enters them all without obstruction;
the various names of realms across the three periods of time—he knows them all completely in every thought-moment.
The oceans of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time—he clearly perceives each and every one without exception.
They are also able to manifest their physical forms and travel everywhere to the abodes of those Tathāgatas;
furthermore, in all lands throughout the ten directions, before all Buddhas, the Teachers,
they cause clouds of every kind of adornment to rain down as an offering to all the Unsurpassed Enlightened Ones.
Furthermore, with an ocean of boundless great questions, they entreat all the World-Honored Ones;
they receive and uphold, without forgetting or losing, the clouds of sublime Dharma rained down by those Buddhas.
Moreover, before the assemblies of all Tathāgatas in immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions, they [uphold the teachings].
Seated upon a throne adorned with manifold wonders, He manifests various supernormal powers;
Furthermore, throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions, He displays all manner of miraculous transformations:
Within a single body he manifests infinite bodies, And within infinite bodies he manifests a single body.
Furthermore, from each and every pore, he emits countless great rays of light;
through various skillful means, he dries up the ocean of afflictions of sentient beings.
Moreover, from each and every pore, he manifests clouds of infinite transformation bodies.
Pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions, They rain down the Dharma everywhere to deliver all beings.
All the children of the Buddhas in the ten directions Enter this inconceivable gate of liberation;
Throughout all future eons until the very end, They dwell securely, practicing the bodhisattva path.
He preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations, causing them all to cast off the net of false views;
he reveals the heavenly realms and the two vehicles, and even the Tathāgata’s omniscience and the places where all sentient beings take birth, manifesting infinite and diverse bodies.
Manifesting myriad forms identical to all classes of beings, They preach the Dharma universally according to their minds;
If one attains this gate of liberation, One dwells in an ocean of boundless merit.
Like the number of atoms in oceans of lands, It is inconceivable and immeasurable.
"Good son, I know only this liberation door of teaching and transforming sentient beings to cause them to give rise to roots of goodness.
As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they transcend all worlds and manifest bodies within the various realms of existence;

they do not dwell upon objects of perception, they are without obstruction, they thoroughly understand the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they are well able to examine all phenomena, and they have attained non-self."
Wisdom that realizes the dharma of selflessness; teaching and taming all sentient beings without ever ceasing;
with a mind always dwelling peacefully in the non-dual gateway to reality; universally entering the ocean of all verbal expressions—how could I now know or describe such an ocean of merit?
Such courageous wisdom, such spheres of mental activity, such realms of samādhi, and such liberation!
"O son of good family, in this Jambudvīpa there is a grove named Lumbinī. In that grove there is a deity named Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhā.
Go to her and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva cultivate the bodhisattva practice?
How is one born into the family of the Tathāgatas and become a light for the world, remaining without weariness throughout all future kalpas? Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated himself."
Circumambulating her feet countless times, he joined his palms in reverence, gazed up at her, took his leave, and departed.

The eighth great vow is entrusted to the Night Goddess of Diligence (*Vīrya-rātridevatā*), for she dwells in the Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*), where the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) universally protects and succors all by means of the wind of great vows.
As for the Immovable Stage, it refers to the spontaneous and continuous succession of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Its characteristics are as follows:

Because he could not be moved by afflictions, at that time the youth Sudhana, following the instructions of his previous spiritual friend, went to the place of the night goddess Sarvajagadrakṣāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhā.
He saw that night goddess seated upon a lion throne called the Universal Manifestation of All Palaces, a Treasury of Maṇi Kings, amidst a great assembly. Well... [he saw her].
Before Vimalakīrti had even had time to inquire further, that night goddess silently bestowed the Dharma-realm upon him by manifesting the physical forms of the sun, moon, and constellations.

These manifested twenty-four types of bodies, each with its own specific revelation. The first ten types were transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that responded to the capacities of sentient beings.
Following those, she manifested the six types belonging to all Buddhas, which correspond to the accomplishment of the Dharma (*dharmasiddhi*).
The body of practice manifests the eight kinds [of bodies] below as being like illusions; this is the body that accords with reality by being free from obstructions.

It predominantly manifests various bodily distinctions in accordance with internal virtues, causing those who see the body to realize the mind. This is precisely the dharma-realm realized by the Night Goddess.
At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld these various bodies, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, and with single-minded devotion prostrated himself.
He immediately realized the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in accordance with what he had seen and gave rise to ten kinds of mind toward the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
This refers to generating a mind of equality toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and so forth. This is a profound realization of complete identity.
Having generated this mind, one attains the same practices as that night goddess and the bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-field.

Because of the prior arousal of the ten minds, such as the mind of equality with oneself, one attains practices identical to those of the Bodhisattva Kalyāṇamitrasama. Regarding what is called "identical," there is an explanation in the *Śāstra*.
There are four meanings. First, the non-duality of person and phenomena, which is identical to the entire dharma-realm. Second, the non-duality of cause and effect, which is identical to all Buddhas.
Third, the non-duality of self and others, which is identical to all Bodhisattvas. Fourth, the non-duality of defilement and purity, which is identical to all sentient beings.
The reason one is able to be thus identical is precisely due to the Bodhisattva of the Eighth Stage.
Having realized the principle of non-arising, he and others act in mutual cooperation; because they have attained mastery over form, all things are without obstruction.
This pervasive clarity is identical [to that of Samantabhadra]. While this was merely a preliminary encounter for Sudhana, it is only here that the actual realization is revealed.

Therefore, what follows—namely, "sharing the same mindfulness," meaning his mind constantly recollects all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and so forth—constitutes these eighty-four kinds of sameness.
Regarding the practices: there are fifty practice-sūtras, which are merely mentioned in brief; in reality, they are even more numerous. Therefore, the conclusion below states:

"At that time, the youth Sudhana, observing the Night Goddess Sarvajagadrakṣāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhā, gave rise to ten kinds of pure minds and attained [qualities] equal in number to the atoms within a Buddha-field."
Having attained this sameness, his mind became further purified. He praised her with ten verses beginning with, "I have generated a firm resolve to seek unsurpassed enlightenment," and so forth.

Having recited these, he manifested a superior state of mind to demonstrate that his profound realization was in perfect accord with hers, thereby expressing the depth of his gratitude for her profound kindness.
This concludes the section where the night goddess, without waiting for Sudhana’s inquiry, first [spoke].
Thus, by silently revealing the Dharma-realm, he has already enabled Sudhana to obtain the benefit of profound realization.
Yet, although Sudhana has beheld the functioning of liberation and received its benefits, he does not yet know the name of this liberation; therefore, he asks below:
"What is the name of this gate of liberation? How long has it been since you first resolved your mind [for enlightenment]? "How much time has passed?"

When one attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood. Sudhana posed these three questions, yet the Night Goddess answered only regarding the name of her liberation and the time she first resolved to attain enlightenment;
she did not answer as to when she would become a Buddha. Her intention was to manifest that she had already attained Buddhahood.
The meaning of the subsequent passage is self-evident. The Night Goddess first answered by stating the name of the liberation:
"O son of good family, this gate of liberation is called 'Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings so that They May Generate Roots of Goodness. Previously, she had only bestowed it through silence;
here, for the first time, she speaks of bestowing her own dharma-realm. Below, she reveals the functional activity of this liberation, saying: "Because I have accomplished this liberation..."

One awakens to the equality of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. There are three scriptural passages that clarify how, although the fundamental reality of the *dharmadhātu* was first realized as equal, the arising of function based upon that reality constitutes the boundless great function of the *dharmadhātu*.
Below, its function is demonstrated, stating: "And it constantly manifests immeasurable form-bodies (*rūpakāya*), namely, various kinds of form-bodies, and so forth."
Briefly stated, one hundred kinds of physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) are manifested. There are thirty-eight lines of scripture [concerning this].
This intent reveals that having realized the equal *dharmadhātu*, one then realizes the "spontaneously born, effortless mental body" (*manomayakāya*) among the three types of mental bodies.
Therefore, it concludes by indicating: "The physical body in the form of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is manifested," thereby manifesting liberation.

The great function of the gates of liberation is boundless. This is also because Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage realize the true suchness of equality (*samatā-tathatā*) and dwell in the stage of mastery over form;
therefore, they manifest manifold physical bodies. Thus, the text below concludes by indicating this, stating:
"In every thought-moment, they manifest such forms and bodies, filling the ten directions," and so forth. There are ten lines of scripture that summarize these great functions.

It is profound and vast, without limit, in order to answer the question concerning the name of liberation. Later, in response to the inquiry regarding the duration and proximity of the arousal of the mind, he said:
"Good son, as to the duration and proximity of the arousal of the mind that you have asked about, such a meaning is extremely profound and difficult to explain."

Receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, I shall now explain this for you. In the following formal exposition, he first praises the profundity of the Dharma to reveal the reason why it is difficult to explain.
He says: "The wheel of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is far removed from all realms of conceptual discrimination;
it cannot be differentiated by such kalpas as long or short, defiled or pure, broad or narrow, many or few, within the cycle of birth and death."
It is revealed as being thus profound, pure by nature, and free from all conceptualization; how, then, could it be expressed through words or conceptual distinctions?
Nevertheless, although it cannot be spoken, those who wish to speak do so in order to universally illuminate [beings] according to their needs for transformation.
Even so, though it is spoken, it is difficult to comprehend; therefore, the following cites the examples of the sun’s orb, the boatman, and the great ocean.

The five metaphors, such as that of an illusion and a magical transformation, appear in the *Twenty-three Practices Sūtra* (*Triṃśatikā-prakaraṇa*), which uses these analogies to reveal meanings that are extremely profound and difficult to fathom.

Therefore, it concludes with the following indication: "O Son of the Buddha, although the wisdom of a bodhisattva is thus profound and difficult to fathom, I shall, relying upon the Buddha’s spiritual power, explain it for you.
The subsequent text then formally narrates the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
This begins as a response to Sudhana’s question regarding the duration of time.

When it says, "O Son of the Buddha, in ages long past, beyond oceans of worlds," it means that many worlds are gathered together to form a single world-system (*lokadhātu-jāti*), and many such world-systems are gathered together to form a single ocean of worlds (*lokadhātu-samudra*).
Now, this entire Buddha-field within that ocean of worlds is to be completely shattered into pieces.
Dust. Taking these particles of dust as the measure for one kalpa—one particle representing one kalpa—how could the number of such kalpas possibly be conceived?
Now, referring to the time prior to this number of kalpas, it is said to be "beyond" (atīta) and so forth. Prior to this, there was a kalpa named *Sūryaprabha* (Good Light).
Within this kalpa, there was a world named *Ratnaprabhā* (Jewel Light), and this world existed during that kalpa.
In the center, ten thousand Buddhas appeared in the world. The first of these Buddhas was named Dharma-Wheel-Sound-Empty-Space-Lamp-King (*Dharmacakranirghoṣagaganapradīparāja*).
In that world, there was a Jambudvīpa, within which was a royal capital.
Not far to the east of that capital was a great forest named Sublime Light (*Prabhāsa*). Within the forest was a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), named Jewel...
Flower. At that time, the Buddha Dharmacakrapravartin attained supreme perfect enlightenment within this forest.
For a full hundred years, he expounded the True Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity. While that Buddha remained in the world, there was a king in the land named Prabhāsa.
During the king’s reign, the human lifespan was ten thousand years; however, his people mostly committed evil deeds and sowed [the seeds of] suffering.

At that time, King Prasenajit, desiring to subdue wicked sentient beings, established prisons, jails, shackles, fetters, and instruments of punishment to confine them; thus, immeasurable sentient beings underwent great suffering.
At that time, the king had a crown prince named Śubha-vinīta who resided within the palace. From afar, he heard the sounds of the prisoners’ agonizing pain. His own...
