that is to say: the vastness of the worlds, the establishment of the worlds, the wheels of the worlds, the fields of the worlds, the distinctions of the worlds, the revolutions of the worlds, the lotuses of the worlds, the Sumerus of the worlds, and the names of the worlds.
Throughout all worlds within this ocean of worlds, by the power of the original vows of the World-Honored One Vairocana,
I am able to fully know and remember them; I also call to mind the ocean of all causal conditions of the Tathāgata in the past,
namely, his cultivation of the skillful means of all vehicles and his dwelling in the purity of bodhisattva practices throughout immeasurable eons.
They transform sentient beings within Buddha-lands, serve all Buddhas, establish dwelling places, listen to and receive the preaching of the Dharma,
and attain various samādhis. They obtain various masteries, cultivate the *dāna-pāramitā*, enter the ocean of the Buddha’s merits,
maintain the precepts and practice austerities, fulfill all forms of patience, exert courageous diligence, accomplish the various *dhyānas*, and perfect pure wisdom regarding all things.
Manifesting birth in various realms, they purify all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. They universally enter all lands and universally purify Buddha-fields.
They universally enter the ocean of wisdom of all Tathāgatas and universally encompass the Bodhi of all Buddhas.

Attaining the light of the great wisdom of the Tathāgatas, they realize the nature of the universal knowledge of all Buddhas and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment, turning the wondrous Dharma wheel.
The wheel, as well as all the assemblies in my various places of enlightenment— within those assemblies,

I fully know all the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings since past lives, from their first aspiration to mature sentient beings, through the cultivation of skillful means that increase moment by moment,
until they attain various samādhis, supernormal powers, and liberations. Why is this so?
Through this liberation of mine, I am able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings; the roots of goodness cultivated by all sentient beings;
the defilement and purification of all sentient beings; the various distinctions among all sentient beings; all the gateways of samādhi of the śrāvakas;
all the peaceful samādhis, supernormal powers, and liberations of the pratyekabuddhas; and all the [qualities] of the bodhisattvas.
Because they have fully realized the light of liberation of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the youth Sudhana said to Gopā, "Noble Lady, how long has it been since you attained this liberation?
She replied, "Son of good family, in a past age, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, there was an eon named Supreme Conduct and a world-system named Fearless. In that world..."
Within this world-system, there is a set of four continents called Peaceful and Secure (*Kṣema*).
Among these four continents, in Jambudvīpa, there is a royal city named High and Victorious Tree (*Uccagrimavṛkṣa*), which is the most preeminent among eighty royal cities.
At that time, there was a king named Lord of Wealth (*Dhanapati*). This king possessed sixty thousand court ladies, five hundred ministers, and five hundred princes.
All those princes were valiant and capable of subduing enemies. The crown prince was named Maheśvara (Lord of Majestic Virtue);
he was exceptionally handsome and pleasing to behold. The soles of his feet were flat and full, complete with the mark of the wheel (*cakrāṅka*), and the insteps were high and prominent.

Between the fingers and toes of his hands and feet, there are webbed membranes. The heels of his feet are even and well-proportioned. His hands and feet are soft and supple. His calves are like those of the eneya deer-king.
He is perfectly rounded in seven places. His male organ is concealed within a sheath. The upper part of his body is like that of a lion king.

His two shoulders are level and full. His arms are long and reach down to his knees. His physical form is upright and straight. There are three lines upon his neck. His cheeks are like those of a lion. He is endowed with these four [marks].
His ten teeth were all perfectly even and closely set. His four canine teeth were bright white. His tongue was long and broad, capable of producing the Brahma-voice.

His eyes were deep blue; his eyelashes were like those of a bull king. Between his eyebrows was the mark of the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft. On the crown of his head was the *uṣṇīṣa*. His skin was fine and soft, like the color of pure gold.
The hairs of his body curled upward. His hair was the color of indigo-blue. His body was large and full, like a *nyagrodha* tree. Thus it was.
At that time, the Crown Prince, having received the instructions of his father, the King, went with ten thousand court ladies to the Gandhahasti Garden to sightsee and enjoy himself.
At that moment, the Prince mounted a magnificent jewel chariot, which was adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
Upon it he sat upon a great lion-throne made of mani-jewels. Five hundred court ladies each took their places at jeweled reins to pull and guide the vehicle as they proceeded.
Their movements were measured, neither slow nor hurried. Hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious parasols;

hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious banners; hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious streamers; and hundreds of thousands of millions of people performed various musical performances.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of people burned various famous incenses; hundreds of thousands of millions of people scattered various exquisite flowers.
They surrounded him from front and back as an escort. The road was level and even, without any elevations or depressions; various jewels and mixed flowers were strewn upon it.
Rows of jewel trees were lined up, covered by a canopy of jeweled nets. Various multi-storied pavilions extended throughout the space.
Within these pavilions, some contained heaps of various precious gems; some displayed all manner of ornamental articles;
some provided various kinds of food and drink; some hung and spread various garments; and some prepared all sorts of necessary provisions.
Furthermore, he stationed beautiful women and an immeasurable number of male and female attendants, granting them all that they required.
At that time, there was a woman named Bhadrottamā who brought a young girl named Guṇavatī;

she was of upright countenance, her features were pure and refined, her proportions were perfectly balanced—neither too stout nor too slender, neither too tall nor too short—and her eyes and hair were deep blue.

He was of a dark-blue complexion. His voice was like the Brahma-voice. He was well-versed in the arts and crafts and proficient in debate. He was respectful, diligent, and untiring; compassionate and non-violent;
endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, gentle, upright, and straightforward. Free from delusion, he had few desires and was devoid of flattery and deception.
Mounted upon a magnificent jeweled chariot and surrounded by handmaidens, he departed from the royal city with his mother, traveling ahead of the Prince. There he saw the Prince...
The son, reciting his words with melodic intonation, felt a surge of passionate attachment and said to his mother, "My heart's desire is to serve this man with reverence.
If my wish is not fulfilled, I shall surely perish. His mother said to her daughter, "Do not harbor such a thought.

Why? Because he is extremely difficult to obtain. This man is fully endowed with all the marks of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin); later, he shall succeed to the throne and become a Universal Monarch."
"There is a jewel-woman who emerges and soars freely through the air; we, being lowly and base, are not her match.
This place is difficult to attain, so do not harbor such thoughts. Beside that Gandhakuṭī garden, there is a site of enlightenment named Dharma-Cloud Radiance.
At that time, a Tathāgata named Jina-sūryakāya, complete with the ten titles, has appeared therein and has already been present for seven days. At that time, he—
The young girl took a brief nap and dreamed of that Buddha. Upon awakening from the dream, a deity in the sky addressed her, saying:
"The Tathāgata Sūryavarcas attained perfect enlightenment at the Dharma-cloud Radiance Bodhimaṇḍa seven days ago.
He is surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras."
Garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and the Brahmā deities up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven;

the earth spirits, wind spirits, fire spirits, water spirits, river spirits, ocean spirits, mountain spirits, tree spirits, garden spirits, medicinal herb spirits, and city-guardian spirits—all gathered together for the sake of seeing the Buddha.
At that time, the maiden Sumati beheld the Tathāgata in a dream.
Therefore, because he had heard of the Buddha’s merits, his mind was peaceful and free from fear. In the presence of the Prince, he spoke these verses:
"My body is most upright and handsome, My fame spreads throughout the ten directions, And my wisdom is without equal."
Skillfully proficient in all arts and crafts, when hundreds of thousands of immeasurable beings behold me, they are all filled with lustful attachment;
yet my mind does not give rise to even a slight desire for them.
Without anger or resentment, without dislike or joy, I simply give rise to a vast and great mind to benefit all sentient beings.
Now that I behold the Prince, endowed with all the marks of merit, my heart is filled with great joy and all my faculties are delighted.
Your complexion is like a radiant jewel; your hair is beautiful, curling to the right;
your brow is broad and your eyebrows are slender and curved. My heart desires to serve you; I gaze upon the body of the Prince.
Like an image of pure gold, and like a mountain of great jewels; with the marks and signs possessing radiance, eyes wide and deep blue-black;
a moon-like face and lion-like jaws; with a joyful countenance and exquisite voice, I pray you deign to accept me out of compassion;
your tongue’s appearance is broad, long, and wondrous, like the color of red copper.
With a Brahma-voice like that of a *kiṃnara*, all who hear it rejoice; His mouth is square and not drawn back, his teeth are white, even, and closely set.
When he speaks and displays a smile, those who see him find joy in their hearts.
With a stainless and pure body, endowed with the thirty-two marks, he shall surely [attain enlightenment] within this world-system.
As he was assuming the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, the prince then addressed the maiden, saying: "Whose daughter are you? By whom are you protected?
If you already belong to another, I ought not to give rise to a mind of passionate attachment. At that time, the prince questioned her with a verse:
Your body is utterly pure, Endowed with the marks of merit.
I now ask you: In whose care do you dwell? Who are your parents? To whom do you now belong?
If you already belong to someone, That person must have taken you in; You would not steal another’s property.
You harbor no harmful intent; you do not commit sexual misconduct. Upon what speech do you abide?
You do not speak ill of others, nor do you destroy the intimacies of others. You do not encroach upon the domains of others, nor do you harbor anger toward them.
You do not give rise to perverse or dangerous views, nor do you perform contradictory actions.
One does not use the power of flattery and crookedness to deceive the world through expedient means. One respects one’s parents and reveres spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Upon seeing those who are poor and destitute, one is able to give rise to a mind of gathering-in (*saṃgraha*).
If there is a spiritual friend who instructs and shows you the Dharma, one is able to give rise to a firm and steadfast mind.
Do you ultimately respect [the Buddha]? Do you love and delight in the Buddha?
Do you understand the ocean of merits of the Bodhisattvas and the Sangha? Are you able to pay them homage?
Are you able to know the Dharma, yet unable to purify sentient beings? Do you abide within the Dharma, or do you abide in what is not the Dharma?
When you see those who are solitary and friendless, are you able to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness?
When you see sentient beings in the evil realms, are you able to produce great compassion? When you see others attain honor and joy, are you able to produce sympathetic joy?
When others come to oppress you, do you remain free from anger and affliction? Have you resolved upon the aspiration for enlightenment?
To awaken sentient beings, one practices for boundless eons; can one do so without weariness?
At that time, the mother of the girl spoke these verses to her son, the prince:
"O Prince, you should listen as I now describe this maiden’s birth and her growth, along with all their causal conditions.
On the very day the Prince was born, she likewise emerged from a lotus;
her eyes were pure, long, and wide, and her limbs and joints were perfectly formed. Once, during the spring month..."
Wandering through the Śāla grove, he saw everywhere the various medicinal herbs, all of them flourishing and lush;
wondrous trees burst forth with exquisite flowers that looked like auspicious clouds from afar. Beautiful birds sang in harmony, finding joy together amidst the woods.
He was accompanied by eight hundred women who traveled with him, their beauty so peerless it captivated the hearts of men.
Their garments were all magnificent and beautiful, and their songs and chants were entirely exquisite.
In that garden there was a bathing pool named Lotus Banner; I sat upon its bank, surrounded by a multitude of female attendants.
Within that lotus pond, a thousand-petaled flower suddenly sprang up, with precious petals and a stem of lapis lazuli.
With a pedestal of Jambū-river gold, at that time when the night had ended, the sun’s rays first appeared;
the lotus flower opened wide, emitting a vast, pure light.
That radiance was exceedingly brilliant, like the sun just rising, illuminating all of Jambudvīpa; the multitude marveled at this unprecedented wonder.
At that time, I saw this jade maiden, born from that lotus flower;
her body was exceedingly pure, and all her limbs were perfectly formed. She is a treasure of the human world, born from pure karma;
her past causes have not been lost, and now she experiences this retribution—her hair is deep blue-black and her eyes are like blue lotuses.
With a Brahma-voice and golden light, Adorned with flower garlands and a crown of various jewels,
Pure and free from all defilements, With every limb and joint fully complete, His body is without deficiency,
Like a statue of pure gold resting amidst precious flowers; From his pores, sandalwood fragrance Pervades and perfumes all things.
Her mouth emits the fragrance of blue lotuses, and she constantly utters the Brahma-sound.
Wherever this woman dwells, there is always the music of the devas. She should not be matched with an inferior person;
indeed, there is no one in the world worthy to be her husband, save for you, whose body is adorned with the marks of excellence.
May you deign to accept me; neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor fine, in every way perfectly adorned—may you deign to accept me.
Having attained complete mastery in the methods of writing, calculation, crafts, and all arts and skills—may you deign to accept me.
Well-versed in all military strategies, Skilled in resolving all disputes and litigation, Able to tame those difficult to tame— I pray you, deign to accept me.
Your body is exceedingly pure; Those who behold it never tire of looking.
Adorned with natural merit, You should deign to accept me. All the ailments of sentient beings—
She is thoroughly proficient in that dependent origination and dispenses medicine according to the illness.
She is capable of extinguishing all the various and immeasurable kinds of linguistic expressions of Jambudvīpa, even down to the sounds of music;
she understands everything that women are able to do—this girl knows it all.
And being free from the faults of women, I pray that you will graciously accept me quickly.
Without envy or stinginess, without greed or anger, upright by nature and gentle, free from all coarseness and evil,
I shall show reverence to my elders, serve them without opposition, and delight in cultivating all virtuous deeds.

This will accord with you: whenever you see those who are old or sick, poor, or beset by suffering—without rescue or refuge—always give rise to great compassion. Constantly contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), seeking neither self-interest nor personal pleasure;
may you only wish to benefit sentient beings, adorning your mind with this resolve.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, He is at all times free from negligence.
In speech and in silence, those who see him Are filled with joy and delight. Though he is in every place, His mind is entirely free from attachment;
Seeing those of virtuous merit, He gazes upon them with never-tiring appreciation, And honors his spiritual friends.
Delighting in seeing those who have left evil behind, her mind is not restless; she acts after first reflecting,
adorned with merit and wisdom, entirely free from resentment— she is the most excellent among women and should serve the Prince.
At that time, having entered the Garden of Fragrant Sprouts, the Prince addressed his daughters, Varaprabhā and Bhadrottamā, saying:
"O virtuous daughters, I am seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I shall do so throughout immeasurable kalpas until the end of the future."
One shall gather all dharmas that assist the path to omniscience; cultivate boundless bodhisattva practices;
purify all perfections; make offerings to all Tathāgatas; uphold and protect all the teachings of the Buddhas; adorn and purify all Buddha-lands;
ensure that the lineage of all Tathāgatas remains uninterrupted; and act in accordance with the dispositions of all sentient beings.
Universally maturing them; I shall extinguish the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings and establish them in the state of ultimate peace and happiness.
I shall purify the eye of wisdom of all sentient beings. I shall cultivate all the practices performed by Bodhisattvas.
I shall abide in the impartial mind of all Bodhisattvas. I shall accomplish all the stages of conduct of all Bodhisattvas. I shall...

May all sentient beings be universally gladdened. One should relinquish all things and practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) throughout the bounds of the future, so that all sentient beings may be universally satisfied.

Clothing, food and drink, wives and concubines, sons and daughters, heads, eyes, hands, and feet—whatever such internal or external possessions one has—one should give them all away without any stinginess. One should...
At that time, you may have created obstacles for me: when I gave away wealth and goods, your heart was stingy; when I gave away my sons and daughters, your heart was pained and distressed;
when I severed my limbs, your heart was filled with grief and despondency; and when I abandoned you to go forth into homelessness, your heart was full of regret.
At that time, the Prince, who was then named Wondrous Virtue (Guṇaprabha), spoke these verses:
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I have resolved to attain bodhicitta;

throughout immeasurable kalpas, I shall practice the cultivation of omniscience. Within those immeasurable great kalpas, I shall purely cultivate the ocean of vows—entering the pools and purifying obstacles—passing through every one of these immeasurable kalpas in the presence of the Buddhas of the three times.
I shall study the six pāramitās and fully accomplish the practice of skillful means;
I shall bring to fruition the path to bodhi. All the defiled lands of the ten directions, I shall purify them all.
From all the hardships of the evil realms, I shall cause all beings to emerge forever. By means of skillful means, I shall extensively deliver all living beings.
May I extinguish the darkness of ignorance and abide in the path of the Buddha’s wisdom.
May I make offerings to all Buddhas and purify all stages. Arising with great compassion, may I relinquish all things, both internal and external.
When I see those who come to beg, may no stinginess or parsimony arise; my mind shall always delight in giving.
Do not disobey me; if you see me giving away my head, take care not to cause me distress.
I speak these words to you first to make your mind firm and steadfast. Even when your hands and feet are cut off, do not feel resentment toward the beggar.
Having now heard my words, you should reflect upon them with careful attention.
"Whatever things are loved by men and women, I shall renounce them all. If you can comply with my heart, I shall fulfill your wish.
At that time, the young maiden addressed the prince, saying, "I respectfully accept your instruction," and then spoke in verse:
Throughout oceans of immeasurable kalpas, may my body be consumed by the fires of hell;
if you would graciously accept me, I am willing to endure this suffering. In immeasurable places of rebirth, may my body be crushed like fine dust;
if you would graciously accept me, I am willing to endure this suffering. For immeasurable kalpas, may I carry you upon my head.
Vast Vajra Mountain, if you would graciously accept me, I shall willingly endure this suffering within the immeasurable ocean of birth and death.
By offering my own body and flesh, may you attain the state of the Dharma King,
and by your graciously accepting me and granting me your lordship, may I likewise become so.
In every life, wherever I practice giving, may my gifts always be for the sake of compassion for the suffering of sentient beings and for the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Having already gathered in sentient beings, may you likewise gather me in as well.
I do not seek wealth or status, nor do I crave the pleasures of the five senses; I desire only to practice the Dharma together.
I pray that you take benevolence as your primary guide; with eyes deep blue, long, and wide, you gaze upon the world with compassion and do not give rise to a mind of attachment.
You will surely accomplish the path of a Bodhisattva. Wherever the Prince treads, the earth brings forth various precious flowers;
you will surely become a Wheel-Turning King. I pray that you will graciously accept me.
I once dreamed of this sublime Dharma site of enlightenment, where the Tathāgata sat beneath the tree surrounded by an immeasurable multitude.
In my dream, that Tathāgata, whose body was like a mountain of pure gold, stroked the crown of my head with his hand.
Upon waking, my heart was filled with joy; he was a celestial being who had been my kinsman in the past.
Named Joyful Radiance, that deity spoke to me: "When a Buddha arises in the world at the site of enlightenment, I once had this thought:
'I pray to behold the body of the Prince. That deity replied to me, saying:
'You shall now behold him. The vows I formerly aspired to have all been fulfilled within my very thoughts.'"
"I only wish that we may go together to pay homage to that Tathāgata.
At that time, having heard the name of the Tathāgata Sun-Victory-Body (Sūryavijaya-kāya), the Prince was filled with great joy and desired to see that Buddha.
He scattered five hundred maṇi jewels over the girl, crowned her with a wondrous treasury of radiant light tiara, and clothed her in fire-like [robes].
Clad in robes of flaming maṇi jewels, the girl at that time remained unmoved in heart and showed no sign of joy;
she merely joined her palms in reverence and gazed up at the Prince without averting her eyes for a moment. Her mother, Suprabhā, then spoke these verses before the Prince:
This maiden is exceedingly beautiful, her body adorned with merit; her former vow to serve the Prince is now fulfilled.
Possessing ethical discipline and wisdom, endowed with all virtues, she is supreme and peerless throughout all worlds—this maiden was born from a lotus.
Her lineage is beyond reproach; she shares the same conduct as the Prince.
Free from all faults, this woman’s body is soft and supple, Like celestial silk or fine cotton wool. Wherever her hands touch and stroke, all ailments are entirely extinguished.
From her pores issues a wondrous fragrance, A perfumed scent most incomparable.
If sentient beings hear [this], they will all abide in pure precepts; their physical forms will be like pure gold as they sit upright upon lotus pedestals.
If sentient beings see them, they will abandon harm and possess a compassionate heart;

their speech and tone will be exceedingly gentle and soft, such that there is none who does not rejoice upon hearing it. If sentient beings are able to hear [it], [they shall likewise attain these qualities].
Completely free from all evil karma, with a pure mind untainted by blemish, Far removed from all flattery and crookedness,
they speak words that accord with the heart, Causing all who hear them to rejoice; Gentle and compliant, endowed with shame and remorse,
they show reverence to their elders and seniors, Free from greed and devoid of deception, they feel compassion for all sentient beings.
This girl’s mind does not rely upon her physical beauty, her appearance, or her retinue;
she honors all Buddhas solely with a pure heart.
At that time, the Prince, together with the girl Sudarśanā, ten thousand court ladies, and their attendants, departed from the Fragrant Sprout Palace.
He went to the Dharma-Cloud Radiance Bodhimanda. Having arrived, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot to where the Tathāgata was.

He beheld the Buddha’s physical marks, which were dignified and serene; his faculties were well-tamed and harmonious; and he was pure within and without, like a great dragon pond free from all turbidity and impurity.
All were moved to pure faith, leaping with joy and delight. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him countless times. At that time...
The Prince and the maiden Sudarśanā each took five hundred exquisite jewel lotuses and scattered them as offerings over that Buddha.
The Prince constructed five hundred vihāras for the Buddha; each was made of fragrant wood, adorned with various jewels, and interspersed with five hundred mani-gems.
At that time, the Buddha preached for him the *Sūtra of the Universal Eye Lamp Gate*. Having heard this—
Having recited this sutra, he attained oceans of samādhis within all dharmas. That is to say, he attained the samādhi of universally illuminating the ocean of vows of all Buddhas;
the samādhi of universally illuminating the treasury of the three periods of time; the samādhi of directly beholding the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas;
the samādhi of universally illuminating all sentient beings; the samādhi of the lamp of wisdom that universally illuminates all worlds; and the samādhi of universally illuminating one...
The Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom that Discerns the Faculties of All Beings; the Samādhi of the Cloud of Radiance that Protects and Saves All Beings;
the Samādhi of the Great Bright Lamp that Universally Illumines All Beings; the Samādhi of Expounding the Dharma-Wheel of All Buddhas;
and the Samādhi of Being Fully Endowed with the Pure Conduct of Samantabhadra. At that time, the daughter Sudarśanā attained a samādhi named "Inconquerable Ocean-Treasury. In...

They shall never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Then the prince, together with the maiden Sumati and their retinue, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and withdrew to return to the palace.

Upon arriving before the father king, after completing his prostrations and kneeling, he addressed the king, saying: "Great King, you should know that the Victorious Sun-body (*Sūryavarcas*) has appeared in the world."
In this world, within this kingdom, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) known as the Radiance of the Cloud of Dharma, he has attained perfect awakening not long ago.
At that time, the Great King said to the Crown Prince: "Who told you such things?
Was it a deva or a human? The Crown Prince replied: "It was this maiden, Endowed with Sublime Virtue. When the King heard this, he rejoiced.
Immeasurable. It is like a poor man who discovers a great hidden treasure and thinks to himself: "The Buddha, the unsurpassed jewel, is difficult to encounter.
If I am able to see the Buddha, I shall forever sever all fear of the evil realms.

The Buddha is like a king of physicians, able to cure the diseases of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and able to rescue one from the great suffering of birth and death. The Buddha is like a guide, able to..."

Having formed the thought that sentient beings have reached the ultimate state of peace and security, he assembled all the minor kings, ministers, retinues, as well as the entire great assembly of kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas. He then abdicated the royal throne and bestowed it upon the crown prince.

Having performed the consecration ceremony, he went together with ten thousand people to the place where the Buddha was staying. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him.
After circumambulating several times, he and his entire retinue withdrew and sat down.

At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed the king and the great assembly, and from within the mark of the white tuft between his brows, he emitted a great radiance called "Lamp of the Minds of All Worlds.
It universally illuminated immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions and stood before all the lords of the world, manifesting the inconceivable [power] of the Tathāgata.
He deliberated upon his great supernormal powers (*mahā-abhijñā*) so as to cause the minds of all those ready for conversion to attain purity.
At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his inconceivable and sovereign supernormal power, manifested a body that transcended all worlds.

With a perfect voice, he universally preached a *dhāraṇī* for the great assembly called "The Lamp that Dispels Darkness from the Meaning of All Dharmas. [It was as vast as] the atoms of Buddha-fields...
With *dhāraṇīs* as numerous as the atoms of dust as their retinue, that king, having heard this, immediately attained the light of great wisdom.
Within that assembly, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust in Jambudvīpa who simultaneously realized this *dhāraṇī*.
Six hundred thousand nayutas of people exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained liberation of mind. Ten thousand [others...]
Upon his birth, he was far removed from dust and free from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye. Immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.

At that time, the Buddha again manifested miraculous transformations through his inconceivable power, extensively expounding the Dharma of the Three Vehicles throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Then, the King, his father, thought to himself: "If I remain at home, I shall not be able to realize [the truth]."
Having attained such a sublime Dharma, he thought, "If I were to leave the household life and study the Path under the Buddha, I would surely achieve success.
Having formed this thought, he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that I may leave the household life and practice under the Buddha. The Buddha said, "As you wish;
know for yourself the proper time. Then, King Dhanapati and ten thousand people simultaneously left the household life under the Buddha. Not long after—
In that interval, they fully attained the *dhāraṇī* of the Lamp Dispelling Darkness that Accomplishes the Meaning of All Dharmas.

They also attained the aforementioned gates of samādhi, as well as the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva, the boundless eloquence (*pratibhāna*) of a bodhisattva, and the unimpeded pure body of a bodhisattva.
They proceeded to the abodes of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions to hear and receive their teachings. For...

The Great Dharma Master expounded the sublime Dharma. Furthermore, by means of his supernatural powers, he pervaded the lands of the ten directions, manifesting his body in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
He praised the appearance of the Buddhas, recounted the Buddhas' original practices, and revealed the Buddhas' past causes and conditions.
He extolled the Tathāgata’s sovereign supernatural powers and upheld the teachings spoken by the Buddhas. At that time, on the fifteenth day, the Prince was at...
In the main hall, the ladies-in-waiting gathered around him, and the seven treasures appeared spontaneously: first, the wheel treasure named Unobstructed Movement;
second, the elephant treasure named Vajra Body; third, the horse treasure named Swift Wind; fourth, the jewel treasure named Sunlight Treasury;
fifth, the woman treasure named Endowed with Wondrous Virtue; sixth, the steward treasure named Great Minister; and seventh—

The Lord of the Military Treasure was named Vimalanetra. Possessing the seven treasures, he became a Wheel-Turning King who ruled over Jambudvīpa, governing the world with the True Dharma so that the people were happy.
The king had a thousand sons, handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing enemies and adversaries.
Within Jambudvīpa there were eighty royal cities, and in each city there were five hundred monasteries. In each [monastery]...
The monasteries and Buddha-stūpas were all exceedingly high and vast, adorned with various exquisite jewels.
In each royal city, they invited the Tathāgata and made offerings with inconceivable and wondrous articles of worship.

When the Buddha entered the cities, he manifested great supernormal powers, causing immeasurable sentient beings to plant various roots of goodness, and [purifying] the minds of immeasurable sentient beings.

They attain purity. Seeing the Buddha, they rejoice and resolve upon bodhicitta. Arousing great compassion, they benefit sentient beings; they diligently cultivate the Buddha-dharma and enter the true meaning.
Abiding in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they realize the equality of all dharmas. They obtain the wisdom of the three periods of time and contemplate the three periods with equanimity.
Knowing the sequence of the appearance of all Buddhas, they preach various teachings to gather in and sustain sentient beings. They give rise to...
A bodhisattva vows to enter the bodhisattva path. Knowing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they accomplish the ocean of Dharma and are able to manifest their bodies universally throughout all lands.
Knowing the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings, they cause them to give rise to the vow for omniscience.
Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is that crown prince who, having attained the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, made offerings to the Buddha, anyone other than this person?
"O person, it is Śākyamuni Buddha who is he now. The King who was the Master of Wealth is Ratnakusuma Buddha.

That Ratnakusuma Buddha currently resides in the east, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, in a world-ocean named Cloud Reflecting the Space of the Manifest Dharma-realm.
Within it is a world-system named Universally Manifesting the Shadows of the Three Times."
Nirvāṇa King. Within that world-system, there is a world named Perfect Light. Within it is a site of enlightenment named Manifesting the Bodies of All World-Leaders.
It was here that the Tathāgata Jewel Flower attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Surrounded before and behind by an assembly of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, he preached the Dharma for them.
Dharma. When the Tathāgata Ratnakusuma was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he purified this world-ocean.

All the Buddhas who appeared in the world throughout the past, future, and present within that world-ocean were those whom Ratnakusuma, while a bodhisattva, had taught and inspired to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the mother of the girl was virtuous...
The one who appeared then as my mother, Sunetra, is now this very person. Those who were the king’s retinue are the assembly gathered here before the Tathāgata.
They have all fully cultivated the various practices of Samantabhadra and brought their great vows to fulfillment.

Although they constantly abide within this assembly at the site of enlightenment, they are able to manifest universally throughout all worlds. Dwelling in the samādhi of the equality of all bodhisattvas, they are always able to see [the Buddha] directly.
All Buddhas, all Tathāgatas, with clouds of wondrous sounds like space itself, turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
he is able to hear and receive them all, attaining mastery over all phenomena, and his fame is heard throughout all Buddha-lands.
They go everywhere to all sites of enlightenment and appear before all sentient beings, teaching and taming them according to what is appropriate for each.
Throughout all future eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva path without ever ceasing, fulfilling the vast vows of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha, that daughter of noble virtue, together with the Wheel-Turning Sage King Lord of Majestic Virtue, by means of the four...
I myself am the one who performed the supreme material offerings to the Tathāgata Sun-body (Sūryakāya).
After that Buddha passed into extinction, sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of Buddhas appeared in that world; I served and made offerings to them all together with the King.
The first of those Buddhas was named Pure Body (Vimalakāya); the next was named All-Knowledge Moon-Light Body (Sarvajñajyotirprabha-kāya); the next...
The first was named Jāmbūnada-gold Radiance King; the second was named Body Adorned with All Marks; the third was named Sublime Moonlight;
the fourth was named Banner of Wisdom Contemplation; the fifth was named Light of Great Wisdom; the sixth was named Vajra Nārāyaṇa Diligence;
the seventh was named Invincible Power of Wisdom; the eighth was named Universal Serene Wisdom; and the ninth was named Cloud of Stainless Supreme Wisdom.
The first is named Lion Wisdom Radiance; the next is named Radiant Topknot; the next is named Banner of Merit Radiance; the next is named Wisdom Sun Banner;
the next is named Body of Blooming Jewel Lotuses; the next is named Pure Light Adorned with Merit; the next is named Cloud of Wisdom Flames;
the next is named Universally Illuminating Moon; the next is named Wondrous Sound of the Ornamented Canopy; and the next is named Lion.
Courageous Wisdom Radiance; next, named Moon of the Dharma Realm; next, named Manifesting the Reflections of Space to Awaken the Minds of Sentient Beings;
next, named Constantly Inhaling the Fragrance of Quiescence; next, named Universally Resounding Silent Sound;
next, named Mountain of Nectar; next, named Sound of the Ocean of Dharma; next, named Firm Net; next, named Buddha-Shadow Topknot; next, named Moonlight.
Vimalaprabha; next is named Pratibhānavaktra; next is named Bodhipuṣpajñāna; next is named Ratnajvālāparvata; next is named Guṇatāraka;
next is named Ratnacandradhvaja; next is named Samādhiśarīra; next is named Ratnaprabharāja;
next is named Samantajñānacaryā; next is named Jvālārṇavapradīpa; next is named Vimaladharmaghoṣarāja; next is named Anupamaguṇakīrti.
Dhvaja. Next was named Bhāvitabhuja. Next was named Praṇidhānaviśuddhicandra. Next was named Arthāvabhāsadīpa. Next was named Gambhīranirghoṣa.
Next was named Vairocanavijayasāgararāja. Next was named Sarvayānadhvaja. Next was named Dharmasāgaramaṇipuṇḍarīka.
O Son of the Buddha, in that eon there were sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of such [Buddhas].
Buddhas appeared in the world, and I approached, served, and made offerings to them all. The last of those Buddhas was named Vistīrṇamatī.

In the presence of that Buddha, I attained the pure eye of wisdom. At that time, as that Buddha entered the city to teach and transform beings, I, as the queen, paid my respects to the King and [the Buddha], making offerings with various exquisite things. In the presence of that Buddha, I heard him preach the Dharma.
This is the Dharma-door for generating the lamp of all Tathāgatas. Immediately, one attains the liberation that observes the ocean-like realm of the samādhis of all Bodhisattvas.
Son of the Buddha, having attained this liberation, I have diligently practiced it together with Bodhisattvas for as many eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field;
and throughout those eons as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, I have served and made offerings to [the Buddhas].
They measure all Buddhas: some serve one Buddha for an eon, or two, or three, or an unspeakable number;
others encounter as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, approaching, serving, and making offerings to them all.

Yet they are still unable to know the dimensions, physical appearance, or color of the Bodhisattvas' bodies, nor their bodily actions, mental activities, wisdom, or the spheres of their samādhis. The Buddha—

"O Son of the Buddha! If there are sentient beings who see a Bodhisattva practicing the path of enlightenment, whether they harbor doubts or possess faith, the Bodhisattva employs various mundane and supramundane skillful means to gather them in as their followers, causing them to attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O Son of the Buddha! I have seen that Buddha attain this..."
Having attained liberation, I have practiced together with bodhisattvas for as many eons as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields.
During those eons, I have personally approached, served, and made offerings to all the Buddhas who appeared in the world;
I have listened to the Dharma they taught, and have read, recited, and upheld it. From all those Tathāgatas, I have obtained this liberation in its various forms.

This Dharma door involves knowing the various worlds of the three periods of time, entering the various oceans of lands, beholding the various attainments of perfect enlightenment, entering the various assemblies of Buddhas, generating the various great vows of Bodhisattvas, cultivating the various sublime practices of Bodhisattvas, and attaining the various liberations of Bodhisattvas;
yet one has not yet been able to know the Samantabhadra liberation door attained by Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s gate of liberation is like great empty space; it is like the names of sentient beings; it is like the ocean of the three periods of time;

it is like the ocean of the ten directions; it is like the ocean of the dharma-realm—immeasurable and boundless. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s gate of liberation is equal to the realm of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, for as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, I have observed this Bodhisattva.
The body knows no satiety. It is like people with great desire who, when gathered together as men and women, become mutually infatuated and give rise to immeasurable deluded thoughts and perceptions;

I am also like this. As I contemplate each and every pore of the Bodhisattva’s body, in every thought-moment I see immeasurable and boundless vast worlds, abiding in various ways, adorned in various ways, and having various forms.
There are various mountains, various lands, various clouds, various names, various Buddhas appearing, various sites of enlightenment, and various assemblies.
They expound various sūtras, proclaim various consecrations, and [reveal] various vehicles.
Through various skillful means and various purities, he also perceives within each and every pore of the Bodhisattva,
at every moment of thought, an infinite ocean of Buddhas seated upon various bodhimaṇḍas, manifesting various supernatural transformations, turning various wheels of Dharma,
and constantly and uninterruptedly preaching various sūtras. Furthermore, within each and every pore of the Bodhisattva, he sees the infinite...
The various abodes of the ocean of sentient beings, their various forms and appearances, their various activities,
and their various faculties; furthermore, within each and every pore of the Bodhisattva, one sees the boundless gateways of practice of all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time—
namely, their boundless and vast vows, their boundless distinct stages, their boundless perfections, and their boundless past deeds.

The gateway of great compassion that reaches all limits; the cloud of great pity that is boundless; the mind of great joy that is limitless; and the boundless skillful means for gathering in sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, I have, in every thought-moment, observed each and every pore of the Bodhisattva in this manner.
Wherever I have gone, I have not gone again; wherever I have seen, I have not seen again.

I sought its limit, but ultimately it could not be found. Even when I saw Prince Siddhārtha dwelling within the palace, surrounded by his court ladies, I used the power of liberation to observe each and every pore of the Bodhisattva, and in all of them, I beheld the events within the dharma-realm of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha, I have attained only this liberation of the ocean-like samādhi that observes the Bodhisattva.
Just as all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have perfected an immeasurable ocean of skillful means,

manifesting bodies that accord with the various types of sentient beings and teaching practices that accord with their inclinations; just as they manifest oceans of infinite forms and appearances from every single pore,
knowing that the nature of all phenomena has non-nature as its nature, and knowing that the nature of sentient beings is identical to the characteristics of empty space.
Free from conceptual discrimination, they know that the Buddha’s spiritual power is identical to suchness (*tathatā*), pervading all places and manifesting infinite realms of liberation.
In a single thought-moment, they are able to enter the vast dharma-realm with mastery and sport within the dharma-gates of all the stages (*bhūmi*).
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Son of good family, this...
In this world there is Māyā, the Mother of Buddhas. Go to her and ask how a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva conduct;
how one remains unstained by any worldly realm; how one makes offerings to all Buddhas without ever ceasing; how one performs the deeds of a bodhisattva without ever regressing;
how one leaves behind all obstacles and enters the liberation of a bodhisattva without depending on others; and how one abides in the One Vehicle.
They encompass the entire path of the bodhisattvas; they go to the abodes of all Tathāgatas; they gather in the realms of all sentient beings;

and throughout all kalpas of the future, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, giving rise to the vows of the Mahāyāna and increasing the roots of goodness in all sentient beings without ever ceasing.
At that time, Śākyaguptā, wishing to clarify further the meaning of this liberation, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
spoke these verses:
“If there are those who see a bodhisattva Practicing various deeds, And giving rise to thoughts of both good and evil...”
All these Bodhisattvas have gathered together from ages long past.
Beyond hundreds of eons as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there was an eon named Pure, and a world-system named Radiant Light.
In this eon, sixty quadrillion Buddhas appeared in the world; the last among them, the Lord of Gods and Men, was named Dharma-Standard Lamp.
After that Buddha entered nirvana, there was a king named Jñānagiri who ruled over all of Jambudvīpa without any enemies.
The king had five hundred sons who were handsome, brave, and strong;
their bodies were entirely pure, and all who saw them were filled with joy—both the king and his princes.
With faith, they made offerings to the Buddha and protected his treasury of Dharma; they also delighted in diligently practicing the Path.
The Prince was named Suprabha (Good Light); free from defilement and possessing many skillful means, all his marks were perfectly complete, such that those who saw him could never tire of looking.
Together with five hundred million people, he left the household life to practice the Way.
Valiant and firm in diligence, he protects and upholds the Buddha’s Dharma.
The royal capital is named Jñānavṛkṣa (Tree of Wisdom), surrounded by a thousand billion cities. There is a grove named Śāntaguṇa (Tranquil Virtue), adorned with various jewels;
Sugati (Excellent Light) dwells in that grove, widely proclaiming the Buddha’s true Dharma through the power of his eloquence and wisdom.
Causing all beings to be completely purified, once, while wandering for alms, I entered that royal capital with extremely composed and steady gait; with right mindfulness, my mind was undisturbed.
In that city there was a householder named Śrīkīrti; at that time, I was his daughter, named Vimalaprabhā.
At that time, while I was in the city, I encountered one of Excellent Radiance, whose various marks were exceedingly sublime and dignified;
my mind gave rise to defiled attachment. Next, as he went begging and arrived at my door, my heart’s passion increased further.
I immediately untied the jeweled necklace from my body and placed it, along with the pearls, into his alms-bowl. Although I did so with a mind of defiled attachment, [I offered it].
Making offerings to that Son of the Buddha for two hundred and fifty kalpas, he did not fall into the three evil realms;
instead, he was born into the family of a celestial king, or became the daughter of a human king.
He constantly beheld the body of the One of Excellent Radiance, adorned with wondrous marks. From that point on, the kalpas that passed numbered two hundred and fifty.

Born into the family of Subhūti, I was named Sumati. At that time, seeing the Prince, I conceived a heart of reverence and wished to serve him with full devotion. Fortunate was I to receive his compassionate acceptance;
I then accompanied the Prince to behold the Buddha Sūryagātra. Having completed our respectful offerings, I remained there.

He immediately gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; during that single eon, among sixty billion Tathāgatas, the final Buddha, the World-Honored One, was named Vast Understanding (Vipula-jñāna).
There he attained the pure eye and clearly understood the characteristics of all phenomena;
he universally perceived the places of rebirth and forever eliminated the mind of inversion.
I have attained the liberation of the samādhi realm of the Bodhisattva of Contemplation.
In a single thought-moment, I enter the inconceivable ocean of lands throughout the ten directions. I behold all worlds, with their various distinctions of purity and defilement;
I do not crave or delight in the pure, nor do I increase aversion toward the defiled, as I universally perceive all worlds.
When the Tathāgata sits at the site of enlightenment, within a single thought-moment he emits immeasurable light;
in a single thought-moment he is able to enter universally into unspeakably many assemblies.
He also knows all the gateways of samādhi attained by them, and in a single thought-moment he is able to fully know all those vast and great practices.
The immeasurable stages and skillful means, As well as the ocean of all vows— I observe that within the body of a Bodhisattva,
who has practiced for boundless eons, The measure of each and every pore cannot be found even when sought;
Within each and every pore are lands, Innumerable and beyond description, With wheels of earth, water, fire, and wind.
There is nothing that is not contained within it: The various foundations, The various forms, the various substances and names, And the boundless varieties of adornments.
I behold the oceans of lands and unspeakable worlds, And I see the Buddhas therein, Expounding the Dharma to transform sentient beings.
He did not comprehend the body of the Bodhisattva, nor the various karmas of that body; he likewise did not know the mind, the wisdom, or the practices traversed throughout the kalpas.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to depart.
The tenth is the maiden Gopā. She is associated with the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). As for the stage of the Cloud of Dharma:

it is so called because the great wisdom-cloud of the Dharma contains the waters of manifold virtues; it covers the coarse obstructions (*dausthulya*) as if they were space, and fills the body of reality (*dharmakāya*).

Having received the instructions of his previous spiritual friend, Sudhana contemplated, practiced, and maintained them in mind without forsaking them. Following those teachings, he sought them out and gradually arrived at the Universal Radiance (*samantaprabha*).
In the lecture hall, before Gopā had even appeared, a deity came to welcome him. This deity was named Aśokadattā.
Together with ten thousand palace-guarding deities, she came to welcome Sudhana and praised him, saying: "Welcome, O noble man! You possess great wisdom and valor;
you are able to cultivate the inconceivable, sovereign liberation of a bodhisattva. Before long..."
In order to attain the unsurpassed fruit, there are thirteen supplementary sūtra passages praising Sudhana’s ability to achieve the Dharma through ultimate diligence.
Sudhana said: "O Noble One, may I obtain all that you have just described. He then proceeded to describe what he himself had attained, saying:
"I vow that all sentient beings shall be relieved of all their burning afflictions. And so forth.

As for being free from weariness amidst birth and death, it is because one gathers all sentient beings through the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
There are fifteen lines of scripture describing the practices attained by oneself. Following that, it says:
"The noble ones; the Bodhisattva acts as an adornment for all sentient beings," and so forth. There are ten lines of scripture clarifying this through the myriad [virtues].

He practices deeds that benefit sentient beings. By visiting many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and realizing numerous Dharma-gates, he reaches this stage where the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are fulfilled.
Because he exclusively gives rise to conduct for the benefit of others, this differs from all preceding stages.
At that time, as Sudhana was about to ascend the Dharma Hall, the spirit Aśoka adorned it with various kinds of exquisite flowers and scattered them [over him].

Sudhana ascended and further spoke in verse, reciting ten stanzas beginning with "You have now appeared in the world, as a great lamp for the world," to express his profound sense of reverence. He then followed after Sudhana, never departing from him.
At that time, Sudhana entered the Lecture Hall of Universal Manifestation of the Dharmadhātu and sought the daughter of the Śākya clan, whom he saw within the hall.
Seated upon a lion throne of precious lotuses, she was surrounded by eighty-four thousand court ladies.
Sudhana praised the extraordinary virtues of the Queen of Śrāvastī and her retinue with more than ten verses, describing their excellence in detail.
The reason for this is that it symbolizes the fulfillment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the realization of the perfected *dharmadhātu*; thus, the eighty-four thousand...
The four thousand afflictions were all transformed into sublime practices for the benefit of sentient beings. First, he was seen and honored;
next, he prostrated and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. He first set forth his own resolve for enlightenment, and then formally asked how to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Yet, [the girl] did not know how a bodhisattva, while within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), is not defiled by the afflictions of birth and death.

There are eleven phrases that universally inquire about the practice of compassion and wisdom, the inverse and the conformative, the provisional and the real, and the unimpeded dual movement of quiescence and activity.
This question is also far removed from all other stages. At that time, the girl Gopā said to Sudhana: [The following is the main text.]

The Cloud of the Dharma Realm said: "Good son, if a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will be able to fulfill the bodhisattva practice of the universal wisdom-light of Indra’s net. This directly illuminates the dharma realm in its entirety."
The infinitely layered and inexhaustible practices of the Imperial Net are called the Wondrous Practices of Samantabhadra.

As one is about to ascend to the stage of enlightenment, these practices of the perfectly fulfilled Dharma-realm are revealed. It is said that these practices are accomplished through ten dharmas; next, the ten dharmas are shown.
Together with the preceding verses of praise, there are sixteen lines of scripture. However, these ten practices arise from and depend upon skillful knowledge.
Because it is accomplished through consciousness, its meaning is reiterated in verse: "First, by approaching spiritual friends, one is able to accomplish the supreme practices of Indra’s net.
This means that each of the ten dharmas mentioned above possesses ten [factors] within itself; thus, they constitute a practice that is infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
There are twelve verses which, in their respective order, versify the preceding ten practices of Indra’s net.
The former [section] merely indicated the method; its intention was that it was difficult to state the name of this "Inexhaustible Dharma-Gate of the Indra-Net of Ten Dharmas.
Therefore, after Gopā below had spoken these verses, she addressed Sudhana, saying:
"I have attained the liberation-door of 'Observing the Ocean of Samādhis of All Bodhisattvas. This precisely indicates its name, namely, Samantabhadra.
Samādhi is as deep and vast as the ocean; it receives this name because one is able to enter the ocean of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
When Sudhana heard the name "dharma-realm," he asked the Great Sage: "What is the sphere of this gate of liberation?
This inquiry regarding the sphere is intended to clarify the functional activity of the dharma-realm. Next, Gopā replied: "O son of good family, I..."
Entering this liberation-samādhi, one merely contemplates the ocean of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and comes to know the subtle matters within that ocean of the dharma-realm.
Below, the method of contemplation is shown; it proceeds from the narrow to the broad and consists of three successive stages.
First, one contemplates that within a single Sahā world-system there are ten dharma-realms. One first contemplates that within this world-system there are...
Regarding the sentient beings of the six realms, from as many eons ago as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, throughout their wanderings in various destinies—dying here and being born there;
their retributions for good and evil; their states of false certainty or right certainty;

and each of their mental activities, inclinations, and afflictions—I know and see every distinction of their faculties and conduct. Next, I contemplate all those within this world-system throughout eons as numerous as its atoms...

I fully know the names of the Buddhas who appear in the world, as well as their initial generation of the bodhicitta, their cultivation of the bodhisattva practices throughout kalpas as numerous as atoms,
their attainment of Buddhahood, their turning of the wheel of Dharma, their transformation of sentient beings,

and their entry into nirvana. Next, I observe the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas, each from their initial generation of the bodhicitta and their cultivation through successive kalpas.

I fully know each and every practice door cultivated by those who have realized their respective vehicles, up to the bodhisattvas, as well as the samādhis, supernormal powers, skillful means, and vows they have attained. The concluding summary states:
"Throughout the ocean of kalpas in this Sahā world, extending to the limits of the future, occurring in continuous succession—I know them all. As it says:
These twenty-three lines of scripture reveal the observation and thorough knowledge of the subtle matters of the ten dharma-realms within a single Sahā world-system.
This, however, merely provides a brief indication of a single layer of the Sahā world’s realm.
Next, by means of analogical knowledge, one gradually understands that the oceans of lands are vast and subtle, and there are six stages to this.
First, just as one knows the Sahā world, one likewise fully understands that within the Sahā world there are worlds as numerous as atoms;
these are merely lands of the same category as the Sahā world, existing in numbers as great as those atoms. Second, likewise...
He knows all the various types of worlds within the Sahā world-system; he likewise understands them in this same way.
Thirdly, he knows the worlds contained within the atoms of the Sahā world-system, because each and every atom contains many, many worlds.
This entry into the subtle is, for now, based on a single world-system, the Sahā.
It is said: next, the fourth section gradually expands, stating that one also knows the worlds situated throughout the ten directions without interval outside the Sahā world.
Now, the Sahā world is located on the thirteenth layer of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), with the Sahā world precisely occupying the center.
Outside of it, there are worlds numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields.
They are surrounded by realms that serve as their retinue. This refers to the worlds surrounding the Sahā world;
one should understand that within each of these realms, there are likewise ten dharma-realms, just as in the Sahā world.
Furthermore, one should know the worlds contained within the world-systems of the Sahā world; this then applies universally.
One contemplates the twenty tiers of the Flower Treasury World-system (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu-vyūha*), which is called a "world-seed" (*lokadhātu-jāti*).
Regarding the worlds contained therein: for instance, the very bottom layer is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in a single Buddha-field;
likewise, up to the topmost twentieth layer, it is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in twenty Buddha-fields. As...
All of these are worlds subsumed within world-systems. Thus, within each and every one of these worlds, there are ten dharma-realms, just as there are in the Sahā world, all of which he fully knows.

Furthermore, he also knows the worlds subsumed within the infinite world-systems of the ten directions within this Flower Treasury World-Ocean. This [passage] then cites the Flower [Treasury World-Ocean] in its entirety.

This refers to the ocean of world-systems within the *garbhadhātu*. Regarding what is called the "ocean of world-systems subsumed within world-germs" (*lokadhātu-jāti*), it refers to the Flower Treasury Ocean (*padma-garbha-sāgara*).
This means that at the center of the great Lotus Treasury, like the pistil of a flower, there is a single twenty-fold world-system contained within one pistil.
Since the flower has inexhaustible pistils, within each and every pistil there is [a world-system].
Each of these consists of twenty layers of worlds, encompassing all the numerous worlds within their filaments and contained within a single vast lotus flower;
collectively, they are called the "Ocean of Worlds. This is infinitely inexhaustible, termed the "Boundless Ocean of Lands.
Within it, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Such is the world-system contained within this ocean.

Regarding the realms: within each and every realm, there are ten dharma-realms just as there are in this Sahā world. All such oceans of lands are entirely contained within the mind of Samantabhadra’s samādhi;
he knows each one with perfect clarity. Therefore, it is called the "liberation gate of the ocean of samādhi.
Thus, the ocean that is observed is used to demonstrate the sphere of samādhi; hence, it is said that he "knows with perfect clarity. This above section merely...
This indicates the extent of the realm to be contemplated. Below, it shows the characteristics of the worlds known therein, stating:
"The so-called worlds are vast and expansive; the worlds are established," and so forth, briefly enumerating ten different types.
These fruits of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) are all accomplished through the original vows of the World-Honored One Vairocana.
Thus, one is able to recollect this vast expanse of cause and effect. Therefore, the subsequent passage concludes by referring to the causal practices of Vairocana, stating:

"One also recollects all the oceans of causes and conditions possessed by the Tathāgata in the past, namely, the cultivation and accumulation of the skillful means of all vehicles, the various pāramitās, and so forth. There are ten chapters of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* that clarify Vairocana.
Regarding the matters of causal practice, it is therefore concluded by saying: "In this way, I fully understand all of these. Consequently, he later explains himself:
"For what reason have I fully understood the vast causes and effects mentioned above?
It is because through this gate of liberation of mine, I am able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings, up to and including the light of liberation of all Tathāgatas."
"By the power of this liberation, I am thus able to know. The above has already answered regarding the sphere of liberation.
The following questions reveal the depth of the root of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, Sudhana said to Gopā: "Noble One, how long has it been since you attained this liberation?
This question seeks the very source of liberation. In the subsequent text, Gopā provides a full answer.
He recounts his past causes, first clarifying the beginning of his initial generation of the mind of enlightenment:
"In a past world, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there was an eon named Supreme Conduct and a world-system named Fearless.
Within that world-system were four continents; in Jambudvīpa, there was a city named High and Victorious Tree, and within that city was a king."

His name was Dhanapati. That king had a crown prince named Tejodhipati, who was exceptionally handsome and pleasing to behold, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. One day, the prince was accompanied by ten thousand court ladies.

He went to the Gandhakuṭī Garden to enjoy himself with sightseeing and recreation. There, he displayed various kinds of precious objects and articles for livelihood and distributed them as gifts within the garden.
At that time, there was a woman whose mother was named Bhadrā;
she brought along a young girl named Guṇavatī, who was of upright countenance and incomparable beauty. By chance, she followed her mother out of the city and saw him.
The son’s heart was filled with love and attachment; he immediately said to his mother, "My heart's desire is to serve this man with reverence.
His mother said, "This man is endowed with the marks of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin). He will surely become a Wheel-Turning King in the future. He already possesses a precious queen;
we are lowly and base, not his equal. Do not harbor such a thought. At that time, there was a certain path within the Gandhamādana Garden.
At that time, the Tathāgata Jitaruci appeared in this place. Then, while the young girl was dozing, she saw that Buddha in a dream.
Upon waking from her sleep, because she had beheld the Tathāgata in her dream, her mind became peaceful and free from fear.
She immediately went before the Prince and spoke these verses: "My body is most upright and beautiful; my wisdom is without..."
The matchmaker then praised the prince, expressing his wish for him to accept her; there were ten verses in total. At that time, the prince addressed the girl, saying:
"Whose daughter are you? By whom are you protected? If you already belong to another, I may not take you.
He further examined the circumstances of her lineage and whether there were any faults by means of twelve verses; all were thorough inquiries.
These were words of truth. At that time, the girl’s mother also spoke a verse, saying to the Prince:
"Prince, you should listen: this girl did not emerge from a womb, but was born from within a lotus; therefore, her appearance is exceptionally sublime."
"Unrivaled among men, she possesses thirty-one verses that fully describe her feminine virtues, concluding with the words:
'She is entirely free from resentment; she is the most excellent among women and should serve the Prince.
At that time, the Prince entered the Gandha-kūṭa Garden and addressed his mother, Sujātā, and his daughter, Kalyāṇī, renewing his solemn vow, saying: 'I wish to proceed to...'"
Seeking unsurpassed bodhi, [he vowed] to exhaust the limits of the future, fully explaining the various practices of a bodhisattva.
It continues until it says: "When I abandoned you to leave the household life, did your heart feel regret?

These words of solemn vow consist of twelve and a half lines of prose, all of which describe his own profound practices and his fears regarding matters that might become obstacles. The Prince further...
The verses spoken consist of ten stanzas, all of which describe profound practice and emphasize the necessity of remaining free from obstacles. It concludes by saying:
"If you can comply with my heart, I shall follow your will. At that time, the young girl addressed the Prince, saying:

"I respectfully accept your instruction," and she also spoke a verse to vow her resolve: "Even if, throughout an ocean of immeasurable kalpas, the fires of hell were to consume my body, if I could..."

"Accept me as your kinsman; I am willing to endure this suffering. Within it, he says that for the sake of pitying sentient beings, he has resolved upon the Bodhicitta—this is the very beginning of the initial resolve.
It continues until he says: 'Because I saw the Tathāgata in a dream, I was able to see the Prince.
Now that my wish is fulfilled, I pray that we may together behold the Tathāgata. There are fourteen verses, all of which recount his forgetfulness."
The Suffering Relative, whose virtue was rare and who aspired to emulate supreme conduct, resolved to generate the bodhicitta.

At that time, the Prince, fully perceiving the maiden’s resolve, immediately accepted her; he then adorned her by scattering exquisite jewels upon her, crowning her with a jeweled tiara, and clothing her in precious garments.
At that time, the girl’s mind remained unshaken, and she showed no sign of joy.
Her mother, Sujātā, stood before the prince and, expressing her own sense of fulfillment, spoke ten verses in praise of her daughter’s virtues; all were words extolling the girl.
Subsequently, the prince and the girl, Suśīlā, together resolved to practice the path and departed together from the city of Gandhavatī.
They went to the Dharma-Cloud Radiance Bodhimanda in the Garden of Teeth and beheld the Tathāgata Victorious Sun-Body. Each offered their worship.
At that time, the Buddha preached for them the *Sūtra of the Universal Eye Lamp Gate*. Having heard it, the prince and the princess immediately attained ten kinds of samādhis.
They returned to the palace and reported in detail to their father, the king, regarding the appearance of the Buddha and all related matters, and they questioned him further.
Upon hearing of the circumstances concerning the maiden Sudarśanā, the king was filled with joy. At that time, the king immediately resolved to see the Buddha;
he then abdicated the throne to the crown prince and went at once to behold the Buddha. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted rays of light to receive him and preached a *dhāraṇī* for him.
Having heard the Dharma, the king immediately attained the radiance of great wisdom. Within that assembly were Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust.
[Sa]. He attained dhāraṇīs, and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta. At that time, having heard the Dharma, the king resolved his mind on renunciation;
through his cultivation and realization, he also attained various samādhis.
Thereupon, the crown prince succeeded to the royal throne and widely propagated the Great Teaching. From the time the prince had seen the Buddha, down to his desire to inspire [others]—one.

The *Sarvajñajñānapraṇidhāna* consists of fifty-eight lines of verse. It narrates the Prince’s encounter with the Buddha, his father the King’s renunciation, and the circumstances surrounding the Prince’s succession to the throne;
it then proceeds to answer in detail questions regarding the duration of his initial resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
Consequently, it concludes by correlating the past with the present, stating: "Was that Prince anyone else? He was none other than Śākyamuni."
The nun Bhadrā was this very person. King Dhanapati was the Buddha Ratnapuṣpa.
At that time, her mother, Bhadrottamā, was my own mother, Bhadranetrī. The king’s retinue were the assembly gathered here before the Tathāgata now.
That girl, Varuṇadevī, was myself. The text summarizing these connections consists of eighteen lines of scripture, beginning from the section on Jyotīrasa.
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, sixty billion nayutas of Buddhas will successively appear in that world;
I shall serve and make offerings to them all with you, O King, and behold many Buddhas therein.
I have briefly cited forty names of Buddhas; there are seventeen lines remaining in the sutra. The last of those Buddhas was named Vistīrṇamatī (Vast Understanding).
When that Buddha entered the city, I was the Queen Consort; together with the King, I paid him homage and heard the Dharma he preached.
Immediately, I attained the liberation of the ocean-like realm of the samādhis for observing all bodhisattvas. This serves as proof of having attained the Dharma.
At that time, there are three and a half lines of sūtra. Following this, it describes the period after attaining liberation, during which he polished his realization over many kalpas, saying:
"I attained this liberation and diligently practiced it for as many kalpas as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
Although I have served and practiced under many buddhas, I have not yet exhausted the realm of the bodhisattva samādhis; indeed, such bodhisattvas are difficult to encounter."
What is seen is also not empty. There are seven lines of scripture that describe the events of practicing the path over many kalpas.

Following that, there are six lines of scripture which further describe how, since I saw that Buddha and attained this liberation, I have practiced for as many kalpas as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields;
although I have attained various liberations, I have still not been able to know the universal... [attainment].
The Gate of Worthy Liberation. This section below investigates and explains the reason for his lack of knowledge, asking: "For what reason has he practiced for many eons yet remained unaware?

It is because the Gate of Samantabhadra’s Liberation is like the great void, like the names of sentient beings, and like the ocean of the Dharma-realm in the ten directions; it is equal to the realm of the Tathāgata, being profoundly deep and vast.
This is because it is difficult to know. The following explains the reason why it is profound, vast, and difficult to know:

"Throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, I have observed each and every pore of the Bodhisattva’s body; in every thought-moment, I have seen immeasurable and boundless vast receptacle-worlds (*bhājanaloka*).
In each and every pore, in every thought-moment, I have seen immeasurable and boundless wisdom and correctness."
Awakening to the world: in every single pore, moment by moment, one perceives immeasurable and boundless worlds of sentient beings;
in every single pore, moment by moment, one perceives the boundless gates of practice of the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time;
and even within each and every pore, one sees all matters within the dharma-realm of the three periods of time. In summary, these are profound, vast, and inexhaustible, comprising nineteen lines.

The Sūtra describes the characteristics of profundity and vastness that are difficult to fathom. The reason they are difficult to fathom is that they accord with the boundlessness of principle and phenomena, and are equal to the realm of all Buddhas.
Thus, even the liberation of Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyikabodhi*) does not know it;
therefore, it is named the "Liberation Gate of Samantabhadra. The preceding response regarding the duration of this liberation is now complete. Below, the author humbles himself.
Viśeṣamati said: "I have attained only this liberation of observing the ocean of bodhisattvas.

As for the oceans of skillful means of those bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate limit of the infinite, and even their entry into the gateways of the dharma that sport within all stages throughout the vast dharma-realm—how could I know them? Then, pointing to a subsequent friend, he said: "In this world..."
"Mother of the Buddha, Māyā, you should go and inquire [about this].
When the Bodhisattva approached all the Tathāgatas and encompassed the realms of all sentient beings, as he was about to depart, he restated and reiterated its meaning in thirty-one verses.
The first verse generally reveals the Bodhisattva’s benefit for others; the next fifteen verses eulogize and clarify events from distant kalpas. [The prose follows.]
[The preceding section] was absent. The subsequent fifteen verses correctly versify the causes and conditions for the daughter’s virtues.

At that time, having heard this, Sudhana prostrated at her feet, took his leave, and departed. This concludes the section on the characteristics of the stages of practice, as manifested through the forty-one spiritual friends beginning with Mañjuśrī.
