Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Seventeen: Entering the Dharmadhātu.
From here begins the second major section, which comprises eleven individuals starting with Māyā.

This section clarifies "Entering the Reality-Phase by Conjoining Conditions," meaning that it causes the various conditions of the preceding stages to converge into the single reality-dharmadhātu, thereby giving birth to the fruit of Buddhahood—just as Māyā gave birth to the Buddha.
Therefore, this is explained next. Although there are eleven individuals, in terms of the Dharma, there are only nine.
The meeting is tenfold: the first is the general, and the remaining nine are the particular. Thus, Māyā attained the dharma-gate of the illusion of wisdom;
in the end, she also attained illusory abiding. Beginning and end meet, encompassing the middle; the general and the particular are perfectly integrated.
Because returning to reality is non-dual, this signifies the appearance of the Buddhas and the various Dharma-gates taught by Bodhisattvas during their practice;

from beginning to end, these are solely the liberation of illusory wisdom. Since various illusory conditions do not depart from the single true Dharma-realm, at this stage of ultimate awakening, one reunites with the previously mentioned illusory conditions to enter the real Dharma-realm.
In sum, nothing transcends the great vow, wisdom, and illusory liberation of Māyā. At the end, Śrīdevī and her spiritual friend likewise realize the liberation of dwelling in illusion.
This signifies that from the beginning to the end of attaining Buddhahood, it is but a single illusory field.

Because the causes of the ten stages are perfected, one enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi); as the position is ultimate and the principle exhausted, Sudhana beholds Māyā as his spiritual friend of Equal Enlightenment.
Furthermore, this stage is not easily perceived; therefore, city deities, rākṣasas, and others act as precursors to manifest the advancement of this position.

This is precisely the single gate of liberation of Māyā, which subsumes the causes and effects of the preceding five stages and constitutes the practice leading to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Its meaning is most profound and mysterious; one must employ the wisdom of contemplation to harmonize and integrate it, thereby grasping its essential point.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded intent, desired to go to the place where Lady Māyā was.
Immediately, he attained the wisdom of contemplating the realm of the Buddhas and formed this thought: "This spiritual friend dwells far removed from the world, abiding in non-abiding."
Transcending the six sense bases, they are free from all attachments. They know the path of non-obstruction and are endowed with the pure Dharma-body.
By means of illusion-like karma, they manifest transformation bodies; by means of illusion-like wisdom, they contemplate the world; and by means of illusion-like vows, they sustain the Buddha-body.
A body born of mental resolve; a body without birth or extinction; a body without coming or going; a body that is neither empty nor substantial;

a body that does not change or decay; a body without arising or ceasing; a body whose all characteristics are but a single characteristic; a body free from the two extremes; a body without a place of dependence.
The inexhaustible body; the body that manifests like a shadow, free from all conceptual discrimination; the body known to be like a dream; the body understood to be like a reflection;
the body like the pure sun, manifesting transformed bodies throughout the ten directions; and the unchanging body abiding in the three periods of time.
It is neither body nor mind; it is like space, moving without obstruction, transcending the eyes of all worldly beings, and visible only to the pure eyes of Samantabhadra.
How may I now draw near to such a person, serve them, and make offerings to them?
While dwelling with them, he observed their physical forms, listened to their voices, reflected upon their speech, and received their instructions.
Having formed this thought, a city-protecting deity named Ratnanetra appeared in the midst of the sky, surrounded by a retinue;
adorned with various exquisite ornaments, she held in her hands immeasurable jeweled flowers of many colors.
He scattered Sudhana and spoke these words: "O son of good family, you should guard the city of the mind;
that is to say, do not covet any realm of birth and death. You should adorn the city of the mind; that is to say, focus your intent on seeking the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
You should purify the city of the mind; that is to say, ultimately sever stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception. You should cool the city of the mind; that is to say, contemplate..."
One should contemplate the true nature of all dharmas. One should cause the city of the mind to increase, which means accomplishing all factors conducive to the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
One should adorn the city of the mind, which means constructing the palaces of the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*).

One should illuminate the city of the mind, which means entering universally into the *bodhimaṇḍas* of all Buddhas to hear and receive the Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*. One should cause it to flourish.
The city of the mind refers to universally encompassing all the skillful means of the Buddhas.

One should make this city of the mind firm and solid by constantly and diligently practicing the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. One should defend this city of the mind by always and single-mindedly warding off evil friends and the armies of Māra.
One should make this city of the mind vast and transparent by opening the way for the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas. One should skillfully repair this city of the mind by listening...
One should receive all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas; one should support the city of the mind, which means having deep faith in the ocean of merits of all Buddhas.
One should expand the city of the mind, which means extending great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) universally to all worlds.

One should well-shelter the city of the mind, which means gathering all wholesome dharmas to cover it from above. One should broaden the city of the mind, which means feeling great compassion (*karuṇā*) and pity for all beings.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one should open the city-gate of the mind, which means relinquishing all that one possesses and bestowing it as gifts according to need.

One should guard the city of the mind closely, which means preventing various evil desires from entering. One should solemnly fortify the city of the mind, which means expelling all unwholesome dharmas so they do not remain.
One should resolve upon the city of the mind, which means constantly accumulating the factors conducive to enlightenment for the sake of attaining omniscience.
One should establish the city of the mind so that it is irreversible, by means of right mindfulness regarding the spheres of all Tathāgatas of the three times.

One should polish the city of the mind until it is transparently clear, by means of penetrating understanding of all the various dependent originations within the Dharma-gates found in the sūtras of the True Wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
One should partition the city of the mind, by means of universally instructing and revealing [the path] to all sentient beings.
They cause all to behold the path to *sarvajñatā* (omniscience). One should maintain the city of the mind by generating the great ocean of vows of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
One should enrich the city of the mind by accumulating the vast mass of great merit that pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*.
One should cause the city of the mind to be clear and lucid by universally knowing the faculties, inclinations, and other such qualities of sentient beings. One should cause the mind...

The sovereignty of the city means universally encompassing the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm. One should purify the city of the mind by maintaining right mindfulness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
One should know the intrinsic nature of the city of the mind, which means knowing that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
One should know that the city of the mind is like an illusion, which means realizing the nature of all phenomena through omniscience. O Son of the Buddha! Bodhi—
Sons of the Great Being, if one can thus purify the city of the mind, then one will be able to accumulate all wholesome dharmas.

Why is this? Because one eliminates all obstacles and difficulties, namely: the obstacle to seeing the Buddha, the obstacle to hearing the Dharma, the obstacle to making offerings to the Tathāgata, the obstacle to gathering in sentient beings, and the obstacle to purifying the Buddha-lands. Sons of good family, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...

Because the Bodhisattva is free from such obstacles and difficulties, if they give rise to the aspiration to seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will see one without exerting effort; eventually, they shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the body-guardian spirits named Padmadharmaguṇa, along with the countless spirits of Wondrous Flower Radiance, surrounded him from front and back as he proceeded on the path.
Emerging from that place, he stood in mid-air before Sudhana and praised Lady Māyā with various wondrous sounds.

From her ear-ornaments, she emitted nets of light of immeasurable colors and forms, which universally illumined the boundless worlds of all Buddhas, causing Sudhana to see all the Buddhas in the lands of the ten directions. These nets of light circled to the right...
After circulating once throughout the world, it returned and entered the crown of Sudhana’s head, eventually pervading all the pores of his body.
Sudhana immediately attained the eye of pure radiance, because he was forever freed from the darkness of all ignorance;
he attained the unobscured eye, because he was able to comprehend the nature of all sentient beings; he attained the stainless eye, because he was able to contemplate the nature of all phenomena.

Because they have attained the gate of the pure eye of wisdom, which is able to perceive the nature of all Buddha-lands; because they have attained the Vairocana-eye, which sees the Dharma-body of the Buddhas;
because they have attained the eye of universal radiance, which sees the inconceivable and equal bodies of the Buddhas;

because they have attained the eye of unimpeded light, which observes the formation and destruction of all oceans of lands; and because they have attained the eye of universal illumination, which sees the ten directions.
Because the Buddha has set in motion the wheel of the sublime Dharma through the exercise of great skillful means;
because he has attained the eye of universal range that sees immeasurable Buddhas and tames sentient beings through the power of mastery;

and because he has attained the eye of universal vision that beholds the appearance of all Buddhas in every land—at that time, there was a rākṣasa king who protected the Dharma Hall of the Bodhisattvas, named Sūryanetra (Good Eye), together with his retinue.
Then, together with ten thousand rākṣasīs, they scattered various exquisite flowers upon Sudhana from the midst of the sky and spoke these words:
"Good son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he is able to draw near to spiritual friends. What are these ten? They are:
a mind that is pure and free from all flattery and deception; great compassion that is impartial and universally embraces all sentient beings."
Knowing that all sentient beings lack any true reality, their resolve for omniscience never regresses.
By the power of faith and understanding, they universally enter the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas. Attaining the eye of pure wisdom, they perceive the nature of all phenomena.

With great compassion that is impartial, they universally cover all sentient beings. With the light of wisdom, they clear away all delusive objects; with the rain of nectar, they wash away attachments to birth and death.
With the vast eye, one thoroughly discerns all phenomena; the mind always accords with all spiritual friends. These are the ten.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten gateways of samādhi, they constantly see all spiritual friends before them.
What are these ten? They are: the samādhi of the pure wheel of the emptiness of phenomena; the samādhi of observing the ocean of the ten directions;
the samādhi of never abandoning or diminishing any objective realm; the samādhi of universally beholding the appearance of all Buddhas;
the samādhi of gathering the treasury of all merit; the samādhi of never forsaking spiritual friends at any time; and the constant...
The Samādhi of Beholding All Spiritual Friends as Giving Birth to the Merits of All Buddhas; the Samādhi of Never Being Separated from All Spiritual Friends;
the Samādhi of Constantly Making Offerings to All Spiritual Friends; and the Samādhi of Having No Faults Before Any Spiritual Friends.
Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these thirteen gates of samādhi, they constantly attain intimacy [with them].
He drew near to various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, he attained the samādhi called "Turning the Dharma-Wheel of All Buddhas.
Having attained this samādhi, he came to know that the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas is equal. Everywhere he encountered various spiritual friends.
While these words were being spoken, the youth Sudhana looked up into the sky and replied, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You..."
Out of compassion and to take me under your care, please employ skillful means to instruct me on how to see virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). I pray that you will tell me:
how should one go to the presence of a virtuous spiritual friend? In which direction, in what city, town, or village should one seek a virtuous spiritual friend?
The rākṣasa replied: "Noble son, you should universally prostrate to the ten directions and seek a virtuous spiritual friend with right mindfulness and reflection."
Seeking spiritual friends in all realms; seeking spiritual friends by traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions with courageous mastery;
and seeking spiritual friends by contemplating the body and the mind as being like dreams and shadows.
Below this, Māyādevī represents the spiritual friend of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*). In Sanskrit, *Māyā* means "Queen of Heaven.

However, this stage represents the culmination of causal practice as one is about to enter the ocean of fruition; thus, she is represented by the Buddha’s mother, for she is capable of giving birth to a Buddha.
Consequently, she brings together the causes of the preceding five stages, converging them all into a single reality. Likewise, Sudhana is also able to bring these together.
Having integrated all the spiritual friends he had consulted and all the Dharma-gates he had realized into a single flavor, he proceeded;
thus, upon reaching this place, he did not see Māyā. Immediately, he attained the realm of the Buddha’s vision and formed this thought:
"This spiritual friend has transcended the world and dwells in non-abiding; he even sustains the Buddha-body through the power of vows and illusion-like wisdom. This was already so.
He is able to harmonize in secret with the illusory gate of Māyā’s vow-knowledge; thus, he beholds seventeen kinds of bodies.
To say that these are seen solely by the pure eyes of Samantabhadra is already to have entered the Buddha-realm, surpassing all other liberations.
These seventeen kinds of bodies are manifested by the Queen of the Dharma (Dharmarājñī); therefore, Sudhana says: "Such a person as I..."
"How can I now draw near to him, make offerings to him, and receive his instructions? This was said because it is difficult to behold him.

After Sudhana had formed this thought, there was a city-protecting goddess named Ratnanetra who, from the midst of the sky, scattered various kinds of precious flowers over Sudhana and addressed him, saying: "O son of good family!"
One should guard the city of the mind. Below this are thirty gates that teach Sudhana the skillful means for seeing spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
these represent the progressive advancement into the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The first twelve gates clarify the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
This clearly demonstrates that there is not a single thing or a single speck of dust that is not a gateway to the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the "city of the mind," it means that this mind is the dwelling place of the Dharma King of Perfect Enlightenment and the locus where all myriad virtues are gathered.

Since the attainment of Buddhahood does not occur outside of this mind, guarding it and so forth constitute sublime practice. Because the ten perfections are what is cultivated throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one should next provide support for them.
There are eleven gates beneath the "Assisting Mind-City," which clarify the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten kinds of superior practices.
Next, there are seven gates beneath the "Maintaining Mind-City," which clarify the perfection of merit and wisdom.

Finally, it is concluded that if one can thus purify and cultivate the mind-city, reaching even unto the ultimate, one will certainly attain Buddhahood; this praises the benefits of accomplishment. In total, there are twenty-eight [gates].

The *Caryā-sūtra* clarifies that the assembly of practices must be unified into a single mind; this is the essential for attaining Buddhahood, and thus constitutes the supreme practice of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Next, there was a body-guard deity named Padmadharmaguṇa who emerged from the site of enlightenment.
Abiding in the midst of space, they praised the virtues of the Queen of Heaven with wondrous voices.
They also emitted light of immeasurable colors and forms, universally illuminating the boundless worlds of all Buddhas, causing Sudhana to see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This light then returned and entered the crown of Sudhana’s head, eventually pervading all the pores of his body. The various deities of this body first empowered Sudhana with their light.
The Dharma-realm is secretly transmitted; this signifies the ultimate stage. The realm of wisdom is profoundly deep and truly not easy to enter.

Therefore, one must rely upon the empowerment and sustenance of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to be able to enter it. Thus, when Sudhana’s pores were completely suffused by light, he suddenly attained the perfect clarity of the eye of wisdom.
Consequently, he immediately obtained the ten kinds of eyes, such as the pure light-eye (*vimalaprabhā-cakṣus*). Then...
Upon attaining the "Eye of Universal Vision," one beholds all Buddha-fields and the emergence of all Buddhas;
this is achieved by relying on the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whereby one is able to see the realm of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, these ten eyes do not merely perceive the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), but also behold the inconceivable Buddha-body in its ten forms, free from obstruction. Having thus received the guidance of the two goddesses, Sudhana—
Regarding the empowerment through instruction: although it is relatively easy to perceive the realm of the Buddha, it is even more difficult to see this spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Why is this? Because he is the mother who gave birth to the Buddhas. Therefore, next, there is a rākṣasī who guards the Dharma Hall in the midst of the void, who instructs Sudhana on the method for perceiving spiritual friends; one should [apply] these eleven [points].
The cultivation of the mind is the foundation. The passage concerning the ten minds consists of seven and a half lines of scripture.

Having already taught the eleven kinds [of mind], he further demonstrates the ten kinds of samādhi as the essential means for perceiving the Knowledge-Being (jñāna-sattva). However, it is only through samādhi that one can perceive;
for this Knowledge-Being takes the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as its body, and all Buddhas of the ten directions arise from it.
This birth is by no means visible through a distracted mind; therefore, one is taught the ten kinds of samādhis with a profound resolve.
Once these samādhis are attained, one realizes that the essential nature of all Buddhas is equal. Only then can one encounter spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) everywhere.
If one enters this samādhi and perfectly realizes the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), then upon every touch of the eye and every encounter with an object, one reaches the ultimate limit.
As for the source of the Dharma, all places are spiritual friends.

When the rākṣasa had spoken these words, Sudhana looked up toward the sky and replied to him, saying, "Since you have compassionately accepted me and taught me through skillful means, I pray that you will tell me in which direction and at which place I should seek a spiritual friend. The rākṣasa said, "Good son, you should..."
"Universally prostrating to the ten directions to seek spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) sweeps away the mind that seeks [the Dharma] only in the south. Furthermore, it says:
"With right mindfulness, contemplating all objective realms to seek spiritual friends sweeps away the tendency to seek only the dharmas realized by those spiritual friends.
It further says: "With courageous vigor and mastery, traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to seek..."
"Good friend," this sweeps away the narrow-minded view of seeking a good friend through individual instances of mind and objects.
The preceding three [lines] have already dissolved the person and the dharma that are sought. Next, it says:

"Contemplate the body and contemplate the mind as being like a dream or a shadow while seeking a good friend. This dissolves the person who seeks and eliminates the persistence of anything that exists as an object.
This is the vision of attaining the Dharma. When person and dharma are both extinguished in this way, and self and other are simultaneously obliterated, one is equal and such-like;
thus, one naturally enters the impartial Dharmadhātu. This teaching that sweeps away all traces and cuts off all footprints is entirely contained within the single word of Rākṣasa.
Yet, although Rākṣasa is an evil spirit, he was able to reveal the subtlety of entering the Dharmadhātu.
How could the dharma of birth and death not be the wondrous function of the Dharma-realm? It is here that Sudhana’s journey of seeking reaches its ultimate consummation;
why, then, must he seek the Queen of Heaven? Nevertheless, it is at this point that Sudhana has already attained realization.
That which was manifested by the Queen of Heaven was precisely the Dharma-gate of the Magical Illusion of Wisdom.
At that time, Sudhana received and practiced her instruction; immediately, he beheld a great jewel lotus flower springing forth from the earth.
Its stem is of vajra; its core is of exquisite jewels; its leaves are of maṇi; its pedestal is made of the king of luminous jewels;
and its filaments are composed of the colors and fragrances of various gems. Countless jeweled nets completely cover it.
Upon that pedestal is a multi-storied pavilion named "The Treasury that Universally Encompasses the Dharma Realms of the Ten Directions," wonderfully and exquisitely adorned, with a ground of vajra.
There were rows of a thousand pillars, all made of maṇi jewels, with walls of Jāmbūnada gold.
Necklaces of various gems hung down on all four sides, and the steps and railings were adorned all around.
Within that pavilion was a seat of wish-fulfilling jewel lotuses, decorated with various kinds of precious gems and exquisite jeweled railings.

Jeweled robes were arranged in alternating rows; jeweled canopies and jeweled nets covered them from above. Various jeweled silk banners hung down on all sides; as a gentle breeze moved them, light flowed and sounds resonated.
From within the jeweled flower-pennants, various exquisite flowers rained down. From within the jeweled bells and chimes, beautiful sounds issued forth.
Between the jeweled doors and windows, various necklaces hung down. From within the bodies of the maṇi-jewels, fragrant water flowed out.

From the mouths of precious elephants emerge nets of lotuses; from the mouths of precious lions issue clouds of exquisite fragrance; from the Brahma-form precious wheels arise sounds according to all desires;
from the vajra-precious bells issue the sounds of the great vows of all bodhisattvas; from within the precious moon-banner appear the transformed bodies of Buddhas;
and from the pure-treasury precious king manifest the sequence of births of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. The sun-treasury maṇi...
They emit great rays of light that universally illumine all Buddha-fields in the ten directions.
The sovereign mani-jewel emits the perfect radiance of all Buddhas. The sovereign Vairocana-mani-jewel raises clouds of offerings to honor all Tathāgatas.
The sovereign wish-fulfilling jewel manifests the spiritual transformations of Samantabhadra in every thought-moment, filling the entire Dharma-realm.
From the precious king Sumeru, celestial palaces emerged. The various celestial maidens sang with manifold exquisite melodies in praise of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and subtle merits.
At that time, Sudhana saw such a throne, surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of seats.
Lady Māyā sat upon that throne, manifesting purity before all sentient beings.
The form-body (*rūpakāya*): that is to say, the form-body that transcends the three realms, for it has already emerged from all states of existence (*gati*).

The form-body that accords with the inclinations of the mind, for it is unattached to anything in all worlds. The universally pervasive form-body, for it is equal to the number of all sentient beings.
The incomparable form-body, for it causes all sentient beings to extinguish their inverted views. It is immeasurable...
The body of various forms manifests in diverse ways according to the minds of sentient beings;
the body of infinite marks universally displays all manner of forms; the body of universal manifestation appears through great sovereign mastery;
the body that transforms all appears before beings as appropriate to their needs; and the eternally manifesting body extends throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.
Because it is inexhaustible; because the color-body that does not go is never extinguished in any realm of existence (*gati*);

because the color-body that does not come does not emerge from any world; because the color-body that does not issue forth has no origination; because the color-body that does not perish is free from verbal expression;
because the color-body that is not real attains suchness (*tathatā*); because the color-body that is not false appears in accordance with the world. It is without...
The moving physical body is because it is eternally free from arising and ceasing; the indestructible physical body is because its *dharmatā* is indestructible;

the signless physical body is because it transcends the path of language; the single-marked physical body is because taking the signless as its mark; the image-like physical body is because it manifests in accordance with the mind;
the illusion-like physical body is because it is produced by illusory wisdom; and the mirage-like physical body is because it consists of mere conceptualization.
Because they are sustained; because the form-body of reflection manifests in accordance with vows; because the form-body of dreams appears in accordance with the mind;
because the form-body of the dharma-realm is pure by nature like space; because the form-body of great compassion constantly protects sentient beings;
because the unimpeded form-body pervades the dharma-realm in every thought-moment; and because the boundless form-body universally purifies all sentient beings.
The immeasurable form-body, because it transcends all speech; the non-abiding form-body, because it vows to deliver all worlds;
the placeless form-body, because it constantly transforms sentient beings without interruption; the birthless form-body, because it is accomplished through illusory vows;
the unsurpassed form-body, because it transcends all worlds; and the form-body as it truly is, because it is manifested by a concentrated mind.
The non-arising form-body, because it appears in accordance with the karma of sentient beings; the wish-fulfilling jewel form-body, because it universally fulfills the vows of all sentient beings;
the non-discriminating form-body, because it arises solely in accordance with the discrimination of sentient beings;
the form-body free from discrimination, because no sentient beings can know it; and the inexhaustible form-body, because it exhausts the births of all sentient beings.
Because it is the limit of death; because the pure form-body is non-discriminative, being identical to that of the Tathāgata;
such a body is not form, for all its formal characteristics are like reflections; it is not sensation, for worldly painful sensations have been utterly extinguished;

it is not perception, for it appears only in accordance with the perceptions of sentient beings; it is not formations, for it is accomplished based on karma that is like an illusion. It is free from...
Consciousness. Because the Bodhisattva’s vow-knowledge is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; because the verbal expressions of all sentient beings have been severed;

and because he has already attained the accomplishment of the body of quiescent extinction—at that time, the youth Sudhana again saw Lady Māyā manifesting a physical form that transcends all worlds according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, namely, she manifested [a form] that transcends...
The body of a goddess of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, up to surpassing the bodies of goddesses of the Caturmahārājakāyika Heaven;
or manifesting as surpassing the bodies of nāga maidens, up to surpassing the bodies of human women—manifesting such immeasurable forms of physical bodies.
Benefiting sentient beings, they gather all the dharmas that assist the path to omniscience. They practice the pāramitā of giving with equanimity.
Their great compassion universally covers all worlds. They give rise to the immeasurable merits of a Tathāgata. They cultivate and increase the mind of omniscience.
They contemplate and reflect upon the true nature of all phenomena, attaining the ocean of profound patience and possessing the various gateways of meditative concentration.
Abiding in the state of the samādhi of equanimity, he attains the perfect radiance of the Tathāgata’s concentration. He dries up the vast ocean of sentient beings’ afflictions;
his mind is always in right concentration, never wavering or disturbed, as he constantly turns the pure, non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.
They are well able to thoroughly understand all Buddha-dharmas. They constantly contemplate the true nature of phenomena with wisdom.

They behold all Tathāgatas without ever feeling weary or satiated. They know the sequential order of the appearance of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. And they see the samādhis of the Buddhas ever present before them.
They thoroughly comprehend the immeasurable and innumerable paths of purity through which the Tathāgatas appear in the world;
they traverse the space-like realm of all Buddhas to universally gather in sentient beings, teaching and bringing them to fulfillment according to their respective inclinations;
they enter the Buddha’s immeasurable, pure Dharma-body; they fulfill great vows to purify all Buddha-fields, and ultimately bring all sentient beings to subdual.
Their minds constantly and universally enter the realms of all Buddhas. They give rise to the sovereign spiritual powers of Bodhisattvas.
Having attained the pure and undefiled Dharma-body, they constantly manifest immeasurable form-bodies.

They crush all demonic forces, accomplish the power of great roots of goodness, give rise to the power of the True Dharma, and are fully endowed with the powers of all Buddhas, attaining the sovereign powers of all Bodhisattvas.
They swiftly increase all powers of wisdom; they attain the light of the Buddha’s knowledge that universally illumines all things;

they fully know the ocean of minds of immeasurable sentient beings, along with the various distinctions of their faculties, natures, desires, and inclinations; and their bodies pervade the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions.
They fully know the characteristics of the formation and destruction of all lands; with their vast eyes, they behold the oceans of the ten directions;

with their pervasive wisdom, they know the oceans of the three periods of time; their bodies universally accomplish the works of the oceans of all Buddhas; and their minds constantly receive and retain the oceans of all dharmas.
I shall cultivate all the merits of the Tathāgatas and give birth to all the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas.
I shall constantly and joyfully observe all Bodhisattvas, from their first aspiration until they achieve the path of practice.
I shall always diligently protect all sentient beings and constantly delight in praising the merits of all Buddhas. May I become the mother of all Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld Lady Māyā manifesting as many gates of skillful means as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa.
Having seen this, Sudhana likewise manifested as many bodies as the number of bodies manifested by Lady Māyā, and in every place before Lady Māyā, he paid respectful homage. Immediately—
He attained immeasurable and innumerable gateways of samādhi, discerning, observing, practicing, and entering them.
Arising from samādhi, he circumambulated Māyā along with her retinue, stood with palms joined, and said:
"O Great Sage, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has instructed me to resolve my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to seek perfect knowledge."
I have approached and made offerings to these spiritual friends; I have gone to serve each one of them without missing an opportunity, and have gradually come here.
I pray that you will tell me how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct so as to achieve its fulfillment.
He replied: "O Son of the Buddha, because I have accomplished the liberation door of the great vow-wisdom illusion of a bodhisattva, for this reason..."

I am always the mother of all bodhisattvas. Son of the Buddha, just as I was born from the right side of Queen Māyā in the house of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu within this Jambudvīpa, giving birth to Prince Siddhārtha, and manifested inconceivable and sovereign spiritual transformations; so it is here.
In this manner, even unto the end of this ocean of worlds, all the Vairocana Tathāgatas enter my body and manifest the sovereign miraculous transformations of their birth. Furthermore, noble son,
when the Bodhisattva was about to descend to be born in the palace of King Śuddhodana, I saw light radiating from every single pore of the Bodhisattva’s body.

This light is named "The Wheel of Merit of the Birth of All Tathāgatas. From every single pore, there appear adornments of the births of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Those rays of light universally illuminate all worlds; having illuminated the worlds, they enter my crown and likewise all my pores.
Within the center of each pore, there further appeared, throughout that light, the names of all bodhisattvas, their births, and their miraculous transformations;

"Good man, I know only this liberation of pure, unimpeded mindfulness. As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they emerge from the night of birth and death with brilliant and penetrating clarity;
forever free from the darkness of delusion, they never fall into昏沉 (stupor) or sleep.

Their minds are free from all hindrances, their physical conduct is light and tranquil, and they possess a pure awakening to the nature of all phenomena. Having accomplished the Ten Powers, they bring enlightenment to all living beings."
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good son, in the city of Kapilavastu there is a teacher of children named Viśvāmitra.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, because he had heard the Dharma, the youth Sudhana leaped for joy with inconceivable goodness.
His faculties naturally increased in breadth; he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, took his leave, and departed.
Second, Sudhana, receiving the instruction of Māyā, went directly to the celestial palace to visit Dyutindhara.

As for the name Dyutindhara, it signifies that his superior application of compassion and wisdom is luminous, pure, and sovereign, in the sense that it destroys darkness; therefore, the dharma-gate is so named.

"Unimpeded and pure mindfulness. The first phrase refers to seeking [the truth] in accordance with the teachings. "Seeing the Light of the Lord of Heaven" and below refers to seeing, paying respect, and inquiring;
it describes having already resolved the mind [for enlightenment] and asking about the practice of the bodhisattva path. The Lord of Heaven replied:
"I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'Unimpeded Mindfulness, Pure Adornment. This precisely demonstrates the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm). It is called 'unim... [The text ends here.]

Regarding "obstruction" and so forth: it means that by means of a single moment of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*), one universally contemplates the three periods of time such that nothing is not clearly manifest.
Thus, the absence of past, future, and present constitutes "unimpeded mindfulness. Not being separated from this distinct mindfulness constitutes "pure mindfulness.

Because one recollects the Buddha’s merits, which are beneficial to compassion and wisdom, it is called "adornment. Now, regarding the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) visited by Sudhana, the first is Guṇākara...

Yun was immediately shown the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*). Thus, all the Dharma-gates bestowed by the spiritual mentors he encountered were expedient means for entering the realm of the Buddha.
Upon the completion of the causes of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), that which is entered—Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*)—is the mother who gives birth to the Buddha.
Although it is clearly realized that the Buddha is accomplished through oneself, there still remains the aspect of giving birth, which is not devoid of coming and going.
[This] is the mark. However, if one harbors views of appearing and disappearing, coming and going, then mindfulness will not be pure.
Now, the Lord has clearly perceived Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in more than Ganges-sand kalpas; I have made offerings to and served them all.
As for the Dharma-gates I received and all that was performed throughout the entire Dharma-realm, I have followed them all in mindfulness, recollecting them with clarity before me.
Maintain this and practice it in accordance with it. In this way, the Buddha-body is eternally abiding and never extinguished;
time has no past or present, nor coming or going; it is distinct and clear, manifest before one without obscuration. This is the true Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is the unimpeded mindfulness, the pure adornment, and liberation. This is the ultimate fulfillment of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. Thus, this goodness...
The Dharma-gate of Friendship should be understood as the initial aspiration for equal enlightenment; it is the sublime practice for attaining Buddhahood.
The twenty-two lines of scripture describing the recollection of many Buddhas over many kalpas already demonstrate the functional efficacy of this Dharma-gate.
Yet, [the Buddha] speaks with humility, deferring to the superior, saying: "I know only this liberation of pure understanding through unimpeded mindfulness. As it says:
All Bodhisattvas emerge from the night of birth-and-death with brilliant and penetrating clarity; forever free from the darkness of delusion, they never fall into昏沉 (torpor) or sleep.
Even unto the pure awakening and realization of the nature of all phenomena—this demonstrates the ground of great awakening, pure and radiant, which is free from conceptual thought.
How could I possibly know this? Then, pointing to a companion behind him, he said: "In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a youth."
His teacher’s name is Samantabhadra. You should go and inquire of him; he will explain it for you.

At that time, because of hearing the Dharma, the inconceivable roots of goodness of the youth Sudhana naturally increased and expanded. He prostrated himself, gazed up at his teacher with reverence, took his leave, and departed.

Descending from the celestial palace, he gradually approached that city. Upon reaching Samantabhadra, he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.

He addressed him, saying: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I...
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
Viśvāmitra replied, "Son of good family, there is a youth here named Śilpabhijña who studies the bodhisattva’s knowledge of scripts. You should question him; he will explain it to you."
At that time, Sudhana went to where he was, prostrated himself with his head at his feet in reverent salutation, and stood to one side.

He said, "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray..."

"Tell me," [he said]. Then that youth addressed Sudhana, saying: "Noble son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Skillful Knowledge of All Arts. I constantly chant and maintain these syllables."
Third, Sudhana heard the teachings of the Great Teacher, further increasing his roots of goodness. He gradually made his way toward the city of Kapilavastu and arrived at the abode of Samantabhadra.
Upon seeing him, he paid his respects and inquired after his well-being, recounting his own initial resolve and requesting instruction on how to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
Samantabhadra replied, "There is a youth here named Śilpabhijña who studies the bodhisattva’s knowledge of scripts; you should go to him."
Question: Regarding the statement that Samantabhadra (Pien-yu) serves as the teacher for the youth, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The principle-vehicle (zong-tong) is for one's own cultivation;

the teaching-vehicle (shuo-tong) is for instructing the ignorant. Thus, this virtuous friend acts as the teacher for the youth to signify that all dharmas prior to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) have not yet transcended the characteristics of speech, words, and letters. As for why Samantabhadra does not speak, it signifies the path of language [is exhausted].
This is because it severs [the notion of] speech by means of the teaching of original non-existence. Yet, while he himself does not speak, he points to the teachings of the various arts (*śilpa*).
This intention indicates that although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness.
Therefore, the forty-two characters taught by the various arts below all enter the gate of *prajñāpāramitā*, clearly manifesting the realization of words.

It is said that all [these] are unattainable. The intention is that one enters the ocean of fruition only by departing from words. Although the ocean of fruition is beyond words, it is precisely because of words that one must enter it.
This meaning has not been elucidated in the commentary; it merely states that Vyāsa did not explain it.
Briefly, there are four meanings: first, because it is identical to the *dharmaparyāya* of various arts; second, because the Dharma has been entrusted [to others] to manifest its circulation;
third, because it signifies that the essence of all *dharmaparyāyas* is non-dual; and fourth, because it signifies that only through non-attainment is there true attainment.

Although these are the correct meanings, they correspond to the literal words of the master; since the meaning should contain [these implications], the commentary refers to them as "various" (*zhòng*).
The arts are the skillful means of illusory wisdom and the good spiritual friends of the alphabet. At that time, the boy said to Sudhana:
"I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Skillfully Knowing All Arts. To say one knows all arts does not refer merely to the alphabet;
it refers to all worldly speech, livelihoods, occupations, and so forth, which accord with the True Dharma and do not contradict the true nature of reality."
This is contradictory. This [passage] is the actual bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*. Below, it reveals its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), stating:
"I constantly chant and maintain these syllables (*akṣara*). For syllables are the most excellent of all arts, being the foundation of writing and speech.
However, the reason why all forty-two letters are said to "enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā" is that one enters the signless (*animitta*) through these letters.
The term "gate" (*mukha*) refers to the meaning of a door, because language is able to manifest meaning.

Therefore, throughout the *Vairocana Sūtra*, it is stated that the wisdom of non-apprehension—that which has nothing to be attained—is itself Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrī Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"By receiving and upholding this dhāraṇī, one enters into the equality of all phenomena and swiftly attains the accomplishment of Mahāprajñā."

If one recites it even once, it is as if one were upholding the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma. Below, the commentary is cited in full with its explanations for the sake of thorough study and reference.
When pronouncing the syllable *A*, one enters a gate of *prajñāpāramitā* called "Entering the Undifferentiated Realm through the Power of the Bodhisattva.
This single syllable *A* signifies non-arising (*anutpāda*). Since the principle of non-arising encompasses all phenomena, it is said:
There is no differentiation. Yet, when a bodhisattva attains this non-arising, they are able to penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena and sever all hindrances;
therefore, it is called "sovereign power.
When pronouncing the syllable *ta*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named the "Gate of Boundless Differentiation."
Regarding the second, the multi-syllable [mantra]: in that five-syllable *sūtra*, the syllable *ra* signifies purity, stainlessness, and freedom from defilement.
Now, as for the term "many" (*ta*), the *Vairocana Sūtra* commentary explains that "many" means liberation through suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Vajraśekhara* states: "Because suchness is unattainable. This means that suchness is precisely the boundless differentiation; since suchness is unattainable, it is "many" (*ra-ta*).
These two characters have similar forms and their pronunciations are easily confused; therefore, I shall now follow the majority interpretation.
When pronouncing the syllable *pa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm."
Regarding the three syllables *ba*, the Five-Syllable Sūtra states: "There is also no ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); all phenomena are equal.
This means that the simultaneous disappearance of both the ultimate and the conventional is the true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). That the equality of all phenomena is itself universal illumination.
When pronouncing the syllable *Cha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Universal Wheel that Severs Differentiation.
Regarding the fourth syllable, *Cha*: it signifies that all phenomena lack any conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); since all formations are empty, it universally crushes differentiation.
When pronouncing the syllable *na*, one enters the gateway to the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Attaining the Unreliant and Unsurpassed.

Regarding the fifth, the syllable *na*: it signifies that all phenomena (*dharmas*) lack intrinsic nature or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and that neither speech nor written words can be apprehended therein.

This means that because both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) have vanished, there is nothing upon which to rely. The simultaneous vanishing of subject and object is called "unsurpassed.
These five characters above are precisely the five-character heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī. To conclude by returning to the contemplation of the mind, it says: "You should know this essential point:
you must contemplate that this mind is originally pure, without defilement and without attachment, free from the marks of conceptual discrimination regarding 'self' and 'what belongs to self.'"
When pronouncing the syllable *la*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Stainless Non-Reliance.
Regarding the sixth syllable, *la*: because one realizes that all phenomena are detached from the world, the causal conditions of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*) never manifest.
Because one is detached from the world, there is no reliance; because craving does not manifest, there is no stain.
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍha* (pronounced lightly), one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Expedient Means of Non-retrogression.

As for the seventh syllable, *ḍha*, it is the expedient means of non-retrogression because one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are tamed and quiescent, being equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and devoid of discrimination.
When pronouncing the syllable *va*, one enters the gateway to the *prajñāpāramitā* named "Vajra-field.
Regarding the eighth syllable, *va*: because one realizes that all phenomena are free from bondage and liberation, one only then enters the vajra.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Wheel.

As for the nine *ṭa* syllables, they signify the realization that all phenomena are free from feverish distress, hypocrisy, and impurity; because one attains cool serenity, this carries the meaning of universal destruction.
When pronouncing the syllable *sa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Oceanic Treasury.
As for the ten instances of the syllable *sa*, it is because one realizes that all phenomena are without obstruction, just as the ocean contains all reflections.
When pronouncing the syllable *va*, one enters the gateway to the *prajñāpāramitā* named "Universal Arising and Abiding.
Regarding the eleventh syllable, *va*: because one realizes that all phenomena are beyond the path of verbal expression, one is thus able to abide everywhere.
When pronouncing the syllable *Ṭha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Perfect Radiance.
As for the twelve *Ṭha* syllables, they signify that all phenomena are truly immovable; being immovable, they radiate perfect light.
When pronouncing the syllable YA, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Accumulation of Differentiations.
Regarding the thirteenth syllable YA: because one realizes that all phenomena are truly non-arisen, the various accumulations of different vehicles are all found to be unobtainable.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṣṭa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Radiance Pacifying Afflictions.
Regarding the fourteenth syllable, *ṣṭa*: one realizes that the characteristics of all dharmas—subjugation and maintenance—are unobtainable.
Universal radiance is that which is able to subjugate; afflictions are that which are to be subjugated. "Pacifying" has the meaning of subjugation.
When pronouncing the syllable KA, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Cloud of Non-differentiation.
Regarding the fifteenth, the syllable KA: one awakens to the fact that an agent for all phenomena cannot be found; thus, the performance of action is like a cloud.
They are all without distinction.

Regarding the sixteen *sa* syllables: one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are immediately equal, for their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.

That is to say, the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) constitutes the long-flowing stream of birth and death; it rushes and surges with violent force.
The conceit of "I" is loftily elevated, like a multitude of peaks standing side by side, for all are attachments to what is "mine."
When pronouncing the syllable *ga*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Establishment.

Regarding the eighteen *ga*-syllables: they signify that the nature of the practice of grasping at all phenomena is unattainable. As for the term "establishment," it means that through the very act of practicing and grasping, one is able to establish [the state of non-grasping].
When pronouncing the syllable *tha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Treasury of the Equality of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
As for the nineteenth syllable, *tha*: it is the realization that the locus and nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) are unattainable;
for true suchness, being equal, is the locus upon which all phenomena depend.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṣa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Entering the Purification of the Ocean of the World.
Regarding this twenty-second syllable *ṣa*: it is the realization that the arising of all phenomena—both the subject that produces and the object produced—is unattainable;
for it is because there exists a producer and a produced that there is an "ocean of the world."
When pronouncing the syllable *kṣa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Mindfulness of the Adornments of All Buddhas.
The twenty-first syllable, *kṣa*, is the realization that the nature of peace and security is unattainable, because the adornment of mindfulness of the Buddha is the most secure of all.
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing and Discerning the Multitude of All Dharmas.
Regarding the twenty-second syllable, *ḍa*—in an alternative translation it is rendered as *dha*—one realizes that the nature of the realm (*dhātu*) which sustains all dharmas is unattainable;
for by discerning the multitude of dharmas, one perceives that they are precisely what sustains the nature of the realm.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṣa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Radiance that Follows the Wheel of All Buddha Teachings.
Regarding the twenty-third syllable, *ṣa*: it is the realization that the quiescent nature of all phenomena is ungraspable; by means of this quiescence...
Because it specifically accords with the Buddha’s teaching,
when pronouncing the syllable *kha*, one enters the gateway to the *prajñāpāramitā* called the "Treasury of Wisdom Cultivated on the Ground.
The twenty-fourth syllable, *kha*, is the realization that all phenomena are like the nature of space and are ungraspable.
Wisdom is like space; therefore, it is able to contain and store all things.
When pronouncing the syllable *kṣa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Treasury that Quells the Ocean of All Karmas.
Regarding the twenty-fifth syllable, *kṣa*: it is the realization that the nature of all dharmas is ultimately ungraspable; this refers to the ocean of karma.
Profound and vast, there is nothing it does not encompass; therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (garbha).
When pronouncing the syllable *sa-ta*, one enters the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā named "Eliminating All Obscurations of Delusion and Opening Pure Radiance."
Twenty-sixth, regarding the syllable *ṣa*: it is the realization that all phenomena are the locus of support and non-support, such that a nature of immovability cannot be found.
Taking delusive obstructions as non-locus and opening up pure radiance as its locus—this takes the true emptiness free from obstructions as the locus of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
When pronouncing the syllable *raṅ*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Gate of Worldly Wisdom.
Regarding the twenty-seventh syllable, *raṅ*: in another translation it is rendered as *nyang*; this means that one awakens to all phenomena and realizes that their nature cannot be apprehended.
That which knows is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that which is known is the gate.
When pronouncing the syllable *hralda*, one enters the gateway to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) called the "Wisdom Wheel of the Realm of Birth and Death.
Regarding the twenty-eighth syllable, *hralda*: it is the realization that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is such that their meaning cannot be grasped through attachment.
It is attained; that is to say, attachment is taken as the object of birth and death. This meaning is the wheel of wisdom (*jñānacakra*).

Because attachment to birth and death is the object observed by wisdom, when pronouncing the syllable *va*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Perfectly Adorned Palace of All-Knowledge."
