Regarding the twenty-ninth syllable, *ba*: it refers to the realization that the nature of all phenomena as being destructible is unattainable.
It is a term for "perfection. Amoghavajra translated it as "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This means that the adornment of the palace-site of enlightenment arises from conditions.
It is destructible; because it is not an adornment, it cannot be apprehended.
When pronouncing the syllable *cha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of the Perfection of Expedient Means through Individual Practice."

Regarding the thirty syllables beginning with "Cha" (車), they are translated separately as "Sra" (縒). This means that one realizes that the nature of being obscured by desire and pleasure (*kāmarati*) regarding all phenomena is unattainable.
Since one has already attained skillful means and rejoices in [the truth], each [perfection] is individually fulfilled; thus, the nature of being obscured is unattainable.
When pronouncing the syllable *sama*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Manifestly Beholding All Buddhas Throughout the Ten Directions.
Regarding the thirty-first syllable, *sama*: it is the realization that the nature of all phenomena as objects of recollection is unattainable.

When pronouncing the syllable HA-VA, one enters a door of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing All Conditionless Sentient Beings," by which means one gathers them through skillful means and causes the birth of unimpeded power.
The thirty-second syllable is *ha-va*. In another translation, it is rendered as *ha-va*. This signifies that the nature of all phenomena as being summonable is unattainable;
that is to say, because there is no conditionless summoning that could cause something to become conditioned.
When pronouncing the syllable *sra*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Cultivating Entry into the Ocean of All Meritorious Qualities.
Regarding the thirty-third syllable, *sra*: it is the realization that the courageous and vigorous nature of all phenomena is unattainable; by means of this courage...
One who is capable and vigorous can cultivate and enter these merits.
When pronouncing the syllable GA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Firm Oceanic Treasury of Clouds of All Dharmas."
Regarding the thirty-fourth syllable, *ga*: it is the realization that the substantiality (*sthūla*) of all phenomena is unapprehendable.

This means that just as the earth is substantial and can support equally, and can likewise contain and store like the ocean's equality—supporting and encompassing—the clouds and rain of the Dharma are preached because they are unapprehendable; thus, they are able to support and contain.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Beholding All Buddhas of the Ten Directions According to One’s Vows.
Regarding the thirty-fifth syllable, *ṭha*, it is translated separately as *cha*. This signifies realizing that the nature of the accumulation of all phenomena is unattainable;
that is, by accumulating the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, one is able to behold them universally.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṇa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Contemplating the Wheel of Syllables. Therein are inexhaustible billions of syllables.
As for the thirty-six *ṇa* syllables, one thereby awakens to the fact that all phenomena are free from all clamor and contention, having neither going nor coming.

The nature of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining cannot be apprehended; this is because one constantly contemplates the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), that is, because of the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*).
When pronouncing the syllable *spha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā, which is the ultimate state of transforming sentient beings.

Regarding the thirty-seventh syllable, *sapha*: alternative translations render it simply as *pha*. It signifies that one awakens to the fact that the pervasive fruit of retribution for all phenomena is unattainable.
That is to say, only when the ultimate transformation of sentient beings is achieved does it constitute a pervasive fruit of retribution.
Only when both cause and effect are empty is there true fulfillment.
When pronouncing the syllable *saka*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Radiant Wheel of Unimpeded Eloquence that Universally Illuminates the Vast Treasury.
Regarding the thirty-eighth syllable, *saka*:
in another translation it is rendered as *saka*; it signifies awakening to the accumulation of all phenomena within the aggregates (*skandha*).
The nature is unattainable; that is to say, it is an accumulated vast treasury, the accumulation of the wheel of unimpeded light.
When pronouncing the syllable *ca*, one enters the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* named "Proclaiming the Realm of All Buddha-Dharmas."
The thirty-ninth is the letter *sa*. This means that one realizes that the nature and characteristics of senescence in all phenomena are unobtainable;
that is to say, the nature of senescence is itself the realm of the Buddha-dharma.
When pronouncing the syllable *Śva*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Universal Roar of the Dharma-Thunder throughout All Realms of Sentient Beings.
As for the forty syllables beginning with *Śva* (alternatively translated as *Śva-tsa*), they signify the realization that all phenomena are the fulfillment of the accumulation [of merit and wisdom].
No trace can be found. This means that the gathering [of the assembly] is all sentient beings. The Dharma-thunder is the footprint; the foot is that which is able to walk.
Because of walking there is a trace, and the trace is that which is walked upon. The pervasive roaring of the Dharma-thunder is precisely the practice of the Dharma.
When pronouncing the syllable *tha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Awakening Sentient Beings by Means of the Dharma of Non-Self.
Regarding the forty-first syllable, *tha*: it is the realization that the nature of all phenomena is characterized by urgency and cannot be apprehended;
that is, awakening them through non-self is precisely what urges them forward to reach the other shore. If this is categorized according to the stages of manifestation, it corresponds to...
Desiring to fulfill the Dharma-body of Equal Enlightenment and to bring the beginning and the fundamental into alignment, one transcends the two shores.
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Treasury of the Differentiation of All Dharma-Wheels."
Regarding the forty-second letter, *ḍa*: it signifies that the ultimate limit of all phenomena (*dharma*) is unattainable. As for the term "Differential Treasury" (*viśeṣagarbha*):
it means that this ultimate limit contains and preserves all wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), and is also the point of final consummation for all wheels of Dharma.
In terms of its corresponding stage, it corresponds to the level of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); it is the ultimate boundary of all phenomena.
Exhausting all locations, it is because there is nothing to be attained, and thus one attains bodhi. The above constitutes the meaning of the commentary (*śū*).
The supplementary explanation states: Regarding the aforementioned syllables, they all speak of entering the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Yet, the reason the spiritual friend at the stage of *samyaksambodhi* (Equal Enlightenment) teaches this dharma-gate of syllables is that his intention lies in departing from the marks of words and departing from the conditions of the mind.
Regarding signs: only by departing from all signs can one enter the wondrous and realize the source of the single Dharma-realm mind.
How is this clarified? It is said that the alphabet is the root of speech and writing.
In our Sahā world, the essence of the teaching consists of the sounds of speech and words—not only in the Buddha-dharma, but even in all worldly matters.
All supramundane dharmas that are expressed through exposition consist of speech and written characters.

Yet these characters flow forth from the one true dharma-realm; therefore, the various languages of all phenomena within the ten dharma-realms—whether mundane or sagely—do not transcend these forty-two characters as their mother.
This is precisely what is expounded in the inexhaustible teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Dharma-realm—the forty-two stages of the teaching on the interpenetration of sequential progression and perfect fusion of cause and effect—is entirely expressed through words, sounds, and vocalization.
Therefore, the forty-two characters comprehensively encompass the dharma-gates of the forty-two stages.
However, the ocean of fruition transcends language; it must be realized by departing from language. Thus, when Sudhana has completed his pilgrimage up to the stage of cause...
Ultimately, it is necessary to transcend words and realize [the truth] instantaneously. Therefore, each of these forty-two characters is described as "entering the gate of Prajñāpāramitā.
Yet, this ultimate Prajñā is the fundamental fruit-wisdom of the Buddha.
The Commentary cites two sutras to explain this "entry into Prajñā," both of which define it through "unobtainability" (*anupalabdhi*). For it is through unobtainability that one truly attains it.
Bodhi. This is the ultimate point of convergence for entering the Dharma-realm. By chanting these syllables, one enters the gateway of Prajñā;
it is not that the letters themselves are Prajñā. The profound meaning of the double mystery of the Dharma-realm reaches its pinnacle here.
Those who aspire to the Great Dharma-gate should contemplate this deeply.
"Good son, when I chant these syllables, with these forty-two gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā* as the foremost, I enter immeasurable and innumerable gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Good son, I know only this liberation of the Bodhisattva Skillful in All Arts (*sarva-śilpa-jña*). As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who are able, regarding all worlds..."
He was skilled in the supramundane Dharma and, through wisdom, reached the further shore. He comprehended all diverse methods and arts without exception.
He possessed profound understanding of writing and mathematics. He was adept at medical prescriptions and incantations for effectively curing various ailments.

There were sentient beings possessed by ghosts and demons, those afflicted by the curses of enemies and hatred, those affected by the portents of malevolent stars, those pursued by wandering corpses, and those who were deranged.
He is able to cure all manner of ailments, such as epilepsy and emaciation, restoring them to full health.

Furthermore, he is skilled in discerning gold, silver, pearls, shells, coral, lapis lazuli, *maṇi* gems, *śaṅkha* conch, *kīcaka* stone, and all other types of treasures—including their origins, their various classifications, and their respective values.
He also knows the villages, camps, towns, small and large cities, and palaces.

Palaces, gardens, groves, rocky crags, springs, marshes, and wetlands—in short, all places where people dwell—the Bodhisattva is able to protect and sustain them according to their respective locations.

Furthermore, he skillfully observes celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, human physiognomy and its auspicious or inauspicious signs, the cries of birds and beasts, clouds, mists, and seasonal climates, the abundance or scarcity of crops, and the security or peril of kingdoms. Regarding all such worldly arts and crafts, there is none that he does not [master].

They are able to exhaustively investigate and refine the very source and foundation [of all things], and they can further discern the supramundane dharmas, defining their names correctly and clarifying their meanings.

They observe their essential natures and characteristics and practice in accordance with them. Their wisdom enters therein, free from doubt and obstruction, devoid of ignorance and dullness, without sorrow or affliction, without sinking, and without anything that is not directly realized. How could I possibly know or speak of them?
"O son of good family, in this kingdom of Magadha there is a village.
Within it is a city named Pāṭalī, where there dwells an upāsikā named Bhadrottamā. Go to her and ask:
'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? Then, the youth Sudhana bowed his head in respectful salutation at the feet of Vidvān.
He circumambulated him countless times, and with longing and reverence, took his leave.

As Mañjuśrī recited these syllables for Sudhana, he declared that these forty-two letters, beginning with the gateway of the *pāramitās*, lead into immeasurable and innumerable gateways of the *pāramitās*; that is to say, they symbolize the forty [virtues].
"O two honorable ones! O all you who are perfectly interfused! From the initial letter 'A' to the subsequent letters, each represents a dharma-gate.
Since dharma-gates are infinite, the letters are likewise infinite. Because not a single one can be apprehended, the gate of Prajñā is also immeasurable and innumerable.
Herein the dharma-gates are brought to their consummation and realization; thus, with humility, he declares: 'I know only this goodness.'"
He knows only the liberation that consists in mastery of all arts.

Just as the various bodhisattvas, through their wisdom and supernormal powers, reach the further shore regarding all worldly skillful methods—down to the various regional and exotic crafts and all worldly technical skills, mastering them without exception and exhausting their very sources—and regarding supramundane dharmas, correctly defining their names and analyzing their meanings. Without...
"How could I possibly know that which has not been directly realized?
He then pointed toward a companion and said, "In this kingdom of Magadha there is a village and a city named Pāṭaliputra. There dwells a female lay disciple (upāsikā) named Bhadrā.
You should go and inquire of her; she will explain it to you. Then, filled with longing and reverence, the youth Sudhana took his leave and departed.
He proceeded toward the city and approached the Venerable Bhadrapāla; having prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and joined his palms in reverence, he stood to one side and said:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able [to explain this]."
"Please instruct me; I pray that you will speak for my sake. Worthy and Victorious replied, "Son of good family, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called the 'Dharma-Seat of Non-Reliance.
Having realized it myself, I further explain it to others. Furthermore, I have attained the inexhaustible samādhi.
It is not that the dharmas of that samādhi are either exhaustible or inexhaustible; rather, it is because the eye of the nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) that it produces is inexhaustible."
Furthermore, it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge because the ear is inexhaustible;
it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge because the nose is inexhaustible; it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge because the tongue is inexhaustible;
it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge because the body is inexhaustible; and it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge because the mind is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, because they can give rise to the inexhaustible waves of merit of the nature of omniscience;

furthermore, because they can give rise to the inexhaustible light of wisdom of the nature of omniscience; furthermore, because they can give rise to the inexhaustible swift supernormal powers of the nature of omniscience.
Good son, I know only this liberation of the place of enlightenment that is without dependence. As...
"How could I possibly know or fully describe all the unattached meritorious practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Good son, to the south there is a city named Kṣetravatī. There dwells an elder named Dṛḍhavimukti.
You should go and ask him how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path. At that time, Śubha...
Sudhana, having paid his respects with offerings, circumambulated her countless times. With deep longing and veneration, he took his leave and traveled south.
Fourth, Sudhana received the instruction on the various arts from the laywoman Bhadrottamā, who was the spiritual friend of Illusionary Wisdom Without Dependence.
Upon arriving, he paid his respects and, having declared his initial resolve for enlightenment, inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. At that time, Bhadrottamā replied:
He said: "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called the 'Dharma-Field of the Non-Abiding Site. Having realized it myself, I shall now explain it to others.

This is the direct transmission of the Dharma-realm, clarifying that first one attains liberation and subsequently attains samādhi; this is what is called the 'Exhaustible and Inexhaustible Nature of Dharmas.
As for the term 'Dharma-Field of the Non-Abiding Site,' it means that there is no dependence on either the internal or the external; this is the Way."
Regarding the term "maṇḍala": Xianshou says that in Sanskrit it is *anālaya-maṇḍala*. *Anā* means "non-" in this language; *ālaya* means "place of reliance";
and *maṇḍala* means "site of practice" (*daochang*), which is a circular field.

This signifies that while the defiled portion of the *ālayavijñāna* as a place of reliance is absent, the pure portion exists as a circular field from which inexhaustible sublime virtues are produced. That is to say:
The ultimate transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) reveals inexhaustible virtues; therefore, it is next called the "samādhi of the exhaustible and the inexhaustible.

This means that the One True Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) simultaneously transcends both defilement and purity, and is thus said to be "exhaustible" [in its dualistic appearance]. It is the empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Based upon this, inexhaustible merits are produced, which is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. Essentially, when the mind has no dependence, it accords with the fundamental source.
Only when [the mind] is empty does one see that which is not empty, endowed with the qualities of its intrinsic nature; hence it is said that "the nature of wisdom is produced.

Thus, the six functions of the eyes and so forth cease their delusions and manifest the great function of wisdom; hence it is said that "the light of wisdom, supernatural powers, and inexhaustibility are produced.
This is the ultimate realization of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); hence it is said that "one attains inexhaustible samādhi. This constitutes the bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*.
He then humbly deferred, saying, "I know only this liberation of the field of practice that is without support.
As for the merits of the conduct of non-attachment belonging to all the bodhisattvas, how could I possibly know them?
Pointing toward a companion behind him, he said, "To the south there is a city named Urubilvā. There dwells an elder named Sthirāvimokṣa; you should go and inquire of him."
"I shall speak for you. Then the youth Sudhana, filled with longing and gazing up at him in reverence, took his leave and traveled south.
Arriving at that city, he went to the householder’s residence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in respectful salutation.

He addressed him, saying, "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The elder replied, "Good son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation."
It is named "Pure Adornment of Unattached Mindfulness. Since I attained this liberation, I have diligently sought the True Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions without ceasing.
Good son, I know only this liberation of the Pure Adornment of Unattached Mindfulness;
as for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have attained fearlessness and the great lion’s roar, [I do not know their ways]. Resting...
Abiding in a vast accumulation of merit and wisdom, how could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
Son of good family, in this very city there is an elder named Moon of Excellence (*Candraprabha*). The residence of that elder is always filled with radiance;
go to him and ask: "How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path? At that time, the virtuous...
The youth Dravya paid homage at the feet of Dṛḍha, circumambulated him countless times, and departed.
Fifth was the elder Dṛḍha, who served as the spiritual friend of Māyājñāna-asaṅga. He resided in the southern region of India known as Ārdra-kṣetra;
because it is near water and richly irrigated, it manifests that the water of non-conceptual emptiness can nourish and grow all things. As for the elder’s name, "Dṛḍha," it signifies firmness.

It is unattached and pure; because it cannot be moved by afflictions, it is liberation. Upon seeing this, Sudhana paid his respects, declared his resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
The elder replied: "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'Unattached Recollection, Pure Adornment.
'Unattached' refers to the objective sphere, as it is free from the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*); 'recollection' refers to the mind."
Because its essence is free from conceptual thought, it is without afflictions; because the two obstacles are forever exhausted, it is called "pure. Being pure, it is able to adorn the Dharma-body.
Since I attained this liberation, I have diligently sought the True Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions without ceasing.
I know only this liberation, whereas the Bodhisattvas are able to roar the lion’s roar.
"I abide in a vast accumulation of merit; how could I possibly know this? Within this very city there is an elder named Candracchattra.
You should go and ask him; he will explain it to you. Sudhana paid his respects and, taking his leave, departed.
He approached Candra-sudatta, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and standing to one side with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well-able to provide instruction; I pray—"
"Tell me," [he said]. Candra-vimalā replied, "Noble son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Wisdom Radiance.

Noble son, I know only this liberation of the radiance of wisdom. As for the immeasurable gates of liberation realized by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"
"Good man, to the south of here there is a city named Utpala. There dwells an elder named Anābhibhūsenāpati.
Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Candracchattra, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and reverence."
The sixth is the Elder Subhacandra. He is the spiritual friend of Māyājñānajyotis. True wisdom that clears away delusion is called "Pure Wisdom" (Vimalajñāna);
subsequent wisdom that illuminates phenomena is called "Wisdom-Light" (Jñānajyotis). Being able both to purify and to illuminate, he is like a crescent moon in the autumn sky.
Therefore, he was named Wondrous Moon (*Candraprabha*). Upon seeing him, Sudhana recounted his own initial aspiration for enlightenment and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
Wondrous Moon replied, "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Light of Wisdom. I have only attained this liberation."
"As for the immeasurable liberations attained by the bodhisattvas, how could I possibly know them? To the south of here is a city named Utpala;
there dwells an elder named Anāthapiṇḍada. You should go and inquire of him. Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Candracchattra and, filled with longing and reverence, took his leave.
Gradually approaching that city, he arrived at the householder’s residence. He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.

He addressed him, saying: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is skilled..."
"You are able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me. The elder replied, "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'Inexhaustible Aspect.
Having realized this bodhisattva liberation, I see immeasurable Buddhas and obtain an inexhaustible treasury."

"Good son, I know only this liberation of inexhaustible marks. As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained infinite wisdom and unimpeded eloquence, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Good son, to the south of this city there is a village named Dharma. In that village there is a brahmin..."
“The brāhmaṇa named Most Tranquil—go to him and ask: how does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Anābhibhū-sena, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.
The seventh was the elder Anābhibhūsenāpati (Invincible Army), who was a spiritual friend characterized by inexhaustible illusory wisdom.

When Sudhana saw him, he recounted his own initial aspiration for enlightenment and respectfully inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. The elder replied, "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'Inexhaustible.
This is the correct teaching of the Dharma-gate; it is called a 'Dharma-gate' because the virtues accomplished therein are infinite."
I have realized this liberation; I see immeasurable Buddhas and attain the inexhaustible treasury. This explains the name through its function:
"attaining the inexhaustible treasury" refers to hearing all the sublime Dharma, wherein both the Buddhas and the Dharma are without end.
Having seen the Buddhas and attained the inexhaustibility of the Dharma, one is thus invincible. Being a gathering of manifold virtues, it is likened to an army, and it is also capable of—
Because it universally conquers all demonic armies, and because everything emerges from its essence, the city is named "Source of Birth" (Janma-bhūmi).
Having already demonstrated the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*) of this Dharma-gate, he then humbly defers, saying: "I know only this liberation.
As for the unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*) of the Bodhisattvas, how could I possibly speak of it? To the south of this city, there is a village; therein dwells a Brahmin..."
"The gatekeeper's name is Most Tranquil (Sāntamati). You should go and inquire of him; he will explain it to you.

With reverence, longing, and veneration, Sudhana took his leave and traveled south by stages until he reached that village and saw Most Tranquil. He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood with palms joined in respectful salutation.

Standing to one side, he addressed him, saying: "Noble One, I have previously resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The brāhmaṇa replied: "Good son, I..."
The liberation of a bodhisattva is called "the speech of sincere vows.
Because of this speech, bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have never regressed.

There is no present regression, nor will there be any future regression. Good son, because I abide in the power of truthful speech, whatever I intend to do is never not fulfilled. Good son, I know only this liberation of truthful speech.
As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, their conduct and abiding do not contradict their truthful speech; their words are invariably truthful and have never been false. There is none...
The arising of the causes for the measure of merit—how could I possibly know or speak of it?
Son of good family, to the south of here there is a city named Sumanāmukha. There dwells a youth named Śrīsaṃbhava and a maiden named Guṇavatī.
Go to them and ask: how does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva practice?
At that time, the youth Sudhana, out of reverence for the Dharma, prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.
[He then met] the eighth spiritual friend, the brahmin Most Tranquil, who was skilled in illusory wisdom and truthful speech; Sudhana beheld him.

"Most tranquil! You have already resolved to attain enlightenment; I shall consult you regarding the essentials of the Dharma. The Brahmin replied, "I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation called 'Speech of Sincere Vows.
This is the gateway to the Dharma that correctly reveals it. Now, as for what is termed 'speech of vows,' the first meaning is that there is no falsehood from beginning to end.
From the initial resolution of the mind, one establishes a solemn vow, ensuring that one's actions necessarily accord with one's words."
Because it does not deviate from previous words; secondly, because its subsequent practice is not in vain. Now, regarding the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in this stage:

they are one who, following the mind of the Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), alone realizes the liberation of truthful vow-words (*satya-praṇidhāna-vāk*). "Truthful" (*satya*) means being without falsehood.

This is because from the very first arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), there was a single momentary vow to reach Buddhahood; that one has certainly reached this point without fail means this vow is without falsehood. This is because...

Once the vow "I shall attain Buddhahood" has been uttered, one resolutely acts in accordance with these words until the attainment of Buddhahood, never retreating, never halting midway, and never considering a small achievement sufficient. This word is not false;
because the vow is not false, one passes through many kalpas until the ultimate goal is reached. Therefore, this stage alone is specifically designated as attaining this liberation.
Therefore, the four grave precepts—namely, refraining from false speech along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—are by no means trivial matters.
Because false and deceptive words are stilled, they are called "tranquil. This tranquility constitutes pure conduct; thus, they are entrusted to the *brāhmaṇa*.
To demonstrate their function, it is said: "By means of these words, [one attains] the past, present, and future," and so forth, up until one attains [liberation].
In unsurpassed bodhi, there is no turning back, because one abides in speech of sincere vows;
whatever is undertaken according to one's will is never not fulfilled—this is its great function. Yet, he modestly defers, saying: "I have only attained the liberation of speech of sincere vows.
Just as all Bodhisattvas ensure their words are necessarily sincere, thereby giving birth to immeasurable merit, how could I possibly [do so]?"
"Know this: to the south of here is a city named Supuṣpākara. There dwells a youth named Guṇākara and a maiden named Guṇavatī. You should go and inquire of them; they will explain it to you.

At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages toward the south until he reached the city of Supuṣpacandra-dvāra.
There he saw the youth Śrīsañcaya and the maiden Śrīmatī. He prostrated at their feet, circumambulated them to the right, and standing before them with palms joined, spoke these words:
"Noble ones, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know..."
"How should a bodhisattva study the bodhisattva conduct? How should they cultivate the bodhisattva path? We pray that you will compassionately explain this for us.
Then the boy and girl said to Sudhana, "Noble son, we have realized a bodhisattva liberation called 'Abiding as an Illusion.
Having attained this liberation, we see all worlds as abiding as an illusion. Because of this...
Because they are produced by conditions, all sentient beings abide as illusions. Because they arise from karma and afflictions, all worlds abide as illusions.
Because they are produced through the successive conditioning of ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth, all phenomena abide as illusions.
Because they are produced by various illusory conditions such as the view of self, all three periods of time abide as illusions. The view of self and so forth...

Because they are produced by inverted cognition, all sentient beings—along with their arising and ceasing, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—are like illusory abodes, produced by false conceptualization.

All lands are like illusory abodes, manifested by the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, the inversion of views, and ignorance. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are like illusory abodes, consisting of wisdom and abandonment.

Because they are accomplished through discernment; because all Bodhisattvas abide in illusion, being accomplished by the dharmas of vows and practices that enable them to self-subdue and transform sentient beings;
and because all the assemblies, transformations, subduings, and activities of all Bodhisattvas are accomplished by the illusion of the power of vows and wisdom.
Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of illusory phenomena cannot...
"Beyond thought, good son! We two can only know this liberation of dwelling in illusion (*māyā-vihāra-vimokṣa*).
As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have skillfully entered the illusory net of infinite phenomena—how could we possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
At that time, the boy and girl, having spoken of their own liberation, [proceeded] with inconceivable virtues...

It is named the *Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha*. It arises from the ripening of the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas;
it arises from the power of the mindfulness, vows, mastery, and supernormal knowledges of bodhisattvas; it arises from the skillful means of bodhisattvas;
it arises from the merit and wisdom of bodhisattvas. Good son, a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation, by means of great compassion...
The mind manifests such realms for the sake of all sentient beings and accumulates such adornments.
Within these, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya dwells, desiring to gather in and bring to maturity the parents, kinsmen, and people of his original birthplace.
Furthermore, he desires to cause those sentient beings who share the same birth and the same practice to [attain] greatness.

Because one attains firm stability within the vehicle; furthermore, because he desires that all those sentient beings may achieve accomplishment according to their respective stages and roots of goodness;
furthermore, because he desires to manifest for you the gate of liberation of the bodhisattvas;
to manifest the bodhisattvas' mastery in taking birth in all places; and to manifest the bodhisattvas universally appearing in various bodies in a single place.

Because they constantly teach and transform all sentient beings; because they demonstrate that Bodhisattvas, through the power of great compassion, universally gather all worldly resources without weariness;
because they demonstrate that Bodhisattvas fully cultivate all practices while knowing that all practices are free from signs;
and because they demonstrate that Bodhisattvas take birth in various places while realizing that all births are signless.
Therefore, go to him and ask: how does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva conduct? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? How does one study the bodhisattva precepts?

Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have mastered all bodhisattva practices, understand the minds of all sentient beings, and constantly manifest before them to teach, transform, and subdue them. That...

they can increase your bodhicitta; they can strengthen your resolve; they can augment your virtues;

Good son, you should not cultivate a single virtue, illuminate a single dharma, or practice a single course of action.
One should form a single vow, receive a single prediction, abide in a single patience, and conceive the thought of ultimate perfection.
One should not practice the six perfections with a limited mind, nor dwell merely on the ten stages, purifying buddha-fields, or serving spiritual friends. Why is this?
Son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should plant immeasurable roots of goodness and should accumulate immeasurable requisites for enlightenment.
One should cultivate immeasurable causes for enlightenment; one should study immeasurable skillful dedications;

one should transform immeasurable realms of sentient beings; one should know the immeasurable conduct of sentient beings; one should know the immeasurable faculties of sentient beings; one should recognize the immeasurable inclinations of sentient beings;
one should observe the immeasurable minds of sentient beings; one should discipline immeasurable sentient beings; and one should sever immeasurable [afflictions].
One should purify immeasurable karmic habituations; one should extinguish immeasurable false views; one should eliminate immeasurable defiled minds; one should generate immeasurable pure minds;
one should extract immeasurable poisonous arrows of suffering; one should dry up immeasurable oceans of craving and desire;
one should shatter immeasurable darknesses of ignorance; one should demolish immeasurable mountains of self-conceit; one should sever immeasurable...
Bound by birth and death, one should cross over the immeasurable currents of existence; one should exhaust the immeasurable ocean of rebirth;
one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to emerge from the mire of the five desires; one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to leave the prison of the three realms;
one should establish immeasurable sentient beings within the Noble Path; one should extinguish immeasurable courses of greedy desire; one should purify and cultivate...

One should destroy immeasurable courses of hatred; one should transcend immeasurable courses of delusion; one should leave behind immeasurable nets of Māra; one should abandon immeasurable deeds of Māra;
one should purify the immeasurable aspirations of a bodhisattva; one should increase the immeasurable skillful means of a bodhisattva;

One should fulfill the power of right mindfulness. One should bring forth the power of immeasurable samādhi. One should give rise to the power of immeasurable pure wisdom.
One should strengthen the power of immeasurable resolute conviction. One should accumulate the power of immeasurable merit. One should increase the power of immeasurable insight.
One should initiate the power of immeasurable bodhisattvas. One should perfect the power of immeasurable Tathāgatas. One should discern immeasurable dharmas.

Gate: One should understand immeasurable Dharma-gates; one should purify immeasurable Dharma-gates; one should give rise to the light of immeasurable Dharmas; one should perform the illumination of immeasurable Dharmas;
one should illuminate the faculties of immeasurable categories of beings; one should know the diseases of immeasurable afflictions;
one should collect the medicines of immeasurable sublime Dharmas; one should treat the illnesses of immeasurable sentient beings; and one should prepare [the remedies].

One should offer immeasurable ambrosial offerings; one should visit immeasurable buddha-fields; one should make offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas; one should enter immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas;
one should receive the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas; one should endure the offenses of immeasurable sentient beings;

One should gather immeasurable sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). One should cultivate immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī. One should give rise to immeasurable gateways of great vows.
One should cultivate immeasurable power of great compassion and great vows. One should diligently seek immeasurable teachings without ever resting.
One should give rise to immeasurable power of reflection; one should manifest immeasurable miraculous feats; one should purify immeasurable radiance of wisdom;
one should traverse the immeasurable realms of sentient beings; one should undergo immeasurable births within existence; one should manifest immeasurable diverse bodies;

One should dwell in the great palace of the Bodhisattvas; one should contemplate the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;

one should know the realm of the Bodhisattvas that is difficult to know; one should practice the various conducts of the Bodhisattvas that are difficult to perform; one should possess the honored majesty and virtue of the Bodhisattvas;
one should tread upon the correct station of the Bodhisattvas that is difficult to enter; one should know the various types of practices of the Bodhisattvas; and one should manifest...
A Bodhisattva’s universal spiritual power should receive the Bodhisattva’s equal cloud of Dharma; it should expand the Bodhisattva’s boundless web of practices;
it should fulfill the Bodhisattva’s boundless perfections; it should receive the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable predictions of enlightenment;
it should enter the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable gates of patience; it should cultivate the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable stages; and it should purify the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable...

This is the Dharma-gate. You should, together with all bodhisattvas, abide for boundless eons, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, adorning and purifying unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, and giving rise to unspeakable bodhisattva vows. Good son, to state it briefly:
One should universally cultivate all bodhisattva practices; one should universally transform all realms of sentient beings;
one should universally enter all kalpas; one should universally be born in all places; one should universally know all worlds; one should universally practice all dharmas;
one should universally purify all lands; one should universally fulfill all vows; one should universally make offerings to all Buddhas; one should universally accord with all...
This is the vow of a bodhisattva: one should universally serve all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Noble son, you should not grow weary in your quest for spiritual friends;
do not feel satisfied merely upon seeing them; and do not shrink from toil and hardship when questioning them.
Draw near to spiritual friends without harboring any thought of turning back. Make offerings to spiritual friends without ceasing.
Receive the instructions of spiritual friends without error. Study the conduct of spiritual friends without doubt.
When hearing spiritual friends expound the gateways to liberation, do not hesitate. Upon seeing spiritual friends engage in actions associated with the afflictions, do not give rise to aversion.
Strange! One should not allow the deep faith and respectful mind toward a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to change.

Why is this? Good son, it is because through a spiritual friend, a bodhisattva hears all the practices of bodhisattvas, accomplishes all the virtues of bodhisattvas, gives birth to all the great vows of bodhisattvas, brings forth all the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas, and accumulates [them].
They gather all the aids to the path of the bodhisattvas; they develop the light of all bodhisattva dharmas; they reveal all gates of renunciation for bodhisattvas;
they train in all the pure precepts of bodhisattvas; they abide securely in all the meritorious qualities of bodhisattvas;
they purify all the vast aspirations of bodhisattvas; they increase all the firm resolve of bodhisattvas; and they are endowed with...
He has perfected the gateways of dharani and eloquence of all bodhisattvas; he has attained the pure treasury of all bodhisattvas;
he has given rise to the light of samādhi of all bodhisattvas; he has obtained the supreme vows of all bodhisattvas; he shares the same vow as all bodhisattvas;
he has heard the supreme teachings of all bodhisattvas; he has attained the secret abodes of all bodhisattvas, reaching...
The island of jewels for all Bodhisattvas; that which increases the sprouts of all Bodhisattva roots of goodness; that which causes the body of wisdom of all Bodhisattvas to grow;
that which protects the profound and secret treasury of all Bodhisattvas; that which sustains the mass of merit of all Bodhisattvas;
that which purifies the path of rebirth for all Bodhisattvas; that which receives the clouds of the true Dharma of all Bodhisattvas; that which enters into all Bodhisattvas.
The path of great vows, which leads to the fruit of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas; which encompasses all the sublime practices of Bodhisattvas; which reveals all the merits of Bodhisattvas;
which travels to all directions to hear and receive the sublime Dharma; which praises the vast majesty and power of all Bodhisattvas;
which generates the power of great compassion of all Bodhisattvas; and which gathers the supreme self-mastery of all Bodhisattvas.
In power, they give rise to all the bodhi-factors of a bodhisattva and perform all the beneficial deeds of a bodhisattva.
Good son, it is by being sustained by a spiritual friend that a bodhisattva does not fall into the evil realms; by being embraced by a spiritual friend that he does not retreat from the Mahāyāna;
by being protected and remembered by a spiritual friend that he does not violate the bodhisattva precepts; and by being guarded by a spiritual friend...
One is protected from following after evil associates; one is nurtured by spiritual friends so as not to lack or diminish the qualities of a bodhisattva;
through being gathered by spiritual friends, one transcends the stage of ordinary worldlings; through the instruction of spiritual friends, one transcends the stages of the two vehicles;
through the guidance of spiritual friends, one attains liberation from the world; and through the cultivation provided by spiritual friends, one is able to...
They are stained by worldly dharmas. By serving spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they cultivate all bodhisattva practices;

by making offerings to spiritual friends, they become endowed with all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). By associating with spiritual friends, they are not overcome by karma or afflictions.
By relying on the power of spiritual friends, they are firm and do not fear any māras. By taking refuge in spiritual friends...
Consciousness increases all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Why is this?
Good son, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) can purify all hindrances, extinguish all sins, remove all calamities, and cease all evils.
They can shatter the long night of darkness of ignorance, destroy the solid prison of false views, enable one to leave the city of birth and death, and cause one to renounce the mundane world.
The House can sever the nets of all Māras; it can extract the arrows of manifold suffering; it can leave behind the perilous places of ignorance;
it can emerge from the great wilderness of false views; it can cross over the currents of existence; it can depart from all deviant paths; and it can reveal the path to Bodhi.
It can teach the Dharma of the bodhisattvas; it can cause them to dwell securely in the bodhisattva practices;
it can cause them to advance toward all-knowledge; it can purify the eye of wisdom; it can increase the bodhicitta; it can give rise to great compassion; it can expound sublime conduct;

it can explain the pāramitās; it can expel evil associates; it can cause them to abide in the various stages (bhūmis); it can cause them to attain the various patiences (kṣāntis); and it can cause them to cultivate...
It cultivates all roots of goodness; it enables the accomplishment of all requisites for enlightenment;
it bestows all great merits; it leads to the stage of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); it causes one to joyfully accumulate merit; it causes one to exultantly practice all spiritual disciplines;
it causes one to enter into the profound meaning; it causes one to reveal the gateway to liberation; it causes one to close off [the gates to the unwholesome].
It cuts off all evil realms. It can cause one to be illuminated by the light of the Dharma; it can cause one to be moistened by the rain of the Dharma;
it can cause the extinction of all delusions; it can cause one to abandon all views; it can cause the increase of all Buddha-wisdom;
and it can cause one to dwell securely in all gates of the Buddha-dharma. Good son, a virtuous friend is like a compassionate mother.
Because they give birth to the lineage of the Buddhas, they are like a compassionate father; because they provide vast benefit, they are like a wet nurse;
because they protect one from committing evil, they are like a teacher; because they show what is to be studied by Bodhisattvas, they are like a skilled guide;

because they can demonstrate the path of the *pāramitās*, they are like a good physician; and because they can cure the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are like the Snowy Mountains, increasing all things.
Because they provide wisdom, they are like brave generals; because they eliminate all fears, they are like guides for travelers;
because they cause one to emerge from the turbulent stream of birth and death, they are like ship captains; because they cause one to reach the jewel island of wisdom, they are like such.
Good son, you should always thus maintain right mindfulness and contemplate spiritual friends. Furthermore, good son, you should serve all spiritual friends.
O Consciousness, you should develop a mind like the great earth, for it bears heavy burdens without weariness.
You should develop a mind like a diamond, for its resolve is firm and indestructible. You should develop a mind like Mount Cakravāḍa, for no suffering can move it.
You should develop a mind like that of a servant, for you comply with all instructions. You should develop...
One should develop a mind like that of a disciple, because one does not oppose any instruction. One should develop a mind like that of a servant, because one does not tire of any task.
One should develop a mind like that of a foster mother, because one undergoes all hardships without complaining of weariness.

One should develop a mind like that of a hired laborer, because one does not oppose whatever instructions are received. One should develop a mind like that of a man clearing away dung, because one is free from arrogance.
One should develop a mind like ripened grain, because one is able to remain humble. One should develop a mind like a fine horse, because one is free from a wicked nature.
One should develop a mind like a great carriage, because it can carry heavy burdens. One should develop a mind like a well-trained...
One should develop a mind that follows an elephant, for it is always submissive and compliant. One should develop a mind like Mount Sumeru, for it is unshakable.
One should develop a mind like a good dog, for it does not harm its master. One should develop a mind like a caṇḍāla, for it is free from arrogance.
One should develop a mind like a castrated ox, for it is devoid of ferocity and anger. One should develop a mind like a boat, for it travels back and forth without weariness.

One should develop a mind like that of a bridge, because one ferries others across without weariness. One should develop a mind like that of a filial son, because one respectfully complies with their countenance.

One should develop a mind like that of a prince, because one obeys their instructions and commands. Furthermore, son of good family, you should conceive the thought of illness and suffering regarding yourself;
conceive the thought of a king of physicians regarding the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); and conceive the thought of [medicine] regarding the Dharma taught.

One should conceive the thought of a skilled physician regarding what is practiced; the thought of being cured of disease regarding that practice; furthermore, one should conceive the thought of a long journey regarding oneself;
the thought of a guide regarding the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); the thought of the right path regarding the Dharma taught;

and the thought of reaching the distant destination regarding what is practiced. Furthermore, one should conceive the thought of seeking deliverance regarding oneself; and the thought of a boatman regarding the spiritual friend.
One should conceive of the Dharma being taught as a boat; of the practice being cultivated as reaching the further shore.
Furthermore, one should conceive of oneself as a crop; of the spiritual friend as a dragon king; of the Dharma being taught as a timely rain;
and of the practice being cultivated as the ripening [of the harvest]. Moreover, one should conceive of oneself as being in poverty. Regarding...
One should conceive of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as King Vaiśravaṇa; of the Dharma taught as wealth and treasure;

and of the practice undertaken as abundance. Furthermore, one should conceive of oneself as a disciple, of the spiritual friend as a skilled craftsman, of the Dharma taught as a craft or skill, and of the practice undertaken as thorough knowledge. Moreover, one should...
One should conceive of oneself as being fearful; of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as being courageous and robust; of the Dharma taught as being weapons;
and of the practice undertaken as being the destruction of enemies. Furthermore, one should conceive of oneself as a merchant.
One should conceive of the spiritual friend as a guide; one should conceive of the Dharma taught as precious jewels;
and one should conceive of the practice undertaken as the gathering of these treasures.

Furthermore, one should conceive of oneself as a son, the spiritual friend as a parent, the Dharma taught as the family inheritance, and the practice undertaken as the succession to that inheritance. Moreover, one should...
One should conceive of oneself as a prince, regard the spiritual friend as a minister, regard the Dharma taught as the king’s decree,
and regard one's practice as donning the royal crown, wearing the royal robes, binding the royal turban, and sitting upon the royal throne. Son of good family,
you should give rise to such a mind and form such an intention to draw near to the spiritual friend.
Why is this? Because by approaching spiritual friends with such a mind, one causes their aspirations to attain eternal purity.
Furthermore, son of good family, spiritual friends cause all roots of goodness to grow, just as the Snowy Mountains cause all medicinal herbs to grow.
A spiritual friend is a vessel for the Buddha-dharma, just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams.
A spiritual friend is the locus of merit, just as the great ocean gives birth to all manner of jewels. A spiritual friend purifies the bodhicitta.
Just as a fierce fire can refine true gold, a spiritual friend transcends worldly phenomena.
Like Mount Sumeru rising out of the great ocean, a spiritual friend is unstained by worldly phenomena, just as a lotus flower is not adhered to by water.
A virtuous friend does not tolerate any evil, just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse.
A virtuous friend increases pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), just as the moon’s radiance becomes full during the bright fortnight. A virtuous friend illuminates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
For example, just as the blazing sun illuminates the four worlds, so does the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) cause the body of a bodhisattva to grow.
Just as parents nourish and raise their children, O son of good family, to speak of it in brief:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can follow the instructions of a spiritual friend, they will attain ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of merits and purify ten [perfections].
One may speak of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of profound intentions; one lengthens hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable roots of the bodhisattvas;
one purifies hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable powers of the bodhisattvas;
one severs ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeyas of hindrances; and one transcends ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeyas.
The realm of Māra. Entering ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* Dharma-gates;
fulfilling ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* aids to the Path; cultivating ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* sublime practices;
and generating ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* great vows. Good son, I shall further explain this briefly.
It explains all bodhisattva practices; all bodhisattva perfections; all bodhisattva stages; all bodhisattva patiences;
all bodhisattva dharani-gates; all bodhisattva samadhi-gates; all bodhisattva supernormal powers and wisdom;
all bodhisattva dedications; all bodhisattva vows; and the accomplishment of all bodhisattvas.
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, it all arises through the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Spiritual friends constitute its root;
one is born from spiritual friends, emerges from spiritual friends, grows by means of spiritual friends, and abides by means of spiritual friends.
Spiritual friends act as the causes and conditions; spiritual friends are able to initiate [the path]. At that time, the youth Sudhana heard that spiritual friends were thus...
Meritorious Virtue was able to reveal the wondrous practices of immeasurable bodhisattvas and was able to accomplish immeasurable, vast Buddha-dharmas.
Leaping for joy, she prostrated at the feet of Śrīgarbha and Guṇākara, circumambulated them countless times, and gazed up at them with earnest devotion.
He took his leave and departed.
Ninth, the virtuous Devasena was led by the illusory friend Bhadrarūpā to the gate called *Sumanāmanojñā*.
*Sumanā* refers to the *sumanā* flower; it grows beside the city gates and also represents the celestial *māndārava* flowers. It signifies...
Because he has received the friend’s instruction and attained the flower of the sublime cause of supreme wisdom, the youth symbolizes pure wisdom and the maiden symbolizes pure compassion;
through the mutual guidance of compassion and wisdom, the two meet together.

At the conclusion of this meeting of conditions, because compassion and wisdom are fulfilled, he is about to behold Maitreya and succeed to the Buddha’s position. At that time, the youth Sudhana proceeded in search according to the instructions.
Traveling south by stages, he arrived at the city of Sumanāmukha and beheld the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī.

Having recounted his own resolve, he respectfully inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. At that time, the youth and the maiden correctly bestowed upon him the Dharma-realm and addressed Sudhana, saying:
"We have realized the bodhisattva liberation called 'Abiding as an Illusion,' which means being able to know both the object and the wisdom."
Profound and pure phenomena all arise from conditions and lack a fixed nature; thus they abide like illusions. This clarifies the preliminary gateway of the Dharma:
that the objects and wisdom realized through cultivation both rely upon the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*. This is because what is produced by conditions is like an illusion.
Therefore, the subsequent section clarifies their functional activity, stating: "Because one attains this liberation, one perceives all worlds as illusions."

Abiding. Because it is produced by causes and conditions, there are ten kinds of illusions. The first clarifies that the world arises through conditions; both the defiled and the pure arise from conditions.

The subsequent nine specifically clarify that both ordinary beings and sages are illusory. The first five concern ordinary beings; they are the dependent nature of the defiled portion, which is like an illusion because it arises through conditions.
The sixth, "all lands," applies in meaning to both the defiled and the pure; these are what ordinary beings and sages rely upon. All...

Because they arise in accordance with conditions, the latter three [stages] rely on the pure levels (*śuddhabhūmi*). Since all noble beings of the Three Vehicles do so through the power of illusion, the conclusion states:

"The self-nature of illusory phenomena is inconceivable. This intends to reveal that all causes and effects—whether of the noble or the ordinary, defiled or pure—are the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, this corresponds to the initial Māyā, forming a single illusory *dharmadhātu* from beginning to end.
The net: the total and the particular are perfectly interfused, for they return to the one reality. This is the ultimate point of entering reality by means of conditions.
After the boy and girl had bestowed the Dharma-realm, they spoke with humility and deference, saying:
"We two can only know this liberation of illusory abiding; as for the Bodhisattvas who enter the illusory net of boundless phenomena, what can we say?"
How is this known? He pointed toward his companion behind him and said: "To the south of here is a land called Pāṭalī (Coastal), where there is a garden named Mahāvyūha (Great Adornment).

Within it stands a vast and lofty tower named Vairocanavyūhagarbha (Treasury of Vairocana’s Adornments), wherein resides the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya. Now, Maitreya is the master of Vijñaptimātra (Consciousness-Only)."
The consciousness-store is the Tathāgata-garbha; because it is adorned by the ten thousand practices and becomes the Dharma-realm store, this pavilion is named the "Vairocana Adornment Store.
Since the cause is exhausted and the fruit is fulfilled, one immediately enters the ocean of fruition;
therefore, it is entrusted to Maitreya, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood, and represented by this vast and great pavilion. Next, for the purpose of gathering and sustaining those below...
There are seven lines of further scripture clarifying the causes for dwelling in this pavilion. Subsequently, it instructs one to go and inquire, saying:
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path. It provides ten questions as a guide.

Next, from the phrase "For what reason" (*kena hetunā*) onwards, there are nine lines of scripture that investigate and explain the reasons for these extensive inquiries, thereby demonstrating the essential purpose of such broad questioning. That is to say:

Because the pursuit of virtue is vast, one must consult extensively before knowledge can be attained. Next, "you should not" [teach them]—this indicates that you should not instruct them with a limited mind;
this section consists of two and a half lines of scripture, which admonishes against a narrow-minded attitude and necessitates extensive inquiry.
Following this, "for what reason" and so forth interrogates and explains the necessity of extensive inquiry and extensive cultivation; this section comprises thirty-six and a half lines of scripture.
The ninety-eight sections all extensively clarify the practices of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below, severing delusions, and realizing the truth.

The commentary divides these into ten segments; next, following the essential words, four lines of scripture conclude the brief exposition to reveal its vastness, so that one may universally practice what is essential.

Therefore, he exhorts them to give rise to the vast and great mind (*mahācitta*). Next, from the passage "You should not grow weary in seeking a spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) downwards, there are one hundred lines of scripture, all of which provide instructions and exhortations regarding the service of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The first five lines admonish that one should diligently seek a virtuous friend. Following the question "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*), there are fifteen lines and thirty-five phrases of scripture which clarify [this point].

A virtuous friend can demonstrate correct practice. Next, from "due to the virtuous spiritual friend" downward, twenty-two lines of sūtra clarify that the virtuous friend can act as an external protector.

Next, from "the virtuous spiritual friend is like a compassionate mother" downward, five and a half lines of sūtra provide instruction and exhortation, meaning the method for serving such a friend. Next, "you should serve all virtuous spiritual friends; you ought to generate..."
As in the twelve lines and a half of the sūtra following "The Earth-like Mind," there are twenty-one phrases that teach the cultivation of the mind toward a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Next, following "Furthermore, you should [regard] yourself," there are seventeen lines of sūtra that teach the cultivation of the mind of remedial application (*pratipakṣa-citta*) by means of distinguishing between oneself and the spiritual friend.
The commentary divides these into ten phrases, each consisting of four matters. Next, "you should generate... [and so forth].
Following this, there are ten lines of sutra text that conclude and exhort regarding how a friend can bring about benefit.

Next, following the essential words, there are twelve lines of sutra text that provide a dual conclusion for both the gates of admonition and exhortation. Because it would be difficult to exhaust these through detailed explanation, they are concluded by summarizing the extensive into the concise;
all state "ten unspeakables," intending to reveal that the benefits of a virtuous friend are indeed inexhaustible. However...

Sudhana has already visited many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Arriving here, [the text] extensively praises the benefits of spiritual friends and deeply instructs the practitioner on the mind with which to serve them.
This is done by subsuming all the teachings received from previous spiritual friends within this [chapter], thereby perfecting the complete cause for entering the fruit.
It is intended that the practitioner may not forget or be deluded regarding these, and it serves to demonstrate that they all ultimately converge upon the spiritual friend.
It is for his benefit. Were it not so, why would his earnest admonitions, warnings, exhortations, and instructions be as fervent as these?

Having heard of the merits of the spiritual benefactors in this way, Sudhana gazed up at them with deep reverence, took his leave, and departed. Thus concludes the upper section on entering the true nature through conditions;
the following section concerns the causal characteristics formed by gathering virtues.
At that time, having heard the instructions of the spiritual friend, Sudhana’s heart was moistened with clarity.

He reflected with right mindfulness upon the practices of all bodhisattvas and set out for the country of Sāgaratīra. Recalling that in past lives he had not cultivated respectful salutation, he immediately resolved to practice with diligent effort.
Furthermore, recalling that in past lives his body and mind had been impure, he immediately resolved to cultivate himself exclusively in purity. Moreover—
Recalling the various evil karmas committed in past lives, he immediately resolved to vigilantly guard against and sever them.
Recalling the various deluded thoughts that arose in past lives, he immediately resolved to always maintain correct contemplation.

Recalling that the practices cultivated in past lives were solely for his own sake, he immediately resolved to expand his mind so that it universally reaches all sentient beings. Furthermore, recalling past lives...
The pursuit of sensual objects constantly causes self-destruction and yields no true flavor.

Thereupon, he resolves to practice the Buddha-dharma to nourish his faculties and achieve personal peace. He further recalls that in past lives he gave rise to perverse thoughts associated with inverted views.
Immediately, he resolved his mind, gave rise to a heart of right view, and made the vows of a bodhisattva.
He further recalled how, in past lives, he had labored day and night performing various evil deeds; immediately, he resolved his mind and aroused great diligence to accomplish the Buddha-dharma.

He further recalled how, in past lives, he had undergone births within the five destinies, which brought no benefit to himself or others; immediately, he resolved his mind, wishing that by means of it—
Benefiting sentient beings with one's own body to bring to fulfillment the Buddha-dharma and serving all spiritual friends—reflecting thus, one gives rise to great joy.
Furthermore, one contemplates that this body is a dwelling place for the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
yet, one vows to cultivate the Bodhisattva path through the end of future kalpas to transform sentient beings and behold the Tathāgatas as they achieve the Buddha-dharma.
They travel to all Buddha-fields, serve all Dharma teachers, uphold all Buddha teachings, seek out all Dharma companions, behold all spiritual friends, and gather all the qualities of the Buddhas.
They act as the causal conditions for the body of vows and wisdom of all Bodhisattvas. When they form such thoughts, their roots of goodness become inconceivable, immeasurable, and vast.
Roots. That is to say, one develops deep faith and respect for all bodhisattvas, conceiving of them as marvelous and as great teachers.

One’s faculties become purified and wholesome qualities increase. One offers respectful worship to all bodhisattvas, bows with palms joined to all bodhisattvas, and gives rise to the vision of all bodhisattvas that universally beholds the world. One brings forth [the aspiration] of all bodhisattvas...
Universally contemplate the perception of sentient beings. Manifest the transformation bodies of the infinite vows of all bodhisattvas.

Produce the pure sounds of praise and exposition of all bodhisattvas. Contemplate seeing all Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the past and present manifesting the supernatural transformations of attaining enlightenment in all places, such that there is not even a single hair-tip’s breadth where they do not pervade.
Furthermore, he attained the eye of the light of pure wisdom, whereby he beheld the spheres of activity of all Bodhisattvas.

His mind universally entered the net of lands throughout the ten directions, and his vows pervaded the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm, remaining equal across the three periods of time without ceasing.
All such things were brought about solely by his faithful acceptance of the instructions of the spiritual friend, O Sudhana.

With such reverence, such offerings, such praise, such contemplation, such power of aspiration, such mental attention, and such immeasurable sphere of wisdom, the youth prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the Great Pavilion of Vairocana’s Adorned Treasury.
For a moment, he withdrew his thoughts to contemplate and observe. By means of this—
By virtue of deep faith and understanding in the power of great vows, they enter the gate of the equality of the wisdom-body that pervades all places.
They universally manifest their bodies before all Tathāgatas, before all Bodhisattvas, and before all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Before the stupas and temples of all Tathāgatas; before the images of all Tathāgatas;
before the abodes of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; before all the Dharma-jewels; before all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and their stupas and temples;
before all the fields of merit of the noble assembly; before all parents and venerable elders; and before all the multitudes of the ten directions.
Throughout their lives, they shall all, as previously described, honor and praise [the Buddha] without ceasing until the end of the future.
This is because they are equal to space, being boundless; equal to the *dharmadhātu*, being without obstruction; equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), pervading all;
and equal to the Tathāgata, being free from discrimination. They are like shadows that appear in accordance with wisdom, and like dreams that arise from thought.
It is like a reflected image, for it manifests all things; it is like an echo, for it arises dependent upon conditions; there is no arising, nor is there successive emergence or passing away;
there is no intrinsic nature that transforms according to conditions. Furthermore, one definitively knows that all retributions arise from karma.
All fruits arise from causes; all karmas arise from habitual practice; the arising of all Buddhas arises from faith;
and all manifested acts of offering arise entirely from resolute understanding.
All emanation Buddhas arise from a mind of reverence; all Buddha-dharmas arise from roots of goodness;
all transformation bodies arise from skillful means; all Buddha-activities arise from great vows; all practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas arise from dedication;
and the vast adornments of the entire Dharma-realm arise from the sphere of omniscience.

They are free from the view of nihilism because they know dedication; they are free from the view of eternalism because they know non-arising; they are free from the view of causelessness because they know the true cause;
they are free from the view of inversion because they know reality as it is; they are free from the view of a creator because they know things do not arise through another;
they are free from the view of self and other because they know arising from conditions; and they are free from the view of grasping at extremes because they know the dharma-realm is boundless.

Therefore, because they are free from the views and cognitions of coming and going, like reflections; because they are free from the views and cognitions of existence and non-existence, being neither arising nor ceasing;

because they are free from the views and cognitions of all phenomena, being empty and unarisen; because they know [all things] are not independent; and because they know they are produced through the power of vows.
Because one enters the limit of signlessness by being free from all marks; because one knows that all phenomena arise like sprouts from seeds;
like characters produced from a seal; because one knows that substance is like a reflection; because one knows that sound is like an echo; because one knows that objects are like dreams;

because one knows that karma is like an illusion; because one understands that the world is a manifestation of the mind; because one understands that results arise from causes; and because one understands the accumulation of retributive karma.
Knowing that all dharmas of merit flow forth from the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the bodhisattva, the youth Sudhana entered into such wisdom with a focused mind and pure mindfulness.
Before the pavilion, he prostrated himself fully upon the ground with earnest reverence.
Inconceivable roots of goodness flowed through his body and mind, making him feel cool, refreshed, and joyful; he then rose from the earth.
With single-minded devotion, they gazed upon him without a moment’s distraction. Joining their palms, they circumambulated him for immeasurable circuits, thinking to themselves:
"This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who have realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
it is the dwelling place of those who are non-discriminative regarding all phenomena; it is the dwelling place of those who have understood that the dharma-realm is without differentiation."
This is the dwelling place of those who know that all sentient beings are ungraspable;
it is the dwelling place of those who know that all phenomena are unborn; it is the dwelling place of those who do not cling to any world;
it is the dwelling place of those who do not cling to any abode; it is the dwelling place of those who do not delight in any village.
This dwelling place is the dwelling place of those who do not rely on any objective realm; it is the dwelling place of those who are free from all conceptualizations;
it is the dwelling place of those who know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; it is the dwelling place of those who have severed all karmic activities of discrimination;
it is the dwelling place of those who are free from all notions of thought, mind, and consciousness.
This dwelling place is the abode of those who neither enter nor emerge from any path;

it is the abode of those who enter all profound *prajñāpāramitā*; it is the abode of those who are able to dwell within the universal dharma-realm through skillful means; and it is the abode of those who extinguish the fires of all afflictions.
Therefore, this is the dwelling place of those who, through superior wisdom, have severed all views, cravings, and conceits;

it is the dwelling place of those who give birth to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and clarities (*vidyā*), and sport therein;
it is the dwelling place of those who observe the spheres of all bodhisattva samādhis; it is the dwelling place of those who abide in all Tathāgatas...
It is the dwelling place of those who come from all places; it is the dwelling place of those who enter one eon into all eons and all eons into one eon without destroying their characteristics;
it is the dwelling place of those who enter one land into all lands and all lands into one land without destroying their characteristics. Thus, with one...
The dwelling place of one who, through the dharma-base, enters all dharmas by means of all dharmas into a single dharma without destroying their characteristics;

the dwelling place of one who, by means of a single sentient being, enters all sentient beings and by means of all sentient beings enters a single sentient being without destroying their characteristics;
and the dwelling place of one who, by means of a single Buddha, enters all Buddhas...
It is the dwelling place of those who enter into a single Buddha while all Buddhas do not lose their distinct characteristics;
it is the dwelling place of those who, in a single thought-moment, know all three periods of time;
