if one’s mind were to regress, all wholesome dharmas would immediately disperse and perish. Good son, it is like a mani jewel named Great Radiance.
There are those who adorn their bodies with this jewel necklace; it outshines all other precious ornaments such that none of their radiance remains visible.

In the same way, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise adorns his body, outshining all the jewel-like ornaments of the minds of those of the two vehicles until they are entirely devoid of luster. Good son!
Just as the water-purifying jewel can clear turbid water, so too is the jewel of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
it can clear away all the defilements and turbidity of the afflictions. Son of good family, it is like a person who possesses the water-dwelling jewel and wears it upon their body;
when they enter the great ocean, they are not harmed by the water. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this.
It is so. Having attained the wondrous jewel that dwells within the water of the bodhicitta, one never sinks into the ocean of all saṃsāra.
Good son, it is like a person who obtains a dragon-jewel and enters a dragon palace; no dragons or snakes can cause them harm.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having obtained the great dragon-jewel of bodhicitta...
When the jewel enters the desire realm, the dragons and snakes of affliction cannot cause it harm.

Good son, it is just as when Śakra wears the maṇi crown, outshining all the other hosts of devas; so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who, wearing the precious crown of the great vow of the bodhicitta, transcends all sentient beings of the triple world. Good son.
For example, suppose there is a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); it eliminates all the suffering of poverty.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise obtains the wish-fulfilling jewel of the bodhicitta, thereby remaining far removed from all fear of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Good son, it is like a person who obtains a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta-maṇi*); when held toward the sunlight, fire is produced.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this. Having obtained the jewel-gem of the mind of bodhicitta, he holds it toward the light of wisdom and thereby produces the fire of wisdom.
Good son, it is as if there were a person who obtains a moon-essence pearl; holding it toward the moonlight, water is produced.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this; having obtained the moon-essence jewel of bodhicitta...
Jewel. Holding this heart-jewel, one reflects the light of dedication to produce the water of all roots of goodness and vows.
Good son, it is like a dragon king who wears a crown of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewels upon his head, thereby remaining far removed from all fear of enemies.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this. Wearing the precious crown of the bodhicitta and great compassion, they remain far removed from all the hardships of the evil realms.
Good son, it is as if there were a jewel named "Treasury of Ornaments for All Worlds."
If there are those who obtain it, their every desire is completely fulfilled, yet this precious jewel suffers no depletion.
The jewel of the bodhicitta is also like this: if there are those who obtain it, all their aspirations are fully satisfied, yet the bodhicitta suffers no depletion.
Good son, it is as if a wheel-turning king possesses a maṇi jewel which he places—

Within the palace, it emits a great radiance that destroys all darkness. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise abides in the desire realm with the great maṇi-jewel of the bodhicitta, emitting the light of great wisdom that completely destroys the darkness of ignorance in all realms of existence.
Good son, for example, if there is anyone for whom this light of the great indranīla maṇi-jewel [shines]...

Whatever it touches becomes identical in color to that object. In the same way, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is such that when one observes all phenomena and dedicates their roots of goodness, there is nothing that does not become identical in color to the bodhicitta.
Good son, it is like a lapis lazuli gem that, even after remaining amidst impurities for hundreds of thousands of years, is never defiled by foul odors or filth; its nature—
Because it is fundamentally pure, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise:

even while dwelling within the desire realm for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is not defiled by the faults and afflictions of the desire realm, just as the nature of the dharmadhātu is inherently pure.
"Good son, it is like a jewel named Pure Radiance that can completely outshine the colors of all other jewels.
In the same way, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can completely outshine the merits of all ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Good son, it is like a jewel named Flame that can completely extinguish all..."
It dispels all darkness. The jewel of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this; it can extinguish all the darkness of ignorance.
Son of good family, it is as if there were a priceless jewel in the ocean, which a merchant obtains and loads onto a ship to bring into the city.
Among all the various mani-jewels numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, none have a radiance or value equal to it. The Bodhi-...
The jewel of the mind is also like this. Dwelling within the great ocean of birth and death, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva boards the ship of the Great Vow;
with a continuous deep resolve, he carries it across to enter the city of liberation. No one among those of the Two Vehicles can equal his merit.
Good son, it is as if there were a precious jewel named Sovereign King (*Īśvararāja*), located on Jambudvīpa... [it is] far from... [the shore].
The solar and lunar discs are forty thousand yojanas in extent; all the adornments within the palaces of the sun and moon, including the reflections of their jewels, appear therein in their entirety.
It is just so with the jewel of the pure merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta.
Abiding within the cycle of birth and death, they illuminate the emptiness of the dharma-realm; the sun and moon of Buddha-wisdom and all its merits are fully manifested therein.

Good son, it is like a precious gem named Sovereign King (*Vajrarāja*): wherever the light of the sun and moon shines upon it, the value of all other treasures, clothing, and goods cannot possibly equal it. So it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Jewel King of Sovereignty over the Aspiration for Bodhicitta is likewise so.

Wherever the light of omniscience shines, all the merits of the gods and humans of the three periods of time, as well as those of the two vehicles—whether with outflows or without outflows—cannot equal it.
"Good son, in the ocean there is a treasure called the 'Ocean Treasury' (*sāgaragarbha*), which universally manifests all manner of adornments within the sea.
In the same way, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise universally manifests all the adornments of the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Good son, it is like the Jāmbūnada gold of the heavens, which [is surpassed] only by the Great Mind-King (*cittarāja*)."
Just as the maṇi jewel has no equal, so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva like Jāmbūnada gold;
with the exception of the great jewel of the sovereign mind of omniscience, nothing else can equal it.
Son of good family, it is as if there were a person skilled in the methods of taming dragons who attains mastery over all dragons; such is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
It is also like this. Having attained the bodhicitta, which is the skillful method for taming dragons, one gains mastery over all the dragons of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Good son, it is just as a valiant warrior clad in armor and wielding weapons cannot be defeated by any enemy;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who is clad in the armor and wields the weapons of the great mind of bodhicitta.
No karmic afflictions or any evil adversaries can ever subdue it. Good son, it is like the black sandalwood of the heavens:
if even one *zhu* is burned, its fragrance pervades a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*).
The total value of all the precious jewels that fill a three-thousandfold world system cannot equal it. Such is the fragrance of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
It is likewise so. The merit of a single thought universally perfumes the entire dharma-realm; all the merits of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot compare to it.

Good son, just as white sandalwood, when applied to the body, can completely eliminate all feverish afflictions and cause both body and mind to attain universal coolness, so too is the incense of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
It is also like this. It can eliminate all the burning afflictions of false conceptualization, greed, anger, ignorance, and so forth, causing one to be endowed with the coolness of wisdom.

Good son, just as Mount Sumeru takes on the same color as anyone who approaches it, so too is the mountain of the bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; if anyone approaches it, [it likewise transforms them].
They all attain a form identical to that of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Son of good family, it is like the *pārijātaka* tree:

the fragrance of its bark cannot be matched by any of the fragrances of flowers such as the *vārṣika*, the *campaka*, or the *sumana* found within Jambudvīpa. Such is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s tree of the bodhicitta.

It is also like this. The fragrance of the merit of the great vows one has made cannot be matched by any of the fragrances of the merits of the two vehicles—their untainted precepts, concentrations, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Good son, it is like the pārijātaka tree: although its flowers have not yet blossomed, you should know that it is already the source from which immeasurable flowers will emerge.
In the same way, the Bodhicitta-tree of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
although it has not yet blossomed the flower of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one should know that it is the place where the Bodhi-flowers of countless devas and humans are produced.
Good son, it is like this: suppose a garment were perfumed for a single day with *pāriyātra* flowers;
even if one were to perfume it for a thousand years with *campaka*, *vārṣika*, or *sumana* flowers, they could not equal its fragrance.

In the same way, the flower of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is such that the fragrance of all merits perfumed throughout a single lifetime pervades everywhere throughout the ten directions.
It cannot be equaled by the untainted merits of all Buddhas or all followers of the two vehicles, even those cultivated for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

Good son, it is like the coconut tree growing on an island in the ocean; its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are constantly utilized by all sentient beings without a moment’s respite. Such is the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s tree of the bodhicitta.

It is also like this. From the initial arousal of the mind of compassionate vows until the attainment of Buddhahood and the continued presence of the True Dharma in the world, it constantly benefits all the world without interruption. Good son, it is as if there were a medicinal juice called *haritaki*;
if someone were to obtain it, even one *liang* of it could transform a thousand *liang* of copper entirely into pure gold. It is not...
Just as a thousand catties of copper can transform this medicinal elixir, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

By means of the wisdom-medicine of the dedication of the bodhicitta, they universally transform all dharmas—such as karma and afflictions—and cause them all to become the marks of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Neither karma nor afflictions are able to transform their mind. Good son, it is like a small fire: as it burns whatever it encounters, its flames grow ever more intense.
The fire of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: as it encounters whatever objects of focus, the flames of wisdom increase.
Good son, it is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; yet that original single lamp remains undiminished.
It does not diminish nor is it exhausted. The lamp of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise:
it universally kindles the lamps of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, yet its own lamp of mind neither diminishes nor is exhausted.

Good son, for example, when a single lamp enters a dark room, it is able to completely dispel the darkness of hundreds or thousands of years. So too is the lamp of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

It is also like this. Entering into the inner chamber of the minds of sentient beings, it is able to completely eliminate all various dark obstructions of karma and afflictions throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable eons.
Good son, it is like a lamp wick that emits light according to its size; if one adds oil, the light will never cease. So it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The lamp of the bodhicitta is likewise. With great vows as its wick, it illuminates the dharma-realm;
with the oil of great compassion, it matures sentient beings and adorns the buddha-fields, performing buddha-works without ceasing.
Good son, it is like the crown of the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations, made of Jāmbūnada true gold, which [surpasses] the crowns of all the devas of the desire realm.
No ornaments whatsoever can equal it. In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise dons the celestial crown of the great vow of bodhicitta;
no virtues of any ordinary beings or followers of the two vehicles can equal it.
Good son, when the lion king roars, the lion cubs who hear it all increase in courage and strength, whereas other beasts, upon hearing it, immediately [flee].
All [other animals] flee and hide. It should be known that the lion-king Buddha’s roar of bodhicitta is likewise: when the bodhisattvas hear it, their merits increase;
those who hold to acquisitions all retreat and scatter upon hearing it. Son of good family, it is as if someone were to use a lion’s sinew as a string for a musical instrument;
once its sound is played, all other strings snap. So too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

It is likewise so. Using the Tathāgata’s lion-like perfection-body and the sinew of bodhicitta as the strings for the lute of Dharma-joy, once its sound is played, all the strings of the five desires and the various merits of the two vehicles are completely severed and extinguished.
Good son, it is like a person who collects various kinds of milk from cattle, sheep, and other animals, until they have accumulated enough to fill—
Just as a single drop of lion’s milk, when cast into the great ocean, causes it all to be transformed and destroyed, passing through without obstruction, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
by placing the lion-like milk of the Tathāgata’s bodhicitta into the great ocean of the milk of karmic afflictions from immeasurable kalpas,
he causes them all to be utterly destroyed and passes through without obstruction, never dwelling therein.

The liberation of the two vehicles. Good son, it is like the kalaviṅka bird, which while still within its egg possesses great power that no other birds can equal. So too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
having given rise to the bodhicitta within the egg of birth and death, the power of all his merits of great compassion is such that the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess it.
"Regarding 'being able to surpass': Good son, it is like the prince of the garuḍa when he is first born;
his eyes are clear and sharp, and his flight is powerful and swift. Although all other birds have been fully grown for a long time, none can surpass him.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having resolved upon bodhicitta, he becomes a prince of the Buddha, possessing pure wisdom and courageous great compassion."
It is fierce. Even though the practitioners of the two vehicles have cultivated their practices for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they cannot reach it.
Good son, it is like a strong man who, grasping a sharp spear in his hand, pierces through solid and dense armor straight through without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: grasping the keen and swift spear of the bodhicitta, he pierces the dense armor of all false views and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They are able to penetrate everything without any obstruction. Good son, it is like a powerful Mahānāga hero who, when he rouses his majestic wrath, inevitably develops a swelling on his forehead;
as long as that swelling has not yet healed, no one among the people of Jambudvīpa can subdue him. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: if he gives rise to...
Great compassion necessarily gives rise to the bodhicitta. As long as the mind has not abandoned it, all the māras of the world and their followers cannot cause harm.

Good son, it is like a master archer who has many disciples; although they have not yet mastered the skills of their teacher, their wisdom and skillful means are such that no other person can surpass them.
Furthermore, it is the same for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva when first generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Although they have not yet become habituated to the practices of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), their vows, wisdom, understanding, and aspirations surpass those of all ordinary worldlings and followers of the two vehicles.
Good son, it is like a person learning archery who first stabilizes their stance and only afterwards practices the technique. Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. Desiring to study the path to the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), one must first abide securely in the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and only thereafter practice all the Buddha-dharmas.
Good son, it is like a magician who, when about to perform a magical feat, must first give rise to the intention and recall the magical arts;
only then will whatever he performs be fully accomplished. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. When about to manifest all the miraculous illusions of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one must first give rise to the intention and resolve for Bodhicitta;
only then will everything be fully accomplished. Son of good family, it is just as the art of illusion manifests forms where there is no form;
the characteristic of the Bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this—though it is non-existent...
There is a form that cannot be seen, yet it can universally manifest various adornments of merit throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Good son, it is just as when a cat merely sees a mouse; the mouse immediately enters its hole and dares not come out again.
It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta: by momentarily observing all [phenomena] with the eye of wisdom...
Delusions and karmic actions all immediately flee and hide away, never to arise again. Good son, it is like a person wearing ornaments made of Jambu-river gold;

they outshine everything else until all appears like a mass of ink. In the same way, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva wearing the ornaments of the bodhicitta outshines all the merits of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.

All their adornments were rendered devoid of luster and color. "Good son, just as the power of even a small portion of a fine magnet can attract and break apart all iron hooks and locks, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has resolved upon Bodhicitta.
If they give rise to a single thought, they are able to destroy and extinguish all the hooks and locks of views, desires, and ignorance. Good son, it is like a magnet..."
Stones and iron, upon seeing it, are immediately dispersed and none remain behind. It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has resolved upon Bodhicitta:
when the various karmas, afflictions, and the liberations of the two vehicles briefly behold it, they are all dispersed and extinguished, with none remaining.
Good son, it is like a person who skillfully enters the great ocean; all the waters—
No kinsmen will be able to cause them harm. Even if they were to enter the mouth of a makara fish, they would not be devoured by it.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: having resolved upon bodhicitta and entered the ocean of birth and death, various karmas and afflictions cannot cause them harm.
Even if they were to enter the sphere of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they would likewise not...
They will encounter obstacles and hindrances. Good son, it is like a person who drinks the nectar-juice of ambrosia;
no other things can cause them harm. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:

having drunk the nectar-juice of the Dharma of Bodhicitta, they do not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, because they are endowed with the power of vast compassion and vows. Good son...
Son, it is like a person who obtains the añjana ointment and applies it to their eyes; though they walk among people, no one sees them.

In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having obtained the añjana ointment of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), is able to enter the realm of Māra through skillful means, yet all the māras are unable to see him. Good son, it is like this:
Just as there are those who, relying on a king, fear no other person, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Relying on the great sovereign power of the bodhicitta, they fear not the obstacles, hindrances, or the perils of the evil realms.
Good son, it is like a person dwelling within water who fears not being consumed by fire; so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who dwells [in the bodhicitta].
Within the water of the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta, one does not fear the fire of the liberative wisdom of the two vehicles.
Good son, it is just as if a person who relies upon a valiant general has no fear of any enemies;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who, relying upon the courageous great general that is bodhicitta, does not fear any enemies of unwholesome conduct. Good son...
"Good man, it is like the Heavenly King Śakra, who wields the vajra-pestle to subdue all the hosts of asuras.
In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise wields the vajra-pestle of the bodhicitta to subdue all māras and non-Buddhists.
Good man, it is as if there were a person who takes an elixir of longevity, remaining forever vigorous and never aging."
It does not diminish. In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise partakes of the life-prolonging medicine of the bodhicitta;
throughout incalculable kalpas, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices with a mind free from weariness or fatigue, and without any defiled attachment.
Good son, it is like a person preparing medicinal decoctions who must first take pure, clear water. So too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
It is likewise so. One who wishes to cultivate all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva must first give rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Good son, just as a person who protects their body must first protect the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
in upholding the Buddha-dharma, one must also first protect the mind of enlightenment. Good son, for example, if a person’s life-faculty...

If it is severed, one cannot benefit one’s parents, kinsmen, or clan. In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who abandons the bodhicitta cannot benefit all sentient beings, nor can they accomplish the merits of the Buddhas.
Good son, for example, there is nothing that can destroy the great ocean; the ocean of bodhicitta is likewise. All karmas...
It cannot be destroyed by the minds of the two vehicles’ afflictions. Good son, it is like the light of the sun, which the light of the stars and constellations cannot eclipse;
the sun of the bodhicitta is also like this, for it cannot be obscured by the light of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of all those of the two vehicles.
Good son, it is as when a prince is first born, he is immediately honored by the great ministers.

It is weighty because of the mastery of its lineage. In the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves their mind upon awakening within the Buddha-dharma, they are immediately respected by the elder śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have long practiced the holy life.
Because of the mastery of great compassion. Good son, it is just as when a prince, though still young in years, is saluted by all the great ministers;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Although he has only recently resolved his mind [on enlightenment] and is practicing the Bodhisattva path, even the elders of the two vehicles should salute him. Good son, it is just as when a prince, although [at one...]

Among all his ministers and assistants, he has not yet attained mastery; yet, having already fulfilled the marks of a king, he is not equal to any of his ministers or assistants because of the supreme excellence of his birth.

In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, although not yet having attained mastery over all karma and afflictions, has nonetheless fully perfected the marks of enlightenment and is not equal to any [others].
The two vehicles are equal [in this regard], because their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is supreme. Good son, it is like a pure and wondrous maṇi jewel;
because the eye has a cataract, one sees it as impure. The bodhicitta-jewel of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this:
those lacking wisdom and faith call it impure. Good son, it is like a medicine that is [rendered ineffective] by a spell...
It sustains. If there are sentient beings who see, hear, dwell with, or even merely remember it, all their various illnesses will be completely extinguished.
It is the same for the medicinal herb of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

When sustained by all roots of goodness, wisdom, skillful means, and the vow-knowledge of the bodhisattva, if there are sentient beings who see, hear, dwell with, or remember it, all their afflictions...
All afflictions and illnesses will be completely eliminated. Good son, it is like a person who constantly holds ambrosia;
their body will ultimately remain unchanging and indestructible. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:

if they constantly recollect and maintain the ambrosia of the bodhicitta, they will cause the body of their vows and wisdom to remain ultimately indestructible. Good son, it is like a wooden mechanical man; if it lacks...
Just as a body with a wedge inserted becomes disjointed and unable to move, so it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
without the bodhicitta, their practice becomes fragmented and they cannot accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.
Good son, it is like the sandalwood treasure of a Wheel-Turning King called "Elephant Treasury"; if this king of incense is burned, the fourfold army will all leap upward.
"O son of good family, the incense of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this.
If one gives rise to this thought, it causes all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva to forever transcend the triple world and proceed within the unconditioned space of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
O son of good family, for example, a diamond is produced only from a diamond mine or a gold mine; it is not produced from the mines of other jewels."
The diamond-like bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise.
It arises solely from the ground of the diamond-like protection of sentient beings through great compassion, and from the ground of the excellence of the knowledge of all-knowledge;
it does not arise from the ground of the roots of goodness of other sentient beings. Son of good family, it is like a tree named "Rootless," which does not grow from a root.
Yet its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all lush and flourishing. It is the same with the Bodhicitta tree of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
though no root can be found, it is able to nurture the superknowledges and great vows of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits spread out in profusion, casting a dense shade that universally covers the world. Good son, it is like a diamond, which is not inferior or base.

Just as only a vessel that is complete and of superior quality can contain and sustain [a liquid], while a broken vessel cannot—excepting only a vessel that is perfectly intact and exquisite—so too is the vajra of bodhicitta.
It cannot be contained or sustained within the vessels of inferior beings who are characterized by stinginess, envy, violation of precepts, laziness, distracted thoughts, and lack of wisdom;
nor can it be sustained by those who have fallen away from their sublime wisdom and vows, or who are distracted by evil conceptions.
It can be contained and sustained within the vessels of those born [as humans], with the sole exception of the jewel-vessel of the Bodhisattva’s profound resolve.
Good son, for example, just as a diamond can pierce all other jewels, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta; it can completely penetrate all the jewels of the Dharma.
Good son, for example, just as a diamond can shatter all mountains, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta...

It is likewise. It is fully capable of destroying all mountains of false views. Good son, for example, although a diamond may be broken and no longer whole, it still surpasses all other jewels. The diamond of the bodhicitta is also like this;
although one’s resolve may be weak and it may suffer some slight impairment, it still excels the merits of all those of the two vehicles. Good son, for example—
Just as a diamond, even if it has flaws or cracks, is still able to eliminate all poverty, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta;
even if it is flawed and does not advance in various practices, it is still able to abandon all of birth and death.
Son of good family, just as even a small amount of diamond can destroy all other substances, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta.
It is likewise. Upon entering even a slight object of focus, it immediately shatters all ignorance and delusions.
Good son, for example, a diamond cannot be obtained by ordinary people; the diamond of the bodhicitta is just the same—it cannot be obtained by sentient beings of inferior intent.
Good son, for example, a person who does not recognize jewels does not know the power of a diamond.
If one does not know how to employ it, its function cannot be realized. It is the same with the vajra of the bodhicitta:
those who do not know the Dharma do not understand its capacity and thus cannot employ its function. Good son, for example, there is nothing that can destroy a vajra;
likewise, the vajra of the bodhicitta cannot be destroyed by any phenomena. Good son, it is like a vajra-pestle.
None of those men of great strength could hold it, except for one possessing the power of Mahānārāyaṇa.
The bodhicitta is likewise: none of those of the two vehicles can uphold it, except for a Bodhisattva’s firm and virtuous power born of vast causes and conditions.
Son of good family, it is like a diamond, which no object whatsoever can destroy. And yet...
It is able to universally destroy all things, yet its essential nature suffers no diminution. The bodhicitta is also like this:
throughout the countless eons of the three periods of time, it teaches and transforms sentient beings and practices asceticism;
it can accomplish all that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot, yet it ultimately never experiences weariness or fatigue.
It is indestructible. Good son, for example, just as nothing else can support a diamond except the diamond-ground, so too is the bodhicitta;
it cannot be supported by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, except by those who are heading toward sarvajñā (omniscience).
Good son, just as a diamond vessel has no flaws or defects when used to hold [substances],...
Water never seeps through to enter the earth; likewise, the adamantine vessel of the bodhicitta never allows the water of roots of goodness to leak away into the various realms of existence.
Noble son, just as the vajra-limit supports the great earth and prevents it from sinking, so too does the bodhicitta support all [the qualities] of a bodhisattva.
As for practice and vows, they do not allow one to fall and sink into the three realms. Good son, it is like a diamond that remains in water for a long time without rotting or becoming wet;

the bodhicitta is also like this, remaining throughout all kalpas within the waters of birth-and-death, karma, and afflictions, without being destroyed or changed. Good son, it is like a diamond [which cannot be burned] by any fire.
It cannot be burned, nor can it be made hot. The bodhicitta is likewise;
the fires of all the afflictions (*kleśa*) within birth and death cannot burn it, nor can they make it hot.

Good son, it is like the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*) within the trichiliocosm, which can support all Buddhas as they sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdue all Māras, and achieve [awakening].
The seat of the Perfectly Enlightened One cannot be sustained by any other seat. The seat of the bodhicitta is likewise:
it can sustain all the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, the perfections (pāramitās), the various patiences (kṣāntis), the stages (bhūmis), the dedications, and the receiving of predictions;

it sustains the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas), the making of offerings to all Buddhas, and the hearing, receiving, and practicing of the Dharma—none of which can be sustained by any other mind.
It cannot be sustained. Son of good family, the bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable, boundless, and even unspeakably unspeakable supreme merits.
If there are sentient beings who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall obtain such supreme meritorious dharmas. Therefore, son of good family, you have obtained...
Excellent, excellent! You have set your mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and sought the conduct of a bodhisattva;
it is because you have already attained such great merit. Son of good family, as to your question regarding how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path:
son of good family, you should enter this Great Vairocana-Adorned Treasury.
Observing thoroughly throughout the towers and pavilions, he was able to understand how to train in the bodhisattva conduct; having trained, he had accomplished immeasurable merit.
After the youth Sudhana had seen Maitreya and offered extensive praise, he finally inquired about the essentials of the Dharma, first presenting [his request].
Having already resolved their minds [on enlightenment] and having inquired about learning the bodhisattva practices, they further requested that he explain all such matters as these.

There are fifty scriptural passages, all of which inquire about the virtues of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results; since these stages correspond to the ultimate state, [they are explained accordingly].
The intention is to encompass all practices; therefore, one should inquire extensively.
Next, Maitreya first extols that person before transmitting the Dharma, pointing to Sudhana and addressing the assembly: "Do you see these merits of this son of a householder?
Pointing to a person to show the assembly is intended so that others may recognize what is worthy of esteem. Next, [he addresses] "all you virtuous ones..."

This section, beginning with "This son of a householder," correctly praises his virtues. The two and a half lines of scripture up to "searching everywhere to attend upon him and request the Dharma" praise his diligence in general.

Next, from "O virtuous ones" down to "never for a moment giving rise to a single thought of weariness or indolence," the two and a half lines of scripture specifically demonstrate the characteristics of his diligence; that is to say, his diligence at a single time was as follows:
There is no need for lamentation; because from beginning to end he maintained a single thought without laxity, he is indeed worthy of praise.
As for the statement that he "passed through one hundred and ten spiritual friends," this signifies the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Since each stage is fully endowed with a single *pāramitā*, and he has now completed the traversal of these stages, it is said that he has "passed through" them. Next, O virtuous ones, as for this son of a householder...
The following twenty-four lines and a half of the sūtra are extremely rare. They praise the vastness of the initial vehicle (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

The first three lines and a half of the sūtra provide a general praise for its rarity. Next, from "Such a person" to "entering the city of omniscience" (sixteen lines of the sūtra), it specifically clarifies the difficulty of encountering it.
Finally, from "O noble ones" to "never having been in opposition" (five lines of the sūtra), it provides the conclusion.
[This section] praises what has been accomplished. Next, "O virtuous ones, if there are sentient beings...

down to "...successively more difficult to encounter than others," consists of thirteen phrases praising the possession of virtues without deficiency. Because each subsequent stage is more difficult to attain than the preceding one, it is said they are "successively more difficult to encounter.
Next, "O virtuous ones, as for other bodhisattvas... down to "...able to fully possess the [vows of] Samantabhadra... [is the next section].
[This is] the practice. There are ten phrases praising the swift realization that transcends expedient means:

that by relying on the practice of the True Teaching (*saddharma*), one attains in a single lifetime the fruit of kalpas of vast eons, for it is through this very ordinary body that one becomes a Buddha in a single lifetime.
Next, at that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva thus praised Sudhana’s various merits and his ability to attain the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
Having caused immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta, [the Buddha] addressed Sudhana, thereby praising him for the excellent benefit he had obtained by resolving upon Bodhicitta;
thus, he extolled the excellence of his vessel for generating that resolve and its resulting benefits.
Therefore, one is embraced by virtuous friends. Next, from the section beginning with "For what reason," the merits of the bodhicitta are extensively set forth in two hundred and twenty-one verses;
these all pertain to the three types of arousal of the mind and instantaneously possess the merits of all stages.
For now, they are divided into two parts: first, from "The bodhicitta is like a seed" up to "all... [the first part].
The Path of Wisdom consists of one hundred and eighteen phrases, clarifying how the bodhicitta universally encompasses all stages (*bhūmi*). Next, from the passage beginning with "For example,
there is a person who obtains the medicine of fearlessness" up to "cannot be sustained by any other mental factors," there are one hundred and three phrases,
which extensively clarify the sovereign merits of the bodhicitta, comprehensively subsuming the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kauśalya*) and the ten stages.
Regarding the merits of the various stages of the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), each section of the text contains both analogies and their applications.

The first seven analogies illustrate the virtues of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*). The twenty analogies illustrate the virtues of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*). The three sets of nine analogies illustrate the virtues of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).

The subsequent four analogies illustrate the virtues subsumed within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). The subsequent three analogies illustrate the virtues subsumed within the second stage. The subsequent four analogies illustrate the virtues subsumed within the third stage. The subsequent four analogies illustrate...
The virtues of the fourth stage are [illustrated by] four similes. Next, four similes encompass the virtues of the fifth stage. Next, six similes encompass the virtues of the sixth stage.
Next, five similes encompass the virtues of the seventh stage. Next, fourteen similes encompass the virtues of the eighth stage.

Next, ten similes encompass the virtues of the ninth stage. Next, six similes encompass the virtues of the tenth stage. Finally, from "like a diamond" onwards, seventeen similes encompass [the virtues of the Buddha-stage].
Regarding the merits of the state of awakening: because one ultimately achieves bodhi through vajra-wisdom, next [the text] states:
"Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable, boundless, and even unspeakably unspeakable supreme merits," and so forth.
These four lines of scripture conclude and explain what they pertain to; that is to say, the many virtues mentioned above all belong to the bodhicitta.
[The text] summarizes the preceding statement regarding the attainment of excellent benefits. Below, it proceeds to formally bestow the Dharma-realm, saying:
"Good son, as to your question concerning how one studies the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path:
you should enter this Great Pavilion of Vairocana’s Adorned Treasury and observe it thoroughly; then you will be able to understand."
Knowing how to learn the bodhisattva practices; having learned them, one accomplishes immeasurable merit.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Essential Outline*, Fascicle 78 and Fascicle 79.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning commented upon by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá Yán Temple;
and extracted and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fǎyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter, Part 39-20.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having respectfully circumambulated the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya to the right, addressed him, saying:
"I only pray that the Great Sage will open the door of this tower so that I may enter. Then, the Bodhisattva Maitreya stepped forward.
He approached the pavilion and snapped his fingers; the door opened immediately. He commanded Sudhana to enter. Sudhana was filled with joy.

Once he had entered, the door closed again. He beheld that pavilion as vast and immeasurable as space, with its ground composed of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, and featuring incalculable palaces, incalculable gates and portals, and incalculable windows and lattices.
The steps and stairways were immeasurable; the balustrades were immeasurable; the roads were all composed of the seven treasures.
Immeasurable banners, immeasurable standards, and immeasurable parasols were arranged in rows all around; there were immeasurable necklaces made of various precious jewels.
Countless pearl necklaces, countless red pearl necklaces, and countless lion-gem necklaces hung down everywhere;
there were countless half-moons, countless silk ribbons, and countless jeweled nets serving as adornments;
countless jeweled bells produced sounds when stirred by the wind, scattering countless celestial flowers.
Various flowers were strewn; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) celestial jewel-garlands and ribbons were suspended;
incalculable censers of various jewels were arrayed; incalculable fine gold dust rained down; incalculable jewel-mirrors were hung; incalculable jewel-lamps were lit;
incalculable jewel-robes were spread; incalculable jewel-canopies were set out; and incalculable jewel-thrones were prepared. Incalculable...
Precious silken cloths were spread upon the seats. There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) images of Jāmbūnada gold boys and girls;
incalculable images of various forms made of diverse jewels; and incalculable images of Bodhisattvas made of exquisite jewels, filling every place.
Incalculable flocks of birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds; there were incalculable precious *utpala* flowers and incalculable precious *padma* flowers.
It was adorned with countless *kubjaka* flowers and countless *puṇḍarīka* flowers made of jewels;
countless jewel trees were arranged in successive rows, and countless mani-jewels emitted great radiance.
Thus, it was adorned with such immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) ornaments.
Furthermore, he saw within it hundreds of thousands of exquisite pavilions; each was decorated exactly as described above.
Vast, magnificent, and beautiful, they were all like space, without mutual obstruction and without confusion. At one location, the youth Sudhana—
Within it, he saw all places; he saw every single location in this very way.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, beholding such various and inconceivable realms of sovereign power within the Pavilion of Vairocana’s Adorned Treasury, gave rise to great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
His body and mind became supple and soft; he was freed from all conceptualizations and removed all [afflictions].
He obstructed all hindrances, extinguished every delusion, and never forgot what he had seen; he was able to remember everything he had heard and his thoughts remained undisturbed.
He entered the gate of unimpeded liberation, universally directing his mind, universally beholding all things, and universally proffering respectful salutations.
As soon as he began to bow his head, through the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, he saw his own body pervading all the towers.
Within the pavilion, he fully beheld various inconceivable and sovereign realms.
That is to say, he saw the original name of Maitreya Bodhisattva when he first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta; his lineage;
the virtuous friend who awakened him and caused him to plant such roots of goodness; the lifespan he maintained; and the place where he resided.
In this kalpa, he encounters such Buddhas; dwelling in such adorned lands, he cultivates such practices and makes such vows.
He clearly perceives all those Tathāgatas—their assemblies, their lifespans, and the duration for which he attends upon and makes offerings to them.
Or, he sees Maitreya first realize the *maitrī-samādhi*, from which point onward...
He has already been known as Maitreya. Some see him practicing various sublime deeds and bringing all the *pāramitās* to fulfillment;
some see him attaining the stages of patience (*kṣānti*); some see him dwelling in the bodhisattva grounds (*bhūmi*); some see him accomplishing a pure buddha-field;

and some see him manifesting as a protector and upholder of the Tathāgata’s true teaching, becoming a great Dharma teacher who has attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At such a time, in such a place, such a Tathāgata...
They have come to receive the prediction of unsurpassed *bodhi*. Some see Maitreya as a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*) exhorting all sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action;
some see him as a world-protector (*lokapāla*) benefiting sentient beings; some see him as Śakra, rebuking the five desires;
some see him as the King of the Yāma Heaven praising heedfulness; and some see him as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven extolling [virtue].

The merit of a bodhisattva throughout a single lifetime: sometimes he appears as the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, manifesting the various transformations and adornments of bodhisattvas for the sake of the assembly of devas;
sometimes he appears as the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, expounding the teachings of all Buddhas for the assembly of devas;
sometimes he acts as a Māra king, teaching that all phenomena are entirely impermanent; or he appears as a Brahmā king.
He speaks of the various meditative concentrations and immeasurable joys and pleasures;

or, as an Asura king, he enters the great ocean of wisdom, realizes that all phenomena are like illusions, and constantly expounds the Dharma for his assembly to sever all arrogance, intoxication, and haughtiness.
Or again, he is seen dwelling in the realm of Yama, emitting great radiance to rescue those suffering in the hells. Or he is seen among the hungry ghosts.

In places where there was hunger and thirst, he bestowed food and drink to relieve their suffering; or he was seen employing various skillful means to tame sentient beings who were in the realms of animals;
or again, he was seen preaching the Dharma for the assemblies of the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings (Lokapālas);
or again, he was seen preaching the Dharma for the assemblies of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; or again, he was seen [preaching] for the assemblies of the King of the Yāma Heaven.
He preaches the Dharma; or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the King of the Tuṣita Heaven;

or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Great Brahma Kings; or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Dragon Kings;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Yakṣa and Rākṣasa Kings;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Gandharva and Kiṃnara Kings; or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Asura and Dhānava Kings.
He is seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly; or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Garuḍa and Mahoraga kings;
or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of all other humans and non-humans;
or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of śrāvakas; or again, he is seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of pratyekabuddhas; or again, he is seen...

He preached the Dharma for the assembly of Bodhisattvas, from those who have first resolved their minds up to those who are bound to only one more birth and have received the empowerment of consecration.
He was seen praising and explaining all the merits of the stages from the first to the tenth; or he was seen praising and explaining the fulfillment of all the *pāramitās*;
or he was seen praising and explaining the entry into the various gates of patience (*kṣānti*); or he was seen praising and explaining the various...
The gate of the great samādhi. In some instances, one sees the praise and exposition of the profound gate of liberation;
in others, the praise and exposition of the realms of various dhyānas, samādhis, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); in others, the praise and exposition of the various practices of bodhisattvas;

in others, the praise and exposition of the various great vows; or in others, the praise and exposition of the various worldly means of livelihood and arts and crafts with fellow-practicing bodhisattvas.
He saw [the Bodhisattva] performing deeds to benefit sentient beings; or he saw him praising and expounding upon the gate of the empowerment of all Buddhas for bodhisattvas who share the same birth;

or he saw Maitreya for hundreds or thousands of years walking back and forth, reciting, copying out scriptures, diligently seeking and investigating, and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude;
or he saw him entering various meditative absorptions and the four immeasurable minds; or he saw him entering the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the various liberations.
They were liberated. Or they entered samādhi and, through the power of skillful means, manifested various supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).
Or they saw various bodhisattvas entering the transformation-samādhi (*nirmāṇasamādhi*), from each and every pore of their bodies emitting clouds of all manner of transformation-bodies;
or they saw them emit clouds of celestial hosts; or they saw them emit clouds of nāga hosts; or they saw them emit clouds of yakṣas and gandharvas.
He saw clouds of bodies of *piśācas*, *kiṃnaras*, *asuras*, *garuḍas*, and *mahoragas*; of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors;
of universal monarchs, minor kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues; and of elders and householders.
Or he saw clouds of bodies emerging as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and various bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas; or he saw clouds of bodies emerging as all sentient beings.
In some instances, they see him emit sublime sounds praising the various Dharma-gates of the bodhisattvas—namely, praising and expounding upon the gate of the merits of the bodhicitta;
praising and expounding upon the gates of the merits of the dāna-pāramitā up to the jñāna-pāramitā;

and praising and expounding upon the means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), the various dhyānas, the immeasurable minds (apramāṇacitta), as well as the various samādhis, samāpattis, superknowledges (abhijñā), and clarities (vidyā).
The dhāraṇīs and eloquence; all truths and all knowledges; tranquility and insight; liberation; all conditions; all supports; all dharma-gates of teaching;
the praise and exposition of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
all vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; all stages, all patiences, all practices, and all vows—such as these.

All such gateways of merit; or again, within them, one sees the Tathāgatas surrounded by great assemblies, and likewise clearly perceives the birthplaces and lineages of those Buddhas, their physical forms and lifespans, the names of their lands, eons, and titles, their preaching of the Dharma and its benefits, the duration for which their teachings remain, and even all the various differences among their sites of enlightenment and their congregations. Furthermore...
Furthermore, within the various pavilions inside that Treasury of Adornments, he saw one pavilion that was exceptionally high, vast, and magnificently decorated, being peerless and supreme.

Within it, he saw throughout the three thousandfold world system—in each of the ten billion sets of four continents and ten billion Tuṣita heavens—a Maitreya Bodhisattva descending from the divine realm to be born;
Śakra and Brahmā, the kings of gods, were supporting him at his crown.
He donned [the robes]. He walked seven steps and surveyed the ten directions with the roar of a great lion. He manifested as a youth dwelling in palaces and sporting in gardens.
For the sake of all-knowledge, he left the home life and practiced austerities. He showed himself receiving the milk-rice porridge and proceeding to the site of enlightenment.
There he subdued the various māras and attained equal and perfect awakening. He gazed upon the Bodhi tree, and the Brahma King exhorted him to turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
The wheels [of their Dharma], the ascent to celestial palaces to expound the Dharma, the number of eons and the span of their lifetimes,
the assemblies and adornments, the lands they purified, the practices and vows they cultivated, the skillful means for teaching and maturing sentient beings,
and the distribution of their relics and the maintenance of the teachings were all entirely different. At that time, Sudhana saw his own body present before all those Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, he perceives all the assemblies and all the Buddha-activities therein, retaining them without forgetfulness and penetrating them without obstruction.

Moreover, he hears from within all the pavilions the sounds of jewel nets, bells, and various musical instruments, all of which proclaim the inconceivable and subtle sounds of the Dharma, expounding various teachings. That is to say, some speak of the bodhisattva’s initial resolve.
The mind of enlightenment; or the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*); or the various vows; or the various stages (*bhūmi*);
or the respectful offerings made to the Tathāgatas; or the adornment of the Buddha-fields;
or the distinctions in the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma—he heard the sounds of all these aforementioned Buddha-dharmas being fully proclaimed and clearly elucidated. Furthermore...

I have heard that in such-and-such a place, a certain bodhisattva, having been exhorted by a certain spiritual friend, heard a certain Dharma-gate and resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
In a certain eon, at a certain buddha-field, in the presence of a certain Tathāgata and within a certain great assembly, they heard of the virtues of a certain Buddha;
they gave rise to such a mind, made such vows, and planted such vast roots of goodness.
Having practiced the bodhisattva path for a certain number of kalpas, one shall attain perfect enlightenment after that duration of time;
such shall be one's name, such the lifespan, and such the land, complete with its adornments; one shall fulfill such vows and transform such assemblies.
Such was the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas. After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for that many kalpas, benefiting such immeasurable sentient beings.

Some heard that in a certain place, a certain bodhisattva was practicing the various pāramitās—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; others heard that in another place...
There is a certain bodhisattva who, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, has renounced his royal throne, various precious jewels, wife, children, and retinue, as well as his hands, feet, head, eyes,
and all other limbs and members, without any sense of stinginess. Or, having heard that in a certain place there is a certain bodhisattva who protects the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata,
acting as a great Dharma teacher, extensively practicing the gift of Dharma, erecting the banner of the Dharma, and blowing [the conch].
They blow the conch of the Dharma, beat the drum of the Dharma, and rain down the rain of the Dharma. They construct stūpas and temples for the Buddha and fashion images of the Buddha.

They bestow all instruments of happiness upon all sentient beings. Or they hear that in a certain place, a certain Tathāgata attained equal and perfect enlightenment during a certain kalpa, in such a land, with such an assembly, with such a lifespan, preaching such a Dharma and fulfilling such vows.

Having thus transformed and taught such immeasurable sentient beings, when the youth Sudhana heard these and other such inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous sounds of the Dharma, his body and mind were filled with joy, becoming supple, delighted, and serene; he immediately attained immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī.

The various gates of eloquence; the various meditations, the various patiences, the various vows, and the various perfections; the various supernormal powers, the various clarities, as well as the various liberations and the gates of samādhi.
Furthermore, they saw within all the precious mirrors various forms and images: namely, some saw the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of the Buddhas;
some saw the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of the Bodhisattvas; and some saw the assemblies of the Śrāvakas.
He may see a bodhimanda; or he may see the assembly of pratyekabuddhas at a bodhimanda; or he may see a pure world; or he may see an impure world;
or he may see a world that is both pure and impure; or he may see a world that is both impure and pure;
or he may see a world where a Buddha resides; or he may see a world where no Buddha resides; or he may see a small world; or he may see a medium world; or he may see a great world.
Worlds— some seeing Indra-net worlds, some seeing inverted worlds, some seeing upright worlds, some seeing level worlds,
some seeing worlds inhabited by hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
and some seeing worlds filled with devas and humans; within such various worlds, they see countless great bodhisattvas.
Whether walking or sitting, the assembly of bodhisattvas engaged in various activities: they gave rise to great compassion out of pity for sentient beings;
they composed various treatises to benefit the world; they received, upheld, wrote down, recited, questioned, or answered [the teachings];

and at the three times of day, they performed repentance, dedicated their merit, and made vows. Furthermore, they saw a great light emanating from the mani-jewel kings within all the precious pillars.
The net of light was sometimes blue, sometimes yellow, sometimes red, or white;
it was the color of crystal, or the color of quartz, or the color of indranīla, or the color of a rainbow, or the color of Jambūnada gold; or it manifested the colors of all manner of radiances.
Furthermore, he saw those Jāmbūnada-gold youths and maidens, as well as various jeweled images. Some held clouds of flowers with their hands;
some held clouds of garments; some held banners and streamers; some held garlands and parasols; some carried various types of unguents and powdered incense;
some held exquisite nets of mani-jewels; some hung golden chains; some draped necklaces; or some raised up their...
They held ornaments in their arms; some lowered their heads, wearing jeweled *maṇi* crowns, and gazed up with bowed bodies, their eyes never wavering for a moment.

Furthermore, from those pearl necklaces there constantly issued fragrant water endowed with the eight virtues, while crystal necklaces emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light, shining simultaneously.
Banners, pennants, nets, and canopies—all such objects were likewise [made of these materials].
Adorned with various jewels, he further beheld blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*),
and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), each producing immeasurable flowers, some as large as a hand and others as long as a cubit.
Or again, they may be as wide and long as a chariot wheel; within each individual flower, various forms and images are manifested as adornments, namely:
the forms of men, the forms of women, the forms of boys, and the forms of girls.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas;
śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas—all such beings with their physical forms joined their palms, bowed their bodies, and paid homage.
They also beheld the Tathāgata sitting cross-legged, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
He adorned his body. Furthermore, he saw upon that ground of pure lapis lazuli, within the space of every single step, inconceivable varieties of forms and images:
namely, the forms and images of world-systems, the forms and images of bodhisattvas, the forms and images of Tathāgatas, as well as the forms and images of the adornments of various pavilions.
Moreover, within each and every thing—the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the jewel-trees—he saw them all.
Various forms of half-bodies appeared, namely: half-body images of Buddhas; half-body images of Bodhisattvas;
and those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, up to the world-protectors, wheel-turning sage-kings, minor kings, princes, ministers, and high officials, as well as half-body images of the fourfold assembly.
These various forms either held flower garlands, or held necklaces, or...

They bore all manner of ornaments. Some bowed their bodies with palms joined in reverence, gazing up at them with single-minded devotion, never for a moment averting their eyes; some offered praises; others entered into samādhi.
Their bodies were all adorned with the primary and secondary marks, universally emitting various colored rays of light—namely, golden light, silver-colored light, and coral-colored light.

There was light: light of the color of *duṣāra*, light of the color of *indranīla*, light of the color of *vairocana* jewels, light of the color of all kinds of precious gems, and light of the color of *campaka* flowers.

Furthermore, he saw from within the crescent-moon images in the various pavilions an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) variety of lights—suns, moons, and stars—shining universally throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, he saw that within every single step of the four surrounding walls of the various pavilions, all manner of precious jewels served as adornments;
within each and every jewel, there appeared Maitreya practicing the bodhisattva path over kalpas past, sometimes giving away his head or eyes.
Some give away their hands and feet, lips, tongues, teeth, ears, noses, blood, flesh, skin, bones, and marrow;
indeed, they are able to relinquish everything, including nails and hair, as well as wives, concubines, sons, daughters, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, and royal thrones.
Whatever they required, he gave it all to them. Those in prison he caused to be released; those who were bound he caused to be liberated.
For those with illnesses, he provided medical treatment; for those who had entered onto wrong paths, he showed them the right path.
Sometimes he acts as a boatman to ferry others across the great ocean; sometimes he acts as a horse-king to rescue and protect them from calamities;

sometimes he acts as a great seer to skillfully expound various treatises; sometimes he acts as a wheel-turning monarch to exhort the cultivation of the ten wholesome paths; and sometimes he acts as a king of physicians to skillfully heal all manner of ailments.
Some are filial and obedient to their parents; some draw near to virtuous friends; some become śrāvakas; some become pratyekabuddhas; some become bodhisattvas;

some become Tathāgatas to teach and subdue all sentient beings; some act as Dharma masters to uphold and practice the Buddha’s teachings, receiving, maintaining, reading, reciting, and reflecting upon them according to principle; they establish stūpas for the Buddha and fashion images of the Buddha. Whether by themselves...
If one makes offerings or encourages others to do so— such as by applying fragrant ointments, scattering flowers, and performing respectful prostrations— and continues such acts without interruption;
or if one sees [the Buddha] seated upon a lion throne extensively expounding the Dharma, encouraging all sentient beings to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action,
to single-mindedly take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, to uphold the five precepts and the eight fast-day precepts, and to leave the household life.
They listen to the Dharma, receive and uphold it, recite and chant it, and practice according to its principles.
They even behold the myriad forms of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s cultivation of all the perfections throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas.
Furthermore, they see all the spiritual friends whom Maitreya once served, adorned with every merit, and they also see Maitreya himself.

In the presence of each and every one of those spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he drew near, made offerings, and practiced their instructions, until he reached the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Then, the spiritual friends said to Sudhana, "Welcome, young man! Behold these inconceivable deeds of the Bodhisattvas;
do not give rise to weariness. At that time, the youth Sudhana attained the power of non-forgetfulness (*asampramoṣa*).
By the power of mindfulness, they obtain the pure eyes that see the ten directions; they obtain the unimpeded wisdom of skillful observation;
they obtain the sovereign wisdom of all bodhisattvas; and they obtain the vast understanding of all bodhisattvas who have already entered the stages of wisdom.
Within every single object of all the towers and pavilions, they see these things as well as other immeasurable and inconceivable phenomena.

Regarding the various adornments of the sovereign realm: it is like a person who, within a dream, sees all manner of things—namely, cities and towns, palaces and gardens, mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds;
clothing, food, and drink, as well as all other requisites for life; or they may see themselves, their parents, brothers, and internal or external relatives; or they may see...
They see the great ocean, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all the celestial palaces of the gods, as well as the affairs of Jambudvīpa and the other four continents;
or they see their own bodies, vast in measure for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, with houses and garments all proportionate to them.
Thus, throughout the day for immeasurable periods, they remain without sleep or slumber, experiencing various states of bliss. From sleep...
Having awakened, he realized it was a dream and was able to clearly remember all that he had seen.
Sudhana the youth was likewise so: because he was sustained by the power of Maitreya Bodhisattva; because he knew that all phenomena of the triple world are like a dream;

because he had extinguished the narrow and inferior conceptions of sentient beings; because he had attained a vast understanding free from obstacles; and because he dwelt in the supreme realm of the bodhisattvas.
Because of the realms, and because they have entered the inconceivable wisdom of skillful means, they are able to perceive such sovereign spheres of experience.
It is like a person who, when about to die, sees the signs of the retribution they will receive according to their karma.
Those who have practiced evil deeds see all the various states of suffering belonging to hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; or they see the wardens of hell holding...
Armed soldiers, either in anger or with curses, seize them and lead them away. They also hear the sounds of wailing and lamentation.

Some see the River of Ashes; some see the Cauldron of Boiling Water; some see the Mountain of Knives; some see the Forest of Swords. Thus they are oppressed by various means and undergo manifold sufferings.
Those who have performed virtuous deeds immediately see all the celestial palaces of the devas and the immeasurable hosts of devas.
The court ladies were fully adorned with various garments, and the palaces and gardens were all exquisitely beautiful.
Although his body was not yet dead, he saw such things through the power of karma. Sudhana the youth was likewise;
by the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva’s karma, he was able to see all these adorned realms. It is like a person who, [possessed] by a ghost...
Just as one who is possessed by a spirit can see various things and answer all questions put to them, so it was with Sudhana;
for, being sustained by the wisdom of the Bodhisattva, he saw all those magnificent adornments and there was no question he could not answer.
It was, for example, like a person possessed by a nāga, who, thinking himself to be a nāga, entered into...
In the Dragon Palace, what was but a short time seemed to him as if it had already passed through days, months, years, and ages. It was the same for the youth Sudhana;
because he dwelt in the perception of bodhisattva wisdom and was sustained by the empowerment of Maitreya Bodhisattva, what was but a short time appeared to him as immeasurable kalpas.
It was, for example, like the Brahma palace named Adorned Treasury (Vyūharatna), within which the entire trichiliocosm is fully perceived.
Just as all things in the world do not become confused or intermingled, so it was with the youth Sudhana.
Within the tower, he universally manifested all varieties of adorned realms, each distinct and without confusion.

It was, for example, like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*); whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remains within the objective sphere of that absorption.
Manifest before him. So it was with the youth Sudhana; he entered the tower and all its environments became perfectly clear to him.
It was as if a person were to see a city of the Gandharvas in the midst of space, complete with all its adornments, discerning them all without any obstruction.
It was as if the palace of a yakṣa and the palace of a human were situated together in one place.

They abide without intermingling, each perceiving differently according to their respective karma. It is like the great ocean, within which all the forms and images of the three thousandfold world system are seen.
It is like a master illusionist who, through the power of illusion, manifests various illusory phenomena and diverse activities.
So it was with the youth Sudhana; by the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva...
By the power [of his vows], and by the power of inconceivable, illusory wisdom, because he is able to know all phenomena through illusory wisdom,
and because he has attained the sovereign power of all bodhisattvas, he beheld within the pavilion the sovereign realm of all its adornments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya withdrew his supernormal powers, entered the pavilion, snapped his fingers to make a sound, and addressed [the assembly]:

Sudhana said, "Noble son, arise! Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). This is a manifestation produced by the gathering of causes and conditions through the Bodhisattva’s wisdom that knows all dharmas.
Thus, their intrinsic nature is like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, and a reflection; it is entirely unestablished.
At that time, Sudhana heard the sound of a finger-snap and arose from his samādhi. Maitreya addressed him, saying, "Excellent!"
"Son of noble family, you abide in the inconceivable sovereign liberation of a bodhisattva; you experience the joy and bliss of the samādhis of all bodhisattvas;

you are able to see the various sublime and wondrously adorned palaces manifested by the power of a bodhisattva’s spiritual authority, the flow of the factors conducive to enlightenment, and the wisdom of vows;
you behold the conduct of bodhisattvas, hear the Dharma of bodhisattvas, and understand the virtues of bodhisattvas as they truly are."
[He made] this aspiration. Sudhana said, "Indeed, O Noble One! This is through the power of the spiritual friend’s empowerment, mindfulness, and majestic authority.

Noble One, what is the name of this gate of liberation? Maitreya replied, "Good son, this gate of liberation is named 'The Adornment of the Treasury of the Wisdom of Unforgetting Mindfulness that Enters All Realms of the Three Times. Good son...
"Son, within this gate of liberation, there are unspeakably unspeakable gates of liberation that can be attained by a bodhisattva in a single lifetime.
Sudhana asked, "Where has this matter of adornment gone? Maitreya replied:
Regarding their coming and going: it was asked, "From where do they come? He replied, "They come from within the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva;
they abide by relying on the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva. They have no place of departure, nor do they have a place of abiding. They are neither accumulated nor permanent."
"Free from all [such things], son of good family. It is like a dragon king sending down rain:
it does not emerge from his body, nor does it emerge from his mind, yet there is no place where it is not seen, for it is not accumulated.
It simply pours down in torrents by the power of the dragon king’s mental intention, pervading the entire world. Such a realm is inconceivable. Son of good family, that same adornment..."
It is likewise so. It does not abide within, nor does it abide without, yet it is not that it is not seen.

Rather, it is by the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority (*anubhāva*) and the power of your own roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that you see such a thing. Son of good family, it is like a master illusionist who performs various illusory feats;
they come from nowhere and go nowhere. Although there is no coming or going, through the power of illusion, they appear with vivid clarity.
It can be seen that these matters of adornment are likewise so: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
Although there is no coming or going, they manifest in this way due to the power of inconceivable illusory wisdom cultivated through habituation, as well as by the power of former great vows.
Sudhana said, "From where, O Great Sage, have you come? Maitreya replied:
"Good son, all bodhisattvas come in such a manner as to have neither coming nor going; they come in such a manner as to have neither movement nor abiding.
They are without location and without attachment; they neither perish nor arise; they neither abide nor shift; they neither move nor originate; they are without longing and without clinging;
they are without karma and without retribution; they are without origination and without cessation; they are neither discontinuous nor eternal—in this way do they come. Good son..."

Sons, Bodhisattvas come from the state of great compassion because they wish to discipline all sentient beings; they come from the state of great loving-kindness because they wish to protect and deliver all sentient beings;
they come from the state of pure ethical discipline because they take birth according to their inclinations;
they come from the state of great vows because they are sustained by the power of their past aspirations; they come from the state of supernormal powers...
Because they manifest according to the inclinations of all beings in every place; because they come from the state of immovability, never abandoning any Buddha;
because they come from the state of neither grasping nor rejecting, not subjecting body or mind to the toil of coming and going;
because they come from the state of wisdom and skillful means, acting in accordance with all sentient beings; because they come from the state of manifesting transformations, just like...
Because they are manifested as reflections. However, noble son, as for your question regarding where I have come from:
noble son, I have come here from my birthplace, the country of Mālava. Noble son, there is a village there called Āvāsika, and a son of a householder named Gopāla.
It was for the sake of transforming that man and leading him into the Buddha’s [teaching] that I came.
He dwells there in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, he teaches the Dharma to all the people of that land according to their various ways of practice.
He also expounds the Mahāyāna to his parents, kinsmen, and Brahmins, causing them to enter it;
thus he dwells there and has come from there. Sudhana said: "Noble One, what is this Bodhi..."
"Regarding the birthplace of a Bodhisattva, he replied: 'Good son, there are ten birthplaces of a Bodhisattva. What are these ten?

Good son, the bodhicitta is the birthplace of a Bodhisattva, for it gives birth to the family of Bodhisattvas. The profound mind (adhyāśaya) is the birthplace of a Bodhisattva, for it gives birth to the family of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
The stages (bhūmi) are the birthplace of a Bodhisattva, for they give birth to the family of the perfections (pāramitā).'"
