Therefore, the Great Vow is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives rise to the family of sublime practices; great compassion is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives rise to the family of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
investigation according to reality is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives rise to the family of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
and the Mahāyāna is the birthplace of bodhisattvas, for it gives rise to the family of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Thus they transform and guide sentient beings.

This is because this bodhisattva is born into the family of the Buddhas as their place of birth. Wisdom and skillful means are the place of birth for this bodhisattva, as they are born into the family of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The cultivation of all dharmas is the place of birth for this bodhisattva, as they are born into the family of all Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. Good son, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
The mother is skillful means; the father is skillful expedient (*upāya-kauśalya*); the wet-nurse is the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*);

the foster-mother is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); the ornaments are the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); the caregiver is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);

the washerwoman is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the teacher; and all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are one’s companions.
All wholesome dharmas are one’s retinue; all bodhisattvas are one’s brothers; the bodhicitta is one’s family;

practice in accordance with reality is the family tradition; the stages (bhūmis) are the family residence; the various patiences (kṣāntis) are the family clan; the great vows are the family instruction;
fulfilling all practices is following the family tradition; exhorting others toward the Mahāyāna is the succession of the family estate; and the water of the Dharma...
The consecrated bodhisattva, bound to only one more birth, acts as a crown prince; having accomplished awakening, he is able to purify his lineage.
Son of good family, in this way the bodhisattva transcends the stage of ordinary beings, enters the rank of bodhisattvas, and is born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
Abiding in the Buddha-lineage, they are able to cultivate all practices without severing the Three Jewels. They are well able to protect the Bodhisattva clan and purify the Bodhisattva seed.
Their place of birth is noble and supreme, free from all faults and evils.
They are revered and praised by all the worlds, including devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. Good son, when a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born into such [a lineage]...
This is the family of the Honored and Exalted. Because they know all phenomena to be like reflections, they harbor no contempt for any in the world.
Because they know all phenomena to be like magical transformations, they are unstained by attachment to any realm of existence (*gati*).
Because they know all phenomena to be without self, they teach and transform sentient beings with minds free from weariness. Great compassion constitutes their essential nature.
Therefore, they embrace sentient beings without perceiving weariness or hardship. Because they thoroughly understand that birth and death are like a dream, they pass through all kalpas without fear.
Because they know that all aggregates are like illusions, they manifest taking birth without fatigue or aversion.
Because they know that the elements and sense bases are identical to the dharma-realm, they do not destroy or annihilate any sensory objects. Knowing all...
Because they perceive thoughts as being like a mirage, they enter the various realms of existence without giving rise to deluded confusion.
Because they realize that all phenomena are like illusions, they enter the realm of Māra without giving rise to defiled attachment. Because they know the Dharma-body, no afflictions can deceive them.
Because they have attained mastery, they penetrate all realms of existence without obstruction. Good son, my body is born everywhere.
The entire dharma-realm is equal to the diverse physical forms of all sentient beings; equal to the various distinct voices and sounds of all sentient beings;

equal to the manifold names and titles of all sentient beings; equal to the manifestation of birth by all pure sentient beings, conforming to the world through the display of preferred modes of conduct for the purpose of teaching, transforming, and subduing them. It is equal to all these things.

All activities are those performed by ordinary beings; they regard all sentient beings with equanimity and manifest their bodies to fill the Dharma-realm in accordance with the vows of all Bodhisattvas.

Good son, I manifest in order to transform and deliver those who previously practiced the same conduct as I but have now fallen away from the bodhicitta, and also to teach and transform my parents and kin.

...belonging to [this category]. Furthermore, in order to teach and transform the various brahmins so that they might abandon their pride regarding their lineage and be born into the Tathāgata-gotra, I was born here in this Jambudvīpa realm, in the country of Mālava, in the village of Koṭa, into a brahmin family.
Good son, I dwell here within this great pavilion, according to the needs of all sentient beings.
That which the mind delights in, I teach through various skillful means to transform and subdue them. Good son, it is because I act in accordance with the minds of sentient beings;
because I wish to bring to maturity those gods in the Tuṣita Heaven who share my same practice;
and because I wish to manifest the transformations and adornments of a Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom, which surpass all realms of desire, so as to cause them to renounce all [attachments].
It is for the sake of sensual pleasure; to cause them to know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; to cause them to know that the prosperity of the devas must inevitably decline;
and to manifest, at the time of his imminent descent into birth, the dharma-gate of great wisdom by engaging in discourse with bodhisattvas in their final birth.

In order to gather and transform those who practice in concert with me, and to cause those sent by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to be fully awakened like lotuses in bloom, you shall pass away from this life and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Son of good family, when my vows are fulfilled and I attain omniscience and realize Bodhi, both you and Mañjuśrī shall behold me together. Son of good family...
"Son, you should go to the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī and ask him: 'How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct?
How does one enter the gateway of Samantabhadra’s conduct? How is it accomplished? How is it expanded? How is it followed?
How is it purified? How is it perfected? Son of good family, he will explain these for you."
He explained this in detail. Why is this? The great vows of Mañjuśrī are not shared by any other bodhisattvas, even those numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas.
Good son, the conduct of the youth Mañjuśrī is vast and his vows are boundless; he brings forth all the merits of a bodhisattva without ever ceasing.
"Good son, Mañjuśrī is constantly the mother of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas;
he is constantly the teacher of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Bodhisattvas.
He teaches and brings to maturity all sentient beings, and his fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions. He constantly expounds the Dharma within the assemblies of all Buddhas."
"O Master, you are praised by all Tathāgatas. You abide in profound wisdom and are able to see all phenomena as they truly are.
You have attained mastery over the realm of all liberations and have brought to ultimate completion all the practices of Samantabhadra. O son of noble family!"
The youth Mañjuśrī is your spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He causes you to be born into the family of the Tathāgatas;
he nurtures all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and gives rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
He brings you to meet with true spiritual friends, causing you to cultivate all merits, to enter the net of all vows, and to abide in all great vows. For your sake, he has taught this one...
All the secret dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and all the inconceivable practices of the bodhisattvas, are manifested.
You were born together with them in the past and have practiced together with them; therefore, noble son, you should go to the place of Mañjuśrī without becoming weary or discouraged.
Mañjuśrī shall explain all merits to you. Why is this? Because of the various virtues that you previously beheld...
That Jñānakīrti entered the gate of liberation through the bodhisattva practices and fulfilled his great vows—all of this was due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.

Mañjuśrī has attained ultimate perfection in all respects. At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.
At that time, having been praised for his bodhicitta by Maitreya, the youth Sudhana was instructed, saying:
"You should enter this Great Pavilion of the Vairocana-Adorned Treasury and observe it thoroughly;
then you will be able to fully understand the training in the conduct of a bodhisattva. Then Sudhana said, "I pray only that the Great Sage would open the pavilion..."
The gatekeeper permitted me to enter because this pavilion is the very treasury of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha*).
Since Sudhana’s practice had reached its ultimate limit, he sought to realize and enter it. At that moment, Maitreya snapped his fingers, and the door opened immediately.

However, it was necessary for Maitreya to snap his fingers because one must rely on external conditions (*pratyaya*) to be added before sudden realization can occur; the underlying intent lies in the transcendence of words.

Therefore, he merely snapped his fingers. As for "having entered, he immediately closed [the door]," it is because one enters the secret and wondrous gate of the *dharmadhātu-garbha* through the characteristic of non-entry;

thus, having entered, he closes it again. That Sudhana saw the pavilion as being like space is to manifest that the *tathāgatagarbha* is empty, and that its nature, which accords with the *dharmadhātu*, is vast and inclusive, containing all phenomena without exception. However...

The phrase "adorned with various kinds of exquisite jewels" symbolizes that the non-empty essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses adornments consisting of merits equal in number to the sands of the Ganges that accord with its nature.
Therefore, below this, twenty-two lines of scripture appear, which fully clarify the various adornments within the pavilion; this precisely clarifies the entry into the *dharmadhātugarbha*.

The realm thus realized is the dependent retribution; this is called the "inferior vision of the primary retribution. As soon as he prostrated himself, he saw his own body pervading all the pavilions.

Furthermore, he saw the Dharma realized by Maitreya from the time he first resolved for enlightenment, through his cultivation over successive kalpas, as well as his performance of bodhisattva practices throughout many lifetimes, and how he gathered in and transformed sentient beings according to their various types. In every place...
In various places, he preached the Dharma; there are thirty-eight lines of sutra that clarify the deeds of Maitreya’s causal practices as seen within the pavilion.
This constitutes the vision of Maitreya alone, his primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Next, there are more than ten lines of sutra where one sees various bodhisattvas entering the *nirmāṇa-samādhi*; these clarify the vision of the various practices of the accompanying bodhisattvas.

This refers to the aforementioned immeasurable retinue. Next, there are two lines and a half of scripture which further reveal the virtues of the various Buddhas and Tathāgatas who gather and transform beings therein. The above constitutes the realm contained within the pavilions;
next, one again sees a principal pavilion among the various pavilions within that Treasury of Adornments. There are ten lines of scripture clarifying this principal pavilion.

Within [this vision], he clearly saw the three thousandfold world-system and the ten billion Tuṣita heavens, each of which contained Maitreya’s eight manifestations of attaining enlightenment, up to the distribution of his relics.

Sudhana also saw himself within each of those assemblies at the sites of Maitreya’s enlightenment, hearing the Dharma and gaining benefit; he recollected these without forgetting and attained thorough penetration.
Without obstruction, he next heard various sounds emerging from within all the various adornments inside the pavilions, proclaiming the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Each individual adornment possessed various functions and spheres of activity.

There are seventy-six lines and a half of sūtra that explain in detail the majestic adornments, activities, and spheres within the pavilion. Next, following this, there are four lines of sūtra stating:
"At that time, Sudhana attained the inconceivable, sovereign sphere of mindfulness and recollection regarding all matters of majestic adornment.
This serves as a summary to manifest the characteristics of what was seen. Next, it says: "For example, suppose there were a person..."
Within dreams, one sees various objects, even up to all the sovereign realms of adornment.
There are thirty-three lines of scripture that use metaphors to clarify the characteristics of what is seen; each has its own underlying reason. The text contains ten such metaphors.
Each metaphor illustrates that the characteristics of the seer and the seen are each distinct from one another. Thus, from the time the noble Sudhana entered the pavilion until this point,

these one hundred and eighty-six lines of scripture collectively reveal the realm within the pavilion and comprehensively manifest the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*) in the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein the environment and the inhabitants are layered upon layer.

The inexhaustible, inexhaustible realm—the fourfold Dharma-realm and ten profound gateways of principle and contemplation expounded throughout the entire sutra—are fully contained within this single pavilion; their subtlety reaches its ultimate peak here.
Because Sudhana enters this Dharma-realm, he is able to perfect the fruits of vast eons within a single lifetime. Yet, while the text of the sutra may appear coarse and easily perceived, its...
The dharma-gate of reality is inconceivable, subtle, and difficult to know;

that is, the causes and effects of the preceding five stages all ultimately converge here, which is what is called the final consummation of entering the Dharma-realm. Nevertheless, it all ultimately returns to being like a dream and like an illusion.
What are called birth-and-death and nirvana are both like a dream from yesterday.

The unobstructed dependent origination of the dharma-realm does not, in its entirety, transcend the *māyopama-samādhi* (the samādhi that is like an illusion). Those who are resolved to enter the dharma-realm should contemplate this deeply.
However, the realm within the upper pavilion was what Sudhana perceived while in samādhi.
Having seen these things, Maitreya then withdrew his supernatural power, snapped his fingers to make a sound, and addressed Sudhana, saying: "O son of good family, arise!
Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). These are signs manifested through the gathering of causes and conditions. Thus it was for himself...
Their nature is like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, and like a reflection; none of them are established.
This demonstrates the tenet of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). "None are established" directly points to the core of the doctrine of dependent origination.

Because the one true *dharmadhātu* is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is able to accord with conditions precisely because it lacks intrinsic nature. Nevertheless, all phenomena...
Phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they arise from conditions; thus, from the perspective of facts, they are not established. They lack intrinsic nature because they arise from conditions;
thus, from the perspective of principle, they are not established. Because each is unestablished, every phenomenon arises from conditions without obstruction or hindrance.

Yet this essential meaning is revealed throughout various passages in the sūtras; it is here, at this ultimate stage, that the fundamental source is directly pointed out, and it is described as being like an illusion.
It was as if he had tied it while dreaming. At that time, Sudhana heard the sound of a finger-snap and arose from samādhi.
Maitreya said to him, "You have dwelt in this inconceivable liberation; this serves to certify that Sudhana has personally realized it.
Sudhana replied, "This is due to the power of the spiritual friend’s majestic empowerment. Thus Sudhana emerged from samādhi.
He arose and asked Maitreya, "What is the name of this gate of liberation?
Maitreya replied, "This gate of liberation is named 'The Adorned Treasury of the Wisdom of Unforgetting Recollection that Enters All Realms of the Three Times.
Because this is a great gate of liberation that encompasses the general characteristics of the entire Dharma-realm, within it there are unspeakably unspeakable [qualities]."

"Liberation. This is the direct designation for the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). However, regarding the statement that "this is what is attained by a Bodhisattva in their final birth," this refers to the person capable of abiding therein, who is at the ultimate limit of the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*).

This sufficiently demonstrates that this Dharma-gate cannot be known by those of the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ pṛthagjanāḥ*) or the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa āryabhūmayaḥ*). Next, Sudhana asked: "From where does this supreme Dharma-realm come?"
This reaches the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-bhūtakoṭi*). Maitreya replied, "It comes from the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
This reveals that the dharma-realm arises from conditions. Since it is said to arise from conditions, there is neither coming nor going;
therefore, it is said to be "far removed from all [extremes]. Thus, the analogy of the dragon king sending down rain is taught to demonstrate that [all things] are but the mind.

Manifestation. Next, the analogy of a magician and his illusions is taught to demonstrate that things lack intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, thereby showing that they are fundamentally unarisen.
Thus, he concludes by pointing his finger and saying: "Through the power of the habitual practice of illusory wisdom, they manifest in this way.

The above clarifies that the dharma-realm, including both the primary and secondary environments, is like an illusion. Below, Sudhana asks Maitreya from where he has come; this question concerns Maitreya’s origin.
Regarding the phrase "coming from a place," the intention is that while the realm of liberation may be admitted to be like an illusion, how could the person who dwells therein be like an illusion?
Therefore, this examines the physical characteristics of the primary retribution (*vipāka*). However, Maitreya answers according to reality by citing three kinds of places from which one comes.
The first answer states: "That which comes is without coming and without going, neither arising nor ceasing. This—
In terms of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, it pervades all places; thus, "coming without coming" refers solely to the principle (*li*).
Next, the statement "coming from the place of great compassion" and so forth refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* coming from the myriad practices (*sambhāra*).
Finally, when it says, "As for your question of where I come from," it explains that [the Buddha] comes from his birthplace, the country of Māratī.

This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*. Because it manifests birth in various places according to the capacities of sentient beings in order to discipline them, it is intended to reveal that Maitreya has perfected the ten thousand practices and fully realized the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Upon hearing Maitreya’s account of his place of birth, Sudhana immediately asked, "What is the place of birth for a bodhisattva? To which Maitreya replied:

Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of birthplaces. Taking the bodhicitta as the root for birth into the Buddha-family, in each of these ten phrases, the preceding clause represents the practice that gives birth, and the following clause represents the family into which one is born.
This continues until, ultimately, all phenomena give birth to the family of all Tathāgatas; this specifically refers to the Reward-Buddha (vipākabuddha) born of conditions. Above.
This clarifies that the ten kinds of mind constitute the primary practice for birth into the Buddha-family. Following this, it clarifies the conditions for the arising of the retinue;
namely, the ten pāramitās serve as the auxiliary practices. Therefore, it is said: "Skillful means is the father, and prajñā is the mother."

This constitutes the parents of the two bodies: the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *sambhogakāya*. Next, there are twelve lines of scripture following the passage "The Bodhisattva thus transcends the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), enters the rank of a Bodhisattva, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata," which provide a comparative evaluation to manifest his excellence.
This means that because he has been born into the family of the Tathāgata as the most honored and supreme, next [the text] says:

"My body is universally born throughout the entire dharma-realm," etc., from the *Wuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Five Practices). This is Maitreya’s own manifestation of his true retribution; having already realized the dharmakāya, he is able to manifest a true body according to his vows, filling the dharma-realm.
Next, it says: "In order to transform and deliver those with whom I shared vows in the past, I abide here."
In the pavilions, he employs skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. There are five sūtras that clarify his manifestation of birth into a brahmin family in the country of Malada;
this was his body manifested in accordance with conditions. Next, it says:
"In order to accord with sentient beings and to bring to maturity those gods of the Tuṣita Heaven who share the same practice as myself, I passed away from here and was born in the Tuṣita Heaven."

There are six lines of sūtra that clarify how one shall be born in Tuṣita as the body of an Ekajātipratibaddha (one bound to only one more birth), revealing this to fellow-practicing bodhisattvas so that they may awaken and enter [the path].
Therefore, it is said: "Those sent by Śākyamuni arrive like the blooming of lotus flowers."
Thus we know that those who hear the Dharma at Maitreya’s first assembly when he appears in the future will all be disciples of our Śākyamuni during the final dharma-age (*mappō*).
All who propagate the Dharma shall be born in Tuṣita Heaven to receive Maitreya’s teachings; therefore, they will serve as his retinue in the future.
Hence, the concluding passage states: "When my vows are fulfilled and I attain bodhi, you and Mañjuśrī..."
All are able to see me. This Mañjuśrī is a Buddha who has already attained realization in the past;
Maitreya is a Buddha who will appear in the future; and Sudhana, moreover, is a future Buddha under Maitreya.
Thus, the three sages have been brought together to conclude the manifestation of the Dharma-gate. Now, he points out the next spiritual friend: "You should go to Mañjuśrī."
Regarding the phrase "at the place of the good spiritual friend," the intention is to direct Sudhana to see Mañjuśrī and inquire about the dharma-gate for entering the ocean of fruition.
This signifies reflecting back upon the source of the mind as the essential means for realization and entry. Next, regarding the section beginning with "For what reason":
The "Investigation and Explanation" (*zhǐshì*) points to the reason why Mañjuśrī was seen. Its intent is: Mañjuśrī has already been seen; why must he be seen again?

The "Explanation" (*shì*) clarifies that because his virtue is profound and vast, and his past affinities (*pūrvapratyaya*) are weighty, there are ten lines and a half of scripture that clarify the reasons for the vastness of his virtue and the depth of his affinities.
Its meaning is that because of Mañjuśrī, Sudhana has now arrived here and attained birth [in this state].
The family of the Tathāgata all relies upon the power of great wisdom. If one wishes to reach the ultimate ocean of fruition, nothing short of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom can bring about such wondrous accord.
This is because the beginning and the source are unified; therefore, you must go to see him. Hence it is said:
"For this reason, you should go to see him. Thus it is said: "All the spiritual friends you have previously encountered were all through the majestic power of Mañjuśrī."
"The power of the deity must now be seen once; only then shall one attain the ultimate realization in all places. He cautioned him, saying, "Do not give rise to weariness or fatigue.
Having heard these instructions, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and took his leave to depart.

Because Maitreya’s practice is perfected and his stage is ultimate, there is no further deference or recommendation. The section on the causal characteristics of the superior gathering of virtues is hereby concluded.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
commentary on the meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
and edited and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fǎyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Entering the Dharma Realm, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Twenty-one. At that time,
following the instructions of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages,
passing through more than one hundred and ten cities, until he arrived at the city of Sumana in the country of Samantamukha, where he stood at its gate.
Mañjuśrī reflected upon this, observing him with sympathetic attention as he wandered about in search of him, desiring to pay his respects.
At that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar across a distance of one hundred and ten *yojanas* and placed it upon Sudhana’s head, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! If one is devoid of the root of faith, with a weak mind and full of regret, [one's] meritorious practice..."
They lack the diligence to avoid regression; they develop attachment to even a single root of virtue; they consider themselves satisfied with meager merit;
they are unable to skillfully initiate practices and vows; they are not sustained by spiritual friends; they are not remembered by the Tathāgatas;
and they are unable to understand such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā) or such a principle (naya).

Regarding this Dharma-gate, its such practice, and its such sphere: whether it be thorough knowledge, manifold knowledge, fathoming the source and bottom, understanding, entering, liberation, discrimination, realization, or attainment—none are able to accomplish these at all.
At that time, Mañjuśrī proclaimed this Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
The youth Sudhana accomplished incalculable dharma-gates and was endowed with the light of immeasurable great wisdom.
He caused [the youth] to attain the boundless *dhāraṇī* of a bodhisattva, boundless vows, boundless samādhis, boundless supernormal powers, and boundless knowledge;
he caused him to enter the site of practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct and established him in his own station.
At that dwelling place, Mañjuśrī withdrew and disappeared from sight. Thereupon, Sudhana reflected and contemplated,
single-mindedly aspiring to see Mañjuśrī and to behold as many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm,
all of whom he would approach, revere, and serve, receiving and practicing their instructions without any opposition.
From here begins the fourth major section, which clarifies that wisdom illuminates the non-dual aspect.

It reveals that the essence of the causal dharmas producing their fruits is free from discrimination, as it transcends all dualistic characteristics such as object and cognition. Furthermore, since Sudhana’s obstacles have been exhausted and his delusions removed, he has never stirred a thought;
therefore, his retrospective illumination is nothing other than his original mind, with no difference whatsoever. Thus, Sudhana’s cause...

The stages have already been exhausted. That one encounters Mañjuśrī once again at this point signifies that, since the very first arousal of the mind directed toward Bodhi originated with Mañjuśrī, it represents the arising of *ādi-kṣānti-jñāna* (initial awakening wisdom) from *mūla-jñāna* (fundamental wisdom). Now, having progressed until delusion is exhausted and reality is fully realized, one desires to enter the ocean of fruition.

To do so, one must necessarily bring *ādi-bodha* (initial awakening) into accord with *mūla-bodha* (original awakening). This non-duality of initial and original awakening is called [the state of] "non-dual name."

Because it is ultimate awakening, it should be seen. As for the statement that "wisdom illuminates non-duality," wisdom is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and illumination is the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*);
because the initial and the fundamental are unified, they are said to be without dual characteristics.
Upon reaching this point, all mental objects and states of mind are resolved into the perfection of the one mind, which constitutes the ultimate. However, as for not seeing Mañjuśrī, it is because...
In this regard, they are utterly transcendent. Because the Dharma-body has no "this" or "that," there is no mutual seeing between them.

When it is said that he extends his right hand from afar across one hundred and ten *yojanas*, and further mentions passing through one hundred and ten cities, this symbolizes that each of the ten *pāramitās* cultivated throughout the ten stages (*bhūmis*) possesses ten aspects, thus totaling one hundred;
while the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) constitutes the one hundred and first.

It encompasses the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Yet, because Sudhana perfectly integrates all virtues, it is said that he "surpasses" them; this truly transcends the dualistic mind and its objects, being free from all relative dependence.
As for the phrase "stretching out his right hand from afar," it signifies that Sudhana’s journey through the various stages is entirely based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
This means that the fulfillment of wisdom is not different from the initial resolve; hence, it is called "stretching the right hand from afar," symbolizing conformity with the *dharmadhātu*.
This is the nature [of the teaching]. According to this, "the crown of Sudhana's head" indicates that his station is the supreme, unsurpassed summit of the Dharma.
As for the expression "Excellent! Excellent!"—the fact that he does not see Mañjuśrī but only hears words of praise signifies that the ineffable Way is manifested through speech.
If one lacks the root of faith, even those at the lowest level will be unable to practice the six lines of the sutra. Thus it is said:
By citing their incapacity, one manifests their capacity. If one were to omit the nine phrases beginning with "the faculty of faith," it would be said that they are incapable.

The fourteen subsequent phrases beginning with "unable to fully comprehend" all serve to conversely manifest their capacity. Regarding the phrase "unable to fully comprehend," it should be stated as "then one would be unable to fully comprehend.
The intended meaning is that if one lacks the faculty of faith and so forth, one will be unable to fully comprehend this.
The fourteen dharmas clearly demonstrate that because Sudhana does not depart from the root of faith and so forth, he is able to comprehend these various gateways.
This specifically elucidates the meaning of not departing from the initial resolve; hence, the subsequent text states:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī proclaimed this dharma, causing Sudhana to accomplish incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) dharma-gateways and the eight kinds of boundlessness."
From "The Great Wisdom" onwards, the entry of wisdom into the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda is entirely the benefit of not being separated from the root of faith;

this concludes the benefits by returning them to the source. The concluding phrase, "and placing Sudhana at his own place of abiding," correctly signifies that initial awakening (ādikṣānti-jñāna) is gathered back into original awakening (mūla-awakening), for they are one and the same awakening. Therefore, it is called "his own place of abiding. Thus says the text.

As for the statement that "the extraordinary [wisdom] further subsumes the unmanifest": once one has entered true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), one is distanced from all characteristics of the mental sphere.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "The site of practice (*caryā-maṇḍala*) of Samantabhadra is the principle of the *dharmadhātu*; the place where he himself abides is the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
Principle and wisdom are of one suchness. This is explained as "entering" and "abiding. When faith reaches the limit of the sphere of wisdom, the characteristics of faith then vanish.

Therefore, it is said that he does not appear. Nevertheless, after Sudhana received from Mañjuśrī the revelation of the *dharma*-gates for accomplishing incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) qualities and so forth, he dwelt in the very place where Mañjuśrī himself resides.

Thereupon, reflecting and observing with single-minded resolve, he wished to see Mañjuśrī as well as the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) numbering as many as the atoms in three thousandfold worlds. This meaning of "dwelling" should be understood as being equivalent to this.
Regarding the mind after awakening: because Sudhana’s realization of the nature [of reality] has not yet been forgotten, he still wishes to see [the Bodhisattvas].

When one’s realization accords with the wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one sees that the ocean-like virtues of the nature are all present within the source of the mind; thus, all dharma-gates do not depart from the present moment of thought.
Therefore, he served all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm without ever showing opposition.
Consequently, it was not necessary for him to seek them out from afar one by one to pay his respects. Thus, it is later said that he "universally observed and universally heard.

Nevertheless, while Sudhana later beheld Samantabhadra, in this instance Mañjuśrī directly proclaims the dharma-gate of accomplishment, simply stating that he causes [beings] to enter into the state of Samantabhadra.
The practice of the Way is exhausted in a single phrase; there is nothing further to instruct later friends.

This intention signifies that the ocean of fruition transcends words, requiring one to reach a wondrous resonance beyond speech, allowing only for self-awakening. Once the superior wisdom has illuminated the non-dual aspect, it is complete.
They increase their pursuit of all-encompassing wisdom, expand the vast ocean of compassion, and augment the great cloud of loving-kindness.

Universally observing the birth of sentient beings, they give rise to great joy and dwell securely in the bodhisattva’s gateways to tranquility. They universally take as their object all vast realms of experience.
They study the vast merits of all Buddhas; they enter the definitive knowledge and vision of all Buddhas; they increase the factors conducive to the path that assist all-encompassing wisdom;
they skillfully cultivate the profound resolve of all Bodhisattvas; and they know the sequence of the appearance of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Entering the ocean of all dharmas; turning all wheels of Dharma; giving birth to all worlds; entering the ocean of all bodhisattva vows;
dwelling through all kalpas to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva; illuminating the spheres of all Tathāgatas; nurturing all the faculties of a bodhisattva;
attaining the pure radiance of omniscience; and universally shining upon the ten directions to eliminate [all darkness].

All dark obstructions are cleared away; wisdom pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Throughout all Buddha-fields and all states of existence, he universally manifests his body, reaching everywhere without exception.
He crushes all obstacles and enters the unimpeded Dharma, abiding in the ground of equality within the Dharma-realm.
Observing the realm of Samantabhadra’s liberation, they immediately heard the names, practices, and vows of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,

as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment, the direct path, the stages (*bhūmi*), the skillful means of the stages, the entries into the stages, the advancements within the stages, the abidings in the stages, and the cultivation of the stages.
Regarding the realm of the earth, the power of the earth, and the coexistence within the earth, they felt a yearning desire to behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Thereupon,
before the lion throne of Vairocana Tathāgata at this Vajragarbha Bodhimanda, upon a seat of a lotus treasury of all jewels,
they gave rise to a mind as vast as the realm of empty space, relinquishing all lands and becoming free from all attachments.
An unobstructed mind; an unobstructed mind that universally practices all unobstructed dharmas; an unobstructed mind that enters everywhere into the oceans of the ten directions;
a pure mind that universally enters the realm of all-knowledge; and a clear and lucid mind that contemplates the adornments of the site of enlightenment.
A vast mind that enters the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas; a pervasive mind that transforms the realms of all sentient beings; an immeasurable mind that purifies all lands;
an inexhaustible mind that abides through all kalpas; and a consummate mind that proceeds toward the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
When the youth Sudhana gave rise to such minds, by the power of his own roots of goodness, [he was sustained] by all the Tathāgatas.
Through the power of empowerment and the power of shared roots of goodness with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, one perceives ten kinds of auspicious signs.
What are these ten? They are: perceiving all Buddha-fields as pure; seeing all Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment;
seeing all Buddha-fields as pure and free from all evil realms; and seeing all Buddha-fields as pure, filled with various wondrous lotuses.
They took these as solemn adornments. They saw all Buddha-fields as pure, with the bodies and minds of all sentient beings being pure;
they saw all Buddha-fields as pure, adorned with various kinds of precious jewels;
they saw all Buddha-fields as pure, with all sentient beings having their bodies adorned by the marks of excellence; they saw all Buddha-fields as pure, with clouds of various adornments.
He covered it with these. He saw all Buddha-fields purified, and all sentient beings arising in mutual compassion for one another, benefiting each other and not causing harm.
He saw all Buddha-fields purified as sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), adorned with splendor.
He saw all Buddha-fields purified, and all sentient beings whose minds were constantly mindful of the Buddha. These are the ten. Furthermore, he saw ten kinds [of things].
The marks of radiance. What are the ten? They are as follows: seeing all the atoms within all worlds;
from each and every atom, clouds of nets of light-rays of Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, emerge and pervasively illuminate;
and from each and every atom, clouds of wheels of light-rays of Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds, emerge with various colors and forms.

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, from within each and every atom there emerge clouds of jewel-like physical forms of Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
From within each and every atom there emerge clouds of flaming wheels of Buddha-radiance, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
From within each and every atom there emerge [clouds of] various wondrous... as numerous as the atoms in all worlds.
Clouds of incense pervaded the ten directions, extolling the great ocean of merit of all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

From within every single atom emerged clouds of suns, moons, and stars as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, all emitting the light of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva that universally illumines the Dharma-realm. From within every single atom emerged [clouds] as numerous as the atoms in all worlds...
From the bodies of all sentient beings, clouds of physical forms emit the Buddha’s light, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.
From within each and every atom, there emerge clouds of mani-jewels in the form of the physical bodies of all Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
From within each and every atom, there emerge clouds of the physical bodies of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, filling the Dharma-realm.
The realms: causing all sentient beings to attain liberation and have their aspirations fulfilled;

from within every single atom, there emerge clouds of the physical forms and images of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, proclaiming the vast vows of all Buddhas that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
These are the ten. At that time, the youth Sudhana, having seen these ten kinds of radiant signs, [prostrated himself].
He then thought to himself: "I shall now certainly behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; I shall increase my roots of goodness and behold all Buddhas;
regarding the vast realm of all Bodhisattvas, I shall give rise to resolute understanding and attain all-knowledge.
At that time, Sudhana fully restrained his senses and sought with a single mind to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, giving rise to a heart of great diligence that never wavered.

Immediately, with the universal eye, one observes the spheres of experience perceived by all Buddhas and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, conceiving in each case the thought that one has attained the vision of Samantabhadra. With the eye of wisdom, one contemplates the path of Samantabhadra;
one’s mind becomes as vast as space, and one’s great compassion becomes as firm as a diamond. One makes the vow to always follow him throughout the entirety of the future.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, practices in accordance with the conduct of Samantabhadra;
having perfected wisdom, he enters the realm of the Tathāgata and dwells on the stage of Samantabhadra.

At that time, the youth Sudhana saw Samantabhadra Bodhisattva seated upon a lion throne of precious lotuses before the Tathāgata amidst the great assembly, surrounded by all the hosts of bodhisattvas. Most...
He was extraordinary, with no equal in the world. The realm of his wisdom was immeasurable and boundless, difficult to fathom and difficult to conceive;
it was beyond the observation of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and all Bodhisattvas.
He beheld from every single pore of Samantabhadra’s body clouds of light, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and all worlds.
They extinguish all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings and cause all bodhisattvas to give rise to great joy.
They see from each and every pore emerge clouds of various colors, fragrances, and flames, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields;
these pervade the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, universally perfuming all the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas. They see from each and every pore emerge...

Clouds of various flowers, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, rained down upon all the sites of enlightenment and assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
From every single pore, there issued clouds of fragrance-trees, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields,
which rained down various wonderful flowers upon all the sites of enlightenment and assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.

Fragrance. He saw from each and every pore emerge clouds of exquisite garments, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, raining down upon the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm and space-realm.
He saw from each and every pore emerge clouds of jewel-trees, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and space-realm. All [Buddhas]...
In the Buddha’s assembly at the site of enlightenment, a rain of maṇi jewels fell.

From each and every pore, clouds of bodies of devas from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields issued forth, filling the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and praising the bodhicitta.
From each and every pore, clouds of bodies of Brahmā deities as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields issued forth, exhorting all Tathāgatas to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
I saw from each and every pore emerge clouds of bodies of kings of the desire realm, as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, protecting and upholding the Dharma wheel of all Tathāgatas.
I saw from each and every pore, in every moment of thought, emerge clouds of Buddha-fields of the three periods of time,
as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, pervading the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space for the sake of sentient beings who have no refuge.
They act as a refuge for those seeking one; they act as a protection for those without protection; they act as a support for those without support.

From every single pore, in every moment of thought, they manifest clouds of pure Buddha-fields, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, wherein all Buddhas appear in the world along with their assemblies of Bodhisattvas.

They were all completely filled. From every single pore, in every moment of thought, they saw clouds of pure and impure Buddha-fields, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, emerge and pervade the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, causing all defiled sentient beings to attain purity.
From every single pore, in every moment of thought, they saw [clouds of] impure [Buddha-fields], as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, emerge...
Clouds of purified Buddha-fields pervade the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, causing all defiled sentient beings to attain purity.
From every single pore, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of impure Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.
Throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, they cause all sentient beings who are purely defiled to attain purity.
From every single pore, in every moment of thought, they manifest clouds of bodies of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-lands;
pervading the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, they teach and transform sentient beings according to their needs, causing them all to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He focused his mind and saw that from every single pore, in each and every moment, there issued forth clouds of bodhisattva bodies as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields.
These pervaded the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, extolling the various names of all Buddhas and causing all sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness.
He saw that from every single pore, in each and every moment, there issued forth [clouds of bodhisattvas] as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields.
The Bodhisattva’s clouds of bodies pervade all Buddha-lands throughout the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space,
proclaiming all the roots of goodness produced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from their first aspiration. From every single pore, in every moment of thought,
there emerge clouds of Bodhisattva bodies as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-lands, pervading the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space throughout all Buddhas...
In each and every buddha-field, he proclaimed the ocean of all bodhisattva vows and the pure, wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

He saw from every single pore, in every moment of thought, clouds of the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva emerging, causing the minds of all living beings to attain fulfillment and enabling them to fully cultivate the path to omniscience. From every single pore, he saw [clouds] emerge...
Clouds of bodies of perfect enlightenment, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment in every Buddha-field,
causing all bodhisattvas to increase in the Great Dharma and achieve omniscience. At that time, the youth Sudhana,
beholding such a realm of sovereign spiritual powers of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, experienced immeasurable joy and exultation throughout his body and mind, and gazed upon it again and again.

Within each and every part of Samantabhadra’s body and within each and every pore, there are all the wind-circles, water-circles, earth-circles, and fire-circles of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems;
as well as great oceans, rivers, and streams; various precious mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains;
villages, camps, cities, towns, palaces, and gardens; all the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the realm of King Yama; and devas and nāgas.
The eight classes of beings, both human and non-human; the realms of the desire, form, and formless worlds;
the sun, moon, stars, constellations, wind, clouds, thunder, and lightning; day and night, months, seasons, and years and eons;

the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, and the adornments of the sites of enlightenment—all such matters were clearly seen, just as this world was seen, including everything that exists throughout the ten directions.
All worlds are seen in this same way. Just as one sees the present worlds of the ten directions, so too are all worlds of the past and future seen, each distinct and without confusion.
Just as these supernatural powers have been manifested by this Vairocana Tathāgata here, so too [are they manifested] in the world-system of Padmaśrī in the eastern direction.
The supernatural power manifested by the Buddha Kṣemaśrī is likewise so. As it was with the Buddha Kṣemaśrī, so it is in all worlds of the eastern direction;

as it is in the eastern direction, so it should be known that the supernatural powers manifested by all Tathāgatas in all worlds of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below are exactly the same. As it is in all worlds of the ten directions, so it is everywhere.
In this way, within every single atom of all Buddha-fields in the ten directions, there are the assemblies of all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm.
At each of those Buddha-sites, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra sits upon a lion throne of precious lotuses and manifests spiritual powers in exactly the same manner.
Within each and every body of that Samantabhadra, all realms of the three periods of time are manifested. One...
In all Buddha-fields, among all sentient beings, and at the manifestation of all Buddhas and their assemblies of Bodhisattvas;
hearing the voices of all sentient beings, the voices of all Buddhas, the wheels of Dharma turned by all Tathāgatas,
the various practices accomplished by all Bodhisattvas, and the playful supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas— Sudhana saw them all.
A wise Bodhisattva, possessing such immeasurable and inconceivable great supernormal powers, immediately attains ten kinds of wisdom-pāramitās.
What are these ten? They are: the wisdom-pāramitā that is able to pervade all Buddha-fields in every thought-moment;
the wisdom-pāramitā that is able to go before all Buddhas in every thought-moment; [and so forth].
The perfection of wisdom that is able to make offerings to all Tathāgatas in every moment of thought;
the perfection of wisdom that hears, receives, and upholds the Dharma from all Tathāgatas everywhere in every moment of thought;
the perfection of wisdom that contemplates the wheel of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas in every moment of thought; [the perfection of wisdom] that knows all in every moment of thought.
The perfection of wisdom regarding the Buddha’s inconceivable great supernormal powers;
the perfection of wisdom regarding inexhaustible eloquence that expounds a single phrase of Dharma in every thought-moment until the end of the future;

the perfection of wisdom regarding the observation of all phenomena with profound *prajñā* in every thought-moment; and the entry into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharma-realms in every thought-moment.
The perfection of wisdom of the ocean of knowledge; the perfection of wisdom that knows the minds of all sentient beings in every thought-moment;
and the perfection of wisdom in which the practices of Samantabhadra’s wisdom are ever-present in every thought-moment.
Once the youth Sudhana had attained these, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra extended his right hand and touched the crown of his head. Having touched his head, Sudhana—
Vasumitra immediately attained as many gates of samādhi as there are atoms in all buddha-fields,
each having as many samādhis as there are atoms in all buddha-fields as its retinue. Within each and every samādhi,
he beheld oceans of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields— Buddhas never before seen— gathering all the aids to omniscience as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields.
The implements: producing all the supreme and wondrous dharmas of omniscience, numbering as many as the atoms in all Buddha-fields;
generating all the great vows of omniscience, numbering as many as the atoms in all Buddha-fields; entering the ocean of great vows, numbering as many as the atoms in all Buddha-fields;
abiding in the essential path of transcendence of omniscience, numbering as many as the atoms in all Buddha-fields; and cultivating [the practices] of all Buddha-fields.
The practices cultivated by bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms, the great vigor for omniscience as numerous as the atoms of all buddha-fields,
and the pure light of omniscience as numerous as the atoms of all buddha-fields— just as in this Sahā world,
the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra placed his hand upon the crown of the head of Sudhana in the presence of the Buddha Vairocana, so it was in these ten [worlds].

In every direction, within all worlds and within every single atom of those worlds—in all such worlds and at the abodes of all Buddhas—Samantabhadra Bodhisattva likewise rubbed the crown of Sudhana’s head. The Dharma gates he attained were also entirely equal [in all places].
At that time, the Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son, do you see me?"
"Is this power of spiritual transformation not so? Indeed, it has been seen, O Great Sage.
This inconceivable matter of great spiritual power can only be known by a Tathāgata. Samantabhadra said:
"Good son, in the past, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, I practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva seeking all-knowledge. One by one..."
Throughout the kalpas, in order to purify the bodhicitta, he served Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
In each and every kalpa, in order to accumulate the merit and virtue of omniscience,
he established great assemblies of giving as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, causing all worlds to hear of them.

I know. They cause all who have requests to be fully satisfied. In each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the dharma of omniscience, they practice giving away material wealth as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
In each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, they give away cities, towns, and villages as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
They cast away their kingdoms, royal thrones, wives, children, and retinues; they gave as alms their eyes, ears, noses, tongues, bodies, flesh, hands, and feet, even unto their very lives.

In each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the head of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they gave as alms heads as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. In each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking one...
Because of their all-encompassing wisdom, they reverently honor, respect, serve, and make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
They present them with all necessities, including robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal elixirs.
Within those teachings, they leave the household life to study the Path, practicing the Buddha-dharma and upholding the true doctrine. Skillfully...
"O son of noble family, throughout that ocean of kalpas, I recall that never for even a single moment did I fail to comply with the Buddha's teachings.
Never for a single moment did I give rise to a mind of anger or malice, a mind of 'I' and 'mine,' a mind of distinction between self and others,
a mind remote from bodhicitta, or a mind of weariness and exhaustion toward saṃsāra, a mind of indolence, a mind of obstruction, or a mind of delusion."
I abide solely in the unsurpassed, indestructible great bodhicitta, which gathers all the dharmas that assist the path to omniscience.
Son of good family, I adorn the buddha-fields and rescue, protect, teach, and bring to maturity sentient beings through the mind of great compassion.
They make offerings to all Buddhas and serve spiritual friends in order to seek the true Dharma, propagate it, and protect and uphold it.

They are able to relinquish everything, both internal and external, and even do not begrudge their own bodies or lives. Even if one were to explain the causes and conditions for this throughout oceans of kalpas, they would never be exhausted.

The oceans of kalpas may come to an end, but this [Dharma] has no end. Good son, within the ocean of my Dharma, there is not a single word or a single phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king, nor was there anything that was not sought by relinquishing all that one possesses.
Good son, the Dharma I have sought is solely for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all beings.
Sentient beings, with single-minded contemplation, made these vows: "May all sentient beings hear this Dharma; may the light of wisdom universally illuminate the world;
may we reveal and demonstrate supramundane wisdom; may all sentient beings attain peace and happiness;
and may we universally praise all the merits of all Buddhas. Through such causes and conditions from my past as these, at [the time of] the...
It could not be exhausted even by speaking for an ocean of eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields.
Therefore, noble son, through such power of the factors conducive to enlightenment, power of all roots of goodness, power of great aspiration, power of cultivating merit,
power of contemplating all dharmas as they truly are, power of the eye of wisdom, power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, and power of great compassion—

By the power of [the perfections], the power of pure supernormal knowledges, and the power of spiritual friends, one attains this ultimate, pure Dharma-body equal throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, one attains a pure and unsurpassed Form-body that transcends all worlds;
according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, it manifests forms and enters all lands, pervading all places, extensively appearing throughout all worlds.
Through my supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), all who behold me are filled with joy and delight. Good son, you should observe this physical body (*rūpakāya*) of mine;
it has been accomplished over an ocean of boundless eons. For immeasurable thousands of billions of *nayuta* eons, it has been difficult to see and difficult to hear.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness, or those who have planted only a small amount of goodness—
Roots. Even Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas cannot yet hear my name, much less see my body.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who hear my name, they shall no longer regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they see me, touch me, welcome me, escort me, or follow me for even a moment—even seeing or hearing me in a dream—[they shall not regress].
I am likewise for all in this way. There are some sentient beings who, by recollecting me for one day and one night, immediately attain maturity;

others do so after seven days and seven nights, half a month, one month, half a year, one year, a hundred years, a thousand years, one eon, a hundred eons, or even for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields while recollecting me.
Those whom I have brought to maturity— whether in a single lifetime, a hundred lifetimes, or even for as many lifetimes as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—
who have matured through mindfulness of me, some see me emitting great rays of light.
Some see me shaking the Buddha-fields; some give rise to fear, while others give rise to joy, and all are brought to maturity.

Good son, by means of such skillful gates as these, numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-field, I cause all sentient beings to attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Good son, if there are sentient beings...
Those who see or hear me in this pure land will surely be born within this pure land.
If there are sentient beings who see or hear my pure body, they will surely be born within my pure body. Good son, you should contemplate this pure body of mine.
At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated the physical marks and signs of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Within each and every joint and every single pore, there are unspeakably unspeakable oceans of Buddha-fields.
In each of these oceans of fields, there are Buddhas appearing in the world, surrounded by assemblies of great Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, one sees all those oceans of fields established in various ways, with various forms and various adornments.
Various great mountains surround them on all sides; clouds of various colors cover the void; various Buddhas appear and expound various Dharmas.

Such matters as these are each distinct. Furthermore, one sees Samantabhadra, from within each ocean of worlds, manifesting clouds of Buddha-nirmāṇakāyas as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, pervading everywhere throughout the ten directions.
In worlds, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to incline toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw himself within the body of Samantabhadra, teaching and transforming sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
Furthermore, the youth Sudhana drew near to as many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as there are atoms in a Buddha-field.

The roots of goodness and the light of wisdom he has attained are such that, compared to the roots of goodness attained by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, they do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-billionth part;
indeed, they cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy. This is from the time when the youth Sudhana first resolved his mind [upon enlightenment] until he attained this vision.

The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra: the oceans of all Buddha-lands entered by him during that interval now exceed, by unspeakably unspeakable multiples of the atoms of Buddha-lands, the oceans of Buddha-lands entered in a single thought-moment within a single pore of Samantabhadra.
As it is with one pore, so it is with all pores. Thus it is, O Sudhana, the youth...
If you were to take a single step within a pore-land of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, you would pass through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Even if you continued walking in this manner for all future eons, you would still be unable to know the sequence of the oceans of lands within a single pore—
the treasury of the oceans of lands, the distinctions of the oceans of lands, the universal entry into the oceans of lands, and the oceans of lands themselves.
They cannot know the limits of the formation and destruction of oceans of lands, nor the limits of all the adornments of oceans of lands.

They also cannot know the sequence of oceans of Buddhas, the treasury of oceans of Buddhas, the distinctions of oceans of Buddhas, the universal entry into oceans of Buddhas, or the arising and ceasing of oceans of Buddhas.
Furthermore, they cannot know the sequence of oceans of bodhisattva assemblies, the treasury of oceans of bodhisattva assemblies, or the [nature of] oceans of bodhisattva assemblies.

The distinctions: the universal entry into the ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas; the gathering of the ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas; and the dispersal of the ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas—regarding all such limits, one cannot know them.
Nor can one know their wisdom that enters the realms of sentient beings, knows the faculties of sentient beings, and teaches and tames all sentient beings.
Such is the profound mastery in which bodhisattvas dwell, and the various stages and paths into which bodhisattvas enter. Thus it is.

Reaching as far as the limits of the ocean of worlds, the youth Sudhana proceeded through the lands within the pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; he traveled in this manner for one eon in a single land,
and even for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, yet he never perished from one land to appear in another.
Manifesting in every thought-moment throughout the boundless oceans of lands, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, leading them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the youth Sudhana successively attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
he became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas, his single body filling all worlds.
The buddha-fields and so forth, the practices and so forth, the perfect awakenings and so forth, the supernormal powers and so forth, the wheels of Dharma and so forth, the eloquences and so forth,
the verbal expressions and so forth, the vocal tones and so forth, the powers, fearlessnesses, and the abodes of the Buddhas and so forth, the great compassion and so forth,
and the inconceivable liberations and masteries— all are entirely equal.

Below this, the fifth major section reveals the characteristics of the vastness of the cause. Because the preceding [section] showed that the illumination of principle is non-dual, it revealed its profundity;

only then is one fit for the vast cause of attaining Buddhahood. Since each and every cause accords with the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, Mañjuśrī’s *Prajñāpāramitā* subsumes the aspects (*lakṣaṇa*) back into the essence (*svabhāva*), while Samantabhadra’s *Dharmadhātu* represents the secret, layered [meaning].
"Reverently increasing and seeking. "Seeking in accordance with the teaching" follows immediately below.

However, because there are the two characters "increasing" (*zēngzhǎng*), the intent is to reveal that whereas the aforementioned spiritual friends merely sought the causal practices of a bodhisattva, here one seeks directly for the fruit of Buddhahood;
hence it says, "increasingly seeking all wisdom. This single phrase provides a general heading for that which is sought: all wisdom.
This concludes the section on the fruit of Buddhahood. Next, the twenty-five phrases beginning with "Vast and Great Compassion" constitute a comprehensive contemplation of the perfect cause.
These are all causes for attaining Buddhahood and are entirely the realm of Samantabhadra’s liberation; therefore, it concludes by stating "contemplating," and so forth.
The causes sought in the above are all the perfect causes of Samantabhadra;
therefore, they differ from the aforementioned stages of the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), where each stage is distinct. Below, one hears the name, practices, and vows of Samantabhadra.
Because Sudhana universally contemplates the *dharmadhātu*, he is able to hear the name of Samantabhadra immediately. Here, the two characters "hears" (*wen*) run through the subsequent sections.

Regarding the phrases such as "practices and vows" and so forth: herein, "hearing" does not mean hearing them from one person or many people; rather, it is hearing them in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*.
These twelve phrases—beginning with "practices," "vows," and the various "stages"—are precisely the stages subsumed within the perfect interfusion of the stage of Samantabhadra.
Because he has heard the Dharma from the former person, he yearns and longs to see him. The following clarifies this longing.

Regarding those who must first cultivate contemplation before beholding that person: because the fruit-realm of Samantabhadra’s Dharmadhātu—perfect, wondrous, and sublime—is not visible to a distracted mind, it is necessary to cultivate contemplation.
Thus, right here before the lion throne of Vairocana Tathāgata at this Vajragarbha Bodhimanda, upon all the precious lotus thrones; herein, the following section correctly elucidates [the matter].

Regarding the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this first points to the locus of what is to be contemplated. Now, "Vajragarbha" refers to the mind at the stage immediately following Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because it relies upon the awakening of the Buddha-fruit, it is called the "Vajra-mind," and it is also the Tathāgata-garbha-mind;

therefore, it is termed "Vajragarbha. This Vajragarbha-mind is the ground of the Buddha-fruit; therefore, it is called the "Bodhimanda. This is precisely that which has been realized by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, it is called the lion throne of Vairocana Tathāgata; the Flower Treasury Adorned World is established upon it, and thus it is called the Lotus Treasury Throne.
This is the Dharma-realm realized by Samantabhadra; therefore, one contemplates Samantabhadra therein. Thus the Commentary states:
"In terms of the symbolic representation, this refers to the Buddha-fruit within one's own mind, which is the object of faith."
Within the essence of bodhi, the arising of all Indra-nets of Samantabhadra’s realm constitutes the contemplation of the mind.
This single phrase reveals the contemplation that performs the observing. The subsequent passage states:
"Arising the vast mind equal to the realm of space," continuing up to "the ultimate mind of the Tathāgata’s ten powers. These eleven phrases are all designated as the realm of Samantabhadra.

He then gave rise to the contemplation of the mind; therefore, he was able to see later on. Because Sudhana performed such a universal contemplation of the mind, there were first ten kinds of auspicious signs, due to:
first, the power of his own roots of goodness; second, the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment;
and third, the power of the shared roots of goodness with Samantabhadra. Next, what are these ten? They are as follows: he saw all...
The Buddha-fields are pure, extending throughout the entire Dharma-realm; this constitutes the tenth.
To correctly behold these rare wonders, one first perceives the ten preceding signs of auspiciousness. Next, one perceives the ten kinds of light;
within those lights, one sees in each and every atom a network of lights equal in number to the atoms of a microcosm, and so forth, until one beholds the world.
The subtle realms within the dust-motes of the world-spheres manifest these karmic functions; yet all are the lands of Samantabhadra’s *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (recompensed environment).

Because Sudhana had thus performed this universal contemplation, he saw only the extraordinary environments of Samantabhadra’s *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* lands, but had not yet seen his *mūla-vipāka* (primary recompense) body; therefore, he beheld these ten kinds of light and resolved that he would certainly see him.

Regarding the mind of Samantabhadra, at that time one again arouses contemplation and further cultivation, universally gathering all the sense faculties. With a single mind, one seeks to behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and gives rise to great diligence.

Thereupon, with the Universal Eye, one contemplates the essence of Samantabhadra, whose body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, until finally entering the realm of the Tathāgata and abiding on the stage of Samantabhadra. There are five sutras that clarify this process of renewed cultivation.
He gave rise to the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). This encompasses all forms of contemplation; therefore, he was subsequently able to see him.
At that moment, Sudhana immediately beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva sitting before the Tathāgata. He marveled, saying: "He is most extraordinary and peerless in the world.
His realm of wisdom is immeasurable and boundless, unfathomable and inconceivable, equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
Upon this single vision of Samantabhadra, one immediately knows that wisdom is inconceivable; this is the sudden realization attained in a single thought-moment.

Therefore, the commentary (śāstra) categorizes what follows as "the clarification of seeing, hearing, realizing, and entering. Now, regarding this entire Great Sūtra, this chapter is judged to be the "realization through entry based on the person.
When Sudhana arrives here, he attains true realization, wherein the causes are perfected and the fruits are fulfilled to their ultimate limit.
In this regard, however, this section from here down to "all are entirely equal" consists of one hundred and sixty-four lines of scripture.
It comprehensively clarifies the realm of realization and entry. Furthermore, this major section is divided into two sub-sections:

first, the general manifestation of the perfection of the causes for attaining benefit, up until the final four lines of scripture beginning with "at that time," which clarify the fulfillment of the fruit.
Equalizing the Buddhas. Regarding the benefits gained, first is the benefit of seeing the body.
This refers to the passage below [in the sutra] concerning each and every pore of Samantabhadra’s body, which contains thirty-six lines of scripture.

It clarifies that from each and every pore of Samantabhadra’s body, clouds of various kinds of inexhaustible bodies emerge, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; in reality, these are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

In this text, twenty stages are briefly enumerated. These all arise from the ten minds born of Sudhana’s longing and desire to see [Mañjuśrī], continuing until the manifestation of perfect enlightenment and the attainment of all-knowledge in all buddha-fields.
Thus one knows that each perceives according to the limits of what is seen by their own mind.

At that time, when Sudhana beheld such a realm of sovereign supernatural power of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, his body and mind were filled with universal joy. However, the above passage describes only what was seen emerging from a single pore;
what is contained within has not yet been seen. In the subsequent text, he again beholds what is contained within, stating: "He observed again each and every..."
Within each and every pore of his body, there are the sentient beings of the three thousand great thousandfold world systems, across the six realms and four modes of birth;
reaching upward to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas, and including all matters pertaining to the ten dharma realms, both the primary and secondary environments.
All are clearly seen. It does not stop at a single trichiliocosm. Just as this world is seen, so too are all the infinite worlds of the ten directions;
each and every one is seen throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, each distinct and without confusion.
This reveals the inexhaustibility of the Indra’s Net and the subtle mutual containment within the Ten Mysterious Gates.
The realm where the pure and the mixed are without obstruction is entirely contained within a single pore;

it is likewise so for every one of all the pores. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "As manifested by this Vairocana Tathāgata, even unto each Buddha before every world in the ten directions, there is Samantabhadra; in each and every body, in each and every..."
The pores all manifest in this manner. There are nine lines and a half of sūtra text that conclude by establishing universal pervasiveness. The Commentary states:

"The final conclusion concerns Samantabhadra within a single mote of dust. This shows that while previously the body contained the Dharma-realm, being vast and boundless, it manifested the meaning of "universal" (samanta);
now, this very body containing the Dharma-realm enters invisibly into a mote of dust, becoming harmonious, supple, and unimpeded.
This clarifies the meaning of his virtue. Because he is all-pervasive both internally and externally, he is named Samantabhadra.
Above, we have merely seen Samantabhadra’s supreme body; below, the text explains the attainment of profound benefit, stating:
"When Sudhana beheld such inconceivable great supernormal powers of Samantabhadra, he immediately attained ten kinds of *jñāna-pāramitā* and the ten *pāramitās*. There are eleven [verses].

This section of the *Sūtra* clarifies the matter of attaining profound benefit. Having already attained the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the perfection of the stages (*bhūmi*) has been manifested; how much more so when the ten [manifestations] are inexhaustible?
From the point of first beholding the body of Samantabhadra up to this point, it comprehensively clarifies the benefit of beholding his body.
