Below, it clarifies the benefit of the touching of the crown of the head, stating: "Once Sudhana had seen this, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra immediately extended his right hand and stroked [his head]."

He touched his crown. Once the crowning had been performed, Sudhana immediately attained samādhi-doors as numerous as the atoms within all buddha-fields, up to the pure light of omniscience. There are eight lines of verse that clarify the matter of these acquired benefits.
Next, just as it was here in this Sahā world, down to the very bottom, all were likewise equal;
that is, within each and every atom mentioned previously, all Samantabhadras likewise rubbed Sudhana’s head.

This shows that not only does Samantabhadra pervade every single atom, but Sudhana himself likewise pervades them all. Thus, it reveals that Sudhana has attained direct realization; therefore, it says:
Samādhi. Next, at that time, Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana, saying: "O son of good family, do you see this supernatural power of mine?
By asking this question, he reveals the profundity and vastness of the cause; for when the cause is profound, the fruit is abundant.
The intent is to show that while Sudhana perceives only the excellence of the fruit-virtue—the realm realized by Samantabhadra—he does not know its profound cause.
This is because he intends to demonstrate its cause; therefore, he specifically inquires about it. Thus, below, Samantabhadra declares:
"In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, I sought all-knowledge," and so forth.
Up to the passage on the great bodhicitta, there are seventeen lines of scripture that specifically clarify the seeking of bodhicitta.

Within this section, it concludes by stating, "There has never been a single thought that was not in accord with the Buddha's teaching," thereby demonstrating the abandonment of faults and the accomplishment of virtues.
Next, from the line "I adorn the buddha-fields with a mind of great compassion" down to "this shall never come to an end," these three lines and the remainder of the scripture collectively clarify...
Regarding the practice of compassion and wisdom, the next section clarifies the practice of seeking the Dharma, stating:
"Within the ocean of my Dharma, there is not a single word or phrase that was not sought after renouncing the status of a Wheel-Turning King. It further states:

"The Dharma I seek is entirely for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings," and so forth. These are the causes and conditions of seeking the Dharma in the past, which are beyond expression.
It could not be exhausted even by explaining for an ocean of eons as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field.
There are six scriptural passages that specifically clarify the practice of seeking the Dharma; since one would not abandon even a single word or phrase, how much less an entire section?
The intent is that because my practice of seeking the Dharma is both difficult and long-lasting, the cause is profound and thus the fruit attained is vast.

Therefore, the subsequent section concludes by establishing the cause and its resulting fruit, stating: "By means of these ten powers, such as the power of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)...
This indicates that the cause is profound; because the cause possesses the efficacy of attaining the fruit, they are all termed "powers" (*bala*).

Next, one attains this ultimate *dharmakāya*, which is equal throughout the three periods of time, as well as the unsurpassed *rūpakāya*. There is nothing about which one does not feel joy. This constitutes the conclusion.

Regarding the fruit thus accomplished: from the point where Samantabhadra first questioned Sudhana up until this passage, there are thirty-four lines of scripture that collectively reveal the profundity and vastness of the cause.
Next, in the section beginning with "You should now observe my physical body as it is," the boundless nature of the contemplative function is clarified.
Although the boundlessness of its manifest function is revealed, the specific reference to observing the physical body is intended to ensure that [the practitioner] actually perceives it.
The essence of the fruit-body of form possesses boundless great function; one should know that this is the result induced by the cultivation of vast causes.
Therefore, it is stated next: "This physical body of mine has been accomplished over an ocean of boundless kalpas. This reveals the profundity of the cause.
To say that it is difficult to see or hear for immeasurable kalpas is intended to give rise to the thought of its rarity, thereby inspiring a longing for the fruit.

Because it is the cause for birth, that which follows clarifies how it is difficult to hear and difficult to see; this is because by seeing it even for a moment, one immediately attains the benefit of non-retrogression.
Next, the passage beginning with "Or there may be some beings" clarifies the benefit of the maturation of roots of goodness.

Next, [the passage] beginning with "By means of such skillful means as these, numbering as many as the atoms in a buddha-field, I cause all beings to [attain] perfect enlightenment... [explains this].
[He] attains non-retrogression and so forth; even up to the point where it is said that he will certainly be born within my pure body.
There are fourteen additional lines in the sutra that clarify matters of benefit gained through what is difficult to see or hear. Therefore, the conclusion follows:
"You should contemplate this pure body of mine. Now, as for Samantabhadra’s desire that Sudhana contemplate his body, it is because of Vairocana...
The Dharma-body is no body, for it takes the Dharmadhātu of Samantabhadra as its body.

If one enters the body of Samantabhadra, one exhaustively reaches the realm of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana; thus, Sudhana was led to contemplate his own body so that he might realize and enter [this state].
If it were not manifested through the body of Samantabhadra, where else could one see the entry into the ocean of fruition? Therefore, Sudhana’s...
As for that which is realized and entered, it is simply entering the body of Samantabhadra. Although this meaning is not explicitly clear in the commentary, the sense of the sūtra is very evident;
therefore, the subsequent passage states: "At that time, Sudhana contemplated the marks and signs, as well as the limbs and joints of Samantabhadra’s body."
Within each and every pore, there are oceans of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
In each of these oceans of fields, Buddhas appear, manifesting various adornments and expounding various Dharma teachings, each distinct from the others.
Thus, a single pore contains the three worlds; furthermore, one sees Samantabhadra within that pore.
In each and every world-ocean that appears, countless transformation bodies of the Buddha emerge to teach and transform sentient beings;

this is the vision of Samantabhadra’s manifestation of great activity. Sudhana further sees his own body within the body of Samantabhadra teaching and transforming sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
this is the vision of his own body equally manifesting universal transformation. These are the eight lines and a half of scripture above.

This collectively reveals the entry into the inconceivable Dharma-realm (*acintya-dharmadhātu*). The following text provides a comparative assessment to manifest its superiority, generally demonstrating that Sudhana has reached the perfection of causes;
it consists of nineteen and a half lines of scripture, divided into four sections.

The first states that the roots of goodness and wisdom obtained by approaching spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field are compared to the merit of a single pore of Samantabhadra.
Even virtues numbering hundreds of thousands of millions could not equal one part of this; thus, the measurement of these roots of goodness is shown to be transcendentally superior.
Next, from the initial generation of the mind downward, the entry into the ocean of lands within the pores of Samantabhadra is clarified;

compared to what was previously entered before this point—that which was entered in a single thought-moment—this present entry exceeds the former by unspeakable multiples. Next, within the pores of Samantabhadra...
Taking a single step within a buddha-field, one immediately traverses worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields.
Traveling in this manner until the end of the future, it can never be exhausted; how much more so the various distinct adornments therein, which are likewise boundless.
This extends even to each and every ocean of buddha-fields, oceans of buddhas, oceans of bodhisattva assemblies, and oceans of sentient beings.
As well as the ocean of sentient beings to be tamed, the profound mastery in which Bodhisattvas dwell, the various stages they enter, the various paths, and so forth—such oceans are without limit.
However, what is presented here consists of three types: the ocean of lands, the ocean of Buddhas, and the ocean of Bodhisattvas.
In fact, these already encompass in total the questions regarding the ten oceans from the first assembly. This is because the intention [of the questions] is supreme.
As for those who did not know at first: this refers to the ten kinds of oceans within the ocean of Vairocana’s fruition; therefore, he specifically raises them as questions.

However, the texts of the preceding nine assemblies have already explained the causes and conditions of these ten oceans; yet, while they were merely spoken of, the actual realization and entry into them had not been revealed.
Now, as Sudhana has perfected his causal practices, he has entirely transcended the former [stages] within a single pore of Samantabhadra.
That which is not known can be understood through the profound realization of the *dharmadhātu*. It is further stated that Sudhana,
within the lands within the pores of Samantabhadra, may traverse for one eon in a single land,
proceeding in this manner until he traverses for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, proceeding in this manner without any distinction between them.
Appearing and disappearing, moment by moment they pervade the boundless ocean of lands, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may attain Bodhi.
Such is the vastness of what Sudhana has realized. Thus, within the boundless ocean of lands, self and others are not separated by even a hair’s breadth;
throughout the ten periods of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment. This is Sudhana—
The perfection of causes does not exceed a single pore of Samantabhadra; this is what is meant by the sudden, complete realization in a single lifetime of the fruits of kalpas of vast eons.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consists of four divisions, the last of which concerns "entrance through reliance on persons.

This refers to the fruit presented in the first assembly, which exhorts sentient beings of great resolve to rely upon it for cultivation and realization. Now, the final fourth division concerns "entrance through reliance on persons."
Thus, the Dharma realized by Sudhana is precisely the boundless ocean of fruition (phala-sāgara) presented in the first assembly;
here, the text merely provides a brief summary. In reality, this has already been exhausted within the nineteen and a half lines of scripture that follow, though it cannot be fully set forth there;
therefore, it is subsequently concluded within the section on the fourteen [qualities] and so forth. Thus, the subsequent scripture says: "At that time..."
The youth Sudhana then successively attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
He became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas. With a single body, he filled all worlds;

he was equal to them in buddha-fields, in practices, in perfect enlightenment, in supernormal powers, in turning the wheel of Dharma, in eloquence, in speech, in voice, and in the powers and fearlessnesses.
Such as these: the equality of the Buddha’s dwelling, the equality of great compassion, and the equality of inconceivable liberation and mastery—all are entirely equal.
These fourteen kinds of equality above are such that there is nothing that is not equal.

The Supplementary Commentary states: The sub-commentary (shu) categorizes these four lines of scripture as clarifying that the perfection of the stages is equal to that of the Buddha. The explanation says:

"Causes are fulfilled and fruits are perfected," which in meaning corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samatā-bodhi). Since the causal stage is already complete and there is nothing further to be cultivated, it is simply called "equal.
If this is used as the criterion for Equal Enlightenment, then it accords with the previous chapter's initial judgment that the single name of Samantabhadra reveals the cause.

The characteristic of vastness means that initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodha) is identical to the fundamental [awakening], and perfect awakening (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) manifests before one, pervading the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) such that nothing is not included.
If this is so, then at this stage, as perfect awakening manifests before one, one should immediately enter the Sublime (Miao).

Yet, the present text states that one "immediately attains Equal Enlightenment" (samyak-saṃbodhi), which appears to be contradictory. This is because the term "equal" (*pingdeng*) here refers to the equality of equanimity (*samatā*), rather than the equality of parity.
"Etc. (ādi): Because the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) transcends all words, it is merely indicated by "etc. Therefore, the subsequent verse praises the Buddha’s virtues as being inconceivable;

this is precisely an exaltation of what Sudhana has realized. Since that which Sudhana has realized is the equal Dharma-realm (*samatā-dharmadhātu*), he borrows the description of the Buddha’s virtues to praise it.
The above concludes the section on seeing, hearing, and realizing entry.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra spoke these verses:
"You all should remove the defilements of all delusions, And listen with single-minded concentration and without distraction as I speak.
The Tathāgata is endowed with all perfections; He is the true path of all liberations."
The World-Transcending Tamer, Supreme among Men, Whose mind is as pure as space,
Constantly radiating the great light of the sun of wisdom, Universally causing all sentient beings to extinguish the darkness of delusion—
A Tathāgata is difficult to see or hear; Only now, after immeasurable billions of kalpas, have you encountered him.
Like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age, one should thus listen to the Buddha’s virtues;
his various activities that accord with the world are like a conjurer manifesting manifold deeds,
intended only to gladden the minds of sentient beings, never giving rise to conceptual discrimination or mental constructions.
At that time, having heard this teaching, all the bodhisattvas were single-mindedly filled with longing and yearning, wishing only to hear of the true merits of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
They all thought to themselves: "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva has fully cultivated all practices;
his essential nature is pure, and all his words are entirely without falsehood. He is praised by all the Tathāgatas. Thus they reflected.

Having already conceived a profound sense of longing and reverence, at that time the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—fully adorned with merit and wisdom, like a lotus flower, unsullied by any of the defilements of the triple world—addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Listen attentively, all of you."
I now wish to speak of a single drop from the ocean of the Buddha’s merits. Thus, he spoke in verse:
The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space, Pervading the minds of all sentient beings;
It fully understands all the delusions of the world, Yet gives rise to no various discriminatory thoughts.
In a single thought, you fully know the phenomena of the three periods of time, And likewise comprehend the faculties of all sentient beings.
Like a skillful master of great illusion, In every moment you manifest boundless deeds;
According to the various activities of sentient beings' minds, Through the power of your past karmic vows.
Causing those who see him to each perceive him differently— Yet the Buddha is fundamentally free from any stirring thought.
Some may see the Buddha seated everywhere, Pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions;
Or there may be those whose minds are not pure, Who do not see the Buddha for immeasurable eons.
Some, possessing faith and understanding, free from pride, Upon resolving their minds, immediately behold the Tathāgata.
Others, with deceitful and impure hearts, Seek for billions of eons yet do not encounter him.
Yet others hear the Buddha’s voice in every place; That voice is exquisite and wondrous, gladdening the heart.
There may be those who, for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, or millions of kalpas, have not heard [this teaching] because their minds were impure;
yet others may see great Bodhisattvas of pure conduct filling the three thousandfold world system,
all of whom are fully endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra, while the Tathāgata sits majestically among them.
Some see this realm, peerless and exquisite, purified by the Buddha through immeasurable eons;
therein the most supreme venerable Vairocana awakens to and attains bodhi.
Others see a lotus blossom, a most wonderful and sublime land, wherein the Tathāgata Bhadraśrī dwells.
Surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom diligently cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra;
some see the Buddha Amitāyus surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others,
all of whom have already attained the stage of consecration and fill the worlds throughout the ten directions.
Some see this trichiliocosm adorned in various ways like the world of Abhirati,
with the Tathāgata Akṣobhya dwelling within it, as well as bodhisattvas such as Gandhahastin;
others see Candrabuddhi of Great Renown together with Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva and his peers.
Abiding in a wondrous adornment like a perfect mirror, He pervades the pure lands throughout the ten directions;
Or he is seen as the World-Honored One, Sun-Treasury, Abiding in the pure land of Excellent Radiance,
Together with all the consecrated bodhisattvas, Pervading the ten directions while preaching the Dharma.
In some, one sees the Buddha Vajra Great Flame together with the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu,
traveling throughout all vast lands, preaching the Dharma to eliminate the cataracts of sentient beings;
within each tip of a single hair, there are unspeakable numbers of Buddhas endowed with the thirty-two marks.
The Bodhisattva is surrounded by his retinue, preaching various teachings to deliver sentient beings.
Some behold a single pore, wherein vast lands are fully adorned and immeasurable Tathāgatas all reside, filled with pure sons of the Buddha.
Some see within a single atom the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
completely filled with immeasurable Bodhisattvas who have practiced all manner of deeds for unspeakable eons;
others see upon the tip of a single hair the ocean of lands as vast as the sands of countless dust motes.
Various karmas arise with their respective distinctions; Vairocana turns the wheel of Dharma.
Some see the world as impure, while others see it as composed of pure jewels.
The Tathāgata dwells for immeasurable eons, manifesting everything up to his final nirvāṇa.

Pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions, He manifests in various ways in inconceivable manners, According to the mentalities, wisdoms, and karmas of sentient beings; There are none whom he does not transform and purify.
Such a Great Teacher of the Unsurpassed, Fills all the lands throughout the ten directions.
I shall describe a small portion of the various supernatural powers he manifests; you should listen.
Some see Śākyamuni having already attained the path of Buddhahood after inconceivable kalpas have passed;
others see him now just beginning as a bodhisattva, benefiting all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Some see this Lion of the Śākyas, who honors all Buddhas and practices the Path;
some see the Most Honored One among men, manifesting various powers and miraculous feats;
some see him practicing generosity or upholding the precepts, or practicing patience, diligence, or the various dhyānas.
Through wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge, they manifest in accordance with the minds of sentient beings;
some see them as having reached the ultimate *pāramitās*, while others see them dwelling in the various stages (*bhūmis*),
or possessing the knowledge of *dhāraṇīs*, *samādhis*, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)— thus they appear in every way, without exception.
Sometimes they manifest practicing for immeasurable eons, abiding in the Bodhisattva stage of patience;
sometimes they manifest abiding on the stage of non-retrogression; sometimes they manifest receiving the consecration of the water of Dharma upon their crowns;
sometimes they manifest the bodies of Brahmā, Śakra, or the World-Protectors; and sometimes they manifest as Kṣatriyas or Brahmins.
Adorned with various forms and marks, like a magician manifesting myriad images—
sometimes appearing as he first descends from Tuṣita, or seen within the palace accepting the ladies-in-waiting,
or seen renouncing all worldly splendors and pleasures, leaving home and departing the secular world to study and practice the Way.
Some see him just born, others see him passing away; Some see him leaving home to practice the extraordinary path, or see him seated beneath the Bodhi tree;
Some see him subduing the armies of Māra and attaining perfect enlightenment, Or see the Buddha’s initial parinirvāṇa, Or see stūpas being erected throughout the world.
In some, he sees a Buddha image standing within a stūpa, manifested in this way because he knows the proper time;
or he sees the Tathāgata Amitāyus bestowing the noble prediction upon various bodhisattvas,
becoming a supreme Great Teacher who will next succeed him in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Some see [the Tathāgatas] entering parinirvāṇa after having performed buddha-work for immeasurable billions of kalpas;
some see them now first attaining bodhi; some see them currently practicing various sublime deeds;
and some see the pure moon of the Tathāgata in the Brahma-world or in the palace of Māra.
In the palaces of the Lord of Sovereignty (Īśvara) and the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), he manifests various kinds of supernatural transformations;
or he is seen dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, surrounded by immeasurable devas.
For their sake, he teaches the Dharma to bring them joy, and they all together resolve to generate the mind [of awakening] and make offerings to the Buddha.
Some see him dwelling in the Yāma Heaven, or in the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the World-Protectors, or the nāgas;
in all such palaces, there is none in which his image does not appear.
There, before the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, he scattered flowers and spread his hair as an offering.
From this, one thoroughly understands the profound and wondrous Dharma, And constantly transforms all sentient beings through this path.
Some see the Buddha having long since entered parinirvāṇa, While others see him first attaining bodhi;
Some see him remaining for immeasurable kalpas, While others see him enter extinction in a mere instant.
The physical marks, radiance, and lifespan; wisdom, bodhi, nirvāṇa, the assemblies, emanations, majestic deportment, and voice—each of these is infinite.
Or they may manifest their bodies as exceedingly vast, like the great jewel mountain Sumeru.
Some see him sitting cross-legged, unmoving, filling boundless worlds;
some see his halo measuring one fathom, or ten thousand million *yojanas*;
some see it illuminating immeasurable lands, or filling all buddha-fields.
Some see the Buddha’s lifespan as eighty years; some see it as hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of years;

or they see him dwelling for inconceivable eons. Thus, successively doubling beyond this, the Buddha’s wisdom penetrates all things with pure non-obstruction, universally knowing the phenomena of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment.
All arise from the conditions of mind and consciousness; Arising and ceasing, impermanent, they lack intrinsic nature.
Within a single land, one attains perfect enlightenment; In all lands, one likewise attains it.
Every land enters into every other, and each is likewise so; Manifesting in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata abides in the unsurpassed path; He has accomplished the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, possessing wisdom that is unimpeded.
He turns the wheel of Dharma of twelve aspects, fully understanding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; He analyzes the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
With unimpeded eloquence regarding the Dharma, its meaning, joy, and expression,
he extensively expounds through these four analytical knowledges that all phenomena are selfless and devoid of marks. That the nature of karma neither arises nor perishes,
being utterly remote like space— this the Buddha distinguishes through skillful means.
The Tathāgata thus turns the wheel of Dharma, universally shaking all lands in the ten directions;
palaces, mountains, and rivers all tremble, yet he causes no sentient beings to feel alarm or fear.
The Tathāgata universally proclaims a vast and sublime sound, enabling all to understand according to their faculties and inclinations.
Causing all to resolve their minds and remove the stains of delusion, yet the Buddha never gives rise to a thought;
whether they hear of generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, Or meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and knowledge;
or they hear of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—these various expressions each differ.
Some hear of the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties and powers,

as well as the factors of enlightenment, the path, the various recollections, the supernormal powers, and tranquility and insight; they hear of the immeasurable skillful means and various Dharma gates,
and of the dragons, spirits, the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, Brahmā, Śakra, and the world-protecting devas.
The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, Causing all to understand according to their respective dispositions.
Whether there be greed, hatred, or delusion, Or anger, concealment, stinginess, envy, pride, and flattery—
Of the eighty-four thousand diverse afflictions, He causes them all to hear the teachings that remedy each.
If one has not yet fully cultivated pure and white dharmas, one should cause them to hear the exposition of the ten precepts;
having been able to practice giving, they shall tame themselves. One should cause them to hear the sound of quiescent nirvana.
If a person’s will is weak and lacks compassion, they will loathe birth and death and seek only their own liberation.
I cause them to hear the teaching of the three gates of liberation, so that they may emerge from suffering and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
If there are those who possess little desire by nature and, weary of and turning their backs on the three realms of existence,
seek tranquility, I cause them to hear the teaching of dependent origination, so that they may achieve deliverance by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

If there are those with pure and vast minds, Endowed with the merits of generosity and precepts, The Pure Tathāgata, possessed of compassion, Causes them to hear the sound of the Mahāyāna being taught.
In some lands, they hear the One Vehicle; In others, two, three, four, or five.
Thus, even unto the immeasurable, all are the Tathāgata’s power of skillful means;

nirvāṇa is quiescent and never otherwise. Though there are distinctions in the superiority or inferiority of wisdom and practice, they are like space, whose essential nature is one, while the flight of birds—far or near—is each different.
The Buddha’s body and voice are likewise; they pervade the entirety of the realm of empty space.
According to the differences in the mental capacities and wisdom of sentient beings, what is heard and seen varies for each.
Because the Buddha cultivated various practices in the past, he is able to manifest wondrous sounds according to their inclinations.
Without conceptualizing this or that, or who I am speaking to and whom I am not speaking to,
the Tathāgata’s face emits a great light; the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates he teaches are likewise all-pervasive, illuminating the world and eliminating afflictions.
Fully endowed with pure merit and wisdom, you always accord with the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
like space, you are free from defilement and attachment, yet for the sake of sentient beings,
you appear and manifest the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, while also demonstrating a long life remaining in the world.
Although appearing thus in accordance with the world, his essential nature is pure like space;
throughout all boundless lands, the faculties and desires of sentient beings are likewise immeasurable,
yet the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom clearly perceives them all, manifesting the Buddha-way according to those who are to be transformed.
Throughout the entirety of the empty space of the ten directions, among all the assemblies of humans and devas,
the Buddha manifests his body in accordance with their various differing forms.
If he is among a great assembly of śramaṇas, he appears with his hair and beard shaven and wearing the *kāṣāya* robe.
Carrying his robes and bowl, guarding his sense faculties, he causes them to rejoice and brings their afflictions to rest.
Whenever he approaches a brahmin, he manifests a frail and emaciated body,
holding a staff and a water jar, ever pure, endowed with wisdom, and skilled in eloquent discourse.
Exhaling the old and inhaling the new to satisfy himself, he draws in the wind and drinks the dew as his sustenance;
whether sitting or standing, he remains unmoving. Manifesting such ascetic practices, he subdues those of heterodox paths;
or upholding their precepts, he serves as a teacher to the world, being well-versed in medical arts and all other treatises.
He fully understands writing, mathematics, astronomy, geography, and all manner of signs, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious omens pertaining to the body;
he has deeply entered the various dhyānas and liberations, the samādhis, supernatural powers, and the practice of wisdom.
Through conversation, chanting, and shared play, he employs skillful means to cause all beings to abide in the Buddha-way.
Sometimes he manifests fine garments to adorn his body, wearing a floral crown upon his head and shaded by a lofty parasol, surrounded before and behind by the fourfold army;
he warns the multitudes and proclaims his majesty to subdue minor kings.
Or he acts as a judge to hear lawsuits and decide legal cases, skillfully understanding all worldly affairs of state.
All matters of giving and taking are clearly discerned, causing all beings to be joyful and submissive;
Or acting as a great minister, he exclusively provides counsel and support,
skillfully employing the kings' laws of governance to benefit the ten directions universally, While all sentient beings remain unaware of it.

Sometimes he appears as minor kings scattered like grains of millet; sometimes he acts as a flying universal monarch (cakravartin), causing all the princes and retinues of women to be transformed by his teaching, such that none can fathom it.
Sometimes he becomes one of the four world-protecting kings (lokapāla), presiding over the nāgas, yakṣas, and other beings.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of the assembled multitude, causing them all to rejoice greatly; or,
as the Great Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, dwelling in the Sudharmā Hall and the Nandana Grove,
he wears a flower crown upon his head and speaks the wondrous Dharma, which the various devas gaze upon with reverence, unable to fathom it.

Sometimes dwelling in the celestial realms of Yāma or Tuṣita, in the Maṇi-jewel palaces where the gods Nirmāṇarati and Vaśavartin and the Māra kings reside, he teaches the practice of truth to subdue them; or,
amidst the assemblies of the Brahmā heavens, he expounds the four immeasurables and the paths of dhyāna.
Causing all to rejoice, he then departs, and none know the manner of his coming or going;
whether he reaches as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, there he speaks of the precious flowers of the factors of enlightenment and other immeasurable noble virtues,
and only then does he depart, leaving those who do not know him.
That which is seen by the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom— within it,
all sentient beings are entirely brought to fulfillment through various means of instruction by means of infinite skillful methods;
it is like a master illusionist skilled in magical arts who manifests all manner of illusory phenomena.
The Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings is likewise: For their sake, he manifests various bodies;
Just as the pure moon in the void Causes the beings of the world to see it wax and wane, And causes its reflection to appear in all rivers and ponds, While all the stars are eclipsed by its radiance.
The moon of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has appeared in the world, And through skillful means, it manifests increase and decrease;
The waters of the bodhisattvas’ minds reflect its image, While the śrāvakas, like stars, possess no radiance.
It is like a great ocean filled with jewels, Pure, free from turbidity, and immeasurable.
All sentient beings throughout the four continents—within them all, his image appears;

so too is the ocean of the Buddha’s qualities of body: stainless, unclouded, and boundless, reaching to the end of the realm of phenomena, there is no sentient being among whom his image does not appear.
Just as the pure sun emits a thousand rays, Shining upon the ten directions without moving from its place, The light of the Buddha-sun is likewise:
Neither going nor coming, it dispels the darkness of the world.
Just as a dragon king sends down a great rain, Which issues neither from his body nor from his mind.
It is able to moisten and saturate everywhere, cleansing away the scorching heat and making it cool;
the Dharma-rain is likewise so, not emerging from the Buddha’s body or mind,
yet it awakens all beings, universally causing the fires of the three poisons to be extinguished.
The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body is peerless throughout all the three realms;
because its nature is neither existent nor non-existent, it transcends the path of worldly speech.
Though it has nothing upon which to rely, there is nowhere it does not abide; though there is nowhere it does not reach, it never departs.
Like a painting in the sky or what is seen in a dream, one should view the Buddha-body in this way:
all phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, cannot serve as a metaphor for the Buddha.
Just as birds and beasts in the mountains and forests have none that dwell relying upon the empty sky.
The great ocean’s maṇi jewels possess infinite colors, And the distinctions of the Buddha’s body are likewise so.
The Tathāgata is neither form nor non-form; He manifests according to need, yet dwells nowhere.
Space, suchness, the limit of reality, Nirvāṇa, the dharma-nature, and cessation—all are thus.
Only such a true Dharma can be displayed, though the thoughts within the minds of atoms in the Buddha-fields could be counted; the waters of the great oceans could be drunk up,
space could be measured, and the wind could be bound— yet none can fully exhaustively describe the virtues of the Buddha.

If there are those who hear of this ocean of merit and give rise to a heart of joy, faith, and understanding, they shall obtain everything as it has been extolled; be careful not to harbor doubts regarding this.
This section, following the previous, clarifies that the Buddha’s supreme virtues are inconceivable. While the preceding prose section merely manifested the perfection of the causes, this [verse]...
The verse now sets forth the function of the fruit; it does not recapitulate the preceding prose. Nevertheless, there are two intentions: first, in relation to Samantabhadra.

Samantabhadra’s intention is as follows: "Previously, you saw my inconceivable [nature], yet that was still within the stage of cause. Now I reveal the fruit to you, which is even more profoundly deep."

Second, regarding Sudhana: Sudhana is equal to the Buddha, yet he is merely one whose causes are perfected. Because the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) transcends verbal expression, it is not said that he has attained Buddhahood.
Now, by relying on the manifestation of the Buddha’s virtues, the characteristics of Sudhana’s fruition are revealed;
thus, in both the prose and the verses, cause and effect are interwoven. First, the four verses mark his virtues, exhort him to listen, and grant permission to speak. Next, at that time, all...

The Bodhisattvas thirstily longed to hear it. Next, at that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva spoke in verse, extensively describing the characteristics of perfected virtues to cause the assembly to seek their fulfillment. Next, the verses are formally recited:

"The Buddha’s wisdom is vast and equal to space," etc., which extensively reveals the inconceivable virtues of the Buddha. There are ninety-five verses, divided into two parts; the first consists of ninety-three verses.
This section separately extols the Buddha’s virtues. The final two verses conclude by showing that these virtues are inexhaustible and exhort one to have faith without doubt.
Within the preceding portion, there are eighty verses of direct exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), followed by thirteen verses of illustrative parables (*dṛṣṭānta*).

These collectively praise the perfection of the ten bodies and the twenty-one kinds of supreme merit of Vairocana, which are divided into twenty-one sections. The first of these consists of two verses.

This refers to the merit of functioning with absolute non-obstruction regarding the objects of knowledge; that is, because the Buddha is unobstructed, he is without attachment or doubt concerning all things, categories, and their specific distinctions.

Second, the single verse beginning with "In accordance with the various activities of the minds of sentient beings" clarifies the merit of being able to enter the most pure *tathatā* (suchness), which is characterized by the non-duality of existence and non-existence. That is to say:

Having realized that suchness is non-dual, there is no movement of thought. Third, the three verses beginning with "Or seeing the Buddha sitting at various places" refer to the merit of the effortless and uninterrupted performance of Buddha-activities;

that is, dwelling in the Buddha’s non-abiding state while performing Buddha-activities without ceasing, hence the phrase "or seeing," and so forth. Fourth, "Or seeing pure great bodhisattvas... [and so on].
The fifteen verses concern the qualities of non-differentiation regarding the basis, intention, and activity within the *dharmakāya*.

That is to say, because the wisdom that serves as the basis for all Buddhas is identical, the altruistic intention (*āśaya*) that benefits others is identical, and the functions of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are identical, the aforementioned sūtra states that they "attain equality with the Buddhas.
Alternatively, the three verses following the passage on Śākyamuni’s attainment of the Buddha-way [refer to this]. Specifically:
One cultivates the merit that serves as the antidote to all obstacles; that is, one constantly cultivates awakened wisdom at all times to counteract the six hindrances and so forth.
Since it is stated that many kalpas have already passed, its initial accomplishment is not fixed. Six:
Or, in the three verses following the "Ultimate Perfection," one sees the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists. Seven: Or, one sees [the Buddha] in Tuṣita.
The initial sixteen verses concerning the descent of the spirit into the world describe the merits of being born in the mundane realm without being obstructed by worldly dharmas.
The first five concern the manifestation of the eight marks of birth without obstruction; the next three concern dwelling in the celestial palaces without obstruction;

the next six concern skillful transformation according to the world without obstruction; and the final two conclude with the capacity of unobstructed wisdom to respond to various capacities. These are the eight [merits] of the Tathāgata.
Below the section on "Abiding in the Unsurpassed Path" are eighteen verses that clarify the merit of establishing the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Among these, the first four verses establish the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), while simultaneously revealing its functional activity (*karmavipāka*). The subsequent three [verses] clarify the establishment of the path of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
This is also an antidote. Next, the seven [verses] clarify how the single sound of the Dharma is heard differently according to the various types of beings, up to an immeasurable extent.

The final four [verses] clarify that the vocal karma is equal and responds to all. The nine [verses] on the "perfection of pure merit and wisdom" and the following three verses clarify the merit of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). This means that the prediction of the past and future is as if it were the present; therefore, it is said "all."
10. The four verses beginning with "Clearly seeing the ten directions of the ultimate empty realm" clarify the merit of manifesting the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
11. The two verses beginning with "Or upholding those precepts to become a teacher of the world" clarify the merit of severing all doubts;
that is, because one is well-determined regarding all objects of knowledge, one is able to sever the doubts of others. 12. [The next section follows.]
Alternatively, the nine verses beginning with "Or seeing [beings] adorned with superior garments" cause one to enter into the merits of various practices;
that is to say, because they universally comprehend the natures and behaviors of all sentient beings and lead them in according with their faculties.

The single verse following "The unimpeded wisdom of the Tathāgata perceives... refers to the merit of sublime wisdom in future lives; that is to say, because the Buddha knows things from the distant past.

14. "For example, like a master illusionist skilled in magical arts"—the five verses following this describe the merit of manifesting according to [beings'] resolute belief (*adhimukti*), meaning that he manifests his body in accordance with their understanding.
15. "For example, like the pure sun emitting a thousand rays"—the three verses following this [describe the merit of]...
This refers to the merit of the application (*prayoga*) for taming sentient beings, which is the basis for the immeasurable;
the meaning is that the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable because it is the basis for the bodhisattvas’ application in taming sentient beings.
The two verses following the [verse on] the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous *dharmakāya* clarify the merit of the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*) within the equal *dharmakāya*.
Verse 17, “All Phenomena Within the Three Realms, Whether Existing or Non-existing,” explains the merit of manifesting distinct Buddha-lands according to superior resolve (*adhimukti*).
Since these are manifested in accordance with resolve, they cannot be compared to anything else.
Verse 18, “The Immeasurable Colors of the Maṇi Jewels of the Eight Great Oceans,” explains the merit of the three types of Buddha-bodies being without spatial limitation.
The single verse beginning with "nineteenth, like space, true suchness, and the limit of reality" subsumes three kinds of merit:
(1) the merit of constantly manifesting the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings until the end of the realm of birth and death, which is equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
(2) the merit of being inexhaustible, which is equal to space; and (3) the merit of being ultimate, which is equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is because [it is] according to reality.

Because they reach the limit of the future limit, even the atoms of lands, the thoughts of the mind, the waters of the great oceans, the measure of space, and the winds that could be counted or known—none can exhaustively describe the virtues of the Buddha.
If there are those who hear this ocean of merit and give rise to a heart of joy, faith, and understanding, they shall obtain everything exactly as it has been extolled. Be careful!
"Do not harbor doubts regarding this. These two verses summarize the inexhaustible [nature of the teaching] and also specifically manifest its inexhaustible merits.
Within them, the former verse praises its virtues, while the latter verse exhorts one to have faith.
Ancient masters have also treated these two verses as a separate section for circulation. The main text is now concluded. The verse of dedication says:
The nature of phenomena is profound and vast, difficult to conceive; I have provided a brief explanation according to my capacity.
May this merit be equal to the limit of reality, Universally causing all sentient beings to attain Bodhi.
